title: Electra/Persona review – Blanchett and Hoss face off in lopsided Sophocles/Bergman double bill | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Benedict Andrews’ intense, interval-free mashup of ancient and modernist classics is a show of two halves
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Benedict Andrews’ intense, interval-free mashup of ancient and modernist classics is a show of two halves
Content: Nina Hoss (Electra), Cate Blanchett (Clytemnestra) and Ella Lily Hyland (Chrysothemis) in Electra/Persona.Photograph: Monika RittershausView image in fullscreenNina Hoss (Electra), Cate Blanchett (Clytemnestra) and Ella Lily Hyland (Chrysothemis) in Electra/Persona.Photograph: Monika RittershausTheatreReviewElectra/Persona review – Blanchett and Hoss face off in lopsided Sophocles/Bergman double billBenedict Andrews’ intense, interval-free mashup of ancient and modernist classics is a show of two halvesArifa AkbarTue 1 Sep 2026 19.10 EDTFirst published on Tue 1 Sep 2026 19.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Electra bit of the title refers to the Sophoclean tragedy of a daughter trapped in a cycle of vengeance, the Persona part to Ingmar Bergman’s 1966 film about an actor who suddenly stops speaking while performing Electra on stage.Benedict Andrews’ drama after Bergman and Sophocles first welds the two together, then raises the concept higher by enlisting his star castings inCate Blanchettand Nina Hoss to share the parts of Electra and her murderous mother, Clytemnestra, as well as Bergman’s inexplicably silent actor, Elisabeth, and her nurse, Alma, who fall into a disturbing, mirrored relationship.The order of who will play whom is decided on the flip of a coin before each show every night. “Heads or tails?” Blanchett asks Hoss, after walking on, and gets an audience member to toss the coin. She wins, so it’s Clytemnestra and Alma for her, while Hoss plays Electra and Elisabeth.It’s a clever twist (too clever?) that seems earnest in its intentions to eke out mother-daughter friction from each drama, as well as exploring ideas on performance, how actors assume roles and who they become when they are off-stage – rather than a production conceived as theatrical sport.Yet, this intense, interval-free show is quite literally a game of two halves, Andrews’ overhaul of the ancient much more successful than his strangely sterile play on Bergman’s classic.Blanchett and Hoss are thrown into a series of gladiatorial face-offs across the night and if Andrews’ idea to join up two such distinct dramas suffers from strain, they become his secret weapon. They shine, even when the awkwardness of Persona reveals its cracks.The ancient comes first, with a searing performance from Hoss (previously in a shimmering production ofThe Cherry Orchard, directed by Andrews). She plays a spittingly angry adolescent, ominously brandishing a hammer, who has an edge of the comic grotesque. She hates her mother but, it is clear, loves her too.Blanchett, for her part, is commanding but less imperious thanStockard Channing’s Clytemnestra in the West End’s kooky Elektra. Beneath the hauteur (and occasional comic touches) she is beseeching, and convinces us of her right to seek vengeance for the death of her daughter, Iphigenia (sacrificed by her father, Agamemnon, to appease the gods), so that mother and daughter seemed justified in their thirsty violence.There is overt theatricality, face paint rubbed on, costumes donned, characters role-playing parts of their family story – Electra assuming the part of Agamemnon, or her brother Orestes, by putting on their respective jackets; her more obedient sister, Chrysothemis (Ella Lily Hyland), trembling in the virgin white dress of Iphigenia.The murder ofClytemnestra’s lover, Aegisthus (Patrick Robinson), consists of blood spat across his face. It is stark and effective on Magda Willi’s ascending staircase set, on which the drama looks like an act of conjuring. An electric heartbeat pumps up the adrenaline in Brendan Aanes’s sound design, without tipping into frenzy. It is all supremely controlled.View image in fullscreenNina Hoss (Elisabeth) and Cate Blanchett (Alma) in the Persona half of Electra/Persona at the National Theatre.Photograph: Monika RittershausIf only Andrews had left it at that. Bergman’s film – regarded as the apex of psychological experimentalism on screen – is trickier to pull off on stage. Andrews introduces a screen and a handheld camera, briefly reflecting the audience but mostly showing us Elisabeth in enigmatically silent closeup.Hoss holds the camera mostly, and the film’s chase across the beach in a fight between the two women is re-enacted as a backstage walk, with handheld camera. It’s now an old trick, beloved of the likes of Ivo van Hove and Jamie Lloyd, which looks hackneyed here.There is some clever overlay between the two parts, with same props and costumes turning up. But Alma’s monologues seem like witterings against Elisabeth’s silences. Bergman’s film is said to have influenced David Lynch, among others, and the endeavour here ends up like a sixth-form imitation of both.As a double bill, of sorts, the first is the showcase, not only of its two central performers but the power of performance itself.At theNational Theatre, London until 10 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreNational TheatreCate BlanchettSophoclesIngmar BergmanreviewsShareReuse this content

title: HRH Helch: the graffiti artist who left an indelible mark on high-rise Britain | Street art | The Guardian
description: He upset Queen Elizabeth II, defied the developers and had to scrap for every inch of graffiti space in a gentrified, urban landscape
Author: Eddy Frankel
Headline: He upset Queen Elizabeth II, defied the developers and had to scrap for every inch of graffiti space in a gentrified, urban landscape
Content: Towering legacy … the artist’s tag sprayed on a railway viaduct near Windsor Castle, 2019.Photograph: REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenTowering legacy … the artist’s tag sprayed on a railway viaduct near Windsor Castle, 2019.Photograph: REX/ShutterstockStreet artHRH Helch: the graffiti artist who left an indelible mark on high-rise BritainHe upset Queen Elizabeth II, defied the developers and had to scrap for every inch of graffiti space in a gentrified, urban landscapeProlific UK graffiti artist Helch diesEddy FrankelTue 1 Sep 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou know you’ve made an impact when the headlines upon your death are filled with words like “iconic”, “infamous”, “world class” and “upset Queen Elizabeth II”. By that measure, graffiti supremo Helch made a pretty serious mark on the world.Hedied this week, leaving behind a country pockmarked by his tag, a giant towering HELCH, though sometimes reduced to just a simple upper-case H. It was on railway bridges and motorway overpasses, on derelict buildings and decrepit high rises. From Bristol to London, Helch was everywhere. He was even on a railway viaduct on the way to Windsor Castle, in 60ft high white letters, “ruining” the view of poor old Elizabeth’s home and apparently leaving our late monarch in an absolute rage.View image in fullscreenAmerican carwash covered in Helch’s street art, Shoreditch, east London, 2022.Photograph: Photozaic/AlamyHe was only 34, which almost doesn’t make sense. It feels like his work has been around for ever, as much a part of the British urban landscape as red phone boxes and uncollected bins. In a post on Instagram, his gallery, BSMT Space, said “an urban landscape without an H in it seems unfathomable”. And it’s true, that towering letter defined the look of late 2010s Britain.Unlike 2000s graffiti megastars such asBen EineorSweet Toof, who operated in an east London that was still filled with squalor and dereliction, a place not yet lost to the endless tide of gentrification, Helch’s England was a more polished, sanitised, pristine place. Where his predecessors could run rampant on the wastelands that would soon be newbuilds, Helch had to work in a city where every inch of grit and urban sprawl had been levelled to make way for high-rise apartment blocks no one lives in and co-working spaces no one works in. Helch had to scrap for every inch of graffiti space, he had to hunt out the final concrete canvases left in the new steel and glass urbanity of England.View image in fullscreenAnother Helch work in Shoreditch, east London, 2021.Photograph: Mark Charnock/AlamyWhen you see Helch, you’re seeing the remains of what the country was before the developers came in and sold it all on. When you see Helch, you’re seeing someone lay claim to the city you’re in, or the road you’re on.It was a comfort to spot a Helch tag as you made your way through London or down some miserable motorway. It meant that someone had persevered, that individuality had won through against the odds. He was just some miscreant from Hayes in London doing what all great graffiti artists do best: leaving his mark, shaping the city in his own image, and upsetting the poshos in the process. But he leaves behind a towering legacy, one that’ll cost the developers a hell of a lot to scrub off, and that makes it worth every penny.Explore more on these topicsStreet artArtfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: One last Starmer U-turn and it’s over to Andy ‘less policy, more vibes’ Burnham | John Crace | The Guardian
description: What former PM could resist upstaging the new one hours before his first dispatch box appearance in 16 years?
Author: John Crace
Headline: What former PM could resist upstaging the new one hours before his first dispatch box appearance in 16 years?
Content: Andy hadn’t come to pick a fight with the opposition. He hoped they would listen to him, realise he was right and work with him.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenAndy hadn’t come to pick a fight with the opposition. He hoped they would listen to him, realise he was right and work with him.Photograph: ReutersThe politics sketchLabourOne last Starmer U-turn and it’s over to Andy ‘less policy, more vibes’ BurnhamJohn CraceWhat former PM could resist upstaging the new one hours before his first dispatch box appearance in 16 years?UK politics live – latest updatesTue 1 Sep 2026 13.43 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTShareNo good deed goes unpunished. Or any deed for that matter. It was only a few weeks ago that Keir Starmer was insisting he would remain an MP until the next general election. So we should all probably have guessed that hewould be off at the earliest opportunity. U-turns were a distinguishing feature of his two years in office.And what former prime minister could resist upstaging the new one hours before his first appearance at the government dispatch box for 16 years? Especially when the new one had been plotting his downfall for at least a year. It’s what everyone would have wanted. Right?Not that Starmer was framing his decision in these terms. This wasn’t a simple matter of revenge. Or a need to still feel relevant. These were the last things on his mind. Keir has only ever wanted what was best for Andy. But he now had his own life to think about. And why tell the world about it on a bank holiday weekend when nobody is paying attention to the news, when you can wait till the first day of the new parliamentary session and grab the headlines?Keir said in his statement that he had really meant it when he said he would remain MP for Holborn and St Pancras, but it had only latterly dawned on him that this would be incompatible with his ambitions to be a player on the international stage. Please spare us from another Tony Blair. There again, Keir is unlikely to be invited on to Donald Trump’s Board of Peace. He should use that as his calling card.In truth though, Keir had never seemed that interested in representing his constituents or serving as a backbencher. He’s not like Theresa May, who remained, sad and alone, on the backbenches for years after being removed by her fellow Tory MPs. Nor does he have the inclination to follow the example of Rishi Sunak and turn up to work every couple of months or so. Perhaps he is more in need of the money that might come from leaving the Commons. And for a prime minister, Starmer had always seemed curiously uninterested in politics. So much so that you wondered why he had ever become a politician. It probably just felt like a normal career progression.Meanwhile, Burnham could probably live with being pushed down the news agenda for the day. He had mixed feelings about Keir’s decision. In the long run, life would probably be easier without Starmer around to cause trouble, but the downside was a potentially tricky byelection. Especially if Zack Polanski chose to stand for the Greens. And never forgetting an almost obligatory appearance from Count Binface. But this would all be for another day. Right now he had a Commons statement on the government’s direction to negotiate.First, it was a time to be gracious. After saying he would be following his predecessors in reaffirming his commitment to Ukraine, Burnhamspent the first few minutes of his speech praising Keir. He had given a lifetime of service, had created a platform for change and had made the Labour party electable again. You could almost believe he was sorry to see him go.View image in fullscreenKemi did at least try to sound as if she had listened and would work at doing better to find common ground.Photograph: House of CommonsThen we got to the heart of the matter. Less policy, more positive vibes. Andy hadn’t come to the Commons to pick a fight with the opposition. Rather he hoped they would listen to him, realise he was right and then work with him. It was a big ask – especially with Kemi Badenoch as leader of the opposition, and so disinhibited she can pick a fight with herself – but probably worth a go. Just on the off-chance. Andy wasn’t going to give in to point scoring without at least attempting to offer a hand of friendship.We ran through a wishlist. The climate crisis. Surely no one was going to argue with that, not after the emergency in Nepal and the hottest summer on record? You could sense Kemi longing to intervene, to say that net zero was a con. It took all her self-control not to make an idiot of herself.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham’s ambitious plans need room to breathe – and Westminster suffocates change | Rafael BehrRead moreBurnham began. Small boat crossings down: tick. More prison places for the right kinds of prisoner: fingers crossed. Defence: that would be sorted later, somehow. The cost of living: we need to be honest that the country has been in decline since 1980.“I will be relentless about achieving change and growth,” he said. First he had taken Manchester, now he takes the UK. A Britain that would work for all of us. A desire to keep upbeat. The country had had enough of being told it was falling apart. Let the good times roll. Ish.We can make the next decade better than the last, he concluded. That suddenly didn’t feel quite so comforting. I mean, the next 10 years can hardly be worse than the shitshow of the last 10 years. Can it? Can it? Please. We need some reason to get out of bed each morning.As for Kemi, let’s also be generous. She did at least try to sound as if she had listened and would work at doing better to find common ground. Though she couldn’t do this without sounding vaguely patronising. As if Burnham was some sort of ingenu who had been parachuted into Westminster without a clue as to what he was doing, and she was the old lag who had seen it all before.“I’ll be gentle,” she said, as if Andy was a halfwit, before going on to say that almost everything he had said was totally wrong. The decline in small boat crossings was just a coincidence. Margaret Thatcher had taken office before she had been born, so therefore anything Thatcher had done was totally irrelevant. Kemi thinks the world began with her birth and will end with her death. The narcissist’s fantasy. She promised to help when it was in the national interest, but the national interest would only be served if she was in charge.Andy tried to let her down gently. He was here to help too.Kemi had gone to Romeand fantasised that Giorgia Meloni had told her not to do a deal with Reform. He would happily have saved her the air fare and told her the same thing. Then he took her by surprise – by pointing out she had just picked a shadow chancellor who had been the author of Liz Truss’s mini-budget. Kemi looked a little shell-shocked. She is going to have to up her game before tomorrow’s prime minister’s questions.Explore more on these topicsLabourThe politics sketchKeir StarmerAndy BurnhamnewsShareReuse this content

title: The Raygun documentary ducks a big question about the Olympic fame of a ‘dorky white academic’ | Sport | The Guardian
description: A new Netflix documentary finds warmth and humor in Rachael Gunn’s Olympic ordeal but sidesteps the larger questions raised by her viral fame
Author: Dvora Meyers
Headline: A new Netflix documentary finds warmth and humor in Rachael Gunn’s Olympic ordeal but sidesteps the larger questions raised by her viral fame
Content: Australia’s Rachael ‘Raygun’ Gunn competes during the women’s breaking competition at the Paris Olympics in August 2024.Photograph: Ezra Shaw/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAustralia’s Rachael ‘Raygun’ Gunn competes during the women’s breaking competition at the Paris Olympics in August 2024.Photograph: Ezra Shaw/Getty ImagesSportThe Raygun documentary ducks a big question about the Olympic fame of a ‘dorky white academic’Untold Raygun: Breaking Badly finds warmth and humor in Rachael Gunn’s ordeal, but never fully reckons with what her notoriety meant for breakingDvora MeyersTue 1 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 16.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarly in Netflix’s new documentary, Untold Raygun: Breaking Badly, Australian B-girl Rachael Gunn, recounts a session she had with her sports psychologist prior to the 2024 Paris Olympics.“Right before the Olympics, I went to my therapist, panicked,” she says. Her therapist asked her what was the worst thing that could happen. And she said, “The whole world could laugh at me.” Her therapist responded: “Do you think that’s reasonable?” Cue Gunn’s hysterical laughter.Raygun: Breaking Badly review – the ridiculed Olympic B-girl gets the last laugh … and it’s a total joyRead moreAnyone who has ever gone to a therapist will be amused at this anecdote. Nine and a half times out 10, the therapist would have been right. No, they’d say, the worst outcome you can imagine probably won’t come to pass. But in Gunn’s case, what she feared the most did, in fact, happen. Her shenanigans – the sprinkler, the kangaroo hops – in the cyphermade her go viralalmost as soon as she was done with her sets. (Perhaps if Gunn had been explicit about what she was planning to do in her sets, her therapist would have reacted differently.) Gunn’s performance launched a thousand memes, more than a couple of late-night TV segments, several conspiracy theories, and even a musical at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival.“She became the most famous breaker on planet Earth overnight,” Flix, a fellow Australian B-girl, says in the documentary. All without winning a single vote from any of the nine judges across her six rounds.Untold Raygun, which premieres globally on Netflix on Tuesday, really doesn’t dwell on what it means for breaking, an art form created by Black and Brown youth in the South Bronx, that its first Olympic foray will be primarily – if not exclusively – remembered for a white woman from Australia doing the sprinkler instead of the dynamic performances of the rest of the contenders. It’s mostly focused on Gunn herself with little time spent on the greater context of the art form and how it ended up in the Olympics. The documentary features interviews with Gunn, her parents, her husband who introduced her to breaking, and a few dancers who know her from the Aussie scene. Through them, we get a coming of almost middle-age story about an academic who meets a B-boy working at a call center, falls in love with him and the art form he’s passionate about, and somehow ends up centerstage at the Olympics.View image in fullscreenAustralia’s Rachael ‘Raygun’ Gunn competes during the women’s breaking round-robin at the Paris Olympics in August 2024.Photograph: Angelika Warmuth/ReutersGunn is likeable in the documentary. She comes across as (mostly) self-aware and self-deprecating. Her parents are charming, laughing heartily when asked if they had ever previously associated “Olympian” with their quirky daughter. Sammy Free seems like a sweet fellow who is completely besotted with his wife. (We should all be so lucky to find someone who loves us the way that Free clearly loves Gunn.) But the most useful voices in Untold Raygun are the two Australian B-girls who offer some critical perspective on the place of women in the breaking scene and Gunn’s performances at the Games. They’re harsh, at times, but also fair.Tinylocks, one of Gunn’s contemporaries, repeatedly invokes “No easy props,” a term that’s something of a hip-hop ethos about having to prove your skill to earn respect. (The phrase is often associated with American B-girl Asia One, who founded a crew called No Easy Props in 1997.) “It was such a male dominated space and B-girls were really fighting to be seen but as more women started entering breaking, it was felt that some girls were getting accolades too early in their careers. The crowd would cheer just for participating,” she says.It is within the context of “no easy props” that Tinylocks offers her assessment of Raygun’s pre-Olympic performances, as she was coming up in the small Australian scene. “There were one or two times when I was like, ‘Oh yeah, that was fresh.’ Maybe not so much the other times.”Tinylocks decided to pass on trying to earn the Oceania qualifying spot. “I’m interested in breaking as an art form,” she says, which is a sentiment I heard from other dancers in the scene after the Olympic trajectory was announced by the IOC and the World DanceSport Federation (WDSF). Flix gave it a go at the Oceania qualifier, but said that, at 41, she didn’t expect much. Gunn was surprised that she kept advancing through the bracket until she was in the final battle against B-girl Molly. If you go back and watch the Oceania qualifier, you won’t see any of Gunn’s “iconic” moves from the Paris Olympics in that final. What she threw down against Molly doesn’t stand out in any way – either for good or for bad. Yes, her movements were slow and lacked sharpness, her sets not particularly intricate. But she showed fairly standard breaking foundation movements. If she had done those sets in Paris, Gunn wouldn’t have advanced out of the preliminary rounds but she also wouldn’t have become a global sensation.View image in fullscreenGunn competes during the women’s breaking competition at the Paris Olympics, where she failed to win a single vote from the nine judges across her six rounds.Photograph: Héctor Vivas/Getty ImagesThe documentary explains the change in her set composition: she realized how far behind she was the top B-girls she was going to be battling at the Olympics. She went to a couple of European battles in the months before the Games and performed poorly in all of them. Gunn and her husband decided to change their approach. Instead of trying to up the difficulty content of her sets through power moves – the acrobatics like headspins and windmills that laypeople associate with breaking – they would go all in on originality, one of the five categories breaking judges evaluate at the Games. (The other four were technique, vocabulary, execution and musicality.) They had gone from hoping to win one battle or even one round to trying to win a single vote from one of the nine judges. Gunn and Free said they looked to Australia for movement inspiration from its famous wildlife (kangaroo) to its dance moves (the sprinkler). They even added a nod to swimming, an Olympic sport at which Australia excels. Despite this strategy, Gunn didn’t get a single vote in Paris.Raygun opens up on her infamous Olympics breakdancing debut: ‘Not as bad as I thought!’Read moreThere’s a world in which this approach could have worked for Gunn but it’s a world where she is much better at breaking fundamentals, where her footwork is sharp and clean, her movements swift but also unhurried. The breaking scene has had its share of well-respected dancers who bring humor and personality to the cypher. B-boys and B-girls often call this “character.” (In fact, one of them,Jeffro, was competing on the men’s side in Paris.) The issue with Gunn’s attempts at character is that those gimmicks were basically all she had. The bunny hop or the kangaroo weren’t simply moments in an otherwise proficient set that ticked other boxes, like technique, execution or musicality. The gimmicks were the main event.As a point of contrast, let’s consider another athlete who became a meme during the Paris Games:Stephen Nedoroscik. The pommel horse specialist doffed his glasses, Clark Kent style, before he saluted the judges. There the tenor of the online discourse had none of the mockery that suffused the Raygun tweets because Nedoroscik was actually world class in his event. He was the 2021 world champion on pommel horse and won bronze in the event at the Olympics. Something similar took place in the sport shooting event where Turkey’s Yusuf Dikecbecame a memedue to his nonchalant stance and lack of gear. But because he was actually good at his sport – he won silver – the online hijinks never turned mean.“People have a lot of opinions about what women do, what women should do, sometimes from women,” Gunn says of the reaction online to her performance. Generally speaking, there is truth to this assertion. Women do get singled out for criticism in a way that often feels disproportionate to the offense. Gunn didn’t commit a crime. She didn’t murder anyone on live TV. And she didn’t cheat her way to the Olympics as many people falsely claimed after Paris. (This is one of the conspiracy theories that Untold Raygun takes pains to dispel.) But it still felt disingenuous for Gunn to invoke this defense as a response to her Olympic performance. The response was not simply about her creative choices but also about the gap between herself and her competitors. She put herself on an Olympic stage where spectators expect elite performance, not a professor who is simply doing her best. The Olympics aren’t really a vehicle for self-expression. They’re supposed to be a vehicle for excellence.View image in fullscreenGunn poses for a portrait in Sydney in April 2024, four months before making her Olympic debut in Paris.Photograph: Cameron Spencer/Getty ImagesGunn isn’t the first person to compete at the Olympics whose skills are decidedly subpar. There wasEddie the Eagle, the British ski jumper who competed at the 1988 Olympics in Calgary, who definitely did not fly through the air with the greatest of ease.Eric Moussambanicompeted in swimming at the 2000 Games though he could barely swim the entire length of an Olympic pool. And in 2018, Elizabeth Swaney, representing Hungary, did nothing of substance in the halfpipe competition,putting together the most basic of runs. What distinguishes Gunn from the other Olympians is that they competed in sports that were already well-established. Though they became well-known, they didn’t become thefaceof their respective sports. But breaking was new to the Games in 2024 and most viewers weren’t familiar with it except from pop-culture products of the 80s. Gunn left Paris as the most famous breaker in the world. The average person on the street couldn’t tell you who won the breaking competition in Paris but they can probably remember Raygun, if not by name, then at least by description of what she did on the floor.There was no way for Gunn to have predicted this outcome, even if she, on some level, feared it before she got on the plane for France. But it would have been welcome to see her reckon with it and what it means for the culture and breaking’s chances of getting on the program of a future Games. (The documentary doesn’t mention this so I’ll do it: that breaking won’t appear at LA2028 has nothing to do with Gunn. The decision was made months before she hopped across the cypher.)Ultimately, Untold Raygun seeks to reassure the viewer that Gunn has survived hervery public bout with global humiliationwith her spirit and sense of whimsy intact. “I’m a dorky white woman who is an academic,” she said. “And I’m OK with that.”Last week WDSFsubmitted breaking for considerationfor the 2032 Olympics, which will be hosted by Brisbane. If the local organizing committee decides to give breaking another shot at Olympic glory then perhaps we’ll see Gunn again, but hopefully not at the center of the cypher.Explore more on these topicsSportBrisbane Olympic Games 2032Paris Olympic Games 2024DanceOlympic GamesAustralia sportfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Olivia Rodrigo is standing up for the vulnerable. I wish Taylor Swift would do the same | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: This weekend, Rodrigo raised millions for charities that benefit women and girls, and she has previously been vocal about Gaza and Ice. With free speech increasingly under threat, her peers should take note, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: This weekend, Rodrigo raised millions for charities that benefit women and girls, and she has previously been vocal about Gaza and Ice. With free speech increasingly under threat, her peers should take note, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: Trying to Make America Somewhat Decent Again … Olivia Rodrigo at the Daisy Chain Fields festival in California, on 29 August.Photograph: Christopher Polk/Billboard/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTrying to Make America Somewhat Decent Again … Olivia Rodrigo at the Daisy Chain Fields festival in California, on 29 August.Photograph: Christopher Polk/Billboard/Getty ImagesOpinionOlivia RodrigoOlivia Rodrigo is standing up for the vulnerable. I wish Taylor Swift would do the sameArwa MahdawiThis weekend, Rodrigo raised millions for charities that benefit women and girls, and she has previously been vocal about Gaza and Ice. With free speech increasingly under threat, her peers should take noteTue 1 Sep 2026 11.21 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTShareDonald Trump, the 80-year-old president of the United States, spent his weekend whiningabout a lakeand posting memes ofDonald’s Ducks. While he was busy with his ducks, Olivia Rodrigo, a 23-year-old pop star, spentherweekend trying to Make America Somewhat Decent Again. On Saturday, Rodrigo hosted the inauguralDaisy Chain Fields festival, bringing together female artists to raise money for women-focused non-profits which have had theirfundingslashedby the Trump administration. The festival raised $10m (£7.4m) whichMelinda French Gatesmatched, bringing the total to $20m.In a perfect world a singer holding a benefit concert for feminist charities wouldn’t be radical stuff. But we don’t live in a perfect world, do we? We live in hell. Trump has successfully bullied US institutions into doing his bidding.Universities have defundeddiversity, equity and inclusion programmes, manymedia outletshave kowtowed to the US’s self-styled king and tech CEOs havejumped intobed with him. Women’s rights are goingbackwards globallyand our civil liberties are under attack.It has become depressingly clear just how many of the rich and powerful are self-serving cowards who will abandon social justice issues as soon as it becomes mildly inconvenient. So it was refreshing to see a young musician rally people together in service of reproductive justice at a festival that was proudly feminist and didn’t pretend to be non-political.Rodrigo has always used her platform to speak out: she’s never been one of those annoying celebrities who insist that remaining apolitical is some sort of noble act. When Roe v Wade was overturned in 2022, the then 19-year-old musician condemned the decisionon stage at Glastonbury. Rodrigo, who is Filipino American, also publicly told the Trump administrationnot to use her musicin their “racist, hateful propaganda” when one of her songs was featured in a government video telling undocumented immigrants to self-deport.Rodrigo has also not been silent about Gaza: a subject many celebrities areterrified to mention, because empathising with Palestinians is a tried-and-tested wayto ruin your career. Last year she wrote on Instagramabout how“mothers, fathers and children in Gaza are starving, dehydrated and being denied access to basic medical care ...” Rodrigo also gave a nod to Palestine (which, thanks to Israel’s attacks onmaternity wardsand healthcare is a reproductive justice issue) at a press conference for her Daisy Chain Fields festival, whereshe wore a dressmade by Palestinian fashion brandNöl Collective.Speaking on the New York Times’sPopcast earlier this year, Rodrigo said acknowledging social issues is part of expressing herself. “I think it would just be disingenuous to be like, I don’t feel heartbroken about what’s going on in Gaza. As an artist, I feel like that’s just what you do. And that’s my job,”she said.Frankly, I think it’s the job of everyone with any sort of platform or power. Celebrities shouldn’t have to get political, some will say. No, of course not. But if you have a huge platform and oodles of money and even just a smidgen of a conscience, then you should probablywantto use your resources and reach for good, shouldn’t you? Giving money to charity is one thing, but it takes more courage to show people where you stand, knowing there may be repercussions for it. I hate this idea of not “taking sides”: the world is not a football match; political parties are not “teams”. It is not divisive to stand with vulnerable people.Taylor Swift,the richest female musician in history, certainly seemed to agree with that at one point. She famously stayed quiet in the lead-up to the 2016 election, but later, when more celebrities were doing so, came out to endorse progressive causes. “I need to be on the right side of history,” she said in the2020 documentaryMiss Americana.But while Swift did endorse Kamala Harris in 2024, she has been very careful about what she says during Trump 2.0. Unlike all the musicians who have publicly condemned the Trump administration for using their music in offensive posts, she seemingly ignored the use of her songs byTrump for months. In recent weeks her songs have beenquietly removedfrom Trump’s ragebait posts, but Swift has not issued any sort of public statement about it. And she certainly hasn’tsaid anythingabout issues such as Gaza or ICE.There are limits to celebrity activism, sure. But in a world where free speech is under attack, it feels increasingly important for celebrities to speak out. Let’s hope Rodrigo’s festival prompts more of her peers to have some guts.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
