title: ‘Not just Hollywood crap’: Mike Leigh on the East End communist who brought world cinema to the UK | Movies | The Guardian
description: A new season celebrates Contemporary Films and its founder Charles Cooper, who bet on Britain taking to Ingmar Bergman, Yasujiro Ozu, Satyajit Ray – and a young Mike Leigh
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: A new season celebrates Contemporary Films and its founder Charles Cooper, who bet on Britain taking to Ingmar Bergman, Yasujiro Ozu, Satyajit Ray – and a young Mike Leigh
Content: ‘It was remarkable that they embraced this thing’ … Eric Allan and Anne Raitt in Mike Leigh’s debut feature film, Bleak Moments (1971).Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘It was remarkable that they embraced this thing’ … Eric Allan and Anne Raitt in Mike Leigh’s debut feature film, Bleak Moments (1971).Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyMovies‘Not just Hollywood crap’: Mike Leigh on the East End communist who brought world cinema to the UKA new season celebrates Contemporary Films and its founder Charles Cooper, who bet on Britain taking to Ingmar Bergman, Yasujiro Ozu, Satyajit Ray – and a young Mike LeighAndrew PulverTue 1 Sep 2026 10.05 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 14.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOccasionally, vital pieces of the cultural jigsaw disappear without anyone really noticing. This, sadly, was the fate of Contemporary Films, the British film distributor that popularised sophisticated, grownup international cinema – foreign language mostly – in the UK, and heralded the arrival of the auteur generation with directors such asIngmar Bergman, Satyajit Ray, Andrzej Wajda and Yasujiro Ozu.Contemporary, and its founder Charles Cooper, weren’t the only game in town –Kenneth Rive’s Galawas a fellow traveller – but Contemporary got there first, setting up shop in 1951, first with short films for the then popular film society sector, and moving into features with the 1952 Japanese filmChildren of Hiroshima. Its marketplace clout faded rapidly in the early 1990s, when it was a victim of changing industry practices. But amazingly, the company is still with us – and is planninga 75th anniversary series of screeningsto showcase its history.View image in fullscreenCharles Cooper.Photograph: Contemporary FilmsSuch is Contemporary’s lustre that, along with screenings of films such as Miloš Forman’s A Blonde in Love, Bergman’s Wild Strawberries and Jack Hazan’s David Hockney documentary A Bigger Splash, the great and good are turning out in support, led byMike Leigh, whose feature film directing debut, Bleak Moments, was picked up by Contemporary in 1971. “It was a great honour,” Leigh says. “One was used to seeing ‘Contemporary Films’ on all the movies one saw that weren’t just Hollywood crap.”Bleak Moments, a studiedly funny and weird film based on Leigh’s own stage play, is about a woman living an isolated life with a sister with a learning disability and a boring job. It was financed by Albert Finney, still riding high on his 1960s acting successes. As a homegrown, off-kilter feature, it was a slightly unusual item for Contemporary to pick up. “We were fresh on the block and innocent,” says Leigh, “and you take everything for granted in some way. But actually, when you think about it, they were pretty remarkable and they embraced this thing.”Now a Palme d’Or and Golden Lion winner, Leigh undoubtedly understands the impact the company had on his own development. But it is its effect on the wider culture, the openness and cosmopolitanism that Contemporary helped to foster, that is arguably its most important contribution. “I grew up in Manchester,” says Leigh, “and I saw movies all the time, but I never saw a film that wasn’t in English. I saw only Hollywood and British movies. So when I came to London, world cinema suddenly presented itself. I have recollections of seeing Russian films, Italian neorealism, you name it. It was all going on, and Contemporary was very much at the centre of that.”View image in fullscreenThe company’s office in Soho, London, in 1969.Photograph: Contemporary FilmsCooper, the driving force behind it all, was an East End Jew – the son of a butcher from Ukraine – and a committed communist who saw cinema as a way to build awareness. Before the second world war, he brought Soviet films to the UK viaKino, the film section of the Workers’ Theatre Movement, then spent the war in New York running a film section for theInternational Workers Order.Deported from the US in 1950, Cooper set about supplying films to hungry fans in film societies, of which there were an estimated 200 across Britain. The increasing interest in foreign “art” films meant Cooper was in tune with the intellectual times, with his special interest in eastern European and underclass-oriented films.Part of Cooper’s strength, it seems, was his devotion to family life and willingness to involve his children in his day-to-day. His daughters from his first marriage agree. Adi Cooper, now a board member of Social Work England, says: “Charles was in the right place at the right time in terms of capturing a market for the sort of films he was interested in, which branched out from political ones into what you would now call, I guess, arthouse cinema. He was prepared to take a risk on people who were unheard of here at the time, some of whom went on to have a much wider appeal.”View image in fullscreen‘There wasn’t much separation between work and home’ … Charles and Kitty Cooper with Satyajit and Bijoya Ray.Photograph: Contemporary FilmsHer twin, Sue Cooper, a founder member of1970s punk act Poison Girls, says: “There wasn’t much separation between work and home with Charles. He really was passionate about film and politics, and he was very motivated to expose people’s thinking to different cultures. He was basically an internationalist and a humanist.” They regale me with anecdotes about screenings in the basement of their Wembley home (“The room is crammed full of people! I’m two feet from the back wall gazing up at this film called Alexander Nevsky”) to messing about in the school holidays at the company’s Frith Street office (“pasting press cuttings into scrapbooks and getting seven and sixpence for three hours’ work”).Also key to Contemporary’s success was the relationship Cooper nurtured with George Hoellering, the Hungarian émigré who ran the celebrated Academy cinema on London’s Oxford Street which, throughout the 1950s and 60s, was the flagship venue for these kind of films. “They were joined at the hip,” says Pete Lawley, Contemporary’s current managing director. “They were the gold standard of the time.”View image in fullscreenContemporary acquired some of the key indie films of the 90s, including Hal Hartley’s The Unbelievable Truth with Julia McNeal and Adrienne Shelly.Photograph: Electric/Kobal/ShutterstockHoellering died in 1984, by which time Cooper had his own cinemas: the Paris Pullman and Phoenix cinema in London and another Phoenix in Oxford. Lawley, who came on board in 2023, outlines Contemporary’s decline: as Cooper’s health began to fail in the late 1980s, he passed control to his second wife, Kitty Furstenberg, who in turn sold it on to their friendEric Liknaitzky, who died in 2023. Although Contemporary did acquire some of the key indies of the late 80s and early 1990s, including Patricia Rozema’s I’ve Heard the Mermaids Singing, Jane Campion’s Sweetie and Hal Hartley’s The Unbelievable Truth, it seems the shift to home entertainment formats in the 90s passed Contemporary by. Instead it stuck to occasional re-releases of tried and tested classics from their archive.Lawley says Contemporary has kept going by licensing clips from their catalogue; he has been sorting through the copious company documentation and says he is now working on plans for the future. “It’s very important to me,” he says. “I really want to keep it going. It can’t be about the money, let’s put it that way. It may be small, but there’s something worthwhile to build upon.”Contemporary 75begins with a screening ofBleak Momentsand Mike Leigh in conversation. at the BFI Southbank, London, on 3 September and runs until 11 October at cinemas across LondonExplore more on these topicsFilmMike LeighSatyajit RayIngmar BergmanAndrzej WajdaYasujiro OzuFilm industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Burnham blames Brexit and Thatcher for ‘wrong turns’ in first Commons speech as PM | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: The prime minister said Britain needed to be brutally honest about the mistakes of the last 40 years of UK politics
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: The prime minister said Britain needed to be brutally honest about the mistakes of the last 40 years of UK politics
Content: Andy Burnham promised to bring optimism and ‘substantial change’ during his term.Photograph: House of CommonsView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham promised to bring optimism and ‘substantial change’ during his term.Photograph: House of CommonsAndy BurnhamBurnham blames Brexit and Thatcher for ‘wrong turns’ in first Commons speech as PMThe prime minister said Britain needed to be brutally honest about the mistakes of the last 40 years of UK politicsPippa CrerarandJessica ElgotTue 1 Sep 2026 14.52 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has blamed Brexit andMargaret Thatcherfor a decade of low growth in the UK, arguing that Britain needs to be brutally honest about having taken “a series of wrong turns” in the last 40 years.In his first Commons appearance since he took over as prime minister about six weeks ago, Burnham told MPs he wanted to build a new sense of optimism so “we can make this next decade better than the last”.The British people wanted “much more substantial change” on the big issues facing the country, he said. “That is what I will bring. Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be. Things are not working as they should.”The UK economy has takena 6% hit from the effects of Brexit, according to economists’ analysis of internal Bank of England data on thousands of British companies since the referendum a decade ago.More public control is the way to grow UK economy, Burnham to tell MPsRead moreShortly before Burnham’s Commons address, Keir Starmer, his predecessor, announced he wouldstand down as an MP, saying he wanted to focus on international affairs, triggering a tricky first byelection test for Burnham in a seat where the Greens fancy their chances.The cabinet was told on Tuesday that the government will have three key priorities: cutting costs of essentials like childcare and mortgages; the regeneration of communities; and greater public control of water, housing and energy.Burnham’s deputy, Louise Haigh, will lead task forces on each of those issues, the Guardian understands. He told his ministers they must be “relentless” in fulfilling his priorities.His plans are set against atough economic backdrop. The chancellor’s headroom against Labour’s fiscal rules could be halved at his first budget if the current global bond sell-off persists, and economists warn mortgage rates could go up this autumn.In his Commons statement, the prime minister also:Hinted that he would commit to spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, saying he had appointed John Healey as his chancellor “precisely because” of hisposition on military spending.Signalled he is open to renationalising the water industry – saying he is looking at “all possible solutions”, as the sector is a “leaking monument” to the failures of privatisation.Opened the door to looking again at electoral reform in Labour’s next manifesto. “I do believe there needs to be a mandate to make that change. There are different views in this house, but I believe we will need to get a consensus at the next election. And if there is that consensus, then a change can be made in the next parliament.”Announced he would attend the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey and continue pursuing green energy – but that he would be “pragmatic” on supply, amid expectations he will approve the Jackdaw gasfield. “The mistake is saying it’s got to be one or the other for political purposes. The truth is, it’s going to have to be both.”Flanked by Healey and Haigh, Burnham suggested to MPs theBrexitvote had been a response to “a series of wrong turns” made by Britain in the 1980s onwards, that were then compounded by leaving the EU.The prime minister, whose Makerfield constituency voted for Brexit, has previously argued it would be amistake to rerun the referendum– but has said that he wants the UK to rejoin in his lifetime. He suggested the next UK-EU reset summit could take place in November.Tax promises, defence targets and Iran: Andy Burnham’s budget headachesRead more“Political power was centralised, economic power privatised, the country de-industrialised. Austerity followed, hollowing out councils and depriving them of the agency to act to reverse any of this,” he said during a three-hour stint in the Commons.“And then Brexit compounded the damage, ushering in a decade of low growth and stalled regeneration. Change begins with honesty … Unless we are blunt about what went wrong, we won’t turn things around.“Far from taking back control, the combination of these policies took control out of the hands of communities up and down Britain for 40 years. Too many places have been drifting.”He added: “The government I lead will be relentless in giving people and places what they were promised 10 years ago: ownership and control, and from that control over their destiny comes change and growth.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch accused Burnham of wanting to take the UK ‘back to the 1970s’.Photograph: House of CommonsThe Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, accused the prime minister of “living in the past” over his attacks on Thatcher – who was in power from 1979 to 1990 – and four decades of neoliberalism.“The year is 2026 but the prime minister said everything has gone wrong since the 1980s, still complaining about Margaret Thatcher. He is talking about a woman who became prime minister before I was born. He is living in the past and he wants to take us back to the 1970s.”In the statement, Burnham paid tribute to Starmer, saying he had created a platform for Britain to be fixed, “and we will use it well”. Just hours earlier, his predecessor announced he would be standing down as MP for Holborn and St Pancras, despite saying in July he planned to stay on until the next election.“It has been a huge honour and privilege to represent the best constituency in the country,” he said. “I will now focus on other things and that will be international affairs, including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast-changing world.”Starmer’s seat, long seen as a safeLabourhold, is likely to be targeted by the Greens, potentially for party leader Zack Polanski, who is a London Assembly member. “Zack has always made it clear he would like to be a London MP. London has been his home for over 20 years,” a Green spokesperson said.Just asthe Makerfield byelectionwas seen as a proof of concept for whether Burnham could beat Reform, so the north London seat will test his progressive credentials. Labour will choose its candidate to replace Starmer next Wednesday under an accelerated selection timetable.Burnham’s first taskforce will be charged with finding bold solutions to tackling “everyday rip-offs”. The cost of living taskforce will look at parking charges, subscription traps and cowboy builders, as well as long-term fixed pressures like mortgages, food costs and childcare.The second will assess the affordability and practicalities of the state taking over failing essential services. Burnham believes that greater state control of essential services is the surest way to economic growth, avoiding the potential for ineffective profiteering by privatised services.Government sources said that Haigh, the first secretary of state, wanted to look beyond sectors such as transport and explore serious opportunities for greater state control in areas like energy and housing – if it would bring down ordinary people’s costs.The third taskforce will explore more radical ideas to revive crumbling high streets and impoverished districts, such as potential legislative options on houses in multiple occupation, as well as devolving powers to mayors and councils to help them regenerate local high streets.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamLabourMargaret ThatcherBrexitnewsShareReuse this content

title: Russia targets Ukraine’s rail network as war enters deadly new phase | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Six employees killed on Tuesday after Moscow escalates attacks on infrastructure and Ukrainian capital
Author: Luke Harding
Headline: Six employees killed on Tuesday after Moscow escalates attacks on infrastructure and Ukrainian capital
Content: Railway workers respond to a call to repair overhead lines after they were destroyed by a Russian drone strike in Boryspil, Kyiv region.Photograph: Jelle KringsView image in fullscreenRailway workers respond to a call to repair overhead lines after they were destroyed by a Russian drone strike in Boryspil, Kyiv region.Photograph: Jelle KringsUkraineRussia targets Ukraine’s rail network as war enters deadly new phaseSix employees killed on Tuesday after Moscow escalates attacks on infrastructure and Ukrainian capitalLuke HardingandDan Sabbaghin KyivTue 1 Sep 2026 13.23 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussia has opened a deadly new phase in its war againstUkraineby deliberately targeting the country’s railway network, with six employees killed on Tuesday in the latest strikes on Kyiv.Ukraine’s state-owned railway company, Ukrzaliznytsia,said its workers diedwhen a ballistic missile plunged into a locomotive depot. The Russians hit other railway facilities, it added, during a massive bombardment of Kyiv and the Kyiv region.At least 12 people died, with a dozen wounded, including three children.“An unbearably difficult night for the entire railway family. Railway staff have been working at the scene since early this morning. The attack has caused significant damage. Rescue workers are still putting out a number of fires,” said Ukrzaliznytsia’s chair,Oleksandr Pertsovsky.View image in fullscreenBoryspil, in the Kyiv region. Trains were evacuated and travellers stranded during Russia’s days-long air assault on KyivPhotograph: Jelle KringsThe grim strike took place as Russia escalated its attacks on the Ukrainian capital.It has carried out continuous raids for six days, beginning last week, in an attempt to disrupt daily life and demoralise the city’s inhabitants. The onslaught took place hours before Ukrainian children began a new school year.Since Russia’s full-scale invasion, 58 railway staff have been killed and at least 318 injured. One wounded railway employee, Volodymyr, was taken to hospital on Tuesday, with people urged to donate blood if they were B positive – his group. “Our colleagues are by his side,” Ukrzaliznytsia said, adding it would support victims’ families.Ukraine’s railway network is Europe’s third largest, with 15,000 miles (24,000km) of track. It has been a lifeline for the country’s wartime civilians, transporting four million people and an estimated 120,000 pets. It has brought world leaders to Kyiv,including Joe Bidenand Andy Burnham,who arrived last week on an overnight servicefrom Poland.View image in fullscreenRailway workers repairing overhead lines after a Russian strike.Photograph: Jelle KringsSerhih Leshchenko, a member of Ukrzaliznytsia’s supervisory board, described the railway as the “backbone of Ukraine’s economy”. It was the main logistical supplier for the country’s army and industry, and every week transported 600,000 people, he told the Guardian. With 170,000 workers, it was also Ukraine’s biggest company.For these reasons Russia was trying to destroy railways, he added. In the first year of the war it attacked bridges, which could be easily replaced. Next, it targeted rails and electricity substations. Ukraine then switched to using diesel engines. This year, Russia started “direct attacks on civilian locomotives”, he said – an insidious tactic, at a time when Ukraine is short of air defences.Several drivers have been killed and locomotives targeted inside depots. Leshchenko said that if a Shahed drone came within 50km of a train, it had to be evacuated, and could only continue once the threat has passed. So far this year Russia has hit the network more than 1,500 times – a higher figure than in the whole of 2025. Overall, 249 carriages and 492 locomotives have been damaged.Once known for their punctuality, trains now suffer regular delays, sometimes lasting as long as 12 to 15 hours. Amid air raid sirens, passengers are forced to disembark and take cover, including during winter.Writing on Facebook, the Ukrainian journalist Tetiana Zaiets described how she hid in April when Russian drones flew overhead.View image in fullscreenA destroyed railway bridge in the Lyman district in eastern Ukraine’s Donetsk oblast.Photograph: Jelle Krings“It was hell. The train stopped at night somewhere in central Ukraine. I don’t even know the name of the town. Half asleep, I just heard the conductor say ‘evacuation’. We took only our personal belongings and valuables with us. It was raining outside. Thank you to the conductors for handing out blankets,” she posted.She added: “That’s how we held out for two hours. While kamikaze drones were buzzing overhead, we crawled under a goods wagon. The last carriage in the train was full of children. They were being taken back from hospital. They were crying in their sleep. I thought I’d ended up in some sort of horror film. But no, this is our life.”Since the incident, Zaiets said she was too frightened to travel by train. “Until the war is over, I won’t be using it,” she said, stressing she respected Ukraine’s “courageous” railway workers.Last week, an enemy drone hit a train in the Odesa region with 600 people on board, including 15 children.“The train was stopped, we were kicked out. We heard explosions, everything was burning. It was scary,” one passenger, Andriy,told the website Suspline.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenRefugees arriving in Lviv on evacuation trains from Kharkiv and Kryvy Rih make their way through the train station.Photograph: Jelle KringsAnother passenger, Eva, said she was evacuated twice, and “dropped off in a field”. “We sat there and heard something flying. Then we saw a drone very close by.” She managed to collect her belongings and was eventually picked up by a bus, she said.Leshchenko admitted the Russian strikes were hurting Ukraine’s economy and had slowed the export of grain from its under-fire Black Sea ports. He saidKyivneeded air defences from western partners, so it could protects its trains from marauding missiles and drones. “If the whole country is under attack, they will attack railways for sure,” he said.Up until this year more than 90% of Ukrainian trains arrived on time. This was in part down to the fact engines never go especially fast, rolling at 55mph. Carriages are clean and comfortable: the best way of getting around a vast country. Stewards look after night train customers and bring them morning tea in filigree holders. There is a trolley on day trains, and patchy wifi.View image in fullscreenA wounded Ukrainian soldier is evacuated on a train.Photograph: Jelle KringsOn international services, border guards scrutinise male passengers, while dogs roam up and down corridors. Since the invasion, men between 18 and 60 have been forbidden from leaving the country, with some exemptions. On trains from Kyiv to Przemyśl, a railway hub in eastern Poland, most travellers are women. Since 2022 about six million people have departed abroad, many exiting by train.‘Everything’s smashed to bits’: Ukrainians turn anger on those storing weapons near their villagesRead moreIn recent days Russia has launched over 1,500 drones at Ukraine, 800 of them jet-fuel models, which are harder to shoot down. In the past, Moscow would send a swarm of drones a couple of times a week, usually at night. Now the attacks continue without a pause, with one or two drones dispatched every hour, paralysing ordinary life. Air raid sirens in Kyiv are non-stop.Pertsovsky, Ukrzaliznytsia’s boss, described the loss of his employees on Tuesday as “terrible”. “We are in touch with their loved ones. Everyone is with them to get through this extremely difficult time. The night is bitter with impossibility,” he wrote.Explore more on these topicsUkraineKyivRail transportEuropeRussianewsShareReuse this content

title: Dozens arrested after fatal pre-dawn shootout in Dutch village  | Netherlands | The Guardian
description: Police urged people in Overasselt to stay indoors after one person died and 34 were arrested
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Police urged people in Overasselt to stay indoors after one person died and 34 were arrested
Content: Police have arrested people from France, Belgium and Algeria, as well as the Netherlands.Photograph: ANP/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPolice have arrested people from France, Belgium and Algeria, as well as the Netherlands.Photograph: ANP/ShutterstockNetherlandsDozens arrested after fatal pre-dawn shootout in Dutch villagePolice urged people in Overasselt to stay indoors after one person died and 34 were arrestedAgence France-PresseTue 1 Sep 2026 18.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 18.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAuthorities have arrested 34 people, including French, Belgian and Algerian nationals, after a person died in a pre-dawn shootout in a Dutch village reportedly linked to a notorious drug lord.Police urged people in Overasselt, near the German border, to stay indoors with doors and windows shut in case further suspects were on the loose.At about 4am on Tuesday, a group of heavily armed men in balaclavas approached a house in Overasselt and shots were fired, resulting in the death of a 51-year-old, reportedly a security guard.Police responding to the scene immediately came under fire, with two officers sustaining non-life-threatening injuries, police spokesperson Jolanda Aalbers said. Several weapons, data storage devices and vehicles were also seized, she said.According to local media, the shootout was likely connected to the criminal underworld of Dutch drug lord Jos Leijdekkers, also known asBolle Jos(fat Jos).Leijdekkers is one of the Netherlands’ most wanted criminals and has previously been convicted for his role in international cocaine trafficking.View image in fullscreenFrom left: Monique Vinkesteijn, Joerie Minses and Jolanda Aalbers at a press conference following the shooting.Photograph: ANP/ShutterstockHe has lived in Sierra Leonefor at least three yearsand is reportedlyin a relationship with the daughter of the country’s president, Julius Maada Bio.The Het Parool newspaper said the gunfight resulted from a conflict over several hundred kilograms of cocaine thought to have been trafficked by Leijdekkers’ gang.Deputy chief prosecutor Monique Vinkesteijn said there had been a shooting at the same house last year related to a “longstanding conflict” but did not reveal further details.“We know that the group currently in custody is international in nature,” Vinkesteijn said. “It includes French and Belgian nationals, people from Algeria, and also individuals from the Netherlands.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe prosecutor said the suspects faced a variety of charges ranging from murder to manslaughter to preparing a kidnapping and that it was possible further arrests would follow.Local mayor Joerie Minses said the whole community was shocked by the violent events.“What happened in Overasselt crosses all boundaries. This is un-Dutch … Overasselt has been shocked by a form of extreme violence that is totally unacceptable,” he said.Explore more on these topicsNetherlandsEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Farage faces questions over his claim of second standards investigation | Nigel Farage | The Guardian
description: Reform leader said inquiry had been widened but watchdog is not believed to have decided whether to do so
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Reform leader said inquiry had been widened but watchdog is not believed to have decided whether to do so
Content: Farage was sworn in as an MP again on Tuesday after winning the Clacton byelection.Photograph: House of CommonsView image in fullscreenFarage was sworn in as an MP again on Tuesday after winning the Clacton byelection.Photograph: House of CommonsNigel FarageFarage faces questions over his claim of second standards investigationReform leader said inquiry had been widened but watchdog is not believed to have decided whether to do soRowena MasonWhitehall editorTue 1 Sep 2026 14.54 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNigel Farage is facing questions about why he claimed his finances were the subject of a second standards investigation, as he was sworn in again as Clacton’s MP.TheReform UKleader said when he resigned in July that the standards system had become a “political tool” because “yet another standards investigation is under way” into his finances.He argued he wanted the people of Clacton to be the judge of his actions, rather than “the establishment”, after revelations in the Sunday Times that his friend and convicted fraudster George Cottrell had paid for social media work, accommodation and security before the 2024 election.However, it is understood the parliamentary standards commissioner had not launched another investigation or widened the scope of the existing one at that point.The commissioner is believed still not to have decided whether to widen the inquiry as recently as two weeks ago, when it was reopened as Farage was returned as MP for Clacton with an increased majority.Arms and the £5m man: Farage megadonor Christopher Harborne’s military empireRead moreThe commissioner launched his first investigation in May into Farage’s £5m gift from the Thailand-based donor Christopher Harborne before the 2024 election, which was not declared on the MPs’ register of interests and wasfirst revealed by the Guardian. Initially Farage said the money was given to pay for his security, then he described it as a reward for campaigning for Brexit.At least two complaints were then submitted in July about Farage’s funding by Cottrell. Faragecalled a byelection on 7 Julyand the initial investigation was paused.However, Westminster sources said the standards commissioner was assessing information. There is no official confirmation that he has widened his inquiry to include the Cottrell donations, and the commissioner’s list of investigations currently only includes the one launched in May.The sources said the commissioner wanted to see further evidence that Farage had broken the rules in relation to donations from Cottrell in the year before the 2024 election, including his payments for social media work.View image in fullscreenNigel Farage swears in as Clacton's MP at the House of Commons. He said on Tuesday he planned to spend less time in parliament while he toured the country.Photograph: House of Commons/ReutersFarage has maintained the videos were personal and likened his public role before that election to the work of an influencer. However, a number of the videos were political in nature, campaigning on immigration issues.Critics say these should be declared under rules that say donations related to politics must be registered in the 12 months before an MP is elected.The standards commissioner declined to comment on the status of the investigation into Farage and whether any decision had been made on widening the inquiry.If there is no second investigation nor a widened scope, it is possible the first investigation into Farage could conclude sooner than expected. The Times reported in July that the Reform leader would be interviewed within weeks but the byelection paused the process.In relation to the investigation, Alex Burghart, the shadow chancellor of the duchy of Lancaster, said: “The questions surrounding Nigel Farage’s £5m gift from Christopher Harborne and the donations from George Cottrell simply aren’t going away.“Farage has already tried to run away with his farcical byelection in Clacton, but he can no longer hide from these questions. He needs to come clean … The public deserves answers and Farage can’t keep hiding.”If the standards commissioner finds a breach of the rules, and the separate standards committee of MPs recommends a sanction of more than 10 days of suspension from parliament, Farage could end up facing a second byelection.As he was sworn in again on Tuesday, Farage told GB News that he planned to spend less time in parliament and would be leaving more Westminster work to [the Reform deputy leader] “Richard Tice and the gang” while he goes on a tour of the country.Farage will set his priorities for the year ahead when he gives his speech at the Reform party conference at the end of this week, where he is expected to attempt to draw a line under the focus on his finances.Explore more on these topicsNigel FarageReform UKParty fundingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Deported Milo Yiannopoulos says he is ‘ashamed’ of support for Trump | ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) | The Guardian
description: British far-right pundit breaks silence on ICE arrest and deportation and says he was ‘really, really terrified’
Author: Anna Betts
Headline: British far-right pundit breaks silence on ICE arrest and deportation and says he was ‘really, really terrified’
Content: Milo Yiannopoulos at a Ukip rally in Exeter in 2019. Yiannopoulos was deported from the US after being arrested by ICE officials in New Orleans.Photograph: Geoff Caddick/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMilo Yiannopoulos at a Ukip rally in Exeter in 2019. Yiannopoulos was deported from the US after being arrested by ICE officials in New Orleans.Photograph: Geoff Caddick/AFP/Getty ImagesICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Deported Milo Yiannopoulos says he is ‘ashamed’ of support for TrumpBritish far-right pundit breaks silence on ICE arrest and deportation and says he was ‘really, really terrified’Anna BettsTue 1 Sep 2026 16.49 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMilo Yiannopoulos, the British far-right commentator who wasarrestedlast week by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers in Louisiana and deported to the United Kingdom, has broken his silence about the experience, saying that “for the first time I know what it feels like to be really, really terrified”.Yiannopoulos on Tuesday appeared onPiers Morgan Uncensored, a YouTube show presented byPiers Morgan, the British broadcaster and media personality. Yiannopoulos, 41, described the experience in the US as “humiliating and disorientating”, “physically degrading” and “frightening”.He also said that he was “ashamed” of his previous support for Donald Trump, who has pursuedan agendaof mass deportation throughout his second presidency.“I didn’t really understand the physical reality of how institutionalized the brutality is in America” he said, adding: “It’s like everybody that’s arrested is anMS-13 gangmember, and it hurts a lot more than it looks like on television.”His remarks came just days after he wasdeportedfrom the US, after beingarrested on Thursdayby ICE officers at New Orleans airport.In a statement last week, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), theparent agencyof ICE, said Yiannopoulos had “legally entered the country” in May 2019, but “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws”.Yiannopoulos was anearly supporterof Trump before he first became US president in 2016. He is aformer editor of Breitbart Newsand later worked to help the rapper Ye, formerly known asKanye West, explore apresidential runin 2024.The homeland security department said Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge on 22 July “after failing to show up for his immigration hearing”.In the Piers Morgan interview, Yiannopoulos disputed the government’s account and denied previously overstaying a visa. He said he is married to an American, and claimed he held a green card that he was “renewing on a two-year basis”.The Guardian has contacted homeland security and the White House for comment on Yiannopoulos’s remarks.Yiannopoulos also said that while he was detained, “no one would tell me anything” – a common complaint from people held in ICE custody.“I don’t think I’ve ever been frightened like that before” he told Morgan. “I think maybe in the past I’ve been a little bit blasé when people talked about their trauma, a little bit cavalier when people talked about stuff kind of lingering with them, but I get it now … I wouldn’t wish it on anyone.”Last year, in posts on social media, Yiannopoulos had beensupportiveof Trump’scrackdown on immigration.Inonepost, he wrote: “There is one concrete thing we must insist on this administration delivering. It matters a lot more than debts measured in imaginary money. We have got to deport millions and millions and millions of people. Without that, nothing else matters.”In anotherpost, Yiannopoulos had said that California “needs ICE checkpoints at supermarket entrances, gas stations, strip malls, intersections and government buildings, with on the spot deportation for anyone who can’t prove they are in the US legally”.During Tuesday’s interview, Yiannopoulos said of his past support for Trump: “If I had any clue that anything remotely like this was even possible, I would never have gotten involved in supporting Trump in the first place and I’m very ashamed that I did.”Explore more on these topicsICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Trump administrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Federal judge dismisses lawsuit against Lizzo brought by former wardrobe stylist | Lizzo | The Guardian
description: The star has denied allegations of bullying and harassment in the workplace in a suit that has now been thrown out of court
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: The star has denied allegations of bullying and harassment in the workplace in a suit that has now been thrown out of court
Content: Lizzo in March 2026.Photograph: Evan Agostini/Invision/APView image in fullscreenLizzo in March 2026.Photograph: Evan Agostini/Invision/APLizzoFederal judge dismisses lawsuit against Lizzo brought by former wardrobe stylistThe star has denied allegations of bullying and harassment in the workplace in a suit that has now been thrown out of courtAdrian HortonTue 1 Sep 2026 15.33 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 20.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA federal judge on Tuesday dismissed the remaining claims in awell-publicized lawsuitagainstLizzo’s production company, declaring that the case brought by her former wardrobe stylist could not proceed.The ruling by US district judge Fernando L Aenlle-Rocha comes nearly two years after he dismissedLizzoas an individual defendant from the case brought by Asha Daniels against the About Damn Time singer and her production company, Big Grrrl Big Touring, Inc Daniels first filed her lawsuit in September 2023, alleging that she was subject to bullying as well as sexual and racial harassment in an “unsafe, sexually charged workplace culture”.Lizzo answers her critics: ‘I’m a fat, black, happy girl – they were always going to try to tear me down’Read moreLizzo denied all allegations and called the lawsuit, as well as aseparate suitfiled by three backup dancers in August 2023, “false” and “outrageous”. At the time of filing, her lawyers characterized Daniels as a “disgruntled” employee with “meritless and salacious” accusations.In his ruling, Aenlle-Rocha said Daniels failed to identify conduct by company employees that would constitute “general hostility” toward women or disparate treatment between men and women at the workplace. “This alleged conduct and these alleged incidents, while inappropriate and unprofessional, fall within the scope of what the Supreme Court has held to be outside the protection of Title VII as part of the ‘ordinary tribulations of the workplace,’” he wrote.Daniels also claimed disability discrimination, citing an injury from a wardrobe manager who allegedly rolled a heavy clothing rack over her foot and pushed her. But while “the court does not seek to minimize or disregard the pain plaintiff felt from these injuries,” the judge decided that said injuries did not meet the requirements set forth by the American Disabilities Act (ADA).In a statement, Daniels’ lawyer Ron Zambrano expressed disappointment with the ruling.“While we respect the court and the judicial process, we believe the decision improperly weighed evidence that should have been evaluated by a jury,” he said. “We disagree that an employee twisting her ankle and limping while trying to work does not meet the legal standard of a disability under the ADA. These are important issues because these claims often depend on how a jury evaluates the full workplace environment, the surrounding context, and disputed facts. We respectfully disagree with the Court’s approach and are considering appropriate next steps.”Lizzo said she was “relieved” about the ruling, writing on Instagram: “I prayed for the truth to come out and thanks to my incredible lawyers, the truth has prevailed.”Daniels’ lawsuit followed on the heels of a separate suit by three former backup dancers who accused the Grammy winner of creating a hostile work environment through sexual, racial and religious harassment. The lawsuit further claimed that the singer, an outspoken advocate for body positivity and self-love, berated a dancer for gaining weight, pressured another dancer to touch a nude performer at a club in Amsterdam and subjected several dancers to an “excruciating” 12-hour audition after making false accusations that they drank while working.The fat-shaming claim was dismissed by a judge in December 2025. In a social media post celebrating that dismissal, Lizzo said she is “not settling” and will fight “every single claim until the truth comes out”. The case remains ongoing.“I could have settled, but I’m a woman who is not afraid of the truth coming out, so I’m continuing to fight,” shetoldthe Today show in June. “I’m really excited for all of the claims to be dropped and for us to just move forward.”Explore more on these topicsLizzonewsShareReuse this content

title: British aid worker mistakenly identified as a survivor of Nepal-Tibet disaster | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: More than 1,000 people confirmed dead and more than 4,000, including 36 British nationals, remain missing
Author: Angus Thomson
Headline: More than 1,000 people confirmed dead and more than 4,000, including 36 British nationals, remain missing
Content: People search for the names of family members on a list posted outside an army training centre in Nuwakot, Nepal.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople search for the names of family members on a list posted outside an army training centre in Nuwakot, Nepal.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesNepal-Tibet flood disasterBritish aid worker mistakenly identified as a survivor of Nepal-Tibet disasterMore than 1,000 people confirmed dead and more than 4,000, including 36 British nationals, remain missingAngus ThomsonTue 1 Sep 2026 18.58 EDTFirst published on Tue 1 Sep 2026 14.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA British aid worker was mistakenly identified by Nepalese authorities as a rescued survivor after returning to Kathmandu on a humanitarian aid flight.Alastair Chambers, a 45-year-old former Gloucester councillor, said he flew to Nepal last week to distribute sleeping bags, food and essentials to communities cut off by collapsed bridges.After spending several days in a village near the Trishuli river in central Nepal, Chambers returned by helicopter to the capital, where he was greeted by police officers asking for his details.“I gave them my details, just abiding by the rules, and they obviously thought that I’d been rescued,” Chambers told the Press Association.Chambers appeared on a list of 119 names released by local authorities on Tuesday. An army spokesperson then told reporters at a press conference that a British national was among those rescued.“I was contacted by about 15 different journalists in the last few hours, just asking how I was and how I’m feeling after being rescued, and I had to say: ‘Well sorry, I haven’t been rescued,’” Chambers told PA.Those rescued included 118 Nepali nationals – 44 women and 74 men.Thirty-six British nationals are missing, the Foreign Office minister, Stewart Wood, told the House of Lords on Tuesday. The figure had previously been put at 33.Chambers was fined £49,000 after pleading guilty in June 2022 to breeding and selling dogs without a licence. The 45-year-old, who was the leader of a group of community independents on Gloucester city council until 2024, is due to face trial in November after denying he used homophobic slurs against a bar owner and former council worker.At least 1,050 people have been confirmed dead in Nepal since Wednesday’s flash floods, while Chinese state media said 66 people had been killed in Tibet. More than 4,000 people are still missing.Nepal’s prime minister, Balendra Shah, said 11,000 people had been rescued across the affected region. This included 330 foreign nationals, the Nepalese tourist board said in an update on Tuesday.How the deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – a visual guideRead morePreliminary analysis of satellite imagery suggests the collapse of a glacier high in the Himalayas was the primary cause of the disaster.The collapse – so large it wasinitially recorded as a magnitude-4.4 earthquake– triggered a deadly torrent of water, mud and ice that tore along the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers on Wednesday.Crews have faced dangerous and difficult conditions while searching unstable terrain and flood debris.Search efforts are now focused on attempts to reach about 600 workers believed to betrapped inside tunnels at several hydropower stationsin the region.“Massive work has been going on in the tunnel, all the tunnels,” the army spokesperson said on Tuesday.A rapid deployment rescue team from the UK arrived in Nepal on Saturday to provide support for Britons and their families as part of the government’s £5m commitment to support relief and recovery efforts.The Red Cross estimates that 93,000 people have been directly affected by the disaster.Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I think he’s sensible’: constituents on Keir Starmer stepping down as MP | Keir Starmer | The Guardian
description: Few regrets voiced in Holborn and St Pancras over decision despite former PM having had ‘rough time of it’
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Few regrets voiced in Holborn and St Pancras over decision despite former PM having had ‘rough time of it’
Content: ‘It would have been tough for him to sit behind the new prime minister,’ said Dominic Ford, outside the Parakeet pub.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘It would have been tough for him to sit behind the new prime minister,’ said Dominic Ford, outside the Parakeet pub.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianKeir Starmer‘I think he’s sensible’: constituents on Keir Starmer stepping down as MPFew regrets voiced in Holborn and St Pancras over decision despite former PM having had ‘rough time of it’UK politics live – latest updatesHelena HortonTue 1 Sep 2026 13.35 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn Keir Starmer’s north London constituency, full of pretty pubs and elegant townhouses, few tears were being shed at thenews of his departure as its MP.One man nursing a pint outside a pub in Kentish Town simply remarked “good” when informed his MP had quit. He added: “I thought he was very nice before he became prime minister; I met him a few times. But he messed the country up and screwed over pensioners.”Keir Starmer to stand down as MP to focus on world affairsRead moreAnnie, a 30-year-old doctor having a coffee and pastry on a bench near the tube station, said: “I think everyone here wanted him to leave. He’s had a rough time of it, sure, but we have all had enough of him.”Dominic Ford, a 75-year-old pensioner reading a book outside the Parakeet pub, was more sympathetic. “I think he’s sensible. It would have been tough for him to sit behind the new prime minister,” he said. “He’s a very nice, honest guy, and he was very visible around here. We used to see him going to the Arsenal with his son. He was a good local MP, and very honest. I felt very sorry for him when he resigned as prime minister.”On a quiet street among rows of pastel-coloured terrace houses is the Pineapple, Starmer’s favourite pub. It is out of the way of the high street, and the former prime minister is frequently seen there drinking a pint.He may have become tired of his pub visits being documented in various newspapers, because when the Guardian visited and asked regulars what they thought about him stepping down, the bar staff firmly said that questions about Starmer were not allowed. Perhaps this commitment to discretion is why he has referred to the pub as his “church” and “the best pub in land”.View image in fullscreenLaura Hyland said she welcomed the decision: ‘[Starmer] gave very little support for Palestine, and I hope Andy Burnham will be more supportive.’Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianStarmer announced hisdeparture as prime ministerin June after several unpopular choices including making Peter Mandelson, a friend of Jeffrey Epstein, ambassador to the US. On Tuesday, Starmertold the Camden New Journalhe wanted to focus on international affairs and “pass the baton to a successor”.Starmer had previously said he would seek to serve out his term as a backbench MP, and his decision to quit will spark a byelection. The Green party leader, Zack Polanski, is understood to be considering a run for the seat.Laura Hyland, a 67-year-old artist, said she was pleased Starmer was stepping down and that she welcomed the prospect of a byelection. “He gave very little support for Palestine, and I hope Andy Burnham will be more supportive. Arresting people for holding signs saying ‘I support Palestine Action’ was disgraceful.”Anita, 52, was doing her shopping on the high street. She also welcomed Starmer standing down, and said: “I can’t stand him. He was completely useless and I am glad he stood down.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreen‘It is a real shame to lose him from this form of public service so prematurely,’ said Lewis Galloway.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianThe former prime ministers Rishi Sunak and Theresa May both committed to serving out a term as an MP for their constituencies after losing a general election.Sunak is still representing his North Yorkshire constituency, now Richmond and Northallerton, two years after Starmer taunted him about whether he would be moving to California to work in tech. Lewis Galloway, 43, who works in marketing, said he would have liked to see the same from Starmer.“It’s a shame that he’s standing down,” he said. “There was something nice about Theresa May and Rishi Sunak when they stood down and still worked for their constituents from the backbenches. It is a real shame to lose him from this form of public service so prematurely.”Explore more on these topicsKeir StarmerLondonByelectionsLabourLabour party leadershipHouse of CommonsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content
