title: Burnham’s ambitious plans need room to breathe – and Westminster suffocates change  | Rafael Behr | The Guardian
description: A summer on the road suited the prime minister’s open style, but now the walls of conventional politics are closing in, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Author: Rafael Behr
Headline: A summer on the road suited the prime minister’s open style, but now the walls of conventional politics are closing in, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Content: Andy Burnham leaving No 10 to address the House of Commons, London, 1 September 2026.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham leaving No 10 to address the House of Commons, London, 1 September 2026.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesOpinionAndy BurnhamBurnham’s ambitious plans need room to breathe – and Westminster suffocates changeRafael BehrA summer on the road suited the prime minister’s open style, but now the walls of conventional politics are closing inTue 1 Sep 2026 12.46 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 14.08 EDTShareNothing stays fresh for long in parliament and no one sounds normal. The air, thick with convention, suffocates originality, tuning every voice to the same Westminster pitch. The need to escape that climate is one reason whyAndy Burnhamquit his Commons seat to run for mayor of Greater Manchester. Or that is how he tells the story.Returning after nearly a decade away, the prime minister says he wants to throw open the windows, let in some air. He thinks devolution can cultivate a healthier political culture. He intends to rebalance England’s centre of gravity with apower basein the new No 10 North.The timing of Burnham’s arrival in Downing Street, just before the summer recess, suited those arguments. He replaced Keir Starmer, thenpromptly went on tour, posting chatty videos on social media, appearing as the antidote to a stuffy predecessor who, perhaps unfairly, had come to be seen as the archetypal Westminster mechanoid. Starmer, who todayannounced his intentionto stand down as an MP, may find his authentic voice on the outside.Meanwhile, Burnham has to bring his free-range prime minister act into the battery farm of the Commons. His mandate and legislative programme are inherited from the Starmer era. He is stuck with the same squeezed budgets in the same sluggish economy imperilled by the same turbulent global climate. His room for fiscal manoeuvre is constrained by Labour’s 2024 manifesto prohibition on broad-based tax rises and by the bond market’s punitive vigilance towards anything that looks like undisciplined spending.In such conditions, politics is reduced to a zero-sum competition for scarce resources. Every promise made to satisfy the needs of one department or constituency contains an undeclared threat to deprive someone else.Starmer’s leadership was ruined by many things, but few were as crippling as his failure to grapple with those dilemmas. He wouldn’t pick sides between irreconcilable demands within his cabinet. When his own ministers couldn’t read his political instincts or decrypt his priorities, the public had no chance. It was a recipe for paralysis, delivering a congealed gruel of continuity to voters who thought they had ordered piping hot change.Determination not to repeat that mistake has shaped Burnham’s approach from his first moments in office. He declared a moral mission – the elimination of rough sleeping – before even crossing the threshold of No 10. He followed it up with emblematic policies to demonstrate that regime change brought a new focus on the cost of living.No one in Downing Street pretends that capping bus fares or cutting VAT on fuel bills is enough to win affection from a sceptical public. The function of modest retail policies is to show that Labour, renewed by fresh leadership, has snapped out of despondency and started listening. Abounce in opinion pollssuggests it is working.But the transition from small-change symbols to big-ticket policy choices is not easy.It is especially hard if the prime minister is conflict averse and prone to flights of empathic urgency. That is the hazard flagged by Burnham’s critics, based on observation of his career as a minister in the New Labour government and later as Manchester mayor. They are traits that generate spontaneous promises that later have to be diluted or retracted.View image in fullscreenA cushion on a chair in Andy Burnham’s office at No 10 North, Manchester, 20 August 2026.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianIn June, Burnham got himself into just such a tangle over acommitment to compensate“Waspi women” who feel they were mistreated by the Department for Work and Pensions when their retirement age was raised. In May, he told a campaigner for party finance reform that he supported the principle of a cap on donations to guard against big money exerting undue influence in politics. A cap has been proposed as an amendment to the representation of the people bill, currently on its way through parliament. But the government, following trade union lobbying,is not backingthe move.The learning curve for any new prime minister is brutally steep.Things that seem obvious from outside No 10 are revealed to be fearsomely complex. What seems compelling on the campaign trail can feel like a ruinous drain on time and political capital in government. The road is especially hard to navigate for those who arrive midterm, scrambling over unfinished and unpopular business bequeathed by an ousted predecessor.The retreat from plans to free up prison capacity by releasing offenders early is a revealing case. Burnham understandably doesn’t want his first months in office marred by a parade of stories about villains walking free. But swerving unfriendly headlines isn’t a plan for reforming the justice system or growing its shrivelled budget.Likewise, the prime minister’sappearance in Kyivto celebrate Ukraine’s independence day, while important as a display of solidarity with Volodymyr Zelenskyy, came with no account of the sacrifices Britain faces as the price of ramping up its own defences against Russian aggression.No one is better briefed on that challenge than the chancellor. As defence secretary, John Healey resigned from Starmer’s government in protest at the former prime minister’s reluctance to boost military spending. Relocated to the Treasury, he finds himselfmanaging a downgradein rearmament expectations ahead of the autumn budget.The seasonal migration of politics back to parliament threatens a sudden narrowing of Burnham’s options. The prime minister has a theory to counter that threat. His argument is that devolution, as well as bringing fresh air to politics, spurs economic growth.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLoosening the dead hand of Whitehall control over public services is supposed to promote innovation and efficiency. A more responsive government, attuned to local market conditions, will unlock investment.Assuming that can work, the mechanism is slow. Burnham accepts that it is a 10-year plan. The opposition calculates that the fiscal walls will close in on Labour a lot faster than that.Kemi Badenoch thinksthe economy is the issuethat will rehabilitate Tory fortunes. To sharpen her attack on that front, she hassacked her shadow chancellor, Mel Stride, for insufficient pugnacity with the Treasury brief. His replacement, Andrew Griffith, is deemed more dynamic, a quality he oncedisplayed in cheerleadingfor Liz Truss’s disastrous 2022 “mini-budget”.Defence spending is an insatiable beast. John Healey is right to tame it | John McTernanRead moreIn Badenoch’s view, Burnham is a “people-pleaser” who lacks the resolve to whip his MPs behind tough budget choices. He will rely on tax rises to pay for policies that the left see as essential maintenance to the social safety net and the right decry as profligate subsidy for fecklessness. The impossibility of feeding Labour’s big-government appetite with hands shackled by the 2024 manifesto will force the prime minister to seek his own mandate with an early election.It is a plausible scenario. It is also unclear how the Tories get match fit on that timetable when they are running third in national polls. Badenoch’s personal ratings aren’t so bad, but she lacks insight into the reasons why so many voters think her party is unfit to govern. Discounting Griffith’s contamination by the Truss project when appointing a shadow chancellor is a symptom of that blind spot.The Tories are flattered into feeling relevant by a sympathetic press and the constitutional crutch of official opposition status. In parliamentary arithmetic, theConservativesstill eclipse Reform UK.Badenoch welcomes the enclosure of politics in the Commons chamber as much as the Labour leader resists it. The theatre of ritual combat is more her style than his. But the prime minister’s judgment is better in thinking voters are turned off by the whole spectacle. Burnham’s fresh manner has breathed life into a government that was expiring. It will take a different order of political skill to dispel the older miasma of cumulative failure that hangs heavy over Westminster.Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Private equity keeps picking off London-listed firms – and Westminster barely notices | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: Bodycote is the latest FTSE 250 industrial company set to fall to an overseas bidder, despite the government’s talk of ‘reindustrialising’
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: Bodycote is the latest FTSE 250 industrial company set to fall to an overseas bidder, despite the government’s talk of ‘reindustrialising’
Content: Bodycote’s offices in Houston, Texas. The company has 130 sites across 22 countries and 4,000 employees.Photograph: Brett Hondow/AlamyView image in fullscreenBodycote’s offices in Houston, Texas. The company has 130 sites across 22 countries and 4,000 employees.Photograph: Brett Hondow/AlamyNils Pratley on financePrivate equityPrivate equity keeps picking off London-listed firms – and Westminster barely noticesNils PratleyBodycote is the latest FTSE 250 industrial company set to fall to an overseas bidder, despite the government’s talk of ‘reindustrialising’Tue 1 Sep 2026 12.56 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 14.08 EDTShareThe UK is in the business of “reindustrialising”, says the prime minister. If we are, an increasing portion of the activity will be under foreign ownership. Tuesday brought yet another overseas private equity swoop on aFTSE250 industrial firm.This time it’s the Macclesfield-based Bodycote, which describes itself as “the world’s largest service provider of heat treatment and specialist metallurgical technologies” – think, for example, processes and coatings to toughen jet engine blades.The buyer is the US buyout firm Veritas for £1.65bnor 940p a share, or £1.85bn including debt. Unless, that is, the rival bidder, CVC, a European private equity firm, comes back for another bite, which the market clearly thinks is a possibility because Bodycote’s shares closed at 955p.The shame is that one cannot call 940p a stunning price. The valuation “does not appear particularly generous on a take-out basis”, said an analyst at the investment bank RBC, noting that it’s only 25% above the pre-bid level and the implied earnings valuation is merely in line with Bodycote’s 10-year average.Indeed, nine-tenths of the “reasons for recommendation” section of Bodycote’s announcement sounded like an argument for doing the opposite. The passage started by saying how well the medium-term “optimise, perform, grow” strategy adopted in late 2024 was going. The plan was designed to find efficiencies and shift towards the expanding aerospace and defence sectors in pursuit of enviable financial metrics, including 20%-plus operating margins and a return on capital employed of 15 to 20% through the cycle. Good progress has been made, say the directors.On the way, there has been enough spare cash for £120m of share buy-backs while maintaining a 38-year record of growing or maintaining the dividend. And the board is “confident in the ongoing execution” of the strategy, with “the majority of remaining improvements under Bodycote’s control”.It was only in the last sentence that the company also said it was “mindful of increasing structural challenges in certain automotive and industrial markets together with macroeconomic uncertainties which create meaningful risk to delivery of Bodycote’s medium term financial targets”.In other words, everything is going splendidly apart from a couple of risks – the sectoral one that the strategy is addressing, and the vague “macroeconomic uncertainty” that is a normal state of affairs for most companies. As a reason for accepting a bid at a mere 25% premium, it’s not terribly convincing.In Bodycote’s defence, one might say the takeover price could yet improve if CVC, which said it was considering its position, comes back. More depressingly, one suspects Bodycote simply lives in that unloved sub-£5bn capitalisation part of the stock market that suffers from lack of attention and lack of regular inward capital flows. It is harder to fight for independence if the unspoken market pressure is to accept a bid for the sake of certainty.The mini-tragedy in this case is that there was a wake-up call of sorts for investors when Apollo, yet another US private equity outfit, expressed an interest in bidding at 885p in the spring before walking away. The net result, though, is that Bodycote’s 54 years of London stock market life will come to an end one way or another. The company joins a long list of departees this year, which on Tuesday alone also took in telecoms company Gamma Communications for £1.1bn and the Scottish energy firm Capricorn for £292m.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBodycote can still prosper under private equity ownership, of course. But a leading UK-based global specialist in its field, with 130 sites across 22 countries and 4,000 employees, is yet another bad one for the London market to lose.The remedies for this rate of exodushave been trawled over in this column many times– and none are easy. But the process surely starts with recognition among politicians that “selling the family silver” – the title of a recent Peel Hunt report that calculated 150-plus bids for UK companies with a market value of more than £100m since the start of 2023 – may not be in the UK’s long-term economic interests. As ever, there was barely a squeak out of Westminster.Explore more on these topicsPrivate equityNils Pratley on financeFTSEStock marketsEconomic policyIndustrial policynewsShareReuse this content

title: It’s September. Time to put your knees away | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: From May to August, social media is awash with photos of brown knees. But summer’s almost over and they’re all starting to blur together
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: From May to August, social media is awash with photos of brown knees. But summer’s almost over and they’re all starting to blur together
Content: ‘The message is universal. I am in a hot place. I am doing what I please, mainly supine. I have knees.’Photograph: Cavan Images/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘The message is universal. I am in a hot place. I am doing what I please, mainly supine. I have knees.’Photograph: Cavan Images/AlamyOpinionSocial mediaIt’s September. Time to put your knees awayZoe WilliamsFrom May to August, social media is awash with photos of brown knees. But summer’s almost over and they’re all starting to blur togetherTue 1 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 12.45 EDTShareIt’s the start of September, so time to bid adieu to the classic holiday selfie: two brown knees. If it’s on the socials there might be a caption – #bestlife, #bliss – and if it’s in a text it needs no explanation at all, because its message is universal. I am in a hot place. I am doing what I please, mainly supine. I have knees.Everyone’s knees look the same, which is weird given the sheer variety of body shapes, and everyone’s background is mainly the same: a body of water, conceivably a mountain. There might be a cocktail to the side, but there will never be anything interesting, such as a dog, because that would dispel the serenity. It would be good if the knees were just a frame, and between them some distant, barely legible scene were playing out, such as a sword fight or a harras of many-coloured horses, but that would run counter to the vibe: “I am completely at peace and definitely not seeking out horses and lying near them for clicks.”The knees arrive in May and by August you will have seen most of your friends’, except that since they are all interchangeable, you don’t remember who’s been where and you have no way of telling whose bliss is the greatest. It would really help if someone would sunburn their knees, but if they do, that’s an image they’ll never share, ditto any mosquito bites or knee imperfections or pastiness. But then, I don’t need a gritty, warts-and-all portrait of the holiday season – I just want to be confident that everyone I’ve ever met and many, many people I haven’t have fully hinged legs.Knee season is countercyclical (almost) with football season, so for the rest of the year we see only elite knees, and that’s fine too. None of this is a criticism, and nobody here thinks there was anything to be said for a time before phones.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsSocial mediaOpinionFriendshipcommentShareReuse this content

title: The rich and powerful are already trying to sway the next election – I have a plan to stop them | Stella Creasy | The Guardian
description: A bill proposing a cap on donations is up for debate this week. We must seize this chance to keep big money out of our politics, says MP Stella Creasy
Author: Stella Creasy
Headline: A bill proposing a cap on donations is up for debate this week. We must seize this chance to keep big money out of our politics, says MP Stella Creasy
Content: ‘On Wednesday, the representation of the people bill will come before parliament.’Photograph: Niklas Halle’n/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘On Wednesday, the representation of the people bill will come before parliament.’Photograph: Niklas Halle’n/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionParty fundingThe rich and powerful are already trying to sway the next election – I have a plan to stop themStella CreasyA bill proposing a cap on donations is up for debate this week. We must seize this chance to keep big money out of our politicsTue 1 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 11.31 EDTShareChristopher Harborne gave Reform£9m in one day– more than double the amount all trade unions combined gave Labour nationally and its MPs directly for the entirety of the last general election. Once such “largesse” in our politics was rare, now it is commonplace. In 2015, just1% of donationswere from individuals and companies giving £1m or more – by 2024, that figure was a third. The chequebooks of the rich and powerful are already circling the next election. The question for Labour is, are we prepared to pay the price if we refuse to stop them?The prime minister deserves credit for recognising how toxic this has become and the public support for action too. As a result, on Wednesday, measures to cap what overseas donors can give will come before parliament in the representation of the people bill. Yet focusing on location rather than the level of a donation misses how wealthy individuals can set up a UK shell company or use a UK postcode to continue to dominate our democracy. With several British millionaires already funding political entities and parties and others waiting in the wings, our goal must be to ensure no one – near or far – can buy Westminster.Labour is yet to commit to this because some are uneasy that capping individual donations could lead to calls to cap collective donations from membership organisations and trade unions. This is not the first time this fear has led to inaction. ThePhillips review of party funding in 2007collapsed over this dilemma, despite support from major Labour donors including Lord Sainsbury for a cap. With hindsight, we can see how this opened the door for the crisis we now face.That is why I have proposed an amendment to the bill – new clause 120 – that would introduce an immediate £500,000 annual cap on donations, falling to £100,000 in the following calendar year. This would give the government until the end of the second year to establish a permanent cap. Whatever level is ultimately chosen could not exceed £500,000 and would have to be approved by parliament, giving all MPs the chance to shape the final scheme.Critically NC120 explicitly exempts trade unions from the cap if they abide by the existing rules around political funds. Thousands of working people pooling their contributions through a democratic membership organisation is not the same as one extraordinarily wealthy individual writing a cheque for millions of pounds. Since 1913, there has been legislation on how trade union funds can be used – making the comparative lack of parity in how we regulate moneys given by companies and individuals even more startling.Most of us could never dream of having £100,000 to give to a political party. We make ourselves heard by voting, campaigning, volunteering, joining political parties and organising collectively. Safeguarding such organisations on all parts of the political spectrum is therefore also part of a healthy democracy because they allow people who could never wield significant financial power individually to act together.The government has now said it will consider lowering the amount of money political parties are permitted to spend. This is welcome if it happens, but is only half the solution to stopping the voices of ordinary people from being increasingly drowned out by those of billionaires and big business. Without a donation cap, too, donors will circumvent rules by using local groups, parties will stockpile funds and enforcement will be retrospective at best.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionArms and the £5m man: Farage megadonor Christopher Harborne’s military empireRead moreIf passed, the proposal coming before parliament would mean the government would not have to agree on the formal limit now. We would only have to agree that there should be one for all donors – whatever passport they hold – and to act before the next election. Such a deadline would also prevent disagreement about details becoming a convenient excuse for doing nothing at all.In common with Donald Trump, Nigel Farage is clear he intends to keep taking the sums in question and celebrates those giving. Inevitably, when political parties can accept unlimited individual donations, politics degenerates into a fundraising arms race. One party attracts a multimillion-pound donor, so another goes searching for its own to be able to compete.As a democratic as well as socialist movement,Labourcannot stand by as our democracy disintegrates under these pressures. Opposing donation caps is at odds with helping to organise the will of working people against the dominance of capital. Political power should not simply belong to whoever has the most money. Without a meaningful cap, each new quarterly donation report for Westminster politics will provide another nail in the coffin for our hopes of doing things differently. If we fail to seize this moment, the largest wallets will become the loudest voices in deciding Britain’s future.Stella Creasy is Labour and Cooperative MP for WalthamstowExplore more on these topicsParty fundingOpinionReform UKChristopher HarborneLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: Forget T-maxxing – the manosphere’s obsession with testosterone is just fear-maxxing | Donna Lu | The Guardian
description: Testosterone replacement therapy comes with serious and potentially irreversible health risks including infertility and early heart disease
Author: Donna Lu
Headline: Testosterone replacement therapy comes with serious and potentially irreversible health risks including infertility and early heart disease
Content: ‘Low testosterone is being blamed in the rightwing manosphere for a crisis of masculinity,’ writes Donna Lu. ‘But the fixation on T-maxxing ignores hard evidence.’Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Low testosterone is being blamed in the rightwing manosphere for a crisis of masculinity,’ writes Donna Lu. ‘But the fixation on T-maxxing ignores hard evidence.’Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesAntiviralMen's healthForget T-maxxing – the manosphere’s obsession with testosterone is just fear-maxxingDonna LuTestosterone replacement therapy comes with serious and potentially irreversible health risks including infertility and early heart diseaseRead more in theAntiviral seriesTue 1 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 19.22 EDTShareAre you tired? Feeling flat and irritable? Finding it difficult to concentrate? Maybe you’re experiencing the seemingly ubiquitous symptoms ofmodern life. Or, if you’re a man, you may have been told by countless uncredentialed online influencers that you’re probably suffering from “low T”.For decades, testosterone has been marketed to men as a means to maximise virility. But in recent years, social media has fuelled the “T-maxxing” trend, in which men are encouraged to maximise their testosterone levels through either natural or artificial means.Low testosterone is being blamed in the rightwing manosphere for acrisis of masculinity; global search interest in the term is up60% from last year.‘Manosphere’ influencers pushing testosterone tests are convincing healthy young men there is something wrong with them, study findsRead morePopular podcasters such asJoe RoganandAndrew Hubermanopenly talk about taking testosterone, as has the 72-year-old Robert F Kennedy Jr, who has said he uses testosterone replacement therapy as part of an “anti-ageing protocol”.Elsewhere in the Trump administration, the US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, announced in July that soldiers 30 and over would betested annuallyto ensure they have the “right testosterone levels”.Social media is awash with testimonies from men on testosterone replacement therapy who say they have lost weight and regained energy, motivation and libido. Prescriptions for testosterone in theUKandUShave risen sharply in recent years.But the fixation on T-maxxing ignores hard evidence: very few men actually have clinically low levels of the sex hormone, and taking exogenous testosterone – through injections or gels – comes with serious and potentially irreversible health risks, especially when treatment is unwarranted.‘Fearmongering’ in the manosphereTestosterone is a steroid hormone we all produce, but is naturally found at higher levels in men.Testosterone levels fluctuate throughout the lifetime, says Prof Ada Cheung, an endocrinologist at the University of Melbourne.Population-based studies show that testosterone rises rapidly during male puberty and that over time “it does tend to decline a bit with age”, she says. “That decline with age we think is largely attributed to the accumulation of chronic health conditions as we get older” – conditions such as obesity, diabetes, high cholesterol and blood pressure. “But it doesn’t mean that every older man needs testosterone [treatment], because that’s not the case at all.”Testosterone levels also vary through the day and in response to physical stressors such as illness and poor sleep. “It’s always low in the afternoon and highest first thing in the morning,” Cheung says. “Testosterone naturally varies when we eat … and if we’re sick in any way.”Research suggests that average testosterone levels in men havedeclined over the last five decades, though they remain within normal reference ranges. Experts, Cheung included, believe the trend may be at least partly explained by lifestyle habits, stress, chronic disease and rising obesity.Clinically low testosterone – also known as male hypogonadism – is “actually pretty uncommon”, Cheung says. “Less than 2% [of men] would have clinical hypogonadism.” It can can be caused by genetic conditions such as Klinefelter syndrome, or conditions that affect the pituitary gland in the brain, which regulates sex hormone production.“Why people often get confused is that the symptoms of low testosterone are very non-specific, like fatigue, low mood, poor concentration, erectile dysfunction, low motivation,” Cheung says. Far more commonly, she points out, these issues are caused by other factors, such as stress, depression, obesity, and iron or thyroid issues.But these symptoms are frequently used to promote testosterone screening and treatments on social media, says Dr Brooke Nickel, a senior research fellow at the University of Sydney’s school of public health.Research she co-authored, published in January in the journalSocial Science & Medicine, found that young men are being aggressively marketed to by testosterone influencers and wellness companies. Their analysis of 46 popular posts – from accounts with a total following of 6.8 million and which had amassed a combined 659,000 likes – found that nearly three-quarters of accounts had vested financial interests, such as being the sellers of testosterone tests and therapies.“The narratives that they were discussing were closely mirrored to those promoted within the manosphere, where hormone levels were being presented as a measure of manhood,” she says.Testosterone tests, they found, were primarily targeting younger men – a group for which mass screening for low testosterone is medically unwarranted. None of the posts, unsurprisingly, presented any evidence to support claims made.Nickel describes such posts as “fearmongering” – using common experiences to suggest “there’s something medically wrong and that testosterone is a solution”.What are the health risks of taking testosterone?“Once you start testosterone and you are on it for a while, it’s very hard to wean. It’s not just a short-term thing,” Cheung says. Taking testosterone shuts off the body’s natural production of the hormone, as well as sperm production.The American “looksmaxxer” Braden Peters, also known as Clavicular, isby his own admission infertilefrom steroid abuse.“People can become infertile and it can take months to years to recover – and the recovery is not always guaranteed, which is probably one of the most serious concerns,” Cheung says.Doctorshave reportedpeople taking testosterone presenting with gynaecomastia, (male breast enlargement), severe atrophy of the testicles, and early heart disease. Testosterone replacement therapy also increases the risk of blood clots.For patients who do have clinical hypogonadism, “it’s often a lifelong commitment when we start treating someone with testosterone therapy”, Cheung says. “It can lead to things like sleep apnoea, acne, prostate issues, urinary difficulties, mood and libido fluctuations, so it’s not without risk.”‘Not approved for human use’: the online frenzy for injectable peptides sweeping AustraliaRead moreMen frustrated by barriers like financial costs and stigma when seeking out testosterone through regulated medical channels have reported getting the hormone through underground sources with relative ease, Australianresearch has found.That poses its own health risks:Australian testingof anabolic steroids obtained from underground markets has found traces of carcinogenic heavy metals such as lead, arsenic and cadmium, as well as product mislabelling.If men are concerned about symptoms and believe low testosterone may be an issue, they should contact a health practitioner, Cheung says. “If you’re worried, go and see your GP and have a conversation, rather than listening to someone trying to tell you something on social media.”Donna Lu is an assistant editor, climate, environment and science at Guardian Australia.Antiviralis a fortnightly column that interrogates the evidence behind the health headlines and factchecks popular wellness claimsAsk AntiviralWhat health trend do you want examined?Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. title: The Guardian view on the global bond shock: Andy Burnham should take note | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Japan’s collision with Donald Trump reveals the dilemma facing Britain: economic independence is becoming more necessary – and more tricky to achieve
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Japan’s collision with Donald Trump reveals the dilemma facing Britain: economic independence is becoming more necessary – and more tricky to achieve
Content: Sanae Takaichi and Donald Trump talk in the Oval Office at the White House in March 2026.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersView image in fullscreenSanae Takaichi and Donald Trump talk in the Oval Office at the White House in March 2026.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersOpinionJapanThe Guardian view on the global bond shock: Andy Burnham should take noteEditorialJapan’s collision with Donald Trump reveals the dilemma facing Britain: economic independence is becoming more necessary – and more tricky to achieveTue 1 Sep 2026 14.15 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 19.44 EDTShare“In the midst of every crisis lies great opportunity” is an aphorism attributed toAlbert Einstein. It seems to be taken to heart by this White House. Aglobal bond sell-offsparked by an inflationary shock emanating from the Gulf sees Donald Trump seeking to restrict plans by Japan – a longtime ally – to reduce dependence on an international system America dominates.Japan, a successful exporter, has long done things its own way. For years Tokyo saw off the bond vigilantes despite running enormous deficits and a huge national debt. It demonstrated how a central bank could fund public spending and keep interest rates low if it wanted to. This economic model was refined by Shinzo Abe, Japan’s longest-serving prime minister. However, this week the US treasury secretary,Scott Bessent, called time onAbenomicsas his price for US help in stabilising Japan’s currency. Japan’s Sanae Takaichi, he indicated, should shrink her $2tnspendingplans and raise rates. Abenomics did not suddenly become financially impossible. It became inconvenient to the issuer of the world’s reserve currency.Kevin Warsh, Mr Trump’s handpicked chair of the US Federal Reserve, has made it clear that he will raiseinterest ratesin response to inflationary pressures. Others will be expected to follow. In Japan’s case, Washington fears that ayen crisiscould become a bond crisis. A disorderly rout could force Japan into ever larger currency interventions – and repeated appeals to Washington to help defend the yen. If such aid proved inadequate, Tokyo could end up defending its currency by dumping US treasury bonds – of which it has more than a trillion dollars worth – and put upward pressure on the very yields Mr Bessent is trying to contain. His demand that Tokyo raise rates and cut spending is not just about Japanese inflation. It is about trying to prevent Tokyo’s adjustment to the Iran shock being exported on to America’s balance sheet.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham on 1 September.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersMr Burnham’s first Commonsspeechas prime minister suggests an expansive programme to raise living standards and get growth through regional reindustrialisation. This, he says, rests on the “bedrock” of fiscal responsibility. Mr Burnham promises an activist state to deal with four decades of underinvestment and privatisation. But retaining Rachel Reeves’s fiscal framework leaves his investment plans hostage to interest rates, debt costs and feverish “headroom” speculation. Turmoil in global bond markets could derail his industrial strategy before it gets going.Japan’s big bazooka spending programme was meant to do what Mr Burnham now says Britain must do on a smaller scale: use the state to rebuildproductive capacity, reduce strategic dependence and build its export competitiveness. Tokyo has the fiscal firepower, a central bank able to dominate the sovereign bond market and trillions invested overseas. The UK government could mimic that and change its fiscal rules, its relationship to the Bank of England and the way investment is accounted for.But Japan is Mr Burnham’s problem writ large. The war in Iran made it urgent to reducedependenceon fossil fuels. But the conflict’s inflationary shock makes that objective harder – though not impossible – to pursue. Mr Trump’s team is using its leverage over the yen to restrain Tokyo’s plan to make Japan resilient to external price spikes. Mr Burnham has been forewarned: the Gulf inflation shock wave bolsters the argument for economic independence while making the means of achieving it more difficult.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on loneliness: the decline in friendship leaves gen Z exposed | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Problems with housing, jobs and technology have dented young people’s confidence in the future and each other
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Problems with housing, jobs and technology have dented young people’s confidence in the future and each other
Content: ‘Adolescence is a complicated time of life … This is one reason why supportive peer relationships are so important.’Photograph: Getty/iStockphotoView image in fullscreen‘Adolescence is a complicated time of life … This is one reason why supportive peer relationships are so important.’Photograph: Getty/iStockphotoOpinionLonelinessThe Guardian view on loneliness: the decline in friendship leaves gen Z exposedEditorialProblems with housing, jobs and technology have dented young people’s confidence in the future and each otherTue 1 Sep 2026 14.14 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 19.45 EDTShareHope, Raye told a crowd at Reading festival on Saturday, was the theme of a set inspired by hersecond album. Having established through a show of hands that most of the audience had just done their GCSEs, and after recounting her own rocky road to stardom, the 28-year-old singer led a series of upbeat chants of “it’s gonna be all right”.For anyone who thinks adolescence ought to be a time of optimism, it was a charming spectacle. But a new report from the Institute for Public Policy Research thinktank paints a much gloomier picture. Building on existing evidence of declining wellbeing, such asAlan Milburn’s reporton young people who are not in education or work, the IPPR’s researchers found that 11- to 24-year-olds in England (gen Z and older members of gen Alpha) areincreasingly lonely. They have fewer friends than young people in the past and are less contented with those they do have. One in 20 say that they have no friends at all. A series of interviews produced worrying evidence of their lack of confidence about the future.They also spoke about problems with concentration that they associated with social media. When asked what they do in their spare time, the most common answer was “doomscrolling”. But while the authors point to “deference to unaccountable tech oligarchs” as one way in which politicians have let younger generations down,their analysisgoes wider. It includes housing costs, a shortage of entry-level jobs, student debt, austerity and the Covid-19 pandemic. They conclude that the social contract with youth is broken and needs fixing.View image in fullscreenRaye at Reading festival.Photograph: James Klug/RedfernsThis is a deliberately broad-brush study that focuses on what the 10 million 11- to 24-year-olds in England have in common. But it does not gloss over socioeconomic differences. The steepest falls in life satisfaction over the past decade have been in deprived areas; housing is a far more serious blockage on the route to independence for those without family wealth. Noting that the average deposit has risen to £78,000, the report states that “owning a home before your mid-30s has become close to an inherited trait”. With social housing all but impossible to access for most young adults, too many are either stuck with parents or in privately rented flats. Labour has already taken steps to boost the supply of new homes, but must do more to improve young people’s prospects. It is a national scandal that so many are locked out.Adolescence is a complicated time of life, and there is an echo of Sigmund Freud’sidea of “ordinary unhappiness”in the report’s reference to the “ordinary challenges” of growing up. It is hard to leave school and parents, and decide what to do next. This is one reason why supportive peer relationships are so important, and why research on friendship is worthwhile.But while gen Z and gen Alpha deserve attention, their problems should not be viewed in isolation. The weakening of the social fabric around them can be seen as part of a wider pattern that the IPPR rightly links to neoliberalism’s assault on collectivism. There is no single policy lever that can be pulled to mend the missing threads. But governments and councils are far from helpless. Housing, job-market reforms (including limits onAI in recruitment) and a stronger overall emphasis on generational fairness would all make the world a friendlier place for under-25s.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Assisted dying, palliative care and patient choice | Assisted dying | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to an article by Dr Zubir Ahmed, who argued that better palliative care should be prioritised before assisted dying is legalised
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to an article by Dr Zubir Ahmed, who argued that better palliative care should be prioritised before assisted dying is legalised
Content: ‘We must work out how to craft these safeguards, not deny patients a choice.’Photograph: MartinPrescott/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘We must work out how to craft these safeguards, not deny patients a choice.’Photograph: MartinPrescott/Getty ImagesAssisted dyingLettersAssisted dying, palliative care and patient choiceReaders respond to an article by Dr Zubir Ahmed, who argued that better palliative care should be prioritised before assisted dying is legalisedTue 1 Sep 2026 12.44 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTShareI work as a renal physician, including on a transplant ward, so I will have had many of the same experiences as Zubir Ahmed, but I do not share his opinion about assisted dying (As a doctor, I say this: before we even consider assisted dying, fix how we care for the most vulnerable, 26 August).It is universally agreed that patients with capacity should be able to make decisions about their treatment. Their decision is the one that matters if they have the ability to use and understand the relevant information and can communicate any decision they make. The doctor needs to explain possible options and their likely outcomes in as fair and balanced a manner as possible.My daily reality, like that of just about everyone working in theNHS(and in other healthcare systems), involves doing the best I can within constrained resources. Palliative care provision and social services are not unique in being limited by the funding and staffing available. To say that patients should not be allowed to choose an assisted death until these reach some arbitrary standard defined as acceptable by Mr Ahmed or others begs many questions, and denies patients the ability to control their destiny now.Kidney doctors such as me look after patients receiving artificial kidney (dialysis) treatment. This gives many years of good life to many, but when the burden of living has become too much, it is not uncommon for them to decide to stop their treatment. “Thank you for looking after me so well, and for letting me go,” is the most moving thing a patient has ever said to me.It is essential that safeguards are incorporated into any legislation that allows a patient to choose an assisted death, but we must work out how to craft these safeguards, not deny patients a choice.Dr John FirthCambridgeZubir Ahmed is right: palliative care needs investment and development before any further debate on assisted dying. Fear of dying badly has increased as NHS services have been squeezed more than ever.Lauren Edwards’ billwould fund assisted dying from the NHS budget, further eroding other services. Specialist palliative care across the UK is patchy, and palliative care in generalist services varies widely.When a doctor says “there’s nothing more that can be done”, few patients know to ask for a specialist opinion. Sadly, many clinicians are unaware of developments in specialist palliative care and what can be done to relieve distress.Without access to adequate symptom relief and competent psychological support, you won’t have a real choice when an assisted death is both offered and delivered by the very clinicians who could and should be working to improve your quality of life.Research reveals that abuse of older people is common, but Edwards’ proposals will do nothing to detect abuse and coercion. The bill does not even require cases of assisted dying to be referred to a coroner; there will be no scrutiny of what really happened. In the last 15 years,209 cases of assisted suicidehave been referred to the director of public prosecutions; eight were prosecuted for homicide or other serious crime (almost 4%). How will these be detected under the current proposals?Andy Burnham is right. This bill is an untimely distraction.Sheila Hollins andIlora FinlayHouse of LordsAs a former nurse and NHS midwife of more than 30 years, and now a full-time unpaid carer for my 88-year-old mother with dementia, I agree that a choice is only meaningful when a viable alternative exists.We rightly worry that seriously ill or disabled people may feel they have become a burden. But we must confront what creates that fear: social care that is rationed, unaffordable or unavailable, while relatives are expected to fill every gap regardless of the cost to their own health and future.I did not freely choose between continuing my career and becoming a full-time carer. I chose not to abandon my mother when suitable, reliable and affordable support was unavailable. Those are not the same thing.I now provide considerably more than 35 hours of care each week for carer’s allowance of £86.45 – no more than £2.47 an hour at the minimum qualifying hours. Caring has cost me my salary, occupational-pension growth, financial independence and much of my freedom. Yet the state treats family care as an almost limitless free resource.A humane social-care system would guarantee appropriate professional support to anyone who needs it, including people without relatives. Families could then choose whether to provide care, how much they could safely manage and when they needed to stop. Carers would receive proper financial support, pension protection and meaningful respite.Before parliament creates another choice at the end of life, it must provide genuine choices throughout life. No vulnerable person should fear being a burden because adequate care is missing – and no relative should have to sacrifice their entire future to prevent that from happening.Jacqueline HyltonLeedsHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: A national commission on voting reform is essential | Electoral reform | The Guardian
description: Letters: Sandy Martin and Joan Ruddock respond to an article on changes to the voting system
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Sandy Martin and Joan Ruddock respond to an article on changes to the voting system
Content: ‘Many people do not realise that the referendum was not about a proportional electoral system.’Photograph: PA Wire/Press Association ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Many people do not realise that the referendum was not about a proportional electoral system.’Photograph: PA Wire/Press Association ImagesElectoral reformLettersA national commission on voting reform is essentialSandy MartinandJoan Ruddockrespond to an article on changes to the voting systemTue 1 Sep 2026 12.43 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTShareYour report (Labour MPs will push Burnham to back voting reform in first 100 days, 25 August) says: “The UK last rejected electoral reform in 2011 after a referendum [on] whether to change to an alternative vote system.” Many people do not realise that the referendum was not about a proportional electoral system. While the alternative vote is the best way to elect a single person, it really doesn’t work for a government.That referendum was primarily a popularity contest for Nick Clegg, and it is no surprise that he was rejected, predominantly by people who were not aware of the actual terms of the referendum. A national commission, taking evidence from people across the country, followed by a general election that includes a manifesto commitment to changing the system, will be a far more reliable and accurate representation of the views of the British people than a referendum is ever likely to be.Sandy MartinChair,LabourCampaign for Electoral ReformThe amendment to the representation of the people bill on which you report is not the only thing to which the government will have to reply. By law they will have to respond to a parliamentary petition, initiated by me, which calls for thesetting up of a national commissionin line with the all-party parliamentary group’s proposal.The petition states that it should be an independent, time limited, expert-led review to build consensus for changing the electoral system for parliament. Already more than 25,000 people have signed – twice the number required to trigger a government response. It is eagerly awaited.Joan RuddockFormer Labour MP and ministerHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Don’t dismiss ‘Woke 1.0’ – young people’s activism should be encouraged  | Politics | The Guardian
description: Letter: Far from being crazy, the grandchildren of the radical ‘permissive’ generation are using their voices to fight for progress, as we taught them to do, writes Paul McGilchrist
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Far from being crazy, the grandchildren of the radical ‘permissive’ generation are using their voices to fight for progress, as we taught them to do, writes Paul McGilchrist
Content: Demonstrators in Rochester, New York, during a protest over the death of a black man, Daniel Prude, after police put a spit hood over his head during an arrest in March 2020.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersView image in fullscreenDemonstrators in Rochester, New York, during a protest over the death of a black man, Daniel Prude, after police put a spit hood over his head during an arrest in March 2020.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersPoliticsLettersDon’t dismiss ‘Woke 1.0’ – young people’s activism should be encouragedFar from being crazy, the grandchildren of the radical ‘permissive’ generation are using their voices to fight for progress, as we taught them to do, writesPaul McGilchristTue 1 Sep 2026 12.43 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 12.46 EDTShareI can’t help feeling that Nesrine Malik’s critique of “Woke 1.0” was more nuanced and focused than the published responses suggest (Letters, 24 August). Yes, it could be puritanical, dogmatic and wrong-headed at times, but to dismiss it on these grounds is to ignore Malik’s entreaty not to “trivialise and dismiss movements that resonated globally, and which had safety, dignity and equal opportunity at their heart”.Far from being “crazy”, so called “Woke 1.0” was the roar of the grandchildren of the radical “permissive” generation – on both sides of the Atlantic – using voices they were always encouraged to believe could change the world. They were schooled in human rights like no others before them, and inducted into activism through historical precedent, armed only with just cause and integrity. They were unashamed to wear conviction on their sleeves and prepared to face the inevitable backlash as readily as their often-celebrated countercultural forebears.Malik argues, persuasively and correctly, that how we “frame” this activism conditions how we appreciate its aims. And it has been comprehensively framed by rightwing reactionaries making space for the recrudescence of attitudes and proclivities which an older progressive generation fought tooth and nail to bury.Paul McGilchristCromer, NorfolkHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Writers’ homes are sites of resistance and renewal | Books | The Guardian
description: Letter: David Devanny on the challenges in running the late poet Charles Causley’s home in Launceston, Cornwall
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: David Devanny on the challenges in running the late poet Charles Causley’s home in Launceston, Cornwall
Content: ‘We owe everything to our volunteers and occasional private philanthropy, supplemented by grants and donations.’ Cyprus Well.Photograph: Mr Standfast/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘We owe everything to our volunteers and occasional private philanthropy, supplemented by grants and donations.’ Cyprus Well.Photograph: Mr Standfast/AlamyBooksLettersWriters’ homes are sites of resistance and renewalDavid Devannyon the challenges in running the late poet Charles Causley’s home in Launceston, CornwallTue 1 Sep 2026 12.43 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 12.46 EDTShareIn response to your letters on preserving writers’ homes (25 August) Cyprus Well was the cottage home of poet Charles Causley (1917-2003) in Launceston, Cornwall. We are a small charity, proud to open the doors to aspiring writers, schoolchildren, residents and tourists as much as we can, year-round. We share Causley’s sanctuary of 50 years with those who love his work or write their own, as well as those who just want to immerse themselves in a peaceful and enriching environment.Like others who run writers’ homes for the public, it’s not easy – particularly with weather impact on the building and demands on shrinking sources of funding. We owe everything to our volunteers and occasional private philanthropy, supplemented by grants and donations from trusts and foundations. It would be wonderful if the town council – some of whom knew Causley in his lifetime – would reconsider their position on supporting us, too.The trust will keep going as best it can, providing opportunities to visit (and stay in) Causley’s home, bidding for much-needed funding, bringing leading poets to Launceston to work with schoolchildren, as well as in the library and independent bookshop, while championing Causley’s own work and supporting his beloved community.It’s about the visitor as much as the writer – perhaps that’s the key. Enter a fine writer’s private domain, and you are reminded of the possibility of a world without such places. We can see these homes as sites of resistance and renewal, a mark of the living impact of creativity, and evidence of the importance of preserving it.David DevannyChair, Charles Causley TrustHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Fernández completes record-equalling £125m move from Chelsea to Manchester City | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Manchester City have equalled the British transfer record with a £125m deal to sign midfielder Enzo Fernández from Chelsea
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Manchester City have equalled the British transfer record with a £125m deal to sign midfielder Enzo Fernández from Chelsea
Content: Enzo Fernández has signed a five-year deal at Manchester City after joining from Chelsea for £125m.Photograph: Manchester City FCView image in fullscreenEnzo Fernández has signed a five-year deal at Manchester City after joining from Chelsea for £125m.Photograph: Manchester City FCManchester CityFernández completes record-equalling £125m move from Chelsea to Manchester CityFernández: ‘This is a club built for success’Chelsea’s move for Monaco’s Camara falls throughJacob SteinbergTue 1 Sep 2026 19.12 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester City have equalled the British transfer record with a £125m deal to sign Enzo Fernández from Chelsea, who were left raging after their attempts to replace the Argentina midfielder were dashed by Monaco reneging on an agreement to sell Lamine Camara last night.On a day of twists and turns, City emerged in a strong position after they bolstered their attack by signing Iliman Ndiaye from Everton for up to £65m and landed one of Enzo Maresca’s biggest targets on a five-year deal.Chelseaheld out for a huge fee for Fernández and it seemed they were going to find a replacement for him as the transfer window drew to a close.The club moved to agree a £47m fee with Monaco for Camara, who was set to sign a six-year contract with the option of an extra year. Chelsea swooped when Everton’s attempts to sign the USA striker Folarin Balogun ran into difficulties. It left Monaco needing to raise funds from elsewhere, prompting Chelsea to revive their move for Camara after having a £38.1m offer for the 22-year-old Senegal midfielder rejected earlier in the day.Transfer deadline day: Man City sign Fernández and Ndiaye, Mudryk and Tosin join Spurs – liveRead moreChelsea had a written agreement with Monaco but were stunned by the Ligue 1 club pulling out of the deal as the deadline approached. Sources called Monaco’s conduct “deeply unprofessional”. As an extraordinary situation developed it emerged that Everton, who have also loaned Jack Grealish from City, had refused to give up on Balogun, renegotiating the fee for the former Arsenal forward only for that deal to also fall down just after midnight.The collapse of Camara’s move did not lead to Chelsea cancelling the sale of Fernández to City. The deal means City have spent £327m on midfielders this summer following the arrivals of Elliot Anderson from Nottingham Forest for £116m and Ayyoub Bouaddi from Lille for £86m.“I could not be happier to be here, and I am ready for the challenge of helping City continue winning trophies. This is a club built for success,” said Fernández, who becomes this country’s most expensive player alongside Alexander Isak, who joined Liverpool from Newcastle for £125m a year ago. “I pride myself on continually improving my game. Anyone who’s worked with me will know how hard I train every single day and how much I put into matches. I give absolutely everything and I can promise Manchester City that will continue now I’m here.”View image in fullscreenIliman Ndiaye also completed his move to Manchester City on a busy deadline day for sporting director Hugo Viana.Photograph: Manchester City FCMaresca has a good relationship with Fernández after coaching him at Chelsea and a reunion has been on the cards for a while. City opened talks with Chelsea on Monday night and will feel they have successfully rebuilt their midfield after selling Rodri to Barcelona and losing Bernardo Silva to Real Madrid, while also selling Nico González to Newcastle. They were also not put off even after Chelsea’s unofficial deadline for clubs to lodge bids of £120m for Fernández passed last month.Fernández has been angling for a way out of Chelsea since March and his departure was announced in a short statement on the club’s website. The 25-year-old, who scored 31 goals after joining from Benfica for £106.7m in January 2023, initially had his sights set on joining Real Madrid. He grew disillusioned following Maresca’s acrimonious split with Chelsea earlier this year. Fernández, the unofficial vice-captain, spoke out after Chelsea were knocked out of the Champions League by Paris Saint-Germain in March. Chelsea responded by banning him for two games.Fernández reported back to training after the World Cup and was booed by Chelsea fans during a pre-season friendly against Real Sociedad at Stamford Bridge. He featured in the club’s opening first game of the season, coming off the bench to help Xabi Alonso’s side beat Fulham, but was left out of Chelsea’s next two fixtures.Chelsea came round to the view a sale was in their interests. There is a feeling within the club that Fernández, who won the Conference League and Club World Cup during his time in west London, had not shown himself to be vice-captain material.Chelsea have made in the region of £500m in loans and sales this summer. They finished the window by selling Marc Guiu to RB Leipzig for £16m and loaning Dário Essugo to Strasbourg, Robert Sánchez to Como andMykhailo Mudryk to Tottenham. Tosin Adarabioyo joined Spurs on a permanent deal.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityChelseaTransfer windownewsShareReuse this content

title: Everton left with only one striker after Balogun deal collapses late on deadline day | Everton | The Guardian
description: Everton’s £40m move for US international Folarin Balogun collapsed late on deadline day to leave manager David Moyes with only one striker for the first half of the season
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Everton’s £40m move for US international Folarin Balogun collapsed late on deadline day to leave manager David Moyes with only one striker for the first half of the season
Content: Folarin Balogun will not be be joining deadline-day signings Jack Grealish and Ainsley Maitland-Niles at Everton.Photograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFolarin Balogun will not be be joining deadline-day signings Jack Grealish and Ainsley Maitland-Niles at Everton.Photograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty ImagesEvertonEverton left with only one striker after Balogun deal collapses late on deadline day25-year-old walks away from £40m deal at last momentBeto and Ndiaye already sold by club to raise fundsAndy HunterTue 1 Sep 2026 19.46 EDTFirst published on Tue 1 Sep 2026 19.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEverton’s £40m move for US international Folarin Balogun collapsed late on deadline day to leave manager David Moyes with only one striker for the first half of the season.Everton had agreed a £40m deal for Balogun only for issues with the striker’s medical to place the transfer in doubt after the Merseyside club had sold Beto to Fiorentina and Iliman Ndiaye to Manchester City. Enquiries were made to Manchester United for Joshua Zirkzee and Aston Villa for Tammy Abraham but proposed loans for both forwards were rejected.The structure of the deal was renegotiated late on – Monaco agreed to accept a lower payment up front and more in add-ons – and Everton submitted a deal sheet to complete the transfer in time. But the 25-year-old is said to have changed his mind over the move and walked away at the final moment. The collapse of the deal leaves Thierno Barry as Everton’s one recognised striker and completed a shambolic end to the window by the club’s hierarchy, who were already under pressure having tried to sell Harrison Armstrong to Nottingham Forest.Transfer deadline day: Man City sign Fernández and Ndiaye, Mudryk and Tosin join Spurs – liveRead moreEverton also hit problems in their attempts to sign right-back Kenny Tete from Fulham. A £9m deal had been agreed for the defender only for Fulham to fail to land their preferred replacement, Andrei Ratiu of Rayo Vallecano. Everton finally concluded their long-running search for a right-back by signing former Arsenal player Ainsley Maitland-Niles from Lyon for a fee of around £4.2m. The 29-year-old has agreed a three year contract.Funds were raised by the sales of Ndiaye to City, for £60m plus £5m in add-ons, Beto to Fiorentina for £15.5m, Tim Iroegbunam to Hull for an initial £15m and Nathan Patterson to Torino for an undisclosed fee.Grealish returns to the Hill Dickinson Stadium on another season loan from City. The 30-year-old enjoyed a productive spell on loan in 2025-26 before sustaining a fractured foot that ended his campaign in February.Grealish, who will be out of contract at City when this latest deal ends next summer, could make his second Everton debut against Manchester United on Sunday. He said: “I’m so happy. I think I’m at my best at everything in life, not just football, when I feel loved. That’s what the manager has given me, what my teammates have given me and especially what the fans have given me. Every time I see an Everton fan, it’s just pure love.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It means a lot to me and hopefully I’ve made a few Everton fans happy. I had a perfect time here for the first six months, then I stayed around after I got injured. I’ve been watching all the Everton games in pre-season and since the season started. Now I feel ready to go.”Explore more on these topicsEvertonTransfer windownewsShareReuse this content

title: Arthur Fery sunk by Lorenzo Musetti in straight sets on US Open debut | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: The Wimbledon semi-finalist Arthur Fery lost 6-3, 6-3, 7-5 to Lorenzo Musetti while Elena Rybakina sailed into the second round with a 6-3, 6-2 success
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: The Wimbledon semi-finalist Arthur Fery lost 6-3, 6-3, 7-5 to Lorenzo Musetti while Elena Rybakina sailed into the second round with a 6-3, 6-2 success
Content: Arthur Fery fought hard but could not find the answers against Lorenzo Musetti.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/APView image in fullscreenArthur Fery fought hard but could not find the answers against Lorenzo Musetti.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/APUS Open Tennis 2026Arthur Fery sunk by Lorenzo Musetti in straight sets on US Open debutBritish Wimbledon semi-finalist loses 6-3, 6-3, 7-5Elena Rybakina into second round with 6-3, 6-2 winTumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowsTue 1 Sep 2026 16.55 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSix weeks on from the fortnight that changed his life, Arthur Fery’s first grand slam appearance since his semi-final run at Wimbledon came under considerably different circumstances. He is now the 33rd best men’s player in the world, a direct entrant for all of the biggest tournaments, and he has continued to gain experience at the highest level of professional tennis each week.As a result of his continued exposure on the tour, though, Fery’s adversaries have also learned a bit more about him. In his first main draw appearance at the US Open, Fery came up against a prepared and sharp Lorenzo Musetti, who knew exactly how to exploit the vulnerable parts of his game in order to secure a win. The Italian comprehensively outplayed the British No 1, reaching the second round with a comfortable 6-3, 6-3, 7-5 victory.Naomi Osaka pays tribute to NBA star Allen Iverson in basketball-themed US Open outfitRead moreThis was an emphatic, impressive performance from Musetti, who handcuffed Fery with his heavy topspin and simply had far too many options for his opponent. Despite fighting hard until the end, Fery’s game looked underpowered as he struggled to consistently hit through one of the best defensive players in the world.Fery had actually started well enough, quickly finding rhythm behind his serve as he eased through his first three service games. However, as the Italian began to take control of the baseline with his forehand, the Briton’s serve capitulated. Down 15-30 at 3-3, Fery threw in his first two double faults of the match on consecutive points to hand over the first break.Once that was secured, Musetti opened up his shoulders and imposed relentless pressure on Fery. Musetti spent much of the match pushing Fery behind the baseline with his heavy spin and height. With the ball consistently bouncing high above his shoulders and out of his strike zone, Fery struggled to counter Musetti effectively. He veered between desperately trying to take the ball on the rise, constantly spraying errors, and being dictated to by Musetti whenever he tried to hang back and wait for the ball to drop. He never really looked comfortable.Over the course of their two hours on court, Musetti also made use of his far greater weaponry. He served well in decisive moments and effortlessly stepped inside the baseline, dominating with his forehand when necessary.He also struck his sweet single-handed backhand supremely well on certain key points, particularly in the second set, where he converted the decisive break point and then saved a later break point with supreme down-the-line backhand winners.In the aftermath of his shock run to the Wimbledon semi-finals, Fery has managed himself well. He performed at a high level in Cincinnati, winning a round and then pushing Alex de Minaur, the world No 8,in two tight sets. Last week, he reached his first ATP final in Winston-Salem, providing more evidence that he belongs at this level.View image in fullscreenElena Rybakina could become world No 1 during this US Open.Photograph: Robert Prange/Getty ImagesHe is yet to lose to any lower-ranked opponent. But the standard at the top of men’s tennis is incredibly high and competing with players of Musetti’s calibre will come with many more losses and lessons. It remains to be seen how much these lessons will enable him to improve.For Musetti, this is a hopeful first performance as he tries to put himself back in contention for big titles after a torrid year. Musetti had started the season ranked No 5 and he was en route to a first Australian Open semi-final in Melbourne when he was forced to withdraw due to injury while leading Novak Djokovic by two sets in their quarter-final match. After a few months out, it has taken even longer for Musetti to rebuild confidence in his game and body. He is finally beginning to resemble his old self again.Elsewhere, Elena Rybakina made a positive step forward in her pursuit of the No 1 ranking as she moved into the second round with a 6-3, 6-2 win over the 17-year-old American wildcard Thea Frodin.View image in fullscreenFlavio Cobolli lets it all out after battling back from two sets down to see off Francisco Comesaña.Photograph: Timothy A Clary/AFP/Getty ImagesThere have been ample doubts surrounding Rybakina after she suffered a foot injury at the Cincinnati Open that forced her to retire from her quarter-final match against Iga Swiatek but she appeared comfortable on the court as she overpowered her inexperienced opponent.Rybakina currently sits at No 1 in the live rankings and she would become the world No 1 for the first time in her career if she reaches the semi-finals or if Aryna Sabalenka, Jessica Pegula and Coco Gauff do not win the tournament.In the men’s draw, the fifth seed and French Open finalist Flavio Cobolli produced one of the best comebacks of his career to escape a tough battle with the Argentinian Francisco Comesaña, recovering from a two-set deficit to reach the second round with a 3-6, 2-6, 6-3, 6-4, 6-4 win.Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026US Open tennisArthur FeryTennisUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Maia Bouchier powers England to record ODI run chase against Ireland | Women's cricket | The Guardian
description: Maia Bouchier hit 104 to power England to victory in the first ODI against Ireland, as they won by six wickets in Leicester
Author: Raf Nicholson
Headline: Maia Bouchier hit 104 to power England to victory in the first ODI against Ireland, as they won by six wickets in Leicester
Content: Maia Bouchier welcomes the applause after reaching her century in Leicester.Photograph: Philip Brown/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMaia Bouchier welcomes the applause after reaching her century in Leicester.Photograph: Philip Brown/Getty ImagesWomen's cricketMaia Bouchier powers England to record ODI run chase against IrelandIreland: 281-5; England: 283-4Bouchier hits 104; fifties for three Ireland battersRaf Nicholsonat Grace RoadTue 1 Sep 2026 14.42 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 19.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA century from Maia Bouchier led England to a record women’s one‑day international run chase against Ireland at Grace Road on Tuesday, as they passed their target of 282 with six wickets and 71 balls to spare.Bouchier missed out on selection for the T20 World Cup in June, but she remains a key part of England’s ODI plans as they try to build a new team following the retirements of Heather Knight and Tammy Beaumont.England beat Ireland by six wickets in first women’s cricket ODI – live reactionRead moreBouchier initially played second fiddle to Sophia Dunkley, who smashed 73 from 61 balls. But when Dunkley drove a return catch to the leg-spinner Cara Murray, it was left to Bouchier to bring up the three-figure score which was there for the taking against a helpless-looking Irish attack.“Obviously gutting that I missed out on the World Cup,” Bouchier said. “But it was a really good way to play some more cricket [for Hampshire] and take the positives instead of the negatives. There’s a lot of opportunity next year which is really exciting. If I can just put my name out there and score those big runs, I hope that will take care of itself.”England are contesting the three ODIs against Ireland without several key players – the regular captain Nat Sciver‑Brunt remains injured, while Lauren Bell, Danni Wyatt-Hodge, Sophie Ecclestone, Amy Jones and Linsey Smith are being rested. The series therefore provides an intriguing glimpse into the future, with the 21‑year‑old Jodi Grewcock batting at No 3 and the off‑spinning all‑rounder Mady Villiers making a white‑ball return after two years in the wilderness.Grewcock failed to shine, bowled through the gate by the wily Murray for nine, while Bouchier holed out to long-on for 104. But Alice Capsey and Freya Kemp continued the momentum with a flurry of boundaries, ensuring England romped home.View image in fullscreenSophia Dunkley survives a stumping attempt. She went on to score 73.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAThe Ireland captain, Gaby Lewis, said: “It’s very disappointing. You’re battling against world-class players who really took on the powerplay, and they put our bowlers off their lines and built that pressure for our bowlers and we struggled with our execution.”Earlier there were half-centuries for three Ireland players – Amy Hunter, Lewis and Rebecca Stokell – although Stokell’s original celebrations proved premature when the umpires ruled that a boundary over fine leg had come off her helmet and counted as leg-byes. She was then given out lbw to England’s stand‑in captain, Charlie Dean, but had the decision overturned on review, allowing her to reach the milestone for real with 10 balls left of the innings.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere remain concerns about England’s lack of bowling depth. Without Bell and Ecclestone, England’s attack – spearheaded by Issy Wong and Lauren Filer – lacked penetration, allowing Lewis and Hunter to stroll to a 136-run partnership for the second wicket.England also leaked 33 extras, including 20 wides – the second-most conceded by England in an ODI in the professional era. Capsey, keeping wicket for the first time in a full international in place of the rested Jones, took a brilliant one‑handed diving grab to see off Alice Tector. On the other hand, might a more experienced keeper have prevented some of those wides?There is an equation to be balanced between the number of runs saved by fielding the best keeper (Jones) against the number of runs gained by playing the more consistent batter (Capsey) – and it is the head coach, Charlotte Edwards, who will be required to do the maths.Explore more on these topicsWomen's cricketEngland women's cricket teamIreland women's cricket teamCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Colin Kaepernick knelt 10 years ago. America responded with a clear warning to Black people | Colin Kaepernick | The Guardian
description: A decade after Kaepernick’s quiet protest shook the NFL, his exile looks less like an aberration than a blueprint for the culture war that followed
Author: Howard Bryant
Headline: A decade after Kaepernick’s quiet protest shook the NFL, his exile looks less like an aberration than a blueprint for the culture war that followed
Content: Colin Kaepernick’s protest dominated off field discussion for much of the 2016 NFL season.Composite: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenColin Kaepernick’s protest dominated off field discussion for much of the 2016 NFL season.Composite: Guardian DesignColin KaepernickColin Kaepernick knelt 10 years ago. America responded with a clear warning to Black peopleHoward BryantA decade after Kaepernick’s quiet protest shook the NFL, his exile looks less like an aberration than a blueprint for the culture war that followedTue 1 Sep 2026 03.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 13.50 EDTShareAmerica likes nice round numbers, perfect for anniversaries and reflections, and it has, suddenly, been 10 years sinceColin Kaepernickfirst protested police killings – more accurately, police killings of Black people that went unpunished either internally or by the courts – by taking a knee during the national anthem for the entirety of the 2016 NFL regular season. He never played in the league again.Ten years covers a lot of ground, especially in these years of American darkness, and many of the important details surrounding Kaepernick, his banishment and significance have disappeared, time replaced by more time and more darkness – time moving faster than ever, at internet speed, where nothing matters, where nothing sticks. We consume by clip, by click, by meme, and knowledge by meme is not knowledge at all.Much of the Kaepernick story was reduced to his personal banishment, but second to Barack Obama, Kaepernick is the face that propelled white anger into a “culture war” that continues earnestly into its second decade. It has traveled through the NFL, through Hollywood, the White House, and now iscorroding the WNBA. Obama’s ascent to the White House confirmed the unlikely prospect that a Black person could be elected president, ostensibly the ultimate symbol of American possibility. It was not a universal sentiment.Sophie Cunningham isn’t rejecting politics.
