She’s cashing in on themRead moreIn the annals of American protest, which has included suffragettes breaking windows, students blocking traffic,Black Panthers armed in public, economic boycotts and marches on Washington, Kaepernick was mild by comparison – he gave voice with 60 seconds of silence. “To me, this is bigger than football and it would be selfish on my part to look the other way,” heexplained on 26 August 2016after a preseason contest between his San Francisco 49ers and the Green Bay Packers (he sat on the bench during the anthem for that game, he would kneel for the first time the following week). “There are bodies in the street and people getting paid leave and getting away with murder.” Combined, however, Obama and Kaepernick represented the realization of the deepest of white fears, the assumptions and expectations of Black equality that has consumed a segment of the collective white American psyche since emancipation.Ten years later, one view of the Kaepernick legacy can be seen through a harsh, retrofitted lens: sports leagues would largely purge the troublemakers and co-opt the protests, reducing them into useless, corporate-friendly gestures; an American electorate that voted Donald Trump into power twice, as his unapologetic, unambiguous racism reflected theirs; media outlets responding in agreement, coalescing around Trump’s whiteness, appeasing their rightsholders, readers and viewers by making the conscious choice – a clear and egregious dereliction of journalistic duty – to silence the voices within who make them uncomfortable; a player class that was never nearly as bold as its greatest legends well aware of Kaepernick’s fate, unwilling to repeat it, and operating as puppets.They didn’t have far to go. While Trump called NFL players “sons of bitches” in his first term and demanded Kaepernick be banned from the league, NFL players undermined him. Dallas Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescottassured his bossesin 2018 that he was no radical, not merely by playing football but demeaning Kaepernick’s protest. “For me, I believe in doing something, action. It’s not about taking a knee,” Prescott said, undermining centuries of evidence to the contrary about the efficacy of physical protest. Even the most devout Cowboys fan could probably not name a single example where Prescott took action. He simply didn’t want to get involved.Michael Vick, ex-convict,killer of dogs, but redeemed by the NFL following his prison sentence, told Kaepernick to “cut his hair” if he sought a pathway to forgiveness. Hall of Famer Ray Lewis told Kaepernick to “keep his mouth shut”. It should be noted that Kaepernick was exiled from the NFL for kneeling –kneeling –while Lewis, connectable to an incident that resulted in two killings as an active player, was fined$250,000 by the NFLfor pleading guilty to obstruction of justice andnever missed a game.View image in fullscreenColin Kaepernick kneels in protest during the national anthem before the San Francisco 49ers’ game against the Los Angeles Rams at Levi’s Stadium in September 2016.Photograph: Robert Reiners/Getty ImagesWhether hostile or oblivious, white Americans have treated this nation as a personal possession they choose to share with others, quite different from a nation that belongs to all that must be shared collectively. This country, Black people know and are harshly reminded by their white countrymen whenever they have the temerity to forget, istheirs,and that proprietorship is codified by the everyday speech of white Americans – Weletyou attendourschools, live inourneighborhoods, be part ofourcommunities, play inourprofessional sports – and is mirrored by Black speech alike. It is the fatal language of integration.Such assumed proprietorship demands white people receive deference for their benevolence, explains their rage when they don’t get it. It also means they believe they can revoke the privilege of being American whenever that proprietorship is challenged, as Kaepernick discovered 10 years ago. The result was a continuum. Kaepernick losing his job has now become a political philosophy at the highest levels of government: Black people have not earned their positions through the grind of hard work, but from diversity initiatives.Only in witnessing the slow-motion murder of George Floyd in 2020 during a global pandemic and the White House overreacting by rolling tanks through town and shooting at white people on the steps of their own houses did the country have a collective moment that it had all gone too far, that Kaepernick had been right all along. Even NFL commissioner Roger Goodell admitted, by pressure not conscience,that the league was wrongin its crackdown on player protest – but only briefly. The simmering hostility, never quieted, has increased anew.The January 6 riotsended the periodknown as athlete activism, and in the wider sense, the Kaepernick era. They also ended whatever shreds of credibility remained from this nation of laws, and exposed the players as having surrendered. Wired to accept challenges and refuse defeat, the players were finally vindicated as hordes of white, real Americans, the ones who told them therewere other ways to protest, wore T-shirts tostand for the flag and kneel for the cross,countered the Black Lives Matter protest without cleverness or style withBlue Lives Matter,and–at the order of the President of the United States – stormed the most symbolically important legislative building in the world. The players – perhaps mollified by Goodell’s apology, or Obama’s advice to NBA players to stop their protests after a weekend work stoppage following Jacob Blake’s shooting in Kenosha, general fatigue or knowing they were overmatched – didn’t say a thing. A cop – a member of that sacred occupation for which they ostensibly held so much respect –died in the aftermathof the January 6 riot. The mob ransacked the Capitol, and the American media tripped over itself debating whether to even call it a riot. It made sense. This istheirs, and you cannot trespass or riot on your own property.There is the lesson of Kaepernick and there is his legacy. They are not the same. The lesson was largely directed toward other players. It was a threat. Kaepernick was the NFL’s Metacomet at Plymouth, head on a stake for the world to see, a warning for the rest to stay in line – and they have. What passes for protest today is a player writing something mildly profound on their cleats, but only on the designated game days when theNFLallows it.The devastating rest is the legacy, far darker and yet in its own sense inspiring. The inspiration lies in the freedom of acknowledgment. There is no reason to continue the naive exercise of negotiation, of waiting for permission, of believing the moral arc of the universe bends toward justice, of believing equality is a shared American goal. It is not. What the country has become in these 10 years,with its 1,500 pardons, the proud anti-Blackness from this White House, the malleable ethics of a cowering corporate media that has largely stamped out the voices it once embraced as a “racial reckoning” – has proven it. Look at the wreckage.Howard Bryant is the author of 11 books, including The Heritage: Black Athletes, A Divided America, and the Politics of Patriotism and Kings and Pawns: Jackie Robinson and Paul Robeson in America.Explore more on these topicsColin KaepernickNFLUS sportsGeorge FloydRoger GoodellBarack ObamaJacob BlakecommentShareReuse this content

title: Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 12: Manchester United | Manchester United Women | The Guardian
description: The departure of Marc Skinner and several senior squad members leaves new manager Eva Olid to guide United into their new era
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: The departure of Marc Skinner and several senior squad members leaves new manager Eva Olid to guide United into their new era
Content: Julia Zigiotti Olme of Manchester United Women during a training session at La Manga Club in Spain. Photograph: Poppy Townson/MUFC/Manchester United/Getty ImagesThe departure of Marc Skinner and senior squad members leaves new manager Eva Olid to guide United into new eraByTom GarryTue 1 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 19.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:7th (NB: this is not necessarily Tom Garry’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:4thProspectsIt was all-change at Manchester United during pre-season, with thedeparture of their head coach Marc Skinnerafter five years followed swiftly by theappointment of Eva Olidas a new era begins. There have been significant outgoings from the playing group, including the senior squad membersMelvine Malard, Gabby George, Millie Turner and Lisa Naalsund, as well as the end-of-contracts exits of Leah Galton and Hannah Blundell, but the signings of the Spain youth international defender Andrea Medina, the former Germany youth international goalkeeper Janina Leitzig and the Sweden forward Monica Jusu Bah will give the squad a fresh feel.Missing out on the Women’s Champions League places by nine points last season was disappointing and after a summer in which other clubs have spent big, it feels more likely United will be looking over their shoulder at challengers coming up from fifth and sixth than mounting a title challenge.Tottenham’s and London City’s ambitious recruitment mean they could threaten United’s position but United have not turned into a bad team overnight. European quarter-finalists last season, their squad retains a strong level of quality international players, despite the sale of Malard to Chelsea in particular. The England internationals Maya Le Tissier and Ella Toone are the senior leaders in a squad that also retains a world-class goalkeeper in Phallon Tullis-Joyce, the dynamic England midfielder Jess Park and the talented Sweden wing-back Anna Sandberg. A top-half finish feels realistic and the club will hope for strong runs in the domestic cups. There is also understood to be a desire at the club to make the playing style more entertaining for supporters.Graphic showing how London City finished in the past five seasonsOff-field pictureAs with the men’s club, the Glazer family own a majority stake and Ineos – led by Sir Jim Ratcliffe – has a minority stake but has control of football operations. The women’s team’s financial history divides opinion in the sport; some argue United are an example of how to run a professional women’s team sustainably, having recorded a profit of £397,000 in their most recent accounts and a profit of £1.34m since reforming their senior women’s team in 2018, while others lament a lack of investment from the ownership compared with the budgets of their rivals such as Arsenal, Chelsea and Manchester City.The managerOlid was appointed on 5 August on a two-year deal with the option of a further year. The Spanish coach, who turned 41 in late August, arrives after an impressive spell at Hearts, where she led the club to their first Scottish Women’s Premier League title in May. That made her the SWPL’s manager of the season. It is understood she was chosen by United’s hierarchy because they feel her CV demonstrates a strong track record of developing and improving young players.Star signingBah, who has 11 caps, looks to be an important signing for United from BK Häcken for a fee reportedly of about £400,000. The 23-year-old helped the Swedish club win last term’s inaugural Women’s Europa Cup – European club-level women’s football’s second competition – and she said the opportunity to work with Olid was “perfect” because she wants to improve. She provided seven assists and scored 16 goals for her club last season and United will hope she can settle into the WSL quickly.View image in fullscreenMonica Jusu Bah arrives in Manchester from Swedish club BK Häcken.Photograph: Poppy Townson/Manchester United/Getty ImagesStat attackUnited made a mockery of underlying data last season. Only Arsenal overachieved against their attacking expected goals by more and only City conceded fewer compared with their xG at the back. They were ranked fourth for expected goal metrics at both ends but the combined variance of +9.86 against those numbers makes them hard to predict this season.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGraphic showing Manchester United were second to the champions for exceeding expected goals in 2025‑26Set for a breakthroughLayla Drury, an academy graduate, became United’s youngest player and goalscorer when given her debut in the Women’s FA Cup in January at 16, and this summer the 17-year-old became the youngest player to sign a professional contract with the club. She has been added to England’s Under-20 squad for September’s World Cup in Poland and last Saturday scored for the Young Lionesses in their 11-0 warm-up victory against New Caledonia. The forward had previously played for Wales’ youth teams.What they say“I always say: ‘My life is football.’ I don’t have other things. I spend probably 24 hours every day on football. It’s my life, my lifestyle and I give everything for the team and for the players. They always have me. Doubts, questions, [it] doesn’t matter the time of the day, I’m going to be there for them. I want to make them better, and that is how I’m going to feel good as a coach, seeing the improvement, seeing that they are better, and of course, winning matches” – Olid to MUTV.Where are they playing their home games?United play at Leigh Sports Village, a 12,000-capacity venue which is also the home of the rugby league club Leigh Leopards and United’s men’s Under-21s. It has been their home ground since 2018. The stadium hosted a quarter-final at 2022’s Euros. United’s final home WSL fixture, against Arsenal in May, has been scheduled for Old Trafford, although that match may have to be rearranged if Arsenal reach the semi-finals of the Women’s Champions League because the second legs are that weekend.On Friday 4 September at 1pm Suzanne Wrack will be answering readers’ questions about the new WSL season for GuardianConversationsExplore more on these topicsManchester United WomenWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Fin Tarling’s death casts shadow over Tour of Britain as safety fears loom large | Tour of Britain | The Guardian
description: A minute’s applause for Tarling will take place in Lincoln on Wednesday following a spate of serious recent crashes which have put safety on the agenda
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: A minute’s applause for Tarling will take place in Lincoln on Wednesday following a spate of serious recent crashes which have put safety on the agenda
Content: The peloton at the Volta a Portugal paid tribute to Fin Tarling, who died when his cycle collided with a non-race vehicle last month.Photograph: Nuno Veiga/EPAView image in fullscreenThe peloton at the Volta a Portugal paid tribute to Fin Tarling, who died when his cycle collided with a non-race vehicle last month.Photograph: Nuno Veiga/EPATour of BritainFin Tarling’s death casts shadow over Tour of Britain as safety fears loom largeMinute’s applause to take place in Lincoln on WednesdaySpate of serious recent crashes have put safety on agendaJeremy WhittleTue 1 Sep 2026 12.40 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 16.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThedeath of the Welshman Fin Tarlingcontinues to cast a long shadow over professional cycling and nowhere will that absence be felt more deeply than at the men’s Tour of Britain which begins on Wednesday.Tarling’s former team NSNCycling, which includes the Olympic medallist Ethan Vernon, also one of his closest friends, will be brought to the start line in Lincoln for the opening 187km stage, for what is expected to be a minute’s applause.Tadej Pogacar shares picture from hospital after Vuelta-ending crashRead moreTarling was killed while racing in the Volta a Portugal last month when he collided with a non‑race vehicle driving towards him. The race operates a rolling road closure, the same security strategy employed by theTour of Britain. The police investigation into Tarling’s death is ongoing.A spate of serious recent crashes, including the high-speed fall endured by theTour de France champion Tadej Pogacar, which forced him to abandon the Vuelta a España this year while leading the race, have yet again put safety at the top of the agenda.Tom Pidcock’s tearful tribute to the Tarling family, when winning the World Mountain Bike title in Italy last weekend, revealed the depth of feeling over the teenager’s death.The double Olympic gold medallist Pidcock, initially expected to start the British race, has opted to focus on preparing for the world championships in Canada by riding warm-up races in Montreal and Quebec.Tarling’s collision in a race operating under a rolling road closure has been thesubject of much scrutinyin the aftermath of his accident and the flaws of that system were highlighted just days later, in the women’s Tour of Britain, when the Australian rider Maeve Plouffe had her own near-miss.“While the race convoy was still in sight, and I was less than two minutes down [behind], there were cars from the general public coming at me from all directions, including one that nearly hit me on a roundabout,” the 27-year-old said.Jonathan Day, director of the race organisers, said: “Rider safety is paramount and will always be treated as a priority in our planning and how we operate any race.”The race organisers maintain that the Tour of Britain is delivered in accordance with the UCI’s road racing regulations, described as the safety and operational standards that govern international and UK-based road racing.Local authorities, emergency services, commissaires, police and event partners are all part of the race planning process. But the efficiency of rolling road closures has also been questioned by Adam Hansen, president of the CPA professional rider association, who said: “There is a hole in rolling road closures and we have to fix this.”After an opening stage based on Lincoln, the convoy will travel through Yorkshire and on to the Scottish Borders. The second day’s racing takes the peloton from Boston to Skegness while stage three, through East Yorkshire, starts in Hull and ends in Beverley.Over the weekend the convoy crosses the Yorkshire moors and dales, before the final stage on Sunday, which starts south of Edinburgh – site of the Grand Départ for the Tour de France next year – and finishes in Earlston.Alongside Vernon, there is a raft of British talent lining up for the five‑day race including Ben Wiggins, son of Sir Bradley. National time trial champion in the under-23 category, the 21-year-old is now on the radar of several leading World Tour teams.The Tour de France stage winners Olav Kooij, Filippo Ganna and Tim Merlier are among the leading World Tour names, while Pogacar’s UAE Emirates XRG team will be led by the Giro d’Italia stage winner Jhonatan Narváez.The move from four days of racing last year to five days in 2026, giving it parity with the women’s Tour of Britain, is hoped to further boost interest as the buildup to the UK-based Grand Départ begins next year.Explore more on these topicsTour of BritainCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘In my heart until I die’: Argentina says a tearful thank you to Lionel Messi | Lionel Messi | The Guardian
description: The Argentinian’s decision to quit international football was met by an outpouring of affection from the country he led to World Cup glory in 2022
Author: Marcela Mora y Araujo
Headline: The Argentinian’s decision to quit international football was met by an outpouring of affection from the country he led to World Cup glory in 2022
Content: Lionel Messi looks overwhelmed after an enthralling 3-2 victory against Egypt in the 2026 World Cup.Photograph: Patrick Smith/Fifa/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLionel Messi looks overwhelmed after an enthralling 3-2 victory against Egypt in the 2026 World Cup.Photograph: Patrick Smith/Fifa/Getty ImagesLionel Messi‘In my heart until I die’: Argentina says a tearful thank you to Lionel MessiThe Argentinian’s decision to quit international football was met by an outpouring of affection from the country he led to World Cup glory in 2022Marcela Mora y AraujoTue 1 Sep 2026 11.05 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnyone who was present at Lionel Scaloni’s press conference immediately after theWorld Cup final between Spain and Argentinain New Jersey on 19 July and saw his tears, the sobs which prevented him from speaking while he got up and walked out, could tell this was a man weeping not because of defeat in a single match but because he was fully aware that what that particular group of men had been through for the past eight years had come to an end.Messi’s announcement that he isretiring from international football, posted on Instagram on Monday complete with photos of three handwritten sheets of some anonymous yet corporate-looking headed paper and a Harry Potter Time Turner pen, to the soundtrack ofBrindis sung by Soledad Pastorutti, instantly dominated the news and unleashed a barrage of homages, gratitude and joy from all corners. But it’s not exactly a surprise.Lionel Messi’s international retirement serves as a reminder: watch him while you still canRead more“How crazy that the day has come, dear Leo,” Cristian Romero posted, making it clear that this was expected in spite of the unexpectedness. “The day no one wanted to arrive has arrived,” echoed Giovani Lo Celso, who said he had “nine years listening to you, admiring you and learning by your side”. His international teammates highlight how in their childhood they dreamed of meeting him one day, let alone actually playing with him. Nico Paz says since he was four years old he “used to watch you play with my dad and we would calculate together whether I would be in time to play with you”.It’s not just his teammates who are expressing gratitude and nostalgia. On a Buenos Aires street corner someone put a red telephone on a table with a sign saying: “What would you say to Messi?” Passersby picked up the receiver and talked into it: “I’m 86 years old and you have given me the greatest joys in my life. You will be in my heart until the day I die,” one gentleman said. A young boy saw the news and “burst into tears even though I was at school”. A well-spoken woman said “we will miss you because you are an extraordinary being”, a little girl added “you’re the best and the greatest”. An old man signed off “bye, son”.Influencers, journalists, artists, cultural commentators and psychologists all expressed their gratefulness for Messi being a great human being. “Messi led by example,” the veteran sportswriter Matías Martin wrote, while the coach and motivational speaker Matias “Coco” Gallo Bevegni posted that theWorld Cupwinner “taught me more in defeat than in victory”.View image in fullscreenA message written by Lionel Messi and posted to Instagram explaining his retirement from the Argentina team.Photograph: Lionel Messi/Instagram/ReutersThe football pundit Morena Beltrán could not hold back the tears as she explained to her older colleagues that for her generation there is a sense of mourning and emptiness which can only be filled by gratitude, which maybe they have already experienced, because they have seen another God. The psychoanalyst Milagros Filgueras praised the decision to hand-write the note, saying some goodbyes need the body involved. The journalist Pablo Perantuono devoted his column to the “epistolary genre”, noting that a handwritten letter in this day and age is almost a countercultural act of originality.The writer Andrés Burgo highlighted that in 10 of the past 12 World Cups, either Maradona or Messi played, so this truly marks the “end of an era in which grandparents, parents, sons and daughters and grandchildren enjoyed an incredible privilege during almost 45 years. The heir will arrive – we hope – but right now is a time of orphanage. And gratitude.”View image in fullscreenArgentina fans wearing T-shirts depicting Lionel Messi and Diego Maradona.Photograph: Amanda Perobelli/ReutersMessi revealed that this letter was actually written two days after the final, a cathartic diary-like release, but that on Monday, after“[what happened with] my dad”he was more convinced than ever. The note said: “It’s a decision that hurt and continues to hurt,” but that he understands this is the moment. The poet Valeria Correa Fiz pointed out that he originally wrote “I think”, crossed it out and replaced it with “I understand”. Messi swore he always gave his all, not only these past few years when “everything was won” (he never says “I won”; it’s always “we” or “it” was won) but he has nothing left to give. He’s emptied.The 39-year-old, however, scored four goals for Inter Miami at the weekend and continues his career at club level, where he clearly still has much to give. He is not retiring from playing football, the thing he loves most. He is retiring fromArgentina.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenMessi shows off the World Cup trophy after winning the 2022 final against France.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianWith two international dates coming up and no rival agreed, no doubt the clarification that there will be no Messi in the squad will impact on the potential fixtures. And not unlike the time when he quit Argentina before, in 2016, the country’s football is in a bit of turmoil.The context and climate include scandals surrounding the Argentinian Football Association, the pressure by some lobbies to privatise football clubs, which are non-profit organisations, and the international furore caused by several incidents during the World Cup which have landed Argentina with some hefty fines, sanctions and suspensions.The heaviness of the Argentina flag which for so many years visibly weighed him down, turned idyllic when it became the cloak of victory, mattered very much to his father, Jorge. Messi said he wanted to win another World Cup for him. Perhaps his death has somehow freed him from that aspect of his Argentinianness.View image in fullscreenSupporters in Sydney, Australia, watch Messi on giant TV screens after Spain defeated Argentina in the 2026 World Cup final.Photograph: David Gray/AFP/Getty ImagesAnd just like last time, the spontaneous visceral response from the Argentinian people is acceptance and relish at the good times lived. That inexplicable sense of pride that comes from being from the same soil as someone who is very good at something and whose magic is still untarnished by the sordid final match against Spain, or any of the criticisms directed at the squad and fans throughout the tournament. If anything, his final tears in front of the stands, like Scaloni’s tears at the press conference, are mirrored in a nation moved profoundly by the generations we have just lived through, perhaps not realising we were living through them.The huge volume of emotive, sentimental outpouring is rather lovely, and amid it all an enduring image of three little boys walking down a Buenos Aires street with No 10 Messi shirts on their backs signals the way forward, towards a future unknown.Explore more on these topicsLionel MessiArgentinaWorld Cup 2022World Cup 2026World CupfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: BBC axes ‘iconic’ Ski Sunday winter sports show after nearly 50 years on TV | Skiing | The Guardian
description: The BBC blamed changing viewing habits and financial concerns after dropping Ski Sunday, amid scrutiny over its approach to sports rights
Author: Tony Paley
Headline: The BBC blamed changing viewing habits and financial concerns after dropping Ski Sunday, amid scrutiny over its approach to sports rights
Content: Ski Sunday helped to make Franz Klammer a household name in the UK.Photograph: Tony Duffy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSki Sunday helped to make Franz Klammer a household name in the UK.Photograph: Tony Duffy/Getty ImagesSkiingBBC axes ‘iconic’ Ski Sunday winter sports show after nearly 50 years on TVCorporation cites audience shifts and financial concernsBroadcaster under fire over approach to sports rightsTony PaleyTue 1 Sep 2026 11.24 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA staple of Sunday afternoon TV for almost 50 years, withan instantly recognisable theme tune, is being axed amid complaints that the BBC’s sports coverage continues to go downhill.TheBBChead of sport, Alex Kay-Jelski, has been under fire of late and will certainly not have endeared himself to some of the licence-paying public who have enjoyed the coverage of winter sports on one of Britain’s longest-running sports shows with the news on Tuesday that Ski Sunday is being dropped.The top 40 theme tunes in sportRead moreThe unruffable David Vine was the first presenter of the weekly show that created household names in the UK out of alpine skiers such as Franz Klammer, Konrad Bartelski and Michela Figini – while there will be no more mentions of glamorous Val-d’Isère and Val Gardena to help brighten the mood under leaden skies on a Sunday winter teatime.Ski Sunday became equally famous for its theme tune, a rousing violin-led arrangement called Pop Looks Bach, which was composed by Sam Fonteyn and wasoften towards the top of pollsand lists of signature TV sports melodies. It was recorded for the Boosey & Hawkes Music Library in 1970.“If music is licensed from a music library, you never know when it might appear,”recalled the composer’s son, Nicholas, when the programme was rebooted in 2008 but with the popular theme retained. “So he’d often be sitting there watching and suddenly say, ‘That’s mine!’ He was always delighted when it was on TV and watched avidly, even when it was on that Barbara Woodhouse programme [1980’s Training Dogs the Woodhouse Way, for which he also wrote the theme].”“Since its debut in 1978, Ski Sunday has become an iconic part of the winter sports calendar, bringing the excitement, drama and beauty of the action on the snow to audiences across the UK. Changing audience behaviours and the tough financial decisions needed to meet savings requirements mean BBC Sport must continually review how it delivers value for licence-fee payers and serves audiences across all platforms. This decision forms part of that process,” was the explanation given in a BBC press release.View image in fullscreenDavid Vine during his days presenting Ski Sunday for the BBC.Photograph: PAThe corporation’s critics will be quick to condemn the move by Kay-Jelski who shocked many earlier this year by arguing that the BBC does not need live rights to a sport to be relevant.Speaking at the Financial Times business of football conference, the director of sport said: “My challenge to us at the BBC all the time is let’s just make sure we are in the conversation of the things that matter. For example, we have audio rights to Formula One but not video rights. But we still have reporting and live pages and digital video that draw in millions and millions and millions of people. You can still be relevant, you can still matter if you don’t show the sport.”Kay-Jelski has been criticised recently for his decision not to have his expert panel leave their Salford base for New York until the semi-finals of the World Cup and for scrapping Saturday lunchtime preview programme Football Focus. Last month there were media reports ofunrest among the Match of the Day production teamon the eve of the Premier League season.In recent years, Ski Sunday had become a magazine-style programme with a wider winter sports remit. Its final presenters were Ed Leigh and British former downhill racer Chemmy Alcott.Explore more on these topicsSkiingBBCnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mark Carney tells US to ‘start being serious’ amid escalating trade war | US news | The Guardian
description: Canadian PM is set to retaliate against tariffs levied by Donald Trump and criticized US officials over insults
Author: Victoria Bekiempis
Headline: Canadian PM is set to retaliate against tariffs levied by Donald Trump and criticized US officials over insults
Content: Donald Trump speaks alongside a map showing Lake Ontario labeled as Lake America in the Oval Office.Photograph: Jim Watson/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump speaks alongside a map showing Lake Ontario labeled as Lake America in the Oval Office.Photograph: Jim Watson/AFP/Getty ImagesUS newsMark Carney tells US to ‘start being serious’ amid escalating trade warCanadian PM is set to retaliate against tariffs levied by Donald Trump and criticized US officials over insultsUS politics live – latest updatesVictoria Bekiempisand Guardian staffTue 1 Sep 2026 11.48 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 11.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMark Carney has rebuked Donald Trump’s administration and urged officials in Washington to “start being serious” amid escalating trade tensions between the US and Canada.Days beforeCanadais due to retaliate against Trump’s sweeping tariffs with its own duties on US goods, the Canadian prime minister criticized US officials for insulting his country. “It is beneath their office,” he said.“When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions” about trade, Carney said.Trump signed an executive order last week directing the US federal government torename Lake Ontario as Lake America– a move that has been rejected by Canadians.The US president’s most senior trade negotiator has meanwhile downplayed the potentially disastrous effects of a US trade war with Canada, declaring the spat to be “more their emergency than ours”.The US trade representative, Jamieson Greer, argued that Canada was more vulnerable after the breakdown in talks set the stage for sweeping tariffs between the two neighbors,tellingPolitico: “There are no negotiations happening on trade right now.”The comment comes just more than a week after US-Canada trade talks imploded. The USlevied50% tariffs on $20bn in Canadian goods.Trump suggests he is reviewing US support for UK over Falkland IslandsRead moreCanada, the US’ssecond-largest trading partner, announced it would impose retaliatory tariffs on $20bn of American goods starting on 8 September. Now, US residents are poised to feel extreme pressure from Trump’s tariffs and Canada’s retaliatory measures, including on day-to-day items.Greer appeared to blame the escalating trade war on Canadian officials, telling Politico: “It’s not clear Canada wants a deal.“If Canada believes that prohibiting and banning American goods and services is appropriate, then obviously that’s something that the United States should consider as well.”‘If it’s made in the US, I don’t buy it’: Canadians on boycotting Trump’s AmericaRead moreUnacceptable asks from Canada included lighter taxes on heavy-duty trucks, according to Greer, who said such requests torpedoed the trade talks.Canadian officials, on the other hand, attributed the collapsed negotiations to a White House disagreement over who was directing trade talks. Mark Carney, the country’s prime minister,also saidthat American negotiators saw the French language in Canada as an “irritant”, but added: “In Quebec, these are rights.”Trump, for his part, has argued in recent weeks that Canada “wants the benefits” of being a US state, without being one – a preoccupation of the US president – as he lashed out at the country’s leaders. “They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of tariffs,” claimed Trump. “No more!!!”Greer suggested that negotiations broke down after a misunderstanding around what was, and wasn’t, on the table. “Was that political? I don’t know,” he told Politico. “Was it economic? … I’m not sure how much economic sense it makes because the choice is not between the current tariffs and … you know, duty-free trade. Like, that is that. Those weren’t the options.”Explore more on these topicsUS newsUS politicsCanadaTrump tariffsUS economyDonald TrumpEconomicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Norway’s new king swears oath of allegiance with daughter at his side | Norway | The Guardian
description: Haakon VIII promises to uphold 1814 constitution but his queen misses ceremony because of post-surgery ‘complications’
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Haakon VIII promises to uphold 1814 constitution but his queen misses ceremony because of post-surgery ‘complications’
Content: King Haakon VIII makes his way to the Norwegian parliament where he gave a oath before cabinet ministers and MPs on Tuesday.Photograph: Amanda Pedersen Giske/ReutersView image in fullscreenKing Haakon VIII makes his way to the Norwegian parliament where he gave a oath before cabinet ministers and MPs on Tuesday.Photograph: Amanda Pedersen Giske/ReutersNorwayNorway’s new king swears oath of allegiance with daughter at his sideHaakon VIII promises to uphold 1814 constitution but his queen misses ceremony because of post-surgery ‘complications’Jon HenleyEurope correspondentTue 1 Sep 2026 10.40 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKing Haakon VIII swore an oath of allegiance before Norway’s parliament on Tuesday in the first major stage in the passing of the crown since the death of his father after 35 years on the throne.Wearing a ceremonial uniform, Haakon, who became king when Harald V died on Friday, promised to uphold Norway’s 1814 constitution with his 22-year-old daughter, Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, by his side.“I promise and swear that I will govern the kingdom of Norway in accordance with its constitution and laws, so help me God, the almighty and omniscient,” the 53-year-old king pledged to cabinet ministers and MPs in the main chamber of the 169-seat parliament.View image in fullscreenKing Haakon at Tuesday’s swearing of the oath ceremony with his daughter, Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra. Norway does not have a formal coronation.Photograph: Per Ole Hagen/Getty ImagesHaakon’s wife, Mette-Marit, 53, was unable to attend the 17-minute ceremony because of complications after a lung transplant in June. Her doctors said such complications were not uncommon.Are ​Holm, a pulmonologist at Oslo university hospital, said the queen had had “complications on some occasions with the operation, including today. As a ​result, she must be put under observation ​throughout the day today.”Harald, whose funeral will be held in Oslo on 9 September, with heads of state from around the world invited to attend, was widely appreciated in Norway for his warmth, unassuming lifestyle and dedication to preserving national unity.Tens ⁠of thousands of Norwegians have flocked to the royal palace to lay flowers, drawings, candles and flags.View image in fullscreenPeople line up on Tuesday to pay their respects to the late King Harald V, whose casket lies in state at the Royal Palace Chapel in Oslo.Photograph: Odd Andersen/AFP/Getty ImagesA poll for the public broadcaster NRK found the monarchy’s popularity had risen over the past few months. The first survey since Harald’s death at the age of 89 found that about 72% of Norwegians supported the monarchy, compared with 54% in May. In February, while the royal family was mired in a succession of scandals, support for the institution fell to 60%.View image in fullscreenQueen Mette-Marit.Photograph: Ho/Newspix InternationalMette-Marit has faced strong criticism for her association withJeffrey Epstein, while her son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, is appealing against a four-year sentence for two rape convictions.Responding to Haakon’s oath, Masud Gharahkhani, the parliament’s president, who arrived in Norway as a child refugee from Iran, said Harald had personified “the values that underpin our liberal democracy”, including compassion.There will be no formal coronation of the new king and queen because Norway abolished the ceremony more than a century ago but Haakon may, like his father and grandfather, choose to have his accession consecrated at Trondheim’s Nidaros Cathedral.Harald, who will be buried in the royal mausoleum at the Akershus Fortress in Oslo, died while being treated in hospital for haemolytic anaemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of red blood cells.Explore more on these topicsNorwayEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Gaps in NHS end-of-life care ‘denying ill children chance to die at home’ | NHS | The Guardian
description: Campaigners say some care boards in England flouting their legal duty, resulting in ‘cruel’ postcode lottery
Author: Denis Campbell
Headline: Campaigners say some care boards in England flouting their legal duty, resulting in ‘cruel’ postcode lottery
Content: Sarah Buchan Cooke needed support from Great Ormond Street children’s hospital and hospice Haven House during her son Dylan’s final days.Photograph: HandoutView image in fullscreenSarah Buchan Cooke needed support from Great Ormond Street children’s hospital and hospice Haven House during her son Dylan’s final days.Photograph: HandoutNHSGaps in NHS end-of-life care ‘denying ill children chance to die at home’Campaigners say some care boards in England flouting their legal duty, resulting in ‘cruel’ postcode lotteryDenis CampbellHealth policy editorTue 1 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 15.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSeriously ill children are being denied the chance to die at home because the NHS in many parts ofEnglandis flouting its legal duty to provide the care needed to make that happen, critics say.The widespread failure to provide at-home end-of-life care is forcing children who want to die at home to instead do so in hospital. Campaigners have described it as “cruel”.The postcode lottery in palliative care means some of the almost 89,000 under-19s in England who have a life-limiting condition may not get their wish to die at home. Medical advances mean theirnumbers have almost trebledsince 2003-04, and the complexities of their illnesses have increased. About 1,600 die each year.Nick Carroll, the chief executive of the charity Together for Short Lives, said: “It is shocking that children with serious illnesses are waiting to leave hospital because the health and care system is not taking responsibility for their community care. To deny families the chance to spend precious moments together at home before their child dies is simply cruel.”He accused theNHSof neglect for not ensuring that all children who want to can die at home with specialist teams including doctors, nurses and therapists on hand during their final days. “Families have every right to be upset as they continue to be overlooked,” Carroll said.The NHS’s 42 integrated care boards (ICBs) are legally obliged under theHealthand Care Act 2022 to ensure such care is provided around the clock at home when a child is dying. But 15 (36%) of them do not commission such services, freedom of information requests by Together for Short Lives show.Only 13 (31%) were able to show they were doing so. Ten (24%) were providing some but not all of the care they should, and three (7%) said they were still organising such care.The lack of provision means very sick children are ending up having to seek help at A&E or be admitted to hospital, some of whom then die there rather than at home.Carroll said: “Our research shows that many families, simply because they live in a certain area, may be denied the chance to have their child die in the safety and comfort of their own home because ministers and the NHS have failed to put the right care in place. That should shame us all.”View image in fullscreenNick Carroll, chief executive of the charity Together for Short Lives.Photograph: HandoutHe blamed the situation on ICBs’ precarious finances and on their “widespread assumption that palliative care is primarily for older adults, despite thousands of children across England living with life-shortening and life-threatening conditions”.He said while an early draft of the government’s forthcoming “modern service framework” for palliative care specifically mentioned babies, children and young people, that reference was not included in the most recent version.Sarah Buchan Cooke said it made a huge difference to the whole family when her son Dylan was able to die at home in January 2023, just before he turned four, after a long spell in hospital. He had Sandhoff disease, a rare neurodegenerative condition that left him needing 24/7 care.Great Ormond Street children’s hospital andHaven House, a children’s hospice, both in London, supported the family in Dylan’s final days.“At the end of his life it was a beautiful thing to have him at home. I can’t really imagine it any other way. I’m very aware of how fortunate we were,” Buchan Cooke said.“It breaks my heart to think of other families in our situation not being able to have that same level of care and support. You’re the one who knows your child best. That ability to choose [between home and hospital] means everything.”In March, Rachel de Souza, the children’s commissioner for England, highlighted that some children, including with life-limiting illnesses, werespending months and sometimes years in hospitalbecause of a lack of “safe or appropriate” alternatives elsewhere.Delays in arranging packages of care, a shortage of children’s social care placements and housing issues were “leaving children and their families in impossible situations”, de Souza said. Such children are disproportionately from poor backgrounds or ethnic minorities, data shows.The NHS Alliance, which represents ICBs, did not respond directly to the findings. It agreed with the charity that access to end-of-life care for children should be universal but emphasised that commissioning such services could be “complex”.Ian Perrin, the alliance’s assistant director of integrated care, said: “Every child with a life-limiting condition, and every family supporting them, should be able to access high-quality, compassionate palliative and end-of-life care, regardless of where they live.“ICBs recognise the vital role that children’s hospices, community services, specialist teams and voluntary sector partners play in supporting children and their families. As the services are delivered through a range of organisations and arrangements vary across the country, this can make commissioning complex and difficult to compare consistently.“However, ICBs remain committed to working with families, providers, charities and national partners to reduce unwarranted variation, improve access to care and ensure more people can receive care closer to home.”Explore more on these topicsNHSHospicesHealthDeath and dyingChildrenEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Autistic boy who took replica knife to school has exclusion quashed by high court | Schools | The Guardian
description: Mother of 10-year-old says she hopes case will help others, as judge says exclusion should be ‘a tool of last resort’
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Mother of 10-year-old says she hopes case will help others, as judge says exclusion should be ‘a tool of last resort’
Content: The boy, who cannot be named, handed the replica knife to a friend to use against another child during an altercation in the playground.Photograph: AlexLinch/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenThe boy, who cannot be named, handed the replica knife to a friend to use against another child during an altercation in the playground.Photograph: AlexLinch/Getty Images/iStockphotoSchoolsAutistic boy who took replica knife to school has exclusion quashed by high courtBoy’s mother says she hopes case will help others, as judge says exclusion should be ‘a tool of last resort’Diane TaylorTue 1 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe mother of a 10-year-old autistic boy who had his permanent exclusion from a primary school quashed by the high court has said she hopes the ruling helps other children.The boy, who cannot be named, was permanently excluded from his primary school, part of the Lift academy chain, after coming to school in July 2025 with a replica butterfly knife, which he handed to a friend to use against another child during an altercation in the playground.The knife was described as having unsharpened blades and rounded ends, and when the child used it against the other child no significant injury was caused.The judge said there had been differences of opinion about whether the knife was made of metal or plastic and that it may have been closer to a “fidget toy” than an unsharpened or training version of a weapon.The school excluded the boy, first temporarily and then permanently, on the basis of the incident.In his judgment, the deputy high court judge Alan Bates identified a range of concerns with the way the school and the governors disciplinary panel had reached their decision, including whether the decision was proportional.He said that permanent exclusion should be “a tool of last resort” and that those considering whether to exclude a child should make a careful assessment of whether allowing the pupil to return to the school would seriously harm the welfare of the pupil or of others at the school.As a result of this case, the judge recommended theDepartment for Education(DfE) update its guidance about permanent exclusions from schools, saying it could “fairly” be said to be unclear or incomplete.According to DfE data, in the autumn term of the 2024-25 year there were 3,700 permanent exclusions from schools in England, 85% in secondary schools, 14% in primary schools and 1% in special schools. It is highly unusual for a school exclusion case of this kind to reach the high court.“I am so happy about this high court ruling,” the boy’s mother said. “I hope it will help the lives of many children and young people in other schools. Both my son and I were so upset about the school’s decision to permanently exclude him. We didn’t think things had been dealt with fairly. I just felt that they wanted to get rid of my son.“It was a long and complicated process to fight this and at one point I nearly gave up. But the situation was so upsetting and frustrating that I was determined to continue to challenge the exclusion.”A spokesperson for Lift schools said: “We respect the court’s judgment and are carefully considering its implications. We are reviewing the published detail and will be reflecting the findings in our own exclusion guidance, training and governance arrangements so that future decisions clearly evidence the factors considered and the reasoning behind them.”Angelo Monni of Duncan Lewis solicitors, representing the boy, said: “The decision provides important guidance for schools, academy trusts, governors, local authorities and families, and is likely to significantly influence how permanent exclusion decisions are approached in future. The judgment provides important guidance that will need to be followed by schools, and is a vindication for our client and his mother.”A DfE spokesperson said:“We will carefully consider the judgment and the judge’s observations. Permanent exclusion should only ever be a last resort, used to protect the education or welfare of the pupil or others in the school community. Headteachers must consider any contributing factors, including whether a pupil’s behaviour may stem from an unmet need or a special educational need or disability. We’ve recently updated our statutory exclusion guidance and will keep it under review, so schools, governing boards and independent review panels have the clarity they need.”Explore more on these topicsSchoolsDepartment for EducationAutismnewsShareReuse this content

title: High winds during El Niño could be deadly for England’s stressed trees, say experts | Trees and forests | The Guardian
description: Head of tree collections at Kew ‘very worried about this autumn’ as hot, dry summer has caused brittleness
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: Head of tree collections at Kew ‘very worried about this autumn’ as hot, dry summer has caused brittleness
Content: Parched grass in Slough, Berkshire. many trees are undergoing ‘early autumn’, losing their leaves early, to cope with the extreme heat.Photograph: Maureen McLean/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenParched grass in Slough, Berkshire. many trees are undergoing ‘early autumn’, losing their leaves early, to cope with the extreme heat.Photograph: Maureen McLean/ShutterstockTrees and forestsHigh winds during El Niño could be deadly for England’s stressed trees, say expertsHead of tree collections at Kew ‘very worried about this autumn’ as hot, dry summer has caused brittlenessPippa NeillEnvironment reporterTue 1 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 16.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHigh winds associated with El Niño could cause widespread mortality among tree species already weakened by a prolonged period of extreme heat and drought, experts have warned.This summer much of Europe has been scorched by a series of record-breaking climate crisis-inducedheatwaves. The impact is notable across much of England’s countryside, where oncegreen landhas turned brown, and many trees are undergoing“early autumn”– wilting and losing their leaves early – to cope with extreme heat.Kevin Martin, head of tree collections at Kew Gardens, said to cope with these extreme conditions, trees had not grown as they normally would, and had become less flexible and more brittle.“If we see the extreme winds that are predicted this year because of El Niño, we’re going to see potentially large impacts on trees,” he said.The UK’s Met Office has said the El Niño event developing over the Pacific Ocean is likely to be thestrongest for more than a century, with increased rainfall and storms forecast to hit the UK this autumn. El Niño is a natural phenomena that has been made worse by global heating.2:58Could ‘Godzilla’ El Niño bring the hottest year on record? – video explainerMartin said this extreme weather could lead to root death, where dry weather followed by heavy rain can undermine the structure of the soil.“We could then start to see some trees actually fail at the root plate. I’m really worried about this autumn,” he said.This year’s weather has been so extreme that Martin thinks some species could be lost completely from certain landscapes. “We may lose species like the silver birch, the common beech and oak from landscapes where we’re used to seeing them,” he said.While the impact is widespread, the heat is disproportionately affecting the oldest trees, with experts warning thatEngland’s ancient oaks are dyingin the hot and dry weather.Martin said that what made 2026 so unprecedented was thespring heatwave, when temperatures reached 35C, making it the hottest May ever recorded. “The whole growing season this year has been under stress, I don’t think we’ve ever experienced environmental impact like this before,” he said.Simon Richmond, a technical officer at the Arboricultural Association, said trees were extremely resilient organisms, able to adapt to one-off years of extreme weather. However, he said the “danger that we face now is the likelihood with climate change of this being a prolonged pattern of weather”.After the 2022 heatwave, Kew Gardens lost more than 400 trees due to heat and drought. Martin thinks the impact of the 2026 heatwave could be much worse.He predicts that at Kew and across the south-east, there will be a “significant amount of mortality”.“From what I can see from the landscape here at Kew, we’re going to see a lot more mortality than what we saw in 2022 because a lot of trees that just got through 2022 are not going to make it through this year.” However, he said the full impact of this year’s extreme weather would not be known for the next two to three years.Marcus Lindner, a principal scientist at the European Forest Institute, said that several years of extreme weather could push certain species over the edge, with almost all tree species at risk from the changing climate.“Species that are normally drought-tolerant are adapted to a certain level of drought stress, but if we have continuous and repeated drought these trees will at some point not be comfortable with that any more,” he said.Explore more on these topicsTrees and forestsEl Niño southern oscillationExtreme heatEnglandDroughtnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘They take the water, the springs dry up’: fear as Guatemalan goldmine plan is revived | Mining | The Guardian
description: After lying dormant for years, the Era Dorada project in Asunción Mita resumed this year and villagers say history is being repeated, despite promises of change
Author: Euan Wallace
Headline: After lying dormant for years, the Era Dorada project in Asunción Mita resumed this year and villagers say history is being repeated, despite promises of change
Content: Lake Güija. A volcanic lake and Ramsar wetland on Guatemala’s border with El Salvador, it connects the Ostúa and Lempa rivers. If the Era Dorada project is activated, environmentalists claim the wetland could be contaminated.Photograph: Euan WallaceView image in fullscreenLake Güija. A volcanic lake and Ramsar wetland on Guatemala’s border with El Salvador, it connects the Ostúa and Lempa rivers. If the Era Dorada project is activated, environmentalists claim the wetland could be contaminated.Photograph: Euan WallaceSouthern frontlines: Latin America and the CaribbeanMining‘They take the water, the springs dry up’: fear as Guatemalan goldmine plan is revivedAfter lying dormant for years, the Era Dorada project in Asunción Mita resumed this year and villagers say history is being repeated, despite promises of changeSupported byAbout this contentEuan Wallaceand Martina Mariano in Asunción Mita, GuatemalaTue 1 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 10.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the community of La Lima inGuatemala, Elda Dinora Ramírez, 58, looks towards a small well at the back of her home. Dusty wooden planks lie across the opening, concealing the faint gleam of water far below. “The well is drying up again,” she says.Ramírez’s home lies less than a mile fromEra Dorada– a goldmining project acquired by the Canadian multinational Aura Minerals in January 2025. After years of inactivity, the project was reactivated this year when the Guatemalan governmentgranted Aura a construction licence.View image in fullscreenElda Dinora Ramírez lives less than a mile from the mine site in La Lima, Guatemala.Photograph: Euan WallaceExploration began in 1997 under the then-owners Entre Mares, a subsidiary of Goldcorp, and the project has faced a significant backlash throughout its 29-year history.“Until all this started happening, we had a happy and peaceful life here,” says Ramírez. “There was no talk of mining; everything was calm.”After initial excavation began in 2007, residents such as Ramírez reported water shortages. They blamed the mine for pumping out large quantities of geothermal water that was filling the tunnels during excavation.“The machines they use draw from deep down; they take all the water and the springs dry up,” she says.Although the mine’s development was suspended in 2013 due to unfavourable market conditions, the project site continued to have water extracted in subsequent years.With operations temporarily halted, locals around the mine reported that water levels in their wells began to recover. Then known as Cerro Blanco, the project was sold by Goldcorp to the Vancouver-based Bluestone Resources in 2017. In 2021, Bluestone announced a controversial plan to convert the project into an open-pit mine.A year later, a community referendum in nearby Asunción Mita rejected the project, with88% of voters opposing it.“It was a great victory for the people,” says Yony Barrera, 51, owner of a hardware store in Asunción Mita and vice-president of an activist group campaigning against the mine.View image in fullscreenEmployees behind a gate to the Era Dorada site. The company says it has begun deforestation, construction of equipment platforms and removal of water from the mine.Photograph: Euan WallaceIn 2024, Guatemala’s new governmentannulled the environmental licencefor Bluestone’s proposed open-pit mine, just months after it had been approved by the previous administration. But activists feared that work on the project would not remain dormant for ever.“I knew it wouldn’t be over,” says Barrera. “This will only stop when they take the gold.”Today, the mining site hums with life once again. Heavy vehicles judder past the rusted coils of barbed wire that mark the site’s borders, clouds of dust rising in their wake. Workers in hard hats and navy-blue overalls gather around the entrance.The company predicts anannual production of 111,000 ouncesof gold in the first four years of operation. In a statement, Aura says industrial operations have not yet begun, although construction and site preparation work are under way, and that vegetation clearance is authorised under its licence and is being carried out within limits set by the project’s EIA.View image in fullscreenArnulfo Díaz says he sustained an injury that left him deaf in one ear while working at the mine in 2008.Photograph: Euan Wallace“They are advancing a lot, and very quickly,” says Arnulfo Díaz, 43. “At the same time, we are advancing towards our own destruction.”Díaz worked on the project in 2008 as part of the excavation team under Entre Mares, where he says he sustained an injury that left him deaf in his right ear. He fears the project’s return may bring wider consequences for his community.“Our fear is that we will lose everyday access to water,” he says. “Where are we going to go?”Ramírez says the effects are already being felt. As well as her well drying up since the project was reactivated in January, her fruit trees are losing their harvest to drought and her livestock are suffering from respiratory illness she attributes to dust from the mine.“When I lie down at night I start to think: there is no hope left,” she says.Aura Minerals says measures are being taken to suppress dust at the site and monitoring has so far shown that the work has had no impact on air quality.Aura says it is approaching the project with a renewed focus on sustainability, pledging to develop it as an underground mine after more than 1,000 hours of dialogue with local communities.In a company statement, Aura’s president and chief executive, Rodrigo Barbosa, points to plans for a water-purification plant and the use of 100% recycled water.View image in fullscreenThe offices of Era Dorada in Asunción Mita.Photograph: Euan Wallace“This ensures we not only do no harm, but go beyond and create positive value for the communities and environment,” he says.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAura says it will recycle water used in the industrial process in a closed-loop system with no discharge and treat excess natural water from the mine to a drinkable standard for local communities. The company also points to continuous water-quality monitoring upstream and downstream of the operation and says hydrogeological studies and monitoring show no evidence of reduced water availability for local communities.But activists claim that the environmental guardrails in place, designed to limit the project’s harmful impact, fall short of what is required.According to Era Dorada’s opponents, the project continues to operate under a widely criticised Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA), which was approved in 2007.A2023 reportcommissioned by the Central American Alliance Against Mining (Acafremin) says experts from Guatemala’s ministry of environment and natural resources rejected the EIA in 2004 and 2005, but the ministry replaced them in 2007, and the new head of the unit approved the EIA shortly afterwards.Julio González, of the Guatemalan environmental organisation Madre Selva, and other activists say these changes are evidence of past corruption and have criticised the EIA for failing to account for key environmental considerations, such as the safe disposal of cyanide – a highly toxic chemical commonly used to separate gold from rock.A 2022 reportby Steven Emerman, a geophysicist and independent mining expert, recommended that all of the mine’s permits be revoked.View image in fullscreenA stretch of the Ostúa River a short distance from the mining site.Photograph: Euan WallaceIn its statement, Aura says the current underground project falls within the scope of the original EIA and its active environmental licence, which it describes as being fully valid and adequate for the operation. Aura confirms it plans to use cyanide in the Era Dorada project, but says the mine is designed to manage it in line with relevant standards, with the process operating in a closed-circuit system and a detoxification stage at the end of the process to neutralise cyanide in the solution.The mine is in the protectedbiological corridor of the Ostúa dry forest, and environmentalists fear that inadequate governance could expose crucial ecosystems to contamination by heavy metals. Aura says the project is not located in an area with legal restrictions, and claims to have plans in place to maintain the ecological integrity of the surroundings.Scientists also warn that geothermal water discharged during tunnel excavation carries high levels of arsenic. A2019 studyby a biologist, Cidia Cortes, reported elevated arsenic levels at points on the Ostúa River where the mine discharged geothermal water.The company says, however, that arsenic occurs naturally at higher than normal levels in the region and that all of the water pumped from the underground workings is treated to reduce arsenic. Era Dorada also says it is investing to upgrade treatment to improve water to drinkable standards.The Ostúa River feeds intoLake Güija, a protected site that straddles the Guatemala-El Salvador border. Here, communities fear that reactivating the mining project could jeopardise their livelihoods.View image in fullscreenMirna Margarita says: ‘These times are very worrying, with all this contamination that could come to us.’Photograph: Euan Wallace“We have eight children,” says Mirna Margarita, 58, who lives in the lakeside community of Cuevitas. “We fished just to sustain them and put them through school.”Looking out over the blue waters of Lake Güija, she leans back on a lopsided sofa. “These times are very worrying, with all this contamination that could come to us.”Her husband, Maximiliano Pérez, 59, who has fished all of his life, sits opposite her. “It worries us greatly that the mine might become active again and start working, with how much we stand to lose,” he says. “We look at the lake like a mother – she is what gives us our food.”View image in fullscreenPedro Arrieta, a resident of the town of Asunción Mita, says mining brings contamination, corruption and death.Photograph: Euan WallaceAmid ongoing uncertainty, many who live close to the mine share concerns about the future. Pedro Arrieta, 55, is a baker from Asunción Mita. He sits in his family home, where a small plate of home-cooked pastries is passed around the room. “What mining brings is contamination, corruption and death,” he says.A collection of family photos is arranged on the wall behind him. Generations of faces look out from within the gold-rimmed frames. “What are we going to leave to our next generation?” he asks.Explore more on these topicsMiningSouthern frontlines: Latin America and the CaribbeanGuatemalaAmericasWaterRiversfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Dry weather sewage discharges soar as water companies face scrutiny | Water industry | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: 7,280 suspected illegal spills in rivers and sea recorded in first five months of 2026
Author: Sandra Laville
Headline: Exclusive: 7,280 suspected illegal spills in rivers and sea recorded in first five months of 2026
Content: A warning sign in Teignouth, Devon, after a sewage discharge incident  in April 2026.Photograph: nidpor/Alamy Live NewsView image in fullscreenA warning sign in Teignouth, Devon, after a sewage discharge incident  in April 2026.Photograph: nidpor/Alamy Live NewsWater industryDry weather sewage discharges soar as water companies face scrutinyExclusive: 7,280 suspected illegal spills in rivers and sea recorded in first five months of 2026Sandra LavilleTue 1 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 08.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe number of suspected illegal discharges of raw sewage into rivers and seas by water companies during dry weather increased significantly during the first five months of 2026.‘Tiny bit of rain and the sewage comes’: Brighton swimmers vent fury at sea pollutionRead moreDumping raw sewage into waterways during dry spells via overflows amounts to pollution. It is considered a breach of the permits given to water companies and is illegal. Discharging during dry weather increases the toxicity of the sewage pollution entering waterways. Rivers have less flow and volume, and there is no rainwater to dilute the sewage pollution entering the waterway.Last year, in what regulators said was tougher action on sewage pollution, water companies in England were for the first time required to report to the Environment Agency the number of times they discharged raw sewage from combined sewer overflows during dry weather.A dry day spill is flaggedwhen an overflow operates despite little to no rainfall that day and the previous day.In 2025, water companies in England and Wales reported 8,576 dry spill pollution discharges. But according to freedom of information requests submitted byEnvironment Agencywhistleblower Robert Forrester, the pollution is getting worse, not better, despite the regulator’s promise of tougher action.Between January and May this year alone, water companies discharged raw sewage into rivers and seas during dry weather 7,280 times. The data is comparable as it is based on the same instruction and taken from the same data recording system.The water industry said the figures were as yet unverified and it was too early to describe them as dry spills.Forrester, an Environment Agency officer for more than 20 years, revealed failures by the agency to take on water companies’ illegal practices before leaving his job.“Dry day spills will almost always be deliberate and illegal, otherwise there would be non-stop raw sewage spilling from pipes,” said Forrester.South West Water has worst environmental record in England, analysis showsRead more“The huge increase in a much drier year appears to show that water companies have quotas of sewage to dump and will do whatever the weather, and whatever the risk to the public and the environment. Making money is the primary focus.” He said the regulator was no deterrent to the actions of the water companies.“This level of criminality shows that water companies do not believe they, or the government, will ever do anything meaningful to stop them.”Combined sewer overflows are an emergency system designed to be used in extreme weather to relieve pressure in the sewage system. But decades of underinvestment by the privatised water industry have led to the outflows being used regularly to discharge sewage.In the first five months of 2026, South West Water, which operates acrossDevon, Cornwall and parts of Dorset and Somerset, discharged raw sewage on dry days 1,299 times. This compares with 2,451 times during the whole of 2025.Water companies are facing outrage across the country for discharging raw sewage via storm outflows in August following the first moderate spell of rain after more than six weeks of drought. Public mapped data revealed water companies including SouthernWaterand South West Water discharging raw sewage from storm overflows within hours of the first significant rain.In the south-west, after weeks of drought, the company’s own data suggested it discharged sewage into rivers and the sea for a combined total of almost 300 hours in the third week of August.Ed Tyldesley, a Liberal Democrat county councillor in north Devon, said the company’s own figures showed 664 separate spills across 184 sites despite just 16.5mm of rain across the south-west, according to data collated byWaterWatch.“They are using a storm system when there are no storms. It is unbelievable. The worrying thing is that this all seems to be getting worse,” he said.Water companies in England and Wales explore ‘surge pricing’ during droughtRead moreTyldesley said he had been told by the water company that its live monitoring data could sometimes contain false readings. “That leaves two possibilities. Either the South West Water data is correct and sewage was discharged into our rivers and seas for 299 hours in a single week, or their legally mandated monitoring system is so unreliable that hundreds of apparent sewage spills are being reported to the public, which may not actually have happened.”A spokesperson for Water UK, the trade association for the water industry, said: “These are unverified figures, and it is too early to describe them as dry day spills. Nonetheless, no spill is ever acceptable. Water companies are working to end them as fast as possible by tripling investment. Companies are investing £12bn to halve spills from storm overflows by 2030, including relining and sealing sewers to prevent groundwater infiltration – one of the main causes of dry day spills.”South West Water has said the company publishes near real-time monitoring data, which has to be validated before being used for regulatory reporting.“Storm overflow activations can happen for a range of reasons and aren’t determined by rainfall figures alone.“We continue to invest in our monitoring and are spending record amounts to reduce storm overflow use across the region. We’re reviewing the locations raised by the councillor so we can provide a full response.”A Defra spokesperson said: “It is totally unacceptable that some water companies are failing to deliver value for money for customers and polluting our rivers, lakes and seas.“After years of failure, we have taken immediate action to make water companies more accountable, and, for the first time ever, they are now required to report dry day spills as pollution incidents, providing the government with the evidence to go after water companies where performance falls short.”Explore more on these topicsWater industryWaterDevonPollutionEnvironment AgencynewsShareReuse this content

title: Could this humble sea sponge clean up the world’s ports?  | Marine life | The Guardian
description: The chicken liver sponge has sailed through a test of its ability to filter pollutants in a harbour in Spain’s Costa Brava
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The chicken liver sponge has sailed through a test of its ability to filter pollutants in a harbour in Spain’s Costa Brava
Content: The survival of the chicken liver sponge in the harsh environment of a Spanish harbour suggests it could be used to help clean up pollution in ports.Photograph: Carlota EscarréView image in fullscreenThe survival of the chicken liver sponge in the harsh environment of a Spanish harbour suggests it could be used to help clean up pollution in ports.Photograph: Carlota EscarréSeascape: the state of our oceansMarine lifeCould this humble sea sponge clean up the world’s ports?The chicken liver sponge has sailed through a test of its ability to filter pollutants in a harbour in Spain’s Costa BravaSeascape: the state of our oceans is supported byAbout this contentSara HashemiTue 1 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the polluted waters of Marina Palamós on Spain’s Costa Brava, Manuel Maldonado, a sponge biologist, noticed something unusual last month: red starfish had started settling in the area.Nearly two years earlier, the Spanish National Research Council scientist and his colleagues had beguntransplanting sea spongesinto the port to study whether they could survive in its polluted waters.Only one species, the chicken liver sponge (Chondrosia reniformis,also called the kidney sponge), which is found along the Mediterranean coast but rarely seen in the harbour, managed to survive. Its resilience, and the arrival of the red starfish, suggests sponges could be used to clean up pollution in ports.View image in fullscreenResearchers monitored the sponges’ health using underwater photography and close inspection.Photograph: Carlota EscarréSea sponges are some of the Earth’s oldest ecosystem engineers. Previousresearch has shownthat abundant communities can reshape their surroundings in positive ways. They can filter pollutants from enormous volumes of water, cycling nutrients in the process. They also enhance biodiversity by attracting marine animals that live within and around them, such as worms and crustaceans.All of this points to their potential as a tool for renaturalising harbours, some of the most disturbed marine environments in the world. The accumulation of pollutants such as rubbish and oil, the introduction of invasive species from ships and persistent noise pollution make it incredibly difficult for marine life to thrive there.But first, it has to be proved that sponges can survive in harsh environments. “So we tested different Spanish species with the idea of finding some that could survive in a harbour environment,” says Maldonado, who led the research.The team focused on five sponge species commonly found on the coast, chosen because their abundance suggests they are good survivors. “You also don’t want to use a very sensitive or protected species,” he says. “It has to be something you can handle and transport to the harbour.”The sponges were collected from a site about 18 miles (30km) south of the harbour where they were transplanted. Maldonado’s student and study co-author, Carlota Escarré, monitored their health using underwater photography and inspection.Escarré conducted dives every 20 to 64 days over the course of 15 months, braving early hours and cold waters at the harbour.View image in fullscreenRegular dives to examine the sponges were conducted over 15 months.Photograph: Per ManuelAll the red encrusting sponges (Crambe crambe), leather sponges (Scalarispongia scalaris)and stinker sponges(Ircinia oros)shrank and eventually died during the study. But almost 92% of the chicken liver spongespecimens survived the polluted water.“It was a surprise for all of us,” says Escarré.
