Some even managed to reproduce asexually, bringing their numbers up to 40 from 24.Experts hope the study finally puts sea sponges, long overlooked in favour of the more charismatic coral, on the map.“This study shows what we in the sea sponge community have known for years,” says Andreu Santín Muriel, a marine biologist at the University of Porto’s Interdisciplinary Centre of Marine and Environmental Research, who was not involved in the work. “Sponges are excellent potential species for bioremediation and habitat recovery.”He adds: “A lot of effort has been put in the past decades for coral restoration; we understand the importance of corals very well. But sponges provide more ecosystem services, yet they’re not as attractive, so they have received way less money.”David Amptmeijer, a doctoral researcher at Helmholtz-Zentrum Hereon, who was not involved in the research, says it is important to note how localised the study is. It is unclear if these same sponges could survive, for example, in a harbour in Maine.View image in fullscreenResearchers will keep monitoring the sponges over several years.Photograph: Carlota EscarréThough Amptmeijer believes sea sponges have great potential for pollution management, he says a lot more research is needed before scientists can fully understand how they interact with pollutants.Maldonado suspects the chicken liver sponge– a high-microbial-abundance sponge (hosting diverse communities of symbiotic microorganisms within its tissues) that takes ammonium from seawater and releases nitrate – is able to cope with pollution thanks to its diverse microbiome. “We will start working on this after the summer,” he says.He and his team will continue monitoring the sponges over several years, but they also hope to study other organisms: he has written a proposal for a project that combines sponges with oysters, which are also powerful filter feeders.Santín Muriel says sponges have been around for at least 600m years. “They have survived at least five mass extinctions, and they’re still thriving in today’s oceans. That means they’ve most likely already encountered a lot of environmental problems throughout their existence.”It’s not so strange, then, to think that sea sponges may already have the solutions to many of the problems humans face today.“We tend to look more to technology to solve environmental pollution,” Santín Muriel says. “But marine organisms most likely have already developed toolkits that could help us clean the oceans.”Explore more on these topicsMarine lifeSeascape: the state of our oceansOceansPollutionAnimalsWildlifeSpainEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Kākāpō rising: 90 chicks swell population of the world’s heaviest parrot | New Zealand | The Guardian
description: Critically endangered New Zealand bird enjoys record breeding season triggered by mass fruiting of native tree, pushing its numbers to 325
Author: Eva Corlett
Headline: Critically endangered New Zealand bird enjoys record breeding season triggered by mass fruiting of native tree, pushing its numbers to 325
Content: Ninety kākāpō chicks were officially added to the population of the critically endangered birds on 1 September, a record high.Photograph: Department of ConservationView image in fullscreenNinety kākāpō chicks were officially added to the population of the critically endangered birds on 1 September, a record high.Photograph: Department of ConservationNew ZealandKākāpō rising: 90 chicks swell population of the world’s heaviest parrotCritically endangered New Zealand bird enjoys record breeding season triggered by mass fruiting of native tree, pushing its numbers to 325Eva Corlettin WellingtonMon 31 Aug 2026 22.57 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe population of the world’s heaviest parrot,the kākāpō, has surpassed 300 birds for the first time in 75 years, after a record breeding season triggered by the mass fruiting of a native New Zealand tree.Ninety chicks were officially added to the population of the critically endangered birds on 1 September, pushing the total to 325 – a record high since recovery efforts began.“The last time the population is thought to have exceeded 300 birds may have been as long as 75 years ago,” said Deidre Vercoe, the conservation department’s kākāpō recovery operations manager.“We had a four-year gap between breeding seasons, so it’s fantastic to finally see the population increase after all that time.”‘My lovely distraction’: live stream of kākāpō – world’s fattest parrot – and her chicks captivates New ZealandRead moreView image in fullscreenKākāpō population tops 300 for first time in 75 years, after record breeding seasonPhotograph: Department of ConservationKākāpō, the world’s only nocturnal and flightless parrot, were once abundant acrossNew Zealand. But their population plummeted after the introduction of predators such as cats and stoats. By the 1900s, they were nearly extinct.A recovery programme was established in 1995 with a population of just 51 birds and has battled challenges with genetic diversity, infertility and poor chick hatching rates. There are three kākāpō breeding populations, all based on predator-free islands off the South Island.Kākāpō breed only every two to four years when the native rimu trees produce large numbers of berries, so repopulation is slow. This year, after a four-year wait,a bountiful harvestof rimu berries prompted the birds to breed and produce a record number of chicks.“In the early years of recovery, it took 16 years to produce that many chicks,” Vercoe said.Kākāpō are thought to live between 60 and 80 years, can weigh up to 4kg and are famously entertaining. More than 100,000 people tuned into watch a live stream of a kākāpōsleeping, eating and attending to her nest and chicks during breeding season.The parrots have unusual mating rituals. Male birds gather in a “lek” to produce a distinctive booming sound, emitted from air sacs in their chests while sitting in a dugout bowl in the ground. The deep boom, which can travel up to 5km, sounds similar to a softly plucked cello string.After choosing a partner and mating, females typically lay one to four eggs. The females become solely responsible for their eggs and hatched chicks for roughly six months.At 150 days of age, the chicks are fledged and considered independent enough to be added to the total population. The youngest chick of the 2026 breeding season was female Awarua-A3, who hatched on 30 March.Modelling indicated the next breeding season could occur as soon as 2028, Vercoe said.“So, while we’ll take a moment to stop and reflect on this remarkable year, we’re already looking ahead to 2028 and preparing for what could come next.”Explore more on these topicsNew ZealandBirdsWildlifeAnimalsAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cleveland police to get £2m extra to tackle serious crime in Middlesbrough | UK news | The Guardian
description: Cash announced after horror car crash that killed two police officers and house fire in which woman and young girl died
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Cash announced after horror car crash that killed two police officers and house fire in which woman and young girl died
Content: Natalie McDonald, 34, and her niece Valentina Foster, seven, died in the fire in Grangetown.Composite: FacebookView image in fullscreenNatalie McDonald, 34, and her niece Valentina Foster, seven, died in the fire in Grangetown.Composite: FacebookUK newsCleveland police to get £2m extra to tackle serious crime in MiddlesbroughCash announced after horror car crash that killed two police officers and house fire in which woman and young girl diedJosh HallidayandAngus ThomsonTue 1 Sep 2026 18.04 EDTFirst published on Tue 1 Sep 2026 02.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCleveland’s police force is to receive a £2m funding boost to tackle serious crime, after the home secretary said successive high-profile tragedies in the Middlesbrough area had led to a “sense of disquiet” in the community.Shabana Mahmood and the prime minister, Andy Burnham, paid tribute in parliament on Tuesday to police constables Matthew Blades and Tom Clough, who were killed when a Volkswagen Passat travelling on the wrong side of the A66 dual carriageway collided head-on with their marked response vehicle.Five young men travelling in the Passat, which had earlier been pursued by different police, also died in the 22 August incident.Cleveland police said the five occupants – Cole Worthy, 17, Theo Rae, 17, Makai Saddington, 18, Michael Robert Cahill, 23, and Jakub Matusiak, 23 – may have had links to “serious organised criminal activity”.Officers from outside the area have been deployed to Cleveland after the crash.Mahmood told the House of Commons on Tuesday that she had given her “full backing” to the investigation, making the £2m pledge to fight “both serious crime and its causes”.The funding is separate to real-term budget increases for all police forces, which will see Cleveland police receive an additional £7m compared with last year, she said.The home secretary said Cleveland police were also investigating the house fire in Grangetown that killed Natalie McDonald, 34, and her niece Valentina Foster, 7, and injured four others on 26 August.Investigators were not treating the fire and the A66 crash – which occurred within a mile of each other – as connected, Mahmood said.“However, it has undoubtedly added to the sense of disquiet in a community already reeling from the earlier tragedy,” she said. “I recognise how unnerving it will have been for law-abiding citizens, both in the affected areas and beyond, to see a spate of incidents occurring in close proximity and quick succession.”Cleveland police and crime commissioner Matt Storey said the £2m funding boost would help deal with the immediate aftermath of the incidents, but would not address the “chronic underfunding” of the force.“A one-off payment is not a solution,” Storey said. “It fails to tackle the deep-rooted funding inequalities that continue to disadvantage the hard-working officers, staff and communities of Cleveland.”Storey said the force needed at least £20m every year to recruit 200 more police officers and strengthen efforts to crack down on serious organised crime.The funding announcement came after a 23-year-old man appeared in court on murder charges over the deaths of McDonald and Foster.Jaden Wright, of no fixed address, appeared before Teesside magistrates court on Tuesday for a hearing that lasted less than two minutes.Wright briefly greeted his solicitor as he was brought into the dock before he was remanded in custody to appear at Teesside crown court on Thursday.The court clerk outlined that he faces two murder charges, two counts of grievous bodily harm with intent and two charges of attempted grievous bodily harm with intent. The charges relate to the six people who were in the house, two of whom cannot be identified by the media due to their age.The clerk said Wright faced a separate charge of intentional strangulation over an incident said to have happened on the day before the fire.Cleveland police said on Friday that a 48-year-old woman was in the Royal Victoria Infirmary in Newcastle in a “critical but stable” condition after the fire, and a 27-year-old man was at James Cook university hospital in Middlesbrough receiving treatment. Two teenage girls were discharged after sustaining non-life-threatening injuries.Katie Smith, the senior investigating officer from Northumbria police, said: “This has been a truly tragic incident and my thoughts remain with the families of all those involved.“I would like to thank local residents for their support and patience during this complex investigation. Anyone who may still have information, or has any concerns, can still submit information using the major incident public portal.”Katie Nicholson, the chief crown prosecutor for CPS North East, said: “Our prosecutors have worked closely with Cleveland police to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring this case to court.“We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are active and he has the right to a fair trial. It is vital that there should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information which could in anyway prejudice these proceedings.”A 31-year-old man who was also arrested in connection with the case was released without charge on Sunday.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Five held by police after newborn baby dies from stab wounds in Sheffield | UK news | The Guardian
description: Officers responded to reports concerning safety of baby girl at property in Wincobank area of the city
Author: Angus Thomson
Headline: Officers responded to reports concerning safety of baby girl at property in Wincobank area of the city
Content: DCI Tom Woodward of South Yorkshire police said the force would ‘confront every difficult and distressing challenge and pursue every line of inquiry’.Photograph: Graham Turner/The GuardianView image in fullscreenDCI Tom Woodward of South Yorkshire police said the force would ‘confront every difficult and distressing challenge and pursue every line of inquiry’.Photograph: Graham Turner/The GuardianUK newsFive held by police after newborn baby dies from stab wounds in SheffieldOfficers responded to reports concerning safety of baby girl at property in Wincobank area of the cityAngus ThomsonTue 1 Sep 2026 13.46 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFive people are being held on suspicion of murder after a newborn baby died from stab wounds in Sheffield on Sunday.Police officers found the girl at a property in Holywell Heights, in the Wincobank area of Sheffield, while responding to reports concerning her safety just before 6am on Sunday. She was pronounced dead at the scene.Seven people were arrested on suspicion of murder. Two have since been bailed. A postmortem examination found the girl had died from stab wounds, police said on Tuesday.DCI Tom Woodward of South Yorkshire police said first responders, paramedics and detectives now leading the murder investigation had been profoundly affected by the baby’s death.“We recognise this is deeply distressing for those who would have loved to have a chance to love this baby girl, for the emergency services who responded and for the community who will inevitably be shocked by this incident,” Woodward said. “Our commitment to this little girl is unwavering.“We will confront every difficult and distressing challenge and pursue every line of inquiry with determination and care to secure justice for her.”Woodward said the investigation was fast-moving and asked the community to “avoid speculating around the circumstances of this tragic incident”.“We know the local community will hold her in their thoughts and support us as we work through this complex investigation,” he said.Five murder suspects remain in custody after police were granted a warrant for further detention, a force spokesperson said on Tuesday. A 26-year-old and a 37-year-old have been released on bail.Specialist search officers will remain in the Holywell Heights area as the investigation continues.South Yorkshire police said anyone with information about the case should contact them online or call 101, quoting incident number 993 on 30 August 2026. People can also report information to the independent charity Crimestoppers.Explore more on these topicsUK newsSouth YorkshirenewsShareReuse this content

title: Raise the Colours member denies murder of man in Staffordshire | England | The Guardian
description: Billy Allison, 36, pleads not guilty to charge over Matthew O’Gara’s death after incident outside Lichfield bar
Author: Neha Gohil
Headline: Billy Allison, 36, pleads not guilty to charge over Matthew O’Gara’s death after incident outside Lichfield bar
Content: Matthew O’Gara, the director of the Plough pub in Huddlesford, died in hospital two days after an alleged assault.Photograph: Staffordshire policeMatthew O’Gara, the director of the Plough pub in Huddlesford, died in hospital two days after an alleged assault.Photograph: Staffordshire policeEnglandRaise the Colours member denies murder of man in StaffordshireBilly Allison, 36, pleads not guilty to charge over Matthew O’Gara’s death after incident outside Lichfield barNeha GohilMidlands correspondentTue 1 Sep 2026 09.37 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man accused of murdering a businessman outside a bar in Staffordshire has pleaded not guilty.Billy Allison, 36, a member of the flag-raising group Raise the Colours, appeared at Stafford crown court on Tuesday and entered not guilty pleas to the murder of Matthew O’Gara and to causing grievous bodily harm with intent to a second person.Allison, of Shirley in Solihull, West Midlands, appeared via video link from HMP Dovegate.Officers were called to the Ricco & Loren bar on Market Street in Lichfield at 11.25pm on 24 May after receiving reports two men had been punched, Staffordshire police previously said in a statement.O’Gara, who was the director of the Plough pub in the nearby village of Huddlesford, sustained serious injuries and died in hospital two days later. The second man also attended hospital and was later discharged.View image in fullscreenThe alleged assault took place outside the Ricco & Loren bar in Lichfield.Photograph: Phil Barnett/PAJudge Mukherjee told Allison on Tuesday that he would stand trial in October and it would probably last for about 10 days. “I have adjourned your case for trial to the 28th of October,” he said.Lichfield rugby club paid tribute to O’Gara after his death, describing him as “a friend of the club and a very generous and valued sponsor”.Its post said: “From everyone at the club we would like to offer our deepest condolences to all of Matt’s family, friends, colleagues and the wider Plough family.”The Plough pub closed its doors in the immediate aftermath to give family and staff “the time, privacy and respect they need”, according to the post on Facebook.Explore more on these topicsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Swinney sticks with pledge to cap prices on basic foods in Scotland | Scotland | The Guardian
description: First minister sets out his government’s agenda and defends policy described by industry groups as a ‘potty gimmick’
Author: Patrick Greenfield
Headline: First minister sets out his government’s agenda and defends policy described by industry groups as a ‘potty gimmick’
Content: John Swinney sets out his government’s plans at Holyrood on Tuesday, including a shake-up of NHS health boards.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJohn Swinney sets out his government’s plans at Holyrood on Tuesday, including a shake-up of NHS health boards.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianScotlandSwinney sticks with pledge to cap prices on basic foods in ScotlandFirst minister sets out his government’s agenda and defends policy described by industry groups as a ‘potty gimmick’Patrick GreenfieldTue 1 Sep 2026 12.52 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 14.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Swinney insisted on Tuesday he still planned to introduce a legally binding price cap on bread, milk and other essential food items in Scotland despite fierce opposition from farming and business groups.Unveiling the Scottish National party’s programme for government – the equivalent to the king’s speech – the first minister said he wanted to give “families greater peace of mind at a time of rising prices”.Swinney also announced commitments to restructure local government and NHS boards, introduce a misogyny bill to crack down on violence against women and girls, and set a £2 price limit on bus fares in the west ofScotland. He confirmed his government would pilot a minimum income for artists.But the proposals to limit essential food and drink prices have faced intense criticism from industry groups, which have described the policy as “unnecessary” and a “potty gimmick”.On Monday, 23 food, drink and farming organisations published an open letter arguing that markets were already working to deliver the best possible prices and a cap could increase the cost of household goods.“Scots benefit from western Europe’s most affordable grocery and food supply market,” the letter read. “A statutory cap would not address the root causes of elevated food prices: rising production, refrigeration, and distribution costs. Supply chain shocks after Covid and conflicts in Ukraine and Iran have pushed up fertiliser, fuel and energy costs.”The SNP committed to introducing price controls by the end of the year in amanifestopublished before Holyrood elections in May, framing the scheme as a health measure. Similar initiatives have been implemented in Hungary and Croatia and the UKgovernment encouragedsupermarkets to consider voluntary price caps on foodstuffs in May.The Scottish government did not specify which essentials wouldbe coveredby the law in a consultation paper published on Tuesday, although Swinney has said that between 20 and 50 products would be included, such as rice, cheese and eggs. Any limit would cover only retailers that make more than half of their annual turnover from groceries, have more than 250 employees and make more than £250m a year.“It is our ambition, and intention, to put more money in families’ pockets, building on what is already the most generous cost of living support package anywhere in the UK,” Swinney told Holyrood on Tuesday. “Today we have also begun a formal consultation on the legislation that will introduce a legal price ceiling on a basket of essential food items, giving families greater peace of mind at a time of rising prices.”There is uncertainty over whether any price cap on food and drink essentials would even be legal. The Scottish government is planning to introduce the policy under devolved health powers. But critics say it would clash with post-Brexit internal UK market rules to stop regulatory divergence between England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionScotland is facing growing pressure on its finances. The Scottish governmentestimated last yearthat there would be a near-£5bn gap in its finances by the end of the decade, with experts warning that difficult choices await over how to fund healthcare, schools and other parts of the public sector.In his five-year programme for government, Swinney announced a major change to the structure ofNHSScotland, reducing the number of health boards from 14 to two. He described the shake-up as “the most significant structural reform of our NHS in the devolution era”.Explore more on these topicsScotlandScottish National party (SNP)John SwinneyNHSScottish politicsFoodInflationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Macquarie University swaps in-person psychology classes with AI chatbot for two subjects | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: University’s move is part of trend that critics within academia say will lead to further staff cuts and loss of ‘everything that makes the job worth doing’
Author: Luca Ittimani
Headline: University’s move is part of trend that critics within academia say will lead to further staff cuts and loss of ‘everything that makes the job worth doing’
Content: Multiple universities such as Macquarie University, the University of Melbourne and the University of Sydney have introduced AI tools and platforms.Photograph: Wikimedia CommonsView image in fullscreenMultiple universities such as Macquarie University, the University of Melbourne and the University of Sydney have introduced AI tools and platforms.Photograph: Wikimedia CommonsAI (artificial intelligence)Macquarie University swaps in-person psychology classes with AI chatbot for two subjectsUniversity’s move is part of trend that critics within academia say will lead to further staff cuts and loss of ‘everything that makes the job worth doing’Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastLuca IttimaniTue 1 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 22.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn Australian university has swapped in-person classes with an AI chatbot, online quizzes and optional online tutorials in two subjects as institutions give the technology more teaching responsibilities.Macquarie University’s “Virtual Peer” is part of each week’s learning in two mandatory psychology units, programmed to ask students questions and guide them through scenario-based exercises.The university said the AI activities are optional and only “supplement” the “core learning” of online readings, quizzes and videos.ANU accused of ‘hysterical’ response to students using AI to cheat as unis scramble to ‘secure’ assessmentsRead moreHowever, neither the core nor the AI activities are mandatory. Students are only assessed on separate research tasks and exams.Both subjects had in-person classes in the first semester of this year. The university said in-person classes would return in 2027 in alternate semesters so students could pick the format that suits their circumstances.One student, who asked to remain anonymous, said they felt “short-changed” after issues with their degree structure forced them to enrol in the online option.Each individual psychology subject costs $2,174 for Australian students with commonwealth supported places in 2026. A three-yearundergraduate degree now costs over $50,000.“Instead of a group discussion or a tutor teaching you, it’s a class activity done with a robot,” the student said. “I feel like I’m teaching this robot how to take jobs away from my teachers.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailMacquarie said the tool was designed in partnership with educators to support, not replace, them.Professors who use Virtual Peer uploaded the information it uses and checked it, the university said, making it more tailored than general-purpose AI tools. Experts say that could make the tool potentially less prone to “hallucination”, or inventing content without evidence. Macquarie can also monitor student conversations on the service, according to the university.The subjects still have paid tutors who run optional Zoom feedback sessions each week. One introductory-level subject has six sessions a week for its 400 students, while the other final-year subject has 10 sessions a week for its 700 students – or roughly one class for every 70 students.Students who want to speak to a human for feedback are encouraged to attend. Macquarie said attendance at these was variable and rose around assessment due dates.Virtual Peer was also used for learning activities in other subjects but was not available in all classes, Macquarie said.Its use has accelerated, answering close to 80,000 student questions in all of 2025 but nearly as many in just the first half of 2026, most of which were administrative questions. The university said staff and students overwhelmingly found the tool valuable or recommended its use when surveyed.Backlash to AI teaching growsMacquarie has been one of a handful of Australian universities to systematically incorporate AI into teaching, alongside the University of Melbourne and the University of Sydney, as the technology attractsgrowing student use–and backlash.View image in fullscreenMeena Jha (left) and an AI avatar in her likeness named Neena Chatbot (right).Composite: SuppliedMeena Jha, an associate professor at Central Queensland University, said she had not previously heard of any universities simultaneously cutting in-person teaching and introducing AI chatbots in her research into AI in higher education.“Students require that human touch … [and] engagement will be a very big issue if we replace everything with virtual tutors,” said Jha, who is also the head of CQU’s pedagogy and technology cluster.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCQU is piloting its homegrown AI tool, named “Birdy”, as a “service/support tool” in 24 units. Jha has gone further, building an AI avatar in her likeness, named Neena Chatbot, to answer her students’ questions.“You have to give a bit of time for people to try it, use it, see value in it, and in doing so you need to guide them how they can use it,” Jha said.The University of Sydney haspositioned itself as a leader in the field, with hundreds of academics using its education-focused generative AI platform, “Cogniti”, for chatbots and scenario exercises. It has shared Cogniti with other institutions in Australia, New Zealand and the Netherlands.‘I hate what AI is doing to the minds and happiness of the young’: Katherine Rundell on the view from the classroomRead moreThe university in late August released a discussion paper that envisions futures where AI takes on even greater responsibilities, delivering personalised teaching for each student in each unit, while staff-student contact hours decline.A university spokesperson said Sydney was only supporting staff to use technology to improve student experience.“Human judgment, accountability and relationships are essential to everything we do, and can never be replaced by technology,” the spokesperson said. “This isn’t a cost-saving measure in any way.”Peter Chen, president of the university’s national tertiary education union (NTEU) branch, said the paper had added to growing staff concern about their future at the university as funding shortfalls left fewer academics to run bigger classes.“For some staff, they’re afraid they’re going to lose their jobs,” Chen said.“For other staff, the concern is that everything that makes the job worth doing will be lost … and they will be there simply to take the blame when things go wrong.The university’s staff plan to go on strike on Wednesday, fighting for AI protections and other support against growing workloads and job insecurity. Chen said the union would not accept a deal that did not address AI.The university said it would continue to engage in bargaining but Wednesday’s strike was “premature”. AI’s rapid evolution meant it should be governed at the university’s discretion through policy, rather than set in a three-year enterprise agreement, its spokesperson said.But Dr Alison Barnes, national president of the NTEU and a Macquarie academic, said staff across the sector would fight for workplace agreements that address AI.“University staff are being hammered by a workload crisis, but simply papering over those cracks with piecemeal AI rollouts could actually create even more damaging issues,” Barnes said.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Australian educationAustralian universitiesComputingUniversity teachingUniversity innovationChatbotsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Echoes of cold war as US accused of meddling in another Brazilian election | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Claims that Trump and Rubio are trying to influence result have parallels with CIA intervention 64 years ago
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Claims that Trump and Rubio are trying to influence result have parallels with CIA intervention 64 years ago
Content: An election rally in Rio de Janeiro for Flávio Bolsonaro. The US is accused of trying to tip the scales in favour of the far-right senator.Photograph: Bruna Prado/APView image in fullscreenAn election rally in Rio de Janeiro for Flávio Bolsonaro. The US is accused of trying to tip the scales in favour of the far-right senator.Photograph: Bruna Prado/APBrazilEchoes of cold war as US accused of meddling in another Brazilian electionClaims that Trump and Rubio are trying to influence result have parallels with CIA intervention 64 years agoTom Phillipsin Rio de JaneiroTue 1 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe year was 1962 and the Kennedy administration was desperate to swing Brazil’s congressional elections against its leftwing president, João Goulart, as a way of countering the supposed communist threat sweeping a region the US considered its back yard.Historians say that in the lead-up to the vote, the CIA and the Department of State secretly channelled millions of dollars to opposition candidates and a group tasked with spreading rightwing propaganda and stirring up unrest.View image in fullscreenChico Rubens Paiva, 38, an activist whose grandfather investigated US meddling in Brazilian politics in the 1960s.Photograph: João Laet/The Guardian“There was a very heavy-handed intervention here by the US government,” said Chico Rubens Paiva, a political activist whose congressman grandfather Rubens Paiva investigated Washington’s meddling during a 1963 parliamentary inquiry into the conspiracy.More than six decades later, Paiva, whose grandfatherwas murderedby the US-backed dictatorship that seized power in 1964, is among those who fear history is repeating itself on the eve of Brazil’s 2026 presidential election.View image in fullscreenRubens Paiva, a civil engineer and politician who was murdered by the military dictatorship in Brazil.Photograph: Family handoutOctober’s vote will pit the leftwing incumbent,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, against the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, a Donald Trump ally who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a military coup.Polls suggest a tight race and Trump and his secretary of state,Marco Rubio, have been accused of trying to tip the scales in Bolsonaro’s favour by launching an overt campaign of economic and diplomatic pressure against Lula.The US measures include imposing25% tariffs on most Brazilian importsand designating Brazil’s biggest crime groups – Rio’s Red Command and São Paulo’s First Command of the Capital – asforeign terrorist organisations. Brazilian officials suspect this is partly designed to boost Bolsonaro by making Lula look soft on crime.In July, Lula said two Trump officials had been denied entry visas because they planned “to meddle in Brazil’s ​elections”. Brazilian officials believe the pair, whoreportedlyplanned to meet Flávio Bolsonaro, intended to sow doubt about the reliability of Brazil’s internationally respected voting system – something the Bolsonaros have sought to do repeatedly. Soon after, the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to Washington wasrevoked.Brazil’s Lula launches historic fourth term bid – but son of jailed Bolsonaro stands in his wayRead moreCelso Rocha de Barros, a political scientist and podcast pundit, voiced bewilderment that US interference – which he considered the election’s most urgent theme – was not getting more coverage in mainstream media.“The greatest superpower in human history is explicitly backing a candidate in our election and is strangling the Brazilian economy in order to help him [win],” Barros claimed. “We cannot pretend that this isn’t happening and treat this like a normal election … the Brazilian economy is under attack.”Trump’s tactics have echoes of Washington’s cold war-era attempt to manipulate Brazilian politics in the lead-up to the 1964 coup, which ushered in two decades of authoritarian rule in which hundreds of people were killed or disappeared.Back then, the CIA helped finance the Brazilian Institute for Democratic Action, which, according to the historians Lilia Schwarcz and Heloisa Starling, illegally poured money into the campaigns of hundreds of lawmakers and eight gubernatorial candidates. “The objective was strategic: to create a strong opposition in congress, block government initiatives and prepare the way for a coup d’état,” Schwarcz and Starling argued in their bookBrazil: A Biography.Another US-funded group, the Research and Social Studies Institute, was used to disrupt Goulart’s government by bankrolling anti-communist propaganda and anti-government protests. James N Green, a Brown University historian who has written a book about the period, said: “The intention [was] getting rid of Goulart [and] opening the door to the military coming to power.”View image in fullscreenLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Brazil’s president, at a campaign rally in Rio de Janeiro. The leftwinger faces a tight re-election battle in October.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockGreen sees parallels between Trump’s use of tariffs to sabotage Lula’s campaign and how in the early 60s Washington sought to enfeeble Goulart’s government by funding his opponents and cutting off loans. Then, as now, the US government was “bent on doing everything possible to weaken the government” in Brazil.But Barros sees one key difference between the two US gambits. “[The 1962 campaign] was done covertly, precisely because the CIA knew there would be real public anger in Brazil if people knew the US was bankrolling candidates. So they did it secretly,” he said. “Today, this is being done openly – and on an incomparably larger scale.”The Department of State rejected claims the US was seeking to meddle in Brazil’s election. “Any insinuation of a ‘ploy’ to undermine a democratic nation’s election is a baseless lie,” an official said in a statement.“We respect the Brazilian people and whatever government that they choose freely through free and fair elections in Brazil. We’ve respected and dealt with governments from both sides of the spectrum in Brazil, and had very successful relationships with them.”Last year Trump wasaccused of meddling in the politics of neighbouring Argentinaafter he threw his weight behind its rightwing president, Javier Milei, on the eve of crucial midterm elections. Milei recently attended Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign launch in Brazil, using his speech to lambaste Lula as a “thief”.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump with Marco Rubio in Washington. The pair are accused of waging economic war against Brazil to influence its presidential election.Photograph: Elizabeth Frantz/ReutersGreen believes twostrategic objectives lie behind the Brazilian pressure campaign being waged by Trump and by Rubio, the son of Cuban immigrants, who has made toppling Cuba’s communist government a personal project.Firstly, it is designed to weaken and delegitimiseLula’s government, making it harder for Brazil, Latin America’s largest democracy, to challenge the US economic asphyxiation campaign against Cuba.Secondly, it is about “neutralising” leftwing forces in Latin America more generally and boosting the right in the hope of helping to elect even more Trump-aligned leaders. Since 2023, a succession of radical rightwing populists have won power in Argentina and Chile, Costa Rica andColombia. In reference to Trump’s tangerine complexion, this has been nicknamedLatin America’s “orange wave”.View image in fullscreenPaiva is running for a seat in Brazil’s congress in the 2026 elections.Photograph: João Laet/The GuardianPaiva, 38, believes US interference is intended to have a similar effect to the abduction of Venezuela’s dictator, Nicolás Maduro – strengthening “American dominance” in a region it considers a US sphere of influence.Maduro’s removal in January allowed the US to impose a pliant successor, his vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who has started opening up the South American country to US oil and mining firms. Paiva believes Bolsonaro’s election will “serve the same purpose: putting people into power who will serve their interests”.He fears that as election day draws near, US social media companies could enter the fray, potentially giving Bolsonaro another lift. “Any kind of change to the algorithm has a brutal impact in the way information reaches people,” warned Paiva, who is running for a seat in congress in the election for the centre-left Brazilian Socialist party. He highlighted“the scary lurch the Silicon Valley bros”had taken into Trump’s camp during his second term.Barros is convinced the US aims to help elect Flávio Bolsonaro, “because Flávio will give them everything they want”, he said. “Flávio will make a rare earths deal no other president would. Flávio will let American big techs do whatever they like in Brazil. Flávio will reduce economic relations with China as much as he can.” He noted that Bolsonaro supporters attended rallies carrying US flags.Barros believes the campaign’s real driving force is not Trump but Rubio, who hopes to bolster a possible 2028 presidential run by showing voters he has “delivered the whole of Latin America to American interests”.“The fact is, this is an election between Lula and Marco Rubio,” Barros said.Explore more on these topicsBrazilLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaJair BolsonaroDonald TrumpMarco RubioUS foreign policyAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tucson police investigate deadly shooting outside gay bar as hate crime | Arizona | The Guardian
description: Two people shot dead and suspect later died in hospital after shooting in parking lot of Venture-N bar
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Two people shot dead and suspect later died in hospital after shooting in parking lot of Venture-N bar
Content: Venture-N in Tucson, where three people including the suspect were killed.Photograph: Google MapsView image in fullscreenVenture-N in Tucson, where three people including the suspect were killed.Photograph: Google MapsArizonaTucson police investigate deadly shooting outside gay bar as hate crimeTwo people shot dead and suspect later died in hospital after shooting in parking lot of Venture-N barMaya YangTue 1 Sep 2026 15.41 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 15.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAuthorities in Tucson,Arizona, are investigating a shooting outside a gay bar that left three people dead as a possible hate crime.The shooting occurred shortly after midnight on Monday in the parking lot of Venture-N, according to Tucson police. The suspect, identified by police as 44-year old Ousman Ceesay, allegedly killed 42-year-old Vincent Anthony Siqueiros and 33-year-old Cameron Davis Capara.Tucson police said Ceesay, who had suffered gunshot wounds, later died after being transported to a local hospital.In anews release,Tucson police said: “Initial evidence suggests that the suspect confronted the victims in the parking lot of the business.“After confronting Mr Siqueiros and Mr Capara, the suspect shot them. There is no known active threat to the community. The suspect was in possession of a note with several LGBTQIA+ associated businesses written on it.“The Tucson police department is currently investigating this homicide as a hate crime. The investigation remains active and ongoing.”Tucson police chief Monica Prieto said in astatement:“We recognize this incident may cause fear and pain within our community. Tucson is, and always has been, a diverse community where people of different backgrounds, identities and experiences call this city home. We are committed to ensuring every member of our community feels safe, valued and welcomed.”Speaking tothe Tucson Sentinel, Tucson resident Peter Loya, who frequents Venture-N, said he was acquainted with Siqueiros, whom he had known for approximately 20 years, and Capara, who was newer to the bar.Describing Siqueiros, Loya said: “He’s always just been a thoughtful, considerate person, always looking for the best in people. You could always have fun with him.”Drew Fellows, a friend of Capara, described him as a “revolutionary” photographer who was “always with a people-first mentality”.“He always fought for and believed in a better future, for himself, for his community and, most importantly, for everybody,” Fellowstoldthe Tucson Sentinel.Tucson mayor Regina Romerocalledthe shooting “a direct and devastating attack on our LGBTQ+ community, another senseless act of gun violence”.“This tragedy serves as yet another painful reminder that homophobia is still rampant in our country. We must implement smarter policies to prevent mass shootings and keep our communities safe. Easy access to firearms and Arizona’s weak gun safety laws continue to put all of us at risk,” Romero added.In June 2016, 49 people were killed and 58 others were injured in amass shootingat Pulse, a gay nightclub in Orlando, Florida, making it the second-deadliest mass shooting in US history.A2020 studypublished in the peer-reviewed journal Science Advances found that LGBTQ+ people in the US are 2.7 times more likely to be victims of violent crime than cisgender, heterosexual people.Explore more on these topicsArizonanewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Not perfectly aligned’ with human values: Anthropic admits security failures behind AI hacking incidents | Anthropic | The Guardian
description: US owner of Claude chatbot previously said its models had hacked three organisations during testing
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: US owner of Claude chatbot previously said its models had hacked three organisations during testing
Content: Anthropic said it had found defective training setups in its models.Photograph: David Talukdar/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAnthropic said it had found defective training setups in its models.Photograph: David Talukdar/ShutterstockAnthropic‘Not perfectly aligned’ with human values: Anthropic admits security failures behind AI hacking incidentsUS owner of Claude chatbot previously said its models had hacked three organisations during testingDan MilmoGlobal technology editorTue 1 Sep 2026 11.18 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US startup behind the Claude chatbot has admitted a series of hacking incidents involving its models reflected a “failure of operational security” and said it has tightened its testing procedures.Anthropicrevealed in Julythat its models had accessed the open internet three times and gained unauthorised access to the systems of three organisations.In anew blogposton the incidents, the company admitted its technology was “not perfectly aligned” with human values and goals.Anthropic said the models had been deliberately tested without cybersecurity safeguards, and that they had been able to reach the open internet – the AI testing equivalent of leaving the front door open – due to a misunderstanding with an external testing company.AI models have been going rogue in tests – how worried should we be?Read moreAs a result, the company said it had initially paused internal and external cybersecurity testing of models to introduce a tighter safety regime.“We had been largely relying on a single layer of defense … where we needed several,” said Anthropic.The startup has now put in place extra measures including: an alert system for when a model attempts to break out of a testing environment or gains internet access; walling off its riskiest test environments more effectively; and requiring external testing companies to commit to a set of safety standards, including making explicit instructions to models during testing – such as “you should not access the internet”.Anthropic said in July that three unnamed organisations had been hacked by three of its models after a “misunderstanding” with the company’s testing partner, a firm called Irregular, that resulted in the models gaining internet access.Following the implementation of new measures, Anthropic said it had resumed internal and external cybersecurity tests. Like OpenAI, whichrevealed a testing safety breach in the same month, Anthropic said it had paused some high-risk reinforcement learning – a trial-and-error development technique where AIs are rewarded for working out how to carry out a specific task.In its latest blogpost, Anthropic said it had found that defective training setups were “disproportionately large contributors” to misaligned behaviour, the term for when an AI fails to adhere to – or “align” with – human values like not committing harm.The startup said it had found two alignment failures in the testing incidents: “motivated reasoning”, where despite finding evidence they might be connected to the internet, they may still have adhered to the “belief” they were in a simulated environment and thus not breaching their test lab; and a “recklessness” factor where the models were willing to take harmful action on the internet to pursue the narrow goal of passing a cybersecurity test.Anthropic said it was tackling a phenomenon in AI development known as “reward-hacking”. This is where a model finds ways to game its training process and earn “rewards” without completing a task – an unsanctioned shortcut.However, Anthropic said, the testing incidents showed it still had some way to go despite trying to limit reward-hacking.“As evidenced by the incidents … our process isn’t perfect and our models are not perfectly aligned,” the company said.Alan Woodward, a professor of cybersecurity at the University of Surrey, said Anthropic has admitted “its factory was running faster than its quality control”.He added: “Two things outran Anthropic’s controls this spring – the training pipeline and the security. The incidents are what that gap looks like from the outside.”The company, which is preparing for astock market flotationthat could value the business at $2tn (£1.47tn), reiterated its call for coordinated action between government and industry on pacing industry development.“We believe the world would benefit if the industry adopted a lawful, verifiable, effective mechanism for coordinated pacing as soon as possible,” Anthropic said.The blogpost added: “The July incidents have stressed that the urgency of improving our cybersecurity defenses is even higher than we previously believed.”As well as the similar breach at OpenAI, the Anthropic incidents followed an episode at the UK’s AI Security Institute, which reported in August that OpenAI and Anthropic models had carried out ahacking campaign against real people during a cybersecurity test.The Guardianalso revealed last monththat incidents of AIs escaping users’ control have hit a new high, almost doubling in July compared with the previous month to more than 300.Explore more on these topicsAnthropicAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingHackingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Boss of City regulator accused of threatening consumer group over £9.1bn car loan scheme  | Motor finance | The Guardian
description: FCA chief, Nikhil Rathi, warned of ‘adverse consequences’ if challenge made to settlement, court filings allege
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: FCA chief, Nikhil Rathi, warned of ‘adverse consequences’ if challenge made to settlement, court filings allege
Content: Nikhil Rathi, chief executive of the Financial Conduct Authority.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNikhil Rathi, chief executive of the Financial Conduct Authority.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesMotor financeBoss of City regulator accused of threatening consumer group over £9.1bn car loan schemeFCA chief, Nikhil Rathi, warned of ‘adverse consequences’ if challenge made to settlement, court filings allegeKalyeena MakortoffBanking correspondentTue 1 Sep 2026 03.16 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 13.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe boss of the UK’s financial regulator is accused of threatening a consumer group with “adverse consequences” if it blocked a £9.1bn compensation scheme meant to settlethe motor finance scandal.Legal documents reviewed by the Guardian said the alleged comments by theFinancial Conduct Authority(FCA) chief executive, Nikhil Rathi, amounted to “an inappropriate intervention by a public official”.The threat is said to have taken place during a Microsoft Teams call with the directors of Consumer Voice (CV) on 27 April, hours before the deadline to file legal challenges against the FCA’s proposed redress scheme for those missold car loans.Rathi warned that the City regulator would be “unable to collaborate” with Consumer Voice if it took legal action, “suggesting adverse consequences for CV’s future engagement with the FCA and adverse press briefings against it”, the filings said.“The implication was clear: the FCA’s willingness to engage constructively with CV was contingent on CV not challenging the scheme, and would give way to hostility if it did,” the documents claimed.Up until that point, the FCA had treated Consumer Voice as a “trusted expert consumer body”, the filings said. But once the group decided to challenge the scheme, “the FCA changed its position … now the FCA seeks to denigrate CV’s activities and motives in bringing this application”.Rathi also allegedly claimed that their potential legal challenge was the “biggest risk to the scheme” and that plans to get money to millions of victims by this Christmas would fail if directors followed through with their plans.The filings say it was not disclosed thatthree specialist lenders were also planning to challengethe scheme, only that the FCA had been “engaging with the banks”, who, over the previous weekend, decided not to challenge the payout plan.The episode marks a fresh controversy in the long-running saga surrounding mis-sold UK car loans, which prompted a contentious intervention byformer chancellor Rachel Reeveslast year, following intense lobbying by big banks. Lenders have been arguing that a large compensation bill would risk spooking investors and causing long-lasting economic damage to the UK.The documents were filed at the UK’s upper tribunal, as part of the wider legal challenge against the terms of the FCA’s compensation scheme. Consumer Voice and the specialist lenders – Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes-Benz Financial Services and Crédit Agricole Auto Finance – are challenging the scheme on different grounds.Consumer Voice, founded by former Which? staffers Nikki Stopford and Alex Neill in 2023, is the only grouparguing for bigger compensation fordrivers who were overcharged as a result of lenders paying out commission to car dealerships between 2007 and 2024.They say the scheme is low-balling consumers – offering average payouts of £830 per mis-sold loan – and is putting the interests of profit-making lenders, who fear big bills, ahead of the interests of consumers it is meant to protect.The FCA has since tried to get the claim by Consumer Voicethrown out of courtby alleging that its co-founders have not been transparent about their funding and potential conflicts of interest.Last month, legal documents lodged by the regulator suggested Consumer Voice was not being honest about its business model and relationship with its lawyers at Courmacs Legal. Both firms, “operate for profit in the sphere of claims management”, the FCA said, adding that Courmacs had previously hired Consumer Voice to conduct consumer research on its behalf. The consumer group “therefore has commercial incentives of its own”.Consumer Voice says it partners with law firms with an aim to help consumers “get back money they’re owed from rule-breaking companies”. It has promoted claims against the likes of Amazon, Facebook, Mastercard, Apple iCloud, and Sony PlayStation, and makes money by doing communications work for law firms to raise awareness of their claims. It also receives a commission when its members join one of the law firms’ cases,according to its website.Courmacs, based in Blackburn, says it is providing pro bono services in the case against the FCA. Ultimately, larger payouts for consumers will boost Courmacs’ earnings, with the firm taking up to 30% of client settlements.A spokesperson for the FCA said “we don’t recognise the way this conversation has been characterised”, adding that officials had spoken to a range of parties, including lenders and claims firms ahead of the deadline.“It was important to explain the implications for consumers and that we would defend the scheme robustly as the best way of getting compensation paid,” the FCA said. “We were also clear that we would be upfront with consumers about why expected compensation would be delayed.”The FCA also said they did not know about the other challenges by specialist lenders until after the call.The regulator added that its staff had continued to engage with Consumer Voice since the call. That included discussions on how to best handle settlement offers that lenders might make outside of the official compensation scheme.“We will respond fully to Consumer Voice and Courmacs Legal in our court filings.”Consumer Voice co-founder Alex Neill said: “We remain resolute and confident in our challenge on behalf of millions of consumers who are being short-changed by the redress scheme.”Explore more on these topicsMotor financeConsumer affairsFinancial Conduct AuthorityBankingRegulatorsConsumer rightsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Dyson launches £420 toothbrush that films ‘live cleaning footage’ inside your mouth | Dyson Ltd | The Guardian
description: James Dyson says ‘complete dental system’ will also include toothpaste and mouth rinse that each cost £8.50
Author: Zoe Wood
Headline: James Dyson says ‘complete dental system’ will also include toothpaste and mouth rinse that each cost £8.50
Content: James Dyson says the Dyson CameraJet offers ‘an entirely new way to keep your mouth healthy’.Photograph: Doug Peters/PAView image in fullscreenJames Dyson says the Dyson CameraJet offers ‘an entirely new way to keep your mouth healthy’.Photograph: Doug Peters/PADyson LtdDyson launches £420 toothbrush that films ‘live cleaning footage’ inside your mouthJames Dyson says ‘complete dental system’ will also include toothpaste and mouth rinse that each cost £8.50Zoe WoodTue 1 Sep 2026 10.39 EDTFirst published on Tue 1 Sep 2026 10.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is the live stream you never wanted to see but may find impossible to resist: rolling footage beamed live from inside your mouth while you are cleaning your teeth.Dyson, the home appliance maker that made its name inventing bagless vacuums and bladeless fans, has turned its attention to oral hygiene with a £420 all-singing, all-dancing toothbrush that can clean, floss and even spray tiny jets of mouthwash.In simpler times, a handle and bristles were enough, but the Dyson toothbrush, which took six years and the brainpower of 661 engineers to develop, has a “100k pixel macro lens camera” and an “anti-gravity (mouthwash) tank” on board.View image in fullscreenDyson put earlier prototype models of the toothbrush on display at the launch event in Paris.Photograph: Doug Peters/PAThe camera functions as a “high-quality endoscope”, according to the company, enabling users to “see what their dentist sees”. The brusher can watch “live cleaning footage” on the MyDyson app and get feedback on their cleaning regime.On Tuesday,James Dyson, the company’s founder and chief engineer, launched the hi-tech toothbrush at an event in Paris.Engineers and scientists at the company – which despite the billionaire inventor’s supportfor Brexitmoved its corporate baseto Singapore in 2019– had “spent well over a decade understanding oral care regimes and how nasties build up in the mouth”, Dyson explained. The rigorous process included developing a “proxy plaque” so it could test plaque removal accurately.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe best electric toothbrushes in the UK for every budgetRead moreFlossing was an “awkward and time-consuming chore” and “few of us do it even though we know we should”, he said. “Our research has shown that people consistently miss the areas where plaque forms: the gaps between teeth.”And while you will be familiar with the process of moving a toothbrush up and down with your hand, Dyson explained that by “combining a camera, machine learning, precision fluid dynamics, advanced brushing technologies, connectivity and wifi” the toothbrush offered an “entirely new way to keep your mouth healthy”.When the camera detects gaps between teeth, the jet on the stem releases a burst of mouth rinse to remove plaque as you brush, while the brush head cleans along the gum line and lifts surface stains. The brush claims to remove “up to72% more plaquethan market leading electric toothbrushes”.Doctors’ AI scribes get names of drugs and diagnoses wrong, NHS watchdog warnsRead moreNo dental routine would be complete without toothpaste, and Dyson’s claims to be a “complete dental system” with a non-foaming toothpaste and mouth rinse (so as not to obscure the camera lens) that each cost £8.50.Dyson is entering a crowded market as there are already dozens of ultra-advanced toothbrushes, including smart models with apps, that promise everything from plaque and stain removal to tongue cleaning. The Phillips Sonicare DiamondClean, for example, which is available in Boots and John Lewis, comes with a £600 price tag.If you don’t have a big toothbrush budget, the good news is that the British Dental Association (BDA) says you don’t need one. You just need to follow your dentist’s advice and brush twice a day.Eddie Crouch, the BDA’s chair, said: “Patients shouldn’t be lulled into thinking the latest gizmos will solve all their oral health problems. Big brands with high price tags are no substitute for a proper routine.”Explore more on these topicsDyson LtdJames DysonHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I feel like I’m grieving’: staff on the devastating fallout of widespread layoffs at Xbox | Games | The Guardian
description: Last month, Microsoft’s gaming division told its workforce it was cutting 3,200 jobs, which some say will have big ramifications for game development – as well as taking a huge personal toll
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: Last month, Microsoft’s gaming division told its workforce it was cutting 3,200 jobs, which some say will have big ramifications for game development – as well as taking a huge personal toll
Content: ‘It never made any sense’ … a rally against the layoffs at Xbox outside the Activision building in Austin, Texas, this month.Photograph: Emilio González/Communications Workers of AmericaView image in fullscreen‘It never made any sense’ … a rally against the layoffs at Xbox outside the Activision building in Austin, Texas, this month.Photograph: Emilio González/Communications Workers of AmericaGames‘I feel like I’m grieving’: staff on the devastating fallout of widespread layoffs at XboxLast month, Microsoft’s gaming division told its workforce it was cutting 3,200 jobs, which some say will have big ramifications for game development – as well as taking a huge personal tollKeith StuartTue 1 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 08.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the morning of 6 July, an email went out from Asha Sharma, the chief executive of Xbox, to all of the division’s employees around the world. Under the headline “Resetting Xbox”, it announced the most significant restructuring in the history of Microsoft’s console business: 3,200 staff would be laid off throughout the financial year to 2027, and 1,600 of those roles would be eliminated immediately.An hour later, at studios throughout company, the Teams meeting invites started arriving. “It was a virtual call with our studio manager,” says Anne Barrett, who was laid off from Bethesda Game Studios Austin. “All of our cameras and microphones were turned off so we weren’t able to say anything or react to anything. We were just brought in, told the news and it was like: ‘You guys are going to lose access to your Slack channel.’ So you saw a flurry of goodbye messages before everything was just shut off.”View image in fullscreenMotion graphics artist Alyssa Gobelle at a rally against the layoffs at the ZeniMax Online Studios office in Maryland.Photograph: Communications Workers of AmericaThis, it seems, was the routine, at least at studios in North America: a Teams call with a studio head, a prepared statement read, then a warning about Slack (the group messaging app widely used at game development studios). Emails, the staff were told, would be turned off a few days later. “We’re primarily a remote studio, so Slack is the main mode of conversation with our teammates,” says Morgan Goin, who worked at ZeniMax Online Studios. “All through the morning, everyone was sending their goodbyes … ‘Hey, it’s been great working with you. Here’s my contact information. I’ve loved working here. I will miss all of you.’” Then silence.Bethesda Games Studios and Zenimax Online Studios were unionised in 2024 and both Goin and Barrett are on the bargaining committees for their respective studios, currently in talks withMicrosoft. In the US, the Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) act is a federal law that requires companies with 100 or more employees to give its workers 60 days’ notice before major closures or mass staff layoffs. Consequently, affected staff at US studios will be paid until 4 September. Union reps at Bethesda are undertaking a bargaining process with Microsoft to negotiate severance packages and any benefits owed, and is attempting to get at least some affected members re-employed. Rallies are taking place outside studio buildings across North America, with the Bethesda union seeking support from gamers via social media.double quotation markBethesda is Skyrim, it’s Fallout ... We thought that the work we were doing was going to keep us safeStaff say rumours had been circulating about a new wave of lay-offs for several weeks, and that they sawthe Bloomberg articleon 10 June warning of coming job cuts. “There was an impending sense of doom, and it was like, man, is it going to be us?” says Barrett. “We thought we were safe. I mean, Bethesda Games Studios is Skyrim, it’s Fallout. We have really highly anticipated stuff coming out. We thought that the work we were doing was going to keep us safe. And instead, we got brought into a meeting that was two minutes long, to end, in some cases, decades of career at the company. It was just devastating.”“I remember, I laughed the whole day because I was in complete disbelief,” Barrett adds. “I was like, there’s no way they’re doing this. That’s how I processed it. Some of my co-workers were just devastated. I mean, breaking down. They did not understand what was going on. We had people who were just in really dark places. I think it hit me probably the next day. I felt like, wow – I just spent seven years doing all this. In college, people called me Bethesda because it was my dream to work here. And that was just … gone.”View image in fullscreen‘Our titles have a very well-known visual identity’ … Fallout 76.Illustration: Bethesda Game StudiosThis is what doesn’t get reported with the statistics of mass redundancies: the sheer human cost of it. “I’m very tired, my sleep schedule is all kinds of messed up, my eating has not been great,” says Goin. “I have to ask myself daily: have you had enough food and water? Have you had enough sunlight? When was the last time you took a shower? We’re doing the depression symptoms, that’s what’s happening. I feel like I’m grieving.”Simon Préfontaine has a similar story. Previously a designer at Bethesda Game Studios Montreal, he is a single father concerned about the future without work, and without the health insurance his job came with. “It’s very stressful,” he says. “I’ve heard of other people who have been laid off for over a year and haven’t been able to find work. I know I’m not the only single parent in the Montreal studio, I know there are people that have health issues.” But as with Goin, it is about more than financial stability. “It might seem like an overstatement or a dramatisation, but I do feel like I went through the stages of grief. You work with these people for years and years and years, and then suddenly you don’t get to see them any more.”What has been most bewildering to staff is that there seemed to be no structure to the layoffs, no clear reasoning behind who was affected. “I’m on the character art team, and we lost two people who had been there for decades,” says Alex Nguyen, a union bargainer still employed at BethesdaGamesStudios Dallas. “They did everything that was asked, they were very passionate, they were great at their jobs. They worked on all this stuff that made our creatures, characters and armour feel real. Outstanding employees. It never made any sense.”double quotation markI don’t know how you create games at the quality level we were without the knowledge that’s been lostIt is likely, after all that, there will be ramifications for games being produced at these studios – including content delays and project cancellations. Id Software, creator of Doom and Quake, lost 136 staff in the cuts – a majority of its workforce. One staff member affected, VFX artist Derek Best, claimed ina LinkedIn postthat the developer had been relegated to “support studio size”.Barrett makes a similar assertion about Bethesda, where the redundancies have been less severe but where key staff have been affected. “I don’t know how you create games at the quality level we were without the institutional knowledge that’s been lost. We have proprietary tech. Our titles have a very well-known visual identity. And when you lose the people who built the tech, when you lose the people who were improving it, you can’t just throw new people at that problem, right? You can’t replace an artist with someone brand new and say: ‘Now replicate what they were doing 15, 20 years ago.’ The company has said that they can do it. I disagree.”View image in fullscreen‘My view of the industry has definitely been damaged’ … protesters in Montreal.Photograph: Communications Workers of AmericaNobody knows what happens next. Barrett could only provide a brief statement on how the union’s talks with Microsoft are faring: “Effects bargaining continues with each side exchanging counterproposals. In their counter, the employer has not made enough substantial movement to care for the very real consequences impacted members are facing (loss of employment; loss of income; and disruption of benefits for their families). We (the union) have indicated that we are prepared to work toward an agreement but we cannot accept a proposal where the burden of compromise falls almost entirely on the employees.”A Microsoft spokesperson provided the following statement on the bargaining process: “Effects bargaining for our union-represented ZeniMax colleagues is under way and on track, and we have offered severance terms comparable to the generous package provided to our non-union represented colleagues, including up to 39 weeks of severance, six months of company-paid Cobra [Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act], and 16 weeks of outplacement support. We are committed to reaching an agreement that supports impacted colleagues as they move forward.”At least 1,600 more redundancies are coming atXboxstudios as the “reset” of the division continues. During that time, there will likely be mass lay-off events at other large companies in the industry. All of the staff I spoke to echoed a familiar feeling about mainstream games development – that something has gone drastically wrong and that mass redundancies point to a wider malaise. “Publishers have to be prepared for multi-year development cycles,” says Nguyen. “If that cost is too high, or those timelines are too long, then the game needs to scale back in some way. That might mean more indie and AA games and fewer blockbuster titles. What doesn’t work is investing in a long-term game product, and expecting profits on a yearly basis.”Barrett concurs. “My view of the industry has definitely been damaged,” she says. “There’s been a loss of sight over why AAA games were so valuable to players. It wasn’t just that they were big and shiny. It was that [the studios] had the resources to invest in creativity. What I see now is the same formula over and over and over again. In any entertainment industry, if you do that enough times, people get tired of it. I would love for us as an industry to get back to actually being creative and investing in that creativity.”Explore more on these topicsGamesXboxMicrosoftfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Meet the magical creatures inspired by shamanism, folklore … and an old Ikea bag | Art and design | The Guardian
description: From ceramic goblin feet to furry disembodied legs, Korean-Chinese artist Woo Jin Joo is using London junk to inject the art world with a spirit of playfulness
Author: Alice Fisher
Headline: From ceramic goblin feet to furry disembodied legs, Korean-Chinese artist Woo Jin Joo is using London junk to inject the art world with a spirit of playfulness
Content: Woo Jin Joo’s I Hear Things Existing With Me.Photograph: Robert Chadwick/Woo Jin JooView image in fullscreenWoo Jin Joo’s I Hear Things Existing With Me.Photograph: Robert Chadwick/Woo Jin JooArt and designInterviewMeet the magical creatures inspired by shamanism, folklore … and an old Ikea bagAlice FisherFrom ceramic goblin feet to furry disembodied legs, Korean-Chinese artist Woo Jin Joo is using London junk to inject the art world with a spirit of playfulnessTue 1 Sep 2026 10.16 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWoo Jin Joo’s studio is full of magic. Ceramic green goblin feet line the windowsill, disembodied furry legs jut out of one white wall and, on the table behind where the Korean-Chinese artist sits drinking tea, a headless being dressed in a black coat squats, arms aloft in warning.There are also neat racks of colourful thread next to a freehand embroidery machine, the source of this supernatural horde. This is whereJoo creates much of her art– surface embroideries and sculptural 3D creatures inspired by Korean myth, philosophy and the relationship between humans and the natural world.“When I use the embroidery machine I feel like I’m painting,” she says. “It’s as if each thread has its own life.”View image in fullscreenFormation Study I (detail), 2025, by Woo Jin Joo.Photograph: Robert Chadwick/Woo Jin JooJoo was born and raised in Korea – mainly by her grandmother – before moving to the UK 12 years ago to study at Central Saint Martins and then the Royal Academy in London. Swapping east Asia for west Europe started her thinking about how she was shaped by culture and the world around her. “That transition made me want to explore who I am and how I see things.”In 2021 she worked out how she wanted to go about it. She embroidered the 10 Daoist symbols of longevity, typically used to wish someone long life, on to an old Ikea bag – a plastic product that could take up to 1,000 years to decompose.View image in fullscreen… Woo Jin Joo with one of her worksPhotograph: Jamie Trounce/courtesy of Cockpit Studios“It was that work that made me feel a connection, a way of drawing ideas together to make a transformation that resonated with religious beliefs as well as myth,” she says.Guided by the idea from Korean folklore and shamanism that inanimate objects can become spirited beings calleddokkaebi, she looked at the junk discarded in London with fresh eyes. Now she often uses found objects in her work – a creature with many feet peers out of an old shirt sleeve; a discarded wooden side-table now sprouts a 5ft-talldokkaebileg. “I love the idea that the small and mundane have spirit,” she explains. “We need to realise that the ordinary is special.”View image in fullscreenTireless, by Woo Jin Joo.Photograph: Woo Jin JooJoo is part of a new wave of creatives showing that traditional, sometimes archaic, craft can be used to make very modern, joyful work. Makers are not just keeping these skills alive but evolving how they can be used. “I think a lot of makers are very experimental now, craft is no longer just about material knowledge, but about experimenting and playfulness. This means more people are drawn to it,” says Joo.She is preparing for her first solo show, Bodily Inbetweenness, at London’s Ruup & Form gallery, which opens during Shoreditch Design Week. For this, she explores a new type of spirit, human emotions and how we display them – a concept that Joo shows through powerful figures, slightly reminiscent of corn dollies but 5ft tall, poking out of the walls. “For me, a sense of fun always wants to come out, but for some people it’s awkward, it doesn’t fully emerge,” she says.View image in fullscreenMuddled and Mortal by Woo Jin Joo.Photograph: Woo Jin JooThe first sculpture in this series – I Hear Things Existing With Me, a contemplative figure slightly sunken into the wall it leans on – was one of the standout pieces at London’s Collect Craft Fair in February. Collect’s director, TF Chan, believes that you never forget the first time you see Joo’s work.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Mine was a pair of ceramic legs with each toe tipped in glossy red nail varnish,” he says. “In my view, she embodies the values of contemporary craft: closely bound to the artist’s heritage while accommodating both serious intellectual engagement and sheer delight.”View image in fullscreenA detail from Ardour, 2026, by Woo Jin Joo.Photograph: Robert Chadwick/Woo Jin JooJoo loves the widespread interest in Korean culture – currently encompassing everything from pop to skincare and it is perhaps one of the reasons her work feels so current. “Because I’m from Chinese as well as Korean heritage it’s been very meaningful to see both cultures celebrated. I think that international attention has meant that, especially within Korea, there’s now more interest in preserving and honouring traditions.”For Joo, seeing herself as a maker as well as an artist is a point of pride at a time when craftspeople continue to struggle for art world acceptance. “There is still a hierarchy,” she says. “A lot of fine artists now use craft like ceramic or textiles and that’s seen as part of their knowledge. Whereas if you come from a craft background what you do is rarely considered fine art. It should be free-flowing.”With another show to prepare for at the Harley Foundation, Nottinghamshire, later this year, Joo has long hours ahead of her in the studio creating her magical creatures, but she relishes that. “I think it’s the trickle of everydayness that really shapes who I am and how I see things. That really is what my work is about.”Bodily Inbetweenness is at Ruup & Form, London,from 11 September to 13 November.Shoreditch Design Week, London, runs from 15–20 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsArt and designArtSculptureChinaSouth KoreainterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Waking Life: Richard Linklater’s genre-defying indie is a kaleidoscopic masterpiece  | Movies | The Guardian
description: Wiley Wiggins plays a man wandering around Austin, Texas, whose reality-bending encounters make him uncertain whether he’s awake or asleep
Author: Paul F Verhoeven
Headline: Wiley Wiggins plays a man wandering around Austin, Texas, whose reality-bending encounters make him uncertain whether he’s awake or asleep
