Content: Julie Delpy and Ethan Hawke in Waking Life, which was originally shot in live action and then animated using the technique known as rotoscoping.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenJulie Delpy and Ethan Hawke in Waking Life, which was originally shot in live action and then animated using the technique known as rotoscoping.Photograph: APStream teamMoviesWaking Life: Richard Linklater’s genre-defying indie is a kaleidoscopic masterpieceWiley Wiggins plays a man wandering around Austin, Texas, whose reality-bending encounters make him uncertain whether he’s awake or asleepPaul F VerhoevenTue 1 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 20.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“I’m gonna tell you about a dream I once had,”Richard Linklater– playing himself in his own film Waking Life – tells Wiley Wiggins, playing the film’s unnamed protagonist. “I know when someone says that usually you’re in for a very boring next few minutes, and you might be,” Linklater adds as he hammers away at a pinball machine. “But it sounds like … what else you gonna do, right?”On paper, that’s the premise – and, if you’re cynical, the central dilemma – of Linklater’s 2001 genre-defying indie masterpiece. Wiggins plays a man wandering around Austin, Texas, who is uncertain whether he’s awake or asleep. He may be stuck in a dream, unable to wake up – or reality might just be this weird.Films often try too hard to capture what dreamsfeellike, with violent, surrealist imagery, or wacky, quasi-Lychian abstractions. In Waking Life, however, Linklater propels our hero through what feels unnervingly like a dream with none of that ham-handed crudeness. We, along with Wiggins’ dreamer, are attempting to stay on track, only to suddenly find ourselves walking down a street talking to a stranger, with no word on why, or how, we got there.That’s what Waking Life is, essentially – a collection of strange, dreamlike moments. We’re riding along with our hero as he meets a kaleidoscopic array of artists, philosophers and eccentrics, who wax lyrical about everything – from dreams, to politics, to the nature of reality itself.“We had a very, very loose script initially which changed a lot as we started shooting,” Wiggins tells me. “There was a sort of open-casting looking for odd characters around town who could speak passionately about special interests, and then that was incorporated. The whole thing was very loose during filming, which was done with little consumer DV handy cams”.Linklater has always told stories about people tussling with big, abstract ideas, whether it’s the walk-and-talk ruminations of Jesse and Céline in the Before trilogy, or the stoner philosophy of Dazed and Confused. His protagonists have the kinds of contemplative conversations wethinkwe’re having when we’re talking the ear off a stranger at a party.View image in fullscreenRichard Linklater in September 2001.Photograph: Wally Skalij/Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesBut Waking Life is not mere dorm room sophistry: it will likely introduce you to some genuinely mind-blowing ideas as you’re carried downstream through its visually sumptuous waters. The entire film is rotoscoped, a technique invented by Max Fleischer back in 1915, where artists hand-draw over each frame of the film, leading to a hyper-real animated style. Each sequence is drawn by a different animator, changing as the film’s tone does.“There were all sorts of people involved in the animation stage, painters, people who might not have any existing animation experience before,” Wiggins says. “It was a very different technique than even other rotoscoped animations … it was jarring to some viewers, but I appreciated that quality.”The Quiet Earth: New Zealand post-apocalyptic classic preys on the fear of being totally aloneRead moreFor some viewers, Waking Life prompted an exploration of lucid dreaming – the act of becoming aware, and maintaining control, during a dream. For others, it made them gently paranoid about whether they were, in fact, awake at all. “It’s funny, but I actually have done the thing where I try to turn lights on and off in a dream and can’t,” Wiggins says (as the film explains, you typically can’t do this in dreams). “I don’t know if that’s an artefact of having been in the movies, or something real.”But does Wiley think he’s awake or asleep right now? He considers this for a moment. “The last 10 years have been a series of rude awakenings, one after another,” he finally says.A great deal has happened since 2001, when Waking Life came out. In the wake of 9/11, Roger Ebert said that the film “could not come at a better time”, praising it for “[celebrating] a series of articulate, intelligent characters who seek out the meaning of their existence and do not have the answers”.“At a time when madmen think they have the right to kill us because of what they think they know about an afterlife, which is by definition unknowable, those who don’t know the answers are the only ones asking sane questions,” Ebert wrote. “True believers owe it to the rest of us to seek solutions that are reasonable in the visible world.”And with that in mind, maybe now is the perfect moment to dive back into this strange film.Waking Life is available to stream on Disney+ in Australia and Prime Video in the US. It’s available to rent or buy on in the UK.Explore more on these topicsFilmStream teamRichard LinklaterAnimation in filmfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Raygun: Breaking Badly review – the ridiculed Olympic B-girl gets the last laugh … and it’s a total joy | Television | The Guardian
description: She spent the biggest moment of her career at the Paris Olympics thrashing around like a toddler having a tantrum – then went viral globally. Now, a new Netflix film reveals how the much-mocked breakdancer got over it
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: She spent the biggest moment of her career at the Paris Olympics thrashing around like a toddler having a tantrum – then went viral globally. Now, a new Netflix film reveals how the much-mocked breakdancer got over it
Content: Out of step … Rachael Gunn in Untold Raygun: Breaking Badly on Netflix.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixView image in fullscreenOut of step … Rachael Gunn in Untold Raygun: Breaking Badly on Netflix.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixTV reviewTelevisionReviewRaygun: Breaking Badly review – the ridiculed Olympic B-girl gets the last laugh … and it’s a total joyShe spent the biggest moment of her career at the Paris Olympics thrashing around like a toddler having a tantrum – then went viral globally. Now, a new Netflix film reveals how the much-mocked breakdancer got over itStuart HeritageTue 1 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNetflix’s Untold is ostensibly a series of sports documentaries. However, since its inception five years ago, it has been most successful when sport collides with the wider celebrity machine. There have been films about Caitlyn Jenner, Jake Paul and Vinnie Jones. The gold tends to come when the subjects spill over into public notoriety. With that in mind, it was only a matter of time before they made a film about Raygun.You may remember Raygun as the Australian breakdancer who spent the biggest moment of her career at the Paris Olympics thrashing around like a toddler having a tantrum in a supermarket. If you didn’t see her routine, you will almost certainly be aware of the memes she inspired. Adele discussed her during a concert. Rachel Dratch did an impersonation of her on Jimmy Fallon. For months, Raygun was everywhere. As this film demonstrates, she really didn’t want to be.This, of course, is part of the great Olympic tradition. In every competition, a country will put up an athlete who – while perhaps the best in their country – finds themselves wildly out of their league on the international stage. Raygun entered the same Olympic pantheon asEddie the Eagle,Eric Moussambaniand theJamaican bobsleigh team; competitors whose limitations made them more famous than most champions.However, there are a couple of key differences here. The first is that Raygun was competing in a sport that had never previously been held at the Olympics, and whose inclusion was already primed for ridicule. The second is that she was competing in the age of social media, allowing every idiot with a phone to mock her performance in real time. Crashing out of the Olympics with zero points was one thing. Knowing that the world considered you a joke turned out to be far worse.Raygun – real name Dr Rachael Gunn, author of the PhD thesis Deterritorializing Gender in Sydney’s Breakdancing Scene: A B-girl’s Experience of B-boying – is understandably front and centre here, which is good because she turns out to be an intensely charismatic person, in turn open and joyful and infectious. The same can be said for her husband, Sam, a breaker whose professional name (at least before he started training children) was Sammy Sex.View image in fullscreenJoyful … Raygun (left) and B-Girl Flix in Untold Raygun: Breaking Badly.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixIt is through their eyes that this textbook Olympic underdog story is told. A country holds trials for the Olympics. The best person on the day gets through, only to realise fairly quickly that the rest of the world is leagues ahead of them. Gunn watches in dismay as she realises that her unique brand of creative breaking doesn’t mesh with the hardcore power moves of the world elite. In effect, Australia entered an interpretive dancer into a gymnastics competition. Of course she was going to do badly. By her own admission, judged by these criteria, she was “pretty shit”.It’s an opinion that, for a time, the world happened to share. A couple of Australian breakers named Tinylocks and Flix form a Greek chorus here, taking uncomfortably gleeful pleasure in Raygun’s public downfall. But their opinions are amplified by reams of social media posts that gradually balloon out of all proportion, with some falsely claiming that Gunn qualified only because her husband was head of the Olympic committee, and others projecting no end of vitriol about her perceived privilege.It was a truly ugly spectacle. Gunn began to take antidepressants and made a video begging the media to leave her alone. Needless to say, the video made the news, in one case above rolling text reporting the latest tally of dead Palestinians.But once the outrage burned off, people started to notice what Gunn had done. Rather than try to keep up with her more conventionally talented competitors, she entered the Olympics on her own terms. Obviously that didn’t work, because she left the group stage without a single point, but what we saw was a woman being her complete, undiluted self.And isn’t that more relatable than almost anything else at the Olympics? Most Olympians have pushed everything else aside for years, pinning the outcome of their lives on a single moment. Raygun, meanwhile, was a bundle of nerves – underprepared and brimming with impostor syndrome – who was simply trying to get through the day unscathed. In that respect, she may have been the most human athlete there.Untold Raygun: Breaking Badly is on Netflix nowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Super Nature review – crowd-sourced Super 8 film is a triumphant collage of hope for the natural world | Movies | The Guardian
description: Film-maker Ed Sayers’ project gathered footage from collaborators all over the world, cleverly edited to combine human and animal contributions
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: Film-maker Ed Sayers’ project gathered footage from collaborators all over the world, cleverly edited to combine human and animal contributions
Content: All manner of flora and fauna … Super Nature.Photograph: BFIView image in fullscreenAll manner of flora and fauna … Super Nature.Photograph: BFIMoviesReviewSuper Nature review – crowd-sourced Super 8 film is a triumphant collage of hope for the natural worldFilm-maker Ed Sayers’ project gathered footage from collaborators all over the world, cleverly edited to combine human and animal contributionsLeslie FelperinTue 1 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis delightful, fleet-footed film represents a labour of love both for its writer-director-producer-editor, Briton Ed Sayers, and his many, many collaborators who shot the film’s footage on Super 8 all over the world. Between them they’ve used decades-old rigs in newfangled setups with stock that, like several of the species seen here, would have gone extinct had it not been for the intervention of enthusiasts.The brief from Sayers was simply to film nature, so we get shots of all manner of flora and fauna, ranging from coral reefs to high deserts, places populated by minute bugs all the way up to whales. Given Super 8 reels can only capture a few minutes’ worth of stock, this must have been a fiendishly complex puzzle in the editing room, so all credit to Sayers not just for his own lovely footage and clever vision but for his nimble collaging of the whole thing together.It is a work embellished by a sweet, swoony original score by Alexandra Hamilton-Ayres and some dainty Foley work (sound design is by David McAuley) to lay in, for example, the sound of two ibex butting horns. Super 8 cameras don’t record sound, and in fact one of the contributions comes from a British woman who has lost her hearing, and now finds communing with nature in silence all the sweeter.Indeed, the secret strength of the film is how it includes the film-makers themselves, underscoring the continuum between nature, animals and people, all one big mostly happy, sometimes murderous family across the globe. The mini self-portraits capture characters like the woman filming the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, another who loves snakes in the Mojave, a man who is so close to the white rhinos that he looks after he cuddles up to them in the sun, and a chap with Parkinson’s who reckons his devotion to filming wildlife is one of the reasons his health hasn’t deteriorated too badly yet.Throughout, we get glimpses of Sayers himself filming seals along the Norfolk coast or lying down in the rain to shoot a snail in his garden, talking a bit about how his mother’s death shaped his feelings towards the project. Altogether, this forms the best kind of crowd-sourced art: a work that is intimate, quirky and intensely accessible.Super Nature is in UK and Irish cinemas from 4 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsBiodiversityConservationWildlifereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Led us down such a dark path’: documentary explores how 9/11 changed America | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: In Netflix film Turning Point: Generation 9/11, the lives of people forever impacted by the terrorist attack in 2001 are explored
Author: David Smith
Headline: In Netflix film Turning Point: Generation 9/11, the lives of people forever impacted by the terrorist attack in 2001 are explored
Content: A still from Turning Point: Generation 9/11.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixView image in fullscreenA still from Turning Point: Generation 9/11.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixDocumentary films‘Led us down such a dark path’: documentary explores how 9/11 changed AmericaIn Netflix film Turning Point: Generation 9/11, the lives of people forever impacted by the terrorist attack in 2001 are exploredDavid Smithin WashingtonTue 1 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 12.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwenty-five years on, memory is giving way to history. Soon the US will cross the point where half its population were born after11 September 2001or were too young to remember the day that terrorists crashed planes into the World Trade Center in New York, the Pentagon in northern Virginia and a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania.‘Environmental violence’: inside the fight to save indigenous land from becoming a nuclear dumping groundRead more“When I do that math, I get to the bomb at Hiroshima – that’s how distant it is,” says Brian Knappenberger, 56, director of a new Netflix documentary,Turning Point: Generation 9/11. “When we talk about the second world war, for our generation it seemed like a long time ago but, for the current generation of 20-year-olds, that’s how long ago it was.”Having previously made series about the “war on terror”, cold war and Vietnam war, Knappenberger felt compelled to address a generation for whom 9/11 is an abstraction they might find in a school history textbook, a solemn annual ceremony or, most disorientingly, a meme circulating on TikTok and Instagram.Speaking via Google Meet from Los Angeles, he adds: “This film is coming from a place of respecting that experience, not assuming that people understand what it felt like to live through 9/11, which is so ingrained to those of us that did. It’s to illustrate not just what terrorism meant and how frightening that was but also how the decisions made in the days and weeks and years that followed – maybe more than the events themselves – changed us as a country.”Indeed, Knappenberger’s film captures a paradox: even as 9/11 fades from living memory, we are still living in a vividly 9/11 world. “We are at a place where it is moving into distant history. But I would like people to understand what we went through and record in a documentary what those decisions did to us – and ask what kind of country we want to be.”Turning Point: Generation 9/11 follows in a long line of documentaries recounting the horror ofa day that killed nearly 3,000 people: the morning TV shows jarringly interrupted, the trapped office workers, the final phone calls, the heroic firefighters, the falling towers, the dust-coated commuters, the sombre presidential address.For older generations, it is a day when everyone remembers where they were and what they were doing. “9/11 changed my life,” Knappenberger reflects. “It changed how I saw the world. It changed how I saw the political system in the United States. It changed the course of my career. It’s hard to even describe with hindsight how profound of a change this was.”But for anyone born in the late 1990s or later, 9/11 feels like an inheritance. The documentary focuses on young people whose entire lives were directly shaped by the catastrophe. Among them is Laurel Homer, whose father,LeRoy Homer, was the co-pilot of United Flight 93. Laurel was just 10 months old when her father and passengers fought back against hijackers over Shanksville. In the film, she describes feeling like “collateral” in a narrative that consumed her family.She confides: “I know he was a hero but I wish he didn’t have to be …My entire life was kind of built around this. I’m just still struggling so much and it has taken over, like, my whole life.” Grieving a father she never knew, Laurel finds herself confronting strangers online who send callous direct messages or peddle conspiracy theories claiming the tragedy was an elaborate inside job.There is also An Nguyen, whose father,Khang Nguyen– an immigrant who grew up amid the Vietnam war before emigrating to the US – was killed while working as an electrical engineer at the Pentagon. An was four years old when his father ran out to kiss him goodbye at the preschool bus on that Tuesday morning, never to return.Knappenberger observes: “It’s incredibly profound to understand what the children of people who lost their parents, lost their loved ones on 9/11, went through on those days. But it’s more profound when you think about how it changed their lives and those events have stayed with them through the evolution that our country also went through.”To view the modern US information ecosystem through the eyes of these families exposes the depth of contemporary political cynicism, he continues. There has been “memeification” of the event, where conspiracy theories and jokes aboutOsama bin LadenorGeorge W Bushcirculate on platforms such as TikTok and Instagram.More perniciously,the “truther” movementrejects the official account of 9/11 in favour of conspiracy theories, including that it was orchestrated by the US government itself.The director says: “9/11 gave birth to the truther movement – this incredibly dark movement that rises in a disinformation environment, claiming 9/11 wasn’t real or that jet fuel can’t burn steel, that it was an inside job. When you look at these disinformation campaigns through the eyes of children who actually lost loved ones, that makes it even more profound and telling.”View image in fullscreenAn Nguyen in Turning Point: Generation 9/11.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixKnappenberger traces a thread from early conspiracy theories to today’s fractured political reality. “There is a direct line from the early 9/11 truther movement through all of the rise of conspiracy theories online, and a direct connection from that to figures likeAlex Jones, who became a leading figure in the movement, all the way through the disinformation and misinformation that we see now that divides and tears our country apart.”The timing proved fateful. Facebook launched in 2004, Reddit in 2005 and Twitter in 2006. “These platforms were coming of age right in the shadow of 9/11 and so you had this massive rise of conspiracy theories and this new technology and ways we’re communicating on social media happening at the same time. I don’t think you can separate these things. The truther movement is an early predecessor to some of the chaotic world of misinformation that we see now.”The domestic fallout of September 11 was not confined to the internet. The film tracks how the institutional apparatus constructed in the immediate aftermath of the attacks permanently altered civil liberties at home. It visits Brooklyn’s “Little Pakistan” to capture the experience of shopkeepers and families who lived the American dream before 2001, only to find their neighbourhoods subjected to FBI monitoring, harassment and suspicion almost overnight.Knappenberger highlights the creation of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and the subsequent formation of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) which, under Donald Trump, has been widely condemned for its aggressive enforcement tactics and arrests of people without criminal recordsin cities such as Minneapolis.“The violence we see ICE perpetrating on the streets of America has a direct line to 9/11,” he says. “We became fearful and suspicious of Muslim communities in America, and that infrastructure we built needed another place to go, and it continued. That fear dominates us and politicians have capitalised on that fear in order to get elected and to get power.”He adds: “There’s no question that when you see violence on the streets of America perpetrated by ICE, that is a shock of 9/11. That is the wave of violence that started on 9/11 and a direct result of decisions that were made then.This is a choice about who are we as Americans, what’s important to us and what do we do moving forward. There’s a new generation who will start to have to answer those questions for themselves.”The US has also projected violence abroad over the past quarter of a century at a cost of millions of lives. The foundational pillar of the “forever wars” was erected just three days after the twin towers fell when Congress passed the2001 Authorization for Use of Military Force (AUMF)with only a single dissenting vote. Intended to target al-Qaida and those who harboured them, the statute became an elastic legal justification for military interventions, drone campaigns and indefinite detentions across sovereign nations spanning four presidential administrations.“We created this thing called the AUMF, which is about as simple as it gets,” Knappenberger says. “That’s simply not how it works or the way our country was set up. It’s pretty clear in the constitution that Congress determines if we get a war or not. After 230 years at that point of being a country, of having a constitution, we decided after 9/11 that we weren’t going to do that any more. We decided we’re going to defer that in these cases to the president – not at all how the founders of this country saw our government working.”The long-term consequence, Knappenberger argues, has been a dangerous expansion of executive power. “That was meant to go after al-Qaida, the people that attacked us on 9/11, and it has morphed into the rationale behind lots of other wars that we’ve engaged in. In that sense we’re still feeling the effects of the ‘war on terror’ in the way that it shifted power in the United States to the executive.“It said now the president gets to decide if we’re engaging in these wars or not. That’s a huge difference in how America is supposed to operate. In that sense we’re definitely very much feeling the effects of the ‘war on terror’ still – this nebulous war on terror that can be applied and used as a justification for all these other wars.”View image in fullscreenThe World Trade Center on 9/11.Photograph: Hubert Michael Boesl/EPAIf 9/11 was the opening salvo of a new geopolitical era, the chaotic August 2021 evacuation from Hamid Karzai international airport in Kabul after a 20-year war in Afghanistan was the closing of a chapter. The mission suffered a disaster when an Isis-K suicide bomberdetonated an explosive vest at Abbey Gate, killing 13 US service members and at least 170 Afghan civilians.Knappenberger weaves the harrowing experiences of young US marines stationed at Abbey Gate into the narrative. They describe the strange experience of having to coordinate security with the Taliban – the very enemy the US had invaded to depose two decades earlier.Knappenberger says: “It didn’t seem possible that we would still have troops in Afghanistan 20 years after 9/11, especially with how fast the Taliban was driven out. Here we are 20 years after that with a new generation of people: some weren’t born, some were too young to remember 9/11. They are the ones closing it out in those final harrowing days and of course 13 people were killed in that bombing. It’s profound and on the Taliban side you have people who were also not born yet or were too young to remember the events of that day.”Alongside the US military trauma, the film foregrounds the plight of Afghan allies who placed their faith in the United States. One former Afghan military pilot, Obaidullah Durani, recounts securing evacuation for his two children to Arizona while hissick wife, Shafaro, was separated from themand left behind under Taliban rule, fracturing the family.For Knappenberger, the visual parallels between Kabul in 2021 and Saigon in 1975 represent an indictment. “One season of Turning Point wasabout the Vietnam warand you saw people who believed in the American cause fleeing in fear for their lives at the end of that war. Many people thought this was a tragedy that we should never repeat as a country but it’s something that very much was repeated when the United States left Afghanistan.“Over the course of 20 years, the United States did some good things in Afghanistan, but when we left so many people who bought into the idea of a new society ended up running for their lives. When you look at history, you think: how do we do this twice? There is no more stark example of the ineffectiveness of these efforts than the fact that these images look almost identical.”Looking back across a quarter-century defined by overseas conflict, the erosion of institutional trust, rising domestic division under Trump and military operations launched without congressional authorisation, Knappenberger goes back to the strategy articulated by Bin Laden and hisal-Qaida terrorist network.“Osama bin Laden knew that that they couldn’t take on or destroy America; they couldn’t go to war and hurt that many Americans ultimately. He was aware that they could cause America to devour itself, that there was a way of getting America so involved in these other wars and to divide America within.“That would be a way of destroying America that would be far beyond any kind of terrorist attack. He saw the way to destroy America was to turn it against itself and in that sense it’s hard to overstate the profound effect those actions had on us.”Knappenberger is left with questions and the hope that those born after 9/11 will make a different choice. “Who is an American, what is an American, how do we welcome people into our society? Those decisions were made out of fear and they were made out of suspicion, and they changed who we were. We are a different country after 9/11 than we were before. I would like the next generation to not fall into the fear and suspicion that led us down such a dark path.”Turning Point: Generation 9/11 is out onNetflixon 2 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsSeptember 11 2001NetflixfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Get up, get breakfast, noise’: the teen going viral for enduring all 400 of Merzbow’s ear-splitting albums | Music | The Guardian
description: The infamous Japanese noise artist has a vast and forbidding catalogue that commands a cult fandom. Sam Andrews, 18, is vlogging his way through the lot – and taking a stand for deep listening
Author: Archie Forde
Headline: The infamous Japanese noise artist has a vast and forbidding catalogue that commands a cult fandom. Sam Andrews, 18, is vlogging his way through the lot – and taking a stand for deep listening
Content: ‘Like Book of Revelation: The Soundtrack’ … Merzbow performing in 2007.Photograph: Aviv Small/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Like Book of Revelation: The Soundtrack’ … Merzbow performing in 2007.Photograph: Aviv Small/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockMusic‘Get up, get breakfast, noise’: the teen going viral for enduring all 400 of Merzbow’s ear-splitting albumsThe infamous Japanese noise artist has a vast and forbidding catalogue that commands a cult fandom. Sam Andrews, 18, is vlogging his way through the lot – and taking a stand for deep listeningArchie FordeTue 1 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnInstagram Reelthat looks like an 80s coming-of-age movie pops up on your feed. It’s four teenage boys in an American-style basement – comfy sofas, guitars, ping pong table – jeering and laughing. But they aren’t secretly drinking beer or planning on sneaking out. They’re brandishing a vinyl copy ofPulse Demon, the most popular album from the cult Japanese noise artist Merzbow, and subjecting themselves to its brutally harsh sound in full, for fun. “I think this is the Book of Revelation: The Soundtrack,” one guy blurts out, a vague look of fear in his eyes.Merzbow, real name Masami Akita, is the world’s most renowned noise artist. Since 1979, Akita has released more than 400 recordings, which range from a10-hour long albummisleadingly titled Merzbient (it’s anything but ambient) to afree-noise supergroupcalled Flying Testicle. Since February, Sam Andrews, the video’s 18-year-old creator, has been attempting to listen to every one, and is documenting his progress online each day. “I think of my day in album-size chunks,” he says, laughing. “It’s like, get up at seven, get breakfast and then headphones in: noise.”Some of Andrews’ videos have garnered half a million views, and drawn attention from Akita himself. More than just a stunt, they are also prompting conversation about how listeners engage with challenging music in an age of streaming services, algorithms and short-form content always pushing us towards the next thing.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueAside from the penchant for harsh noise and a love for experimental bands such as Swans and Godspeed You! Black Emperor, Andrews is a pretty regular teenager. His messy bedroom is blurred behind him on our video call. He lives in Georgia, wears a T-shirt from summer camp, is passionate about his Christian faith and tells me he works part-time at a cinema in between mainlining Merzbow and applying for college. “With Merzbow, I need to take breaks on Fridays,” he says. “I need time off.”Like Akita, Andrews got into music through drumming, but began thinking critically about it after discovering YouTube music criticAnthony Fantanoand using reviewing services such as Rate Your Music (RYM). He keeps a colour-coded spreadsheet documenting his Merzbow listening and rates every release onInstagramandRYM. His favourite so far is 1990’s Rainbow Electronics, which he gives an 8/10 for how intentional it feels. The worst: 1996’s Merzbow Loves Emil Beaulieau. “The whole second half of the album is 30 minutes of one frequency,” he says. “It’s like tinnitus. That was my breaking point. I was like, what am I getting here as the listener?”Andrews’ videos are absurd in character, a testament to how music criticism is changing online and a nod towards Akita’s own unpredictable ethos: his commitment to animal rights and veganism, sparked after raising four pet bantam chickens in 2002; more recently, a strange and unpopular choice to use AI art in his onstage backdrops.View image in fullscreenMerzbow performing at No Fun Fest at The Hook in Red Hook Brooklyn in 2007.Photograph: Aviv Small/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockDespite his age, Andrews comes from an older school of music lovers that values full albums and discographies, rarely individual songs or playlists. “It’s almost like a medal of honour to say that I had actually sat through an impossibly long discography, one that no one would ever do in its entirety,” he says.Merzbow’s music isn’t alien to younger listeners. Online, gen Z wield its shock factor to soundtrack everything from trolls telling older people toplay the music on their Alexa, memes comparingnoise and K-popand cinematic shots ofbroken tech. Andrews sees this short-form content as more mind-numbing than noise music. Deep listening, he says, will “do wonders for your attention span: being able to sit down and see something as a 40-minute piece rather than a song that you’ll hear 30 seconds of and skip”.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueMerzbow has about 23,000 monthly listeners on Spotify, but those numbers “do not accurately reflect his relevance”, argues Andrew. As Anohni says in Liz Pelly’s bookMood Machine: The Rise of Spotify and the Costs of the Perfect Playlist, the fact that you might only ever want to listen to highly impactful music twice isn’t a comment on its value. Challenging music such as Merzbow forces listeners to think outside an economy where quality is often conflated with popularity, worth measured by consumption.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAndrews has been shocked to see how much people who don’t usually engage with experimental music have to say when they’re exposed to it. “I had a sleepover and convinced my friends to sit through Pulse Demon with me. What I expected was: ‘What is this? That’s just noise.’ But one friend said he could hear the silence afterwards. One hated it, but he still had more to say than I thought he would.” Even at church, his friends’ parents ask bemused questions about how he listens to such abrasive music. “I love explaining to them how I feel, and they do genuinely listen.”Piercing feedback and pig noises: what’s the most out-there album ever?Read moreStill, only 1.6% of Andrews’ audience are his age; most viewers are in their 30s and 40s. “I’ve had people comment things like: ‘I remember back in my college dorm listening to Merzbow in 1990.’ That’s an insane thing to hear. Not only are those people interested in my content, but he really did have a dedicated fanbase back when you had to know a guy who knows a guy to even get your hands on his music.”Akita himself also found his way to Andrews’ page. “Strangely enough he followed me, liked a reel and collabbed on a post, only to remove himself from the post and unfollow me. The hothead probably saw a comment criticising his use of AI or just didn’t like a score I gave out, who’s to say?” Nevertheless, Andrews remains in awe. “It’s fun to take a mic and mash it into the floor and throw things around. But in terms of actually sticking with that and experimenting, making it something that people really want to listen to, that’s admirable. Fifty to 100 years in the future, people will still probably talk about Pulse Demon and Venereology.”Explore more on these topicsMusicExperimental musicSocial mediaInstagramJapanAsia PacificfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The man who shaped Trump: book sheds fresh light on ruthless Roy Cohn | Books | The Guardian
description: American Scoundrel tells story of McCarthy attack dog, mob lawyer and Trump mentor – will the president be thumbing its pages?
Author: Martin Pengelly
Headline: American Scoundrel tells story of McCarthy attack dog, mob lawyer and Trump mentor – will the president be thumbing its pages?
Content: Donald Trump with Roy Cohn at Trump Tower in Manhattan in 1983.Photograph: Sonia Moskowitz/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump with Roy Cohn at Trump Tower in Manhattan in 1983.Photograph: Sonia Moskowitz/Getty ImagesBooksThe man who shaped Trump: book sheds fresh light on ruthless Roy CohnAmerican Scoundrel tells story of McCarthy attack dog, mob lawyer and Trump mentor – will the president be thumbing its pages?Martin Pengellyin WashingtonTue 1 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 09.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKai Bird and Susan Goldmark have written a book Trumpworld doesn’t want you to read. Published on Tuesday,American Scoundrelis a propulsive, horrifying biography of Roy Cohn, the New York mob lawyer whose extraordinary life charted, as the book’s subtitle has it, a “Dark Journey from Joe McCarthy to Donald Trump”.“I told my publicist to reach out to any of the Fox News hosts and reporters, to Joe Rogan, Steve Bannon,” Bird said. “We haven’t gotten a peep, other than Joe Rogan. He said he looked at the galleys, and he got back to my publicist and said, ‘I’m not interested.’ I’m kind of surprised. This is a serious biography of the president’s mentor, whom he publicly admires and says he still misses.”From the mid-70s to the mid-80s, Cohn guided Trump through the cutthroat world of New York real estate. Everything brutal about Trump, in business and politics, he probably learned from Cohn. How to profit fromties to organized crime? Check. How to stay a step ahead of the law? Check. How to remorselessly lie and never admit wrong or defeat? Check.Small wonder thatin 2017, amid scandal over links to Russia that aides couldn’t master, Trump memorably demanded:“Where’s my Roy Cohn?”Trump does know about American Scoundrel, because Bird called him four times on his personal number.“The interviews were eight, nine, 10 minutes,” Bird said. “He told some stories. They were of use to me. I asked, ‘Well, how did you first meet Roy Cohn?’ And I was expecting what he had said before inThe Art of the Dealand in interviews, and instead he flipped the story all the way upside down. Instead of him going up to the older man, recognizing the powerful lawyer sitting at a nearby table at Le Club in Manhattan [in 1973], he said, ‘Oh, Roy Cohn recognized me. I was making a name for myself as a young developer in Manhattan.’”View image in fullscreenKai Bird and Susan Goldmark.Photograph: ScribnerAnother lesson from Cohn: tell the story however the hell you want.Describing his final Trump call, Bird said: “It’s so weird. You cold-call him, and he picks up. This time, instead of politely listening to my questions, he says, ‘Oh, I can’t do this. I don’t have time for this. You shouldn’t be using this number. I’m the president. I have Russia calling. I have China calling.’ And I say, ‘OK, I understand, Mr President, but I just have two questions.’“And I ask, ‘Did you know that Roy Cohn in 1976 voted for Jimmy Carter?’ And he says, ‘Ah, that’s unbelievable. Why would he do that?’ And I said, ‘Well, Roy was kind of fed up and impatient with the old guard Republican party symbolized by Gerald Ford, and he thought Jimmy Carter was a fresh face.’ And Trump said, ‘Oh, I can understand that. That makes sense.’ You know his frustrations with the Republican party establishment. So that must have resonated with him.“Then I said, ‘Well, Cohn quickly got disillusioned with Carter, particularly over the Panama canal treaty, and of course Trump jumped in and said, ‘Yeah, that was a terrible deal. What a terrible deal!’ He’s trying to get off the phone, and I say, ‘Well, I just want you to know this book is coming out in the autumn, and he says, ‘Oh, terrific, maybe I can promote it. Anything I promote goes to number one.’ And then there’s a pause, and he says, ‘Of course, it would have to be fair.’”American Scoundrel is certainly fair. Birdwon a Pulitzer prizefor American Prometheus, a life of the nuclear scientist J Robert Oppenheimer co-written with Martin J Sherwin and the basis for Christopher Nolan’sOscar-winning biopic. Bird’s last subject wasCarter. Cohn kept cropping up, so Bird and Goldmark (his wife, “director of research” and “muse”) got down to work. Then Trump was re-elected. Cohn was current again.“At 27, Cohn was onthe cover of Time magazine,” Bird said, pointing to a rise that saw Cohn graduate from Columbia Law School at 20, prosecute Julius and Ethel Rosenberg,executed for spying for Russia, then become the GOP senator Joe McCarthy’s aide inthe Red Scare, the brutal 1950s witch-hunt of liberals and homosexuals.“Joe McCarthy is a much less complicated and driven kind of figure than Roy Cohn,” Bird said. “Joe McCarthy was a populist senator from Wisconsin who was simply looking to generate some headlines, and he kind of stumbled on the idea of communists and the government.”Cohn was “the ideologue. He’s the svengali, the real brain, who tells Joe McCarthy how he can take advantage of this issue. He runs the hearings, actually conducts the interrogations of these witnesses and is driven out of ideological certainty that there is a danger to the nation from internal communism, and a desire as a Jewish American – this is, I think, important to his identity – to prove his own loyalty, to prove not all Jews are leftwing.”Cohn’s rightwing credentials were impeccable: he was close to Rupert Murdoch, Ronald Reagan and other major reactionary figures.View image in fullscreenThe cover of American Scoundrel.Photograph: ScribnerAs thehorrorsof McCarthyism now echo in Trump’sextralegal war on “woke”, so do inquisitors’ unenforced errors. The Army-McCarthy hearings, whichbrought McCarthy downin 1954, were spawned by Cohn’s attempts to get another young inquisitor, G David Schine, out of overseas service. Senators insinuated Cohn and Shine were lovers. Cohn was certainly gay but never came out of the closet. He was also, Bird said, “quite definitely attracted to Donald Trump. When he met him, Trump was 27 years old. He was tall, blonde, blue-eyed. Wealthy, somewhat. So he was Roy’s type. I don’t think anything sexual went on between them but there was a dynamic, and a pattern to Roy’s friendships.”Cohn could be generous. Bird considers the case of Gary Belis, who dated Cohn, 25 years his senior, but didn’t sleep with him and remained fond. But that story is told in a chapter titled “Predator”, which also containsthe horrific story of Richard Kerr, a Northern Irish boy abused in care then trafficked around the world, including to Roy Cohn.“He could be very charming with someone like Gary Belis and sort of decent,” Bird said. “He courted him, gave him favors as Roy would, but he backed off when Gary indicated he couldn’t go down that path. And yet Cohn was a sexual addict, and he had these ‘boy toys’” – teen hustlers paid for sex.Cohn is an American villain. He features inAngels in America, Tony Kushner’s stage epic of the Aids crisis. In 2024,Jeremy Strongplayed him in The Apprentice, Ali Abbasi’s Trump biopic. A portion of his archive is owned by Michael Stipe of REM, author of the songExhuming McCarthy.He died in 1986, aged 59, from Aids. As he always denied his sexuality, so he denied his final illness, claiming liver cancer even as he received experimental Aids treatment thanks to Washington connections. Not long before he died, he wasdisbarredfor unethical conduct, three indictments having failed to bring him down. (He still had 36 character witnesses, among them Trump, William F Buckley Jr and the TV host Barbara Walters, once Cohn’s “beard”, or fake romantic interest.) In extremis, Trump is commonly said to have abandoned Cohn, causing him to say: “Donald pisses ice water.” Bird said: “That’s not entirely true.“I quote the switchboard operator Chris Seymour at Cohn’sNew Yorktownhouse law firm. He said that when Trump recognized that Roy was dying of Aids, he began to keep his distance. He didn’t rely on him as much, as his lawyer. The calls were fewer. But that didn’t mean he cut him off. He did invite him down to his new estate in Mar-a-Lago for this fabulous dinner, March 86, so just five months before he dies. And it was a touching farewell dinner, with many toasts.”Cohn’s memorial service was held in midtown Manhattan. A witness saw Trump weeping.American Scoundrel isout nowExplore more on these topicsBooksDonald TrumpNew YorkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Anita Brookner by Hermione Lee review – an enigmatic literary great given her due | Anita Brookner | The Guardian
description: This exhaustive biography of the Booker winner brings her properly out of the shadows for the first time
Author: Lucy Atkins
Headline: This exhaustive biography of the Booker winner brings her properly out of the shadows for the first time
Content: Anita Brookner in 1987.Photograph: Mike Abrahams/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenAnita Brookner in 1987.Photograph: Mike Abrahams/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.Book of the dayAnita BrooknerReviewAnita Brookner by Hermione Lee review – an enigmatic literary great given her dueThis exhaustive biography of the Booker winner brings her properly out of the shadows for the first timeLucy AtkinsTue 1 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 05.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Dr Weiss, at forty, knew that her life had been ruined by literature.” The first fictional sentenceAnita Brooknerever published, aged 53, in A Start in Life, certainly set a tone. If people have heard of Brookner today, Hermione Lee says, they imagine a lonely, cardiganed woman yearning for an absent lover. “This,” says Lee (an emeritus English professor at the University of Oxford), “won’t do.”The cardiganed image confuses the author with her protagonists. Of 24 novels written across 30 years, only the first four – A Start in Life, Providence, Look at Me and Hotel du Lac – are about a single woman pining for love. There is certainly a “Brooknerian” style, characterised by elegance, restraint and melancholia, but her fiction engaged with our emotional lives broadly, examining family, exile, home, trauma, ageing and much more.Born in 1928 and raised in south London by a fearsome Polish-Jewish grandmother and absurdly ineffectual parents (a tobacco salesman and a failed singer), Brookner was a highly academic only child. After a degree at King’s College London, she briefly tasted freedom as a student in Paris, but was soon dragged back to care for her extraordinarily needy mother. Yoked to home for the next decade, she managed, nevertheless, to become a brilliant art critic and a charismatic lecturer at the Courtauld Institute, where she stayed until retirement.In the introduction, Lee describes hearing the author’s voice saying, repeatedly, “Go away”, and Brookner’s 20s and 30s were the “most hidden, the least witnessed” of all. Brookner did her utmost to erase her life, and Lee is forced, therefore, to mine any detail she can find. As well as Brookner’s academic work and extensive reading habits, we get her poor handwriting, fear of trains, love of perfumes and at one particularly desperate point, salary increases over two decades. A couple of love affairs in her 30s fizzled out, but if there was ever a record of her feelings, Brookner expunged it. The first 200 pages, then, can be hard going. She was, says Lee, through gritted teeth, “an object of mystery and puzzlement”.double quotation markPrivate Eye snarked about 'Hotel du Lac of Interest' and a grim pattern of critical disdain was setBut Lee persists – always rake thin, Brookner kept slimming biscuits in her handbag; she loved babies; she doled out tranquillisers to nervous PhD candidates – and just as this enterprise starts to feel doomed, something miraculous happens. The tireless details begin to cohere and Brookner steps out of the shadows, intriguing, contradictory – the super brain who shaved 10 years off her age in her own Who’s Who entry; the self-proclaimed “loneliest woman in London” who had loads of friends.The older she gets, the more interesting this book becomes. In 1979, her beloved Courtauld mentor, friend and boss, Anthony Blunt, was exposed as a Soviet spy. Shaken, Brookner remained loyal until she discovered he’d used her to extract information from a hospitalised colleague.Reeling and depressed, facing another lonely summer, she found herself writing fiction. Her process was extraordinary. Each novel took only three months from start to finish. She’d roam London forming sentences in her head, then simply write them down, at speed. Hilary Mantel, a fervent admirer, said Brookner arrived as a novelist perfectly formed, “as if she had hatched from a marbled egg”. She would repeat this process, annually, for more than two decades.In 1984, her fourth novel, Hotel du Lac,about a woman who jilts her fiancee and retreats to a Swiss hotel,won the Booker prize. Pretty much everyone expected JG Ballard’s Empire of the Sun or Julian Barnes’s Flaubert’s Parrot to win. The misogyny was mind-bending. At the ceremony, Ballard hissed, “You stole my Booker.” Private Eye snarked about “Hotel du Lac of Interest” and a grim pattern of critical disdain was set. For the rest of Brookner’s writing life, critics would carp about “doily” novels and compare her to Mills & Boon. Profiles were invariably illustrated with sad spinsters holding cups of tea. It tormented her. But she kept on writing.She was, personally, far from isolated. She had devoted friends, including the Virago publisher Carmen Callil and fellow writers such as Rosamond Lehmann or Julian Barnes, who offers loving memories here. He was so intimidated by her eloquence when they lunched that he’d feel himself inserting semicolons into his own speech.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWas she a literary genius? She once, brilliantly, described novel-writing as “trying very hard to remember something which has not yet taken place”. Lee offers genuinely transporting literary criticism, unearthing the elegance and complexity of the work, but admits the compulsive production of a book a year diluted the impact and sometimes the quality. Still, she singles out three – Family and Friends, Latecomers and The Next Big Thing–as truly “outstanding” novels. Thankfully, it is no longer cool to Brookner-bash. This astute and tireless biography succeeds, against the odds, in unearthing the author – who would be appalled by our scrutiny. Above all, it shows that the work deserves our full attention.Anita Brookner: Art and Life by Hermione Lee is published by Chatto & Windus (£28). title: Under Story by Chloe Benjamin review – this time-reversal melodrama is quantum hokum | Science fiction books | The Guardian
description: A grieving couple who have lost their son find a way to a mirror universe where time runs backwards – but the narrative machinery is shonky and distracting
Author: Beejay Silcox
Headline: A grieving couple who have lost their son find a way to a mirror universe where time runs backwards – but the narrative machinery is shonky and distracting
Content: ‘Will the suffragettes fight to relinquish the vote?’ … Chloe Benjamin.Photograph: David EnloeView image in fullscreen‘Will the suffragettes fight to relinquish the vote?’ … Chloe Benjamin.Photograph: David EnloeScience fiction booksReviewUnder Story by Chloe Benjamin review – this time-reversal melodrama is quantum hokumA grieving couple who have lost their son find a way to a mirror universe where time runs backwards – but the narrative machinery is shonky and distractingBeejay SilcoxTue 1 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is something farcical – grotesque, even – about life played in reverse. A child falling into a tree. A sandwich emerging from a mouth, bite by reconstituted bite. A doctor unstitching a wound. The world is strange in any order, but rewind helps us notice – makes the ordinary absurd.Novels that pick a fight with forward momentum tend to harness this absurdity, revel in it. InThe Cockroach(2019), Ian McEwan gives us a sneering Brexit fable about political nostalgia. If voters want to turn back the clock, let them. He unleashes “Economic Reversalism”, which sees employees pay for the privilege of work, and every pound sent back to where it came from. In Time’s Arrow (1991), Martin Amis inverts the Holocaust. Just imagine it, he dares us: a network of sanatoriums instead of death camps. A vast machinery of reparation run by benevolent Nazis. How monstrously laughable.Joining this backwards bunch is Chloe Benjamin with her third novel, Under Story. It conjures a universe that mirrors our own (a “duoverse”), populated by doppelgangers; a place where the past might be undone, because it hasn’t happened yet.Here are the fictional facts. In the duoverse, ordinary human life begins underground. Mycelium grow a corpse from rot, like a 3D printer for gizzards. A heart starts beating, for reasons, and a fully grown human crawls up from the soil riddled with elderly ailments, but with a box-fresh brain. Once they’re cleaned up and DNA profiled – the work of “overtakers” – these new/old people are delivered to their children, but in the postal, rather than the obstetric, sense. The doorbell rings.Brains grow older; bodies grow younger. Cancers unbloom. Cataracts fade. Children raise their parents until they’re spry enough to cope on their own. Nursing homes are convalescent kindergartens. And down at the other end of life, kindergartens are dementia clinics full of geriatric toddlers. Death is birth: neonates are shoved up their mothers in maternity morgues, swallowed by the amniotic dark.It’s ghoulish stuff, body horror territory: wards of women surgically forced to eat their babies with their hungry vaginas. You might expect – even hope for – some literary depravity: Benjamin Button reimagined by William Burroughs orAgustina Bazterrica. But Under Story is a love story. We follow a forward-born couple, Laurel and Eli, who are grieving their son, Silas. Could a round trip to the duoverse summon him back? Might it also help them to forgive one another? What follows is a 500-page melodrama of parental devotion and quantum hokum. Imagine Orpheus and Eurydice meets Interstellar, but starring Tom Hanks from Big.Using a combination of speculative physics and prophetic dreams, Laurel and Eli find their way to a portal under the ice of Antarctica and into the duoverse. They adjust quickly to its topsy-turvy logic: September follows October, Obama follows Trump, and the analogue revolution is under way (the record player has just been invented). Handily, the climate is also unravaging – extinct species popping up from the ground like the mushrooms that remade them.double quotation markIt’s meant to make us weep, to rouse mighty questions about love, free will and our connection to the planetThe key to it all is entropy: “this universe moves toward the Big Bang, and entropy is reversed,” Eli explains. He’s a physicist; Laurel is a mycologist. They’ll both do a great deal of explaining.There can be no life without entropy, but that’s not the problem here. Plenty of imagined worlds are nonsense, and gloriously so. The problem is that Benjamin keeps drawing our attention to her shonky narrative machinery. She answers questions we’d never thought to ask. We learn that “Christmas exists here, even though Jesus won’t be born for two thousand years” and that reverse folks can’t choose to procreate, because the decision is already waiting for them when they grovel out of the placental dirt.Benjamin’s last novel, 2018’sThe Immortalists, was also about foretold lives: four siblings who learn the dates of their deaths from a fortune teller. But the point – and lure – of that novel was doubt. Was the prophecy real or self-fulfilling? Is there a difference? Benjamin left those questions with us. In Under Story, she seems unsure her cosmic premise can carry its own mysteries.But the more we learn, the more distracted we are. And that’s before Benjamin busts out some last-act theatrics – mystical anagrams and fortuitous gadgetry – or subjects us to a death-birth. It’s hard to trust a novel that doesn’t trust itself.Part of the problem is length. Rewound life is a gimmick, a thought experiment. The books that do it best are wry, incisive and short (the anticlockwise archetype, F Scott Fitzgerald’s The Curious Case of Benjamin Button, is a fleet 40-page story). The longer Laurel and Eli stay in the duoverse, the more contrived it all feels, because the more contrived it has to be. It’s hard to live backwards with dignity, and Benjamin knows it. And so she picks and chooses which bodily functions work in which direction. People walk and talk normally. Have conceptionless sex. Breathe and eat and excrete. It’s entropy galore, except for the life cycle. The author has her backwards cake, and eats it too.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTop 10 novels that interrupt time | Ross RaisinRead moreBut there are much easier ways to meddle with the past and its sorrows (see Scott Alexander Howard’sThe Other Valleyor Aja Gabel’sLightbreakers), which makes all of Benjamin’s picking and choosing feel particularly gruesome. Her duoverse has been elaborately rigged to produce a scene of filial reunion. She has violated the laws of physics, reanimated the dead and turned women’s bodies into tombs all in order to weaponise parental grief.It’s meant to make us weep, to rouse mighty questions about ageless love, free will and our intimate connection to the planet. But here are some of the questions I scribbled in the margins of Under Story: if every fossil is a future creature, are palaeontologists dino-killers? Will the suffragettes fight to relinquish the vote? If vaginas work backwards, are penises the same: meaty little vacuum cleaners, hoovering up sperm? Once you’ve written a line like that you know your suspension of disbelief has well and truly snapped. And maybe something else has too.Under Story by Chloe Benjamin is published by Tinder (£20). title: ‘There’s always a fresh fury’: Tracey Scott Wilson on Black America and her play about a fraudulent journalist | Stage | The Guardian
description: As The Story – inspired by a scandal that ended a young Black reporter’s career – makes its London debut, its author explains why, two decades on, it’s more relevant than ever
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: As The Story – inspired by a scandal that ended a young Black reporter’s career – makes its London debut, its author explains why, two decades on, it’s more relevant than ever
Content: ‘I could’ve been a star’ … Tracey Scott Wilson photographed at the National Theatre in London.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I could’ve been a star’ … Tracey Scott Wilson photographed at the National Theatre in London.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.StageInterview‘There’s always a fresh fury’: Tracey Scott Wilson on Black America and her play about a fraudulent journalistArifa AkbarAs The Story – inspired by a scandal that ended a young Black reporter’s career – makes its London debut, its author explains why, two decades on, it’s more relevant than everTue 1 Sep 2026 07.13 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 07.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf our ability to discern fake news from fact is a hot topic today, Tracey Scott Wilson was on to it more than two decades ago. As a child, the playwright’s father trained her to watch the news every night and discuss it with her three siblings. It meant that she was well placed in the early 00s to spot how stations such as Fox News were veering away from objective reporting to become angled towards a given agenda.By this point a real-life story had been percolating in Wilson’s mind for more than two decades: in 1981, Janet Cooke, a young, ambitious Black American reporter at The Washington Post, had been exposed as a liar. Cooke had just won the Pulitzer prize for her news story about an eight-year-old drug addict, which turned out to be invented. Cooke was discredited, both for her reporting and for embellishing her CV, and was forced to hand back her prize two days after receiving it.View image in fullscreenLinseigh Green  and Jay Simpson  in rehearsals for  The Story.Photograph: © Feruza AfewekiThat scandal became the engine for The Story, Wilson’s breakthrough play at the Public Theater in New York in 2003, now being staged at theNational Theatrein LondonWilson, a rangy, affable presence, is delighted by her play’s revival at a time when the notion of truth, and the media’s part in producing it, couldn’t be more contested. She was a teenager when the Cooke story emerged and a conversation with her father has stayed with her. “He said ‘It’s such a shame she won it for writing something so negative [about the Black community].’ And then when they said the story was a lie, it was a whole other thing.”A few years later, when she was working at the University of Minnesota at a student magazine, she returned to the story. “We had access to [the digital newspaper archive] LexisNexis. I was bored half the time in that job so I’d just look up stories and one day I thought ‘I wonder what happened to Janet Cooke.’ So I put it in LexisNexis and went down a rabbit hole. I thought ‘what a great character she is’.”Her play’s protagonist, Yvonne, is quite the character too, a Black American junior reporter with a CV that takes in an Ivy League educationby way of the Sorbonne. She is assigned to a section whose raison d’etre is to put a positive spin on the newspaper’s race coverage – happy stories featuring the local Black American community to offset the negative ones. It is too niche to hold Yvonne’s ambition so she begins her hunt for a story that will fast-track her to the national news desk, populated by, one imagines, white, male, big beasts.Serendipitously, the play’s original run coincided with the breaking of another newspaper scandal involving Jayson Blair, a Black reporter who admitted to inventing and plagiarising stories while working for the New York Times. That story had race and class elements, just like Wilson’s play: Yvonne is a middle-class woman who sparks resentment and friction because of her (apparent) privilege. Through her, Wilson examines notions of who is deemed inside/outside the fold of the Black community.View image in fullscreenTracey Scott Wilson  and Ashley Thomas in rehearsals for The Story.Photograph: © Feruza Afewerki“I was drawn to the idea of authenticity,” says Wilson, “which is a conversation we are having every single day around class, race, sexuality, and who is allowed to be the spokesperson.”The play is also about women and ambition – the hard, raw kind that Yvonne encapsulates so uncompromisingly, especially now after a series of re-writes. “I wanted to bring Pat [a senior editor and Black woman] into this conversation. Pat and Yvonne are two sides of the same coin, they are both women who are being constantly punished for their ambition and being forced to do things because of their ambition.”There was a false start for a London revival soon after its original staging in New York, when the Soho theatre, in London, invited Wilson to the UK for a reading. “I had never been overseas, I had to go and get a passport,” she says. “I was so excited. They put me up here for a week. I barely remember the reading because I was going to Westminster Abbey, and doing all the tourist things.”It wasn’t picked up and Wilson went back home. “I was disappointed but I forgot about it. It was done a few times in the United States but I didn’t think it would be done again.”It was only when she got the call from the NationalTheatrelast year that she realised that her London trip hadn’t been wasted at all. Clint Dyer, this production’s director, had been at the Soho theatre reading as a twentysomething actor. “I had a Zoom with [the NT] and Clint was there. I didn’t remember him but he said he had loved [the reading in 2003] and every single time he went to do a play in a theatre he would say ‘Have you read The Story?’”Ironically, Wilson herself wanted to be a journalist and majored in the subject as a freshman until her professor at Rutgers University told her she wasn’t cut out for it because she editorialised too much: “He said ‘you just can’t be objective’.” She switched to English, first trying her hand at writing prose before hitting on her gift for script-writing. It’s not lost on her that everything her university professor told her about news journalism has ceased to matter for some organisations. “If I had carried on as a journalism major, I could’ve been a star!’” she jokes.View image in fullscreen‘Reading the news that fits your perspective’ … Tracey Scott Wilson and Clint Dyer in rehearsals for The Story.Photograph: © Feruza AfewekiThe Story is still set in 2003 but it seems like a pertinent – and potent – moment to stage it. The debate on who controls the narrative continues to rise in volume while the death of former Cambridge professor,Jason Arday,has revived charges of racial scapegoating. For Wilson, the concern is not just over news production but also the way we consume it. “I used to play basketball in high school. I remember when my team [theLos Angeles Lakers] lost, I didn’t want to read about it because it would make me feel bad. But it’s just sport so it doesn’t matter, right? Now it applies to everything, so if I don’t like reading this economic data because it makes me feel stressed out or I don’t like reading about this conflict in this country because it makes me feel bad … it’s become a case of reading the news that fits your perspective so you don’t have to feel bad about reality.”Yet while it is evident that many media outlets are focusing on views-journalism, has news production ever really been neutral or objective? “There’s always been rags,” Wilson concedes, “but I think what’s happening now is that there is resignation and acceptance that this is what it is, as opposed to ‘I know that that’s a rag, but this is a paper of note that tries to tell an objective truth.’”She thinks the scandal at the heart of her play would resonate differently today too. “Everything that happens would now happen in a week and we’d forget about it, or it would live on in a particular niche on the internet. The fury only lasts 20 minutes now because there’s another fresh fury.”So is this her condemnation of the media machine that she once dreamed of joining?“I don’t want to say it’s a blanket condemnation. You can criticise the big mainstream papers, but you also have these people on the internet who are saying ‘This is the news from Gaza’. There are people committed to trying to tell the truth.”The Story is at theNational Theatre until 24 OctoberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreNational TheatreRaceNewspapersBlack US cultureinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Emily Wilson to retranslate the Odyssey from scratch | Books | The Guardian
description: Wilson, whose 2017 English translation of Homer’s epic poem inspired Christopher Nolan’s box office hit, is revisiting it after criticising the film adaptation
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: Wilson, whose 2017 English translation of Homer’s epic poem inspired Christopher Nolan’s box office hit, is revisiting it after criticising the film adaptation
Content: ‘It’s a complete retranslation. It’s not a revision of the old version’ … Emily Wilson.Photograph: Matt Rourke/APView image in fullscreen‘It’s a complete retranslation. It’s not a revision of the old version’ … Emily Wilson.Photograph: Matt Rourke/APBooksEmily Wilson to retranslate the Odyssey from scratchWilson, whose 2017 English translation of Homer’s epic poem inspired Christopher Nolan’s box office hit, is revisiting it after criticising the film adaptationEmma LoffhagenTue 1 Sep 2026 11.09 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEmily Wilson, the first woman to translate Homer’s Odyssey into English, is to retranslate the ancient Greek epic poem from scratch less than a decade after the publication of her acclaimed version.The announcement comes after Wilson attracted controversy this summer with a scathing assessment of Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster film adaptation of the Odyssey, which sheslammed forits “abysmal” writing and lack of sex scenes.Wilson’s2017 translationbecame a bestseller and was praised for making the 3,000-year-old epic poem modern and accessible.“I’m now retranslating the Odyssey from scratch, with an approach closer to that of my translation of the Iliad, using somewhat more lines than the original, enabling more varied word-length and pacing,” she told the New York Times.“It’s a complete retranslation. It’s not a revision of the old version,” she told the AP. “I’m about halfway through.”Nolan cited Wilson’s 2017 translation, including its opening sentence, “Tell me about a complicated man”, as an influence on his adaptation of the poem, released in Julythis year and starring Tom Holland, Zendaya, Matt Damon and Anne Hathaway.Nolan’s adaptationtook the global box office by storm,making $264m (£196m) during its opening weekend, marking the director’s best ever opening. Book sales saw a huge bump too: UK print sales of the poemincreased by 1,400% in the four weeks to 25 July compared with the same period in 2025, after the film’s release in the middle of the month.Wilson made headlines forher attack on Nolan’s version. Writing in the London Review of Books, she said: “Nolan’s Odyssey lacks many of the elements that make the poem great … The writing is abysmal.”She continued: “None of the characters has convincing motivation for their actions or words. There are no sex scenes, and all the food looks horrible,” adding, “I would be ashamed to have written any part of this script.”Her criticism attracted strong reactions, includingfrom novelist Joyce Carol Oates,whoaccusedWilson of “haughty superiority”.Wilson’s decision to retranslate the poem predates the row over the film. In an interview recorded in the spring for the ancient-history podcast Instant Classics, she discussed her desire to return to Homer and approach the poem differently from her first translation.“I’m proud of my Odyssey translation … I think there are lots of good things about the kinds of compression and choices that I was forced into,” Wilson said then.She has indicated that she will “probably” keep the opening line, “Tell me about a complicated man”. Wilson also added that her original translation relied too heavily on the word “slave”, when more precise terminology could have better reflected the different forms of enslavement depicted in the poem.The new translation will also give readers far more of Wilson’s scholarly commentary. “I’m also going to quadruple the number of endnotes because endnotes are really fun to write,” she said.While Wilson’s decision to retranslate Homer’s poem is unusual, it is not without precedent.“Translators quite often rework or rewrite their own previous translations,” said Matthew Reynolds, professor of English and comparative criticism at Oxford University. “Elizabeth Barrett Browning completely rewrote her translation of Aeschylus’s Prometheus Bound, Ezra Pound repeatedly revised his translations of Guido Cavalcanti, and Yu JongHo (유 종호) translated Jane Eyre into Korean first in 1970 and again in 2004.”He added: “It shows that translation – especially literary translation – is not just a matter of right or wrong, good or bad, but a continual exploratory process of interpretive reimagining and re-making.”Wilson’s new Odyssey does not yet have a publication date.Explore more on these topicsBooksThe OdysseyPoetryChristopher NolanHomerFilm adaptationsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s more freaky, more balls to the wall’: how alt-country won over a new generation | Americana | The Guardian
description: From Waxahatchee and Florry in the US to Brown Horse and Little Grandad in the UK, a wave of young songwriters are reinvigorating the subgenre’s earnest emotion and twang
Author: Michael Hann
Headline: From Waxahatchee and Florry in the US to Brown Horse and Little Grandad in the UK, a wave of young songwriters are reinvigorating the subgenre’s earnest emotion and twang
Content: Waxahatchee performing at London’s Kentish Town Forum in 2024.Photograph: Sonja Horsman/Sonja Horsman / The GuardianView image in fullscreenWaxahatchee performing at London’s Kentish Town Forum in 2024.Photograph: Sonja Horsman/Sonja Horsman / The GuardianAmericana‘It’s more freaky, more balls to the wall’: how alt-country won over a new generationFrom Waxahatchee and Florry in the US to Brown Horse and Little Grandad in the UK, a wave of young songwriters are reinvigorating the subgenre’s earnest emotion and twangMichael HannTue 1 Sep 2026 06.14 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 06.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘It’s so important to talk about this before it’s gone,” says Francie Medosch, singer, guitarist and songwriter of the band Florry, “because it’s really a flash in the pan.” The flash she means is a brief moment where it feels as though on both sides of the Atlantic, scores of exciting indie bands are playing something that, without slavish copying, has plainly drawn inspiration from alt-country, the music that emerged in the US in the late 1980s and early 90s, when former punks such as Uncle Tupelo – featuring futureWilcoco-founder Jeff Tweedy – and the Bottle Rockets picked up picked up fiddles, banjos and acoustic guitars.In the UK, Brown Horse and Vegas Water Taxi have the weeping pedal steel, in the former case tied to something very heartland and in the latter paired with a very English indie sensibility.Westside Cowboyand Little Grandad both borrow from the spiky rootsiness of early Wilco, while Wyatt play slacker country rock. Over in the US, where there’s always going to be more of this sort of thing, you can point to the current indie-rock holy trinity ofWaxahatchee, Wednesday andMJ Lenderman, plus Florry, Ratboys, Thomas Dollbaum, Fust, SG Goodman, Lily Seabird, Ryan Davis and the Roadhouse Band and more.View image in fullscreen‘There’s a genuine desire among young people to embrace earnest storytelling’ … Ratboys.Photograph: Miles Kalchik“It seems to be a real language right now in the music world,” says Julia Steiner, singer-guitarist of Ratboys, from the rockier end of this moment, “and I’m stoked about it. It’s been a long time coming – it’s so exciting to me when bands take really simple ingredients and find ways to make really progressive recipes with them. What’s exciting to me about alt-country is that the same cowboy chords are in play here, but the filter they come through is more freaky, more balls to the wall. It’s fun to see how many places people can take these essential ideas.”London quartet Little Grandad, who earlier this summer signed a three-album deal with Communion, didn’t even know about alt-country when they started playing last year. “Tim from [buzzy London venue] Brixton Windmill told me, ‘You’ve got to check out this whole scene of bands,’” says their singer-guitarist Harry Lower. “I knew about Wilco, but I didn’t know about Uncle Tupelo and all of that world. I’ve listened to a lot of music in the last year.”One of those discoveries was Jason Molina, of Songs: Ohia and the Magnolia Electric Co, who died in 2013 of organ failure following long-term alcohol abuse. “I love how fragile he is,” Lower says of the midwestern singer-songwriter. “I just believe him. I believe his songwriting. I watched an interview of him, and he’s saying how he’s so confused that he makes this music because he listens to Metallica and metal bands, and he’s like, ‘How has it turned out like this?’ That makes me feel better about what we make, because you stumble into it.”By chance, in the week all these interviews were conducted, London became alt-country central. On the Tuesday night, the Norfolk band Brown Horse were the house band at a night honouring the songs of Molina, with a rotating cast of singers including Alexis Taylor of Hot Chip and Lottie Pendlebury of Goat Girl. On Wednesday, Wilco were in town, with alt-country band Hovvdy opening and a set that didn’t eschew the country end of their catalogue, and on Thursday and Friday Greg Freeman, from Vermont, played two sold-out club shows.Everyone seems to have taken different routes to get to similar places, though all these musicians in their 20s or early 30s came to it via their own discovery, rather than hearing it in the cars of gen X parents. Steiner grew up with country in the air in Kentucky, and added the alternative rock later. Medosch hailsLucinda Williamsas the source of all things alt-country (a complete music head, she offers an eloquent disquisition on why powerpop, and Big Star in particular, must be considered part of this lineage).View image in fullscreen‘You can say so much with a country song’ … Francie Medosch of Florry.Photograph: John McSweeney“All this stuff comes under Neil Young,” says Lower. Thomas Dollbaum, who lives in New Orleans, remembers hearing the music you can’t avoid, such as Bob Dylan, then having uncles send him John Prine CDs, “because they knew I was interested in that kind of music. And then I found stuff on my own. I listened to a lot of Jason Molina, a lot of Damian Jurado, a lot of Bill Callahan and Richard Buckner growing up. In early college I had a friend and we’d send tapes back and forth.”Brown Horse came to alt-country via a eureka moment.
