They were already a band, playing an approximation of American folk music, when they were booked to play the Black Deer festival in 2022. “We’d been so fucking bored for a year and a half,” says their pedal steel player, Emma Tovell. “We had a euphoric moment watching Drive-By Truckers. We could really see where they’d come from that kind of gothic old southern country music, but they were really rocking, and we absolutely loved that. And we saw Wilco at that festival, and SG Goodman, who played at 1pm to 30 people. We got home and decided it was time to start amplifying stuff. That felt like a concentration point.”Tovell remembers an early Brown Horse tour of Scandinavia, where “95% of the gigs were seated and the average age of the audience was 65”. In the last few years, the audience for live guitar music seems to have become much younger. It’s hardly rockism’s revenge on poptimism, but in a culture in which people sit in front of screens all day, for work or for leisure, there’s something resonant about seeing people making music in which raggedness is celebrated, in which edges are the result of friction rather than having been generated by computer.“I think there’s a genuine desire among young people – millennials like myself included – to embrace earnest storytelling and our humanity, in the face of this monolith of corporate suits drooling over AI and the internet and trying to tell us what’s cool,” says Steiner. “There’s something to the idea of stripping that away and getting to the bare essentials of storytelling, and putting your perspective out there in ways that feel accessible and honest. I’m just happy that people are trying to make music that feels really human.”View image in fullscreen‘We’d been so fucking bored’ … Emma Tovell of Brown Horse performing at  the Moth Club, London, in 2024.Photograph: Brown Horse/Facebook“You can say so much with a country song,” Medosch says. “You can be so earnest, or you can be detached, you can mess with the form so much.” She was amazed when she realised British bands felt the same. “What’s happening in England is really shocking to American musicians.”Pixar, Catholic shame, and urine-drinking podcast bros: the mixed-up rock of MJ LendermanRead moreWhile the British bands are still forming their futures, many of the American bands have several years and several albums in the books, and they’re already changing. Florry’s next album will have a Broadway show tune and a Caribbean rock song, says Medosch, hence her pleasure in this moment being captured for posterity.Before our call ends, Steiner asks if I am familiar with the term “post-country”. “I’m just curious because I first used that term 10 years ago as a joke, but I’ve seen people using it nowadays. When I first met Dave, our guitar player – he’s my partner – in university and he started showing me all these bands I had never heard of, he was using terms like post-hardcore and post-rock, and I was like, ‘What the fuck? Post-rock? Like, what are you talking about?’ I just thought it was hilarious, and we started calling our music post-country.”This is still a genre in search of a name – one online wag suggested “the Lendermen” – and maybe it’s not a genre at all, so much as a shared sense of purpose. But it’s real, and it sounds wonderful.Among the acts mentioned in this piece, Ratboys, Lily Seabird, Ryan Davis and the Roadhouse Band, SG Goodman and Little Grandad playthe End of the Road festival from 3-6 September. Most have other UK dates around the festival; check artist websites for detailsExplore more on these topicsAmericanaCountryWilcoWaxahatcheeIndiePop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’m not nervous, I’m ready’: Tschabalala Self on racist vandals and her bold striding woman for the Fourth Plinth | Fourth plinth | The Guardian
description: The last time she displayed a sculpture in public in Britain, someone covered it in white paint. But, undeterred, the acclaimed artist is a placing a black woman in Trafalgar Square
Author: Eddy Frankel
Headline: The last time she displayed a sculpture in public in Britain, someone covered it in white paint. But, undeterred, the acclaimed artist is a placing a black woman in Trafalgar Square
Content: ‘My work is meant to represent humanity. It’s not limited by racial identity’ … Tschabalala Self.Photograph: Christian DeFonte/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘My work is meant to represent humanity. It’s not limited by racial identity’ … Tschabalala Self.Photograph: Christian DeFonte/The GuardianFourth plinth‘I’m not nervous, I’m ready’: Tschabalala Self on racist vandals and her bold striding woman for the Fourth PlinthThe last time she displayed a sculpture in public in Britain, someone covered it in white paint. But, undeterred, the acclaimed artist is a placing a black woman in Trafalgar SquareEddy FrankelTue 1 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTschabalala Self is relentlessly positive and unstoppably optimistic. The US artist is waiting for the unveiling of Lady in Blue, her new sculpture for the fourth plinth in Trafalgar Square, London, a towering, colourful painted bronze of a black woman striding (positively, optimistically) into the future. Self seems resolutely hopeful about the work, which is pretty impressive considering what happened to her last public sculpture in the UK. “Yeah,” she says, speaking from her home in upstate New York. “I mean, that was a completely racist act.”In 2022, Self unveiled Seated at Coal Drops Yard in King’s Cross, London. Like Lady in Blue, it was a vast, brightly painted bronze depiction of a black woman, this time seated demurely on a chair. After being shown at Coal Drops Yard without incident, it was moved to the De La Warr Pavilion in Bexhill-on-Sea, where the reception wasn’t quite as warm. “Within the first week,” says Self, “it was spraypainted white, but only on the skin of the sculpture.” As vandalism goes, it doesn’t get much more pointed, or racist. “The first feeling I had was just pain that my sculpture had been harmed. That someone had enacted violence on an object I had imbued with love and affection.”double quotation markMere personhood is an act of dignity. It’s courageous to be a human beingThe Pavilion wanted to organise a protest in response to the vandalism, but Self pushed for a community cleanup day instead. “I felt like that would be more cathartic, because a lot of people were appalled.” Hundreds queued to take part and, by the end of the day, all the paint had been removed, leaving nothing for the restorers to do. “That wasn’t my first time experiencing racism,” says Self, “but it was the first time my sculpture had been defaced.”View image in fullscreenSelf’s public sculpture Seated in Bexhill On Sea, where it was defaced – then restored in a community cleanup effortPhotograph: Thierry BalBorn in Harlem, New York, in 1990, Self has an ultra-distinctive approach to collaged pop figuration and political idealism, which has made her a young star in the art world. Her work is in MoMA, the Guggenheim and the Whitney in New York and the Albertina Museum in Vienna. She has had exhibitions at the Hammer Museum in Los Angeles and the ICA Boston and is represented by some of the world’s chicest commercial galleries. Her work is a lurid, vivid, super-colourful, mega-joyful celebration of everyday bodies. She’s like a politically engaged, millennial New York version of the French pop modernistNiki de Saint Phalle, famed for her appealingly exuberant “Nanas”.“The central message of my work is that all people should feel embodied,” she says. “They should feel confident and comfortable: empowered in their body. I think that’s a human right. My work is really about allowing people to understand that their physical experience is something they should relish, and to enjoy the physicality of a lived experience.”Self talks like this a lot – positively, optimistically, almost politically, about the idea of bodies and “vessels” and confidence. “Mere personhood,” she says, “is an act of dignity. It’s courageous to be a human being. That is an act worth valuing.”View image in fullscreenGiant steps … Self with a model of Lady in Blue, at the announcement of the shortlist for the fourth plinth commission.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesThis empowering, direct, hopeful message sets Self a little at odds with the hyper-critical, seriously conceptual and often lofty artworks that have sat on the fourth plinth in recent years. How does Lady in Blue sit withTeresa Margolles’s wall of life-maskstaken from hundreds of transgender and non-binary people, which it’s replacing, orSamson Kambalu’s defiantly anti-colonialist portrait of Pan-African preacher John Chilembwe in 2022? Self’s work looks almost shockingly simple and joyful in comparison. Where’s the invective, the anger, the criticality, the radicalism we’ve come to expect from contemporary art?It turns out that joy twinned with simplicityisthe radical thing. “Let’s say you’re a designer, right?” says Self. “To make something simple but functional is seen as the height of conceptual rigour. But somehow when it comes to fine arts, people equate simplicity with something being devoid of conceptual rigour.”So Self rejects all of that, opting for legibility above all else. “If an artwork doesn’t move a large group of people from different educational, class and racial backgrounds, if it doesn’t move people in a relatively uniform way, I would say that’s more of a deficit of the maker than the audience. If the art’s strong enough, it should be legible to some degree to whoever comes across it. That’s part of the skill of being a great artist.”View image in fullscreenWork by Self at the Whitechapel Gallery, London, in 2020.Photograph: Guy Bell/Rex/ShutterstockWhen people discuss Self’s work, they often emphasise that this is art that celebrates black bodies. Does she feel this is too reductive for someone with such a wide-ranging message? “It is over-simplistic and very limiting. The work is often described in that context, but that’s very superficial. All of the figures are black because I make figures that reflect my physical experience. But they are meant to represent human experience that’s not limited by racial identity.”So Self wants Lady in Blue to be seen as a quotidian figure. Viewers have been willing to acceptAntony Gormley’s use of his own body as a stand-in for wider humanity for decades, but the idea that a black woman could be an “everyperson, an everywoman” is still “a large intellectual leap for a lot of people”, Self says. “One of my first prompts was to present the figure as a woman. If people are not able to readily identify with the figure because she is black, that’s a larger social phenomenon that needs to be unpacked.”Some of that unpacking was done in the wake of the vandalism of her work at the De La Warr Pavilion, but that traumatic event must still cast a shadow over this new project. Especially because the fourth plinth isn’t in the grounds of an art gallery in a small seaside town: it’s smack bang in the middle of the most famous public square in London. That means a much bigger audience, with a lot more opinions. Is she worried?View image in fullscreenSelf in her studio in Catskills, New York.Photograph: Christian DeFonte/The Guardian“I’m ready for a whole gamut of reactions. I’m not nervous – I think everyone is entitled to their own opinion of the sculpture. Each will shed light on to some facet of the reality we’re all currently living.”I believe her, but she’d be forgiven for feeling anxious about people disliking her work on this huge public stage after what has happened previously. “It’s not about the artwork being liked. It’s not about the artwork being loved. It’s about the artwork doing its work. And the work is challenging people to have conversations, to unpack previously held beliefs and make room for new ones.”One thing seems certain: Lady in Blue is going somewhere. Striding, stomping, marching forwards, she’s got places to be and no one is getting in her way. Self says the figure is walking towards our collective future, and in the process rejecting all the heavy history embodied in the other sculptures and the architecture of Trafalgar Square. “It’s about there being space for all in places that were formerly weighted down by antiquated gestures, belief systems and impossibilities,” she says. “I didn’t want to make an artwork that was reactionary to the history that has already happened. I wanted to make something that was a beacon that could shed light into a possible future.”Hip-hop honeys and sitting as a political act: why Tschabalala Self is one of America’s hottest artistsRead moreSo what is this possible future? What does Self see coming our way? “I hope all of us can have physical, mental, political space to live our lives freely, without our freedoms interrupting the freedoms of others.” She laughs and adds: “Not that that sounds too American.” It’s the most American thing I’ve ever heard, I reply. “I just want everyone to be able to be free,” she adds. “Doesn’t everyone want that?”Simplicity, joy, embodiment and – above all – freedom. Self’s future sounds as bright and colourful as her towering blue sculpture.Lady in Blue by Tschabalala Self is unveiled on 10 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFourth plinthSculptureArtWomenRacefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘She inspired my proposal’: Readers on Yayoi Kusama | Yayoi Kusama | The Guardian
description: From wedding ceremonies to sunsets with pumpkins, even in urinals, Kusama’s work brought joy, mischief and inspiration to so many
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From wedding ceremonies to sunsets with pumpkins, even in urinals, Kusama’s work brought joy, mischief and inspiration to so many
Content: Pumpkin queen … Great Gigantic Pumpkin, an art installation at the Matsumoto City Museum of Art, Japan.Photograph: Tomohiro Ohsumi/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPumpkin queen … Great Gigantic Pumpkin, an art installation at the Matsumoto City Museum of Art, Japan.Photograph: Tomohiro Ohsumi/Getty ImagesYayoi Kusama‘She inspired my proposal’: Readers on Yayoi KusamaFrom wedding ceremonies to sunsets with pumpkins, even in urinals, Kusama’s work brought joy, mischief and inspiration to so manyGuardian readersTue 1 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 10.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘She inspired my proposal … and our wedding day’View image in fullscreenCiaran and Liam.Photograph: Unknown/Guardian CommunityI have always loved Yayoi Kusama’s work, and when I visited an exhibition of hers on a gap year in Sydney I was spellbound by her infinity mirror rooms. I immediately thought, despite being single at the time, this is a fantastic space to propose in. Fast forward around eight years and I am on one knee holding a ring out to my partner inside an infinity mirror room in Helsinki, with excited and expectant Finns looking on. He said yes. At the wedding, the breakfast was held under polka dotted pink lanterns. Kusama was a fantastic artist, who also protested for my ability to marry – performing her own gay wedding ceremonies before it was legally recognised – and inspired key aspects of my wedding.Liam, 40, Surrey‘I saw her work and dissolved’Two years ago, while researching in Porto, I was encouraged by a friend to go see the Kusama retrospective at the museum in Parque de Serralves. I was fortunate to experience her remarkable installation Dots Obsession – Aspiring to Heaven’s Love. The powerful effect she termed as self-obliteration viscerally connected with me in that room. I didn’t exist, as I dissolved, the dots were everywhere. Humanity is blessed for her work and I’m grateful and humbled to have experienced it.David, Florida, US‘I watched the sunset while sat next to her yellow pumpkin’I’ve been lucky enough to see a huge amount of Yayoi Kusama’s work in Japan and in Europe. Hunting down remote galleries in rural Japan to see her work, and spending time viewing it with no one else there has been an absolute treat. Sitting on the shore next to the yellow pumpkin on Naoshima [an “art island”] watching the sun set was one of the most beautiful experiences I’ve had. Her work brings me a sense of peace and calm. She was truly inspirational.Rachel, London‘She connected with people who didn’t know about art’A lot has been written about Yayoi Kusama’s life and artistic achievements, but perhaps her greatest legacy lies in her ability to bring people into the experience of art, including people who don’t consider themselves art lovers, such as my mother. I loved seeing how my mum was drawn to Kusama’s image and polka-dot works when we visited Tokyo together. You don’t need pretentious art-speak or an understanding of art history to appreciate her work. That direct, instinctive response made the encounter pure and joyful. I bought her a little Kusama plush key chain, which she attached to her bag and carries wherever she goes. It has become a small part of her life; and, for me, a part of our memories together.Vivienne Chow, London‘I climbed inside a red pumpkin on Naoshima’View image in fullscreenSandie in the red pumpkin on Naoshima, Japan’s art island.Photograph: Guardian CommunityI only recently became aware of her work from a visit to Naoshima, Japan’s art island, where two of her pumpkins are on display. Red Pumpkin is particularly great as you can climb inside. On returning home I was surprised and delighted that a pumpkin sculpture had arrived at GoodwoodArtFoundation in Sussex. I’m now researching where to find more pumpkins as they always make me smile.Sandie, 61, London‘I used to pee beneath a photo of her chopping a penis with a knife’From 2008 to 2012 I worked in Tokyo. On weekends I’d go to a gay bar in Shinjuku 2-chome for their ¥1000 “all you can drink” beer for several hours. Above the toilet was a black-and-white photo of Yayoi Kusama looking directly at the camera while holding a big knife chopping a penis (it was really a dildo) on a chopping board. Her eyes were powerful and drew you in. The picture was quite daunting to be looking at while you were peeing. I love that picture and her – she had a very mischievous face and her art was amazing.Peter Allison, 51, Stockton-on-Tees‘Like losing a favourite neighbourhood auntie’We live around the corner from the Kusama Museum in Tokyo. It opened in 2017 when our now 11-year-old son was just two. We’ve visited every year since, watching him grow bigger among Kusama’s pumpkins and infinity rooms. We’ve often visited the museum as a pick-me-up when feeling down. My son and I watched the sunset from the roof on the day the UK exited the EU. Losing Kusama San is like losing a favourite neighbourhood auntie who was always there to bring us good cheer.Tina Burrett, 49, Tokyo, Japan‘The world is a more colourful, whimsical, magical place”’I found her art rather late in my life, after 50, but it resonated with me so much that now I have one of her prints in nearly every room of my home. I find them all extremely uplifting and endlessly fascinating. The more I learned about her the more inspired I felt. From her devastating mental health struggles she found such a brilliant way of harnessing the most unique forms of creativity. There is a true magic in that, and we can all benefit from the lessons she has left us with. An enormous talent she was, and the world is a more colourful, whimsical and magical place graced with the art she made over her long and interesting life. Rest in Power dear Yayoi. You were loved and will be greatly missed.Susan, 55, Florida, USExplore more on these topicsYayoi KusamaInstallationArtfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Demonic oppression’ and ‘girly convos’: the podcast wooing young women back to Christianity | Christianity | The Guardian
description: Girls Gone Bible is on tour in the US, touting a regressive ideal of femininity through discussions of abstinence and mental health struggles
Author: Alaina Demopoulos
Headline: Girls Gone Bible is on tour in the US, touting a regressive ideal of femininity through discussions of abstinence and mental health struggles
Content: Followers of the Christian podcast Girls Gone Bible cry during their live show stop at the Atlanta Symphony Hall in Atlanta, Georgia, on 14 November 2025.Photograph: Jessie Wardarski/APView image in fullscreenFollowers of the Christian podcast Girls Gone Bible cry during their live show stop at the Atlanta Symphony Hall in Atlanta, Georgia, on 14 November 2025.Photograph: Jessie Wardarski/APIs nothing sacredChristianity‘Demonic oppression’ and ‘girly convos’: the podcast wooing young women back to ChristianityGirls Gone Bible is on tour in the US, touting a regressive ideal of femininity through discussions of abstinence and mental health strugglesAlaina DemopoulosTue 1 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 08.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt first glance, the crowd gathering outside a music venue in Red Bank, New Jersey, could have passed for a group of sorority rush hopefuls – or Ella Langley fans on their way to the country star’s show. Most of them were under the age of 30. They wore cowboy boots, maxi sundresses and soft, bouncy blowouts, scrolling on their phones outside the doors as they waited for friends to arrive.But one accessory gave them away: the Bibles they toted. These women were there to pray.Specifically, they were there to see the Girls Gone Bible tour. Hosted by two “Bible-thumping bombshells” (perthe Daily Mail), the Girls Gone Bible podcast is often sold as the conservative woman’s answer to Alex Cooper’s secular, sexual Call Her Daddy franchise. The hosts have “girly convo[s]” about some of the same issues you might hear on Call Her Daddy:datingdos and don’ts, goingsober-curious, or battlinginsecurities. But Cooper never invited an Eastern Orthodox priest on toexplainwhy the Greek church “makes manly men” orblamedthe attention economy on Satan himself.View image in fullscreenAngela Halili prays during their Atlanta live show.Photograph: Jessie Wardarski/APSince debuting in 2023, Girls Gone Bible has become a brand all its own, with more than 1 million followers on Instagram and ranking 42nd for the religion and spirituality genre on Spotify. Its Revival tour began in April, bringing evenings of music, prayer and religious testimony to the east coast, as well as Alabama, Tennessee and California.Girls Gone Bible hosts Angela Halili, 30, and Arielle Reitsma, 36, call themselves “two imperfect girls serving an absolutely perfect God”, though neither grew up very religious or married into the faith. In fact, neither host is married, earning them relatability points among listeners who are still stuck in the dating scene. Both are relatively new Christians who spent their early careers as working actors in Los Angeles, a city usually depicted by conservatives as a den of sin. To that point: Reitsma played a character called “Slutty Girl” in the jukebox musical film Rock of Ages; Halili once appeared in a Marilyn Manson music video.double quotation markOne of the tactics of the Christian right is to narrow the definition of what it means to be a ChristianKelsey Hanson WoodruffBoth converted in moments of personal crisis. Halilitoldthe Christian publication Relevant that her anxiety and alcoholism stemmed from the pressures of working in the industry, and she first “met” God in 2019 when she started praying to help her through an anxiety attack. Reitsma, meanwhile, walked into a church “on a whim” after a rough breakup and “found peace like [she’d] never known”.The success of the podcast led to guest stints on Fox Newssegmentsabout gen Z seeking faith. They opened Donald Trump’s “victory rally” the day before his 2025 inauguration with a prayer thatincludedthe lines “in the life of President Donald Trump, as it is in heaven” and “President Trump … we declare that no weapon formed against you will prosper.”This association with the ascendant Christian right, of course, makes them Maga figures. But unlikepodcasters in theconservative-alignedwomanospherewho regularly toe the party line when it comes to topics such asimmigration, abortion orbirth control, Halili and Reitsma prefer a more lobotomized hang.Speaking softly, with matching vocal fry, they dispense vague platitudes about “healing” and soothe listeners with promises they are not alone in their struggles. They stay away from explicitly political messages in the same way that a pastor’s wife would not want to offend a congregant while making small talk during a post-service coffee hour.View image in fullscreenAngela Halili (left) and Arielle Reitsma speak before Donald Trump arrives at a rally in Washington DC before his inauguration on 19 January 2025.Photograph: Matt Rourke/APIt’s easy to fall into the Girls Gone Bible universe. Episode titles promise juicy discussions of topics that matter to young women: “Codependency and People-Pleasing”, “Overcoming an Eating Disorder”, “Honest Convo About Anxiety”. The hosts remind listeners that they are still figuring all of this out, too. It’s a welcoming space.Kelsey Hanson Woodruff, a scholar of American religious history and postdoctoral fellow at Wesleyan University, said that this come-as-you-are branding has deep roots in evangelism. “Evangelical Christians love a conversion story,” Woodruff said. “It can provide a lot of credibility to someone’s authentic Christian experience.”“They’re not shoving their opinions down people’s throats like some of these other podcasts [such as] Andrew Tate and all that stuff,” Alicia Reicis, a 30-year-old stay-at-home mom told me before the show.The hosts’ everygirl approachability belies their mission to woo women back into a faith that increasingly preaches their oppression. Adult women under 30 arerejectingorganized religion at record rates; a study released this April found that 40% of female respondents claimed no affiliation – up from 29% in 2013. This is probably due in part to the very visible rise of Christian nationalism tied to Trump’s administration. (The secretary of defense, Pete Hegseth,brought a pastorwho does not believe in a woman’s right to vote to speak at the Pentagon; the health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, hasinvokedterms like “spiritual warfare” and “malevolent forces” in speeches.)Despite this, Girls Gone Bible has found success with women who seem able to compartmentalize. Every woman I spoke to at the show declined to talk politics, or how they feel about the hosts supporting Trump. “I don’t really have a full opinion on that,” Reicis told me before politely excusing herself.Outside the venue, Genesis Gesualdo texted her friend who was running late. Gesualdo, 33, works at a salvage yard, which she called “a man’s job”. She told me that she had converted toChristianityless than a week ago because she felt she had strayed from a more modest lifestyle. “I wasn’t walking with him [Jesus], I didn’t obey him,” she said. “The way I dressed was provocative.” Gesualdo came to the event wearing a floor-length floral skirt. She said she was looking forward to “rejoicing”.I couldn’t know the political leanings of every person in attendance. Yes, there were a lot of women sporting what’s become known as “Republican face” – heavy makeup, plumped lips, fake tans – but there were others I would not feel comfortable pegging as such. I lost track counting the number of full-arm tattoo sleeves I saw; I watched a young woman hit her vape while waiting in the concessions line.‘A husband expects a yes’: how wife schools are shaping submissive Christian womenRead moreI wondered if these fans – maybe new converts themselves – would soon find themselves evolving into what the hosts consider to be “godly” women: conservative in appearance, faithandpolitical ideology. “One of the tactics of the Christian right is to narrow the definition of what it means to be a Christian,” Woodruff said. “[Girls Gone Bible] may not talk directly about policies, but they may put forth a certain definition of what it means to be a Christian woman, which is inherently political.”Girls Gone Bible touts aregressive ideal of femininity, encouraging women to be “modest” andabstain from sex before marriage, which Halili oncecalled“demonic oppression”. Harsh, but both women often insist that they’re not trying to shame anyone for prior transgressions – after all, both have pasts of their own. And their audience is perhaps already comfortable with the idea of celibacy. More young women, religious or not,are going “boy sober”, as voluntary abstinence is sometimes called on social media, due to their dismal dating pool and past bad experiences with men.View image in fullscreenFollowers of Girls Gone Bible take a group photo before their Atlanta live show.Photograph: Jessie Wardarski/APIn fact,Girls Gone Bible’s message about dating gets very close to pop feminism. “It’s been genuinely the greatest joy of my life to enter into complete purity,” Halili said on a recent episode taped after she returned from a trip to Miami, a party city synonymous with bikinis and bottle service. “Living a life where I’m not seeking that sort of validation from men, for men to think that I am hot or to think that I’m sexy.”At the New Jersey tour stop, Halili continued preaching girl power. “Marriage isn’t the reward,” she said, as groups of friends cheered and nodded along from their seats. Then she veered back: “Jesus’s presence in your marriage is the reward.”Melissa, a 58-year-old woman grabbing a drink at an Italian restaurant before the show, told me that she wanted to bring her son in hopes of finding him “a Christian girl”. He couldn’t make it; she brought her hairdresser instead. Two college friends, Grace Colucci and Taylor Garvey, might have been just who Melissa was looking for in a potential set-up. Both are 22, and first encountered Girls Gone Bible through TikTok clips. Colucci has never had a boyfriend, but she still appreciates the hosts’ dating advice. “They just make [abstinence] so normalized,” Colucci said. “It’s very inspirational and it makes you feel good.”But Colucci and Garvey were most interested in what Halili and Reitsma say about their mental health struggles. Halili has spoken extensively about living with OCD and disordered eating; for Reitsma, it was suicidal ideation. Colucci listens to their podcasts on stress and burnout. “What they go through is similar to us, and they’re good at [talking about it] in a way that’s fun and easy to learn from. It’s not too heavy.”Now comes the ‘womanosphere’: the anti-feminist media telling women to be thin, fertile and RepublicanRead moreAt the top of the show, Halili and Reitsma led a group singalong of worship music. When the pianist riffed that the “power in the name” of Jesus is “stronger than depression”, the crowd burst into the loudest cheers I heard all night.It makes sense that members of the most depressed and isolated generation in history would gravitate toward this subject matter. In her book Esther’s Army: The Christian Women Who Power the American Right,sociologist Katie Gaddini calls this audience “a post-pandemic female populace eager to hear ‘the truth’”. A recent Pewsurveyfound that 44% of 18- to 29-year-olds listen to “religious audio programs”, which they overwhelmingly digest as podcasts (as opposed to radio programs). Thirty-nine per cent of Americans of all ages who consume this content say they listen for “life advice or guidance”.A young woman whopostedon the subreddit r/Christianity seeking recommendations for podcasts geared toward “girls in their 20s” received this answer from another user: “Girls Gone Bible may not be the most theologically deep but they are a good starting place … Treat them [like] a source of relatability (a lot of their topics are highly relatable).”Evangelicals have long touted the Bible as a cure for mental anguish, and many pastors view depression as a spiritual attack.Reitsma told the audience she “met Jesus on the bathroom floor” during a time in which “everything in the world was telling me to end [her] life”. She explained needing “healing beyond what medication can fix”, meaning antidepressants. She quickly added, “there’s nothing wrong with medications,” but this felt like a concession.In general, the hostsspeak of burnout without addressing the economic forces behind their generation’s collective exhaustion and despair. They detail their mental health struggles, but fall short of interrogating the institutional roadblocks women face when they do try to get help. The intended takeaway: Jesus alone will cure you.View image in fullscreenAngela Halili, right, prays over a follower.Photograph: Jessie Wardarski/APThe night ended with Halili praying for “sexual sinners” (that’s anyone who has sex outside of marriage) and women struggling with infertility. Reitsma hugged audience members who lined up at the foot of the stage.Womencried, holding up their Bibles. Some wore newly purchased tour merch, sweatshirts with phrases such as “Keep the Faith” and “Thank You Jesus.” They would bring home a sense of validation: they were not alone in their pain.The tour has two more stops remaining, both in Florida in September, but there was something about the New Jersey show that especially delighted the hosts: it wasn’t happening in the Bible belt, or even a red state. “I feel such a hunger in here tonight,” Halili said. “It must be the east coast in ya.” Clearly, they believe their message is spreading.Explore more on these topicsChristianityIs nothing sacredReligionPodcastingWomenInternetDigital mediafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A walking tour of Andalucía’s historic white villages: ‘Nightingales serenade us as we wind along lush river valleys’ | Andalucia holidays | The Guardian
description: The famous pueblos blancos in southern Spain’s Sierra de Grazalema natural park teem with wildlife amid a limestone wonderland of peaks
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The famous pueblos blancos in southern Spain’s Sierra de Grazalema natural park teem with wildlife amid a limestone wonderland of peaks
Content: ‘The conditions couldn’t be more perfect’ … Zahara de la Sierra in Andalucía.Photograph: Antonio Ciero Reina/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘The conditions couldn’t be more perfect’ … Zahara de la Sierra in Andalucía.Photograph: Antonio Ciero Reina/AlamyAndalucia holidaysA walking tour of Andalucía’s historic white villages: ‘Nightingales serenade us as we wind along lush river valleys’The famous pueblos blancos in southern Spain’s Sierra de Grazalema natural park teem with wildlife amid a limestone wonderland of peaksMike UnwinTue 1 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 04.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘The wind is in from Africa / Last night I couldn’t sleep.” Joni Mitchell has ear-wormed her way into my head as my wife and I step out from Zahara de la Sierra into the mountains of Sierra de Grazalema natural park. The Africa bit probably comes from yesterday’s visit to Zahara’s castle museum. Here, high above the tiled terracotta mosaic of village rooftops, we learned how the recapture of this picturesque hill town was a turning point in theReconquista– the military campaign of the 1400s that saw the Catholics retake southern Spain after seven centuries of Moorish control. As for sleep deprivation, I may just have overdone it on last night’s tapas.Either way, Africa feels present as we tramp through the countryside of Andalucía, if only in the wildlife. The painted lady butterflies drifting over the flower-spangled verges, the turtle doves purring from the olive groves and the booted eagle drifting overhead: all are summer visitors recently blown in from the great continent to our south.View image in fullscreenBee-eaters in Sierra de Grazalema natural park.Photograph: Nature Picture Library/AlamyIt’s day two of our White Villages of the Ronda Mountains walking tour, a self-guided seven-day route from On Foot Holidays that explores this alluring corner of southern Spain. We arrived yesterday by bus from Málaga, winding up through the mountains until the whitewashed dwellings of Zahara appeared like teeth in the hillside ahead. This was the first of the week’s fourpueblos blancos, all tucked picturesquely into the natural park’s rugged 51,695 hectares (127,740 acres) of limestone peaks and serpentine river valleys.I’ve walked with On Foot before, so the routine is familiar: water bottles and packed lunches stashed in daypacks, laminated map around neck on lanyard and route app open on phone (belt-and-braces navigation). Best of all, our luggage is already wending its way by taxi to the next destination.double quotation markLunch is in a high meadow, where we unwrap our bocadillos while bees buzz and butterflies busy themselves among the bloomsThe conditions couldn’t be more perfect. The hillsides burst with blossom and birdsong, the May temperature is a pleasant mid-20s (midsummer out here would be punishing), and the peaks stand proud against the clear blue sky. It’s hard to believe February brought such heavy rains that much of our route was then impassable – and some areas of the park were affected by wildfires later in the summer.View image in fullscreenWalking to GrazalemaBut each month here has its own character. September/October – also prime walking season – sees the chestnuts and cork oak forests turn russet and gold, and the spring irises and orchids replaced by the post-summer bloom of wild asparagus and autumn crocus. Overhead, those booted eagles will be massing for their return journey – along with bee-eaters, honey buzzards and other winged voyagers – back to Africa.Eight of the best secluded and affordable places to stay in Andalucía, SpainRead moreToday’s hike takes us south towards Grazalema:pueblo blanconumber two. We skirt a reservoir then wind along a lush river valley, nightingales serenading us from the oleander thickets, and by late morning are rising into the mountains, the vista gaining grandeur as we gain height.Lunch is in a high meadow, where we unwrap ourbocadilloswhile bees buzz and butterflies busy themselves among the blooms. Afternoon brings a long uphill slog, then finally a cool descent through shady pines to sleepy Grazalema. Another 11 miles (18km) under our belts.We stay two nights in Grazalema at theHotel la Mejorana, meeting wild ibex on a mountain circuit high above town, and eating at the cosyCádiz el Chicorestaurant, where a menu featuring partridge and wild boar (though, thankfully, not ibex) reflects the region’s hunting traditions. At night, the cobbled streets are quiet beneath a canopy of stars.Benaoján, the third of ourpueblos blancos, lies about 16 miles to the south-east. We exit Grazalema early in the morning, beneath the Los Peñascosmirador. Roosting griffon vultures line the cliffs like pterodactyls, warming up in the morning sun before, one at a time, flapping off on table-top wings for another day combing the plains.View image in fullscreenBenaoján.Photograph: Japhotos/AlamyOur route leads down through the oak woods before rising again into the hills. Here we enter a limestone wonderland, the karst formations sculpted by wind and rain into Henry Moore-like statues. Bee-eaters dart overhead, their liquid chirrups audible long before we lay eyes on them. A passing walker greets us with a cheery “Buen camino!” He’s returning with his father to see the farmhouse where they grew up. We find Dad sitting on a nearby rock, devouring an empanada. They’re the only other walkers we meet all day.Our hideaway at Benaoján is theMolino del Santohotel, where we dine beside a chuckling stream on a terrace crowded with potted geraniums. From here, it takes us two hours to hike to theCueva de la Pileta, an immense cave system discovered in 1905 when a local farmer spotted bats streaming from a fissure in the hillside.Local guide Ainhoa Bullón leads us down cool, narrow passages into measureless caverns, her thin torch beam illuminating flowstone formations as enormous and elaborate as a Gaudí cathedral – formed, she explains, by the drip-drip of lime at the rate of 1cm every 400 years. The farthest recesses hold exquisite shamanic rock art, some more than 25,000 years old. Ainhoa overflows with information, talking us through the cave’s successive ages of antiquity, from Neanderthal to Neolithic. Most important, she delivers us safely back to the blazing sunshine outside.View image in fullscreenRonda, perched atop El Tajo gorge.Photograph: M Viliam /AlamyOur week ends at Ronda, perched atop the precipitous El Tajo gorge. The celebrated clifftop town seems to beckon us onward like some mythical sky citadel as we tramp our final kilometres towards it. Below the cliffs, we find ourselves back in tourist land, sharing the steep climb to the top with a gaggle of selfie-snapping day trippers.We make it, slumping at the first available cafe table to lever off boots, fold away the map and order a celebratory coldcerveza. Tomorrow, we catch our bus back to Málaga. For now, a final night lies ahead, with a stirring panorama from our room at theParador de Rondaand the promise of a slap-up meal down in the old town. Our beers arrive, and any lingering strains of Joni are soon lost to a busker’s volley of flamenco guitar.The trip was provided byOn Foot Holidays.It costs from £985pp for aseven-night self-guided route in Grazalemanaturalpark, ending in Ronda;five-,six- andeight-night routes also available.The walking season is February-May and September-December (April, May, Septemberand October being optimum)Explore more on these topicsAndalucia holidaysSpain holidaysEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sami Tamimi’s recipes for musabaha (warm chickpea dip) and turmeric and nigella seed flatbreads | Food | The Guardian
description: This rubbly cousin of hummus is flavourful and satisfying at any time of day, served warm, topped with a colourful salad and just made to eat with homemade flatbreads
Author: Sami Tamimi
Headline: This rubbly cousin of hummus is flavourful and satisfying at any time of day, served warm, topped with a colourful salad and just made to eat with homemade flatbreads
Content: Sami Tamimi’smusabaha, or warm chickpeas with spicy cherry tomato and coriander salad, served with turmeric and nigella seed flatbread.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Georgia Rudd.View image in fullscreenSami Tamimi’smusabaha, or warm chickpeas with spicy cherry tomato and coriander salad, served with turmeric and nigella seed flatbread.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Georgia Rudd.FoodSami Tamimi’s recipes for musabaha (warm chickpea dip) and turmeric and nigella seed flatbreadsThis rubbly cousin of hummus is flavourful and satisfying at any time of day, served warm, topped with a colourful salad and just made to eat with homemade flatbreadsSami TamimiTue 1 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFew things make me happier than a bowl of warmmusabahaserved with freshly baked bread straight from the pan. It’s a combination that shouts comfort, generosity and the simple pleasure of sharing food. Across the Levant, musabaha is a much-loved breakfast or brunch dish, though I’d happily eat it at any time of day. Served with the buttery, soft turmeric and nigella-seed flatbreads, it becomes a meal that is nourishing, intensely satisfying and perfect for gathering family and friends around the table.Musabaha(warm chickpeas with spicy cherry tomato and coriander salad)View image in fullscreenSami Tamimi’smusabaha, or warm chickpeas with spicy cherry tomato and coriander salad.When I’m short of time but craving something nourishing, full of flavour and genuinely satisfying, I turn to murabaha time and again. Unlike hummus, the chickpeas are left whole, then gently warmed and topped with a vibrant salad of spicy cherry tomatoes, fresh coriander and good olive oil. Serve with plenty of the warm flatbreads below for scooping.Prep15 minCook15 minServes42400g tins chickpeas,drained3 tbsp olive oil, plus extra to drizzle5 large garlic cloves, peeled and crushed1 large green chilli, finely chopped seeds and all1 tbsp ground cumin100g tahini, plus extra to serve120ggreek-style yoghurt3 tbsp lemon juiceSaltFor the cherry tomato salad150g cherry tomatoes,halved1 mini cucumber(100g), finely diced½ red pepper(75g), finely diced20g fresh coriander, finely chopped2 spring onions, trimmed and very thinly sliced1 green chilli, thinly sliced seeds and all1 large garlic clove,peeled and crushed2 tbsp lemon juice1 tbsp white-wine vinegar2 tbsp olive oil1 tbsp sumac1 tsp dried mint½ tsp aleppo chilli, plus extra for sprinklingPut the chickpeas in a medium saucepan with enough water just to cover them., put on a medium heat and bring to a simmer. Leave to cook for about five minutes, just to soften them a bit more, then drain, reserving about 300ml of the cooking liquid.Meanwhile, put all ingredients for the cherry tomato salad in a medium bowl with half a teaspoon of salt, and mix well.Put the oil in a medium saucepan on a medium heat. Add the garlic and cook, stirring often, for two minutes, until the garlic starts to colour, then add the chilli and cook for another minute. Add the drained chickpeas, the reserved cooking liquid, cumin, tahini, yoghurt, lemon juice and a teaspoon of salt, bring to a boil, then turn down the heat to low and simmer, stirring from time to time, for two minutes.To serve, transfer the warm chickpeas to a large serving plate with a lip or a wide, shallow bowl. Drizzle over some tahini, then spoon the cherry tomato salad on top. Finish with a good drizzle of olive oil and a sprinkling of aleppo chilli, and serve with the flatbreads below.Turmeric and nigella seed flatbreadView image in fullscreenSami Tamimi’s turmeric and nigella seed flatbread.I come from a culture where offering freshly baked, warm bread is one of the greatest traditions of hospitality. Whether welcoming unexpected guests or gathering loved ones around the table, bread is always the first thing shared. These golden flatbreads, scented with earthy turmeric and nutty ghee, are perfect for scooping up the warm chickpeas and spicy tomato salad oppositebelow, but they’re equally delicious served with dips or simply drizzled with good olive oil.Prep5 minRest10 minCook25 minMakes8150gfull-fatgreek yoghurt1 tsp bicarbonate of soda350g 00 flour, or plain flour,plus extra for dusting100g wholewheat flour¾ tsp ground turmeric1 tbsp nigella seeds1½ tsp salt35g ghee, or butter, meltedPut the yoghurt and bicarb in the bowl of a free-standing mixer with the dough hook attached, and stir well with a spoon. The mix should start bubbling. Add 150ml water, stir again, then add all the remaining ingredients apart from the ghee and mix on low speed for five minutes, until the dough is soft but not sticky.Divide the dough in 10 equal pieces of about 110g each. Roll each piece into a ball, cover with a damp towel and leave to rest for 10 minutes – this will stop the dough drying out.On a lightly floured surface, roll out each piece of dough into a 16cm disc about ½cm thick.Heat a grill pan until it’s very hot. Lay in one or two dough discs and cook for a minute or two on each side, until the bread is cooked through and has char marks. Remove from the pan, keep warm and repeat with the remaining dough. Brush each flatbread with melted ghee or butter, and serve.Explore more on these topicsFoodBeans, pulses and legumesMain courseSaladBreadBakingHerbs and spicesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Smart ideas for preserving summer fruit and veg | Chefs | The Guardian
description: From fermenting plums in honey and pickling courgettes in vinegar brine to a British take on kimchi, there are many ways to make the most of the warm-weather harvest
Author: Anna Berrill
Headline: From fermenting plums in honey and pickling courgettes in vinegar brine to a British take on kimchi, there are many ways to make the most of the warm-weather harvest
Content: Kenji Morimoto’s mirepoix kimchi is a great way to preserve late-summer vegetables.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull.View image in fullscreenKenji Morimoto’s mirepoix kimchi is a great way to preserve late-summer vegetables.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull.Kitchen aideChefsSmart ideas for preserving summer fruit and vegFrom fermenting plums in honey and pickling courgettes in vinegar brine to a British take on kimchi, there are many ways to make the most of the warm-weather harvestAnna BerrillTue 1 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 08.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat’s the best way to preserve late-summer fruit and veg?Jess,by emailFruit, fruit everywhere, so try fermenting it in honey, says Rachel de Thample, author ofThe Fermentation Year(published in September). “I’m currently looking at a jar of blackberries, but whole plums would be gorgeous, too,” she says, especially when eaten with blue cheese – “or any cheese, really” – meat or fish; you can also use the syrup like maple syrup or cordial. De Thample packs the fruit into sterilised jars and pours in just enough honey to cover it: “If the fruit has a low acidity, add a spoonful of lemon juice or a splash of cider vinegar as well.” Pop on the lid and leave for a few weeks. “It gets fizzy, but it doesn’t get to that explosive stage, because it has quite a concentrated sugar content. It’ll keep for up to a year at room temperature, but I normally pop it in the fridge after a few weeks.”Kimchi is another option to keep Jess enjoying summer fruits all year round. “In Korea, apples and pears are traditional, but there’s a kimchi for every season and region,” says De Thample, who takes a British approach with a courgette, blackcurrant and strawberry number: “You can use up tomatoes in the paste, too.” Otherwise, if you have plums and damsons, take inspiration from Japanese umeboshi: “That has a high percentage of salt – I use 15% per 100g fruit. Layer the salt and plums in jars and, if it’s really dry, pour over water; otherwise, just crush a couple of the plums so their juices create a brine with the salt.” The brine can then be used like a plummy soy sauce, De Thample says: “Having a few jars stored away always makes me feel like I’m winning.” Damsons are also a dream in flavoured liquors, says Kenji Morimoto, regular Guardian contributor and author ofFerment: “That’s a really nice way to capture their flavour, and all you need is vodka, the fruit and rock [or granulated] sugar.Cheong, a Korean form of maceration, will also prolong the goodbyes, Morimoto says. “It’s an easy concept: you want equal parts sugar and fruit, then let that sit, stirring occasionally, and you’ll end up with this candied fruit and a delicious syrup, or just a delicious syrup.” That’s good for glazing tarts, spooning over ice-cream or drizzling over cakes, and in cocktails, as well as for adding a balancing sweetness to savoury dishes such as stews.Otherwise, Morimoto would bring “a bite of effervescence and briny tang” to the winter dearth by making lacto-fermented cherry tomatoes, which he stores and uses chopped in grain bowls and salsas, and in pasta and other savoury sauces. And there aren’t many summer vegetables that won’t taste great pickled, though courgettes in a classic sweet vinegar brine should be high on Jess’s list. “In many ways, courgettes are better to pickle than cucumbers, because they retain that crunch,” Morimoto says, so slice them, salt them, drain them, then add the brine. “You can then take them in any flavour direction you fancy: mustard seeds, fennel seeds and celery seeds; soy sauce, ginger and garlic; dill and allspice.”Whichever route you go down is sure to get you out of a pickle come autumn.Got a culinary dilemma? Emailfeast@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsChefsKitchen aideFoodSummer food and drinkFruitPickling, fermenting and preservingVegetablesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘A huge learning curve’: apprentices on the benefits and pitfalls of vocational training | Apprenticeships | The Guardian
description: While many young people have found jobs and built careers, some have struggled to complete their courses
Author: Jane Clinton
Headline: While many young people have found jobs and built careers, some have struggled to complete their courses
Content: An apprentice engineer works on an aircraft interior in an aerospace engineering factory.Photograph: Monty Rakusen/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn apprentice engineer works on an aircraft interior in an aerospace engineering factory.Photograph: Monty Rakusen/Getty ImagesApprenticeships‘A huge learning curve’: apprentices on the benefits and pitfalls of vocational trainingWhile many young people have found jobs and built careers, some have struggled to complete their coursesJane ClintonandMajidah ChowdhuryTue 1 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe crisis in the youth employment market, withalmost a million young people not in education, employment or training (Neet)across the UK, has placed fresh emphasis on ways of getting employees into the workforce.The government hopes to increase focus on technical and vocational learning inEnglandfrom the age of 14. In parallel, there is an ambition to create thousands more apprenticeships.The work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, has alsoannounced a new bursaryaimed at ensuring families will not be left financially worse off if their teenager starts an apprenticeship.Research from theNational Foundation for Educational Research(NFER) found that black and mixed-ethnicity learners from poorer backgrounds and those for whom English is an additional language are less likely to complete their apprenticeships.The Guardian asked people to share their experiences of apprenticeships.View image in fullscreenThe government hopes to increase the focus on technical and vocational learning from the age of 14 in England.Photograph: Johnny Greig/Getty Images‘I am progressing faster than colleagues with degrees’Ellen*, 24, from Worcester, decided an apprenticeship would work better for her than university, although it was “never suggested” as an option at school.“It was just assumed that uni was going to be the way I went,” she says. “I did my own research on my other options.”Securing an apprenticeship was not easy, and she experienced “a lot of rejections” before she won a place at a medium-sized MEP (mechanical, electrical and plumbing) consultancy.Her three-year apprenticeship was four days a week with a day at college for her higher national certificate (HNC) studies. Her HNC course was two years, but the apprenticeship requirement of submitting evidence added an additional year.Burnham to tell schools in England to adapt teaching to local business needsRead moreEllen passed, gaining a BTec level 4 HNC as well as a CIBSE (Chartered Institute of Building Services Engineers) Licentiate, and EngTech certification through CIBSE as an end-point assessment organisation and the UK regulatory body, the Engineering Council.“It was a huge learning curve and I had to ask for extra help from my teachers,” she says. “At 18, being thrown into the deep end, you just want to do well, you just want to try your best to get all the answers right.“I had a really good experience at the company that took me on as an apprentice and then gave me a job – really supportive managers – but I found it difficult to balance work, study and having a social life. All my friends chose to go to university and were all over the country, and there was no one around my age at work so having any social life was very difficult.”Ellen says a “lack of female role models” within her industry and office was also “a difficulty”.“I have since moved into fire sprinkler design, but starting my new career with a construction qualification and four years of industry experience has meant I am progressing faster than my colleagues who have degrees,” she says.View image in fullscreenA ‘lack of female role models’ can be hard for young women taking apprenticeships in some sectors.Photograph: Caia Image/Getty Images‘I was effectively being paid to learn’Harry, 26, a machinist, says he feels “gratitude” that he has a job, as he sees friends who went to university now questioning that decision.“Some have needed uni to get the jobs that they have now, but some of them I don’t think have needed it, and they’re starting to realise that,” he says.Harry, from Billingshurst, West Sussex, says that, after achieving three A-levels, he briefly flirted with the idea of studying business at university.“The cost put me off,” he says. “Also, it didn’t sit right with me in my gut to go to university. I just didn’t think I had the mental strength for full-time education while balancing a part-time job and watching my money.”Instead, he worked two ski seasons as a chaperone in France and was planning a third when the Covid pandemic closed down tourism.“I was lucky and privileged enough to be able to come back home to stay with my family,” he says. “They obviously wanted me to get a job to pay rent.”Harry knew about apprenticeships through his father, who had done an electrician’s apprenticeship in the late 1980s, and applied for “about five”. He got a four-year level 3 engineering machine technician work placement, involving a day a week of study. He started his apprenticeship in 2020, but delays due to Covid meant he finished it in 2025.Harry threw himself into his studies. “While I was at college, I made sure that all the time I was there, I was doing as much work as I could because I was effectively being paid to learn,” he says.At the end of his apprenticeship, he gained an engineering technician (machinist – advanced manufacturing engineering) level 3 qualification. The apprenticeship had a guaranteed job if he passed. Harry was offered a role, but he decided to go elsewhere for a better wage.He adds: “I do take gratitude in the fact that I have a job. People are meant to come out of uni and find a career, but I don’t think many of them can.”View image in fullscreenThere is a government ambition to create thousands more apprenticeships.Photograph: Monty Rakusen/Getty Images‘Some people were not ready to come to work’Hannah*, a metalworker, says while her apprenticeship was “amazing”, she saw how others struggled and missed out on completing theirs because of a lack of support.“The work suited me, and I received plenty of affirmation after a long spell of unemployment and low self-confidence,” she says. “The college qualification opened a lot of doors.“I took maths and English functional skills tests as part of the process, having not taken any exams as a school-refusing teenager, but the course had some shortcomings when it came to material and delivery – my cohort on the course were almost universally disengaged.”Hannah, who is in her 30s and lives in south-west England, dropped out of school aged 14, only returning sporadically. She was “in that category ofNeetfor quite a while”, turning to the apprenticeship after periods in college, cleaning part-time and picking up “little bits of work” in her 20s.While she is encouraged by the government’s plans regarding technical learning and apprenticeships, she sounds a note of caution. Hannah saw several people unable to continue with their apprenticeship and believes more guided support would have helped, adding that some of the cohort “struggled with attendance and emotional regulation”.“I think apprenticeships can be fantastic, but they aren’t the panacea for joblessness,” she says. “There’s a lot of really good intentions to try and use the apprenticeship programme to get people who might have been a bit like me, though I was also very privileged because I had a supportive family and wasn’t from a really deprived background.“But I saw some people on the apprenticeship, particularly the younger ones, who were just not ready to come into work. Some of them had quite complex emotional problems or difficult backgrounds as well, which makes it even harder.”View image in fullscreenA new bursaryis aimed at ensuring families will not be left financially worse off if their teenager starts an apprenticeship.Photograph: sturti/Getty Images‘Not having any debt is very freeing’Jotham, 24, from Buckinghamshire, says he regarded his three-year degree apprenticeship as the “safest route” to securing a job.“I knew before I did my A-levels that I wanted to do an apprenticeship,” he says. “My dad had said it was a good option and I looked at the government list. University was a backup option if it hadn’t worked out.”He applied for “about 20 to 30 apprenticeships” and chose a scheme with one day a week studying at university in London that meant he could live at home and commute. It started in 2019.“The company I chose had two apprentices at the same time, so that was an advantage, as you had someone to do it with, and the previous apprentice was also there and would help us,” he says.The Guardian view on apprenticeships: young people need help getting started at work | EditorialRead moreHe achieved a first in his digital and technology solutions apprenticeship BSc. Although there was no guarantee of a job at the end of his course, Jotham “carried on working at the same place and was offered a job”.“It’s a very practical option, isn’t it?” he says. “It has all of the advantages of university and none of the disadvantages. Not having any debt is very freeing.”However, he knew of some apprentices who were not so lucky: one had to stop “a year in” because the firm collapsed.“Others either had to stop completely or change how they did the course because the company wasn’t able to employ them for the whole three years,” he adds. “That was a lot of bother for them, because there was no backup plan built into the course.”Jotham is now working in database management.“In the job market, really what’s wanted is experience, but people coming out of their degree may struggle to get that,” he says. “With an apprenticeship, you get the experience. The degree is almost like a checkbox item.”*Names have been changedExplore more on these topicsApprenticeshipsYoung peopleYouth unemploymentCareersWork & careersUnemploymentJob huntingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: My abusive and aggressive partner left me but O2 insists I meet him in person  | Consumer rights | The Guardian
description: I need to take him off my family account, but it says the only way is for him to join me for a joint call with O2
Author: Anna Tims
Headline: I need to take him off my family account, but it says the only way is for him to join me for a joint call with O2
Content: Trying to  take an abusive partner off a family phone account proved traumatising and risky.Photograph: IanDagnall Computing/AlamyView image in fullscreenTrying to  take an abusive partner off a family phone account proved traumatising and risky.Photograph: IanDagnall Computing/AlamyConsumer championsConsumer rightsMy abusive and aggressive partner left me but O2 insists I meet him in personI need to take him off my family account, but it says the only way is for him to join me for a joint call with O2Anna TimsTue 1 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy partner packed up anddisappeared with his children while I was out with friends. I was left having to foot all our bills, including rent, which has made me financially stressed.We had a family plan withO2which meant family phones were all registered to my account. When my partner left, he stopped paying his share of the monthly phone bill, so I set about trying to remove his, and his children’s, phones from the account. O2 explained he would need to join a conference call with me and O2 to agree the transfer of the numbers in question.Getting my ex to engage with this involved support from a mutual friend; then he claimed he could not join the conference calls. O2 had only one suggestion: that he and I meet in person for the call.My ex is an emotionally aggressive and manipulative man. He does not know where I now live, and I want to keep it that way, so I met him in a busy park, and we spent an hour on the phone together with O2. His children’s numbers successfully transferred. His number did not. O2 said it would keep working on it and ended the call.Two weeks on, nothing has happened. O2 insists I either make another joint call with my ex, or pay his outstanding bills and cancel his phone plan.I’ve explained about my financial situation and concerns about meeting up with him.I discovered an O2 form allowing customers to flag up difficult family situations and filled it out but was told I did not qualify. I have now been sent a £164 early termination fee for the children’s numbers that were removed from the plan.My ex is deliberately manipulating this situation. I am baffled that O2 does not have a better process for women during relationship breakdown as forced meet ups could be really risky in some cases.Name and address withheldMy mother has Alzheimer’s but O2 won’t refund unused phone contractRead moreI felt rage when I read of your plight. You had, by then, spent four weeks trying to get O2 to understand the potential risks of meeting your ex and the financial hardship his departure caused. Its response that you meet up, or pay up, was almost certainly in breach of the regulatory duty of care to vulnerable customers telecoms companies are obliged to fulfil.When I pointed this out, O2 managed, within hours, what it had failed to do in weeks, and called you. It admitted you had been led on a debilitating wild goose chase.Instead of subjecting you to a painful encounter in a public park, it should have served a disconnection notice giving him seven days to transfer the numbers to a new account. It duly did after a push from its press office, and cancelled the £164 charge. It has offered you £200 in compensation but you, understandably, feel this does not reflect the anguish and expense the blunders caused you.O2 says: “We have a range of policies to protect and support customers who have been victims of domestic abuse, ensuring they can safely disconnect unwanted numbers without having to meet an ex-partner in person. This existing support was not accurately offered, and we apologise for the experience she had, and the time taken to resolve her issue.”We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. Email us atconsumer.champions@theguardian.comor write to Consumer Champions, Money, the Guardian, 90 York Way, London N1 9GU. Please include a daytime phone number. Submission and publication of all letters is subject toour terms and conditions.Explore more on these topicsConsumer rightsConsumer championsConsumer affairsO2TelecomsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From milk to sausage rolls: how vending machines could help tackle UK ‘food deserts’ | Food & drink industry | The Guardian
description: Selling direct to public helps squeezed farmers control prices and improves access to food in rural areas
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Selling direct to public helps squeezed farmers control prices and improves access to food in rural areas
Content: Emma Poulter and her daughter Bonnie, three, stock up on milk. ‘The machine is fun for little ones,’ says Poulter.Photograph: Sam Frost/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEmma Poulter and her daughter Bonnie, three, stock up on milk. ‘The machine is fun for little ones,’ says Poulter.Photograph: Sam Frost/The GuardianFood & drink industryFrom milk to sausage rolls: how vending machines could help tackle UK ‘food deserts’Selling direct to public helps squeezed farmers control prices and improves access to food in rural areasJoanna PartridgeTue 1 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 05.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFizzy drinks, packets of crisps and bars of chocolate: for decades, vending machines were known as a place to grab a quick snack.Now one family of farmers is trying to change that by bringing vending machines offering fresh milk and local produce – including scotch eggs, sausage rolls and brownies – to villages and other rural locations.Mark James, 70, and his sons Sam, 39, and Jacob, 36, first trialled vending machines as a way of selling their milk directly to consumers, giving themselves more control over the price they receive.“For the first time ever, we’re price makers rather than price takers,” Mark says. “If we weren’t doing [the vending machine business], we’d have to think about giving up milk.”Just under a third (30%) of the 4,500 litres of milk produced each day by the family’s herd of 130 dairy cows at Bodenham in Herefordshire is sold at their 17 Whole Moo World vending machines, located across Herefordshire and the neighbouring counties ofGloucestershire, Worcestershire and Shropshire. The remaining 70% is sold to a local milk processor.View image in fullscreenMark James (right) and his son Sam at the Whole Moo World and Tuckshop vending machines at the Primrose Vale pick-your-own and farm shop near Cheltenham.Photograph: Sam Frost/The GuardianWhen Whole Moo World took off, Jacob and Sam branched out into retailing cakes, sandwiches and other treats made by small local producers from vending machines. Their business, Tuckshop, now has 22 sites, mostly alongside the milk machines, and also allows them to sell empty glass bottles for milk.Jacob says farmers are “waking up” to the advantages of selling directly to consumers, even if they do not have a suitable location or the funds needed to build their own farm shop.View image in fullscreenJacob James believes farmers are ‘waking up’ to the advantages of selling directly to consumers.He believes vending machines could be the answer for villages and small rural communitiesat risk of becoming “food deserts”, where lower-income households struggle to find fresh healthy food amid closures of local shops and poor public transport.They also promise a more profitable way for squeezed farmers to reach customers directly and avoid expensive fees for intermediaries.Dairy producers in Britain and beyond have suffered in recent years from aboom and bust price cycle, where the price of milk, a globally traded commodity, has been extremely volatile. Strong global demand for dairy has usually led to farmers increasing their herd size and upping production, followed by oversupply and a crash in the milk price.Farmgate milk pricesbegan to tumbleagain earlier this year, Mark says. “In August last year we were paid 44p a litre, and ever since the beginning of February it’s been down at 30p a litre.”For many dairy farmers, including the Jameses, this price does not cover the cost of production. Margins in the industry have always been tight and UK supermarkets have traditionally used low milk prices to tempt shoppers through the door, and the milk processing sector is dominated by three main players – Arla, Müller and FirstMilk.British supermarkets are currently charging between £1.20 and £1.30 for a two-pint, or 1.1-litre, bottle of milk.Whole Moo World customers pay £1.50 for a litre of the family’s unhomogenised milk – where the cream has not been separated from the milk during processing – delivered into a refillable glass bottle, which customers can buy once in the vending machines and wash and reuse.A litre of milkshake – with flavours including chocolate, strawberry, banana and specials such as mint choc and blueberry muffin – costs £2.90.View image in fullscreenMoo World customers pay £1.50 for a litre of the family’s unhomogenised milk in a glass bottle.Photograph: Sam Frost/The GuardianMark James says customers are prepared to pay a small premium for milk that, he says, tastes creamier and is more environmentally friendly thanks to the use of glass bottles.This is the Jameses’ second stint as dairy farmers. Mark took over his parents’ farm but quit milk production duringthe 2015 crisis, when low wholesale prices made it impossible to remain profitable.The family subsequently diversified their business, farming beef cattle and opening holiday lets, but the rolling banks of their land did not make it particularly suited to growing arable crops.The younger generation of the James family only supported a return to milk production if they ran the business differently.“It is only through doing this [the vending machines] that I have any interest in being a dairy farmer,” Sam says.It is not just the machines that make a difference: the mixed herd of dairy cows are milked by robots at a time of each cow’s choosing, freeing the family from 4am alarms and the labour-intensive nature of traditional milk production.View image in fullscreenVending machines sell brownies, banoffee pie, cakes, sandwiches and other treats made by small local producers.Photograph: Sam Frost/The GuardianOn the day the Guardian visited one vending machine located next to the Primrose Vale pick-your-own and farm shop on the outskirts of Cheltenham, there was a steady flow of customers who arrived to fill up their glass bottles from the machines.“Our big issue is how to break the habit of [customers] picking milk up in a supermarket, and that is the difficulty because this means that someone is going to make a special trip to come here,” Mark says.For this, finding the right location is vital. Placing the vending machines next to a farm shop has mutual benefits for both businesses, says Jon Henley, one of the managers at Primrose Vale.“The machines seem to be bringing customers in 24/7, and then they see our strawberries and come back for the pick-your-own or the charging points [for electric vehicles]. It can also be helpful in winter when there isn’t much seasonal picking.”The machines are also a novelty for children. “We come to pick berries and then get milk. The machine is fun for little ones,” says Emma Coulter, buying a bottle of milk with help from her three-year-old daughter, Bonnie.Sam Carter-Campbell, who admits to treating himself to a strawberry milkshake as he drives around Gloucestershire for his job as an electrician, says: “I feel like I’m their best customer as I’m at the machine every day. I occasionally have a brownie, too, but sometimes I look and think, ‘I’d better not.’”View image in fullscreenSam Carter-Campbell, an electrician, says he visits the Whole Moo World vending machine every day.Photograph: Sam Frost/The GuardianOne customer, who gave her name as Vicky, describes the machines as a good idea, provided they are installed in the right places in pretty villages and do not become an “eyesore”.The technology that powers vending machines has made significant advances in recent years, according to David Llewellyn, the chief executive of the Vending and Automated Retail Association.“It’s no longer just a standalone mechanical machine, which you don’t have any control over. Now with cashless payments, telemetry and connected equipment, you can see what’s happening, what needs replenishing and it will maintain a range of different temperatures,” he says.Machines stocked with fresh local produce have been available for consumers in France and Italy for some time, adds Llewellyn, while there is one machine for every 35 people in Japan. That compares with one for every 169 in the UK, where most are coffee and hot beverage outlets, usually found in factories and other workplaces.Although the James family can now monitor their machines remotely, they still refill them with milk themselves, travelling to locations within a 30-mile radius of their farm. They plan to keep expanding and may have to take on staff to support the business.“There is a new site we are looking at at the moment, a village of a couple of thousand people, where we think we could provide basic food like milk, eggs, cheese and sandwiches,” Jacob says. “We can do that fairly quickly. The place would support a a farm shop, but vending is much cheaper to install and run.”Explore more on these topicsFood & drink industrySupermarketsRetail industryMilkFarmingFoodRural affairsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Houseplant hacks: can a lint roller banish pests? | Houseplants | The Guardian
description: It’s a great detection tool, but if your plant is infested with thrips or spider mites it may not be enough …
Author: Gynelle Leon
Headline: It’s a great detection tool, but if your plant is infested with thrips or spider mites it may not be enough …
Content: Composite: Olga Yastremska/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Olga Yastremska/Getty ImagesHouseplant hacksHouseplantsHouseplant hacks: can a lint roller banish pests?It’s a great detection tool, but if your plant is infested with thrips or spider mites it may not be enough …Gynelle LeonTue 1 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 13.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe problemThe worst pests are the ones you can’t see; thrips and spider mites are tiny and very good at hiding on the undersides of leaves, in leaf joints and along stems. By the time you notice the damage – silvery streaks, speckling or fine webbing – the infestation is usually well under way. Early detection is the difference between a quick fix and a full-blown outbreak.The hackUse a sticky lint roller to pick up pests that are hard to see. The idea is it works as both a detection tool, and a light physical intervention, lifting adults and eggs before they multiply.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHouseplant hacks: can willow water act as a rooting hormone?Read moreThe methodRoll a lint roller lightly across the leaves, focusing on the undersides where most pests gather, as well as along the stems. Use it gently to prevent tearing or bruising the foliage. Peel off the used layer and inspect it closely: look out for thrips, which show up as thin dark or pale slivers, and mites, which appear as tiny moving dots. Repeat every few days if you suspect a problem, and pair with the appropriate insecticide or treatment.The testI ran a lint roller over a plant that I suspected of harbouring thrips. The sheet had several thin dark specks stuck to the surface – exactly the confirmation I needed.The verdictAs a detection tool, the lint roller is a surprisingly clever little trick. It turns an invisible problem into something you can actually see, which is often the hardest part of catching pests early. But it isn’t a cure: rolling alone will never lift every pest, egg and larva from a plant, so treat anything you find properly.Explore more on these topicsHouseplantsHouseplant hacksGardening adviceGardensfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Thirty years of waiting, a memoir and a trial: conviction in Tupac Shakur killing brings closure | US news | The Guardian
description: A Las Vegas jury on Monday found Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis guilty in the 1996 murder of the hip-hop icon
Author: Dani Anguiano
Headline: A Las Vegas jury on Monday found Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis guilty in the 1996 murder of the hip-hop icon
