title: Mark Carney tells US to ‘start being serious’ amid escalating trade war | US news | The Guardian
description: Canadian PM is set to retaliate against tariffs levied by Donald Trump and criticized US officials over insults
Author: Victoria Bekiempis
Headline: Canadian PM is set to retaliate against tariffs levied by Donald Trump and criticized US officials over insults
Content: Donald Trump speaks alongside a map showing Lake Ontario labeled as Lake America in the Oval Office.Photograph: Jim Watson/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump speaks alongside a map showing Lake Ontario labeled as Lake America in the Oval Office.Photograph: Jim Watson/AFP/Getty ImagesUS newsMark Carney tells US to ‘start being serious’ amid escalating trade warCanadian PM is set to retaliate against tariffs levied by Donald Trump and criticized US officials over insultsUS politics live – latest updatesVictoria Bekiempisand Guardian staffTue 1 Sep 2026 11.48 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 11.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMark Carney has rebuked Donald Trump’s administration and urged officials in Washington to “start being serious” amid escalating trade tensions between the US and Canada.Days beforeCanadais due to retaliate against Trump’s sweeping tariffs with its own duties on US goods, the Canadian prime minister criticized US officials for insulting his country. “It is beneath their office,” he said.“When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions” about trade, Carney said.Trump signed an executive order last week directing the US federal government torename Lake Ontario as Lake America– a move that has been rejected by Canadians.The US president’s most senior trade negotiator has meanwhile downplayed the potentially disastrous effects of a US trade war with Canada, declaring the spat to be “more their emergency than ours”.The US trade representative, Jamieson Greer, argued that Canada was more vulnerable after the breakdown in talks set the stage for sweeping tariffs between the two neighbors,tellingPolitico: “There are no negotiations happening on trade right now.”The comment comes just more than a week after US-Canada trade talks imploded. The USlevied50% tariffs on $20bn in Canadian goods.Trump suggests he is reviewing US support for UK over Falkland IslandsRead moreCanada, the US’ssecond-largest trading partner, announced it would impose retaliatory tariffs on $20bn of American goods starting on 8 September. Now, US residents are poised to feel extreme pressure from Trump’s tariffs and Canada’s retaliatory measures, including on day-to-day items.Greer appeared to blame the escalating trade war on Canadian officials, telling Politico: “It’s not clear Canada wants a deal.“If Canada believes that prohibiting and banning American goods and services is appropriate, then obviously that’s something that the United States should consider as well.”‘If it’s made in the US, I don’t buy it’: Canadians on boycotting Trump’s AmericaRead moreUnacceptable asks from Canada included lighter taxes on heavy-duty trucks, according to Greer, who said such requests torpedoed the trade talks.Canadian officials, on the other hand, attributed the collapsed negotiations to a White House disagreement over who was directing trade talks. Mark Carney, the country’s prime minister,also saidthat American negotiators saw the French language in Canada as an “irritant”, but added: “In Quebec, these are rights.”Trump, for his part, has argued in recent weeks that Canada “wants the benefits” of being a US state, without being one – a preoccupation of the US president – as he lashed out at the country’s leaders. “They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of tariffs,” claimed Trump. “No more!!!”Greer suggested that negotiations broke down after a misunderstanding around what was, and wasn’t, on the table. “Was that political? I don’t know,” he told Politico. “Was it economic? … I’m not sure how much economic sense it makes because the choice is not between the current tariffs and … you know, duty-free trade. Like, that is that. Those weren’t the options.”Explore more on these topicsUS newsUS politicsCanadaTrump tariffsUS economyDonald TrumpEconomicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: MapQuest app reaches No 1 on US Apple list after defying Trump’s Lake Ontario order | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Navigating app surpasses Google and Apple Maps on top-downloaded US chart after posting ‘we’re not changing it’
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: Navigating app surpasses Google and Apple Maps on top-downloaded US chart after posting ‘we’re not changing it’
Content: MapQuest was openly dismissive of the president’s order to rename Lake Ontario amid a trade spat with Canada.Photograph: MapQuestView image in fullscreenMapQuest was openly dismissive of the president’s order to rename Lake Ontario amid a trade spat with Canada.Photograph: MapQuestDonald TrumpMapQuest app reaches No 1 on US Apple list after defying Trump’s Lake Ontario orderNavigating app surpasses Google and Apple Maps on top-downloaded US chart after posting ‘we’re not changing it’Richard LuscombeTue 1 Sep 2026 09.49 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 10.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA pioneering online mapping app that defiedDonald Trumpby refusing torenameLake Ontario has become the most in-demand navigation tool in the US.MapQuest, which wasopenly dismissiveof the president’s 27 August executive orderdirecting federal agenciesto refer to the smallest of the Great Lakes as “Lake America” amid atradespatwith Canada, leapfrogged rivals Google Maps and Apple Maps to top the most-downloaded list, as first reported byTechCrunch.The app held the No 1 spot on Apple’s App Store as of Tuesday morning, the Guardian confirmed.Google quicklycapitulatedto Trump’s demand, showing Lake America to US customers, while Apple is reportedly mulling a decision underpressurefrom the White House to make the same change.But MapQuest, a 30-year-old company that bills itself as “the OG” (original) of the internet mapping era, appears to have been rewarded for standing firm.Canada erects giant ‘Lake Ontario’ sign as spat with Trump over name escalatesRead moreTechCrunch said the app’s downloads had “soared” in recent days to become the fourth most popular of all apps in the US, excluding games – and to lead the Apple app store’s navigation chart, with Google at No 2.InCanada, meanwhile, MapQuest was the second-most downloaded app overall by Sunday night.It comes as polls show Trump’s efforts at renaming the lake found favor with only14% of Americans, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll published on Tuesday. And that survey found only slightly more, 20%, approved of higher tariffs imposed by the Trump administration on Canadian goods, with 57% opposed.MapQuest’s general manager, Doug Berger, said in a statement that usage of its app was running at about 50 times its usual rate. As a bit of fun, he said, the company was also offering subscribers the chance to generate their own name for the lake.That was courtesy of atoolit first introduced after Trump rebranded theGulf of Mexicoto the “Gulf of America” among US federal government agencies in 2025 – to which Google alsoacquiescedin the American market.Berger said in a statement: “We took the same approach we did with the Gulf of Mexico: be part of the conversation, and give people an app that keeps the names they’re familiar with.“Hundreds of thousands of people signaled to us this weekend that we got it right, by downloading our app.”MapQuest has maintained its defiance, and some might say mockery, of Trump’s Lake Ontario order since an original “We’re not changing it” post on social media on 27 August.The following day, in an all-capital letterpostsimilar in style and language to those favored by the president, it wrote: “Our maps are big and beautiful. People come up to us and say we’ll get them places. And we do!”It also responded to a poster who expressed surprise that MapQuest still existed and was not “in the same grave” asRadioShack, the once prominent US technology and electronics company that went through two bankruptcies and shuttered its retail locations a decade ago.Trump the renamer-in-chief keen to leave his mark – or his stain – on worldRead more“Understandable but the other OG, @RadioShackUSA, is still here too,” MapQuest replied, noting its continued existence as an e-commerce operation.On Tuesday morning, Apple Mapscontinued to showthe body of water spanning the US-Canada border as Lake Ontario, despite the insistence on Monday of Doug Burgum, Trump’s interior secretary, that he was “confident” it would soon show Lake America after the president contacted the company directly.On Google, its map for US users reflects the change – but remains Lake Ontario, a name it has had for about 400 years, for users in the rest of the world.Elsewhere, protests continue to escalate. A giant “Lake Ontario – Now and Always” sign in English and Frenchwas erectedover the weekend near Grimsby, Ontario. Ontario’s premier, Doug Ford, told ABC News: “No one’s going to call it Lake of America. It’s been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years. It’s going to continue being Lake Ontario.”On Monday, three Democratic US representatives, Tim Kennedy and Joe Morelle of New York, and Debbie Dingell of Michigan,introduced legislationcalled the Hands Off Our Great Lakes act, seeking to block the Republican president’s federal order to rename the lake, and prevent future changes.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpTrump administrationCanadaAmericasUS politicsMapsApplenewsShareReuse this content

title: Echoes of cold war as US accused of meddling in another Brazilian election | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Claims that Trump and Rubio are trying to influence result have parallels with CIA intervention 64 years ago
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Claims that Trump and Rubio are trying to influence result have parallels with CIA intervention 64 years ago
Content: An election rally in Rio de Janeiro for Flávio Bolsonaro. The US is accused of trying to tip the scales in favour of the far-right senator.Photograph: Bruna Prado/APView image in fullscreenAn election rally in Rio de Janeiro for Flávio Bolsonaro. The US is accused of trying to tip the scales in favour of the far-right senator.Photograph: Bruna Prado/APBrazilEchoes of cold war as US accused of meddling in another Brazilian electionClaims that Trump and Rubio are trying to influence result have parallels with CIA intervention 64 years agoTom Phillipsin Rio de JaneiroTue 1 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe year was 1962 and the Kennedy administration was desperate to swing Brazil’s congressional elections against its leftwing president, João Goulart, as a way of countering the supposed communist threat sweeping a region the US considered its back yard.Historians say that in the lead-up to the vote, the CIA and the Department of State secretly channelled millions of dollars to opposition candidates and a group tasked with spreading rightwing propaganda and stirring up unrest.View image in fullscreenChico Rubens Paiva, 38, an activist whose grandfather investigated US meddling in Brazilian politics in the 1960s.Photograph: João Laet/The Guardian“There was a very heavy-handed intervention here by the US government,” said Chico Rubens Paiva, a political activist whose congressman grandfather Rubens Paiva investigated Washington’s meddling during a 1963 parliamentary inquiry into the conspiracy.More than six decades later, Paiva, whose grandfatherwas murderedby the US-backed dictatorship that seized power in 1964, is among those who fear history is repeating itself on the eve of Brazil’s 2026 presidential election.View image in fullscreenRubens Paiva, a civil engineer and politician who was murdered by the military dictatorship in Brazil.Photograph: Family handoutOctober’s vote will pit the leftwing incumbent,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, against the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, a Donald Trump ally who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a military coup.Polls suggest a tight race and Trump and his secretary of state,Marco Rubio, have been accused of trying to tip the scales in Bolsonaro’s favour by launching an overt campaign of economic and diplomatic pressure against Lula.The US measures include imposing25% tariffs on most Brazilian importsand designating Brazil’s biggest crime groups – Rio’s Red Command and São Paulo’s First Command of the Capital – asforeign terrorist organisations. Brazilian officials suspect this is partly designed to boost Bolsonaro by making Lula look soft on crime.In July, Lula said two Trump officials had been denied entry visas because they planned “to meddle in Brazil’s ​elections”. Brazilian officials believe the pair, whoreportedlyplanned to meet Flávio Bolsonaro, intended to sow doubt about the reliability of Brazil’s internationally respected voting system – something the Bolsonaros have sought to do repeatedly. Soon after, the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to Washington wasrevoked.Brazil’s Lula launches historic fourth term bid – but son of jailed Bolsonaro stands in his wayRead moreCelso Rocha de Barros, a political scientist and podcast pundit, voiced bewilderment that US interference – which he considered the election’s most urgent theme – was not getting more coverage in mainstream media.“The greatest superpower in human history is explicitly backing a candidate in our election and is strangling the Brazilian economy in order to help him [win],” Barros claimed. “We cannot pretend that this isn’t happening and treat this like a normal election … the Brazilian economy is under attack.”Trump’s tactics have echoes of Washington’s cold war-era attempt to manipulate Brazilian politics in the lead-up to the 1964 coup, which ushered in two decades of authoritarian rule in which hundreds of people were killed or disappeared.Back then, the CIA helped finance the Brazilian Institute for Democratic Action, which, according to the historians Lilia Schwarcz and Heloisa Starling, illegally poured money into the campaigns of hundreds of lawmakers and eight gubernatorial candidates. “The objective was strategic: to create a strong opposition in congress, block government initiatives and prepare the way for a coup d’état,” Schwarcz and Starling argued in their bookBrazil: A Biography.Another US-funded group, the Research and Social Studies Institute, was used to disrupt Goulart’s government by bankrolling anti-communist propaganda and anti-government protests. James N Green, a Brown University historian who has written a book about the period, said: “The intention [was] getting rid of Goulart [and] opening the door to the military coming to power.”View image in fullscreenLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Brazil’s president, at a campaign rally in Rio de Janeiro. The leftwinger faces a tight re-election battle in October.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockGreen sees parallels between Trump’s use of tariffs to sabotage Lula’s campaign and how in the early 60s Washington sought to enfeeble Goulart’s government by funding his opponents and cutting off loans. Then, as now, the US government was “bent on doing everything possible to weaken the government” in Brazil.But Barros sees one key difference between the two US gambits. “[The 1962 campaign] was done covertly, precisely because the CIA knew there would be real public anger in Brazil if people knew the US was bankrolling candidates. So they did it secretly,” he said. “Today, this is being done openly – and on an incomparably larger scale.”The Department of State rejected claims the US was seeking to meddle in Brazil’s election. “Any insinuation of a ‘ploy’ to undermine a democratic nation’s election is a baseless lie,” an official said in a statement.“We respect the Brazilian people and whatever government that they choose freely through free and fair elections in Brazil. We’ve respected and dealt with governments from both sides of the spectrum in Brazil, and had very successful relationships with them.”Last year Trump wasaccused of meddling in the politics of neighbouring Argentinaafter he threw his weight behind its rightwing president, Javier Milei, on the eve of crucial midterm elections. Milei recently attended Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign launch in Brazil, using his speech to lambaste Lula as a “thief”.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump with Marco Rubio in Washington. The pair are accused of waging economic war against Brazil to influence its presidential election.Photograph: Elizabeth Frantz/ReutersGreen believes twostrategic objectives lie behind the Brazilian pressure campaign being waged by Trump and by Rubio, the son of Cuban immigrants, who has made toppling Cuba’s communist government a personal project.Firstly, it is designed to weaken and delegitimiseLula’s government, making it harder for Brazil, Latin America’s largest democracy, to challenge the US economic asphyxiation campaign against Cuba.Secondly, it is about “neutralising” leftwing forces in Latin America more generally and boosting the right in the hope of helping to elect even more Trump-aligned leaders. Since 2023, a succession of radical rightwing populists have won power in Argentina and Chile, Costa Rica andColombia. In reference to Trump’s tangerine complexion, this has been nicknamedLatin America’s “orange wave”.View image in fullscreenPaiva is running for a seat in Brazil’s congress in the 2026 elections.Photograph: João Laet/The GuardianPaiva, 38, believes US interference is intended to have a similar effect to the abduction of Venezuela’s dictator, Nicolás Maduro – strengthening “American dominance” in a region it considers a US sphere of influence.Maduro’s removal in January allowed the US to impose a pliant successor, his vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who has started opening up the South American country to US oil and mining firms. Paiva believes Bolsonaro’s election will “serve the same purpose: putting people into power who will serve their interests”.He fears that as election day draws near, US social media companies could enter the fray, potentially giving Bolsonaro another lift. “Any kind of change to the algorithm has a brutal impact in the way information reaches people,” warned Paiva, who is running for a seat in congress in the election for the centre-left Brazilian Socialist party. He highlighted“the scary lurch the Silicon Valley bros”had taken into Trump’s camp during his second term.Barros is convinced the US aims to help elect Flávio Bolsonaro, “because Flávio will give them everything they want”, he said. “Flávio will make a rare earths deal no other president would. Flávio will let American big techs do whatever they like in Brazil. Flávio will reduce economic relations with China as much as he can.” He noted that Bolsonaro supporters attended rallies carrying US flags.Barros believes the campaign’s real driving force is not Trump but Rubio, who hopes to bolster a possible 2028 presidential run by showing voters he has “delivered the whole of Latin America to American interests”.“The fact is, this is an election between Lula and Marco Rubio,” Barros said.Explore more on these topicsBrazilLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaJair BolsonaroDonald TrumpMarco RubioUS foreign policyAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump suggests he is reviewing US support for UK over Falkland Islands | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Comments signal president prepared to use dispute to push UK to raise defence spending and Nato contributions
Author: Robert Tait
Headline: Comments signal president prepared to use dispute to push UK to raise defence spending and Nato contributions
Content: Donald Trump at the White House on Monday.Photograph: Annabelle Gordon/Pool/CNP/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenDonald Trump at the White House on Monday.Photograph: Annabelle Gordon/Pool/CNP/ShutterstockDonald TrumpTrump suggests he is reviewing US support for UK over Falkland IslandsComments signal president prepared to use dispute to push UK to raise defence spending and Nato contributionsRobert Taitin WashingtonTue 1 Sep 2026 04.31 EDTFirst published on Mon 31 Aug 2026 19.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has suggested he is reconsidering US support for Britain’s sovereignty over theFalkland Islands, in a move likely to strain the “special relationship” between Washington and London.“I always review every position – that’s just one of many,” the US president told reporters in the White House, in response to a question about whether he was reviewing the US’s position over the South Atlantic islands, an archipelago whose status has long been disputed byArgentina, which claims sovereignty.Officially, the US takes a neutral position on who has rightful sovereignty over the islands, which Britain first claimed in the late 17th century and has held almost continually since 1833. In practice, it recognizes British administration over the territory, which was the subject of an Argentinian invasion and subsequent military conflict with Britain in 1982.Trump’s remarks were the clearest sign yet that the administration is prepared to use the dispute as leverage to pressure the government of the new British prime minister, Andy Burnham, to raise defence spending and contributions to Nato.A spokesperson for Burnham said on Tuesday that the UK’s position on the Falkands was “crystal clear”.“The Falkland islanders are British with a right to determine their own future. The islanders have expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory, and our commitment to them is unwavering,” he said.“The prime minister was clear on his first day in office that we’ll meet our international commitments to our allies on defence spending, and he hasn’t wavered from that.”Trump’s comments came after an unnamed US officialtold the Telegraphlast week that Washington could change its position over the islands if Britain failed to meet its defence spending commitments.That followed reports that John Healey, the UK chancellor, was preparing to drop Britain’s prior commitment to devote 3% of its GDP to defence spending by 2030 when he delivers his first budget on 28 October.Trump has made a priority of pressuring the US’s allies into boosting defence budgets and raising their Nato contributions during both his presidencies, accusing other countries of “freeloading”. At a summit in The Hague last year, allies committed to spending 5% of GDP on defence and security-related expenditures by 2035.Speculation about a US switch of allegiance over the islands has been swirling for months.In April, aleaked Pentagon emailsuggested reviewing Britain’s claim in response to its lack of support for Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran.A switch of US position would represent a psychological blow to Britain’s sovereignty over the Falklands.After Argentina invaded the islands in 1982, the decision by Margaret Thatcher’s government to dispatch a naval taskforce that eventually resulted in their recovery was bolstered by staunch diplomatic support from Ronald Reagan, who came down on Britain’s side, even though Washington was also an ally of the Argentinian ruling military junta.A total of 649 Argentinian and 255 British personnel died in fighting before Argentina’s forces surrendered in June 1982.The episode played a central role in cementing the bond between Thatcher and Reagan, who were political allies and ideological kindred spirits.In recent times, Trump has become close to Argentina’s populist president, Javier Milei, who attended his second inauguration in January last year.Last year, Trumpauthorized a $20bn financiallifeline to Argentina to help it navigate a financial crisis, but made the funds contingent on Milei’s party winning subsequent congressional elections.Milei’s La Libertad Avanza party duly won the election, confounding pollsters’ forecasts. Trump later authorized the importation of Argentinian beef in an effort to reduce US grocery prices.Milei has vocally supported Argentina’s claim to the islands. In a 2013 poll, 1,513 out of 1,517 Falklands residents who cast a ballot said they wanted the territory remain a part of the UK.Feelings over the islands surfaced after Argentina’s 2-1 victory over England in the semi-final of the World Cup in July, when celebrating Argentinian players unfurled a banner reading “Las Malvinas son Argentinas” – the Falklands are Argentinian.The Argentinian football association was subsequently fined $235,000 by Fifa for violating its rules on non-sporting demonstrations.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpFalkland IslandsUS foreign policyArgentinaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Canada’s ruling Liberals sweep byelections in boost to Mark Carney | Canada | The Guardian
description: Three projected victories are a message to US that Carney has support of the Canadian people, says one MP
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Three projected victories are a message to US that Carney has support of the Canadian people, says one MP
Content: Carney said the results of Monday’s votes amounted to an endorsement of his government’s approach.Photograph: Chris Tanouye/ReutersView image in fullscreenCarney said the results of Monday’s votes amounted to an endorsement of his government’s approach.Photograph: Chris Tanouye/ReutersCanadaCanada’s ruling Liberals sweep byelections in boost to Mark CarneyThree projected victories are a message to US that Carney has support of the Canadian people, says one MPAssociated Press in TorontoTue 1 Sep 2026 03.42 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 12.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCanada’s ruling Liberal party has swept three byelections, a result that showed voters backing the prime minister, Mark Carney, after his face-offwith Donald Trump.The Canadian Press, Canada’s national news agency, projected Liberal victories in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord in Quebec, Beaches-East York in Toronto and North Vancouver-Capilano in British Columbia.Carney said the results of Monday’s votes amounted to an endorsement of his government’s approach. “At this consequential time for Canada, voters have placed their trust in our government’s plan,” he said in a statement.The Quebec result was the most dramatic shift. The Liberal candidate Daniel Gobeil was projected to win big in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord, a district held by the opposition Conservatives since 2018. The region is home to aluminium producers, dairy farms and other industries caught in an escalating trade war with the US.“This victory means we can maintain Canadian unity all across the country,” Gobeil said.‘You’re at war when you get attacked’: Mark Carney shows combative nature in face-off with TrumpRead moreThe other two seats were previously held by Liberals. In British Columbia, Carney’s former deputy chief of staff Braeden Caley won North Vancouver-Capilano.The Liberal MP Hedy Fry told CBC: “The United States is getting a message tonight. Our leader has the support of the Canadian people.”US-Canada trade talks collapsed on 21 August after the two sides failed to reach a deal, and Trump imposed 50% tariffs on roughly $20bn of Canadian goods. Canada responded with plans for tariffs on US products.Trump has escalated his attacks on Canada since the talks failed. He signed an executive orderrenaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America”, and on Monday the US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said Canada had limited leverage in the dispute because the US economy was roughly 13 times larger. Trump has repeatedly talked about making Canada the 51st state.Meanwhile, Carney has accelerated efforts to deepen economic ties with Europe and other partners.The Liberal sweep would bring Carney’s party to 173 seats in the 343-seat House of Commons, further strengthening its position.The byelections were called after the MPs who previously held the three seats resigned from parliament earlier this year.Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University, said the sweep showed Carney retaining strong support across regions, and he called the Quebec result the most significant. He said the easy win in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord probably reflected, in part, the popularity in Quebec of Carney’s decision “to pull the plug on trade negotiations with the White House”.He said the Conservative collapse there was bad news for the party’s leader, Pierre Poilievre. The party had about 41% of the vote in last year’s federal elections but fell to about 13% and third place on Monday. “These numbers do look bad,” Béland said.Carney won Canada’s election last year, fuelled by public anger over Trump’s annexation threats, and he has vowed to reduce Canada’s reliance on the US.Explore more on these topicsCanadaMark CarneyAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Thai resort prepares to host USS Abraham Lincoln sailors after more than 270 days at sea | Thailand | The Guardian
description: Security stepped up in Pattaya before arrival of thousands of sailors and marines whose deployment was extended due to US war in Iran
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Security stepped up in Pattaya before arrival of thousands of sailors and marines whose deployment was extended due to US war in Iran
Content: Pattaya has become hugely popular with foreign tourists, known for its beaches and nightlife scene.Photograph: Алексей Облов/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPattaya has become hugely popular with foreign tourists, known for its beaches and nightlife scene.Photograph: Алексей Облов/Getty ImagesThailandThai resort prepares to host USS Abraham Lincoln sailors after more than 270 days at seaSecurity stepped up in Pattaya before arrival of thousands of sailors and marines whose deployment was extended due to US war in IranGuardian staff and agencies in PattayaTue 1 Sep 2026 04.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 05.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAuthorities in the Thai resort city of Pattaya have stepped up security as they prepare to welcome thousands of sailors and marines from the USS Abraham Lincoln who have spentmore than 270 consecutive days at sea.“About 600 officials will provide security and other necessary assistance,” the provincial governor, Narit Niramaiwong, told AFP.The nuclear-powered aircraft carrier sailed past Singapore over the weekend on its way back to the US after a lengthy deployment in the Middle East as part of the US war against Iran.It left California in November 2025 for duty in the South China Sea and was rerouted to the Middle East before the US-Israeli attacks on Iran that began six months ago.Reports of deteriorating living conditions andpoor mental health onboard, including attempted suicides, have made headlines in the US and provoked criticism of Donald Trump’s war against Iran.Pattaya’s mayor, Poramase Ngampiches, said the carrier would dock just after midnight on Wednesday (about 5pm GMT on Tuesday) at Laem Chabang port. About 40 buses have been laid on to transport the sailors to Pattaya and back in staggered groups before the carrier departs on Sunday.After meeting US officials on Monday, Poramase said service members would be banned from certain recreational activities such as parasailing and cannabis use. Medical cannabis was legalised inThailandin 2022 and dispensaries have become common in Thai cities.Once a sleepy fishing village, Pattaya was transformed by the Vietnam war in the 1960s, when US soldiers on leave began coming for rest and recreation.In Thailand’s sex tourism hub, bright lights flash, loud music blares – and underage girls are exploitedRead moreThe city has since become hugely popular with foreign tourists, known for its beaches and a nightlife scene that has long drawn scrutiny over sex tourism.Poramase told AFP there had been a recent crackdown on sex workers but denied this was linked to the US arrivals.Government officials are warning local businesses not to overcharge US sailors, and Poramase said there would be a greater police presence in popular areas along Pattaya beach and Walking Street.The city’s police chief, Anek Srathongyoo, said law enforcements agencies had been ordered to step up security measures to prevent undesirable situations. He said that if any US service members broke Thai law, they would be prosecuted accordingly.Local business owners feeling the tourism slump from the Iran war are eager for the new arrivals. A banner hung over a local bar near a beach read: “Welcome allUS militarypersonnel. Thank you for your service.”Bualuang Ponok, a bar employee, said she had seen US service members during past visits but she did not expect many from this crew. “They said 5,000 people will come here but how many will reach us?” she said.Earlier in August, the usually Asia-based USS George Washington relieved the long-deployed Lincoln in the Middle East. The Lincoln, one of the US navy’s largest warships, was part of American efforts in the Iran war, whichflared back up over the weekendfor the first time in a month.The deployment included a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 270 days. Trump downplayed concerns over conditions onboard and said the deployment was “not nearly long enough”.Thai officials have said the Lincoln will return to the US after its port call in Thailand.Associated Press and Agence France-Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsThailandUS militaryAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Shein shares slide on fast-fashion retailer’s stock market debut | Shein | The Guardian
description: Hong Kong flotation at $26bn by firm once valued at $100bn follows failure to list in US and UK
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: Hong Kong flotation at $26bn by firm once valued at $100bn follows failure to list in US and UK
Content: Shein company executives and employees at the listing ceremony in Hong Kong.Photograph: May James/EPAView image in fullscreenShein company executives and employees at the listing ceremony in Hong Kong.Photograph: May James/EPASheinShein shares slide on fast-fashion retailer’s stock market debutHong Kong flotation at $26bn by firm once valued at $100bn follows failure to list in US and UKMark SweneyTue 1 Sep 2026 03.11 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 14.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShares in the fast-fashion brand Shein slumped by as much as 10% as the China-founded company made itslong-anticipated trading debuton the Hong Kong stock exchange.The Singapore-headquartered company, once valued at almost $100bn (£74bn), went public on Tuesday pricing shares at HK$48.56, valuing the business at just over $26bn.However, minutes after the flotation, which raised HK$13.6bn, the stock fell as much as 10%, pushing the online retailer’s valuation below $25bn.Shein’s share price recovered most of its early trading plunge, closing at HK$48.50, just 0.12% down on its opening price.“Let global consumers enjoy the sound of fashion,” said Leigh Gui, Shein’s chief financial officer, after a gong was struck to mark the start of trading.The lacklustre launch as a publicly listed company comes after one of the longest-awaited initial public offerings in recent years, afterplans to list in New Yorkwere blocked by regulators over forced labour concerns.Shein also considered a£50bn flotation in Londonbut faced similar questions about its supply chain from campaigners, MPs and investors.Nevertheless, the company has still floated as one of the world’s biggest listed fashion groups, with a valuation around the same as the Swedish retailer H&M. The Zara owner, Inditex, has a market capitalisation of about $213bn.Shein reached a valuation of $100bn in an April 2022 fundraising round, making it the third most valuable startup in the world at the time. The plunge in its value since has been driven by regulatory changes around the world that threaten its business model of shipping goods in small packages out ofChinato take advantage of tax breaks on low-value imported goods.The company swung to a loss of $99m in the first three months of this year, compared with a net income of $395m the year before, after the USremoved its “de minimis” import duty exemptionon small packages, hitting its sales in the country.The EU is also cracking down on the loophole, introducing a€3 (£2.56) dutyon small parcels imported from outside the trading bloc in June, and intends to phase it out, while the UK has said it will do the same by October 2028.On Tuesday, France began imposing penalties on some fast-fashion items to curb the surge in sales of cheap products sold by retailers such as Shein and its Chinese rival Temu.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionParis passed a fast-fashion law in June to address concerns about overproduction, with the penalties calculated using a formula that factors in the number of products sold, their prices and repairability.The penalties, which are set to increase in 2030, range from €0.25 for a pair of boxer shorts or socks to €12 for a coat, with the amount capped at 50% of the product’s pre-tax sales price.China’s commerce ministry has called the French law discriminatory and a trade barrier and said it could be in violation of World Trade Organization principles.Shein, founded by theentrepreneur Chris Xu, runs most of its operations from China but sells all its goods outside the country. It moved its headquarters to Singapore at about the start of 2022, a move viewed by analysts as designed to avoid increasing scrutiny of Chinese companies.Afterforced labour concerns were raised, Shein said it had tightened its supplier policies, enforced through regular audits, with any child or forced labour violations becoming grounds for immediate termination of contract.Explore more on these topicsSheinRetail industryIPOsHong KongChinaAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kākāpō rising: 90 chicks swell population of the world’s heaviest parrot | New Zealand | The Guardian
description: Critically endangered New Zealand bird enjoys record breeding season triggered by mass fruiting of native tree, pushing its numbers to 325
Author: Eva Corlett
Headline: Critically endangered New Zealand bird enjoys record breeding season triggered by mass fruiting of native tree, pushing its numbers to 325
Content: Ninety kākāpō chicks were officially added to the population of the critically endangered birds on 1 September, a record high.Photograph: Department of ConservationView image in fullscreenNinety kākāpō chicks were officially added to the population of the critically endangered birds on 1 September, a record high.Photograph: Department of ConservationNew ZealandKākāpō rising: 90 chicks swell population of the world’s heaviest parrotCritically endangered New Zealand bird enjoys record breeding season triggered by mass fruiting of native tree, pushing its numbers to 325Eva Corlettin WellingtonMon 31 Aug 2026 22.57 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe population of the world’s heaviest parrot,the kākāpō, has surpassed 300 birds for the first time in 75 years, after a record breeding season triggered by the mass fruiting of a native New Zealand tree.Ninety chicks were officially added to the population of the critically endangered birds on 1 September, pushing the total to 325 – a record high since recovery efforts began.“The last time the population is thought to have exceeded 300 birds may have been as long as 75 years ago,” said Deidre Vercoe, the conservation department’s kākāpō recovery operations manager.“We had a four-year gap between breeding seasons, so it’s fantastic to finally see the population increase after all that time.”‘My lovely distraction’: live stream of kākāpō – world’s fattest parrot – and her chicks captivates New ZealandRead moreView image in fullscreenKākāpō population tops 300 for first time in 75 years, after record breeding seasonPhotograph: Department of ConservationKākāpō, the world’s only nocturnal and flightless parrot, were once abundant acrossNew Zealand. But their population plummeted after the introduction of predators such as cats and stoats. By the 1900s, they were nearly extinct.A recovery programme was established in 1995 with a population of just 51 birds and has battled challenges with genetic diversity, infertility and poor chick hatching rates. There are three kākāpō breeding populations, all based on predator-free islands off the South Island.Kākāpō breed only every two to four years when the native rimu trees produce large numbers of berries, so repopulation is slow. This year, after a four-year wait,a bountiful harvestof rimu berries prompted the birds to breed and produce a record number of chicks.“In the early years of recovery, it took 16 years to produce that many chicks,” Vercoe said.Kākāpō are thought to live between 60 and 80 years, can weigh up to 4kg and are famously entertaining. More than 100,000 people tuned into watch a live stream of a kākāpōsleeping, eating and attending to her nest and chicks during breeding season.The parrots have unusual mating rituals. Male birds gather in a “lek” to produce a distinctive booming sound, emitted from air sacs in their chests while sitting in a dugout bowl in the ground. The deep boom, which can travel up to 5km, sounds similar to a softly plucked cello string.After choosing a partner and mating, females typically lay one to four eggs. The females become solely responsible for their eggs and hatched chicks for roughly six months.At 150 days of age, the chicks are fledged and considered independent enough to be added to the total population. The youngest chick of the 2026 breeding season was female Awarua-A3, who hatched on 30 March.Modelling indicated the next breeding season could occur as soon as 2028, Vercoe said.“So, while we’ll take a moment to stop and reflect on this remarkable year, we’re already looking ahead to 2028 and preparing for what could come next.”Explore more on these topicsNew ZealandBirdsWildlifeAnimalsAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Is flying a shark drone a boring job? Possibly – until suddenly it isn’t | Sharks | The Guardian
description: Taha Kafil-Hussain flies a drone above Coogee beach. Mostly he zooms in on seaweed or turtles – but occasionally he spots a shark and clears the water
Author: Penry Buckley
Headline: Taha Kafil-Hussain flies a drone above Coogee beach. Mostly he zooms in on seaweed or turtles – but occasionally he spots a shark and clears the water
Content: 3:55Could shark drones keep swimmers safe at Australian beaches? – videoSharksIs flying a shark drone a boring job? Possibly – until suddenly it isn’tTaha Kafil-Hussain flies a drone above Coogee beach. Mostly he zooms in on seaweed or turtles – but occasionally he spots a shark and clears the waterFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastPenry BuckleyTue 1 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 20.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Hey Taha, what’s the visibility like?” shouts a man with a towel slung over his shoulder.“Uh, nice,” says Surf Life SavingNew South Walesdrone operator Taha Kafil-Hussain.“Good?” the man asks.“Very good,” Kafil-Hussain assures him.Thanking him, the early morning swimmer turns and heads down the steps to Coogee beach.Kafil-Hussain, who Guardian Australia has joined on his early morning shark surveillance flight, says: “When they’re local, they just want to see what the weather, what the water looks like, [if there’s] anything scary.”The 22-year-old has been flying drones for SLS NSW for four years, but only at Coogee beach for a matter of weeks. Before a shark attack on 34-year-oldSydneyteacher and mother Leah Stewart in June, drone surveillance was not permitted at Coogee because it lies directly under the flight path from Sydney airport’s east-west runway.In an interview with 60 Minutes broadcast on Sunday, Stewart described the horror encounter with a four-metre white shark, after which her left arm was amputated, as“like fighting a dinosaur”. The attack, one of a series of high-profile incidents in Sydney in the past 12 months, has prompted the state government to massively ramp up its shark mitigation program.View image in fullscreenDuring each drone flight, Taha Kafil-Hussain rakes the bay in sections from left to right, backwards and forwards, leaving a chequerboard pattern on his control screenPhotograph: Rémi Chauvin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenKafil-Hussain has now flown drones at most Sydney beaches, from Palm beach in the north to Cronulla in the south.Photograph: Rémi Chauvin/The GuardianUnder a $34m initiative by the state government which rolled out on 1 July, 38 of Sydney’s ocean beaches, including Coogee, now receive dawn-to-dusk drone monitoring year round.Seventy NSW beaches in total are part of the dawn-to-dusk program, while others will benefit from increased surveillance throughout the summer and school holidays. From Tuesday, surveillance hours increased, running from 6.15am to 5pm each day for the start of spring, as daylight increases.When Guardian Australia meets Kafil-Hussain in mid-winter, he arrives at 6.30am to throw up a marquee, before checking a radio to determine which direction the planes are flying in (drone surveillance at Coogee has been allowed with special permission from the airport).Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailNot long after, the drone takes off in a whir of plastic from a miniature landing pad, rising 60 metres into the air before heading out to sea. During each 20-minute flight, Kafil-Hussain rakes the bay in sections from left to right, backwards and forwards, leaving a chequerboard pattern on his control screen.He says he’s looking for “anything moving in a different way than normal”.“Anything moving against the flow of water, anything that looks a little bit long – anything alive, really.”He pauses when he thinks he’s spotted something, to zoom in. “Looks like seaweed,” he says.University of Sydney shark policy expert and associate professor Christopher Pepin-Neff agrees that “drones are the best technology that we have at the moment”.But they say there are “important caveats that we need to give to the public”.“On days that are windy, if the shark is too small, the drone operator is not going to be able to see a shark if it’s there.“I’m slightly nervous that, in the absence of [a] large public education campaign, we have the possibility that we’re going to scare the shit out of people,” says Pepin-Neff.With more drone surveillance comes more regular shark sightings. The NSW government says there have been more 750 sightings and more than 200 intervention actions by Surf Life Saving NSW since 1 July.Shark listening stations are now tracking 1,698 white sharks, 938 tiger sharks and 374 bull sharks – the “target sharks” which are most frequently involved in serious shark bites.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKafil-Hussain says he has seen more bull and tiger sharks than whites, and has raised the alarm a few times, most recently for a bronze whaler – involved in rare attacks – which he initially thought was a target shark.If it’s early and he’s on his own, raising the alarm means making the call to clear the water himself – otherwise he shares what he has seen with lifeguards and they make the decision, with the time from spotting a hazard to fully clearing the water about two or three minutes.The SLS drones have a speaker attached to them, allowing him to communicate directly with surfers and swimmers.It’s a technology familiar to followers of the Instagram account Drone Shark App, run by Jason Iggleden, who has been using a drone since 2018 to surveil beaches including Bondi, Tamarama and Bronte.View image in fullscreenChristopher Pepin-Neff says the drone program will ‘restore confidence’ ahead of a busy summer, but there is ‘no silver bullet’.Photograph: Steven Markham/AFP/Getty ImagesVideos on the account show an enormous seal barrel-rolling through the water and a swirling vortex of Australian salmon, while in another a whale lingers beneath a kayaker in Tamarama.“I just had a bit of a vision to help … with getting people out of water with sharks, and just showing them the beauty of what’s out there,” he said.The licensed and insured drone flyer, who continues to work independently, now passes on any sightings to SLS NSW. He is a firm believer in the drone surveillance, saying the ability to spot target sharks grows with experience.“I don’t think you really need to consider much more than drones, to be honest,” he says.Pepin-Neff is supportive of other non-lethal technologies, such as SMART drum lines. They say a trial of new artificial intelligence detection software on drones will take the pressure off humans to discern between more and less dangerous sharks. But their message on controversial measures such as shark nets, here to stay on NSW beaches, and culling, is unequivocal: “They do not work.”‘Not a perfect solution’Kafil-Hussain, who drives each day from his home in Parramatta, has now flown drones at most Sydney beaches, from Palm beach in the north to Cronulla in the south. Every beach is different – he sees turtles, dolphins, the occasional whale. Coogee is home to a wobbegong, a low-swimming carpet shark which does not hunt humans but can attack if threatened.“He’s not around. He’ll pop out eventually,” says Kafil-Hussain.When Guardian Australia visits the beach, arriving before sunrise, it is already heaving with eastern suburbs dog walkers, swim clubs and surfers. Just weeks after the attack on Stewart, Kafil-Hussain says numbers at the beach have only been growing.Pepin-Neff says the drone program will “restore confidence” ahead of a busy summer, but there is “no silver bullet”. “Drones are a great tool but they’re not a perfect solution.”Pepin-Neff swims at fully enclosed beaches, like Marrinawi Cove in Barangaroo, but their advice for those that swim at unenclosed beaches is: “Swim between the flags.”“The ocean is the wild and we need to treat the beach like the bush.”Explore more on these topicsSharksNew South WalesSydneyMarine lifeWildlifenewsShareReuse this content

title: NSW government to resume pill testing at music festivals but rejects calls for wider community rollout | New South Wales | The Guardian
description: Use of sniffer dogs and searches will continue despite health and harm reduction groups arguing they could lead to riskier drug taking
Author: Melissa Davey
Headline: Use of sniffer dogs and searches will continue despite health and harm reduction groups arguing they could lead to riskier drug taking
Content: The ACT and Victoria have both moved beyond festivals to fund community drug checking, where staff provide people with the results along with non-judgmental health and harm reduction advice.Photograph: Jonny Weeks/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe ACT and Victoria have both moved beyond festivals to fund community drug checking, where staff provide people with the results along with non-judgmental health and harm reduction advice.Photograph: Jonny Weeks/The GuardianNew South WalesNSW government to resume pill testing at music festivals but rejects calls for wider community rolloutUse of sniffer dogs and searches will continue despite health and harm reduction groups arguing they could lead to riskier drug takingFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastMelissa DaveyMedical editorTue 1 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 17.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDrug testing will resume atNew South Walesmusic festivals from October, but will not be rolled out into the wider community despite calls from peak health and harm reduction groups, while the controversial use of sniffer dogs and searches will continue.On Wednesday the state government announced NSWHealthwill consult with the music festival industry and harm reduction organisations to roll out pill testing at up to 15 music festivals each year.Sniffer dogs deployed as NSW pill-testing trial begins in WollongongRead moreThere will be no change to the use of sniffer dogs at music festivals, a government spokesperson confirmed, which has been found toprompt risky drug taking. Police, security guards, bag searches and sniffer dogs at music festivalscan lead to riskier drug useas people may “pre-load”, or take all of their substances at once, to avoid detection.Detection of drugs through sniffer dogshas also been used by policeto justifystrip-searches, whichcourts and legal experts have found to be unlawful.The testing rollout follows a 12-month trial which ended in February and which saw 1,480 drug samples tested across 12 NSW music festivals.The trial was free and anonymous, and meant festival goers could hand over a small sample of substances they intended to use to health staff to test for purity, potency and contaminants.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailAn independent evaluation led by the University of Sydney, also made public on Wednesday, found people changed their approach to drug taking after getting their drugs tested, particularly when substances differed from what they expected.Unexpected substances were found in 8% of samples, while high-dose MDMA was found in 4% of MDMA samples where a dose could be calculated. High doses of MDMAincrease the riskof organ failure and death, especially in hot environments or when combined with other substances.A range of unexpected psychoactive substances were detected through the testing, including ketamine analogues (human-made substances which copy ketamine’s chemical makeup, but can produce different and dangerous effects) and heroin.The University of Sydney evaluation also surveyed people about their views towards pill testing and found “a consistent concern … was the conflict between policing activities (such as drug detection dogs) and access to the service site, which may have dissuaded potential service users from accessing harm reduction services”.A report from a landmark summit into how to reduce drug-related harms, published in 2025, recommended NSWconsider ceasing the use of drug detection dogs and strip-searches at music festivals.The chief executive of Unharm, Dr Will Tregoning, said the searches need to be scrapped.“Drug detection dogs are intensive operations that have a track record of clearly contributing to increased overdoses,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSniffer dogs and bag searches can make drug danger at festivals more likely, Victorian coroner findsRead more“People see the dogs and take all of their drugs at once out of fear of being detected, and we know police have beenstrip-searching people at an industrial scale. These searches are also deeply traumatic for people, and affects predominantly young people.”Ahead of the announcement, peak health and harm reduction groups including the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners, the Alcohol and Drug Foundation, and Unharm wrote to NSW’s premier, Chris Minns, and health minister, Ryan Park, on Tuesdaycalling for pill testing services to be offered in the community.TheACTandVictoria have both movedbeyond festivals to fund community drug checking, where staff provide people with the results along with non-judgmental health and harm reduction advice.“Drug checking at festivals reaches people who can get to a festival. It cannot reach the people dying at home,” the letter says.“We ask you to commit to a next phase of drug checking in NSW that includes community-based services, designed for the communities they serve and independently evaluated from the start.”The letter said that 72% of fatal drug overdoses in Australia happened at home in 2024.Minns told budget estimates in August that there were no plans to roll out testing to the community.Explore more on these topicsNew South WalesHealthDrugsMusic festivalsAustralian police and policingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Dozens arrested after fatal pre-dawn shootout in Dutch village  | Netherlands | The Guardian
description: Police urged people in Overasselt to stay indoors after one person died and 34 were arrested
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Police urged people in Overasselt to stay indoors after one person died and 34 were arrested
Content: Police have arrested people from France, Belgium and Algeria, as well as the Netherlands.Photograph: ANP/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPolice have arrested people from France, Belgium and Algeria, as well as the Netherlands.Photograph: ANP/ShutterstockNetherlandsDozens arrested after fatal pre-dawn shootout in Dutch villagePolice urged people in Overasselt to stay indoors after one person died and 34 were arrestedAgence France-PresseTue 1 Sep 2026 18.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 18.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAuthorities have arrested 34 people, including French, Belgian and Algerian nationals, after a person died in a pre-dawn shootout in a Dutch village reportedly linked to a notorious drug lord.Police urged people in Overasselt, near the German border, to stay indoors with doors and windows shut in case further suspects were on the loose.At about 4am on Tuesday, a group of heavily armed men in balaclavas approached a house in Overasselt and shots were fired, resulting in the death of a 51-year-old, reportedly a security guard.Police responding to the scene immediately came under fire, with two officers sustaining non-life-threatening injuries, police spokesperson Jolanda Aalbers said. Several weapons, data storage devices and vehicles were also seized, she said.According to local media, the shootout was likely connected to the criminal underworld of Dutch drug lord Jos Leijdekkers, also known asBolle Jos(fat Jos).Leijdekkers is one of the Netherlands’ most wanted criminals and has previously been convicted for his role in international cocaine trafficking.View image in fullscreenFrom left: Monique Vinkesteijn, Joerie Minses and Jolanda Aalbers at a press conference following the shooting.Photograph: ANP/ShutterstockHe has lived in Sierra Leonefor at least three yearsand is reportedlyin a relationship with the daughter of the country’s president, Julius Maada Bio.The Het Parool newspaper said the gunfight resulted from a conflict over several hundred kilograms of cocaine thought to have been trafficked by Leijdekkers’ gang.Deputy chief prosecutor Monique Vinkesteijn said there had been a shooting at the same house last year related to a “longstanding conflict” but did not reveal further details.“We know that the group currently in custody is international in nature,” Vinkesteijn said. “It includes French and Belgian nationals, people from Algeria, and also individuals from the Netherlands.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe prosecutor said the suspects faced a variety of charges ranging from murder to manslaughter to preparing a kidnapping and that it was possible further arrests would follow.Local mayor Joerie Minses said the whole community was shocked by the violent events.“What happened in Overasselt crosses all boundaries. This is un-Dutch … Overasselt has been shocked by a form of extreme violence that is totally unacceptable,” he said.Explore more on these topicsNetherlandsEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Russia targets Ukraine’s rail network as war enters deadly new phase | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Six employees killed on Tuesday after Moscow escalates attacks on infrastructure and Ukrainian capital
Author: Luke Harding
Headline: Six employees killed on Tuesday after Moscow escalates attacks on infrastructure and Ukrainian capital
Content: Railway workers respond to a call to repair overhead lines after they were destroyed by a Russian drone strike in Boryspil, Kyiv region.Photograph: Jelle KringsView image in fullscreenRailway workers respond to a call to repair overhead lines after they were destroyed by a Russian drone strike in Boryspil, Kyiv region.Photograph: Jelle KringsUkraineRussia targets Ukraine’s rail network as war enters deadly new phaseSix employees killed on Tuesday after Moscow escalates attacks on infrastructure and Ukrainian capitalLuke HardingandDan Sabbaghin KyivTue 1 Sep 2026 13.23 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussia has opened a deadly new phase in its war againstUkraineby deliberately targeting the country’s railway network, with six employees killed on Tuesday in the latest strikes on Kyiv.Ukraine’s state-owned railway company, Ukrzaliznytsia,said its workers diedwhen a ballistic missile plunged into a locomotive depot. The Russians hit other railway facilities, it added, during a massive bombardment of Kyiv and the Kyiv region.At least 12 people died, with a dozen wounded, including three children.“An unbearably difficult night for the entire railway family. Railway staff have been working at the scene since early this morning. The attack has caused significant damage. Rescue workers are still putting out a number of fires,” said Ukrzaliznytsia’s chair,Oleksandr Pertsovsky.View image in fullscreenBoryspil, in the Kyiv region. Trains were evacuated and travellers stranded during Russia’s days-long air assault on KyivPhotograph: Jelle KringsThe grim strike took place as Russia escalated its attacks on the Ukrainian capital.It has carried out continuous raids for six days, beginning last week, in an attempt to disrupt daily life and demoralise the city’s inhabitants. The onslaught took place hours before Ukrainian children began a new school year.Since Russia’s full-scale invasion, 58 railway staff have been killed and at least 318 injured. One wounded railway employee, Volodymyr, was taken to hospital on Tuesday, with people urged to donate blood if they were B positive – his group. “Our colleagues are by his side,” Ukrzaliznytsia said, adding it would support victims’ families.Ukraine’s railway network is Europe’s third largest, with 15,000 miles (24,000km) of track. It has been a lifeline for the country’s wartime civilians, transporting four million people and an estimated 120,000 pets. It has brought world leaders to Kyiv,including Joe Bidenand Andy Burnham,who arrived last week on an overnight servicefrom Poland.View image in fullscreenRailway workers repairing overhead lines after a Russian strike.Photograph: Jelle KringsSerhih Leshchenko, a member of Ukrzaliznytsia’s supervisory board, described the railway as the “backbone of Ukraine’s economy”. It was the main logistical supplier for the country’s army and industry, and every week transported 600,000 people, he told the Guardian. With 170,000 workers, it was also Ukraine’s biggest company.For these reasons Russia was trying to destroy railways, he added. In the first year of the war it attacked bridges, which could be easily replaced. Next, it targeted rails and electricity substations. Ukraine then switched to using diesel engines. This year, Russia started “direct attacks on civilian locomotives”, he said – an insidious tactic, at a time when Ukraine is short of air defences.Several drivers have been killed and locomotives targeted inside depots. Leshchenko said that if a Shahed drone came within 50km of a train, it had to be evacuated, and could only continue once the threat has passed. So far this year Russia has hit the network more than 1,500 times – a higher figure than in the whole of 2025. Overall, 249 carriages and 492 locomotives have been damaged.Once known for their punctuality, trains now suffer regular delays, sometimes lasting as long as 12 to 15 hours. Amid air raid sirens, passengers are forced to disembark and take cover, including during winter.Writing on Facebook, the Ukrainian journalist Tetiana Zaiets described how she hid in April when Russian drones flew overhead.View image in fullscreenA destroyed railway bridge in the Lyman district in eastern Ukraine’s Donetsk oblast.Photograph: Jelle Krings“It was hell. The train stopped at night somewhere in central Ukraine. I don’t even know the name of the town. Half asleep, I just heard the conductor say ‘evacuation’. We took only our personal belongings and valuables with us. It was raining outside. Thank you to the conductors for handing out blankets,” she posted.She added: “That’s how we held out for two hours. While kamikaze drones were buzzing overhead, we crawled under a goods wagon. The last carriage in the train was full of children. They were being taken back from hospital. They were crying in their sleep. I thought I’d ended up in some sort of horror film. But no, this is our life.”Since the incident, Zaiets said she was too frightened to travel by train. “Until the war is over, I won’t be using it,” she said, stressing she respected Ukraine’s “courageous” railway workers.Last week, an enemy drone hit a train in the Odesa region with 600 people on board, including 15 children.“The train was stopped, we were kicked out. We heard explosions, everything was burning. It was scary,” one passenger, Andriy,told the website Suspline.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenRefugees arriving in Lviv on evacuation trains from Kharkiv and Kryvy Rih make their way through the train station.Photograph: Jelle KringsAnother passenger, Eva, said she was evacuated twice, and “dropped off in a field”. “We sat there and heard something flying. Then we saw a drone very close by.” She managed to collect her belongings and was eventually picked up by a bus, she said.Leshchenko admitted the Russian strikes were hurting Ukraine’s economy and had slowed the export of grain from its under-fire Black Sea ports. He saidKyivneeded air defences from western partners, so it could protects its trains from marauding missiles and drones. “If the whole country is under attack, they will attack railways for sure,” he said.Up until this year more than 90% of Ukrainian trains arrived on time. This was in part down to the fact engines never go especially fast, rolling at 55mph. Carriages are clean and comfortable: the best way of getting around a vast country. Stewards look after night train customers and bring them morning tea in filigree holders. There is a trolley on day trains, and patchy wifi.View image in fullscreenA wounded Ukrainian soldier is evacuated on a train.Photograph: Jelle KringsOn international services, border guards scrutinise male passengers, while dogs roam up and down corridors. Since the invasion, men between 18 and 60 have been forbidden from leaving the country, with some exemptions. On trains from Kyiv to Przemyśl, a railway hub in eastern Poland, most travellers are women. Since 2022 about six million people have departed abroad, many exiting by train.‘Everything’s smashed to bits’: Ukrainians turn anger on those storing weapons near their villagesRead moreIn recent days Russia has launched over 1,500 drones at Ukraine, 800 of them jet-fuel models, which are harder to shoot down. In the past, Moscow would send a swarm of drones a couple of times a week, usually at night. Now the attacks continue without a pause, with one or two drones dispatched every hour, paralysing ordinary life. Air raid sirens in Kyiv are non-stop.Pertsovsky, Ukrzaliznytsia’s boss, described the loss of his employees on Tuesday as “terrible”. “We are in touch with their loved ones. Everyone is with them to get through this extremely difficult time. The night is bitter with impossibility,” he wrote.Explore more on these topicsUkraineKyivRail transportEuropeRussianewsShareReuse this content

title: Russia kills at least 12 on sixth night of drone attacks on Kyiv  | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Zelenskyy says Moscow is capitalising on shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors to lower morale in capital
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Zelenskyy says Moscow is capitalising on shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors to lower morale in capital
Content: A firefighter responds to a Russian overnight attack on a railway depot in Kyiv.Photograph: State Emergency Service of Ukraine/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenA firefighter responds to a Russian overnight attack on a railway depot in Kyiv.Photograph: State Emergency Service of Ukraine/AFP/GettyUkraineRussia kills at least 12 on sixth night of drone attacks on KyivZelenskyy says Moscow is capitalising on shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors to lower morale in capitalEurope live – latest updatesDan Sabbaghin KyivTue 1 Sep 2026 11.06 EDTFirst published on Tue 1 Sep 2026 05.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least 12 people have been killed in and around Kyiv overnight as Ukraine’s capital endured asixth consecutive night of Russian drone and missile attacksaimed at shattering infrastructure and lowering the morale of the city.Eight of the dead were reported killed in Kyiv, including seven at a railway depot on the city’s left bank, and four were killed in Boryspil, to the east of the city, in a wave of strikes at about 2.30am after hours of air alerts.A further four people were killed in other parts ofUkraine, regional officials said, in 28 waves of attacks that included a strike on a border crossing point with Romania on the Danube at Orlivka.Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s president, said “a significant number of jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles were used in the attack” and thatRussiawas taking advantage of a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors.In a morning post on social media, Zelenskyy said: “Russia always plans its strikes specifically to cause as much destruction to people’s lives as possible, and it succeeds only when air defence capabilities are insufficient.”Kyiv and the surrounding towns and villages havecome under sustained attackin the past few days. Thirty-eight people were killed after a Russian dronestruck an ammunition store in Myla, 15 miles west of Kyiv, on Thursday, the hit causing hours of secondary explosions and damaging nearby homes.View image in fullscreenA woman collects belongings from her apartment damaged by a Russian missile strike in the town of Boryspil in the Kyiv region.Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersUkraine’s air force said Russia had attacked 28 locations, focusing on the cities of Kyiv and Odesa and their surroundings. Air defences shot down five Iskander ballistic missiles, two Banderol and five Kalibr cruise missiles and 187 out of 218 drones. Officials no longer reveal the total numbers of missiles fired.Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, the chief executive of Ukrainian Railways, said six of the seven people killed in and around the depot were employees of the network. Another rail worker was hospitalised, he added.Kyiv has been chronically short of air defence systems since the supply of Patriot interceptors dried up. The Patriots are the only weapon that can effectively stop high-speed Russian ballistic missiles, made at the rate of about 60 a month.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKyiv suffers hours of daytime air raids as Russia deploys new jet-powered dronesRead moreLockheed Martin, the US company that makes the most capable Pac-3 interceptors, produces about 600 a year, but US military supplies have been depleted during the US war with Iran. Ukraine is trying to secure a stockpile of about 300 for the winter, paid for by European allies, in a supply deal agreed with the US.Moscow appears to be trying to take advantage of an absence of air defence capability before winter, in an escalation of a conflict nearly deadlocked on the frontline. Ukraine has been responding by attacking oil refineries, warehouses and other military facilities deep inside Russia,aiming to hurt the country’s economy.Ukraine’s GUR military intelligence said it had attacked an oil refinery at the Baltic port of Ust-Luga, about 550 miles (885km) from its border. Russian officials said a civilian was killed in the border Belgorod region in an attack.Russia captured 35 square miles (56 sq km) of Ukraine’s territory during August, analysis by the AFP news agency concluded. It was Moscow’s largest advance since February but still much lower than the 150 square mile a month average of 2025.There remains little serious diplomatic effort to end the war, although on Monday India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, urged Vladimir Putin to end the war in public remarks at a bilateral meeting in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan.“Every day that the war continues, humanity is, in effect, set back ​a step, while every step towards peace gives all of humanity real hope for peace. We need to move from endless war to an end to the war,” Modi ⁠said.Putin appeared impatient, tapping his feet as he listened. “Thank you very much, prime minister. We are moving forward along this path,” he replied.Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Ed Miliband promises ‘comprehensive reset’ of UK policy toward Israel | Foreign policy | The Guardian
description: Foreign secretary tells MPs he will try to stop illegal settlements carving up the West Bank
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Foreign secretary tells MPs he will try to stop illegal settlements carving up the West Bank
Content: Ed Miliband has promised to stop UK involvement in settlement projects in the West Bank despite a warning of repercussions from Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, left.Photograph: Debbie Hill/Yui Mok/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEd Miliband has promised to stop UK involvement in settlement projects in the West Bank despite a warning of repercussions from Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, left.Photograph: Debbie Hill/Yui Mok/AFP/Getty ImagesForeign policyEd Miliband promises ‘comprehensive reset’ of UK policy toward IsraelForeign secretary tells MPs he will try to stop illegal settlements carving up the West BankKiran StaceyPolicy editorTue 1 Sep 2026 14.37 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEd Miliband has promised to “reset” Britain’s policy on Israel, saying he will try to stop British companies helping build settlements in the West Bank.Speaking to the Commons for the first time as foreign secretary, Miliband said he would set out measures to prevent UK involvement in projects such as theillegal E1 plan, which critics say would split the West Bank in half.Tuesday’s comments came after Israelissued tendersfor around a third of the 3,400 homes planned for the project. Miliband called the settlement “the crossing of a red line”.He said: “It cuts through the heart of theWest Bankand risks making a Palestinian state unviable. This government will not acquiesce in the destruction of the two-state solution. We will act, and I will set out a comprehensive set of measures in the coming weeks.“I want a comprehensive reset of our approach on these issues because it is necessary, it is high time.”Ministers have been under pressure for weeks to place tighter sanctions onIsrael, specifically in relation to the E1 plan.Last month, Israel invited companies to bid for contracts to build 1,200 homes for the project between East Jerusalem and the settlement of Ma’ale Adumim.View image in fullscreenMa’ale Adumim in the E1 area of the occupied West Bank, where the Israeli government plans to build thousands of homes.Photograph: Debbie Hill/UPI/ShutterstockA group of former British diplomatscalled on the governmentin May to threaten action against any companies bidding to build any illegal settlement “designed to divide the West Bank in two and destroy Palestine’s viability”. They warned that E1 was part of Israel’s “systemic West Bank annexation”.Other governments have condemned the project. The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz – usually one of Israel’s staunchest defenders – called it a “big mistake”.The UK joined a group of 20 other countries, including France, Germany and Italy, as well as the European Union, to issue a joint statement calling E1 “unacceptable”.The statement said: “The E1 settlement will undermine the prospect of the two-state solution by driving a wedge through the West Bank and harming the territorial contiguity of the Palestinian territories.”Miliband said: “We need to look, and we are looking indeed, at our wider economic relationship with the occupied territories and the different tools we have to tackle it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I want to be very clear: we do not want British companies financing, constructing, or advertising new settlements. The work we are now undertaking is how we can stop that. And as I say, I’ll have more to say soon.”Ministers are under pressure to go further and ban trade in goods and services with people or organisations linked to illegal settlements.James Naish, the Labour MP for Rushcliffe in Nottinghamshire, said: “Does the foreign secretary accept that this pace of expansion shows that current UK measures are failing to change Israeli government behaviour, and that a trade ban is now the necessary next step?”Stephen Doughty, a Foreign Office minister, indicated this could be included in the government’s measures. He said: “We have absolutely condemned the settler violence, the settler terrorism that we have seen, absolutely our condemnation of the proposals for E1 and all illegal settlements, and indeed we have joined other countries around the world in condemning this proposal and been very, very clear with the government of Israel that this must stop.“Theprime minister has been very clearthat we need to do more, including looking at further sanctions, both those involved in the violence in Gaza, but also looking at measures to ban trade in goods with illegal settlements.”The Israeli embassy to London responded by referring to previous comments by Gideon Sa’ar, Israel’s foreign minister, who said: “If Britain acts against the state of Israel, the state of Israel will act against Britain. We have the tools. The period is over when people act against the state of Israel and the state of Israel doesn’t respond.”Explore more on these topicsForeign policyIsraelEd MilibandWest BankPalestineMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: British aid worker mistakenly identified as a survivor of Nepal-Tibet disaster | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: More than 1,000 people confirmed dead and more than 4,000, including 36 British nationals, remain missing
