Author: Angus Thomson
Headline: More than 1,000 people confirmed dead and more than 4,000, including 36 British nationals, remain missing
Content: People search for the names of family members on a list posted outside an army training centre in Nuwakot, Nepal.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople search for the names of family members on a list posted outside an army training centre in Nuwakot, Nepal.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesNepal-Tibet flood disasterBritish aid worker mistakenly identified as a survivor of Nepal-Tibet disasterMore than 1,000 people confirmed dead and more than 4,000, including 36 British nationals, remain missingAngus ThomsonTue 1 Sep 2026 18.58 EDTFirst published on Tue 1 Sep 2026 14.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA British aid worker was mistakenly identified by Nepalese authorities as a rescued survivor after returning to Kathmandu on a humanitarian aid flight.Alastair Chambers, a 45-year-old former Gloucester councillor, said he flew to Nepal last week to distribute sleeping bags, food and essentials to communities cut off by collapsed bridges.After spending several days in a village near the Trishuli river in central Nepal, Chambers returned by helicopter to the capital, where he was greeted by police officers asking for his details.“I gave them my details, just abiding by the rules, and they obviously thought that I’d been rescued,” Chambers told the Press Association.Chambers appeared on a list of 119 names released by local authorities on Tuesday. An army spokesperson then told reporters at a press conference that a British national was among those rescued.“I was contacted by about 15 different journalists in the last few hours, just asking how I was and how I’m feeling after being rescued, and I had to say: ‘Well sorry, I haven’t been rescued,’” Chambers told PA.Those rescued included 118 Nepali nationals – 44 women and 74 men.Thirty-six British nationals are missing, the Foreign Office minister, Stewart Wood, told the House of Lords on Tuesday. The figure had previously been put at 33.Chambers was fined £49,000 after pleading guilty in June 2022 to breeding and selling dogs without a licence. The 45-year-old, who was the leader of a group of community independents on Gloucester city council until 2024, is due to face trial in November after denying he used homophobic slurs against a bar owner and former council worker.At least 1,050 people have been confirmed dead in Nepal since Wednesday’s flash floods, while Chinese state media said 66 people had been killed in Tibet. More than 4,000 people are still missing.Nepal’s prime minister, Balendra Shah, said 11,000 people had been rescued across the affected region. This included 330 foreign nationals, the Nepalese tourist board said in an update on Tuesday.How the deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – a visual guideRead morePreliminary analysis of satellite imagery suggests the collapse of a glacier high in the Himalayas was the primary cause of the disaster.The collapse – so large it wasinitially recorded as a magnitude-4.4 earthquake– triggered a deadly torrent of water, mud and ice that tore along the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers on Wednesday.Crews have faced dangerous and difficult conditions while searching unstable terrain and flood debris.Search efforts are now focused on attempts to reach about 600 workers believed to betrapped inside tunnels at several hydropower stationsin the region.“Massive work has been going on in the tunnel, all the tunnels,” the army spokesperson said on Tuesday.A rapid deployment rescue team from the UK arrived in Nepal on Saturday to provide support for Britons and their families as part of the government’s £5m commitment to support relief and recovery efforts.The Red Cross estimates that 93,000 people have been directly affected by the disaster.Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Nepal-Tibet flood deaths pass 1,000 as police ask relatives for DNA to identify victims | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Relatives of missing tourists asked for blood samples and photos, as efforts continue to rescue trapped hydropower workers
Author: Cait Kelly
Headline: Relatives of missing tourists asked for blood samples and photos, as efforts continue to rescue trapped hydropower workers
Content: The aftermath of the devastating flood in Betrawati Bazaar in Rasuwa district, Nepal.Photograph: Angad Dhakal/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe aftermath of the devastating flood in Betrawati Bazaar in Rasuwa district, Nepal.Photograph: Angad Dhakal/ReutersNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepal-Tibet flood deaths pass 1,000 as police ask relatives for DNA to identify victimsRelatives of missing tourists asked for blood samples and photos, as efforts continue to rescue trapped hydropower workersNepal-Tibet floods – latest updatesVisual guide: How the Nepal-Tibet flash flood unfoldedCait Kellyin Kathmandu and agenciesTue 1 Sep 2026 13.32 EDTFirst published on Tue 1 Sep 2026 06.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNepali rescuers have built temporary bridges to reach remote areas and dug through the ruins of hydropower projects in the Himalayas to rescue hundreds of trapped workers, as the death toll passed 1,000 nearly ⁠a week after devastating ​floods left a trail of destruction across the country’s towns and valleys.About 600 people remain stuck in several devastated hydropower stations that have become the focus of rescue efforts. The prime ⁠minister, Balendra Shah, said more than 11,000 people had been rescued across the affected region, and power and communication lines had been restored in some areas.“Thousands of citizens have lost their homes, families, loved ones and property,” Shah said.Headteacher saves 900 children from deadly flash flood in NepalRead moreSix days after the catastrophe struck the Himalayan border region, 4,400 people were still missing in Nepal and Tibet. Police in Kathmandu have urged relatives of missing tourists to provide DNA samples to assist identification efforts.In a statement posted to social media, Nepal police on Monday asked relatives of those missing to “provide a fresh blood sample for DNA profiling and two passport-sized photographs” to the pathology laboratory at the Nepal police hospital in Kathmandu, or the nearest district police office.1:24Drone footage shows scale of destruction after Nepal floods – videoAmong Nepal’s list of the missing are 592 foreigners, including tourists who had come for mountain trekking and Hindu pilgrims seeking spiritual peace at Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash, from countries such as India, the US, UK, Australia and Canada.Relatives abroad have been requested to undergo DNA profiling at an authorised laboratory and to “send a soft copy of the DNA profile to Nepal police’s official email address”.In some of Nepal’s flood-affected areas, hundreds of unidentified bodies have already been buried because they are decomposing and there isno room left in hospitals or morgues.At the police hospital in Kathmandu on Tuesday, more than 100 people were waiting to have their blood sampled.People search posters of those missing in Nepal floodAmong them was Prakaiti Jurnj. Her mother was still missing, but the family had been able to identify her father’s body from a photograph on the wall outside the teaching hospital, where images of the deceasedhave been postedin an effort to identify the victims.“Both my father and mother, they were in the village in Nukawot. They were both swept away by the flood,” she said. “We haven’t heard from them since Wednesday. We found my father’s body; my brother saw the photo on the wall.”She was waiting for her two other siblings, who live in the UK, to arrive on Tuesday so they could all try to get up to the village. She said she wanted to contact her grandmother or sister-in-law, who she thinks both survived the flood because their house is further up the mountain. Their village was still in a blackout, and making contact was impossible.“I can’t go there; the situation is very bad,” she said. “I can’t go up there alone. I am not sure if we’ll be able to get them.”Map showing areas damaged by the flood and mud flows caused by the avalancheThe disaster was triggered by a glacier collapse that sent a deluge of ice, rock and mud through Nepal’s border region withChina, posing a massive challenge for the country’s six-month-old government.The region is vulnerable to flooding and landslides, and extreme weather events such as intense monsoons and melting glaciers have become more common because of warming due to human-caused climate change.In a late-night social media post, Shah said aid worth more than $42m had poured into the country, but that Nepalis were reeling. “The government understands the ​immense pain they are enduring. The path ahead is to ‌support them through this suffering and help ‌them return to normal life through rehabilitation,” the prime minister said.Shah also said that 279 workers had so far been rescued from hydropower projects, where authorities estimated close to 1,000 people had been trapped. Days after the disaster, hope was rapidly diminisging that any of those trapped in a series of tunnels could be alive.1:02Nepal rescue teams work to reach over 900 people believed trapped in hydropower tunnels - videoPictures and videos shared by rescue teams showed earth-moving equipment digging and shovelling mud and rocks under lights in the dark of the night. Soldiers used torchlight in a big pit they had created to look for space to get into one tunnel.Chinese state media coverage has focused largely on the official response, highlighting the deployment of firefighters, the People’s Liberation Army and instructions from top leaders.Little is known about victimson the Chinese side.The flood was “caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming”, China’s state broadcaster said on Monday.Shah said the ​catastrophic event signalled the growing risks that the Himalayan region faces. “The region must therefore remain vigilant. The time has come for us to strongly raise before the international community the disasters we are experiencing as a consequence of climate change,” he wrote in his post.Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalChinaFloodingSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The mountains are changing’: What the floods tell us about the future of India’s Himalayas | World news | The Guardian
description: As families await news of missing loved ones, the disaster is a stark reminder of how the climate crisis is creating a fast-growing threat. Plus, the town considered India’s ‘Jurassic Park’
Author: Niha Masih
Headline: As families await news of missing loved ones, the disaster is a stark reminder of how the climate crisis is creating a fast-growing threat. Plus, the town considered India’s ‘Jurassic Park’
Content: A drone view shows mud covering properties following a flash flood in Trishuli, Nuwakot district, Nepal.Photograph: Navesh Chitrakar/ReutersView image in fullscreenA drone view shows mud covering properties following a flash flood in Trishuli, Nuwakot district, Nepal.Photograph: Navesh Chitrakar/ReutersThis Is IndiaWorld news‘The mountains are changing’: What the floods tell us about the future of India’s HimalayasAs families await news of missing loved ones, the disaster is a stark reminder of how the climate crisis is creating a fast-growing threat. Plus, the town considered India’s ‘Jurassic Park’Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereNiha MasihTue 1 Sep 2026 02.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 04.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt has been hard not to despair while watching the ruinous floodsswallow parts of Nepal, and harder, still knowing that the agony compounds each passing day for dozens of Indian families whose members remain unaccounted for.Social media is awash with desperate pleas, photos and details of the young and old, men and women, from Mumbai to Kolkata, posted by families searching for traces of life. Thedisaster unfoldedwhen a melting glacier slammed into the valley below, unleashing a deadly cascade of rock and ice down the Bhote Kashi River, which flows from Tibet into Nepal.Among the 275 Indiansmissingat the time of writing are workers of a hydropower project and people undertaking the Hindu pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet. Another 128 people of Indian origin, including a large group of Sadhguru’sIsha Foundationspiritual group, are also missing; 149 Indian people have beenrescued as of Monday.For Gauri Joshi, whose five relatives remained unaccounted for over the weekend, the last few days have been a blur of calling their numbers in vain, watching news of rescue operations and trying to reach Indian officials – over and over again. What she has pieced together so far is that her relatives, part of a pilgrim tour group from Maharashtra, cleared immigration at the Gyirong border between Nepal and Tibet and boarded buses shortly before the flood waters destroyed the crossing.“Chances appear very bleak now. But maybe a miracle will happen,” Joshi said.The tragedy has reignited the question of how vulnerable the Himalayas are to climate change, and what its implications are for India. To understand the risks of glacier collapse and thawing permafrost leading to sudden floods and debris flows, I spoke toDr Ashim Sattar, a professor at Indian Institute of Technology Bhubaneswar and an expert onglacial lake outburst floods. The conversation has been edited and condensed.What are the climate- or glacier-relatedrisks emerging across the Himalayas?“There are different forms of cryosphere and how they pose a hazard. In a layperson’s terms, the cryosphere is where water exists in solid form, for example a glacier. When it melts, it forms glacial lakes. If they have an outburst, they can cause damage downstream.Another cryospheric component is glacier ice. This is what we’ve seen in Nepal, where a glacier detachment happened. The frontal part of the glacier detached from the main glacier and eventually led to a debris flow.The third component is permafrost. They exist widely in the Himalayas, but there has not been much monitoring because it’s very difficult. Everything – these lakes, glaciers and permafrost – are all hazards. Unless they’re triggered, they would not cause damage.With climate change, these grounds will go above zero degrees and will start to degrade. These would need very little … to mobilise debris. We might expect a higher frequency of debris flows in the future. We won’t know how they are getting conditioned, unless we have some monitoring stations and scientific investigation.And given the Himalayas are very vast, monitoring every part of it becomes tricky. It can be the mountain ranges within India, or maybe outside India, eventually, which drains into the Indian subcontinent. That needs to be well studied.”View image in fullscreen‘[Floods] might happen any time’ … a Devighat resident retrieves some of his belongings.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianHow big are the downstream risks for India?“Right now, this is a gap in scientific studies; nothing [is] quantified yet. There is direct evidence of climate impacts, even in the Indian part of the Himalayas. The number of glacial lakes is increasing, the size of glacial lakes is increasing, the volume of glacial lakes is increasing, and glaciers are retreating. The risk exists because it might happen any time.”Which parts of India are the most vulnerable?“Everyone in the Himalayas, every Himalayan state has hazards. We can’t deny it. If you look at the eastern side, they have a lot of glacial lakes. They have already reached their maximum extent. Most full-grown lakes are about to reach their limits, like maximum extent. In the western Himalayas or even the central Himalayas, there’s a lot of scope for the lakes because they have not reached their full extent. As the glaciers would retreat, they would keep on growing.We are still unsure when the status is going to change for any of these states. That’s a very, very difficult question, and I don’t think anyone [can] answer it at this moment without any scientific investigation.”How would you describe India’s earlywarning systems and disaster preparedness?“The National Disaster Management Authority is taking proactive steps now with the glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF)Risk Mitigation Programmeto install early-warning systems.Maybe an early warning system should be community-based. It should be for the people and by the people. It’s not always the scientist or the policymakers who can actually make this work at its full potential. We need to have local knowledge, involve the communities to make them more effective.”How long will it take to have these systems in place?“I have no idea because each of these organisations are working at their own pace. They have their own style of working. I’m sure it is going to happen soon. I can just comment on the areas where I know, and I’ve been in touch.”Is prevention possible, orcan it only minimise the damage?“Prevention is possible, but it is very expensive: computationally, financially and manpower-wise. Minimising is also possible. It would require a lot of intervention in the high mountains, which is very difficult in those terrains.We know that the mountains are changing and the hazard levels are increasing, so the only way forward is to minimise the exposure to the risk below. That means how much of the hazard is going to interact with the downstream. If something is in the path, we remove them.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is IndiaNiha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern IndiaEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTo support relief efforts in Nepal, you can contribute totheprimeminister’s Disaster Relief Fund here.What else we’re reading aboutView image in fullscreenPeople protest against an appearance by Mohan Bhagwat, a leader of the far-right paramilitary group RSS, in New York.Photograph: Ryan Murphy/APRSS in New York| Last weekend, Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) chief Mohan Bhagwat addressed Indian Americans at New York’sMadison Square Gardencalling for global unity. The Quintreportedthat the newly formed group behind the event has RSS links. The visitwas opposedby several diaspora groups that reject the RSS’ Hindu nationalist ideology and criticise its record on minority rights.Books and backlash| A reading session organised in Ahmedabad after a private school was forced to drop books by Malala Yousafzai and Anne Frank was allegedly disrupted by a group affiliated with the rightwingBajrang Dal. Three peoplehave been arrested.Indian cinema abroad| Two Indian films have been selected for theBusan International film festival, which begins on 6 October. Birds in the Dark, by Shashank Walia, explores an unexpected human connection while Tamil writer-director Sailesh Rathnakumar’s Selviis set in the world of home-care workers.Guest shelfA recommendation from someone with great tasteView image in fullscreen‘Jurassic Park of India’ … a dinosaur museum in Raiyoli.Photograph: Ajit Solanki/APPhotographer Aashim Tyagi (@aashim), who once documentedArt Deco architecturein Gujarat’s Balasinor, suggests a prehistoric side quest: “I was intrigued by the town’s reputation as the ‘Jurassic Park of India’ and a little digging led me to a dinosaur museum in neighbouring Raiyoli. It’s set amid open fields near one of Asia’s largest fossil beds where Rajasaurus narmadensis and a dozen other species once roamed. Much of the museum and the village’s paleontological preservation is owed to Aaliya Babi of Balasinor’s erstwhile royal family, earning her the nickname ‘Dinosaur Princess’. Balasinor and its dinosaur museum are a worthwhile detour from Ahmedabad or Baroda.”Count itA number worth knowingView image in fullscreenIndia ranked 176th out of 177 countries in the 2026 Environmental Performance Index.Photograph: Anushree Fadnavis/Reuters176India ranked 176th,second from the bottom, in the 2026 Environmental Performance Index, which evaluates countries on environmental health, climate change and ecosystem vitality. The country recorded negative values on air-quality indicators but showed animprovementon the index’s 10-year change metric. In 2022, when India had been ranked last, the central government haddismissed the EPI’s conclusions, saying it used “unscientific methods”.Get in touchDo you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us atthisisindia@theguardian.comand we may include your response in a future edition.Explore more on these topicsWorld newsThis Is IndiaIndiaSouth and central AsiaNepal-Tibet flood disasterFloodingExtreme weathernewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Fund defence spending from tax rise on middle earners, thinktank tells Healey | Defence policy | The Guardian
description: Resolution Foundation argues that UK’s internationally low ‘tax wedge’ must rise to pay for defence ambitions
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Resolution Foundation argues that UK’s internationally low ‘tax wedge’ must rise to pay for defence ambitions
Content: John Healey visiting UK troops in Cyprus in 2024 as defence secretary, before his appointment as chancellor by Andy Burnham.Photograph: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJohn Healey visiting UK troops in Cyprus in 2024 as defence secretary, before his appointment as chancellor by Andy Burnham.Photograph: Getty ImagesDefence policyFund defence spending from tax rise on middle earners, thinktank tells HealeyResolution Foundation argues that UK’s internationally low ‘tax wedge’ must rise to pay for defence ambitionsHeather StewartEconomics editorTue 1 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe chancellor,John Healey, must be prepared to raise taxes for middle earners if he wants to fund significantly higher defence spending, the Resolution Foundation thinktank has said.Healeyresigned from Keir Starmer’s government in June, protesting against what he argued was the then prime minister’s failure to adequately fund defence.But in his new post in No 11 Downing Street, Healey has made clear thathe will wait until next year’s spending reviewbefore presenting a plan to meet Labour’s pledge of devoting 3.5% of GDP to defence by 2035.Defence spending is an insatiable beast. John Healey is right to tame it | John McTernanRead moreIn a new report, entitled Thin End of the Wedge, economists at the Resolution Foundation suggest he will not be able to raise the £28bn a year it would take to meet that promise without asking average workers to pay more.They say that despite historically large tax rises sinceLabourcame to power in 2024, amounting to £70bn a year, the “tax wedge” – taxes on earnings, minus benefits – remains low by international standards.“Despite recent increases, the UK still taxes average earners less than most of our international peers,” says the foundation’s chief economist, James Smith.The analysis shows that tax rises under Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, resulted in a 2.4 percentage point jump in the tax wedge last year – the largest for any country in the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD).Yet at 32.4% for a single earner on average pay, it remains below the average for the OECD and the G7 major economies, they say.When the economists looked at countries with higher public spending, they found these tended to ask their average workers to contribute more – instead of relying on business or wealth taxes, for example.“No other OECD rich country has a bigger state and a lower burden on average workers, so any politician promising both is not being realistic,” Smith said.“There is a strong case that any benefits of increased defence spending will be broadly shared, so the tax rises needed to find this should be too, including higher rates on middle earners.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe tax wedge on a worker paid the median salary, of £33,000 as at April last year, is also low by historic standards, they argue – and is still below the level before the global financial crisis in 2008.In Reeves’s two tax-raising budgets before she was sacked by Andy Burnham, the biggest revenue-raisers wereemployer national insurance contributionsandfiscal drag– where income tax thresholds were left unchanged, so that more people end up paying higher rates.She was constrained by Labour’s pre-election promise not to increase the rates of income tax, VAT or employee national insurance – whichBurnham has promised to stick to.As well as the longer-term defence pledge, Burnham’s government faces pressure to do more to cushion households against rising energy bills over the coming winter, and to beef upefforts to help unemployed young people into work.Healey will present his first budget on 28 October and needs to find approximately £1.4bn a year over the next three yearsto pay for Starmer’s defence investment plan– which Healey in his last job derided as inadequate.Explore more on these topicsDefence policyTax and spendingIncome taxJohn HealeyLabourMilitaryTaxnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cleveland police to get £2m extra to tackle serious crime in Middlesbrough | UK news | The Guardian
description: Cash announced after horror car crash that killed two police officers and house fire in which woman and young girl died
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Cash announced after horror car crash that killed two police officers and house fire in which woman and young girl died
Content: Natalie McDonald, 34, and her niece Valentina Foster, seven, died in the fire in Grangetown.Composite: FacebookView image in fullscreenNatalie McDonald, 34, and her niece Valentina Foster, seven, died in the fire in Grangetown.Composite: FacebookUK newsCleveland police to get £2m extra to tackle serious crime in MiddlesbroughCash announced after horror car crash that killed two police officers and house fire in which woman and young girl diedJosh HallidayandAngus ThomsonTue 1 Sep 2026 18.04 EDTFirst published on Tue 1 Sep 2026 02.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCleveland’s police force is to receive a £2m funding boost to tackle serious crime, after the home secretary said successive high-profile tragedies in the Middlesbrough area had led to a “sense of disquiet” in the community.Shabana Mahmood and the prime minister, Andy Burnham, paid tribute in parliament on Tuesday to police constables Matthew Blades and Tom Clough, who were killed when a Volkswagen Passat travelling on the wrong side of the A66 dual carriageway collided head-on with their marked response vehicle.Five young men travelling in the Passat, which had earlier been pursued by different police, also died in the 22 August incident.Cleveland police said the five occupants – Cole Worthy, 17, Theo Rae, 17, Makai Saddington, 18, Michael Robert Cahill, 23, and Jakub Matusiak, 23 – may have had links to “serious organised criminal activity”.Officers from outside the area have been deployed to Cleveland after the crash.Mahmood told the House of Commons on Tuesday that she had given her “full backing” to the investigation, making the £2m pledge to fight “both serious crime and its causes”.The funding is separate to real-term budget increases for all police forces, which will see Cleveland police receive an additional £7m compared with last year, she said.The home secretary said Cleveland police were also investigating the house fire in Grangetown that killed Natalie McDonald, 34, and her niece Valentina Foster, 7, and injured four others on 26 August.Investigators were not treating the fire and the A66 crash – which occurred within a mile of each other – as connected, Mahmood said.“However, it has undoubtedly added to the sense of disquiet in a community already reeling from the earlier tragedy,” she said. “I recognise how unnerving it will have been for law-abiding citizens, both in the affected areas and beyond, to see a spate of incidents occurring in close proximity and quick succession.”Cleveland police and crime commissioner Matt Storey said the £2m funding boost would help deal with the immediate aftermath of the incidents, but would not address the “chronic underfunding” of the force.“A one-off payment is not a solution,” Storey said. “It fails to tackle the deep-rooted funding inequalities that continue to disadvantage the hard-working officers, staff and communities of Cleveland.”Storey said the force needed at least £20m every year to recruit 200 more police officers and strengthen efforts to crack down on serious organised crime.The funding announcement came after a 23-year-old man appeared in court on murder charges over the deaths of McDonald and Foster.Jaden Wright, of no fixed address, appeared before Teesside magistrates court on Tuesday for a hearing that lasted less than two minutes.Wright briefly greeted his solicitor as he was brought into the dock before he was remanded in custody to appear at Teesside crown court on Thursday.The court clerk outlined that he faces two murder charges, two counts of grievous bodily harm with intent and two charges of attempted grievous bodily harm with intent. The charges relate to the six people who were in the house, two of whom cannot be identified by the media due to their age.The clerk said Wright faced a separate charge of intentional strangulation over an incident said to have happened on the day before the fire.Cleveland police said on Friday that a 48-year-old woman was in the Royal Victoria Infirmary in Newcastle in a “critical but stable” condition after the fire, and a 27-year-old man was at James Cook university hospital in Middlesbrough receiving treatment. Two teenage girls were discharged after sustaining non-life-threatening injuries.Katie Smith, the senior investigating officer from Northumbria police, said: “This has been a truly tragic incident and my thoughts remain with the families of all those involved.“I would like to thank local residents for their support and patience during this complex investigation. Anyone who may still have information, or has any concerns, can still submit information using the major incident public portal.”Katie Nicholson, the chief crown prosecutor for CPS North East, said: “Our prosecutors have worked closely with Cleveland police to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring this case to court.“We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are active and he has the right to a fair trial. It is vital that there should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information which could in anyway prejudice these proceedings.”A 31-year-old man who was also arrested in connection with the case was released without charge on Sunday.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Deported Milo Yiannopoulos says he is ‘ashamed’ of support for Trump | ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) | The Guardian
description: British far-right pundit breaks silence on ICE arrest and deportation and says he was ‘really, really terrified’
Author: Anna Betts
Headline: British far-right pundit breaks silence on ICE arrest and deportation and says he was ‘really, really terrified’
Content: Milo Yiannopoulos at a Ukip rally in Exeter in 2019. Yiannopoulos was deported from the US after being arrested by ICE officials in New Orleans.Photograph: Geoff Caddick/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMilo Yiannopoulos at a Ukip rally in Exeter in 2019. Yiannopoulos was deported from the US after being arrested by ICE officials in New Orleans.Photograph: Geoff Caddick/AFP/Getty ImagesICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Deported Milo Yiannopoulos says he is ‘ashamed’ of support for TrumpBritish far-right pundit breaks silence on ICE arrest and deportation and says he was ‘really, really terrified’Anna BettsTue 1 Sep 2026 16.49 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMilo Yiannopoulos, the British far-right commentator who wasarrestedlast week by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers in Louisiana and deported to the United Kingdom, has broken his silence about the experience, saying that “for the first time I know what it feels like to be really, really terrified”.Yiannopoulos on Tuesday appeared onPiers Morgan Uncensored, a YouTube show presented byPiers Morgan, the British broadcaster and media personality. Yiannopoulos, 41, described the experience in the US as “humiliating and disorientating”, “physically degrading” and “frightening”.He also said that he was “ashamed” of his previous support for Donald Trump, who has pursuedan agendaof mass deportation throughout his second presidency.“I didn’t really understand the physical reality of how institutionalized the brutality is in America” he said, adding: “It’s like everybody that’s arrested is anMS-13 gangmember, and it hurts a lot more than it looks like on television.”His remarks came just days after he wasdeportedfrom the US, after beingarrested on Thursdayby ICE officers at New Orleans airport.In a statement last week, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), theparent agencyof ICE, said Yiannopoulos had “legally entered the country” in May 2019, but “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws”.Yiannopoulos was anearly supporterof Trump before he first became US president in 2016. He is aformer editor of Breitbart Newsand later worked to help the rapper Ye, formerly known asKanye West, explore apresidential runin 2024.The homeland security department said Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge on 22 July “after failing to show up for his immigration hearing”.In the Piers Morgan interview, Yiannopoulos disputed the government’s account and denied previously overstaying a visa. He said he is married to an American, and claimed he held a green card that he was “renewing on a two-year basis”.The Guardian has contacted homeland security and the White House for comment on Yiannopoulos’s remarks.Yiannopoulos also said that while he was detained, “no one would tell me anything” – a common complaint from people held in ICE custody.“I don’t think I’ve ever been frightened like that before” he told Morgan. “I think maybe in the past I’ve been a little bit blasé when people talked about their trauma, a little bit cavalier when people talked about stuff kind of lingering with them, but I get it now … I wouldn’t wish it on anyone.”Last year, in posts on social media, Yiannopoulos had beensupportiveof Trump’scrackdown on immigration.Inonepost, he wrote: “There is one concrete thing we must insist on this administration delivering. It matters a lot more than debts measured in imaginary money. We have got to deport millions and millions and millions of people. Without that, nothing else matters.”In anotherpost, Yiannopoulos had said that California “needs ICE checkpoints at supermarket entrances, gas stations, strip malls, intersections and government buildings, with on the spot deportation for anyone who can’t prove they are in the US legally”.During Tuesday’s interview, Yiannopoulos said of his past support for Trump: “If I had any clue that anything remotely like this was even possible, I would never have gotten involved in supporting Trump in the first place and I’m very ashamed that I did.”Explore more on these topicsICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Trump administrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Farage faces questions over his claim of second standards investigation | Nigel Farage | The Guardian
description: Reform leader said inquiry had been widened but watchdog is not believed to have decided whether to do so
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Reform leader said inquiry had been widened but watchdog is not believed to have decided whether to do so
Content: Farage was sworn in as an MP again on Tuesday after winning the Clacton byelection.Photograph: House of CommonsView image in fullscreenFarage was sworn in as an MP again on Tuesday after winning the Clacton byelection.Photograph: House of CommonsNigel FarageFarage faces questions over his claim of second standards investigationReform leader said inquiry had been widened but watchdog is not believed to have decided whether to do soRowena MasonWhitehall editorTue 1 Sep 2026 14.54 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNigel Farage is facing questions about why he claimed his finances were the subject of a second standards investigation, as he was sworn in again as Clacton’s MP.TheReform UKleader said when he resigned in July that the standards system had become a “political tool” because “yet another standards investigation is under way” into his finances.He argued he wanted the people of Clacton to be the judge of his actions, rather than “the establishment”, after revelations in the Sunday Times that his friend and convicted fraudster George Cottrell had paid for social media work, accommodation and security before the 2024 election.However, it is understood the parliamentary standards commissioner had not launched another investigation or widened the scope of the existing one at that point.The commissioner is believed still not to have decided whether to widen the inquiry as recently as two weeks ago, when it was reopened as Farage was returned as MP for Clacton with an increased majority.Arms and the £5m man: Farage megadonor Christopher Harborne’s military empireRead moreThe commissioner launched his first investigation in May into Farage’s £5m gift from the Thailand-based donor Christopher Harborne before the 2024 election, which was not declared on the MPs’ register of interests and wasfirst revealed by the Guardian. Initially Farage said the money was given to pay for his security, then he described it as a reward for campaigning for Brexit.At least two complaints were then submitted in July about Farage’s funding by Cottrell. Faragecalled a byelection on 7 Julyand the initial investigation was paused.However, Westminster sources said the standards commissioner was assessing information. There is no official confirmation that he has widened his inquiry to include the Cottrell donations, and the commissioner’s list of investigations currently only includes the one launched in May.The sources said the commissioner wanted to see further evidence that Farage had broken the rules in relation to donations from Cottrell in the year before the 2024 election, including his payments for social media work.View image in fullscreenNigel Farage swears in as Clacton's MP at the House of Commons. He said on Tuesday he planned to spend less time in parliament while he toured the country.Photograph: House of Commons/ReutersFarage has maintained the videos were personal and likened his public role before that election to the work of an influencer. However, a number of the videos were political in nature, campaigning on immigration issues.Critics say these should be declared under rules that say donations related to politics must be registered in the 12 months before an MP is elected.The standards commissioner declined to comment on the status of the investigation into Farage and whether any decision had been made on widening the inquiry.If there is no second investigation nor a widened scope, it is possible the first investigation into Farage could conclude sooner than expected. The Times reported in July that the Reform leader would be interviewed within weeks but the byelection paused the process.In relation to the investigation, Alex Burghart, the shadow chancellor of the duchy of Lancaster, said: “The questions surrounding Nigel Farage’s £5m gift from Christopher Harborne and the donations from George Cottrell simply aren’t going away.“Farage has already tried to run away with his farcical byelection in Clacton, but he can no longer hide from these questions. He needs to come clean … The public deserves answers and Farage can’t keep hiding.”If the standards commissioner finds a breach of the rules, and the separate standards committee of MPs recommends a sanction of more than 10 days of suspension from parliament, Farage could end up facing a second byelection.As he was sworn in again on Tuesday, Farage told GB News that he planned to spend less time in parliament and would be leaving more Westminster work to [the Reform deputy leader] “Richard Tice and the gang” while he goes on a tour of the country.Farage will set his priorities for the year ahead when he gives his speech at the Reform party conference at the end of this week, where he is expected to attempt to draw a line under the focus on his finances.Explore more on these topicsNigel FarageReform UKParty fundingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham blames Brexit and Thatcher for ‘wrong turns’ in first Commons speech as PM | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: The prime minister said Britain needed to be brutally honest about the mistakes of the last 40 years of UK politics
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: The prime minister said Britain needed to be brutally honest about the mistakes of the last 40 years of UK politics
Content: Andy Burnham promised to bring optimism and ‘substantial change’ during his term.Photograph: House of CommonsView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham promised to bring optimism and ‘substantial change’ during his term.Photograph: House of CommonsAndy BurnhamBurnham blames Brexit and Thatcher for ‘wrong turns’ in first Commons speech as PMThe prime minister said Britain needed to be brutally honest about the mistakes of the last 40 years of UK politicsPippa CrerarandJessica ElgotTue 1 Sep 2026 14.52 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has blamed Brexit andMargaret Thatcherfor a decade of low growth in the UK, arguing that Britain needs to be brutally honest about having taken “a series of wrong turns” in the last 40 years.In his first Commons appearance since he took over as prime minister about six weeks ago, Burnham told MPs he wanted to build a new sense of optimism so “we can make this next decade better than the last”.The British people wanted “much more substantial change” on the big issues facing the country, he said. “That is what I will bring. Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be. Things are not working as they should.”The UK economy has takena 6% hit from the effects of Brexit, according to economists’ analysis of internal Bank of England data on thousands of British companies since the referendum a decade ago.More public control is the way to grow UK economy, Burnham to tell MPsRead moreShortly before Burnham’s Commons address, Keir Starmer, his predecessor, announced he wouldstand down as an MP, saying he wanted to focus on international affairs, triggering a tricky first byelection test for Burnham in a seat where the Greens fancy their chances.The cabinet was told on Tuesday that the government will have three key priorities: cutting costs of essentials like childcare and mortgages; the regeneration of communities; and greater public control of water, housing and energy.Burnham’s deputy, Louise Haigh, will lead task forces on each of those issues, the Guardian understands. He told his ministers they must be “relentless” in fulfilling his priorities.His plans are set against atough economic backdrop. The chancellor’s headroom against Labour’s fiscal rules could be halved at his first budget if the current global bond sell-off persists, and economists warn mortgage rates could go up this autumn.In his Commons statement, the prime minister also:Hinted that he would commit to spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, saying he had appointed John Healey as his chancellor “precisely because” of hisposition on military spending.Signalled he is open to renationalising the water industry – saying he is looking at “all possible solutions”, as the sector is a “leaking monument” to the failures of privatisation.Opened the door to looking again at electoral reform in Labour’s next manifesto. “I do believe there needs to be a mandate to make that change. There are different views in this house, but I believe we will need to get a consensus at the next election. And if there is that consensus, then a change can be made in the next parliament.”Announced he would attend the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey and continue pursuing green energy – but that he would be “pragmatic” on supply, amid expectations he will approve the Jackdaw gasfield. “The mistake is saying it’s got to be one or the other for political purposes. The truth is, it’s going to have to be both.”Flanked by Healey and Haigh, Burnham suggested to MPs theBrexitvote had been a response to “a series of wrong turns” made by Britain in the 1980s onwards, that were then compounded by leaving the EU.The prime minister, whose Makerfield constituency voted for Brexit, has previously argued it would be amistake to rerun the referendum– but has said that he wants the UK to rejoin in his lifetime. He suggested the next UK-EU reset summit could take place in November.Tax promises, defence targets and Iran: Andy Burnham’s budget headachesRead more“Political power was centralised, economic power privatised, the country de-industrialised. Austerity followed, hollowing out councils and depriving them of the agency to act to reverse any of this,” he said during a three-hour stint in the Commons.“And then Brexit compounded the damage, ushering in a decade of low growth and stalled regeneration. Change begins with honesty … Unless we are blunt about what went wrong, we won’t turn things around.“Far from taking back control, the combination of these policies took control out of the hands of communities up and down Britain for 40 years. Too many places have been drifting.”He added: “The government I lead will be relentless in giving people and places what they were promised 10 years ago: ownership and control, and from that control over their destiny comes change and growth.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch accused Burnham of wanting to take the UK ‘back to the 1970s’.Photograph: House of CommonsThe Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, accused the prime minister of “living in the past” over his attacks on Thatcher – who was in power from 1979 to 1990 – and four decades of neoliberalism.“The year is 2026 but the prime minister said everything has gone wrong since the 1980s, still complaining about Margaret Thatcher. He is talking about a woman who became prime minister before I was born. He is living in the past and he wants to take us back to the 1970s.”In the statement, Burnham paid tribute to Starmer, saying he had created a platform for Britain to be fixed, “and we will use it well”. Just hours earlier, his predecessor announced he would be standing down as MP for Holborn and St Pancras, despite saying in July he planned to stay on until the next election.“It has been a huge honour and privilege to represent the best constituency in the country,” he said. “I will now focus on other things and that will be international affairs, including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast-changing world.”Starmer’s seat, long seen as a safeLabourhold, is likely to be targeted by the Greens, potentially for party leader Zack Polanski, who is a London Assembly member. “Zack has always made it clear he would like to be a London MP. London has been his home for over 20 years,” a Green spokesperson said.Just asthe Makerfield byelectionwas seen as a proof of concept for whether Burnham could beat Reform, so the north London seat will test his progressive credentials. Labour will choose its candidate to replace Starmer next Wednesday under an accelerated selection timetable.Burnham’s first taskforce will be charged with finding bold solutions to tackling “everyday rip-offs”. The cost of living taskforce will look at parking charges, subscription traps and cowboy builders, as well as long-term fixed pressures like mortgages, food costs and childcare.The second will assess the affordability and practicalities of the state taking over failing essential services. Burnham believes that greater state control of essential services is the surest way to economic growth, avoiding the potential for ineffective profiteering by privatised services.Government sources said that Haigh, the first secretary of state, wanted to look beyond sectors such as transport and explore serious opportunities for greater state control in areas like energy and housing – if it would bring down ordinary people’s costs.The third taskforce will explore more radical ideas to revive crumbling high streets and impoverished districts, such as potential legislative options on houses in multiple occupation, as well as devolving powers to mayors and councils to help them regenerate local high streets.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamLabourMargaret ThatcherBrexitnewsShareReuse this content

title: Shein shares slide on fast-fashion retailer’s stock market debut | Shein | The Guardian
description: Hong Kong flotation at $26bn by firm once valued at $100bn follows failure to list in US and UK
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: Hong Kong flotation at $26bn by firm once valued at $100bn follows failure to list in US and UK
Content: Shein company executives and employees at the listing ceremony in Hong Kong.Photograph: May James/EPAView image in fullscreenShein company executives and employees at the listing ceremony in Hong Kong.Photograph: May James/EPASheinShein shares slide on fast-fashion retailer’s stock market debutHong Kong flotation at $26bn by firm once valued at $100bn follows failure to list in US and UKMark SweneyTue 1 Sep 2026 03.11 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 14.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShares in the fast-fashion brand Shein slumped by as much as 10% as the China-founded company made itslong-anticipated trading debuton the Hong Kong stock exchange.The Singapore-headquartered company, once valued at almost $100bn (£74bn), went public on Tuesday pricing shares at HK$48.56, valuing the business at just over $26bn.However, minutes after the flotation, which raised HK$13.6bn, the stock fell as much as 10%, pushing the online retailer’s valuation below $25bn.Shein’s share price recovered most of its early trading plunge, closing at HK$48.50, just 0.12% down on its opening price.“Let global consumers enjoy the sound of fashion,” said Leigh Gui, Shein’s chief financial officer, after a gong was struck to mark the start of trading.The lacklustre launch as a publicly listed company comes after one of the longest-awaited initial public offerings in recent years, afterplans to list in New Yorkwere blocked by regulators over forced labour concerns.Shein also considered a£50bn flotation in Londonbut faced similar questions about its supply chain from campaigners, MPs and investors.Nevertheless, the company has still floated as one of the world’s biggest listed fashion groups, with a valuation around the same as the Swedish retailer H&M. The Zara owner, Inditex, has a market capitalisation of about $213bn.Shein reached a valuation of $100bn in an April 2022 fundraising round, making it the third most valuable startup in the world at the time. The plunge in its value since has been driven by regulatory changes around the world that threaten its business model of shipping goods in small packages out ofChinato take advantage of tax breaks on low-value imported goods.The company swung to a loss of $99m in the first three months of this year, compared with a net income of $395m the year before, after the USremoved its “de minimis” import duty exemptionon small packages, hitting its sales in the country.The EU is also cracking down on the loophole, introducing a€3 (£2.56) dutyon small parcels imported from outside the trading bloc in June, and intends to phase it out, while the UK has said it will do the same by October 2028.On Tuesday, France began imposing penalties on some fast-fashion items to curb the surge in sales of cheap products sold by retailers such as Shein and its Chinese rival Temu.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionParis passed a fast-fashion law in June to address concerns about overproduction, with the penalties calculated using a formula that factors in the number of products sold, their prices and repairability.The penalties, which are set to increase in 2030, range from €0.25 for a pair of boxer shorts or socks to €12 for a coat, with the amount capped at 50% of the product’s pre-tax sales price.China’s commerce ministry has called the French law discriminatory and a trade barrier and said it could be in violation of World Trade Organization principles.Shein, founded by theentrepreneur Chris Xu, runs most of its operations from China but sells all its goods outside the country. It moved its headquarters to Singapore at about the start of 2022, a move viewed by analysts as designed to avoid increasing scrutiny of Chinese companies.Afterforced labour concerns were raised, Shein said it had tightened its supplier policies, enforced through regular audits, with any child or forced labour violations becoming grounds for immediate termination of contract.Explore more on these topicsSheinRetail industryIPOsHong KongChinaAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Everton left with only one striker after Balogun deal collapses late on deadline day | Everton | The Guardian
description: Everton’s £40m move for US international Folarin Balogun collapsed late on deadline day to leave manager David Moyes with only one striker for the first half of the season
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Everton’s £40m move for US international Folarin Balogun collapsed late on deadline day to leave manager David Moyes with only one striker for the first half of the season
Content: Folarin Balogun will not be be joining deadline-day signings Jack Grealish and Ainsley Maitland-Niles at Everton.Photograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFolarin Balogun will not be be joining deadline-day signings Jack Grealish and Ainsley Maitland-Niles at Everton.Photograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty ImagesEvertonEverton left with only one striker after Balogun deal collapses late on deadline day25-year-old walks away from £40m deal at last momentBeto and Ndiaye already sold by club to raise fundsAndy HunterTue 1 Sep 2026 19.46 EDTFirst published on Tue 1 Sep 2026 19.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEverton’s £40m move for US international Folarin Balogun collapsed late on deadline day to leave manager David Moyes with only one striker for the first half of the season.Everton had agreed a £40m deal for Balogun only for issues with the striker’s medical to place the transfer in doubt after the Merseyside club had sold Beto to Fiorentina and Iliman Ndiaye to Manchester City. Enquiries were made to Manchester United for Joshua Zirkzee and Aston Villa for Tammy Abraham but proposed loans for both forwards were rejected.The structure of the deal was renegotiated late on – Monaco agreed to accept a lower payment up front and more in add-ons – and Everton submitted a deal sheet to complete the transfer in time. But the 25-year-old is said to have changed his mind over the move and walked away at the final moment. The collapse of the deal leaves Thierno Barry as Everton’s one recognised striker and completed a shambolic end to the window by the club’s hierarchy, who were already under pressure having tried to sell Harrison Armstrong to Nottingham Forest.Transfer deadline day: Man City sign Fernández and Ndiaye, Mudryk and Tosin join Spurs – liveRead moreEverton also hit problems in their attempts to sign right-back Kenny Tete from Fulham. A £9m deal had been agreed for the defender only for Fulham to fail to land their preferred replacement, Andrei Ratiu of Rayo Vallecano. Everton finally concluded their long-running search for a right-back by signing former Arsenal player Ainsley Maitland-Niles from Lyon for a fee of around £4.2m. The 29-year-old has agreed a three year contract.Funds were raised by the sales of Ndiaye to City, for £60m plus £5m in add-ons, Beto to Fiorentina for £15.5m, Tim Iroegbunam to Hull for an initial £15m and Nathan Patterson to Torino for an undisclosed fee.Grealish returns to the Hill Dickinson Stadium on another season loan from City. The 30-year-old enjoyed a productive spell on loan in 2025-26 before sustaining a fractured foot that ended his campaign in February.Grealish, who will be out of contract at City when this latest deal ends next summer, could make his second Everton debut against Manchester United on Sunday. He said: “I’m so happy. I think I’m at my best at everything in life, not just football, when I feel loved. That’s what the manager has given me, what my teammates have given me and especially what the fans have given me. Every time I see an Everton fan, it’s just pure love.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It means a lot to me and hopefully I’ve made a few Everton fans happy. I had a perfect time here for the first six months, then I stayed around after I got injured. I’ve been watching all the Everton games in pre-season and since the season started. Now I feel ready to go.”Explore more on these topicsEvertonTransfer windownewsShareReuse this content

title: Colin Kaepernick knelt 10 years ago. America responded with a clear warning to Black people | Colin Kaepernick | The Guardian
description: A decade after Kaepernick’s quiet protest shook the NFL, his exile looks less like an aberration than a blueprint for the culture war that followed
Author: Howard Bryant
Headline: A decade after Kaepernick’s quiet protest shook the NFL, his exile looks less like an aberration than a blueprint for the culture war that followed
Content: Colin Kaepernick’s protest dominated off field discussion for much of the 2016 NFL season.Composite: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenColin Kaepernick’s protest dominated off field discussion for much of the 2016 NFL season.Composite: Guardian DesignColin KaepernickColin Kaepernick knelt 10 years ago. America responded with a clear warning to Black peopleHoward BryantA decade after Kaepernick’s quiet protest shook the NFL, his exile looks less like an aberration than a blueprint for the culture war that followedTue 1 Sep 2026 03.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 13.50 EDTShareAmerica likes nice round numbers, perfect for anniversaries and reflections, and it has, suddenly, been 10 years sinceColin Kaepernickfirst protested police killings – more accurately, police killings of Black people that went unpunished either internally or by the courts – by taking a knee during the national anthem for the entirety of the 2016 NFL regular season. He never played in the league again.Ten years covers a lot of ground, especially in these years of American darkness, and many of the important details surrounding Kaepernick, his banishment and significance have disappeared, time replaced by more time and more darkness – time moving faster than ever, at internet speed, where nothing matters, where nothing sticks. We consume by clip, by click, by meme, and knowledge by meme is not knowledge at all.Much of the Kaepernick story was reduced to his personal banishment, but second to Barack Obama, Kaepernick is the face that propelled white anger into a “culture war” that continues earnestly into its second decade. It has traveled through the NFL, through Hollywood, the White House, and now iscorroding the WNBA. Obama’s ascent to the White House confirmed the unlikely prospect that a Black person could be elected president, ostensibly the ultimate symbol of American possibility. It was not a universal sentiment.Sophie Cunningham isn’t rejecting politics. She’s cashing in on themRead moreIn the annals of American protest, which has included suffragettes breaking windows, students blocking traffic,Black Panthers armed in public, economic boycotts and marches on Washington, Kaepernick was mild by comparison – he gave voice with 60 seconds of silence. “To me, this is bigger than football and it would be selfish on my part to look the other way,” heexplained on 26 August 2016after a preseason contest between his San Francisco 49ers and the Green Bay Packers (he sat on the bench during the anthem for that game, he would kneel for the first time the following week). “There are bodies in the street and people getting paid leave and getting away with murder.” Combined, however, Obama and Kaepernick represented the realization of the deepest of white fears, the assumptions and expectations of Black equality that has consumed a segment of the collective white American psyche since emancipation.Ten years later, one view of the Kaepernick legacy can be seen through a harsh, retrofitted lens: sports leagues would largely purge the troublemakers and co-opt the protests, reducing them into useless, corporate-friendly gestures; an American electorate that voted Donald Trump into power twice, as his unapologetic, unambiguous racism reflected theirs; media outlets responding in agreement, coalescing around Trump’s whiteness, appeasing their rightsholders, readers and viewers by making the conscious choice – a clear and egregious dereliction of journalistic duty – to silence the voices within who make them uncomfortable; a player class that was never nearly as bold as its greatest legends well aware of Kaepernick’s fate, unwilling to repeat it, and operating as puppets.They didn’t have far to go. While Trump called NFL players “sons of bitches” in his first term and demanded Kaepernick be banned from the league, NFL players undermined him. Dallas Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescottassured his bossesin 2018 that he was no radical, not merely by playing football but demeaning Kaepernick’s protest. “For me, I believe in doing something, action. It’s not about taking a knee,” Prescott said, undermining centuries of evidence to the contrary about the efficacy of physical protest. Even the most devout Cowboys fan could probably not name a single example where Prescott took action. He simply didn’t want to get involved.Michael Vick, ex-convict,killer of dogs, but redeemed by the NFL following his prison sentence, told Kaepernick to “cut his hair” if he sought a pathway to forgiveness. Hall of Famer Ray Lewis told Kaepernick to “keep his mouth shut”. It should be noted that Kaepernick was exiled from the NFL for kneeling –kneeling –while Lewis, connectable to an incident that resulted in two killings as an active player, was fined$250,000 by the NFLfor pleading guilty to obstruction of justice andnever missed a game.View image in fullscreenColin Kaepernick kneels in protest during the national anthem before the San Francisco 49ers’ game against the Los Angeles Rams at Levi’s Stadium in September 2016.Photograph: Robert Reiners/Getty ImagesWhether hostile or oblivious, white Americans have treated this nation as a personal possession they choose to share with others, quite different from a nation that belongs to all that must be shared collectively. This country, Black people know and are harshly reminded by their white countrymen whenever they have the temerity to forget, istheirs,and that proprietorship is codified by the everyday speech of white Americans – Weletyou attendourschools, live inourneighborhoods, be part ofourcommunities, play inourprofessional sports – and is mirrored by Black speech alike. It is the fatal language of integration.Such assumed proprietorship demands white people receive deference for their benevolence, explains their rage when they don’t get it. It also means they believe they can revoke the privilege of being American whenever that proprietorship is challenged, as Kaepernick discovered 10 years ago. The result was a continuum. Kaepernick losing his job has now become a political philosophy at the highest levels of government: Black people have not earned their positions through the grind of hard work, but from diversity initiatives.Only in witnessing the slow-motion murder of George Floyd in 2020 during a global pandemic and the White House overreacting by rolling tanks through town and shooting at white people on the steps of their own houses did the country have a collective moment that it had all gone too far, that Kaepernick had been right all along. Even NFL commissioner Roger Goodell admitted, by pressure not conscience,that the league was wrongin its crackdown on player protest – but only briefly. The simmering hostility, never quieted, has increased anew.The January 6 riotsended the periodknown as athlete activism, and in the wider sense, the Kaepernick era. They also ended whatever shreds of credibility remained from this nation of laws, and exposed the players as having surrendered. Wired to accept challenges and refuse defeat, the players were finally vindicated as hordes of white, real Americans, the ones who told them therewere other ways to protest, wore T-shirts tostand for the flag and kneel for the cross,countered the Black Lives Matter protest without cleverness or style withBlue Lives Matter,and–at the order of the President of the United States – stormed the most symbolically important legislative building in the world. The players – perhaps mollified by Goodell’s apology, or Obama’s advice to NBA players to stop their protests after a weekend work stoppage following Jacob Blake’s shooting in Kenosha, general fatigue or knowing they were overmatched – didn’t say a thing. A cop – a member of that sacred occupation for which they ostensibly held so much respect –died in the aftermathof the January 6 riot. The mob ransacked the Capitol, and the American media tripped over itself debating whether to even call it a riot. It made sense. This istheirs, and you cannot trespass or riot on your own property.There is the lesson of Kaepernick and there is his legacy. They are not the same. The lesson was largely directed toward other players. It was a threat. Kaepernick was the NFL’s Metacomet at Plymouth, head on a stake for the world to see, a warning for the rest to stay in line – and they have. What passes for protest today is a player writing something mildly profound on their cleats, but only on the designated game days when theNFLallows it.The devastating rest is the legacy, far darker and yet in its own sense inspiring. The inspiration lies in the freedom of acknowledgment. There is no reason to continue the naive exercise of negotiation, of waiting for permission, of believing the moral arc of the universe bends toward justice, of believing equality is a shared American goal. It is not. What the country has become in these 10 years,with its 1,500 pardons, the proud anti-Blackness from this White House, the malleable ethics of a cowering corporate media that has largely stamped out the voices it once embraced as a “racial reckoning” – has proven it. Look at the wreckage.Howard Bryant is the author of 11 books, including The Heritage: Black Athletes, A Divided America, and the Politics of Patriotism and Kings and Pawns: Jackie Robinson and Paul Robeson in America.Explore more on these topicsColin KaepernickNFLUS sportsGeorge FloydRoger GoodellBarack ObamaJacob BlakecommentShareReuse this content

title: Stan Kroenke, owner of Arsenal and LA Rams, to buy MLB’s Angels for reported $4bn | MLB | The Guardian
description: Arte Moreno will sell the Los Angeles team he bought in 2003 for a reported final price of $4bn, a record valuation for a baseball franchise
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Arte Moreno will sell the Los Angeles team he bought in 2003 for a reported final price of $4bn, a record valuation for a baseball franchise
Content: The Los Angeles Angels have struggled for most of Arte Moreno’s tenure as owner.Photograph: Katelyn Mulcahy/MLB Photos/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Los Angeles Angels have struggled for most of Arte Moreno’s tenure as owner.Photograph: Katelyn Mulcahy/MLB Photos/Getty ImagesMLBStan Kroenke, owner of Arsenal and LA Rams, to buy MLB’s Angels for reported $4bnArte Moreno sells after owning team since 2003Deal gives KSE teams in NFL, MLB, NBA, NHL and MLSAgenciesTue 1 Sep 2026 16.27 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 16.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKroenke Sports + Entertainment announced Tuesday that it will buy a controlling interest in theLos Angeles Angelsfrom Arte Moreno in a deal that is expected to close in the first quarter ⁠of 2027.The sale will require the approval of Major LeagueBaseballand its owners.According to ESPN, the Angels sold for $4bn, beatingthe previous MLB recordof $3.9bn set in the sale of the San Diego Padres earlier this year. Moreno bought the Angels for $183.5m in 2003.Kroenke Sports + Entertainment is run by Stan Kroenke and is the owner of the NFL’s Los ⁠Angeles Rams, the NBA’s Denver Nuggets, the NHL’s Colorado Avalanche and MLS’s Colorado Rapids, in addition toArsenalof the English Premier League.MLB suspends Dominican prospect after age-fraud plot involving fake graveRead moreThe entity, which is based in Denver, also owns a professional lacrosse team based in Colorado ⁠as well as Arsenal’s women’s team.Kroenke also developed a 300-acre property just south of Los Angeles in Inglewood, California that includes SoFi Stadium, which ​is home to the Rams. SoFi Stadium was built for more ‌than $5bn and opened in 2020. It ‌will play host to its second Super Bowl at the end of the upcomingNFLseason as well as the 2028 Summer Olympics/Paralympics.When Moreno ‌bought the Angels in 2003, he became the first Mexican American to own a major sports franchise in the United States.Moreno took over the team one year after it won the World Series under ownership by the Walt Disney Co. The Angels advanced to the playoffs in five of the first seven years after Moreno became owner but have made the postseason just once in the past 16 seasons and has not won a playoff game in that time.The Angels have been led by outfielder Mike Trout since 2011, but the 12-time All-Star ‌has seen the playoffs just once when the Angels were swept in a best- of-five series in 2014 against the Kansas City Royals. Trout was a teammate with Shohei Ohtani for six seasons but the duo never made it ​to the postseason.Between 2014 and 2023, Trout and Ohtani combined to win five MVP Awards while wearing an Angels uniform but the team never made the postseason. In 2018 alone, Ohtani was the American League Rookie of the Year while Trout finished second in MVP voting.“The Angels are a storied franchise anchored in a great market,” Kroenke said in a release. “We look forward to an exciting future with the Angels organization.“Disgruntled fans have taken to protesting during games this season. Groups of young fans take to the upper deck in the right ​field corner, take their shorts off, wave them over ​their heads and implore Moreno to “sell the team,” among ​other nightly chants.The Angels are just 53-85 heading into Tuesday and are headed for their 11th consecutive ​losing season.During the 2022 season, ‌Moreno said he would ​explore the possibility of selling the ​Angels but less than one year later he abandoned that plan.“The Angels organization is pleased to announce this transaction with Kroenke Sports + Entertainment,” Moreno said in Tuesday’s news release. “The Moreno family has been honored to steward the Angels for 23 years and we believe with KSE’s experience and success they are the best next owner for the franchise. The Angels organization looks forward to continuing its commitment to the fans, our employees, the players and our business ‌partners.”Explore more on these topicsMLBNFLArsenalUS sportsLos Angeles AngelsBaseballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Former NFL star Tony Romo given driving ban and vows to ‘own my mistakes’ after OWI arrest | NFL | The Guardian
description: CBS NFL analyst and former Dallas Cowboys quarterback Tony Romo has pleaded no contest to a charge of operating while intoxicated
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: CBS NFL analyst and former Dallas Cowboys quarterback Tony Romo has pleaded no contest to a charge of operating while intoxicated
Content: Tony Romo played for the Dallas Cowboys before his retirement as a player.Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/CBS/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTony Romo played for the Dallas Cowboys before his retirement as a player.Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/CBS/Getty ImagesNFLFormer NFL star Tony Romo given driving ban and vows to ‘own my mistakes’ after OWI arrestCBS analyst was arrested in July after traffic stopFormer QB has been absent from CBS dutyAssociated PressTue 1 Sep 2026 14.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 14.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCBS NFL analyst and former Dallas Cowboys quarterback Tony Romo has pleaded no contest to a charge of operating while intoxicated and has apologized for the actionsthat led to his July arrest.Romowas arrested on 23 Julyfollowing a traffic stop in Wisconsin. CBS has since placed him on leave from his role as its lead NFL analyst.The rise and fall of Tony Romo: what comes next for CBS’s $180m NFL analyst?Read moreAccording to Milwaukee County court records, Romo lost his driving privileges for six months and was ordered to complete an alcohol assessment program. He also owes $834. An interlock device must be installed on any vehicle owned or operated by Romo or registered to his name, and that order will remain in effect for at least one year after he is issued a license.“The past month has been difficult, but it has also been personally significant,” Romo said in a statement on Instagram. “It has required me to confront and own my mistakes fully – to the Lord, to myself, to my family and now to the public.”Romo said the multiple back surgeries that led to his retirement as a player “left me with constant, debilitating pain”. He noted that the pain “led to a dependence on pain medication, and my efforts to get off those medications led to an over-reliance on alcohol.”Romo added: “None of this is an excuse. These are my failures and I take responsibility for them.”Romo said he is working with a team of doctors to address his health and “make the necessary changes.” He thanked his family, friends and theNFLcommunity for their support.“As I turn my attention to my health, my family, and, in time, my return toCBS, I kindly ask for privacy,” Romo said.CBS Sports president David Berson said last month that he does not have a timeline for a decision about Romo’s future with the network.Romo, 46, has been the lead game analyst for CBS’s NFL coverage since 2017 after making four Pro Bowl appearances during a playing career that ran from 2004-16 and was spent entirely with Dallas.Analyst JJ Watt will join play-by-play announcer Jim Nantz and sideline reporter Tracy Wolfson on CBS Sports’ lead NFL team during Romo’s absence.Citations released by the Milwaukee county sheriff’s office indicated that Romo performed poorly on field sobriety tests and that an open bottle of an alcoholic beverage was found in the passenger’s side of his Jeep.Body camera footage showed Romo telling deputies he had been coming from a golf course and was on his way “to visit grandma and grandpa” when he was stopped. A deputy told Romo he suspected him of being impaired because he had “red glassy eyes” and an “odor of an intoxicating alcoholic beverage”.Romo went to high school about 35 miles southwest of Milwaukee in Burlington,Wisconsin.Explore more on these topicsNFLUS sports mediaDallas CowboysCBSWisconsinUS sportsUS television industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: The Raygun documentary ducks a big question about the Olympic fame of a ‘dorky white academic’ | Sport | The Guardian
description: A new Netflix documentary finds warmth and humor in Rachael Gunn’s Olympic ordeal but sidesteps the larger questions raised by her viral fame
Author: Dvora Meyers
Headline: A new Netflix documentary finds warmth and humor in Rachael Gunn’s Olympic ordeal but sidesteps the larger questions raised by her viral fame
Content: Australia’s Rachael ‘Raygun’ Gunn competes during the women’s breaking competition at the Paris Olympics in August 2024.Photograph: Ezra Shaw/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAustralia’s Rachael ‘Raygun’ Gunn competes during the women’s breaking competition at the Paris Olympics in August 2024.Photograph: Ezra Shaw/Getty ImagesSportThe Raygun documentary ducks a big question about the Olympic fame of a ‘dorky white academic’Untold Raygun: Breaking Badly finds warmth and humor in Rachael Gunn’s ordeal, but never fully reckons with what her notoriety meant for breakingDvora MeyersTue 1 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 16.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarly in Netflix’s new documentary, Untold Raygun: Breaking Badly, Australian B-girl Rachael Gunn, recounts a session she had with her sports psychologist prior to the 2024 Paris Olympics.“Right before the Olympics, I went to my therapist, panicked,” she says. Her therapist asked her what was the worst thing that could happen. And she said, “The whole world could laugh at me.” Her therapist responded: “Do you think that’s reasonable?” Cue Gunn’s hysterical laughter.Raygun: Breaking Badly review – the ridiculed Olympic B-girl gets the last laugh … and it’s a total joyRead moreAnyone who has ever gone to a therapist will be amused at this anecdote. Nine and a half times out 10, the therapist would have been right. No, they’d say, the worst outcome you can imagine probably won’t come to pass. But in Gunn’s case, what she feared the most did, in fact, happen. Her shenanigans – the sprinkler, the kangaroo hops – in the cyphermade her go viralalmost as soon as she was done with her sets. (Perhaps if Gunn had been explicit about what she was planning to do in her sets, her therapist would have reacted differently.) Gunn’s performance launched a thousand memes, more than a couple of late-night TV segments, several conspiracy theories, and even a musical at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival.“She became the most famous breaker on planet Earth overnight,” Flix, a fellow Australian B-girl, says in the documentary. All without winning a single vote from any of the nine judges across her six rounds.Untold Raygun, which premieres globally on Netflix on Tuesday, really doesn’t dwell on what it means for breaking, an art form created by Black and Brown youth in the South Bronx, that its first Olympic foray will be primarily – if not exclusively – remembered for a white woman from Australia doing the sprinkler instead of the dynamic performances of the rest of the contenders.
