It’s mostly focused on Gunn herself with little time spent on the greater context of the art form and how it ended up in the Olympics. The documentary features interviews with Gunn, her parents, her husband who introduced her to breaking, and a few dancers who know her from the Aussie scene. Through them, we get a coming of almost middle-age story about an academic who meets a B-boy working at a call center, falls in love with him and the art form he’s passionate about, and somehow ends up centerstage at the Olympics.View image in fullscreenAustralia’s Rachael ‘Raygun’ Gunn competes during the women’s breaking round-robin at the Paris Olympics in August 2024.Photograph: Angelika Warmuth/ReutersGunn is likeable in the documentary. She comes across as (mostly) self-aware and self-deprecating. Her parents are charming, laughing heartily when asked if they had ever previously associated “Olympian” with their quirky daughter. Sammy Free seems like a sweet fellow who is completely besotted with his wife. (We should all be so lucky to find someone who loves us the way that Free clearly loves Gunn.) But the most useful voices in Untold Raygun are the two Australian B-girls who offer some critical perspective on the place of women in the breaking scene and Gunn’s performances at the Games. They’re harsh, at times, but also fair.Tinylocks, one of Gunn’s contemporaries, repeatedly invokes “No easy props,” a term that’s something of a hip-hop ethos about having to prove your skill to earn respect. (The phrase is often associated with American B-girl Asia One, who founded a crew called No Easy Props in 1997.) “It was such a male dominated space and B-girls were really fighting to be seen but as more women started entering breaking, it was felt that some girls were getting accolades too early in their careers. The crowd would cheer just for participating,” she says.It is within the context of “no easy props” that Tinylocks offers her assessment of Raygun’s pre-Olympic performances, as she was coming up in the small Australian scene. “There were one or two times when I was like, ‘Oh yeah, that was fresh.’ Maybe not so much the other times.”Tinylocks decided to pass on trying to earn the Oceania qualifying spot. “I’m interested in breaking as an art form,” she says, which is a sentiment I heard from other dancers in the scene after the Olympic trajectory was announced by the IOC and the World DanceSport Federation (WDSF). Flix gave it a go at the Oceania qualifier, but said that, at 41, she didn’t expect much. Gunn was surprised that she kept advancing through the bracket until she was in the final battle against B-girl Molly. If you go back and watch the Oceania qualifier, you won’t see any of Gunn’s “iconic” moves from the Paris Olympics in that final. What she threw down against Molly doesn’t stand out in any way – either for good or for bad. Yes, her movements were slow and lacked sharpness, her sets not particularly intricate. But she showed fairly standard breaking foundation movements. If she had done those sets in Paris, Gunn wouldn’t have advanced out of the preliminary rounds but she also wouldn’t have become a global sensation.View image in fullscreenGunn competes during the women’s breaking competition at the Paris Olympics, where she failed to win a single vote from the nine judges across her six rounds.Photograph: Héctor Vivas/Getty ImagesThe documentary explains the change in her set composition: she realized how far behind she was the top B-girls she was going to be battling at the Olympics. She went to a couple of European battles in the months before the Games and performed poorly in all of them. Gunn and her husband decided to change their approach. Instead of trying to up the difficulty content of her sets through power moves – the acrobatics like headspins and windmills that laypeople associate with breaking – they would go all in on originality, one of the five categories breaking judges evaluate at the Games. (The other four were technique, vocabulary, execution and musicality.) They had gone from hoping to win one battle or even one round to trying to win a single vote from one of the nine judges. Gunn and Free said they looked to Australia for movement inspiration from its famous wildlife (kangaroo) to its dance moves (the sprinkler). They even added a nod to swimming, an Olympic sport at which Australia excels. Despite this strategy, Gunn didn’t get a single vote in Paris.Raygun opens up on her infamous Olympics breakdancing debut: ‘Not as bad as I thought!’Read moreThere’s a world in which this approach could have worked for Gunn but it’s a world where she is much better at breaking fundamentals, where her footwork is sharp and clean, her movements swift but also unhurried. The breaking scene has had its share of well-respected dancers who bring humor and personality to the cypher. B-boys and B-girls often call this “character.” (In fact, one of them,Jeffro, was competing on the men’s side in Paris.) The issue with Gunn’s attempts at character is that those gimmicks were basically all she had. The bunny hop or the kangaroo weren’t simply moments in an otherwise proficient set that ticked other boxes, like technique, execution or musicality. The gimmicks were the main event.As a point of contrast, let’s consider another athlete who became a meme during the Paris Games:Stephen Nedoroscik. The pommel horse specialist doffed his glasses, Clark Kent style, before he saluted the judges. There the tenor of the online discourse had none of the mockery that suffused the Raygun tweets because Nedoroscik was actually world class in his event. He was the 2021 world champion on pommel horse and won bronze in the event at the Olympics. Something similar took place in the sport shooting event where Turkey’s Yusuf Dikecbecame a memedue to his nonchalant stance and lack of gear. But because he was actually good at his sport – he won silver – the online hijinks never turned mean.“People have a lot of opinions about what women do, what women should do, sometimes from women,” Gunn says of the reaction online to her performance. Generally speaking, there is truth to this assertion. Women do get singled out for criticism in a way that often feels disproportionate to the offense. Gunn didn’t commit a crime. She didn’t murder anyone on live TV. And she didn’t cheat her way to the Olympics as many people falsely claimed after Paris. (This is one of the conspiracy theories that Untold Raygun takes pains to dispel.) But it still felt disingenuous for Gunn to invoke this defense as a response to her Olympic performance. The response was not simply about her creative choices but also about the gap between herself and her competitors. She put herself on an Olympic stage where spectators expect elite performance, not a professor who is simply doing her best. The Olympics aren’t really a vehicle for self-expression. They’re supposed to be a vehicle for excellence.View image in fullscreenGunn poses for a portrait in Sydney in April 2024, four months before making her Olympic debut in Paris.Photograph: Cameron Spencer/Getty ImagesGunn isn’t the first person to compete at the Olympics whose skills are decidedly subpar. There wasEddie the Eagle, the British ski jumper who competed at the 1988 Olympics in Calgary, who definitely did not fly through the air with the greatest of ease.Eric Moussambanicompeted in swimming at the 2000 Games though he could barely swim the entire length of an Olympic pool. And in 2018, Elizabeth Swaney, representing Hungary, did nothing of substance in the halfpipe competition,putting together the most basic of runs. What distinguishes Gunn from the other Olympians is that they competed in sports that were already well-established. Though they became well-known, they didn’t become thefaceof their respective sports. But breaking was new to the Games in 2024 and most viewers weren’t familiar with it except from pop-culture products of the 80s. Gunn left Paris as the most famous breaker in the world. The average person on the street couldn’t tell you who won the breaking competition in Paris but they can probably remember Raygun, if not by name, then at least by description of what she did on the floor.There was no way for Gunn to have predicted this outcome, even if she, on some level, feared it before she got on the plane for France. But it would have been welcome to see her reckon with it and what it means for the culture and breaking’s chances of getting on the program of a future Games. (The documentary doesn’t mention this so I’ll do it: that breaking won’t appear at LA2028 has nothing to do with Gunn. The decision was made months before she hopped across the cypher.)Ultimately, Untold Raygun seeks to reassure the viewer that Gunn has survived hervery public bout with global humiliationwith her spirit and sense of whimsy intact. “I’m a dorky white woman who is an academic,” she said. “And I’m OK with that.”Last week WDSFsubmitted breaking for considerationfor the 2032 Olympics, which will be hosted by Brisbane. If the local organizing committee decides to give breaking another shot at Olympic glory then perhaps we’ll see Gunn again, but hopefully not at the center of the cypher.Explore more on these topicsSportBrisbane Olympic Games 2032Paris Olympic Games 2024DanceOlympic GamesAustralia sportfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Arthur Fery sunk by Lorenzo Musetti in straight sets on US Open debut | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: The Wimbledon semi-finalist Arthur Fery lost 6-3, 6-3, 7-5 to Lorenzo Musetti while Elena Rybakina sailed into the second round with a 6-3, 6-2 success
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: The Wimbledon semi-finalist Arthur Fery lost 6-3, 6-3, 7-5 to Lorenzo Musetti while Elena Rybakina sailed into the second round with a 6-3, 6-2 success
Content: Arthur Fery fought hard but could not find the answers against Lorenzo Musetti.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/APView image in fullscreenArthur Fery fought hard but could not find the answers against Lorenzo Musetti.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/APUS Open Tennis 2026Arthur Fery sunk by Lorenzo Musetti in straight sets on US Open debutBritish Wimbledon semi-finalist loses 6-3, 6-3, 7-5Elena Rybakina into second round with 6-3, 6-2 winTumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowsTue 1 Sep 2026 16.55 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSix weeks on from the fortnight that changed his life, Arthur Fery’s first grand slam appearance since his semi-final run at Wimbledon came under considerably different circumstances. He is now the 33rd best men’s player in the world, a direct entrant for all of the biggest tournaments, and he has continued to gain experience at the highest level of professional tennis each week.As a result of his continued exposure on the tour, though, Fery’s adversaries have also learned a bit more about him. In his first main draw appearance at the US Open, Fery came up against a prepared and sharp Lorenzo Musetti, who knew exactly how to exploit the vulnerable parts of his game in order to secure a win. The Italian comprehensively outplayed the British No 1, reaching the second round with a comfortable 6-3, 6-3, 7-5 victory.Naomi Osaka pays tribute to NBA star Allen Iverson in basketball-themed US Open outfitRead moreThis was an emphatic, impressive performance from Musetti, who handcuffed Fery with his heavy topspin and simply had far too many options for his opponent. Despite fighting hard until the end, Fery’s game looked underpowered as he struggled to consistently hit through one of the best defensive players in the world.Fery had actually started well enough, quickly finding rhythm behind his serve as he eased through his first three service games. However, as the Italian began to take control of the baseline with his forehand, the Briton’s serve capitulated. Down 15-30 at 3-3, Fery threw in his first two double faults of the match on consecutive points to hand over the first break.Once that was secured, Musetti opened up his shoulders and imposed relentless pressure on Fery. Musetti spent much of the match pushing Fery behind the baseline with his heavy spin and height. With the ball consistently bouncing high above his shoulders and out of his strike zone, Fery struggled to counter Musetti effectively. He veered between desperately trying to take the ball on the rise, constantly spraying errors, and being dictated to by Musetti whenever he tried to hang back and wait for the ball to drop. He never really looked comfortable.Over the course of their two hours on court, Musetti also made use of his far greater weaponry. He served well in decisive moments and effortlessly stepped inside the baseline, dominating with his forehand when necessary.He also struck his sweet single-handed backhand supremely well on certain key points, particularly in the second set, where he converted the decisive break point and then saved a later break point with supreme down-the-line backhand winners.In the aftermath of his shock run to the Wimbledon semi-finals, Fery has managed himself well. He performed at a high level in Cincinnati, winning a round and then pushing Alex de Minaur, the world No 8,in two tight sets. Last week, he reached his first ATP final in Winston-Salem, providing more evidence that he belongs at this level.View image in fullscreenElena Rybakina could become world No 1 during this US Open.Photograph: Robert Prange/Getty ImagesHe is yet to lose to any lower-ranked opponent. But the standard at the top of men’s tennis is incredibly high and competing with players of Musetti’s calibre will come with many more losses and lessons. It remains to be seen how much these lessons will enable him to improve.For Musetti, this is a hopeful first performance as he tries to put himself back in contention for big titles after a torrid year. Musetti had started the season ranked No 5 and he was en route to a first Australian Open semi-final in Melbourne when he was forced to withdraw due to injury while leading Novak Djokovic by two sets in their quarter-final match. After a few months out, it has taken even longer for Musetti to rebuild confidence in his game and body. He is finally beginning to resemble his old self again.Elsewhere, Elena Rybakina made a positive step forward in her pursuit of the No 1 ranking as she moved into the second round with a 6-3, 6-2 win over the 17-year-old American wildcard Thea Frodin.View image in fullscreenFlavio Cobolli lets it all out after battling back from two sets down to see off Francisco Comesaña.Photograph: Timothy A Clary/AFP/Getty ImagesThere have been ample doubts surrounding Rybakina after she suffered a foot injury at the Cincinnati Open that forced her to retire from her quarter-final match against Iga Swiatek but she appeared comfortable on the court as she overpowered her inexperienced opponent.Rybakina currently sits at No 1 in the live rankings and she would become the world No 1 for the first time in her career if she reaches the semi-finals or if Aryna Sabalenka, Jessica Pegula and Coco Gauff do not win the tournament.In the men’s draw, the fifth seed and French Open finalist Flavio Cobolli produced one of the best comebacks of his career to escape a tough battle with the Argentinian Francisco Comesaña, recovering from a two-set deficit to reach the second round with a 3-6, 2-6, 6-3, 6-4, 6-4 win.Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026US Open tennisArthur FeryTennisUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Lionel Messi in his 30s was one of the best international players ever | Lionel Messi | The Guardian
description: In the decade after his short-lived first retirement, the Argentina talisman upended previous narratives and solidified his place in history
Author: Jeff Rueter
Headline: In the decade after his short-lived first retirement, the Argentina talisman upended previous narratives and solidified his place in history
Content: Lionel Messi enjoyed many of his best moments in the back half of his international careerPhotograph: Jacob Kupferman/APView image in fullscreenLionel Messi enjoyed many of his best moments in the back half of his international careerPhotograph: Jacob Kupferman/APLionel MessiAnalysisLionel Messi in his 30s was one of the best international players everJeff RueterIn the decade after his short-lived first retirement, the Argentina talisman upended previous narratives and solidified his place in historyTue 1 Sep 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 14.03 EDTSharePerhaps somewhere, in some dusty journal that’s surely been lost in Rosario,Lionel Messimade clear his destiny: that if he were to one day represent Argentina, his national team careermustend in East Rutherford, New Jersey.A decade and two months before the playmaker posted hishand-written retirementfrom international football, Messi made his first attempt to leaveLa Albiceleste. They had just lost the Copa América Centenario – a special edition of the South American championship held in the United States for the tournament’s 100th anniversary – inexcruciating fashion, with Messi having missed his attempt in a shootout defeat to Chile at East Rutherford, the same venue where Argentina lost this year’s World Cup final. It was the third consecutive major final that saw Argentina receive silver medals as parting gifts, after the2014 World Cupand2015 Copa América.It wasn’t as though he’d underperformed whenever he donned their fabled white and blue. His five Ballon d’Ors – already a record – weren’t awardedin spite ofhis international record. After theCopa AméricaCentenario, the 29-year-old Messi had made 112 international appearances after debuting in 2005. In that tournament’s semi-final, he overtook Gabriel Batistuta as Argentina’s leading scorer with his 55th goal, to complement his 37 assists.‘In my heart until I die’: Argentina says a tearful thank you to Lionel MessiRead moreA month later, Cristiano Ronaldo, Messi’s great foil, led Portugal to their first European Championship despite exiting the final due to injury. It seemed that their legacies had been largely cast: Messi, a talisman for his club but a regular at heartbreak hotel for his country; Ronaldo, an unstoppable force in front of goal and finally a continental champion.And so, for roughly six weeks, Messi bore the distinction of being aformerArgentina international. Not exactly a memorable stretch of his career – the only games he would have played in that span were Barcelona’s preseason tune-ups – but with Conmebol’sWorld Cupqualifiers in process and his team struggling to secure a place in the field for Russia, Messi framed his return as a necessity.“A lot of things went through my mind on the night of the final and I gave serious thought to quitting,” Messi said on 12 August 2016, “but my love for my country and this shirt is too great.”What followed over his decade-long second act transformed his legacy from one of individual success and international heartbreak into the culmination of the sport’s greatest-ever career and the establishment of his team as South America’s dominant force of the past quarter-century. In its own right, the second international act of Messi, played almost entirely in his 30s, ranks among the greatest careers in international men’s soccer history.The trophy case certainly looks more robust in that back half of his career. In the earlier stage sits five Ballon d’Ors, a World Cup golden ball, a U20 World Cup and an Olympic gold. In the latter: three more Ballon d’Ors, another World Cup golden ball and a second one in silver, a World Cup, two Copa Américas, and a Finalissima.His individual output after retiring the first time is staggering, too: 95 caps, 70 goals, 31 assists. Only 23 men have scored at least 70 goals across full international careers.Lionel Messi’s international retirement serves as a reminder: watch him while you still canRead moreRegardless of era, goals have come more easily for Messi in his 30s than most greats ever find. Geoff Hurst played his 49th and final England match aged 30 in 1972, the same summer he left West Ham for Stoke City. Pelé, in total, scored 77 goals in 92 caps before retiring at age 31. World Cup icon Miroslav Klose scored his 71 Germany goals across 137 caps. Luis Suárez has bagged 69 goals from 143 appearances for Uruguay. Ronaldo had 62 goals in 98 caps for Brazil. Even Kylian Mbappé, who is already on 66 goals and won’t turn 28 until December, has made 106 appearances for France.Of course, numbers and trophies don’t tell the full story. The tale of Messi’s return is one of redemption, finally finding a place in Argentinian hearts after spending so long in Diego Maradona’s shadow. Every national team appearance over the last four years hasbordered on being a worship service, tens of thousands chanting his name.A decade before this summer’s World Cup final, at the same site in New Jersey, the masses jeered as he was left in tears after losing a tournament final. On 19 July, withArgentinaagain suffering a defeat in an even grander competition, they instead wept with him.So well-documented is Messi’s career that it’s tough to find fresh superlatives. Even data-driven comparisons of his output compared to esteemed rivals cause the mind to glaze over. But now, with clarity that the World Cup final was indeed his final turn in an Argentina shirt, the narratives that followed his shock announcement a decade ago have a payoff.Messi retired from Argentina as a 29-year-old, already arguably his sport’s greatest ever. Upon coming back, his second act wasn’t just better than his first – it was arguably better than any other player’s entire career.Explore more on these topicsLionel MessiArgentinaWorld Cup 2026Copa AméricaWorld CupCopa America 2016analysisShareReuse this content

title: Fin Tarling’s death casts shadow over Tour of Britain as safety fears loom large | Tour of Britain | The Guardian
description: A minute’s applause for Tarling will take place in Lincoln on Wednesday following a spate of serious recent crashes which have put safety on the agenda
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: A minute’s applause for Tarling will take place in Lincoln on Wednesday following a spate of serious recent crashes which have put safety on the agenda
Content: The peloton at the Volta a Portugal paid tribute to Fin Tarling, who died when his cycle collided with a non-race vehicle last month.Photograph: Nuno Veiga/EPAView image in fullscreenThe peloton at the Volta a Portugal paid tribute to Fin Tarling, who died when his cycle collided with a non-race vehicle last month.Photograph: Nuno Veiga/EPATour of BritainFin Tarling’s death casts shadow over Tour of Britain as safety fears loom largeMinute’s applause to take place in Lincoln on WednesdaySpate of serious recent crashes have put safety on agendaJeremy WhittleTue 1 Sep 2026 12.40 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 16.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThedeath of the Welshman Fin Tarlingcontinues to cast a long shadow over professional cycling and nowhere will that absence be felt more deeply than at the men’s Tour of Britain which begins on Wednesday.Tarling’s former team NSNCycling, which includes the Olympic medallist Ethan Vernon, also one of his closest friends, will be brought to the start line in Lincoln for the opening 187km stage, for what is expected to be a minute’s applause.Tadej Pogacar shares picture from hospital after Vuelta-ending crashRead moreTarling was killed while racing in the Volta a Portugal last month when he collided with a non‑race vehicle driving towards him. The race operates a rolling road closure, the same security strategy employed by theTour of Britain. The police investigation into Tarling’s death is ongoing.A spate of serious recent crashes, including the high-speed fall endured by theTour de France champion Tadej Pogacar, which forced him to abandon the Vuelta a España this year while leading the race, have yet again put safety at the top of the agenda.Tom Pidcock’s tearful tribute to the Tarling family, when winning the World Mountain Bike title in Italy last weekend, revealed the depth of feeling over the teenager’s death.The double Olympic gold medallist Pidcock, initially expected to start the British race, has opted to focus on preparing for the world championships in Canada by riding warm-up races in Montreal and Quebec.Tarling’s collision in a race operating under a rolling road closure has been thesubject of much scrutinyin the aftermath of his accident and the flaws of that system were highlighted just days later, in the women’s Tour of Britain, when the Australian rider Maeve Plouffe had her own near-miss.“While the race convoy was still in sight, and I was less than two minutes down [behind], there were cars from the general public coming at me from all directions, including one that nearly hit me on a roundabout,” the 27-year-old said.Jonathan Day, director of the race organisers, said: “Rider safety is paramount and will always be treated as a priority in our planning and how we operate any race.”The race organisers maintain that the Tour of Britain is delivered in accordance with the UCI’s road racing regulations, described as the safety and operational standards that govern international and UK-based road racing.Local authorities, emergency services, commissaires, police and event partners are all part of the race planning process. But the efficiency of rolling road closures has also been questioned by Adam Hansen, president of the CPA professional rider association, who said: “There is a hole in rolling road closures and we have to fix this.”After an opening stage based on Lincoln, the convoy will travel through Yorkshire and on to the Scottish Borders. The second day’s racing takes the peloton from Boston to Skegness while stage three, through East Yorkshire, starts in Hull and ends in Beverley.Over the weekend the convoy crosses the Yorkshire moors and dales, before the final stage on Sunday, which starts south of Edinburgh – site of the Grand Départ for the Tour de France next year – and finishes in Earlston.Alongside Vernon, there is a raft of British talent lining up for the five‑day race including Ben Wiggins, son of Sir Bradley. National time trial champion in the under-23 category, the 21-year-old is now on the radar of several leading World Tour teams.The Tour de France stage winners Olav Kooij, Filippo Ganna and Tim Merlier are among the leading World Tour names, while Pogacar’s UAE Emirates XRG team will be led by the Giro d’Italia stage winner Jhonatan Narváez.The move from four days of racing last year to five days in 2026, giving it parity with the women’s Tour of Britain, is hoped to further boost interest as the buildup to the UK-based Grand Départ begins next year.Explore more on these topicsTour of BritainCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Naomi Osaka pays tribute to NBA star Allen Iverson in basketball-themed US Open outfit | Naomi Osaka | The Guardian
description: Naomi Osaka channeled former NBA star Allen Iverson before her US Open first-round victory over Anastasia Zakharova on Monday
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Naomi Osaka channeled former NBA star Allen Iverson before her US Open first-round victory over Anastasia Zakharova on Monday
Content: Naomi Osaka walks on to the court at the US Open.Photograph: Julian Finney/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNaomi Osaka walks on to the court at the US Open.Photograph: Julian Finney/Getty ImagesNaomi OsakaNaomi Osaka pays tribute to NBA star Allen Iverson in basketball-themed US Open outfitJapanese player wears Iverson’s signature cornrowsOutfit also has newspaper clippings about OsakaGuardian sportand agenciesTue 1 Sep 2026 08.02 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 12.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNaomi Osaka channeledformer NBA star Allen Iversonbefore her US Open first-round victory over Anastasia Zakharova on Monday.Osaka made her usual fashionable entrance for her tournament opener, which she won in straight sets. The two-time US Open champion emerged on to the court at Arthur Ashe Stadium wearing a long, white skirt and a gray, hooded robe featuring newspaper clippings about her.Naomi Osaka’s jellyfish-inspired outfit steals the show at Australian OpenRead moreShe then removed her hood revealing her cornrows under a headband, Iverson’s signature look when he was theNBAMVP while playing for the Philadelphia 76ers. She also wore an arm sleeve, a look made popular by Iverson during his playing career.Osaka is not the only Nike-sponsored athlete to wear a basketball-themed outfit at the US Open. World No 1 Aryna Sabalenka is wearing an orange dress at the tournament, one of the colors of the New York Knicks, whowon their first NBA titlesince 1973 in June.View image in fullscreenAllen Iverson was known for his cornrows during his NBA career.Photograph: Jeff Haynes/AFP/Getty Images“It’s my, I guess, my tribute to Iverson. I really like him a lot,” Osaka said after her 7-6, 7-6 victory. “I mean, Nike said basketball, so I said: ‘OK, you want basketball, I’ll give you basketball.’”Osaka wore a shirt with Iverson’s picture when she spoke to reporters on Saturday, praising the Hall of Famer as a fashion trailblazer.“I think he’s also someone that I look up to a lot, because he’s kind of done a lot in fashion, whether it’s on purpose or not, but he’s shiftedthe way that NBA players dress,” Osaka said on Saturday. “I also think the whole conversation around clothes in sports and also just expressing yourself through style, I feel like he’s someone that I look up to in that regard.”View image in fullscreenNaomi Osaka wore a hood when she entered the court on Monday.Photograph: Adam Hunger/APShe added that she had never spoken to Iverson, but he posted a message to Osaka on his Instagram page on Monday, writing: “Wow, what a honor!! BIG FAN can’t wait to meet you.”Osaka hasgained attention for her adventurous styleat tournaments. At this year’s Wimbledon, the Japanese starwore a kimono-inspiredoutfit. At January’s Australian Open, she wore a jellyfish-themed outfit shesaid was inspiredby her daughter’s bedtime stories.Explore more on these topicsNaomi OsakaUS Open Tennis 2026US Open tennisTennisUS sportsNBABasketballShareReuse this content

title: Fernández completes record-equalling £125m move from Chelsea to Manchester City | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Manchester City have equalled the British transfer record with a £125m deal to sign midfielder Enzo Fernández from Chelsea
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Manchester City have equalled the British transfer record with a £125m deal to sign midfielder Enzo Fernández from Chelsea
Content: Enzo Fernández has signed a five-year deal at Manchester City after joining from Chelsea for £125m.Photograph: Manchester City FCView image in fullscreenEnzo Fernández has signed a five-year deal at Manchester City after joining from Chelsea for £125m.Photograph: Manchester City FCManchester CityFernández completes record-equalling £125m move from Chelsea to Manchester CityFernández: ‘This is a club built for success’Chelsea’s move for Monaco’s Camara falls throughJacob SteinbergTue 1 Sep 2026 19.12 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester City have equalled the British transfer record with a £125m deal to sign Enzo Fernández from Chelsea, who were left raging after their attempts to replace the Argentina midfielder were dashed by Monaco reneging on an agreement to sell Lamine Camara last night.On a day of twists and turns, City emerged in a strong position after they bolstered their attack by signing Iliman Ndiaye from Everton for up to £65m and landed one of Enzo Maresca’s biggest targets on a five-year deal.Chelseaheld out for a huge fee for Fernández and it seemed they were going to find a replacement for him as the transfer window drew to a close.The club moved to agree a £47m fee with Monaco for Camara, who was set to sign a six-year contract with the option of an extra year. Chelsea swooped when Everton’s attempts to sign the USA striker Folarin Balogun ran into difficulties. It left Monaco needing to raise funds from elsewhere, prompting Chelsea to revive their move for Camara after having a £38.1m offer for the 22-year-old Senegal midfielder rejected earlier in the day.Transfer deadline day: Man City sign Fernández and Ndiaye, Mudryk and Tosin join Spurs – liveRead moreChelsea had a written agreement with Monaco but were stunned by the Ligue 1 club pulling out of the deal as the deadline approached. Sources called Monaco’s conduct “deeply unprofessional”. As an extraordinary situation developed it emerged that Everton, who have also loaned Jack Grealish from City, had refused to give up on Balogun, renegotiating the fee for the former Arsenal forward only for that deal to also fall down just after midnight.The collapse of Camara’s move did not lead to Chelsea cancelling the sale of Fernández to City. The deal means City have spent £327m on midfielders this summer following the arrivals of Elliot Anderson from Nottingham Forest for £116m and Ayyoub Bouaddi from Lille for £86m.“I could not be happier to be here, and I am ready for the challenge of helping City continue winning trophies. This is a club built for success,” said Fernández, who becomes this country’s most expensive player alongside Alexander Isak, who joined Liverpool from Newcastle for £125m a year ago. “I pride myself on continually improving my game. Anyone who’s worked with me will know how hard I train every single day and how much I put into matches. I give absolutely everything and I can promise Manchester City that will continue now I’m here.”View image in fullscreenIliman Ndiaye also completed his move to Manchester City on a busy deadline day for sporting director Hugo Viana.Photograph: Manchester City FCMaresca has a good relationship with Fernández after coaching him at Chelsea and a reunion has been on the cards for a while. City opened talks with Chelsea on Monday night and will feel they have successfully rebuilt their midfield after selling Rodri to Barcelona and losing Bernardo Silva to Real Madrid, while also selling Nico González to Newcastle. They were also not put off even after Chelsea’s unofficial deadline for clubs to lodge bids of £120m for Fernández passed last month.Fernández has been angling for a way out of Chelsea since March and his departure was announced in a short statement on the club’s website. The 25-year-old, who scored 31 goals after joining from Benfica for £106.7m in January 2023, initially had his sights set on joining Real Madrid. He grew disillusioned following Maresca’s acrimonious split with Chelsea earlier this year. Fernández, the unofficial vice-captain, spoke out after Chelsea were knocked out of the Champions League by Paris Saint-Germain in March. Chelsea responded by banning him for two games.Fernández reported back to training after the World Cup and was booed by Chelsea fans during a pre-season friendly against Real Sociedad at Stamford Bridge. He featured in the club’s opening first game of the season, coming off the bench to help Xabi Alonso’s side beat Fulham, but was left out of Chelsea’s next two fixtures.Chelsea came round to the view a sale was in their interests. There is a feeling within the club that Fernández, who won the Conference League and Club World Cup during his time in west London, had not shown himself to be vice-captain material.Chelsea have made in the region of £500m in loans and sales this summer. They finished the window by selling Marc Guiu to RB Leipzig for £16m and loaning Dário Essugo to Strasbourg, Robert Sánchez to Como andMykhailo Mudryk to Tottenham. Tosin Adarabioyo joined Spurs on a permanent deal.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityChelseaTransfer windownewsShareReuse this content

title: Sunderland pip Crystal Palace in battle of the private jets to land Malick Fofana | Sunderland | The Guardian
description: Both clubs sent planes to France to bring the Belgium winger to UK, but Sunderland’s owner sealed the deal by flying to speak to Fofana personally
Author: Louise Taylor
Headline: Both clubs sent planes to France to bring the Belgium winger to UK, but Sunderland’s owner sealed the deal by flying to speak to Fofana personally
Content: Malick Fofana found himself in demand and in transit on transfer deadline day.Photograph: Mohammed Badra/EPAView image in fullscreenMalick Fofana found himself in demand and in transit on transfer deadline day.Photograph: Mohammed Badra/EPASunderlandSunderland pip Crystal Palace in battle of the private jets to land Malick FofanaBoth clubs send planes to France to acquire Lyon wingerSunderland submit deal sheet for £31m transferLouise TaylorTue 1 Sep 2026 18.15 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSunderland andCrystal Palacewere involved in an extraordinary deadline-day tug of war that concluded with Malick Fofana agreeing to swap Lyon for the Stadium of Light in a club-record £31m move.On Tuesday morning it had seemed that the 21-year-old Belgium winger was heading forSunderlandon a five-year contract, but then Pierre Sage led an attempt to hijack the deal. Palace’s manager coached Fofana at Lyon and forged a strong bond with a player he was keen to bring to Selhurst Park. After speaking to Sage on the phone, Fofana seemed to have changed his mind and decided he wanted to reunite with his old boss in south London. Sunderland, though, refused to surrender.‘A great feeling’: Mykhailo Mudryk seals loan move from Chelsea to TottenhamRead moreThat meant Lyon had a bidding war on their hands and responded by agreeing improved deals with both clubs. Agents’ fees and Fofana’s personal terms were also understood to have risen accordingly. Meanwhile, two private jets, one dispatched by Sunderland and the other by Palace, sat on the tarmac at Lyon airport.At one point Fofana was said to have been seen boarding the former aircraft before a flight to Newcastle airport but, in reality, he was headed to a private hospital in France for a medical commissioned jointly by Palace and Sunderland. With time running out, both clubs accepted this unusual arrangement was the only way a player targeted by Arsenal throughout much of the window would be heading to England.In an attempt to remind Fofana, who scored 11 goals in 59 appearances for Lyon since arriving from Gent in 2024, why he had originally been so excited about playing for Régis Le Bris on Wearside, Kyril Louis-Dreyfus, Sunderland’s owner, flew to Lyon – presumably on a third jet – and spoke to him privately. It appears to have proved an inspired intervention as, shortly after 9pm, Fofana announced that he had made his choice and would be travelling to the Stadium of Light after all.Although the initial fee agreed is £26m, add-ons dictate it should eventually rise to £31m. That leaves a forward capped five times by Belgium set to become Sunderland’s record signing, eclipsing the £30m paid to Strasbourg formidfielder Habib Diarralast summer. Sunderland have submitted a deal sheet and expect it to be concluded shortly.Explore more on these topicsSunderlandCrystal PalaceTransfer windownewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A great feeling’: Mykhailo Mudryk seals loan move from Chelsea to Tottenham | Tottenham Hotspur | The Guardian
description: Tottenham have thrown a Premier League lifeline to the forgotten Chelsea winger, Mykhailo Mudryk, signing him on loan just before the transfer deadline
Author: David Hytner
Headline: Tottenham have thrown a Premier League lifeline to the forgotten Chelsea winger, Mykhailo Mudryk, signing him on loan just before the transfer deadline
Content: Mykhailo Mudryk relished working with ‘my football father’ Roberto De Zerbi while they were at Shakhtar Donetsk.Photograph: Chloe Knott/Tottenham Hotspur FC/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMykhailo Mudryk relished working with ‘my football father’ Roberto De Zerbi while they were at Shakhtar Donetsk.Photograph: Chloe Knott/Tottenham Hotspur FC/ShutterstockTottenham Hotspur‘A great feeling’: Mykhailo Mudryk seals loan move from Chelsea to TottenhamDeal for Ukrainian winger has £75m purchase optionMudryk: ‘I’m so excited to be reunited with De Zerbi’David HytnerTue 1 Sep 2026 17.24 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTottenham have thrown a Premier League lifeline to the forgottenChelseawinger, Mykhailo Mudryk, signing him on loan just before the transfer deadline and challenging him to revive his career.Mudryk became a €100m (£89m) player when Chelseatook him from Shakhtar Donetsk in January 2023; the deal comprised an initial €70m and €30m in add-ons. Chelsea beat Arsenal to his signature at a point when the Ukrainian was among the most in-demand players in Europe.Aston Villa sign Mbaye and Harwood-Bellis as Newcastle get Fernandez-PardoRead moreThe move to Chelsea did not work out and Mudryk hit rock bottom when he was banned for returning an adverse reading for the banned substance, meldonium, which can increase respiratory capacity and stamina. His last competitive game for Chelsea was on 28 November 2024.Mudryk was suspended before being given a four-year ban by the Football Association. But after anappeal to the court of arbitration for sport, he was able to resolve his case with the FA at the end of July, beingcleared for an immediate return to playing. He accepted breaking anti-doping rules and agreed to a suspension that was equal to the time he had already served. The FA noted that changes have been made to the World Anti-Doping Agency’s rules on meldonium and had Mudryk’s test been conducted today then “the concentration of meldonium in the sample would not have been reported” and no adverse finding would have been recorded.Spurs have taken a punt on Mudryk on the recommendation of their manager, Roberto De Zerbi, who worked productively with the 25-year-old at Shakhtar, overseeing his breakthrough season in 2021-22. De Zerbi was in the market for a left winger to complete a new-look front line with the right-sided attacker Sávio and the central striker Omar Marmoush; both have joined from Manchester City.Spurs failed with moves for Cody Gakpo and Iliman Ndiaye. The former was retained by Liverpool; the latter went from Everton to City. And so De Zerbi, who has started the season with Mathys Tel on the left, pivoted to Mudryk. The deal for him has a £75m purchase option.“It’s a great feeling. I can’t wait to start training and playing for the club, and I’m so excited to be reunited with Roberto De Zerbi,” said Mudryk. “He’s my football father. I believe in him. I trust him. I know what he wants from me and with him I always feel I’m improving.”Speaking during Spurs’s pre-season tour of Australia when Mudryk’s ban ended, De Zerbi said: “He’s my son. I’m very happy. He deserves to play. He’s a cool guy, a top player. Hopefully he can show what he suffered in the last two years in this next season.”Spurs have not done business with Chelsea since 2009 when the goalkeeper, Carlo Cudicini, was allowed to join them from Stamford Bridge on a free transfer. Yet they added another Chelsea player on deadline day with the centre-half Tosin Adarabioyo signing for £7m.Adarabioyo replaces Kevin Danso, who went to Sunderland on an initial season-long loan which will be followed by a mandatory £25m purchase. Spurs also moved the midfielder, Pape Sarr, to Juventus on an initial loan with a buy option. The deal is valued at €30m.Explore more on these topicsTottenham HotspurChelseaTransfer windownewsShareReuse this content

title: West Ham fight off Wolves as Divine Mukasa double eases pressure on Nuno | Championship | The Guardian
description: Divine Mukasa, a loan signing from Manchester City, scored twice as West Ham won for the first time in the league this season, beating Wolves 4-2
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: Divine Mukasa, a loan signing from Manchester City, scored twice as West Ham won for the first time in the league this season, beating Wolves 4-2
Content: Divine Mukasa (third left) opened the scoring for West Ham with a superb long-range strike.Photograph: Anthony Hanc/Wired Photos/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenDivine Mukasa (third left) opened the scoring for West Ham with a superb long-range strike.Photograph: Anthony Hanc/Wired Photos/ShutterstockChampionshipWest Ham fight off Wolves as Divine Mukasa double eases pressure on NunoPaul MacInnesat the London StadiumTue 1 Sep 2026 17.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was a match between two disjointed sides, two teams trying to carve out new identities following the drop into theChampionship. In the end West Ham won thanks to a bit of luck, a degree of resolve and, crucially, a sharpness in front of goal that took them away from Wolves and reduced the pressure on Nuno Espírito Santo, for a few days at least.First-half goals from Divine Mukasa and Jarrod Bowen, the latter from the penalty spot, were complemented by two more in the second; Mukasa secured his brace alongside a goal for Konstantinos Mavropanos. The defender doubled up himself too, albeit by scoring at his own end, as Wolves tried to claw their way back into contention. The visitors also added a decent goal from the midfielder Marshall Munetsi to their tally. For all their obvious technical ability, however, César Peixoto’s side lacked the hosts’ sang-froid at the crucial moments and that proved the decisive factor.Nuno’s mantra after the match was “I think we can do better”, but he was clearly grateful for the win. “We all know that it was much needed,” he said. “Looking back even on today, we have mistakes again but we’ve been much more effective in our attacking actions.”With West Ham’s uncertainty extending beyond the field of play, there was much interest taken from the appearance of Amanda Staveley in the stands here. The former Newcastle shareholder remains in the running to acquire a stake in West Ham and could be seen punching the air at Mukasa’s first-half banger. The Manchester City loanee was not the only new recruit to impress, with Arne Engels excellent alongside him in midfield.What gave off the vibes of being an uninspiring opening half ended up being blessed by three goals. West Ham were on the back foot for much of the opening half-hour but established a two-goal lead by the 40th minute after a short spell of improved play. The opening goal was a memorable one, hit by Mukasa from 25 yards and cannoning into the net off the underside of the bar. It was a memorable way for the teenager to open his account, and it came after a piece of smart attacking play that got Kyle Walker-Peters behind Wolves’ defensive line. Seven minutes later, Bowen converted a penalty after swift feet from Joel Piroe confused André into an untimely tackle.View image in fullscreenJarrod Bowen doubles West Ham’s lead from the penalty spot.Photograph: Saud Ahmed/PPAUK/ShutterstockBefore Nuno could get his troops into the dressing room and preach the importance of a clean sheet, Wolves hit back. With West Ham’s defence pushing up, a fortunate deflection off the previously bewildered André opened up the opportunity for Munetsi to run into space, check inside Mavropanos and finish coolly inside Mads Hermansen’s left-hand post.With nascent enthusiasm tempered by the late concession, the atmosphere among the home support quietened as the second half began, perhaps in anticipation of further trials for West Ham. Instead they extended their lead in short order and it was Mukasa who struck again. This was a lovely move, starting with a cute through ball from Bowen that Pablo dummied to take four Wolves players out of the equation. Receiving on the edge of the box, Mukasa stood up Toti Gomes, shifted to his left and hit a shot that deflected off the Wolves skipper and beyond the despairing José Sá.“I’m delighted by the way he played,” Nuno said of Mukasa. “All the young lads, not just those who joined this summer, have brought us energy and talent. There’s a lot of things to improve but I’m delighted to have him.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWolves responded to the third goal by grabbing hold of possession once more, but the sprightly Fer López spurned two chances. Up the other end, however, and an Engels corner was deep and dangerous and, after Mavropanos saw a towering header crash off the bar, the Greek defender smashed the rebound home on the volley. Six minutes after celebrating, Mavropanos got the final touch to a cross from Jackson Tchatchoua to turn the ball into his own net.Wolves created no further chances, but could take solace from the performance of the full-back Tchatchoua, who looked impactful at both ends, while Mateus Mané was dominant on the left. “We created a lot of chances to score, they scored more goals,” said Peixoto. “West Ham took their chances and that’s the difference.”Explore more on these topicsChampionshipWest Ham UnitedWolverhampton Wanderersmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Aston Villa sign Mbaye and Harwood-Bellis as Newcastle get Fernandez-Pardo | Transfer window | The Guardian
description: Aston Villa have added to their summer overhaul with the signings of Ibrahim Mbaye and Taylor Harwood-Bellis while Newcastle have added Matias Fernandez-Pardo to their squad from Lille
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: Aston Villa have added to their summer overhaul with the signings of Ibrahim Mbaye and Taylor Harwood-Bellis while Newcastle have added Matias Fernandez-Pardo to their squad from Lille
Content: Ibrahim Mbaye has joined Aston Villa for £47m from European champions, Paris Saint-Germain.Photograph: Emma Da Silva/APView image in fullscreenIbrahim Mbaye has joined Aston Villa for £47m from European champions, Paris Saint-Germain.Photograph: Emma Da Silva/APTransfer windowAston Villa sign Mbaye and Harwood-Bellis as Newcastle get Fernandez-PardoGabriel Jesus completes move from Arsenal to BarcelonaHarvey Elliott joins Valencia on loan from LiverpoolBen FisherandLouise TaylorTue 1 Sep 2026 13.58 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAston Villacompleted the signings of Ibrahim Mbaye and Taylor Harwood-Bellis on deadline day, with Unai Emery confident the club’s radical summer overhaul has left Villa in position to replicate their recent success. Villa, who have lost both of their Premier League games this campaign, have qualified for the Champions League in two of the past three seasons and won their first major trophy in 30 years after lifting the Europa League.The £47m arrival of the 18-year-old winger Mbaye from Paris Saint-Germain and £25m deal for Harwood-Bellis from Southampton represented Villa’s ninth and 10th summer signings respectively. Villa had generated more than £300m from the sales of nine players, six of whom started May’s Europa League triumph in Istanbul; Morgan Rogers, Ollie Watkins, Ezri Konsa, Youri Tielemans, Lucas Digne and Emiliano Martínez all departed Villa Park in recent weeks, Rogers and Martinez joining Chelsea.Football transfer deadline day: Man City sign Ndiaye and agree Fernández deal, Chelsea close on Camara – liveRead moreWatkins’s £50m exit to the Saudi Pro League club Al-Hilal, after rejecting Villa’s offer of a new contract, led to Villa signing Nicolas Jackson for an initial £47.5m that could rise to a club-record £65m. Earlier in the window, Villa signed Johan Manzambi for a club-record £52m from Freiburg but the Switzerland midfielder is yet to make his debut as he continues his recovery from a knee injury he sustained at the World Cup.AfterMonday’s 1-0 home defeat by Arsenal, Emery struck an upbeat tone. “We are happy how we are closing the transfer window,” said Villa’s manager. “We are not regretting anything and the players who are joining are players that should be enough to rebuild the team with the structure we want. I think we replaced the players as we planned.”Zion Suzuki, a £30m arrival from Parma, made his Villa debut against Arsenal and Villa’s new No 1 accepts the task of replacing Martínez is a “good challenge”. “It was my priority to play games so that is why I made the decision and I played in Belgium for one year, in Parma for two years,” said the 24-year-old, who joined Villa after a move to PSG collapsed in the final stages. “In the end I am here and playing for Villa. I just wanted to come here for this club. There are so many expectations. It is not easy to play after [Martínez] but I want to help the team and be like him.“It was very important to play in Serie A for two years and now I am confident. I made good steps and now I am here to play for the club. I want to enjoy this moment and help the team. I am really looking forward to [playing in] the Champions League but before that, I want a first Premier League win to get some momentum.”Newcastle, meanwhile, concluded a “transformational” transfer window by securing the target that topped their shopping list in May with only hours of the transfer window remaining.The £51m signing of the Belgium forward Matias Fernandez-Pardo from Lille on deadline day is regarded as a considerable coup and prompted boardroom celebration at the end of a turbulent summer. The 21-year-old is Newcastle’s eighth signing of a transfer window that has also seen Eddie Howe replaced as manager by Matthias Jaissle and three of the team’s biggest names – Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimarães – sold for a total approaching £250m.Ross Wilson, Newcastle’s sporting director, kept in frequent contact with Fernandez-Pardo’s advisers. “Matias is a strong example of how a transfer window can unfold with twists and turns along the way,” said Wilson. “Back in May he was our top target and we always remained engaged with him. Now at the end of the window he becomes our eighth addition to a refreshedNewcastle Unitedand we are excited to welcome him.”View image in fullscreenMatias Fernandez-Pardo is seen as having the ability and verstatilty to be an ideal fit for Matthias Jaissle’s Newcastle.Photograph: Jean-François Badias/APFernandez-Pardo’s elusive movement and ability to operate as a No 10, a No 9 or wide-left attacker explains why Newcastle were prepared to stay patient for his signature. “A lot of hours went into this one,” acknowledged Wilson. “But we’re clear on our identity and Matias has speed, intensity and work rate in abundance. We believe in his profile a great deal. Our fans will enjoy him and I know he will also enjoy our amazing St James’ Park atmosphere.”Jaissle seemed equally delighted to have reinforced his frontline with a versatile attacker. “We were all delighted when we knew we could complete this deal,” said the German, who has made three key signings in the £39m Amar Dedic, the £52m Nico González and now Fernandez-Pardo since arriving on Tyneside in early August. “Matias is a highly technical player with explosiveness in his game. He can score and assist, he has courage and the ability to take players on. We’re sure our supporters will enjoy watching him play.”“I’m really happy to be here and very proud to be at such a big club,” said the Belgian. “I spoke to the head coach and he really showed me how much he wanted me to be here. In terms of my career progression it made complete sense to come; I didn’t hesitate at all. I can’t wait to start my wonderful adventure here.”Nick Woltemade’s failure to fit into Jaissle’s high-intensity gameplans explains why Germany forward,signed for £70m from Stuttgart last August, has joined Juventus on a year-long loan.Elsewhere,Barcelonahave confirmed that Gabriel Jesus has joined fromArsenalon a permanent basis for a fee that is thought to be €10m (£8.6m). The Brazil striker was in attendance for Barcelona’s 5-2 win over Rayo Vallecano on Monday night after a deal was struck over the weekend and he leaves north London as only the 12th player to win the Premier League title with two different clubs, having also done so with Manchester City.Harvey Elliott has also joinedValenciaon loan fromLiverpool,while across Merseyside, Beto has sealed a £15.5m move fromEvertontoFiorentina.Kevin Danso has joinedSunderlandon a year-long loan fromTottenhamthat should lead to a formal £25m transfer for the Austria centre-half next summer.Fulhamhave completed the signing of Manuel Ángel fromReal Madrid, having already signed César Palacios and Gonzalo García from the Spanish giants.Explore more on these topicsTransfer windowAston VillaNewcastle UnitedBarcelonaArsenalValenciaLiverpoolnewsShareReuse this content

title: Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 12: Manchester United | Manchester United Women | The Guardian
description: The departure of Marc Skinner and several senior squad members leaves new manager Eva Olid to guide United into their new era
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: The departure of Marc Skinner and several senior squad members leaves new manager Eva Olid to guide United into their new era
Content: Julia Zigiotti Olme of Manchester United Women during a training session at La Manga Club in Spain. Photograph: Poppy Townson/MUFC/Manchester United/Getty ImagesThe departure of Marc Skinner and senior squad members leaves new manager Eva Olid to guide United into new eraByTom GarryTue 1 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 19.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:7th (NB: this is not necessarily Tom Garry’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:4thProspectsIt was all-change at Manchester United during pre-season, with thedeparture of their head coach Marc Skinnerafter five years followed swiftly by theappointment of Eva Olidas a new era begins. There have been significant outgoings from the playing group, including the senior squad membersMelvine Malard, Gabby George, Millie Turner and Lisa Naalsund, as well as the end-of-contracts exits of Leah Galton and Hannah Blundell, but the signings of the Spain youth international defender Andrea Medina, the former Germany youth international goalkeeper Janina Leitzig and the Sweden forward Monica Jusu Bah will give the squad a fresh feel.Missing out on the Women’s Champions League places by nine points last season was disappointing and after a summer in which other clubs have spent big, it feels more likely United will be looking over their shoulder at challengers coming up from fifth and sixth than mounting a title challenge.Tottenham’s and London City’s ambitious recruitment mean they could threaten United’s position but United have not turned into a bad team overnight. European quarter-finalists last season, their squad retains a strong level of quality international players, despite the sale of Malard to Chelsea in particular. The England internationals Maya Le Tissier and Ella Toone are the senior leaders in a squad that also retains a world-class goalkeeper in Phallon Tullis-Joyce, the dynamic England midfielder Jess Park and the talented Sweden wing-back Anna Sandberg. A top-half finish feels realistic and the club will hope for strong runs in the domestic cups. There is also understood to be a desire at the club to make the playing style more entertaining for supporters.Graphic showing how London City finished in the past five seasonsOff-field pictureAs with the men’s club, the Glazer family own a majority stake and Ineos – led by Sir Jim Ratcliffe – has a minority stake but has control of football operations. The women’s team’s financial history divides opinion in the sport; some argue United are an example of how to run a professional women’s team sustainably, having recorded a profit of £397,000 in their most recent accounts and a profit of £1.34m since reforming their senior women’s team in 2018, while others lament a lack of investment from the ownership compared with the budgets of their rivals such as Arsenal, Chelsea and Manchester City.The managerOlid was appointed on 5 August on a two-year deal with the option of a further year. The Spanish coach, who turned 41 in late August, arrives after an impressive spell at Hearts, where she led the club to their first Scottish Women’s Premier League title in May. That made her the SWPL’s manager of the season. It is understood she was chosen by United’s hierarchy because they feel her CV demonstrates a strong track record of developing and improving young players.Star signingBah, who has 11 caps, looks to be an important signing for United from BK Häcken for a fee reportedly of about £400,000. The 23-year-old helped the Swedish club win last term’s inaugural Women’s Europa Cup – European club-level women’s football’s second competition – and she said the opportunity to work with Olid was “perfect” because she wants to improve. She provided seven assists and scored 16 goals for her club last season and United will hope she can settle into the WSL quickly.View image in fullscreenMonica Jusu Bah arrives in Manchester from Swedish club BK Häcken.Photograph: Poppy Townson/Manchester United/Getty ImagesStat attackUnited made a mockery of underlying data last season. Only Arsenal overachieved against their attacking expected goals by more and only City conceded fewer compared with their xG at the back. They were ranked fourth for expected goal metrics at both ends but the combined variance of +9.86 against those numbers makes them hard to predict this season.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGraphic showing Manchester United were second to the champions for exceeding expected goals in 2025‑26Set for a breakthroughLayla Drury, an academy graduate, became United’s youngest player and goalscorer when given her debut in the Women’s FA Cup in January at 16, and this summer the 17-year-old became the youngest player to sign a professional contract with the club. She has been added to England’s Under-20 squad for September’s World Cup in Poland and last Saturday scored for the Young Lionesses in their 11-0 warm-up victory against New Caledonia. The forward had previously played for Wales’ youth teams.What they say“I always say: ‘My life is football.’ I don’t have other things. I spend probably 24 hours every day on football. It’s my life, my lifestyle and I give everything for the team and for the players. They always have me. Doubts, questions, [it] doesn’t matter the time of the day, I’m going to be there for them. I want to make them better, and that is how I’m going to feel good as a coach, seeing the improvement, seeing that they are better, and of course, winning matches” – Olid to MUTV.Where are they playing their home games?United play at Leigh Sports Village, a 12,000-capacity venue which is also the home of the rugby league club Leigh Leopards and United’s men’s Under-21s. It has been their home ground since 2018. The stadium hosted a quarter-final at 2022’s Euros. United’s final home WSL fixture, against Arsenal in May, has been scheduled for Old Trafford, although that match may have to be rearranged if Arsenal reach the semi-finals of the Women’s Champions League because the second legs are that weekend.On Friday 4 September at 1pm Suzanne Wrack will be answering readers’ questions about the new WSL season for GuardianConversationsExplore more on these topicsManchester United WomenWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I was scared to tell my old teammates’: Victoria Pelova on making leap from Arsenal to Spurs | Tottenham Hotspur Women | The Guardian
description: While her move across north London has been amicable, the Netherlands midfielder tells Suzanne Wrack she is relishing a reunion with her former club
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: While her move across north London has been amicable, the Netherlands midfielder tells Suzanne Wrack she is relishing a reunion with her former club
Content: Victoria Pelova at her Tottenham unveiling. ‘You need to put us on as underdogs. The underdog position is the place to be.’Photograph: THFCView image in fullscreenVictoria Pelova at her Tottenham unveiling. ‘You need to put us on as underdogs. The underdog position is the place to be.’Photograph: THFCTottenham Hotspur WomenInterview‘I was scared to tell my old teammates’: Victoria Pelova on making leap from Arsenal to SpursSuzanne WrackWhile move across north London has been amicable, the Dutch midfielder is relishing clash with former clubTue 1 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is not the same intensity to club rivalries between women’s teams as there is between their men’s counterparts, but as the game grows that is changing. Increasingly, there is animosity from fans if a player leaves for a rival side.Victoria Pelova’s movefrom Arsenalto Tottenham firmly bucks the trend, though. Despite arguably having her best years ahead of her, the 27-year-old departed with a lot of well wishes and love.‘Now is a good time for players to speak up’: Lucy Bronze on Fifa and helping refugeesRead more“I was really scared to tell my old teammates that I was going here,” Pelova says. “My close friends knew about it, obviously, but everyone responded so well. Everyone tells me that it reflects on the person I am. So, I’m actually really glad about that.”Pelova has been an Arsenal fan favourite despite limited minutes in her three years at the club, during which she was hampered by an anterior cruciate ligament injury sustained on international duty in June 2024. Why is she so liked? She comes across as fun and is loved by her teammates, with a wicked and dry sense of humour.Pelova was not worried what people would make of her move to Spurs, but the Netherlands midfielder did think about it. Ultimately, it was “an easy decision” to join Martin Ho’s squad.“The way Martin approached me, what he said about how he sees me as a player, the videos he showed me and how he wants me to be, I’ve actually never had a coach talking like that about me. So, for me, it was a good decision. I talked a lot with my mum about it and she immediately said yes. That was actually the most important thing for me, what my mum thought.”At the start of June, Pelova shared online that her mum had died. A carousel of moving photos of the pair through the years was captioned: “Your biggest fear was leaving me behind. My biggest fear was losing you. Rest now, Mum.”Pelova is not ready to talk about the loss, but it sits in the background of the interview. Not having to move home as a result of her leaving Arsenal was important. “It does really help me that I have friends and family around me that take care of me,” she says.View image in fullscreenPelova slides in on Chelsea’s Alyssa Thompson during Arsenal’s 2-0 win at Stamford Bridge in January.Photograph: Alex Broadway/WSL Football/Getty ImagesReflecting on her spell at Arsenal, with her ACL injury coming at a time when it was believed she would start to get more playing time, she says: “There was a private situation going on, my mum was ill, and I didn’t get minutes. So, it was a really tough time and people didn’t know what I was going through.”The goal now? “To be happy again, in football and outside football, and just day by day see how it goes.“It sounds like I have not been happy, but I have been happy in the last year and in being with my friends. But when you’re not playing as regularly as you want to it’s inevitable that you’re not going to be totally happy, and when I’m the happiest person, I will be the best footballer I can be.”The fresh start at Tottenham has been rejuvenating. “It’s nice to have no one know you. For me, that’s the way to go. I don’t know if I can explain it, but I feel like when everyone knows you, they focus on the things they know.”Ho made an instant impression on Pelova. “All the coaches I’ve met are always like: ‘Oh, you can play there and there and there.’ Martin was like: ‘You’rethisfor me.’ He knew exactly where he wanted me and what he wanted from me. That, right away, set the tone for me and it was where and how I see myself as well. What I’ve seen so far is that he’s so detailed. He just wants to make you better. He’s very strict, but he wants to make you a better player and that’s why I’m here.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHo has “a lot” of confidence in her, and that is hugely freeing. “That’s the part I don’t have to worry about … and I can focus on other things.”Pelova’s experience of Tottenham had been playing against them, and the more difficult that got, the more it contributed to her decision to join. “Defending was so hard,” she says of facing Spurs last season. “So, I already liked the style Martin had the team playing. I also already know Caitlin Dijkstra; I’ve known her for eight years and we lived together in Amsterdam so we know each other so well. She’s like my sister. I know Lize Kop, they’re also one of my closest friends. So, that has made the transition easy because I can always rely on them.Aston Villa’s Rachel Daly: ‘It’s given me more of a focus: club football is my one job’Read more“I’m quite social so I’ve been trying to get to know everyone, the youngsters. It’s quite a hard job in the beginning, it’s intense, but I like it. On the pitch, you’re building relationships, pre-season is always heavy, you just need to grind, but it has been good.”Pelova has belief in herself and her body, too. “We trainreallyhard. That’s different to what I’m used to. So, obviously it goes up and down, but I’m confident that in a few weeks everything as a team will have progressed so much. Always with new players, it needs time. I’ve been in football a really long time so I know how it goes.”Asked about Tottenham’s chances of disrupting things at the top, she flips the question, then says she relishes being outsiders. “You need to put us on as underdogs. The underdog position is the place to be.”Now, Pelova is ready for the intensity of pre-season to end and for the games to begin at home against West Ham on Sunday. One, in particular, stands out, and it comes on 25 October at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. “Please, stop pre-season,” she says with a laugh. “I just want to start. I can’t wait to play against all the teams. I can’t wait to play against Arsenal.”Explore more on these topicsTottenham Hotspur WomenWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballArsenal WomeninterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘In my heart until I die’: Argentina says a tearful thank you to Lionel Messi | Lionel Messi | The Guardian
description: The Argentinian’s decision to quit international football was met by an outpouring of affection from the country he led to World Cup glory in 2022
Author: Marcela Mora y Araujo
Headline: The Argentinian’s decision to quit international football was met by an outpouring of affection from the country he led to World Cup glory in 2022
Content: Lionel Messi looks overwhelmed after an enthralling 3-2 victory against Egypt in the 2026 World Cup.Photograph: Patrick Smith/Fifa/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLionel Messi looks overwhelmed after an enthralling 3-2 victory against Egypt in the 2026 World Cup.Photograph: Patrick Smith/Fifa/Getty ImagesLionel Messi‘In my heart until I die’: Argentina says a tearful thank you to Lionel MessiThe Argentinian’s decision to quit international football was met by an outpouring of affection from the country he led to World Cup glory in 2022Marcela Mora y AraujoTue 1 Sep 2026 11.05 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnyone who was present at Lionel Scaloni’s press conference immediately after theWorld Cup final between Spain and Argentinain New Jersey on 19 July and saw his tears, the sobs which prevented him from speaking while he got up and walked out, could tell this was a man weeping not because of defeat in a single match but because he was fully aware that what that particular group of men had been through for the past eight years had come to an end.Messi’s announcement that he isretiring from international football, posted on Instagram on Monday complete with photos of three handwritten sheets of some anonymous yet corporate-looking headed paper and a Harry Potter Time Turner pen, to the soundtrack ofBrindis sung by Soledad Pastorutti, instantly dominated the news and unleashed a barrage of homages, gratitude and joy from all corners. But it’s not exactly a surprise.Lionel Messi’s international retirement serves as a reminder: watch him while you still canRead more“How crazy that the day has come, dear Leo,” Cristian Romero posted, making it clear that this was expected in spite of the unexpectedness. “The day no one wanted to arrive has arrived,” echoed Giovani Lo Celso, who said he had “nine years listening to you, admiring you and learning by your side”. His international teammates highlight how in their childhood they dreamed of meeting him one day, let alone actually playing with him. Nico Paz says since he was four years old he “used to watch you play with my dad and we would calculate together whether I would be in time to play with you”.It’s not just his teammates who are expressing gratitude and nostalgia. On a Buenos Aires street corner someone put a red telephone on a table with a sign saying: “What would you say to Messi?” Passersby picked up the receiver and talked into it: “I’m 86 years old and you have given me the greatest joys in my life. You will be in my heart until the day I die,” one gentleman said. A young boy saw the news and “burst into tears even though I was at school”. A well-spoken woman said “we will miss you because you are an extraordinary being”, a little girl added “you’re the best and the greatest”. An old man signed off “bye, son”.Influencers, journalists, artists, cultural commentators and psychologists all expressed their gratefulness for Messi being a great human being. “Messi led by example,” the veteran sportswriter Matías Martin wrote, while the coach and motivational speaker Matias “Coco” Gallo Bevegni posted that theWorld Cupwinner “taught me more in defeat than in victory”.View image in fullscreenA message written by Lionel Messi and posted to Instagram explaining his retirement from the Argentina team.Photograph: Lionel Messi/Instagram/ReutersThe football pundit Morena Beltrán could not hold back the tears as she explained to her older colleagues that for her generation there is a sense of mourning and emptiness which can only be filled by gratitude, which maybe they have already experienced, because they have seen another God. The psychoanalyst Milagros Filgueras praised the decision to hand-write the note, saying some goodbyes need the body involved. The journalist Pablo Perantuono devoted his column to the “epistolary genre”, noting that a handwritten letter in this day and age is almost a countercultural act of originality.The writer Andrés Burgo highlighted that in 10 of the past 12 World Cups, either Maradona or Messi played, so this truly marks the “end of an era in which grandparents, parents, sons and daughters and grandchildren enjoyed an incredible privilege during almost 45 years. The heir will arrive – we hope – but right now is a time of orphanage. And gratitude.”View image in fullscreenArgentina fans wearing T-shirts depicting Lionel Messi and Diego Maradona.Photograph: Amanda Perobelli/ReutersMessi revealed that this letter was actually written two days after the final, a cathartic diary-like release, but that on Monday, after“[what happened with] my dad”he was more convinced than ever. The note said: “It’s a decision that hurt and continues to hurt,” but that he understands this is the moment. The poet Valeria Correa Fiz pointed out that he originally wrote “I think”, crossed it out and replaced it with “I understand”. Messi swore he always gave his all, not only these past few years when “everything was won” (he never says “I won”; it’s always “we” or “it” was won) but he has nothing left to give. He’s emptied.The 39-year-old, however, scored four goals for Inter Miami at the weekend and continues his career at club level, where he clearly still has much to give. He is not retiring from playing football, the thing he loves most. He is retiring fromArgentina.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenMessi shows off the World Cup trophy after winning the 2022 final against France.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianWith two international dates coming up and no rival agreed, no doubt the clarification that there will be no Messi in the squad will impact on the potential fixtures. And not unlike the time when he quit Argentina before, in 2016, the country’s football is in a bit of turmoil.The context and climate include scandals surrounding the Argentinian Football Association, the pressure by some lobbies to privatise football clubs, which are non-profit organisations, and the international furore caused by several incidents during the World Cup which have landed Argentina with some hefty fines, sanctions and suspensions.The heaviness of the Argentina flag which for so many years visibly weighed him down, turned idyllic when it became the cloak of victory, mattered very much to his father, Jorge. Messi said he wanted to win another World Cup for him. Perhaps his death has somehow freed him from that aspect of his Argentinianness.View image in fullscreenSupporters in Sydney, Australia, watch Messi on giant TV screens after Spain defeated Argentina in the 2026 World Cup final.Photograph: David Gray/AFP/Getty ImagesAnd just like last time, the spontaneous visceral response from the Argentinian people is acceptance and relish at the good times lived. That inexplicable sense of pride that comes from being from the same soil as someone who is very good at something and whose magic is still untarnished by the sordid final match against Spain, or any of the criticisms directed at the squad and fans throughout the tournament. If anything, his final tears in front of the stands, like Scaloni’s tears at the press conference, are mirrored in a nation moved profoundly by the generations we have just lived through, perhaps not realising we were living through them.The huge volume of emotive, sentimental outpouring is rather lovely, and amid it all an enduring image of three little boys walking down a Buenos Aires street with No 10 Messi shirts on their backs signals the way forward, towards a future unknown.Explore more on these topicsLionel MessiArgentinaWorld Cup 2022World Cup 2026World CupfeaturesShareReuse this content
