I’ve received ZERO effort from anyone in the tech industry to even try to explain datacenters …”Read more:One of east coast’s largest datacenters accused of ‘violating federal law’Palihapitiya argues the backlash will grow.“Data centers have unfortunately become THE symbolic representation of the asymmetric upside for a very narrow tech elite and a class that are untrustworthy. Inasmuch, the safer bet may be that the pushback and resistance grows …” he wrote.The technorati on X seem to have recently woken up to the new hostile political reality, and over the weekend spilled some ink bristling at it. Many rejected the backlash as myopic, shallow and short-lived. “Any politician opposed to data centers is unqualified to hold public office,” Gavin Baker, an influential venture capitalist,tweetedon Saturday.On Monday, Donald Trump weighed in. “Let data reign,” he wrote on Truth SocialTruth Social users answered the president’s post en masse and with uncharacteristic rage.As these battles reach a boil in the US, they’re heating up in other parts of the world.ScotlandandAustraliaare seeing their own backlashes unite bitter political foes in opposition to datacenters, fueled by the widespread perception of Silicon Valley as an extractive, neocolonial force.Monday was Tim Cook’s last day as Apple CEOSiri, where does Apple go next? – podcastApple’s Tim Cook leaves behind complicated legacy on privacyFifteen years after Steve Jobs, Tim Cook leaves a dramatically different AppleWho is John Ternus, Apple’s next CEO?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAI and medicine‘Superhuman’ AI tool spots heart disease in less than 2 secondsDoctors’ AI scribes get names of drugs and diagnoses wrong, NHS watchdog warnsAI can detect heart disease in women using mammograms, study suggestsAI on the job: answering your questions about artificial intelligence in the workplaceWe’re trying something new! As part of our year-longReworked series of stories on AI and work, editor Danielle Abril will answer readers’ questions about the changing workplace. You can ask a question for future editions by emailing us attechscape.us@theguardian.com.***This week, readers ask: what skills do I need to learn to stay employable as more companies adopt AI?For workers whose jobs may be affected by AI, the takeaways from several studies all point to a somewhat counterintuitive answer: yes, you should familiarize yourself with generative AI tools. But at least as important: sharpen your human skills. Judgment, adaptability, analytical thinking and leadership all may become differentiators as AI gets embedded in work.Ask yourself: can you critically judge AI’s output? Can you quickly adapt to change? Can you problem-solve and delegate tasks efficiently to humans and AI?“Learn to work with AI in your field, while continuing to build the human and domain skills that help you apply it well,” said Elena Magrini, head of global research for labor market intelligence firmLightcast.io.The tasks that employers are adding to AI-exposed jobs often rely on human skills such as empathy, judgment and creativity, according to PwC’s2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer report, which is based on 1bn job ads from six continents. Junior roles are now more likely to require traditionally senior skills like emotional intelligence and leadership, the report stated. In LinkedIn’s 2026 Skills on the Rise report, based on skills members added to their profiles along with those held by recent hires, in-demand skills included team management, cross-functional collaboration and mentorship, as well as prompt engineering and AI business strategy.One way to start developing experience in leadership and problem solving is at your own company. Work with your boss to find internal training and mentorship programs. And consider volunteering for tasks that may allow you to boost your weaker skills like leading a cross-functional project that requires you to delegate and communicate often. Beyond your employer, companies such as LinkedIn and Coursera offer free online courses for soft and technical skills and OpenAI and Anthropic provide educational materials on how to use AI.***Ask us about AI and work! Emailtechscape.us@theguardian.comwith your questions, and we’ll answer them in future editions of the newsletter.The wider TechScape‘Scary’: how misinformation and AI hallucinations are infiltrating Australia’s parliamentAI slopper in chief: Trump turns to social media amid tough questionsThe datacenter backlash is bringing the entire political spectrum together – against big tech billionairesExplore more on these topicsTechnologyTechScape newsletterDatacenters – USSilicon ValleynewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Olivia Rodrigo is standing up for the vulnerable. I wish Taylor Swift would do the same | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: This weekend, Rodrigo raised millions for charities that benefit women and girls, and she has previously been vocal about Gaza and Ice. With free speech increasingly under threat, her peers should take note, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: This weekend, Rodrigo raised millions for charities that benefit women and girls, and she has previously been vocal about Gaza and Ice. With free speech increasingly under threat, her peers should take note, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: Trying to Make America Somewhat Decent Again … Olivia Rodrigo at the Daisy Chain Fields festival in California, on 29 August.Photograph: Christopher Polk/Billboard/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTrying to Make America Somewhat Decent Again … Olivia Rodrigo at the Daisy Chain Fields festival in California, on 29 August.Photograph: Christopher Polk/Billboard/Getty ImagesOpinionOlivia RodrigoOlivia Rodrigo is standing up for the vulnerable. I wish Taylor Swift would do the sameArwa MahdawiThis weekend, Rodrigo raised millions for charities that benefit women and girls, and she has previously been vocal about Gaza and Ice. With free speech increasingly under threat, her peers should take noteTue 1 Sep 2026 11.21 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTShareDonald Trump, the 80-year-old president of the United States, spent his weekend whiningabout a lakeand posting memes ofDonald’s Ducks. While he was busy with his ducks, Olivia Rodrigo, a 23-year-old pop star, spentherweekend trying to Make America Somewhat Decent Again. On Saturday, Rodrigo hosted the inauguralDaisy Chain Fields festival, bringing together female artists to raise money for women-focused non-profits which have had theirfundingslashedby the Trump administration. The festival raised $10m (£7.4m) whichMelinda French Gatesmatched, bringing the total to $20m.In a perfect world a singer holding a benefit concert for feminist charities wouldn’t be radical stuff. But we don’t live in a perfect world, do we? We live in hell. Trump has successfully bullied US institutions into doing his bidding.Universities have defundeddiversity, equity and inclusion programmes, manymedia outletshave kowtowed to the US’s self-styled king and tech CEOs havejumped intobed with him. Women’s rights are goingbackwards globallyand our civil liberties are under attack.It has become depressingly clear just how many of the rich and powerful are self-serving cowards who will abandon social justice issues as soon as it becomes mildly inconvenient. So it was refreshing to see a young musician rally people together in service of reproductive justice at a festival that was proudly feminist and didn’t pretend to be non-political.Rodrigo has always used her platform to speak out: she’s never been one of those annoying celebrities who insist that remaining apolitical is some sort of noble act. When Roe v Wade was overturned in 2022, the then 19-year-old musician condemned the decisionon stage at Glastonbury. Rodrigo, who is Filipino American, also publicly told the Trump administrationnot to use her musicin their “racist, hateful propaganda” when one of her songs was featured in a government video telling undocumented immigrants to self-deport.Rodrigo has also not been silent about Gaza: a subject many celebrities areterrified to mention, because empathising with Palestinians is a tried-and-tested wayto ruin your career. Last year she wrote on Instagramabout how“mothers, fathers and children in Gaza are starving, dehydrated and being denied access to basic medical care ...” Rodrigo also gave a nod to Palestine (which, thanks to Israel’s attacks onmaternity wardsand healthcare is a reproductive justice issue) at a press conference for her Daisy Chain Fields festival, whereshe wore a dressmade by Palestinian fashion brandNöl Collective.Speaking on the New York Times’sPopcast earlier this year, Rodrigo said acknowledging social issues is part of expressing herself. “I think it would just be disingenuous to be like, I don’t feel heartbroken about what’s going on in Gaza. As an artist, I feel like that’s just what you do. And that’s my job,”she said.Frankly, I think it’s the job of everyone with any sort of platform or power. Celebrities shouldn’t have to get political, some will say. No, of course not. But if you have a huge platform and oodles of money and even just a smidgen of a conscience, then you should probablywantto use your resources and reach for good, shouldn’t you? Giving money to charity is one thing, but it takes more courage to show people where you stand, knowing there may be repercussions for it. I hate this idea of not “taking sides”: the world is not a football match; political parties are not “teams”. It is not divisive to stand with vulnerable people.Taylor Swift,the richest female musician in history, certainly seemed to agree with that at one point. She famously stayed quiet in the lead-up to the 2016 election, but later, when more celebrities were doing so, came out to endorse progressive causes. “I need to be on the right side of history,” she said in the2020 documentaryMiss Americana.But while Swift did endorse Kamala Harris in 2024, she has been very careful about what she says during Trump 2.0. Unlike all the musicians who have publicly condemned the Trump administration for using their music in offensive posts, she seemingly ignored the use of her songs byTrump for months. In recent weeks her songs have beenquietly removedfrom Trump’s ragebait posts, but Swift has not issued any sort of public statement about it. And she certainly hasn’tsaid anythingabout issues such as Gaza or ICE.There are limits to celebrity activism, sure. But in a world where free speech is under attack, it feels increasingly important for celebrities to speak out. Let’s hope Rodrigo’s festival prompts more of her peers to have some guts.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick hereExplore more on these topicsOlivia RodrigoOpinionUS politicsTrump administrationDonald TrumpTaylor SwiftcommentShareReuse this content

title: What should we do with Trump’s monstrous architectural legacy? | Jan-Werner Müller | The Guardian
description: Questions over Trump’s ballroom and other structures might not feel urgent. But when his reign ends, Trumpism must be repudiated
Author: Jan-Werner Müller
Headline: Questions over Trump’s ballroom and other structures might not feel urgent. But when his reign ends, Trumpism must be repudiated
Content: ‘The built environment, and especially the civic landscape of a capital, is never just an afterthought.’Photograph: Manuel Balce Ceneta/APView image in fullscreen‘The built environment, and especially the civic landscape of a capital, is never just an afterthought.’Photograph: Manuel Balce Ceneta/APOpinionTrump administrationWhat should we do with Trump’s monstrous architectural legacy?Jan-Werner MüllerQuestions over Trump’s ballroom and other structures might not feel urgent. But when his reign ends, Trumpism must be repudiatedTue 1 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 10.33 EDTShareOn Monday, a majority on the supreme court found a technical way to overrule a lower court’s imperative to stop work, while not taking a stance on whether the whole enterprise might be illegal to begin with. Preservationists, the majority held, appear to lack legal grounds for filing a suit blocking Trump’s ballroom; that means construction will proceed, even if none other than John Roberts, in a dissent, held that “those responsible” were breaking the rules in deciding “what to build up at the People’s House”. The solicitor general, John Sauer, ison recordclaiming that 65% of the project is completed (of course, he might have exaggerated – such things are known to have happened in Trump administrations). Either way, it is thus likely that there will be a massive structure next to the original White House; and, given that the ruling will embolden the president dramatically to change Washington DC’s landscape by spending money never approved by Congress, we might be cursed with a triumphal arch as well. All of which raises the question: what to do with a monstrous architectural legacy in post-Trump America?Some might dismiss the question as a bit of a luxury problem. After all, a war that also demonstrates the ongoing disempowerment of Congress keeps dragging on; ICE continues its cruel day-to-day work; Trump is trying every tactic to make the midterms go his way. But the built environment, and especially the civic landscape of a capital, is never just an afterthought. Buildings and monuments make values visible, as the philosopher Susan Neimanonce put it. And the decision to leave Trump’s structures in place as if his reign had just been another normal era in US history is not neutral – just like leaving Confederate monuments in place is not neutral.For those who dismiss talk of civic values made visible as all too idealistic, there is another, hard-nosed argument to consider: after all, for anyone around the globe ever to trust a US government again, Trumpism will need to be thoroughly repudiated. Without a clear distancing from his toxic reign – during which the whims and obsessions of one evidently incompetent conman wreaked havoc with old alliances – other countries might well conclude that the US has failed to learn any lessons. And the built environment is a prime candidate for making that distancing visible to the outside world.The ballroom in particular has become a central symbol of Trump 2.0, as it combines core features of Trump’s governance: the shameless corruption, as private companies are invited to “donate” for the project; the sheer destructiveness, as the East Wing was brutally torn down without discussion, let alone permission – something that Trumpists might try to repeat with the Kennedy Center, asHoward Lutnick and others are threateningthat it will have to be demolished unless Trump gets to “renovate” and have his name on it (notice theabuser’s logicof “if I cannot have it, no one can have it”).Democrats, noticing the symbolic importance of the structure, have started to weigh in on its future: Gavin Newsom, the California governor, affirming that “we have to be builders” and not destroyers, would just leave things alone; Senator Chris Murphy has suggested that all “dirty” – which seems to mean: corrupt – projects under Trump might need to go; meanwhile, Senator Ruben Gallego wants to sell the ballroom off “piece by piece” (it is unclear whether that would be some sort of political performance art, intended as a comment on corruption, or an act of symbolic catharsis, copying the way people demolished the Berlin wall piece by piece).The prior, fundamental question is whether a structure honors a particular person or at least affirms a set of political values. This was always the strongest reason why monuments of those defending slavery could simply not be left standing; as Neiman also pointed out, there was no way a Germany that still had Hitler street names – let alone Hitler statues – could have regained the trust of anyone. So, as painful as it might be for members of the Maga cult, no official building should bear Trump’s name, and no publicly funded statues of him must ever be erected – unless the country decides that we should honor a man bent on establishing autocracy in the US.Trump administration threatens to demolish Kennedy Center if $250m renovation not doneRead moreThen again, some republics have preciselynoterased all traces of a tyrannical ruler because they wanted such traces to serve as a warning to future generations. Visitors to Venice’s most famous palace can marvel at portraits of all the doges, except one that is painted over with a black shroud; here the dishonor of the person – Doge Marino Faliero, who attempted a coup – is immortalized, and the moral meaning of history unmistakably clarified.Political iconoclasmwants to leave remnants of an image in place to remind people why iconoclasm had been necessary in the first place. That is why some have suggested that problematic monuments should ideally not be removed at all, but come with explicit statements, such as plaques that disavow their initial political message – or even be legitimatelyvandalized, such that both original and acts of vandalism remain clearly visible.Contextualization has a pedagogical impulse similar to that of museums; hence, there is something coherent about the congressman Jamie Raskin and the progressive politicianSaikrat Chakrabartisuggesting the ballroom should at least partly be turned into exhibition spaces documenting corruption, autocracy and what Raskin described as attempts to “undermine and thwart popular democracy in American life” (though, as Raskin seeks to keep a space for dining, too, guests might end up awkwardly sipping champagne next to depictions of January 6).Perhaps there is a more straightforward approach: the edifice could be named after Renee Good and Alex Pretti, the way some places in the south ended up testifying to those who fought injustice. This could teach a history lesson in a way that, for instance, turning the ballroom into a soup kitchen, as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortezhas suggested, might not – worthy as that idea might also appear.Jan-Werner Müller is a Guardian US columnist and a professor of politics at Princeton UniversityExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationOpinionUS politicsDonald TrumpWashington DCcommentShareReuse this content

title: Once again, Trump wants the FCC to put a bandage on his thin skin | Tom Wheeler | The Guardian
description: The president is lashing out at an NBC host. As the agency’s former chair, I can only hope it stands up for free speech
Author: Tom Wheeler
Headline: The president is lashing out at an NBC host. As the agency’s former chair, I can only hope it stands up for free speech
Content: ‘Once again, the president has said “jump,” and Carr will be judged by his audience of one on how high he goes.’Photograph: Daniel Cole/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Once again, the president has said “jump,” and Carr will be judged by his audience of one on how high he goes.’Photograph: Daniel Cole/ReutersOpinionTrump administrationOnce again, Trump wants the FCC to put a bandage on his thin skinTom WheelerThe president is lashing out at an NBC host. As the agency’s former chair, I can only hope it stands up for free speechTue 1 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 10.38 EDTShareWill the FCC chairperson again abuse his authority over broadcast licenses to put a Band-Aid on Donald Trump’s thin skin?Since the opening days of the Trump presidency, Brendan Carr has acted as the president’sattack dogto coerce broadcasters to say things that please his client. Only days after taking office in January 2025, Carr revived apreviously dismissedcomplaint against CBS for the editing of 60 Minutes that tracked candidate Trump’s specious lawsuit on the matter. At the time, the FCC was considering the transfer of CBS licenses to Skydance, a decision that did not come until after CBSagreed to pay$16m to settle with Trump. In September, after Jimmy Kimmel’s remarks about Charlie Kirk, Carr urged broadcasters to take action,saying “we can do this the easy way or the hard way”– an attack even the senator Ted Cruz said sounded “right out of Goodfellas”. In March 2026, hethreatened broadcastersover their coverage of the Iran war after the president complained on Truth Social. In April, heorderedDisney’s eight ABC-owned television stations to submit their licenses for premature review, even though most aren’t even halfway through their license term (Disney, ABC and the stationsare suing).On Sunday, as the morning talkshows aired, the presidentpostedon Truth Social that Kristen Welker, the host of NBC’s Meet the Press, “will be reported” for her claim that his primary endorsements yielded “mixed results”. “I hope that Chairman Brendan Carr, and the fine people of his Commission, will take this Threat to our Country very seriously,” the post instructed. NBC is owned by Comcast, a company that haslong beenin the president’s crosshairs.With New York Times subpoenas, Trump is brazenly escalating his attacks on the press | Margaret SullivanRead morePutting aside the question of whether an interpretation of primary results is a “Threat to our Country”, as a former FCC chair, I almost feel sorry for Brendan Carr. Once again, the president has said “jump”, and Carr will be judged by his audience of one on how high he goes.The FCC was created by Congress as an independent commission. Early in his term, Trumpissued an executive orderthat brought the FCC and other formerly independent agencies under White House supervision. Now, before taking any significant action, the agency must get approval from the White House. It appears that also includes following White House orders to initiate action.Enforcing his total control, in March, the presidentfired both Democratic commissioners(whose positions were mandated by Congress) from another formerly independent agency, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC). When the commissioner, Rebecca Slaughter, sued, the supreme courtsided with the president.For almost a century, the FCC hasfollowed the statutethat the five-member commission have a 3-2 majority in favor of the president’s party. Today there are two Republicans and only one Democrat on the FCC, Anna Gomez, because Trump won’t appoint another. Trump hasnominated another Republicanto the commission. Many fear that as soon as that appointment is confirmed by the Senate, the president will be able tofire Gomezand eliminate her effective voice while maintaining the required three-person quorum.There is a parallelism here. Trump wants the FCC to control what broadcasters say, while he controls what it can do.As chair of the FCC, Brendan Carr has immense authority to set the agenda and the decisions of the agency. Thus far he has wielded that power against journalism the president dislikes. The first amendment, however, does not have an exception for Donald Trump’s thin skin.Carr’s 2019 comments as a sitting commissioner should be his answer to what President Trump is asking him to do. At that time hetook a firm stand: “The FCC does not have a roving mandate to police speech in the name of the ‘public interest’.” Hopefully, the chairperson will tire of doing the opposite and once again stand for the principle of free speech.Tom Wheeler was chairperson of the Federal Communications Commission from 2013 to 2017Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationOpinionDonald TrumpNBCUS politicsUS television industrycommentShareReuse this content

title: The media’s Hasan Piker obsession is letting Republican Mike Rogers off the hook | Mehdi Hasan | The Guardian
description: Mike Rogers isn’t merely campaigning alongside a controversial supporter. His campaign put an extremist on its faith leadership team
Author: Mehdi Hasan
Headline: Mike Rogers isn’t merely campaigning alongside a controversial supporter. His campaign put an extremist on its faith leadership team
Content: ‘Why aren’t reporters asking Rogers whether he disavows [Lorenzo] Sewell’s description of Islam as a “death cult”?’Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Why aren’t reporters asking Rogers whether he disavows [Lorenzo] Sewell’s description of Islam as a “death cult”?’Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesOpinionUS politicsThe media’s Hasan Piker obsession is letting Republican Mike Rogers off the hookMehdi HasanMike Rogers isn’t merely campaigning alongside a controversial supporter. His campaign put an extremist on its faith leadership teamTue 1 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 07.11 EDTShareHasan Piker.Turn on cable news. Pick up a newspaper. Log on to Twitter. It doesn’t seem to matter where you get your political news: for the past month, the leftist Twitch streamer has become one of the dominant subjects of coverage, conversation and controversy surrounding the crucialMichiganSenate race between the Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and the Republican Mike Rogers.“I can’t stop talking about him,” the conservative pundit Hugh Hewitt recentlyadmittedon Fox, the rightwing network that also can’t stoptalkingabout Piker, day after day, from morning until night.And it isn’t just Fox. The media analysis platform Ground News aggregated242 separate storiesmentioning Piker from across the political spectrum over the past three months – almost three stories a day.Think about that.Piker doesn’t live in Michigan. He isn’t running for office. He isn’t a member of El-Sayed’s campaign. Most Americans have probably never heard of him.Yet the political press is obsessed. The incessant, relentless coverage of him is bad enough. Worse is the gaslighting – including fromDemocratsand liberal commentators – over why Piker has attracted so much attention, and why El-Sayed is apparently expected to spend his campaign answering for every provocative thing the streamer has ever said.By disparaging 2020 protests as ‘Woke 1’, liberals are following the rightwing’s leadRead more“You can’t deploy Hasan Piker aggressively in factional primaries and then turn around after you win and say ‘why is everyone talking about Hasan Piker,’” influential liberal pundit Matt Yglesiaspostedon Twitter/X. “If you don’t want people to talk about him, don’t campaign with him!!”There is just one rather large problem with that argument.Mike Rogers isn’t merely campaigning alongside a controversial supporter. His campaign gave a Michigan-based extremist and religious bigot a leadership title in its faith outreach operation.His name is Lorenzo Sewell.And you’ve probably never heard of him.Sewell, a former gang leader and Black evangelical pastor in Detroit whospokeat Donald Trump’s second inauguration in January 2025, wasunveiledby the Rogers campaign last year as one of seven members of the “senior leadership team” of “Faith Leaders for Mike Rogers”.And Sewell’s views are not exactly difficult to discover. He has publicly and proudly described Islam as a “conquering religion” and a “death cult”. He has called El-Sayed an “Islamic jihadist” who wants to impose “Sharia law all over this land”. The United States, he insists, is “not a nation of Muslims. We are a nation of Christians.”Imagine, for a moment, that a senior member of El-Sayed’s campaign had described Judaism as a “death cult”. Imagine that he had accused Rogers of being a white nationalist terrorist. Imagine the headlines. Imagine the cable-news panels. Imagine the demands – fromRepublicans, Democrats and journalists alike – that El-Sayed denounce him, disavow him, fire him.But Sewell’s vile rhetoric is only part of the story. On 18 August, the pastor co-organized the “Christian Crusader March on Dearborn City Council Meeting” with the far-right anti-Muslim agitator Jake Lang. Lang waschargedwith assaulting police officers with a deadly weapon over his actions on 6 January 2021, before receiving a pardon from Trump. He also says he doesn’t believe the Holocaust happened “at that level” and hasused the N-wordand wasarrestedin Texas in June on a charge of making a terroristic threat.The Dearborn “Crusader” rallyco-organizedby Sewell and Lang attracted neo-Nazis waving aswastika flagand wearing Nazi armbands. There were also reports of pro-KKK material being distributedduringandafterthe event. Dearborn police made22 arreststhat day.This is the question Democrats should ask voters in order to win this November | Robert ReichRead moreAgain: imagine the reaction if a senior faith leader affiliated with El-Sayed’s campaign had co-organized an event that drew people wearing Nazi armbands and waving a swastika flag, and that ended with a bunch of arrests?Would we ever hear the end of it?And unlike El-Sayed and Piker, who first campaigned together in April this year, Rogers and Sewell’s relationship goes back much further, to the former’s previous Senate run in 2024. Rogers spoke alongside Sewell atmultipleeventsduring the final weeks of that campaign.So you might assume that the Republican candidate has faced a barrage of questions about his political relationship with Sewell. You might assume that the same reporters demanding answers from El-Sayed about a Twitch streamer would be demanding answers from Rogers about a man his own campaign identified as part of a “senior leadership team”.You would be wrong.I searched the websites of the New York Times, the Washington Post and CNN. Not one of them appears to have mentioned Sewell in its coverage in 2026. The Timescoveredthe “Christian Crusader” rally in Dearborn, including Jake Lang’s role in it, but made no mention of Sewell – or of Sewell’s connection to Rogers.To be clear: this isn’t whataboutism. I am not asking anyone to excuse anything Piker has said, or saying journalists shouldn’t scrutinize him. Nor am I saying they shouldn’t question El-Sayed’s decision to appear with him.What I am asking for is that our so-called liberal media simply apply the same standard to both candidates. If242 storiesabout Piker are justified because El-Sayed campaigned with him, how many stories are justified about Sewell, whom Rogers’s own campaign named to a senior leadership team?If El-Sayed keeps getting asked about Piker’s rhetoric, why shouldn’t Rogers have to answer for Sewell’s?Why aren’t reporters asking Rogers whether he disavows Sewell’s description ofIslamas a “death cult”? Why aren’t they asking whether he agrees that El-Sayed is an “Islamic jihadist” trying to impose sharia law on Michigan? Why aren’t they asking him to condemn Nazi flags at a “Christian Crusader” rally organized by a senior faith leader on his campaign?Why does the New York Times keep calling the left ‘divisive’?Read moreOh, and why aren’t top Democrats also asking those same questions, and demanding answers for them?The near-erasure of Sewell, Lang, and those Nazi flags from the media coverage of the Michigan Senate race, combined with the silence from so many Democratic party leaders about Mike Rogers’ extremist ties, tells us something important.Three things, in fact.First, this was never really about antisemitism. Otherwise, why aren’t literal Nazi flags at an event organized by a Rogers ally a much bigger story than any of Piker’s remarks?Second, anti-Muslim bigotry continues to be seen and treated as a lesser offense in American public life. Calling Islam a “death cult” doesn’t apparently merit a single panel discussion on primetime cable news.And third, Republicans and Democrats continue to be held to radically different rules. If you’re a Democratic candidate, you have to repeatedly answer for the views of someone who isn’t even on your campaign team. If you’re a Republican candidate, your campaign can put someone on its faith leadership team who has a long record of brazenly bigoted rhetoric and never have to worry about any kind of media backlash.That is the real scandal here. Not that Abdul El-Sayed has been asked endless questions about a controversial ally. But that Mike Rogers has been asked none.Mehdi Hasan is the founder, CEO, and editor-in-chief ofZeteoExplore more on these topicsUS politicsOpinionFar right (US)RepublicansIslamChristianityNazismReligioncommentShareReuse this content

title: Nepal’s glacial collapse foreshadowed a future of climate disaster | Michael Mann | The Guardian
description: The deluge capped a summer of extreme climate events, from deadly heatwaves to wildfires. We must take action now
Author: Michael Mann
Headline: The deluge capped a summer of extreme climate events, from deadly heatwaves to wildfires. We must take action now
Content: ‘The Nepal flooding was was the exclamation point on a summer of extremes.’Photograph: Prabin Ranabhat/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The Nepal flooding was was the exclamation point on a summer of extremes.’Photograph: Prabin Ranabhat/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepal’s glacial collapse foreshadowed a future of climate disasterMichael MannThe deluge capped a summer of extreme climate events, from deadly heatwaves to wildfires. We must take action nowTue 1 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 05.02 EDTShareFor millennia, the high peaks of the Himalayas were held together by an invisible, frozen cement – permafrost and glacial ice that bound ancient rock into seemingly unshakable fortresses. But as the planet continues to warm, this alpine glue is liquefying.The glacial collapse and deluge in Nepal and Tibet wasnot a freak weather event; it was the structural failure of a mountain itself, nature’s latest commentary on the deadly consequences of human-caused planetary warming. And it was the exclamation point on a summer of extremes, illustrating with a soleunnatural disasterthe apocalyptic future that lies in store if we fail to take dramatic climate action.As the death toll continues to mount –the latest countshowed more than 900 dead and more than 4,400 individuals missing – this event has crystalized the climate crisis for many.One reason is undoubtedly the sheer horror of what unfolded here. Chilling surveillance and eyewitness footagecaptured the horrificmoment a 40mph wall of “liquid concrete” violently overtook fleeing crowds, instantly swallowing entire families and burying them beneath feet of thick, red-soaked silt. Another reason, however, is that the connection with climate change was unassailable in this case.The Nepal floods seem a world away – but make no mistake, climate breakdown will affect us all | Nesrine MalikRead moreThe torrent was the direct result of warming-induced glacial collapse, which dumped millions of tons of rock, unleashing a high-velocity wave of mud and debris. The new reality in the era of human-caused climate change, aCNN headlineput it, is that “living downstream from a glacier has become a deadly liability”.The impact of climate change on extreme weather, by contrast, is usually established though a statistical, rather than direct causal, connection. Through what is known asattribution science, climate scientists demonstrate the influence of climate change on the characteristics of an extreme weather event. It is analogous to how epidemiologists establish a linkage between cause (eg smoking cigarettes) and effect (lung cancer), through massive statistical evidence.In the case of climate attribution, scientists run parallel climate model simulations, including a “control” simulation that represents a counterfactual world without human impact, and a “treatment” simulation where human drivers – primarily the increase in greenhouse gas concentrations – are included. They then compare how often a particular event happens in the two cases. If there is a substantial increase in occurrence of a particular event in the “treatment” simulation relative to the “control” simulation, then the extremeness of the event – and its human, societal or environmental impacts – can be “attributed” to climate change.Critics might say that the connection here is merely statistical – almost circumstantial. But much as we are willing to attribute causality when a lifetime smoker contracts lung cancer because they wereas much as30 times more likely to do so because of their use of tobacco products, the extreme characteristics (unusually massive precipitation totals, high temperatures or destructive winds) of the weather event can be attributed to human-caused warming.While the tragic and deadly Tibetan flood might have been the most prominent climate change-induced disaster this summer, it followed an unprecedented series of deadly, destructive and dangerous extreme weather events that can be connected to rising carbon pollution and the warming of our planet.This summer of extremes began early. It started out with aMarch “heat dome”in the south-western US that yielded extremes of heat we only expect to see in mid-summer. The unprecedented extreme March heat was found by climate scientists to have been “virtually impossible” in the absence of human-caused warming.Then came a midsummer-like May heat dome in the eastern US thatsmashed temperature recordsin my home city of Philadelphia. And within weeks, a European heat dome brought deadly triple-digit temperatures tolarge parts of Franceleading to the deaths of more than 3,000 people in Paris and nearly 6,000 for all of France. That was just the first offour record-breaking, back-to-back heatwavesin Europe that, by summer’s end, has cost the lives of more than 35,000 people. And yes, the deadly heatwas attributedto climate change.The record July heat combined with extreme dryness over large parts of western Europe – particularly France and Spain – to generate catastrophic wildfires that dominated the headlines for weeks, along with aviral photoof vacationers calmly lounging under a colorful umbrella while apocalyptic wildfire smoke billows in the background. The fires forced the evacuation of hundreds of thousands of people from their homes. And at the risk of sounding like a broken record: yes, it wasformally attributedto human-caused warming.Back in the US, we had our own wildfire problems. A combination of very hot and dry conditions over southern Ontario and the upper midwest led to huge wildfires generating plumes of smoke that choked the east coast for weeks. Air qualitywas ratedhazardous in my home city of Philadelphia.Nepal-Tibet flood: this is the cost of not acting in the face of the climate crisis | Sunil AcharyaRead moreAnd yes, these wildfires – and indeed, the Canadian wildfires we now see summer after summer –can be attributedto climate change.The summer of extreme weather disasters wasn’t done with us yet. In mid-August a historic “derecho” (a very wide, fast-moving line of severe thunderstorms associated typically with destructive, hurricane-strength straight-line destructive winds) struck the midwestern US with winds exceeding 100mph and devastating flooding, thebetter part of a millionpeople from Illinois to Virginia were left without power.While it is a challenge to apply attribution methods to these rare events, there is emerging evidence that climate change is making them more frequent and more damaging.This past summer’s collective extreme weather disasters were an unmistakable consequence of the continued warming of our planet. The currentadministration’s policies– which werewritten by pollutersthemselves – are making things worse. Donald Trump and enabling congressional Republicans continue to double down on policies favoring fossil fuel extraction and dependenceat the very timewe need to be moving even more quickly away from fossil fuels toward clean energy.These extreme events underscore the urgency of taking action now, and – while there are many things we can do – one of the greatest opportunities Americans will have to affect climate policy is the upcoming midterm election. You can make support for urgent and dramatic climate action a litmus test issue as you go to the voting booth.Michael Mann is presidential distinguished professor and director of the Penn Center for Science, Sustainability and the Media at the University of Pennsylvania, and co-author with Peter Hotez, of the recent bookScience Under SiegeExplore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterOpinionNepalClimate crisisSouth and central AsiaExtreme weatherWildfiresUS wildfirescommentShareReuse this content

title: Colin Kaepernick knelt 10 years ago. America responded with a clear warning to Black people | Colin Kaepernick | The Guardian
description: A decade after Kaepernick’s quiet protest shook the NFL, his exile looks less like an aberration than a blueprint for the culture war that followed
Author: Howard Bryant
Headline: A decade after Kaepernick’s quiet protest shook the NFL, his exile looks less like an aberration than a blueprint for the culture war that followed
Content: Colin Kaepernick’s protest dominated off field discussion for much of the 2016 NFL season.Composite: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenColin Kaepernick’s protest dominated off field discussion for much of the 2016 NFL season.Composite: Guardian DesignColin KaepernickColin Kaepernick knelt 10 years ago. America responded with a clear warning to Black peopleHoward BryantA decade after Kaepernick’s quiet protest shook the NFL, his exile looks less like an aberration than a blueprint for the culture war that followedTue 1 Sep 2026 03.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 13.50 EDTShareAmerica likes nice round numbers, perfect for anniversaries and reflections, and it has, suddenly, been 10 years sinceColin Kaepernickfirst protested police killings – more accurately, police killings of Black people that went unpunished either internally or by the courts – by taking a knee during the national anthem for the entirety of the 2016 NFL regular season. He never played in the league again.Ten years covers a lot of ground, especially in these years of American darkness, and many of the important details surrounding Kaepernick, his banishment and significance have disappeared, time replaced by more time and more darkness – time moving faster than ever, at internet speed, where nothing matters, where nothing sticks. We consume by clip, by click, by meme, and knowledge by meme is not knowledge at all.Much of the Kaepernick story was reduced to his personal banishment, but second to Barack Obama, Kaepernick is the face that propelled white anger into a “culture war” that continues earnestly into its second decade. It has traveled through the NFL, through Hollywood, the White House, and now iscorroding the WNBA. Obama’s ascent to the White House confirmed the unlikely prospect that a Black person could be elected president, ostensibly the ultimate symbol of American possibility. It was not a universal sentiment.Sophie Cunningham isn’t rejecting politics. She’s cashing in on themRead moreIn the annals of American protest, which has included suffragettes breaking windows, students blocking traffic,Black Panthers armed in public, economic boycotts and marches on Washington, Kaepernick was mild by comparison – he gave voice with 60 seconds of silence. “To me, this is bigger than football and it would be selfish on my part to look the other way,” heexplained on 26 August 2016after a preseason contest between his San Francisco 49ers and the Green Bay Packers (he sat on the bench during the anthem for that game, he would kneel for the first time the following week). “There are bodies in the street and people getting paid leave and getting away with murder.” Combined, however, Obama and Kaepernick represented the realization of the deepest of white fears, the assumptions and expectations of Black equality that has consumed a segment of the collective white American psyche since emancipation.Ten years later, one view of the Kaepernick legacy can be seen through a harsh, retrofitted lens: sports leagues would largely purge the troublemakers and co-opt the protests, reducing them into useless, corporate-friendly gestures; an American electorate that voted Donald Trump into power twice, as his unapologetic, unambiguous racism reflected theirs; media outlets responding in agreement, coalescing around Trump’s whiteness, appeasing their rightsholders, readers and viewers by making the conscious choice – a clear and egregious dereliction of journalistic duty – to silence the voices within who make them uncomfortable; a player class that was never nearly as bold as its greatest legends well aware of Kaepernick’s fate, unwilling to repeat it, and operating as puppets.They didn’t have far to go. While Trump called NFL players “sons of bitches” in his first term and demanded Kaepernick be banned from the league, NFL players undermined him. Dallas Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescottassured his bossesin 2018 that he was no radical, not merely by playing football but demeaning Kaepernick’s protest. “For me, I believe in doing something, action. It’s not about taking a knee,” Prescott said, undermining centuries of evidence to the contrary about the efficacy of physical protest. Even the most devout Cowboys fan could probably not name a single example where Prescott took action. He simply didn’t want to get involved.Michael Vick, ex-convict,killer of dogs, but redeemed by the NFL following his prison sentence, told Kaepernick to “cut his hair” if he sought a pathway to forgiveness. Hall of Famer Ray Lewis told Kaepernick to “keep his mouth shut”. It should be noted that Kaepernick was exiled from the NFL for kneeling –kneeling –while Lewis, connectable to an incident that resulted in two killings as an active player, was fined$250,000 by the NFLfor pleading guilty to obstruction of justice andnever missed a game.View image in fullscreenColin Kaepernick kneels in protest during the national anthem before the San Francisco 49ers’ game against the Los Angeles Rams at Levi’s Stadium in September 2016.Photograph: Robert Reiners/Getty ImagesWhether hostile or oblivious, white Americans have treated this nation as a personal possession they choose to share with others, quite different from a nation that belongs to all that must be shared collectively. This country, Black people know and are harshly reminded by their white countrymen whenever they have the temerity to forget, istheirs,and that proprietorship is codified by the everyday speech of white Americans – Weletyou attendourschools, live inourneighborhoods, be part ofourcommunities, play inourprofessional sports – and is mirrored by Black speech alike. It is the fatal language of integration.Such assumed proprietorship demands white people receive deference for their benevolence, explains their rage when they don’t get it. It also means they believe they can revoke the privilege of being American whenever that proprietorship is challenged, as Kaepernick discovered 10 years ago. The result was a continuum. Kaepernick losing his job has now become a political philosophy at the highest levels of government: Black people have not earned their positions through the grind of hard work, but from diversity initiatives.Only in witnessing the slow-motion murder of George Floyd in 2020 during a global pandemic and the White House overreacting by rolling tanks through town and shooting at white people on the steps of their own houses did the country have a collective moment that it had all gone too far, that Kaepernick had been right all along. Even NFL commissioner Roger Goodell admitted, by pressure not conscience,that the league was wrongin its crackdown on player protest – but only briefly. The simmering hostility, never quieted, has increased anew.The January 6 riotsended the periodknown as athlete activism, and in the wider sense, the Kaepernick era. They also ended whatever shreds of credibility remained from this nation of laws, and exposed the players as having surrendered. Wired to accept challenges and refuse defeat, the players were finally vindicated as hordes of white, real Americans, the ones who told them therewere other ways to protest, wore T-shirts tostand for the flag and kneel for the cross,countered the Black Lives Matter protest without cleverness or style withBlue Lives Matter,and–at the order of the President of the United States – stormed the most symbolically important legislative building in the world. The players – perhaps mollified by Goodell’s apology, or Obama’s advice to NBA players to stop their protests after a weekend work stoppage following Jacob Blake’s shooting in Kenosha, general fatigue or knowing they were overmatched – didn’t say a thing. A cop – a member of that sacred occupation for which they ostensibly held so much respect –died in the aftermathof the January 6 riot. The mob ransacked the Capitol, and the American media tripped over itself debating whether to even call it a riot. It made sense. This istheirs, and you cannot trespass or riot on your own property.There is the lesson of Kaepernick and there is his legacy. They are not the same. The lesson was largely directed toward other players. It was a threat. Kaepernick was the NFL’s Metacomet at Plymouth, head on a stake for the world to see, a warning for the rest to stay in line – and they have. What passes for protest today is a player writing something mildly profound on their cleats, but only on the designated game days when theNFLallows it.The devastating rest is the legacy, far darker and yet in its own sense inspiring. The inspiration lies in the freedom of acknowledgment. There is no reason to continue the naive exercise of negotiation, of waiting for permission, of believing the moral arc of the universe bends toward justice, of believing equality is a shared American goal. It is not. What the country has become in these 10 years,with its 1,500 pardons, the proud anti-Blackness from this White House, the malleable ethics of a cowering corporate media that has largely stamped out the voices it once embraced as a “racial reckoning” – has proven it. Look at the wreckage.Howard Bryant is the author of 11 books, including The Heritage: Black Athletes, A Divided America, and the Politics of Patriotism and Kings and Pawns: Jackie Robinson and Paul Robeson in America.Explore more on these topicsColin KaepernickNFLUS sportsGeorge FloydRoger GoodellBarack ObamaJacob BlakecommentShareReuse this content

title: How misconceptions and woeful PR allowed Musk to shred USAID so easily | Jeremiah A Carew | The Guardian
description: A year on from the purge, with thousands of jobs cut and billions in foreign aid lost, a former leader reflects on the sorry saga – and why it would never happen to Nasa
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A year on from the purge, with thousands of jobs cut and billions in foreign aid lost, a former leader reflects on the sorry saga – and why it would never happen to Nasa
Content: Protesters in Washington march in support of USAID in February 2025.Photograph: Drew Angerer/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenProtesters in Washington march in support of USAID in February 2025.Photograph: Drew Angerer/AFP/GettyOpinionGlobal developmentHow misconceptions and woeful PR allowed Musk to shred USAID so easilyJeremiah A CarewA year on from the purge, with thousands of jobs cut and billions in foreign aid lost, a former leader reflects on the sorry saga – and why it would never happen to NasaTue 1 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTShareAyear has passed since I and thousands of colleagues lost our jobs atUSAID. Asking myself “Why us?” I have come to the conclusion that the American public had very little idea of what we were doing and why.Doge, the “department of government efficiency”, began its work in January 2025, with USAID as its first target, in a reckless campaign that even ElonMusk has said he would not repeat. At that moment of chaos, Americans lacked the knowledge that could contradict thefalse narrative presented by Musk, who called the agency a “criminal organisation” and “aviper’s nest of radical left-marxistswho hate America”.But what if Doge had eliminatedNasa, not USAID? Such a scenario seems highly implausible. Despite the rise of private space companies, Nasa remains an icon of national prestige, with broad bipartisan congressional support. How many kids want to be astronauts when they grow up? I sure did. And that’s because Nasa has spent decades carefully communicating its results and cultivating its image with the public.In contrast, USAID is not well known or understood. One expert on USAID’s brand noted that the agency’s handclasp emblem and the tagline “from the American people” were “well known in the developing world, even if not well known in Washington”. How much worse is that brand recognition in middle America?Misunderstandings around foreign aid abound. In March 2025, aKaiser Family Foundation survey reported: “Nearly nine in 10 (86%) adults overestimate the share of the federal budget spent on foreign aid, saying on average that the US spends about a quarter (26%) of its budget on foreign aid.” In fact, about 1% of the federal budget goes on foreign aid.Unfortunately, that lack of recognition and those gross misunderstandings were key factors in USAID’s elimination. It may never be resurrected, but the question remains important: what could future foreign assistance learn from Nasa’s approach to public communications, to ensure broad public understanding and support?Without a doubt, stories were there to be told. In Colombia, where I was deputy director of the largest USAID mission in the hemisphere from 2021 to 2025, we contributed to solving major regional challenges. We helped tens of thousands of Venezuelans take advantage of generous Colombian migration policies by processing legal residency cards, training them for jobs and establishing healthcare access. That meant they could stay in Colombia legally, rather than add to the thousands of migrants trying to enter the US.View image in fullscreenA community kitchen set up by USAID and the World Food Programme in Cucuta, Colombia, 2019.Photograph: Marco Bello/ReutersWe guaranteed hundreds of millions of dollars in loans Colombian banks made to new businesses. These businesses promoted tropical forest products such as açaí to keep the Amazon’s trees standing. Other loans helped poor farmers build businesses with legal crops instead of coca, which is turned into cocaine, causing addiction and death in the US and Europe. These loan-guarantee programmes cost the US government pennies on the dollar to reduce risk so that Colombian banks would extend their loans to new, unfamiliar businesses.And after Colombia’s government successfully negotiated a historic peace accord in 2016, ending 50 years of civil conflict, USAID was the largest donor to help them implement it. Among many things, that meant helping prosecutors gather testimony from thousands of victims of violence so the truth could be told and justice done.When fighters turned in their guns to lead peaceful lives, efforts such as ours helped Colombians achieve some form of reconciliation and turn the page.These are not simple stories to tell. As these examples illustrate, real development work is not handing out goodies for a photo op. It is making strategic nudges to a country’s own efforts to do the things that solve global challenges – illegal migration, climate breakdown, illegal drugs and yes, world peace – while reflecting its national interest.Telling USAID’s story to the American public accurately – describing projects far from home, in complex and unfamiliar foreign contexts – is challenging.Yet faced with its own challenges in communicating technically complex scientific work performed thousands of miles from home, Nasa succeeded where USAID failed. The 2014 book Marketing the Moon, by David Meerman Scott and Richard Jurek, focuses on the Apollo programme, when 94% of American televisions were tuned to the first lunar landing. They argue that “without strong public support abetted by high-profile, enthusiastic public relations, the entire achievement and its funding would have been unthinkable”.Echoes of these strategies are still seen, and Nasa still excels in communicating with the public. There are three ways it does this:Helping voters understandRather than use woolly phrases such as “capacity building” and “democracy strengthening”, as we did at USAID, Nasa goes to great efforts to help viewers grasp what it is doing. Computer visualisations and animations show orbits and flight paths. Saying a Mars rover is “about the size of a small SUV” explains in everyday terms what its scientists have built. The media are willing allies to show these graphics and allow Nasa spokespeople to explain the mission and its impact.Telling stories that link tothe US’s highest national aspirationsIn the Apollo programme, astronauts became superheroes, signing exclusive agreements with Life magazine to profile them. On unmanned missions, Nasa has linked its efforts to timeless questions of science: was there water on Mars, for instance, and did it support life? As its website says: “For more than 65 years, Nasa has made the seemingly impossible, possible.” Nasa has connected its work to national pride, reminding Americans of its cutting-edge science, world-class innovative tech and heroic astronauts.View image in fullscreenThe Nasa headquarters in Washington DC.Photograph: Kevin Carter/Getty ImagesTalking about positive side-effectsNasa is highly vocal about how technology developed for space missions has been repurposed for everyday use and benefited our lives, from memory foam to infrared ear thermometers to cordless tools. Given the prestige associated with Nasa, there is even a small cottage industry of inventions that are falsely attributed to the space programme, such as lasers, Velcro and Teflon.Decades of effective PR and brand recognition may not have been enough to overcome the onslaught of misinformation that USAID faced in 2025. Its international focus – on cultures and contexts completely unfamiliar to Americans – made it vulnerable. The sheer quantity of projects made it easy to find some that would appear indefensible, so when the attacks did come, the gas tank of “brand equity” was nearly empty and the public outcry was muted, with many only just learning of the agency’s existence. USAID was shuttered with startling speed.When an information vacuum allows Americans to overestimate how much of the federal budget goes to foreign assistance, they fail to see it for the bargain it truly is for our nation. Americans spend several times more on pet food and treats than the government did on USAID. What USAID spent on some aid programmes in a year was the equivalent of a few dozen Patriot missiles.In short, as the US aspires to be a great nation – generous, admired and strategic in solving global challenges – the work USAID did seems an absolute bargain. As we reimagine what foreign assistance looks like, let’s be more like Nasa, communicating that value and making Americans proud.Jeremiah A Carew was a senior Foreign Service Officer for USAID; his final tour was as deputy mission director of USAID/Colombia from 2021 until the mission’s closing in 2025.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentOpinionUSAIDAidElon MuskUS politicsUS foreign policyTrump administrationcommentShareReuse this content

title: Populist One Nation’s latest victory points to a thirst for unity. But there are better ways to feel connected | Peter Lewis | The Guardian
description: When we last polled attitudes to membership, I argued the first act of resistance is to join something. Ten years on, that project is even more urgent
Author: Peter Lewis
Headline: When we last polled attitudes to membership, I argued the first act of resistance is to join something. Ten years on, that project is even more urgent
Content: ‘Like other populist movements around the globe, One Nation is rising at a time of social atomisation and isolation.’Photograph: Jessica Hromas/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Like other populist movements around the globe, One Nation is rising at a time of social atomisation and isolation.’Photograph: Jessica Hromas/The GuardianOpinionEssential pollPopulist One Nation’s latest victory points to a thirst for unity. But there are better ways to feel connectedPeter LewisWhen we last polled attitudes to membership, I argued the first act of resistance is to join something. Ten years on, that project is even more urgentGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastTue 1 Sep 2026 19.23 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 20.06 EDTShareOne Nation’sbyelection win at Secret Harbouron the weekend can be dismissed as the result of the politics of anger and exclusion, but if we are serious about understanding the surge in support for Pauline Hanson’s party, we should also recognise a nostalgia for belonging and shared identity. At a time when people are feeling more distant from their leaders and each other, the party’s name seems to offer a patriotic resistance to the status quo.Like other populist movements around the globe,One Nationis rising at a time of social atomisation and isolation. This week’s Guardian Essential report shows this plainly: fewer people are joining things. One-third of those surveyed have never joined anything, ever.Table titled: Are you currently a member or have you ever been a member of any of the following groups?The last time we asked this question was a decade ago in the shock and fug after Trump’s first election win;at the time, I noted thatthe shift away from membership was undermining our faith in an increasingly remote political system.These trends have only been accelerated by technology: the growth of the gig economy, algorithms that reduce citizens to universes of one, and now emerging applications of AI such as personal agents and intimate companions.One Nation is dismissed as divisive, discriminatory and dangerous, but there is an alternate narrative running through theirdisarmingly effective “Please Explain” propaganda cartoons: progressives are the ones dividing the nation into warring identities and turning people against each other. One Nation is here to unite the common people against the elites.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailTake away the red hair and you could be describing the mission of the Australian trade union movement, which emerged as a response to the excesses of the Industrial Revolution (and for its first 75 years displayed asimilarly nativist bent).The Australian union movement was built on the struggles of shearers and miners to first resist the oppressive power of the bosses and then to shape the political system through elected representatives.At its peak in 1975, the movement represented about 60% of the workforce; today it is in the low teens with private-sector coverage in the single digits. The reasons for this are varied: structural shifts from large blue-collar factories, active deunionisation drives, and the shift from permanent to contract labour.Despite this, the majority of Australians still see unions as playing an important role, with 60% saying unions are important for working people today (more than four times the actual membership levels).Table titled: How important are unions for Australian working people today?As a new wave of technological disruption hits, the leadership of theAustralian union movement is in its own transitionwith Sally McManus and Michele O’Neil handing over power to a new generation after close to a decade of fighting the good fight.They leave a movement in a contradictory state, with deep institutional influence within a centre-left government that has a strong hold on power but a membership density at historically low levels.The battle over AI adoption will be fought on multiple fronts, including the workplace, and the different approaches of the union movement and One Nation will be decisive. Whether its wages, job security or the actual deployment of these tools, Australians are already on red alert.Table titled: Thinking about your working life over the next five years, to what extent are you concerned about the following?Early legislative skirmishes are already emerging; fromroutine worker surveillanceto thewholesale theft of creative worksto new forms ofworker control and exploitation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEach demands a level of support for workers’ rights absent fromHanson’s parliamentary voting recordover 30 years where she has reflexively sided with big business and those holding the levers of economic power.Whether it’s nurses or retail workers, home-delivery drivers or teachers, workers will be the canaries in the coalmine when the technology is dangerous, destructive or just plain dumb.The good news is unions are not alone. The Catholic church, buoyed up byPope Leo’s intervention, is entering the fray,gender advocatesare demanding control of their algorithms and theenvironment movementis waking up to the energy demands of datacentres. From here we can see the beginnings of a broader national movement that is neither nativist nor reactionary.One Nation’s Secret Harbour byelection win shows Labor is at a loss when it comes to calming angry voters | AnalysisRead moreWhen we last polled attitudes to membership, I argued the first act of resistance is to join something. Ten years on, that project is even more urgent.From there comes the power to organise and engage and, where necessary, demand governments intervene, such as withMeta’s “pervert glasses”which have finally prompted real progress this week on privacy law reform.The final challenge is not to cede our future to those with authority. As Pope Leostresses in his encyclical: the source of power comes from the ground up, what he calls “subsidiarity”, an idea that resembles the network of workplace delegates, shop stewards and elected organisers that were the hallmark of the union movement at its zenith.The future is not going to write itself. If we didn’t have workers with enforceable legal rights, we would need to invent them. Unions are the bedrock from which a real resistance to oppressive power can grow.If not, we will cede the common ground to the likes of Pauline and Barnaby, sponsored by a billionaire, with no unifying principle apart from a sense of grievance and a track record of voting against the interests of the people they claim to unite.Peter Lewis is the executive director of Essential, a progressive strategic communications and research company that undertook qualitative research for Labor in the last federal election. He is the host ofBurning Platforms, a weekly podcast focusing on the politics of technology. title: Burnham’s ambitious plans need room to breathe – and Westminster suffocates change  | Rafael Behr | The Guardian
description: A summer on the road suited the prime minister’s open style, but now the walls of conventional politics are closing in, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Author: Rafael Behr
Headline: A summer on the road suited the prime minister’s open style, but now the walls of conventional politics are closing in, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Content: Andy Burnham leaving No 10 to address the House of Commons, London, 1 September 2026.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham leaving No 10 to address the House of Commons, London, 1 September 2026.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesOpinionAndy BurnhamBurnham’s ambitious plans need room to breathe – and Westminster suffocates changeRafael BehrA summer on the road suited the prime minister’s open style, but now the walls of conventional politics are closing inTue 1 Sep 2026 12.46 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 14.08 EDTShareNothing stays fresh for long in parliament and no one sounds normal. The air, thick with convention, suffocates originality, tuning every voice to the same Westminster pitch. The need to escape that climate is one reason whyAndy Burnhamquit his Commons seat to run for mayor of Greater Manchester. Or that is how he tells the story.Returning after nearly a decade away, the prime minister says he wants to throw open the windows, let in some air. He thinks devolution can cultivate a healthier political culture. He intends to rebalance England’s centre of gravity with apower basein the new No 10 North.The timing of Burnham’s arrival in Downing Street, just before the summer recess, suited those arguments. He replaced Keir Starmer, thenpromptly went on tour, posting chatty videos on social media, appearing as the antidote to a stuffy predecessor who, perhaps unfairly, had come to be seen as the archetypal Westminster mechanoid. Starmer, who todayannounced his intentionto stand down as an MP, may find his authentic voice on the outside.Meanwhile, Burnham has to bring his free-range prime minister act into the battery farm of the Commons. His mandate and legislative programme are inherited from the Starmer era. He is stuck with the same squeezed budgets in the same sluggish economy imperilled by the same turbulent global climate. His room for fiscal manoeuvre is constrained by Labour’s 2024 manifesto prohibition on broad-based tax rises and by the bond market’s punitive vigilance towards anything that looks like undisciplined spending.In such conditions, politics is reduced to a zero-sum competition for scarce resources. Every promise made to satisfy the needs of one department or constituency contains an undeclared threat to deprive someone else.Starmer’s leadership was ruined by many things, but few were as crippling as his failure to grapple with those dilemmas. He wouldn’t pick sides between irreconcilable demands within his cabinet. When his own ministers couldn’t read his political instincts or decrypt his priorities, the public had no chance. It was a recipe for paralysis, delivering a congealed gruel of continuity to voters who thought they had ordered piping hot change.Determination not to repeat that mistake has shaped Burnham’s approach from his first moments in office. He declared a moral mission – the elimination of rough sleeping – before even crossing the threshold of No 10. He followed it up with emblematic policies to demonstrate that regime change brought a new focus on the cost of living.No one in Downing Street pretends that capping bus fares or cutting VAT on fuel bills is enough to win affection from a sceptical public. The function of modest retail policies is to show that Labour, renewed by fresh leadership, has snapped out of despondency and started listening. Abounce in opinion pollssuggests it is working.But the transition from small-change symbols to big-ticket policy choices is not easy.It is especially hard if the prime minister is conflict averse and prone to flights of empathic urgency. That is the hazard flagged by Burnham’s critics, based on observation of his career as a minister in the New Labour government and later as Manchester mayor. They are traits that generate spontaneous promises that later have to be diluted or retracted.View image in fullscreenA cushion on a chair in Andy Burnham’s office at No 10 North, Manchester, 20 August 2026.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianIn June, Burnham got himself into just such a tangle over acommitment to compensate“Waspi women” who feel they were mistreated by the Department for Work and Pensions when their retirement age was raised. In May, he told a campaigner for party finance reform that he supported the principle of a cap on donations to guard against big money exerting undue influence in politics. A cap has been proposed as an amendment to the representation of the people bill, currently on its way through parliament. But the government, following trade union lobbying,is not backingthe move.The learning curve for any new prime minister is brutally steep.Things that seem obvious from outside No 10 are revealed to be fearsomely complex. What seems compelling on the campaign trail can feel like a ruinous drain on time and political capital in government. The road is especially hard to navigate for those who arrive midterm, scrambling over unfinished and unpopular business bequeathed by an ousted predecessor.The retreat from plans to free up prison capacity by releasing offenders early is a revealing case. Burnham understandably doesn’t want his first months in office marred by a parade of stories about villains walking free. But swerving unfriendly headlines isn’t a plan for reforming the justice system or growing its shrivelled budget.Likewise, the prime minister’sappearance in Kyivto celebrate Ukraine’s independence day, while important as a display of solidarity with Volodymyr Zelenskyy, came with no account of the sacrifices Britain faces as the price of ramping up its own defences against Russian aggression.No one is better briefed on that challenge than the chancellor. As defence secretary, John Healey resigned from Starmer’s government in protest at the former prime minister’s reluctance to boost military spending. Relocated to the Treasury, he finds himselfmanaging a downgradein rearmament expectations ahead of the autumn budget.The seasonal migration of politics back to parliament threatens a sudden narrowing of Burnham’s options. The prime minister has a theory to counter that threat. His argument is that devolution, as well as bringing fresh air to politics, spurs economic growth.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLoosening the dead hand of Whitehall control over public services is supposed to promote innovation and efficiency. A more responsive government, attuned to local market conditions, will unlock investment.Assuming that can work, the mechanism is slow. Burnham accepts that it is a 10-year plan. The opposition calculates that the fiscal walls will close in on Labour a lot faster than that.Kemi Badenoch thinksthe economy is the issuethat will rehabilitate Tory fortunes. To sharpen her attack on that front, she hassacked her shadow chancellor, Mel Stride, for insufficient pugnacity with the Treasury brief. His replacement, Andrew Griffith, is deemed more dynamic, a quality he oncedisplayed in cheerleadingfor Liz Truss’s disastrous 2022 “mini-budget”.Defence spending is an insatiable beast. John Healey is right to tame it | John McTernanRead moreIn Badenoch’s view, Burnham is a “people-pleaser” who lacks the resolve to whip his MPs behind tough budget choices. He will rely on tax rises to pay for policies that the left see as essential maintenance to the social safety net and the right decry as profligate subsidy for fecklessness. The impossibility of feeding Labour’s big-government appetite with hands shackled by the 2024 manifesto will force the prime minister to seek his own mandate with an early election.It is a plausible scenario. It is also unclear how the Tories get match fit on that timetable when they are running third in national polls. Badenoch’s personal ratings aren’t so bad, but she lacks insight into the reasons why so many voters think her party is unfit to govern. Discounting Griffith’s contamination by the Truss project when appointing a shadow chancellor is a symptom of that blind spot.The Tories are flattered into feeling relevant by a sympathetic press and the constitutional crutch of official opposition status. In parliamentary arithmetic, theConservativesstill eclipse Reform UK.Badenoch welcomes the enclosure of politics in the Commons chamber as much as the Labour leader resists it. The theatre of ritual combat is more her style than his. But the prime minister’s judgment is better in thinking voters are turned off by the whole spectacle. Burnham’s fresh manner has breathed life into a government that was expiring. It will take a different order of political skill to dispel the older miasma of cumulative failure that hangs heavy over Westminster.Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
