title: Forget T-maxxing – the manosphere’s obsession with testosterone is just fear-maxxing | Donna Lu | The Guardian
description: Testosterone replacement therapy comes with serious and potentially irreversible health risks including infertility and early heart disease
Author: Donna Lu
Headline: Testosterone replacement therapy comes with serious and potentially irreversible health risks including infertility and early heart disease
Content: ‘Low testosterone is being blamed in the rightwing manosphere for a crisis of masculinity,’ writes Donna Lu. ‘But the fixation on T-maxxing ignores hard evidence.’Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Low testosterone is being blamed in the rightwing manosphere for a crisis of masculinity,’ writes Donna Lu. ‘But the fixation on T-maxxing ignores hard evidence.’Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesAntiviralMen's healthForget T-maxxing – the manosphere’s obsession with testosterone is just fear-maxxingDonna LuTestosterone replacement therapy comes with serious and potentially irreversible health risks including infertility and early heart diseaseRead more in theAntiviral seriesTue 1 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 19.22 EDTShareAre you tired? Feeling flat and irritable? Finding it difficult to concentrate? Maybe you’re experiencing the seemingly ubiquitous symptoms ofmodern life. Or, if you’re a man, you may have been told by countless uncredentialed online influencers that you’re probably suffering from “low T”.For decades, testosterone has been marketed to men as a means to maximise virility. But in recent years, social media has fuelled the “T-maxxing” trend, in which men are encouraged to maximise their testosterone levels through either natural or artificial means.Low testosterone is being blamed in the rightwing manosphere for acrisis of masculinity; global search interest in the term is up60% from last year.‘Manosphere’ influencers pushing testosterone tests are convincing healthy young men there is something wrong with them, study findsRead morePopular podcasters such asJoe RoganandAndrew Hubermanopenly talk about taking testosterone, as has the 72-year-old Robert F Kennedy Jr, who has said he uses testosterone replacement therapy as part of an “anti-ageing protocol”.Elsewhere in the Trump administration, the US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, announced in July that soldiers 30 and over would betested annuallyto ensure they have the “right testosterone levels”.Social media is awash with testimonies from men on testosterone replacement therapy who say they have lost weight and regained energy, motivation and libido. Prescriptions for testosterone in theUKandUShave risen sharply in recent years.But the fixation on T-maxxing ignores hard evidence: very few men actually have clinically low levels of the sex hormone, and taking exogenous testosterone – through injections or gels – comes with serious and potentially irreversible health risks, especially when treatment is unwarranted.‘Fearmongering’ in the manosphereTestosterone is a steroid hormone we all produce, but is naturally found at higher levels in men.Testosterone levels fluctuate throughout the lifetime, says Prof Ada Cheung, an endocrinologist at the University of Melbourne.Population-based studies show that testosterone rises rapidly during male puberty and that over time “it does tend to decline a bit with age”, she says. “That decline with age we think is largely attributed to the accumulation of chronic health conditions as we get older” – conditions such as obesity, diabetes, high cholesterol and blood pressure. “But it doesn’t mean that every older man needs testosterone [treatment], because that’s not the case at all.”Testosterone levels also vary through the day and in response to physical stressors such as illness and poor sleep. “It’s always low in the afternoon and highest first thing in the morning,” Cheung says. “Testosterone naturally varies when we eat … and if we’re sick in any way.”Research suggests that average testosterone levels in men havedeclined over the last five decades, though they remain within normal reference ranges. Experts, Cheung included, believe the trend may be at least partly explained by lifestyle habits, stress, chronic disease and rising obesity.Clinically low testosterone – also known as male hypogonadism – is “actually pretty uncommon”, Cheung says. “Less than 2% [of men] would have clinical hypogonadism.” It can can be caused by genetic conditions such as Klinefelter syndrome, or conditions that affect the pituitary gland in the brain, which regulates sex hormone production.“Why people often get confused is that the symptoms of low testosterone are very non-specific, like fatigue, low mood, poor concentration, erectile dysfunction, low motivation,” Cheung says. Far more commonly, she points out, these issues are caused by other factors, such as stress, depression, obesity, and iron or thyroid issues.But these symptoms are frequently used to promote testosterone screening and treatments on social media, says Dr Brooke Nickel, a senior research fellow at the University of Sydney’s school of public health.Research she co-authored, published in January in the journalSocial Science & Medicine, found that young men are being aggressively marketed to by testosterone influencers and wellness companies. Their analysis of 46 popular posts – from accounts with a total following of 6.8 million and which had amassed a combined 659,000 likes – found that nearly three-quarters of accounts had vested financial interests, such as being the sellers of testosterone tests and therapies.“The narratives that they were discussing were closely mirrored to those promoted within the manosphere, where hormone levels were being presented as a measure of manhood,” she says.Testosterone tests, they found, were primarily targeting younger men – a group for which mass screening for low testosterone is medically unwarranted. None of the posts, unsurprisingly, presented any evidence to support claims made.Nickel describes such posts as “fearmongering” – using common experiences to suggest “there’s something medically wrong and that testosterone is a solution”.What are the health risks of taking testosterone?“Once you start testosterone and you are on it for a while, it’s very hard to wean. It’s not just a short-term thing,” Cheung says. Taking testosterone shuts off the body’s natural production of the hormone, as well as sperm production.The American “looksmaxxer” Braden Peters, also known as Clavicular, isby his own admission infertilefrom steroid abuse.“People can become infertile and it can take months to years to recover – and the recovery is not always guaranteed, which is probably one of the most serious concerns,” Cheung says.Doctorshave reportedpeople taking testosterone presenting with gynaecomastia, (male breast enlargement), severe atrophy of the testicles, and early heart disease. Testosterone replacement therapy also increases the risk of blood clots.For patients who do have clinical hypogonadism, “it’s often a lifelong commitment when we start treating someone with testosterone therapy”, Cheung says. “It can lead to things like sleep apnoea, acne, prostate issues, urinary difficulties, mood and libido fluctuations, so it’s not without risk.”‘Not approved for human use’: the online frenzy for injectable peptides sweeping AustraliaRead moreMen frustrated by barriers like financial costs and stigma when seeking out testosterone through regulated medical channels have reported getting the hormone through underground sources with relative ease, Australianresearch has found.That poses its own health risks:Australian testingof anabolic steroids obtained from underground markets has found traces of carcinogenic heavy metals such as lead, arsenic and cadmium, as well as product mislabelling.If men are concerned about symptoms and believe low testosterone may be an issue, they should contact a health practitioner, Cheung says. “If you’re worried, go and see your GP and have a conversation, rather than listening to someone trying to tell you something on social media.”Donna Lu is an assistant editor, climate, environment and science at Guardian Australia.Antiviralis a fortnightly column that interrogates the evidence behind the health headlines and factchecks popular wellness claimsAsk AntiviralWhat health trend do you want examined?Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. title: The rich and powerful are already trying to sway the next election – I have a plan to stop them | Stella Creasy | The Guardian
description: A bill proposing a cap on donations is up for debate this week. We must seize this chance to keep big money out of our politics, says MP Stella Creasy
Author: Stella Creasy
Headline: A bill proposing a cap on donations is up for debate this week. We must seize this chance to keep big money out of our politics, says MP Stella Creasy
Content: ‘On Wednesday, the representation of the people bill will come before parliament.’Photograph: Niklas Halle’n/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘On Wednesday, the representation of the people bill will come before parliament.’Photograph: Niklas Halle’n/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionParty fundingThe rich and powerful are already trying to sway the next election – I have a plan to stop themStella CreasyA bill proposing a cap on donations is up for debate this week. We must seize this chance to keep big money out of our politicsTue 1 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 11.31 EDTShareChristopher Harborne gave Reform£9m in one day– more than double the amount all trade unions combined gave Labour nationally and its MPs directly for the entirety of the last general election. Once such “largesse” in our politics was rare, now it is commonplace. In 2015, just1% of donationswere from individuals and companies giving £1m or more – by 2024, that figure was a third. The chequebooks of the rich and powerful are already circling the next election. The question for Labour is, are we prepared to pay the price if we refuse to stop them?The prime minister deserves credit for recognising how toxic this has become and the public support for action too. As a result, on Wednesday, measures to cap what overseas donors can give will come before parliament in the representation of the people bill. Yet focusing on location rather than the level of a donation misses how wealthy individuals can set up a UK shell company or use a UK postcode to continue to dominate our democracy. With several British millionaires already funding political entities and parties and others waiting in the wings, our goal must be to ensure no one – near or far – can buy Westminster.Labour is yet to commit to this because some are uneasy that capping individual donations could lead to calls to cap collective donations from membership organisations and trade unions. This is not the first time this fear has led to inaction. ThePhillips review of party funding in 2007collapsed over this dilemma, despite support from major Labour donors including Lord Sainsbury for a cap. With hindsight, we can see how this opened the door for the crisis we now face.That is why I have proposed an amendment to the bill – new clause 120 – that would introduce an immediate £500,000 annual cap on donations, falling to £100,000 in the following calendar year. This would give the government until the end of the second year to establish a permanent cap. Whatever level is ultimately chosen could not exceed £500,000 and would have to be approved by parliament, giving all MPs the chance to shape the final scheme.Critically NC120 explicitly exempts trade unions from the cap if they abide by the existing rules around political funds. Thousands of working people pooling their contributions through a democratic membership organisation is not the same as one extraordinarily wealthy individual writing a cheque for millions of pounds. Since 1913, there has been legislation on how trade union funds can be used – making the comparative lack of parity in how we regulate moneys given by companies and individuals even more startling.Most of us could never dream of having £100,000 to give to a political party. We make ourselves heard by voting, campaigning, volunteering, joining political parties and organising collectively. Safeguarding such organisations on all parts of the political spectrum is therefore also part of a healthy democracy because they allow people who could never wield significant financial power individually to act together.The government has now said it will consider lowering the amount of money political parties are permitted to spend. This is welcome if it happens, but is only half the solution to stopping the voices of ordinary people from being increasingly drowned out by those of billionaires and big business. Without a donation cap, too, donors will circumvent rules by using local groups, parties will stockpile funds and enforcement will be retrospective at best.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionArms and the £5m man: Farage megadonor Christopher Harborne’s military empireRead moreIf passed, the proposal coming before parliament would mean the government would not have to agree on the formal limit now. We would only have to agree that there should be one for all donors – whatever passport they hold – and to act before the next election. Such a deadline would also prevent disagreement about details becoming a convenient excuse for doing nothing at all.In common with Donald Trump, Nigel Farage is clear he intends to keep taking the sums in question and celebrates those giving. Inevitably, when political parties can accept unlimited individual donations, politics degenerates into a fundraising arms race. One party attracts a multimillion-pound donor, so another goes searching for its own to be able to compete.As a democratic as well as socialist movement,Labourcannot stand by as our democracy disintegrates under these pressures. Opposing donation caps is at odds with helping to organise the will of working people against the dominance of capital. Political power should not simply belong to whoever has the most money. Without a meaningful cap, each new quarterly donation report for Westminster politics will provide another nail in the coffin for our hopes of doing things differently. If we fail to seize this moment, the largest wallets will become the loudest voices in deciding Britain’s future.Stella Creasy is Labour and Cooperative MP for WalthamstowExplore more on these topicsParty fundingOpinionReform UKChristopher HarborneLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: Happy 60th anniversary, Notting Hill carnival – a symbol of all that London can be | Sadiq Khan | The Guardian
description: Its founders understood the power of culture to challenge racism, build understanding and turn strangers into neighbours. We need that now as much as ever, says London mayor Sadiq Khan
Author: Sadiq Khan
Headline: Its founders understood the power of culture to challenge racism, build understanding and turn strangers into neighbours. We need that now as much as ever, says London mayor Sadiq Khan
Content: Notting Hill carnival 2026 in London, 31 August 2026.Photograph: Krisztián Elek/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenNotting Hill carnival 2026 in London, 31 August 2026.Photograph: Krisztián Elek/SOPA Images/ShutterstockOpinionNotting Hill carnivalHappy 60th anniversary, Notting Hill carnival – a symbol of all that London can beSadiq KhanIts founders understood the power of culture to challenge racism, build understanding and turn strangers into neighbours. We need that now as much as everSadiq Khan is the mayor of LondonTue 1 Sep 2026 06.15 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 06.19 EDTShareThis bank holiday weekend, the streets of Notting Hill once again set the stage for one of the greatest celebrations on Earth.Children danced through the streets in a blaze of colour. Costume-makers with deft fingers created masterpieces from feathers, sequins and gems. Street vendors served up world-class pepperpot, Trinidadian roti and jerk chicken, and sound systems and steelpan bands shook the streets with the unmistakable sound of carnival.On its 60th anniversary,Notting Hill carnivalproved itself to be bigger, bolder and more vibrant than ever. It’s now the world’s second-largest street festival, attracting people from around the globe and generating a whopping £400m for our economy each year.But carnival has always been much more than just a party. It’s a loud and proud celebration of Caribbean culture and the extraordinary contribution that Caribbean communities have made to our capital city. For me, it representsLondonat its very best: people of different ages, backgrounds, colours and creeds coming together, sharing in the joy of one another’s traditions and cultures, and celebrating the incredible diversity that has come to define the city we all call home.View image in fullscreenNotting Hill carnival, 31 August 2026.Photograph: Alberto Pezzali/APThat’s why I was delighted to step forward with an additional £4.66m of funding – more than triple the amount we provided last year – to help ensure Londoners and visitors could once again enjoy this incredible event. The money we made available was vital for supporting organisers to implement increased safety measures, including doubling the number of stewards and allowing more signs and temporary CCTV cameras to be installed.The 60th anniversary of carnival is a landmark moment for London and I was determined City Hall should pull out all the stops to assist because it’s also a reminder of how far we’ve come as a city.From the late 1940s, thousands of Caribbean migrants sailed to London as part of theWindrush generation, to help rebuild a postwar nation on its knees. Despite coming at Britain’s invitation, however, many of the new arrivals found themselves unwelcome in their new home. Forced to live in cramped, poor-quality housing, they were frequently excluded from public spaces and jobs, and subjected to widespread racism and abuse – fuelled by the far right and fascist groups who sought to stir up hatred and division.In 1958, racist violence erupted on the streets of Notting Hill, with Black Londoners attacked and homes damaged. The following year, Black Londoners across the city demanded justice after the police failed to properly investigate the racist murder ofKelso Cochrane, a young carpenter from Antigua.It was in the face of this appalling racism and violence thatthe seeds of carnivalwere planted. First, Trinidadian activist and journalistClaudia Jonesdecided to organise Britain’s first Caribbean carnival at St Pancras town hall. Broadcast on the BBC, the carnival used the power of music and dance to help heal a hurting community and show the rest of the country the richness and joy of Caribbean culture.A few years later, local activistRhaune Laslettorganised a community fair designed to bring her diverse Notting Hill neighbourhood together. It was then that something magical happened. As their set finished, Russ Henderson and his steelpan band carried on playing as they walked up Portobello Road, taking the crowd with them. A neighbourhood party became a street procession – and the rest, as they say, is history.View image in fullscreenDancers at Notting Hill carnival on 30 August 2026.Photograph: Krisztián Elek/SOPA Images/ShutterstockSixty years later, the seeds planted by Claudia, Rhaune, Russ and countless others have grown into something extraordinary. Today, London without carnival is almost impossible to imagine. It’s become a much-loved fixture of our city’s cultural calendar, and for many Londoners, one of the most highly anticipated weekends of the year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut as the event has grown, the challenge of keeping carnival-goers safe has grown with it. That’s why this year I again stepped in to provide the necessary funding to support the delivery of a safer carnival. And let me be clear: as long as I’m mayor, carnival will remain where the local community wants it to be – on the streets of Notting Hill.Our city has come a long way since those first celebrations. But we know that racism has not disappeared. Indeed, the frightening rise of nativist populist movements in recent years demonstrates that the urgent work of tackling prejudice and building a fairer city is far from finished.But what carnival’s founders understood is the extraordinary power of culture: to challenge racism, build understanding and turn strangers into neighbours. They responded to a moment of division and fear with unadulterated joy – and in doing so, they helped shape a more open and inclusive London for all of us.So to everyone who has carried carnival forward over the past 60 years – the pioneers, organisers, masqueraders, musicians, costume-makers, volunteers, police officers, paramedics and generations of Londoners who have made it their own – thank you. Here’s to another 60 years of celebrating our incredible communities and this beautiful city we have built together.Sadiq Khan is mayor of LondonDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Nimbys can’t stand in the way of Labour’s legacy: a 21st-century new town boom | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: Which do Enfield’s Tories and Greens value more – a golf course or thousands of new homes? It’s a question of political values, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: Which do Enfield’s Tories and Greens value more – a golf course or thousands of new homes? It’s a question of political values, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: A satellite image of Crews Hill and Chase Park in Enfield, north London, April 27, 2026.Photograph: Maxar/DigitalGlobe/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA satellite image of Crews Hill and Chase Park in Enfield, north London, April 27, 2026.Photograph: Maxar/DigitalGlobe/Getty ImagesOpinionHousingNimbys can’t stand in the way of Labour’s legacy: a 21st-century new town boomPolly ToynbeeWhich do Enfield’s Tories and Greens value more – a golf course or thousands of new homes? It’s a question of political valuesTue 1 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 08.19 EDTShareNew towns will again be a lasting Labour legacy, just as in the eras of Clement Attlee and Harold Wilson. Those monuments to optimism, created in the mid-20th century by pulling down slums and building better, will bejoined by seven morein an attempt to ease the housing crisis.Enfield has been the exemplar, its proposed 21,000-home new town enthusiastically backed by its previous Labour council, which was struggling with3,000 familiesexpensively dumped into miserable temporary accommodation, and, I’m told, 7,000 on the waiting list. But in May’s elections, the great anti-Labour storm brought in a regime resisting the new town in every way it can. A minority Conservative group, propped up by the Greens (yes, Tory-backing Greens), informed the government thatit was “withdrawing”. Both parties had run on an anti-new town campaign.Enfield council’s Tory leader, Alessandro Georgiou, gave me this quote, but no interview: “We were elected on a clear mandate to protect Enfield’s green belt, and we have honoured that commitment by formally withdrawing from the new town process.” But there is no “process”, as it was never in a council’s power to block a new town.Devolution and localism? Only so far. Major infrastructure of national importance can’t, won’t and shouldn’t be stopped by local nimbys. Extending the grid, new power generation, waste recycling, transport by rail, air or ports, reservoirs and water treatment would never happen without planning from above. Building a new town falls under the regional control of the mayor, who has oversight of the interests of a far wider population. The London mayor, Sadiq Khan, is faced with adesperate housing shortage. He has the say-so here, and strongly supports new town plans for Enfield and Thamesmead. But pleading the interests of unhoused people rather than the voters in their patch will get councillors unseated, which is why they’re always brandishing alternative plans for building elsewhere, not here.Enfield is the perfect borough for a new town, with excellent rail connections. Opponents protest that it is green belt land, but that’s not how much of it feels. Step out at Crews Hill station and all around is a cluster of glasshouses and garden centres, an unplanned sprawl. There is some charm in its haphazardness, but it is exactly what the government calls “grey belt” – technically green belt, but concreted over, one way or another. Chase Park, the other part of the plan, is described ingovernment plansas “low-quality agricultural land”.I was taken round by Ergin Erbil, who was the Labour council leader until he was defeated in May. He understands housing need: he has just moved into a privately rented two-bedroom flat with his wife and children. “I’ve a degree, a reasonable job, but we’ll never afford to buy,” he tells me. He agrees with Khan’s office: when the mayor and the then housing minister Steve Reed last year proposed cutting the affordable housing quota for fast-tracked developments from 35% to 20%,one official said: “20% of something is better than 35% of nothing.”Local campaigners call Enfield London’s “green lungs”. But do golfing greens really count? Weirdly unnatural and often closed to the public, they are estimated to swallow billions of litres of water a year in England. The new town would mean building 5,500 homes over an area including Crews Hill golf club, to great protest from its members, who each pay up to£1,980 a year. Enfield hasfive other golf courses, part of a London “golf belt”.Weighing some green belt loss against gaining 21,000 homes goes to the heart of political values. Enfield’s Green councillors made their choice: by protesting against the new town, they gave the council to theConservatives.New towns were always mocked by Tories for their New Jerusalem optimism. But the housing minister, Matthew Pennycook, tells me he has been speaking to planners from the last wave who can warn him of things they got wrong, and steer him towards what worked best. Don’t build them around the car, but rather public transport. Don’t build suburban garden cities when only high-density housing guarantees a big enough community to support frequent buses, busy shops, schools, clinics, leisure and new enterprises. Lack of civic planning failed to build enough housing for decades, while covering the countryside with isolated clumps of executive homes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd these planners have proved themselves: after the contemptuous snobbery that greeted its birth almost 60 years ago, Milton Keynes has recently been declaredone of the UK’s best places to live.Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsHousingOpinionLocal governmentSadiq KhanConservativesGreen partyLabourLondoncommentShareReuse this content

title: Cities sweltering and the smell of the middle ages: has the climate crisis killed Instagram’s Euro summer? | Brigid Delaney | The Guardian
description: Who dreams of having a Euro summer now when staying in an ancient, uncooled building in the Old Town is like trying to sleep in a wood-fired pizza oven?
Author: Brigid Delaney
Headline: Who dreams of having a Euro summer now when staying in an ancient, uncooled building in the Old Town is like trying to sleep in a wood-fired pizza oven?
Content: A youth drinks from a can near the Eiffel Tower during hot weather in June in Paris, France. This summer broke temperature records in western Europe and made for an uncomfortable travel experience for hundreds of millions of tourists.Photograph: Annice Lyn/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA youth drinks from a can near the Eiffel Tower during hot weather in June in Paris, France. This summer broke temperature records in western Europe and made for an uncomfortable travel experience for hundreds of millions of tourists.Photograph: Annice Lyn/Getty ImagesOpinionExtreme heatCities sweltering and the smell of the middle ages: has the climate crisis killed Instagram’s Euro summer?Brigid DelaneyWho dreams of having a Euro summer now when staying in an ancient, uncooled building in the Old Town is like trying to sleep in a wood-fired pizza oven?Tue 1 Sep 2026 01.03 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 05.15 EDTShareThis week the Euro summer comes to an end – and so does a certain type of posting on Instagram.Waiting at the bus stop in the grey winter dawn, a slanting rain soaking your trouser leg, you can warm yourself by scrolling your feed and seeing pictures of Australians enjoying a Euro summer. There it is again – azure Greek coves, plates of barbecued sardines, the yachts rented by the hour, and selfies on the balcony of some Paris Airbnb, drinking wine in the long, blue night.But this year, just out of the frame but never far away, wasthe heat. You can’t easily photograph heat but it infused the season so monumentally that it might just have killed the Euro summer dream cold.With extreme heat starting in late May, this summer broke temperature records in westernEuropeand made for an uncomfortable travel experience for hundreds of millions of tourists.France to relax cheese production rules after drought takes toll on grazing landRead moreWho dreams of having a Euro summer now when staying in an ancient, uncooled building in the Old Town is like trying to sleep in a wood-fired pizza oven? How aspirational and glamorous is it to spend your days in an air-conditioned shopping centre (if you can find one) because to try to see a cathedral or historic site is to risk heatstroke?To travel to the usual European vacation spots in high season now is to endure. It’s to plan your travel so that you aren’t outside in the middle of the day. It’s to stay in places that have air conditioning – if you can find them – and pay a premium to try to stay cool.It’s major monuments and attractions being closed because it’s too dangerous for them to remain open. (In June, Notre-Dame Cathedralrestricted access to its towers, while the Eiffel Tower, which is normally open late, announced a 4pm closure, as did the Louvre.)It’s the cities sweltering, smelling of the middle ages – decomposing rubbish, sweat and hot bodies. It’s the feeling of being drained of energy, jet-lagged and damp, lying on a hard mattress in your shuttered hotel room, face close to the fan, as the thick air turns.It’s a population driven mad by the weather, throwing themselves into the canals at 2am because the heat gets trapped in their apartments at night, making it impossible to cool down and sleep.Travel is meant to be pleasurable. Holidays are supposed to be relaxing. But heat of this intensity and duration is incompatible with tourism. It becomes dangerous.Take, for example, the new trees planted to provide shade in Rome’s Piazza Risorgimento, near St Peter’s Basilica. They were burnt to a crisp,according to CNN, and the benches in dark plastic and wood were searingly hot and unable to be used.Across Europe, critical infrastructure failed – with overheated signal systems, melting asphalt that affected tram tracks, andtrain rails bucklingin the extreme heat.As well as making things outside unbearable and dangerous, the weather creates its own confusion and disorientation in the body.When you have heatstroke, you need to sweat to cool down but your skin stays parched and dry. Your body craves fluid but you get confused and forget to drink.At least35,000 more people died than expected in Europe this summerdue to back-to-back heatwaves, with heatstroke a culprit.It’s a strange aspect of human psychology that once summer passes we can remember it washot, we can remember it washorrible, but the actual sensations of physical and mental distress we experienced fade. The body forgets, until next time. The brain stores the fact of heat but not the sensation.But now is the time to prepare for next year, whichcould be even hotter.Australia is imperfect when it comes to climate adaptation and often our approach has been reactionary, piecemeal and ad hoc. But we have experience with long and increasingly uncomfortable summers – and over the years some approaches have been useful.‘It’s like a furnace’: French struggle with heat-trap homes as climate inequality growsRead moreDevelop public education campaigns about the sun and its power. Erect shade cloths in schools and public places. Introduce sunhats as part of your childrens’ school uniforms in summer. Rethink work from home rules if workers don’t have access to air conditioning at home, or consider splitting the working day so workers without cooling are not working in the hottest parts of the day.Make major investments in urban design that presume more extreme temperatures (large plazas like those seen all over Europe are not suitable for our changing climate, as stone absorbs and radiates heat ferociously). Install air conditioning or other cooling measures on public transport, in offices and public buildings. Plant more trees. Install water fountains across public spaces, indoor and outdoor. Have labour laws that protect workers who are on building sites or outdoors in extreme conditions, and make those conditions mandatory. Introduce a heat-warning system with legal obligations attached (ie school and outdoor work cancelled, outdoor events cancelled). Make it socially acceptable towear shorts to the office.And the other big change to consider? Australians could skip the annual Euro summer pilgrimage and enjoy the chill in the air at home.Brigid Delaney is the author of five books, including The Seeker and the SageExplore more on these topicsExtreme heatOpinionEuropeTourism (Australia)Climate crisiscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Nepal and Tibet flood is a warning: melting snow and ice will bring more disasters around the world | Bill McGuire | The Guardian
description: In Alaska, the Himalayas, the Andes, Greenland, and perhaps also the Alps, deadly chain reactions are just waiting to be triggered, says climate professor Bill McGuire
Author: Bill McGuire
Headline: In Alaska, the Himalayas, the Andes, Greenland, and perhaps also the Alps, deadly chain reactions are just waiting to be triggered, says climate professor Bill McGuire
Content: Survivors in Nepal walk past destroyed houses on Sunday, as the search for salvageable belongings began after the flash floods.Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSurvivors in Nepal walk past destroyed houses on Sunday, as the search for salvageable belongings began after the flash floods.Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionNepal-Tibet flood disasterThe Nepal and Tibet flood is a warning: melting snow and ice will bring more disasters around the worldBill McGuireIn Alaska, the Himalayas, the Andes, Greenland, and perhaps also the Alps, deadly chain reactions are just waiting to be triggeredTue 1 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 11.54 EDTShareYou may not have felt it, but the earth beneath our feet is getting twitchier, and global heating is to blame. As temperatures surge and climate breakdown accelerates, interactions between climate and geology are becoming ever more apparent – as marked by last week’s horrific events inNepal and Tibet. We still have a bit of a blind spot when it comes to the idea that a changing climate can impact what scientists call the geosphere, but the evidence has long been incontestable.In 2021, a similar deluge ripped through a series of mountain valleys in theIndian Himalayan state of Uttarakhand, severely damaging two hydroelectric power plants and taking about 200 lives. In August 2025, a colossal landslide in an Alaskan fjordcreated a 500-metre-high wavein an area frequented by cruise ships. A few months earlier, the collapse of part of a glacier in Switzerland’s Valais canton caused a debris-laden torrent thatdestroyed and buriedmost of the already evacuated village of Blatten.What all four events have in common is that they involve what is known as the cryosphere – the sum total of the planet’s frozen water. The fact that ice, snow and permafrost are severely affected by global heating should come as no surprise, and this means that the poles and high mountain regions are bearing the brunt. Everywhere, the cryosphere is receding rapidly, and this is bad news.As glaciers retreat, they expose unstable terrain that is oftenripe for landslides. The swift thawing of permafrost as global heating causes freezing levels to progressively rise also means that mountain faces become unstable rock masses looking for any excuse to collapse. At the same time, wherever there is an available dip or hollow, glacial meltwater is accumulating, forming expanding lakes that are increasingly prone to overtopping or breaching, dumping prodigious volumes of water into inhabited valleys downslope.In such circumstances, there are manifold ways in which climate-driven responses from the earth under our feet can drive dangerous and deadly hazards. As in Nepal and Tibet, the collapse of a weakened glacier can promote a flood, either directly, or by throwing a dam across a river valley that is eventually breached. Permafrost thawing, heavy rains or an earthquake can lead to the formation of landslides that can also block rivers, or obliterate communities completely.In Alaska – one of the fastest-heating places on the planet – the loss of huge amounts of ice has reduced the load on active faults in the crust beneath, and isfacilitating earthquake activity. A similar seismic backlash can be expected in other rapidly melting icy strongholds, including the Himalayas, the Andes, Greenland, and perhaps also the European Alps. Ice melt-related quakes have themselves the potential to provoke devastating landslides or glacier collapses, and to cause the breaching of meltwater lakes, resulting in what are known as glacial lake outburst floods. These will become increasingly common as more water from melting ice and snow accumulates at high altitudes. There are thousands of glacial lakes across the Himalayan region alone,about 200 of whichhave been diagnosed as presenting a threat to communities downslope.There is no question that high mountain communities sit on the frontline of climate breakdown, but it would be a mistake to think that the planet isn’t getting jittery elsewhere, too. The reality is that the geosphere is extraordinarily sensitive, so that a tiny change in environmental conditions can result in apotentially hazardous geological response.This is why there is actuallya volcano “season” – more eruptions happen between November and April than at other times of the year, promoted by minute-scale deformation of the Earth’s crust linked to an annual redistribution of water mass around the planet. It’s why a seismologist colleague of mine is fond of warning that if a dangerous earthquake fault is locked and loaded, it can be triggered by just the same pressure as you’d apply in a handshake. What this all means is that a minuscule variation in some environmental metric – be it air pressure, crustal stress, precipitation, sea level or ice load – can provide the final straw that prompts a geological reaction.Add in the fact that environmental parameters such as temperature,precipitationandsea levelsare all on the rise, and you have that extra nudge that can goad an inactive volcano into erupting, cause a long-dormant fault to rupture, or coax the snout of an unstable glacier to collapse. The end product can be a devastating geological event that is out of all proportion to the size of the initial trigger.There are places that have historically been geologically quiet where a heating climate islikely to result in an awakening. Greenland is ground zero in this regard. Here, the weight of the ice cover, at 2km to 3km thick, has meant that any faults beneath have not been able to move for thousands of years. Now, though, the ice is melting and the load on the faults is reducing. A future rise in earthquake activity is predicted as a consequence.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIceland is also worth keeping an eye on. There, the reduced load arising from the rapid retreat of the Vatnajökull ice sheet is forecast toincrease activity from volcanoes lurking beneath. The huge impact on aviation of the2010 eruption of Eyjafjallajökullprovides us with some inkling of the chaos this could bring to the UK and northern Europe.The increasingly temperamental behaviour of the earth beneath our feet teaches us that global heating is all-pervasive. It will intrude into every aspect of our lives and livelihoods, and leave no part of the planet untouched. As the world processes the horror of the events in Nepal and Tibet, it is a lesson that we ignore at our peril.Bill McGuire is professor emeritus of geophysical and climate hazards at UCL. His latest book is The Fate of the World – a History and Future of the Climate CrisisExplore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterOpinionClimate crisisFloodingEarthquakesTsunamisLandslidesNatural disasterscommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘We’re hunky in our own way’: Modern Family’s Mitch and Cam on their hilarious and groundbreaking love | Television | The Guardian
description: Jesse Tyler Ferguson and Eric Stonestreet proved that opposites really do attract in the smash hit sitcom. But beyond the bickering and and pranks, there was a romance so special that it changed many fans’ lives
Author: Hannah Verdier
Headline: Jesse Tyler Ferguson and Eric Stonestreet proved that opposites really do attract in the smash hit sitcom. But beyond the bickering and and pranks, there was a romance so special that it changed many fans’ lives
Content: ‘They’re two imperfect people who’ve found the perfectness in each other’ … Jesse Tyler Ferguson as Mitchell(left)and Eric Stonestreet as Cameron.Photograph: FoxFast/Sky TVView image in fullscreen‘They’re two imperfect people who’ve found the perfectness in each other’ … Jesse Tyler Ferguson as Mitchell(left)and Eric Stonestreet as Cameron.Photograph: FoxFast/Sky TVMaking loveTelevision‘We’re hunky in our own way’: Modern Family’s Mitch and Cam on their hilarious and groundbreaking loveJesse Tyler Ferguson and Eric Stonestreet proved that opposites really do attract in the smash hit sitcom. But beyond the bickering and and pranks, there was a romance so special that it changed many fans’ livesHannah VerdierTue 1 Sep 2026 07.59 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpposites attract. And spend most of their time arguing. But the love between Cameron and Mitchell Tucker-Pritchett remained strong throughout the 11 years of Modern Family.The two met at a games night when Mitch rolled his eyes every time Cam “got a little boisterous”. They married in two of the most romantic and near-disastrous TV episodes in living memory and raised two adopted children, Lily and Rexford. Being a groundbreaking gay TV couple came at a price: critics wanted more PDAs and less fighting, but Cam and Mitch’s love shone bright.“Mitch and Cam were a gay couple raising a child on TV, so the microscope was zoomed in with a little more focus so a lot of their flaws were heightened,” says Jesse Tyler Ferguson, who plays Mitch. “But I think, when you sit back and look at it, you can see how much love there is between those two people and the family they created.”The chemistry between Tyler Ferguson and TV partner Eric Stonestreet is so strong that talking to them is like watching an episode of Modern Family. “There was never any doubt, even in the early years when we were getting to know each other, that this was going to be someone who’d be in my life for ever,” says Tyler Ferguson. Stonestreet remains tight-lipped, but the affection is powerful. “If I’m in your world jacking with you, then you can take it to the bank that I’m in love with you,” he says.Modern Family ran from 2009 to 2020, when Cam and Mitch drove off to live happily ever after in Missouri. Tyler Ferguson and Stonestreet live in different cities, but still see each other and talk regularly – and their love for the characters lives on.Do you remember meeting for the first time?ES:We met when the producers were testing potential Cams with their already-cast Mitchell.JTF:It was like speed dating, meeting all these different guys and waiting for chemistry to happen. I was certainly drawn to Eric as a person. He was very kind, sweet and excited to be there. Do you want to bring up the Z snap or not?ES:I’ll set it up and you finish it. I’d had three auditions and I’d learned where the laughs were and had a take on the character, so I was very confident. Then we get to the big moment – the network test – and I wasn’t feeling it. So …View image in fullscreenNear disastrous … Cam and Mitch’s wedding.Photograph: Peter “Hopper” Stone/Disney General Entertainment Content/Getty ImagesJTF:The room was a little less warm than Eric had been experiencing before. In this moment where he thought that there should be a laugh and there wasn’t one, he panicked and did a gay Z snap.ES:To this day I have no knowledge of where that came from. I knew it was a ridiculous thing to do and I left thinking I’d messed up. But Jesse was very kind. I remember you saying: “Really good job, that was awesome.”What do Cam and Mitch love about each other?JTF:The most iconic romances develop when opposites attract, like Sam and Diane in Cheers or Ross and Rachel in Friends. Mitch lived a very sheltered life as far as being in the closet and he finds a lot of comfort in Cam’s free spirit.ES:Here are these two imperfect people who’ve found each other and the perfectness in each other. That makes the characters likable immediately. It gets the relationship so much further down the road when it’s not two hunky dudes. Well, we’re hunky in our own way.What were your favourite romantic moments?JTF:The whole PDA thing was so interesting to me. When you looked at all the couples on the show, there’s not a tonne of PDA between Jay and Gloria either, but because we were the gay couple we took the heat.ES:What really hurt my feelings in the beginning was people saying because I was straight I didn’t want to kiss Jesse. First of all, that’s stupid and secondly I’d been in a very gay cult classic movie called Girls Will Be Girls where I’d made out with a drag queen, soplease, girl.JTF:The writers’ response to that is that Mitch has a fear of PDA and then they made this wonderful episode called The Kiss where there’s a moment between Mitch and his dad showing affection and then in the background you see Cam and Mitch kiss. I found it so moving.Is there anything you wish that Cam and Mitch did differently?ES:I got caught up when people were saying Mitch and Cam argue a lot. There were times when I’d look at Jesse and go,“Here we go again,” but it was our job to make those arguments relatable.JTF:I wish they had a better ground plan for their house. We’d always say it’s strange that they only have one bathroom and it’s right off the kitchen.ES:It’s sprawling in Missouri, trust me.When did you realise this was a love story for the ages?JTF:Only in hindsight. I grew up gay and closeted in Albuquerque, New Mexico, and didn’t have anyone on television who was aspirational for me, like “I could get married and have kids”. To know that Eric and I are that for people makes this job feel like a gift.View image in fullscreen‘It was our job to make those arguments relatable’ … a Christmas episode of Modern Family.Photograph: Richard Cartwright/ABC/Getty ImagesES:I don’t even know how to process it when a 14-year-old kid to comes up to me now and says: “I’m gay and I love your character and thank you so much.” The fact we have an effect on people’s lives who weren’t even born when we shot Modern Family is unreal and I’m so grateful.What has been the most intense fan reaction to Cam and Mitch?JTF:Tears. People wanting to give me a hug and being so moved. That’s the good version. There’s also the ones where people are screaming and running down the street.ES:People will come up to me and say: “I watched three episodes during my chemo and you helped me get through those treatments.” I was in New York City seeing a Broadway show and this woman stops me and she says: “Seeing you here tonight has brought my daughter back to life. You were my daughter’s favourite character and the last time I saw her laugh was watching you on Modern Family and you being here right now is like her being here.” I lost it and gave her the biggest, warmest hug I could.How romantic are you in real life?ES:My dad was this big, burly guy and sometimes they’re the most romantic ones. You feel like you’ve won a different kind of prize because it’s not all out there for everyone to see. I think I’m romantic – I have the best gift for our one-year wedding anniversary[Eric is married toLindsay Schweitzer].JTF:I do my best to be romantic. Small acts of affection are very important to me and I show my love by planning date nights. I’m a great cook and I like to cook for Justin [Mikita, Jesse’s husband].Did you keep anything from the set that reminds you of Cam and Mitch?ES:I have the portrait that was above our fireplace of Mitch, Cam and Lily and a basket of fake lemons just because it was an inside joke with one of the producers, Chris Lloyd.JTF:There were a few pieces that we fought over. I have this painting from the Cam and Mitch house and I don’t remember the details of why I was in a scene, but I ended up taking it.View image in fullscreen‘One of his love languages is pranks’ … Cam and Mitchell.Photograph: Peter “Hopper” Stone/Disney General Entertainment Content/Getty ImagesWhat was your real relationship like off camera?ES:I’m more Mitchell off camera and Jesse’s more Cam. He’s breezy and will let things go and I’m the one who’s uptight and constantly worrying about everything. I really enjoyed strapping on my loafers and poufing my hair up because it gave me the chance to be a better version of myself, which is what Cam is.JTF:Eric is very thoughtful as a friend and one of his love languages is pranks. He’s really good at the long-game prank, so he will show affection by creating scenarios that will bring joy to people but also give him pleasure. A lot of our relationship is him ruthlessly pranking me and teasing me and it all comes from a place of love.What can Cam and Mitch teach us about love?JTF:It’s a long game. There are different phases of love – it has peaks and valleys that come with kids, jobs and getting to know each other and you have to allow fights to happen. My father-in-law always says: “We’ve been married 52 years, 33 happily” and he never specifies which they are.ES:We wanted Mitch and Cam to reflect real relationships. My wife, Lindsay, gives me permission to be myself and I desperately want her to be herself and although Mitch would raise a judging eyebrow every once in a while at something Cam would do, they love each other in the face of imperfection.JTF:I have the utmost faith in them and their relationship, so I think they’re still together. Absolutely.Jesse Tyler Ferguson stars in Tru at theMenier Chocolate Factory, London, from 19 September to 14 November.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionMaking loveUS televisionTV comedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Not just Hollywood crap’: Mike Leigh on the East End communist who brought world cinema to the UK | Movies | The Guardian
description: A new season celebrates Contemporary Films and its founder Charles Cooper, who bet on Britain taking to Ingmar Bergman, Yasujiro Ozu, Satyajit Ray – and a young Mike Leigh
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: A new season celebrates Contemporary Films and its founder Charles Cooper, who bet on Britain taking to Ingmar Bergman, Yasujiro Ozu, Satyajit Ray – and a young Mike Leigh
Content: ‘It was remarkable that they embraced this thing’ … Eric Allan and Anne Raitt in Mike Leigh’s debut feature film, Bleak Moments (1971).Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘It was remarkable that they embraced this thing’ … Eric Allan and Anne Raitt in Mike Leigh’s debut feature film, Bleak Moments (1971).Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyMovies‘Not just Hollywood crap’: Mike Leigh on the East End communist who brought world cinema to the UKA new season celebrates Contemporary Films and its founder Charles Cooper, who bet on Britain taking to Ingmar Bergman, Yasujiro Ozu, Satyajit Ray – and a young Mike LeighAndrew PulverTue 1 Sep 2026 10.05 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 14.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOccasionally, vital pieces of the cultural jigsaw disappear without anyone really noticing. This, sadly, was the fate of Contemporary Films, the British film distributor that popularised sophisticated, grownup international cinema – foreign language mostly – in the UK, and heralded the arrival of the auteur generation with directors such asIngmar Bergman, Satyajit Ray, Andrzej Wajda and Yasujiro Ozu.Contemporary, and its founder Charles Cooper, weren’t the only game in town –Kenneth Rive’s Galawas a fellow traveller – but Contemporary got there first, setting up shop in 1951, first with short films for the then popular film society sector, and moving into features with the 1952 Japanese filmChildren of Hiroshima. Its marketplace clout faded rapidly in the early 1990s, when it was a victim of changing industry practices. But amazingly, the company is still with us – and is planninga 75th anniversary series of screeningsto showcase its history.View image in fullscreenCharles Cooper.Photograph: Contemporary FilmsSuch is Contemporary’s lustre that, along with screenings of films such as Miloš Forman’s A Blonde in Love, Bergman’s Wild Strawberries and Jack Hazan’s David Hockney documentary A Bigger Splash, the great and good are turning out in support, led byMike Leigh, whose feature film directing debut, Bleak Moments, was picked up by Contemporary in 1971. “It was a great honour,” Leigh says. “One was used to seeing ‘Contemporary Films’ on all the movies one saw that weren’t just Hollywood crap.”Bleak Moments, a studiedly funny and weird film based on Leigh’s own stage play, is about a woman living an isolated life with a sister with a learning disability and a boring job. It was financed by Albert Finney, still riding high on his 1960s acting successes. As a homegrown, off-kilter feature, it was a slightly unusual item for Contemporary to pick up. “We were fresh on the block and innocent,” says Leigh, “and you take everything for granted in some way. But actually, when you think about it, they were pretty remarkable and they embraced this thing.”Now a Palme d’Or and Golden Lion winner, Leigh undoubtedly understands the impact the company had on his own development. But it is its effect on the wider culture, the openness and cosmopolitanism that Contemporary helped to foster, that is arguably its most important contribution. “I grew up in Manchester,” says Leigh, “and I saw movies all the time, but I never saw a film that wasn’t in English. I saw only Hollywood and British movies. So when I came to London, world cinema suddenly presented itself. I have recollections of seeing Russian films, Italian neorealism, you name it. It was all going on, and Contemporary was very much at the centre of that.”View image in fullscreenThe company’s office in Soho, London, in 1969.Photograph: Contemporary FilmsCooper, the driving force behind it all, was an East End Jew – the son of a butcher from Ukraine – and a committed communist who saw cinema as a way to build awareness. Before the second world war, he brought Soviet films to the UK viaKino, the film section of the Workers’ Theatre Movement, then spent the war in New York running a film section for theInternational Workers Order.Deported from the US in 1950, Cooper set about supplying films to hungry fans in film societies, of which there were an estimated 200 across Britain. The increasing interest in foreign “art” films meant Cooper was in tune with the intellectual times, with his special interest in eastern European and underclass-oriented films.Part of Cooper’s strength, it seems, was his devotion to family life and willingness to involve his children in his day-to-day. His daughters from his first marriage agree. Adi Cooper, now a board member of Social Work England, says: “Charles was in the right place at the right time in terms of capturing a market for the sort of films he was interested in, which branched out from political ones into what you would now call, I guess, arthouse cinema. He was prepared to take a risk on people who were unheard of here at the time, some of whom went on to have a much wider appeal.”View image in fullscreen‘There wasn’t much separation between work and home’ … Charles and Kitty Cooper with Satyajit and Bijoya Ray.Photograph: Contemporary FilmsHer twin, Sue Cooper, a founder member of1970s punk act Poison Girls, says: “There wasn’t much separation between work and home with Charles. He really was passionate about film and politics, and he was very motivated to expose people’s thinking to different cultures. He was basically an internationalist and a humanist.” They regale me with anecdotes about screenings in the basement of their Wembley home (“The room is crammed full of people! I’m two feet from the back wall gazing up at this film called Alexander Nevsky”) to messing about in the school holidays at the company’s Frith Street office (“pasting press cuttings into scrapbooks and getting seven and sixpence for three hours’ work”).Also key to Contemporary’s success was the relationship Cooper nurtured with George Hoellering, the Hungarian émigré who ran the celebrated Academy cinema on London’s Oxford Street which, throughout the 1950s and 60s, was the flagship venue for these kind of films. “They were joined at the hip,” says Pete Lawley, Contemporary’s current managing director. “They were the gold standard of the time.”View image in fullscreenContemporary acquired some of the key indie films of the 90s, including Hal Hartley’s The Unbelievable Truth with Julia McNeal and Adrienne Shelly.Photograph: Electric/Kobal/ShutterstockHoellering died in 1984, by which time Cooper had his own cinemas: the Paris Pullman and Phoenix cinema in London and another Phoenix in Oxford. Lawley, who came on board in 2023, outlines Contemporary’s decline: as Cooper’s health began to fail in the late 1980s, he passed control to his second wife, Kitty Furstenberg, who in turn sold it on to their friendEric Liknaitzky, who died in 2023. Although Contemporary did acquire some of the key indies of the late 80s and early 1990s, including Patricia Rozema’s I’ve Heard the Mermaids Singing, Jane Campion’s Sweetie and Hal Hartley’s The Unbelievable Truth, it seems the shift to home entertainment formats in the 90s passed Contemporary by. Instead it stuck to occasional re-releases of tried and tested classics from their archive.Lawley says Contemporary has kept going by licensing clips from their catalogue; he has been sorting through the copious company documentation and says he is now working on plans for the future. “It’s very important to me,” he says. “I really want to keep it going. It can’t be about the money, let’s put it that way. It may be small, but there’s something worthwhile to build upon.”Contemporary 75begins with a screening ofBleak Momentsand Mike Leigh in conversation. at the BFI Southbank, London, on 3 September and runs until 11 October at cinemas across LondonExplore more on these topicsFilmMike LeighSatyajit RayIngmar BergmanAndrzej WajdaYasujiro OzuFilm industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Meet the magical creatures inspired by shamanism, folklore … and an old Ikea bag | Art and design | The Guardian
description: From ceramic goblin feet to furry disembodied legs, Korean-Chinese artist Woo Jin Joo is using London junk to inject the art world with a spirit of playfulness
Author: Alice Fisher
Headline: From ceramic goblin feet to furry disembodied legs, Korean-Chinese artist Woo Jin Joo is using London junk to inject the art world with a spirit of playfulness
Content: Woo Jin Joo’s I Hear Things Existing With Me.Photograph: Robert Chadwick/Woo Jin JooView image in fullscreenWoo Jin Joo’s I Hear Things Existing With Me.Photograph: Robert Chadwick/Woo Jin JooArt and designInterviewMeet the magical creatures inspired by shamanism, folklore … and an old Ikea bagAlice FisherFrom ceramic goblin feet to furry disembodied legs, Korean-Chinese artist Woo Jin Joo is using London junk to inject the art world with a spirit of playfulnessTue 1 Sep 2026 10.16 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWoo Jin Joo’s studio is full of magic. Ceramic green goblin feet line the windowsill, disembodied furry legs jut out of one white wall and, on the table behind where the Korean-Chinese artist sits drinking tea, a headless being dressed in a black coat squats, arms aloft in warning.There are also neat racks of colourful thread next to a freehand embroidery machine, the source of this supernatural horde. This is whereJoo creates much of her art– surface embroideries and sculptural 3D creatures inspired by Korean myth, philosophy and the relationship between humans and the natural world.“When I use the embroidery machine I feel like I’m painting,” she says. “It’s as if each thread has its own life.”View image in fullscreenFormation Study I (detail), 2025, by Woo Jin Joo.Photograph: Robert Chadwick/Woo Jin JooJoo was born and raised in Korea – mainly by her grandmother – before moving to the UK 12 years ago to study at Central Saint Martins and then the Royal Academy in London. Swapping east Asia for west Europe started her thinking about how she was shaped by culture and the world around her. “That transition made me want to explore who I am and how I see things.”In 2021 she worked out how she wanted to go about it. She embroidered the 10 Daoist symbols of longevity, typically used to wish someone long life, on to an old Ikea bag – a plastic product that could take up to 1,000 years to decompose.View image in fullscreen… Woo Jin Joo with one of her worksPhotograph: Jamie Trounce/courtesy of Cockpit Studios“It was that work that made me feel a connection, a way of drawing ideas together to make a transformation that resonated with religious beliefs as well as myth,” she says.Guided by the idea from Korean folklore and shamanism that inanimate objects can become spirited beings calleddokkaebi, she looked at the junk discarded in London with fresh eyes. Now she often uses found objects in her work – a creature with many feet peers out of an old shirt sleeve; a discarded wooden side-table now sprouts a 5ft-talldokkaebileg. “I love the idea that the small and mundane have spirit,” she explains. “We need to realise that the ordinary is special.”View image in fullscreenTireless, by Woo Jin Joo.Photograph: Woo Jin JooJoo is part of a new wave of creatives showing that traditional, sometimes archaic, craft can be used to make very modern, joyful work. Makers are not just keeping these skills alive but evolving how they can be used. “I think a lot of makers are very experimental now, craft is no longer just about material knowledge, but about experimenting and playfulness. This means more people are drawn to it,” says Joo.She is preparing for her first solo show, Bodily Inbetweenness, at London’s Ruup & Form gallery, which opens during Shoreditch Design Week. For this, she explores a new type of spirit, human emotions and how we display them – a concept that Joo shows through powerful figures, slightly reminiscent of corn dollies but 5ft tall, poking out of the walls. “For me, a sense of fun always wants to come out, but for some people it’s awkward, it doesn’t fully emerge,” she says.View image in fullscreenMuddled and Mortal by Woo Jin Joo.Photograph: Woo Jin JooThe first sculpture in this series – I Hear Things Existing With Me, a contemplative figure slightly sunken into the wall it leans on – was one of the standout pieces at London’s Collect Craft Fair in February. Collect’s director, TF Chan, believes that you never forget the first time you see Joo’s work.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Mine was a pair of ceramic legs with each toe tipped in glossy red nail varnish,” he says. “In my view, she embodies the values of contemporary craft: closely bound to the artist’s heritage while accommodating both serious intellectual engagement and sheer delight.”View image in fullscreenA detail from Ardour, 2026, by Woo Jin Joo.Photograph: Robert Chadwick/Woo Jin JooJoo loves the widespread interest in Korean culture – currently encompassing everything from pop to skincare and it is perhaps one of the reasons her work feels so current. “Because I’m from Chinese as well as Korean heritage it’s been very meaningful to see both cultures celebrated. I think that international attention has meant that, especially within Korea, there’s now more interest in preserving and honouring traditions.”For Joo, seeing herself as a maker as well as an artist is a point of pride at a time when craftspeople continue to struggle for art world acceptance. “There is still a hierarchy,” she says. “A lot of fine artists now use craft like ceramic or textiles and that’s seen as part of their knowledge. Whereas if you come from a craft background what you do is rarely considered fine art. It should be free-flowing.”With another show to prepare for at the Harley Foundation, Nottinghamshire, later this year, Joo has long hours ahead of her in the studio creating her magical creatures, but she relishes that. “I think it’s the trickle of everydayness that really shapes who I am and how I see things. That really is what my work is about.”Bodily Inbetweenness is at Ruup & Form, London,from 11 September to 13 November.Shoreditch Design Week, London, runs from 15–20 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsArt and designArtSculptureChinaSouth KoreainterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘She inspired my proposal’: Readers on Yayoi Kusama | Yayoi Kusama | The Guardian
description: From wedding ceremonies to sunsets with pumpkins, even in urinals, Kusama’s work brought joy, mischief and inspiration to so many
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From wedding ceremonies to sunsets with pumpkins, even in urinals, Kusama’s work brought joy, mischief and inspiration to so many
Content: Pumpkin queen … Great Gigantic Pumpkin, an art installation at the Matsumoto City Museum of Art, Japan.Photograph: Tomohiro Ohsumi/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPumpkin queen … Great Gigantic Pumpkin, an art installation at the Matsumoto City Museum of Art, Japan.Photograph: Tomohiro Ohsumi/Getty ImagesYayoi Kusama‘She inspired my proposal’: Readers on Yayoi KusamaFrom wedding ceremonies to sunsets with pumpkins, even in urinals, Kusama’s work brought joy, mischief and inspiration to so manyGuardian readersTue 1 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 10.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘She inspired my proposal … and our wedding day’View image in fullscreenCiaran and Liam.Photograph: Unknown/Guardian CommunityI have always loved Yayoi Kusama’s work, and when I visited an exhibition of hers on a gap year in Sydney I was spellbound by her infinity mirror rooms. I immediately thought, despite being single at the time, this is a fantastic space to propose in. Fast forward around eight years and I am on one knee holding a ring out to my partner inside an infinity mirror room in Helsinki, with excited and expectant Finns looking on. He said yes. At the wedding, the breakfast was held under polka dotted pink lanterns. Kusama was a fantastic artist, who also protested for my ability to marry – performing her own gay wedding ceremonies before it was legally recognised – and inspired key aspects of my wedding.Liam, 40, Surrey‘I saw her work and dissolved’Two years ago, while researching in Porto, I was encouraged by a friend to go see the Kusama retrospective at the museum in Parque de Serralves. I was fortunate to experience her remarkable installation Dots Obsession – Aspiring to Heaven’s Love. The powerful effect she termed as self-obliteration viscerally connected with me in that room. I didn’t exist, as I dissolved, the dots were everywhere. Humanity is blessed for her work and I’m grateful and humbled to have experienced it.David, Florida, US‘I watched the sunset while sat next to her yellow pumpkin’I’ve been lucky enough to see a huge amount of Yayoi Kusama’s work in Japan and in Europe. Hunting down remote galleries in rural Japan to see her work, and spending time viewing it with no one else there has been an absolute treat. Sitting on the shore next to the yellow pumpkin on Naoshima [an “art island”] watching the sun set was one of the most beautiful experiences I’ve had. Her work brings me a sense of peace and calm. She was truly inspirational.Rachel, London‘She connected with people who didn’t know about art’A lot has been written about Yayoi Kusama’s life and artistic achievements, but perhaps her greatest legacy lies in her ability to bring people into the experience of art, including people who don’t consider themselves art lovers, such as my mother. I loved seeing how my mum was drawn to Kusama’s image and polka-dot works when we visited Tokyo together. You don’t need pretentious art-speak or an understanding of art history to appreciate her work. That direct, instinctive response made the encounter pure and joyful. I bought her a little Kusama plush key chain, which she attached to her bag and carries wherever she goes. It has become a small part of her life; and, for me, a part of our memories together.Vivienne Chow, London‘I climbed inside a red pumpkin on Naoshima’View image in fullscreenSandie in the red pumpkin on Naoshima, Japan’s art island.Photograph: Guardian CommunityI only recently became aware of her work from a visit to Naoshima, Japan’s art island, where two of her pumpkins are on display. Red Pumpkin is particularly great as you can climb inside. On returning home I was surprised and delighted that a pumpkin sculpture had arrived at GoodwoodArtFoundation in Sussex. I’m now researching where to find more pumpkins as they always make me smile.Sandie, 61, London‘I used to pee beneath a photo of her chopping a penis with a knife’From 2008 to 2012 I worked in Tokyo. On weekends I’d go to a gay bar in Shinjuku 2-chome for their ¥1000 “all you can drink” beer for several hours. Above the toilet was a black-and-white photo of Yayoi Kusama looking directly at the camera while holding a big knife chopping a penis (it was really a dildo) on a chopping board. Her eyes were powerful and drew you in. The picture was quite daunting to be looking at while you were peeing. I love that picture and her – she had a very mischievous face and her art was amazing.Peter Allison, 51, Stockton-on-Tees‘Like losing a favourite neighbourhood auntie’We live around the corner from the Kusama Museum in Tokyo. It opened in 2017 when our now 11-year-old son was just two. We’ve visited every year since, watching him grow bigger among Kusama’s pumpkins and infinity rooms. We’ve often visited the museum as a pick-me-up when feeling down. My son and I watched the sunset from the roof on the day the UK exited the EU. Losing Kusama San is like losing a favourite neighbourhood auntie who was always there to bring us good cheer.Tina Burrett, 49, Tokyo, Japan‘The world is a more colourful, whimsical, magical place”’I found her art rather late in my life, after 50, but it resonated with me so much that now I have one of her prints in nearly every room of my home. I find them all extremely uplifting and endlessly fascinating. The more I learned about her the more inspired I felt. From her devastating mental health struggles she found such a brilliant way of harnessing the most unique forms of creativity. There is a true magic in that, and we can all benefit from the lessons she has left us with. An enormous talent she was, and the world is a more colourful, whimsical and magical place graced with the art she made over her long and interesting life. Rest in Power dear Yayoi. You were loved and will be greatly missed.Susan, 55, Florida, USExplore more on these topicsYayoi KusamaInstallationArtfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘There’s always a fresh fury’: Tracey Scott Wilson on Black America and her play about a fraudulent journalist | Stage | The Guardian
description: As The Story – inspired by a scandal that ended a young Black reporter’s career – makes its London debut, its author explains why, two decades on, it’s more relevant than ever
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: As The Story – inspired by a scandal that ended a young Black reporter’s career – makes its London debut, its author explains why, two decades on, it’s more relevant than ever
Content: ‘I could’ve been a star’ … Tracey Scott Wilson photographed at the National Theatre in London.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I could’ve been a star’ … Tracey Scott Wilson photographed at the National Theatre in London.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.StageInterview‘There’s always a fresh fury’: Tracey Scott Wilson on Black America and her play about a fraudulent journalistArifa AkbarAs The Story – inspired by a scandal that ended a young Black reporter’s career – makes its London debut, its author explains why, two decades on, it’s more relevant than everTue 1 Sep 2026 07.13 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 07.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf our ability to discern fake news from fact is a hot topic today, Tracey Scott Wilson was on to it more than two decades ago. As a child, the playwright’s father trained her to watch the news every night and discuss it with her three siblings. It meant that she was well placed in the early 00s to spot how stations such as Fox News were veering away from objective reporting to become angled towards a given agenda.By this point a real-life story had been percolating in Wilson’s mind for more than two decades: in 1981, Janet Cooke, a young, ambitious Black American reporter at The Washington Post, had been exposed as a liar. Cooke had just won the Pulitzer prize for her news story about an eight-year-old drug addict, which turned out to be invented. Cooke was discredited, both for her reporting and for embellishing her CV, and was forced to hand back her prize two days after receiving it.View image in fullscreenLinseigh Green  and Jay Simpson  in rehearsals for  The Story.Photograph: © Feruza AfewekiThat scandal became the engine for The Story, Wilson’s breakthrough play at the Public Theater in New York in 2003, now being staged at theNational Theatrein LondonWilson, a rangy, affable presence, is delighted by her play’s revival at a time when the notion of truth, and the media’s part in producing it, couldn’t be more contested. She was a teenager when the Cooke story emerged and a conversation with her father has stayed with her. “He said ‘It’s such a shame she won it for writing something so negative [about the Black community].’ And then when they said the story was a lie, it was a whole other thing.”A few years later, when she was working at the University of Minnesota at a student magazine, she returned to the story. “We had access to [the digital newspaper archive] LexisNexis. I was bored half the time in that job so I’d just look up stories and one day I thought ‘I wonder what happened to Janet Cooke.’ So I put it in LexisNexis and went down a rabbit hole. I thought ‘what a great character she is’.”Her play’s protagonist, Yvonne, is quite the character too, a Black American junior reporter with a CV that takes in an Ivy League educationby way of the Sorbonne. She is assigned to a section whose raison d’etre is to put a positive spin on the newspaper’s race coverage – happy stories featuring the local Black American community to offset the negative ones. It is too niche to hold Yvonne’s ambition so she begins her hunt for a story that will fast-track her to the national news desk, populated by, one imagines, white, male, big beasts.Serendipitously, the play’s original run coincided with the breaking of another newspaper scandal involving Jayson Blair, a Black reporter who admitted to inventing and plagiarising stories while working for the New York Times. That story had race and class elements, just like Wilson’s play: Yvonne is a middle-class woman who sparks resentment and friction because of her (apparent) privilege. Through her, Wilson examines notions of who is deemed inside/outside the fold of the Black community.View image in fullscreenTracey Scott Wilson  and Ashley Thomas in rehearsals for The Story.Photograph: © Feruza Afewerki“I was drawn to the idea of authenticity,” says Wilson, “which is a conversation we are having every single day around class, race, sexuality, and who is allowed to be the spokesperson.”The play is also about women and ambition – the hard, raw kind that Yvonne encapsulates so uncompromisingly, especially now after a series of re-writes. “I wanted to bring Pat [a senior editor and Black woman] into this conversation. Pat and Yvonne are two sides of the same coin, they are both women who are being constantly punished for their ambition and being forced to do things because of their ambition.”There was a false start for a London revival soon after its original staging in New York, when the Soho theatre, in London, invited Wilson to the UK for a reading. “I had never been overseas, I had to go and get a passport,” she says. “I was so excited. They put me up here for a week. I barely remember the reading because I was going to Westminster Abbey, and doing all the tourist things.”It wasn’t picked up and Wilson went back home. “I was disappointed but I forgot about it. It was done a few times in the United States but I didn’t think it would be done again.”It was only when she got the call from the NationalTheatrelast year that she realised that her London trip hadn’t been wasted at all. Clint Dyer, this production’s director, had been at the Soho theatre reading as a twentysomething actor. “I had a Zoom with [the NT] and Clint was there.
