title: Monet’s Riviera, 90s nostalgia and Bayeux à gogo! The best art and architecture of autumn 2026 | Art and design | The Guardian
description: A self-confident woman strides on to the Fourth Plinth, Nan Goldin captures sex, cats and death and even the Turner Prize shows promise this year
Author: Catherine Slessor
Headline: A self-confident woman strides on to the Fourth Plinth, Nan Goldin captures sex, cats and death and even the Turner Prize shows promise this year
Content: Statue of  Crouching Aphrodite (left) and an Eddie Otchere photo of Metalheadz Sunday Sessions.Composite: Guardian Design/Eddie Otchere/ The Royal Collection/ HM King Charles IIIView image in fullscreenStatue of  Crouching Aphrodite (left) and an Eddie Otchere photo of Metalheadz Sunday Sessions.Composite: Guardian Design/Eddie Otchere/ The Royal Collection/ HM King Charles IIIAutumn arts preview 2026Art and designMonet’s Riviera, 90s nostalgia and Bayeux à gogo! The best art and architecture of autumn 2026A self-confident woman strides on to the Fourth Plinth, Nan Goldin captures sex, cats and death and even the Turner Prize shows promise this yearSee all of our unmissable autumn arts recommendations hereJonathan Jones,Ben EasthamandCatherine SlessorTue 1 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTShareThe Bayeux tapestryThe most anticipated exhibition of the year centres on an embroidered epic of war and conquest that miraculously preserves an intimate window on the Norman invasion of Britain in 1066. Yet, you may find yourself simply fascinated by the artistry of the Anglo-Saxon women who used coloured wool to depict billowing sails, charging horses and King Harold’s spectacular moustache.Jonathan JonesBritish Museum, London, 10 September to 11 JulyLady in Blue by Tschabalala SelfThis joyously comic, exuberant celebration of life on the streets – or in this case, the plinth – is likely to be a sensation. A young woman in a blue dress and blocky shoes strides boldly across the rectangular Fourth Plinth in Trafalgar Square. Her body is big in every sense, her rollicking form a surreal overstatement. An assertive, optimistic work of infectious self-confidence.JJFourth Plinth, Trafalgar Square, London, from 10 SeptemberSunil Gupta: Life With a Camera, 1970-NowLife With a Camera is an apt description of the career of Sunil Gupta, whose portraits of anonymous gay men in Delhi, queer couples in the UK, and cruisers in New York combine a deep commitment to the principle that all forms of love and community should be made visible with a classical eye for composition.Ben EasthamKettle’s Yard, Cambridge, 19 September to 31 JanuaryTurner prizeView image in fullscreenTragicomic tableaux … Kira Freije: Unspeak the Chorus.Photograph: Lewis RonaldThis year’s Turner prize promises powerful art. Kira Freije creates tragicomic tableaux of human figures whose bodies are empty metal frames but whose faces are cast from real people; Simeon Barclay tells stories of working-class northern life through performance and sculpture; Marguerite Humeau makes sculptures out of materials such as wasp venom; and Tanoa Sasraku exhibits textiles and drawings. Should be a good one.JJMIMA, Middlesbrough, 26 September to 29 MarchBeverly Buchanan: WeatheringWhen making permanent monuments has come to seem hubristic (who will be left to appreciate them?) and even irresponsible (do we really need morestuff?), Beverly Buchanan’s tumbledown “shack sculptures” celebrate the organic processes of decay and ruin, restoring the proper hierarchy between art and nature.BESpike Island, Bristol, 26 September to 31 JanuaryPainting the French RivieraView image in fullscreenDoing beach … Bathers by Paul Cézanne, 1890-92. Showing in Painting the French Riviera at the Royal Academy, London.Photograph: Saint Louis Art Museum, Funds given by Mrs Mark C SteinbergArtists didn’t just paint the Riviera; they helped invent it. The rise of France’s Mediterranean coast as a holiday resort from the 1870s onwards coincided with the new, savage embrace of raw sunlight by Monet and Cézanne. Matisse andthe Fauves painted the Riviera in psychedelic colours, but it was Picasso who saw beach life as erotic and shockingly modern.JJRoyal Academy, London, 2 October to 31 JanuarySalman Toor: Someone Like YouRendered in his signature emerald-absinthe tones, Toor’s paintings tell the imagined lives of young, queer south Asian men. Much like near-contemporary Lynette Yiadom-Boakye, he inserts fictionalised subjects into paintings in the traditions of the masters to tell enigmatic, evocative, and gently subversive stories.BECourtauld, London, 2 October to 10 JanuaryWakaliga UgandaThis film studio in Kampala makes action movies on budgets of a few hundred pounds – using props made out of scrap metal and editing rigs built from discarded computer parts – which are shown in makeshift cinemas to live commentaries by charismatic “video jokers”. The challenge? How to reproduce that culture in a gallery without sucking the life out of it.BEChisenhale Gallery, London, 2 October to 6 DecemberSophie Calle: Something MissingIn the language of wellness culture, Sophie Calle lacks boundaries. She has followed a stranger to Venice to secretly photograph him, rifled through the personal effects of hotel guests, and written a newspaper column exposing the private life of a man she had never met. In the fifth decade of her career, it will be interesting to see how her particular brand of mischief lands in our increasingly puritanical culture.BETurner Contemporary, Margate, 3 October to 24 JanuaryKatherine Hubbard: The Great RoomDuring the pandemic, Katherine Hubbard’s mother started to show the effects of a progressive brain disease. They have been working together ever since, with the artist’s profoundly moving photographs, sculptural installations and writings reflecting on how memory and identity is constructed, breaks down, and might be rebuilt.BEStudio Voltaire, London, 7 October to 10 JanuaryThe 90s: Art and FashionView image in fullscreenRaw talent … Chicken Knickers by Sarah Lucas, showing at The 90s at Tate Britain.Photograph: Tate Photography/Courtesy the artist and Sadie Coles HQ, LondonIt was the decade when British art started to be taken seriously around the world, while shocking and scandalising Britain itself. It was also the great decade of the Turner prize. Curator Edward Enninful, former editor-in-chief of Vogue, sets YBAs including Damien Hirst and Sarah Lucas alongside fashion icons such as Alexander McQueen and photographer Juergen Teller.JJTate Britain, London, 8 October to 14 FebruaryRobert Ryman: The Real ThingRyman’s paintings are “the real thing” in the sense that they rejected illusion: his delicate white-on-white works were the logical conclusion of minimalism’s mania to cut art down to its fundamentals. Exquisite refinement or tiresome navel-gazing? Go make up your own mind.BEBarbican, London, 8 October to 28 FebruaryAphrodite: The Making of a GoddessView image in fullscreenCobalt classic … Blue Venus (The Venus of Alexandria) by Yves Klein, showing as part of Aphrodite: The Making of a Goddess.Photograph: Estate of Yves Klein courtesy ADAGP Paris/2026 Succession Yves Klein c/o DACS, LondonForget the Bayeux tapestry, Botticelli’s Venus is coming to Britain. Well, not quite The Birth of Venus, but a similar Botticelli nude that shows he did a nice trade in images of the ancient deity of love and desire. This exhibition starts in ancient Greece with the cult of Aphrodite and follows her reincarnation as the Roman Venus into modern times.JJAshmolean Museum, Oxford, 8 October to 11 AprilWillem de Kooning at workThe greatest painter of the second half of the 20th century? No one can match his range; from shockingly violent (the notorious Womanseries) to heart-stoppingly pretty. The most anticipated show of the season.BERijksmuseum, Amsterdam, 9 October to 17 JanuaryPope.L: Five DecadesPope.L’s business card introduced him as “The friendliest black artist in America” and he became famous for crawling across New York to protest against the neglect of its poor. This survey should be a fitting tribute to an artist who was incandescently angry, shockingly funny and never looked away. More like him are needed.BEModern Art, London, 13 October to 14 NovemberTarek Atoui: Hyundai CommissionThe sound of music comes to Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall, with a difference. Beirut-born, Paris-based Atoui is an artist of delicate multisensory, but mostly aural, environments. He turns everyday stuff – including, in the past, camping gear, stones and water – into musical instruments. It should be engaging and poetic, sending strong echoes of Lebanon’s history echoing in this vast space.JJTate Modern, London, 13 October to 11 AprilConstantinople to Istanbul: One City, Two EmpiresView image in fullscreena 17th-century Ottoman processional scroll showing as part of Constantinople to Istanbul: One City, Two Empires at the V&A.Photograph: Tony Richards/The John Rylands Research Institute and Library, The University of Manchester, Turkish MS4Istanbul really was Constantinople once – the eastern capital of the Roman empire that survived as the centre of Byzantine civilisation. When the Ottomans conquered it in 1453 they respected this, preserving the ancient domed church Haghia Sophia and modelling mosques on it. This survey of art and design from one of the world’s most hypnotic cities, from Byzantine icons to Turkish tamburs, sounds stupendous.JJV&A, London, 7 November to 9 MayVan Eyck: The PortraitsThis mesmerising painter turned a camera-like eye on the people of the early Northern Renaissance period. It was said he was an alchemist, which feels true when you contemplate the glassy perfection of his portraits. That eerie, magical sense of power must have helped his business no end. He is, quite simply, one of the greatest artists ever to have lived.JJNational Gallery, London, 21 November to 11 AprilAlfred Wallis: An Artists’ ArtistWallis was the fisherman turned painter whose discovery by Ben Nicholson gave British modernism its own “primitive” connection to the native landscape, freeing it from models pioneered elsewhere. But these luminous pictures of boats sailing across dreamlike seas – loaded with personal and collective memory – are more than a missing link in art history.BEPallant House Gallery, Chichester, 21 November to 2 MayNan Goldin: You Never Did Anything WrongView image in fullscreenPaws for effect … You Never Did Anything Wrong, Part II by Nan Goldin.Photograph: Nan GoldinLife itself is Nan Goldin’s art. No one rivals her raw truth-telling camera and the total conviction that, when you look at her photographs and films, you are seeing the way her world is. She’s got the lyrical brutality of Andy Warhol and Lou Reed, and her people are their people, updated. Sex and suffering, beauty and death … it’s all here.JJHayward Gallery, London, 24 November to 7 MarchDesign andarchitecture by Catherine SlessorEs Devlin: Other WorldsCurrently plotting the staging for the Met’s much anticipated Ring Cycle, artist and theatre designer Es Devlin has reframed the visual language of opera, theatre, music and fashion. From Wagner to Stormzy, this retrospective illuminating 30 years of creative practice features immersive installations and a replica of her studio.Design Museum, London, 2 October to 4 AprilMichael Landy: Future RuinsView image in fullscreenDouble rubble … Oh! What a falling off do these ruins present. Sir John Soane’s Museum as a ruin, 2026, by Michael Landy.Photograph: Prudence Cuming Fine Art PhotographyThe atmospheric labyrinth that is the Sir John Soane’s Museum hosts Michael Landy’s fantastical drawings of buildings in ruins, inspired by 18th-century draughtsman Joseph Gandy’s romantic vision of a crumbling Bank of England. Landy’s less romantic subjects include Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago compound and Mussolini’s fascist monument, the Palazzo della Civiltà in Rome.Sir John Soane’s Museum, London, 14 October to 17 JanuaryJames StirlingTo mark the 30th anniversary of architecture’s Stirling prize, established in honour of the irreverent and iconoclastic James Stirling, this show looks at his career through his links with Liverpool, where he was brought up and studied. Stirling was fascinated by the city’s industrial past, which shaped his quixotic approach to design.RIBA North, Liverpool, 23 October to 24 JanuaryThe Nue Black AestheticValorising the work of contemporary Black designers across furniture, architecture, fashion and installation, this show looks at how design systems are being radically redefined by the nuances of the Black experience, with designers from diasporic communities balancing shared perspectives with the richly distinctive traditions of their individual heritage.Design Museum, London, 2 November to 8 AugustGuggenheim Abu DhabiView image in fullscreenGehry area … The Guggenheim Abu Dhabi.Photograph: Emic Works/Courtesy of Guggenheim Abu DhabiThe American architect Frank Gehry,who died last year, didn’t live to see his final magnum opus completed after 20 years’ gestation. This Guggenheim satellite in the Gulf bookends a career that took off in Bilbao with the first modern Guggenheim – but will its typically hectic design be as memorable? Or a bloated, extravagant excess?Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, the United Arab Emirates, 11 December

title: Todd Haynes and Wallace Shawn among signatories of letter backing Mark Ruffalo amid antisemitism charge | Mark Ruffalo | The Guardian
description: More than 170 Jewish artists, also including Joel Coen, Hannah Einbinder and Miranda July, have supported the actor after he criticized Paramount
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: More than 170 Jewish artists, also including Joel Coen, Hannah Einbinder and Miranda July, have supported the actor after he criticized Paramount
Content: Wallace Shawn, Hannah Einbinder and Todd Haynes have signed a letter supporting Mark Ruffalo, who spoke out on Paramount’s merger with Warner Bros Discovery.Composite: GettyView image in fullscreenWallace Shawn, Hannah Einbinder and Todd Haynes have signed a letter supporting Mark Ruffalo, who spoke out on Paramount’s merger with Warner Bros Discovery.Composite: GettyMark RuffaloTodd Haynes and Wallace Shawn among signatories of letter backing Mark Ruffalo amid antisemitism chargeMore than 170 Jewish artists, also including Joel Coen, Hannah Einbinder and Miranda July, have supported the actor after he criticized ParamountAdrian HortonTue 1 Sep 2026 14.42 EDTFirst published on Tue 1 Sep 2026 11.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA collective of more than 170 prominent Jewish artists and academics – includingTodd Haynes,Joel Coen,Miranda July,Hannah Einbinder,Wallace ShawnandNaomi Klein– have signed an open letter supportingMark Ruffalo.The actor had beenaccusedof invoking antisemitic tropes after he criticized Paramount Skydance, the media company owned by David Ellison, a Donald Trump ally. Ruffalo had spoken out about the$111bn mergerwith Warner Bros Discovery (WBD).In a statement posted to social media last week, the actor had highlighted the links between Paramount Skydance, poised to become one of the biggest media conglomerates in the USpending a court decision, and Oracle, the technology company owned by Ellison’s father, Larry, that has long supplied software to the Israel Defense Forces and government. Paramount responded to Ruffalo, saying it was “troubled when antisemitic tropes are invoked in purported service of a business dispute”.The letter, titled “Enough!”, dismisses the accusation against Ruffalo as part of an “outrageous smear campaign” and calls for the end to “the false and dangerous weaponization of charges of antisemitism against those who are brave enough to point out the obvious: that the assault on the Palestinian people and the assault on our liberties at home are deeply interconnected, and there is nothing antisemitic about recognizing that fact”.Mark Ruffalo fires back at Paramount Skydance after it accuses him of using ‘antisemitic tropes’Read more“CallingMark Ruffaloantisemitic because he is questioning a massive corporate merger is not only absurd – it’s a dangerous way to shut down legitimate criticism,” Ilana Glazer, the former Broad City star, said in an additional statement.In his original post, Ruffalo shared a video of Safra Catz, former Oracle CEO and the current executive vice-chair, describing the “really profoundly scary technology” the company provided to Israel after the 7 October attack by Hamas in 2023. The actor accused Larry Ellison – who is worth an estimated $189bn and agreed to personally backstop $40.4bn in equity financing to help Paramount Skydance acquire WBD – of “using [Oracle] to fund his son David’sWarner Brosacquisition” and linked the software deals with the IDF to the merger that would unite two of the remaining five legacy studios in Hollywood, as well as a host of networks and news operations.“These ‘really profoundly scary technologies’ will most likely be merged into one of the largest media conglomerates in the world and one day used on you,” Ruffalo wrote.Ruffalo urged his followers to oppose the merger, which he claimed would be “catastrophic” for the entertainment industry. In a separate statement after Paramount’s response, Ruffalo said: “Criticizing the actions of the Israeli prime minister, a military technology contract, or the executives who supply it is not the same as criticizing Jewish people,” Ruffalo wrote. “This critical and necessary dialogue is then dishonestly framed as being anti-Israel.”The letter, whose signatories include Jewish artists, writers, creative professionals and faith leaders as well as several prominent Holocaust and genocide scholars, affirmed Ruffalo’s argument against the $111bn merger that alreadysecured approvalfrom the Trump administration in June: “The proposed merger of Paramount and Warner Brothers Discovery is no mere combination of two huge multinational companies. Yes, it will destroy thousands upon thousands of livelihoods. Yes, it will further consolidate the oligarchic control of our media (witness the gutting ofCBS News). Yes, it will strangle competition and creativity in film and television production and distribution.“But it will do all this and more as part of a larger project of tech-driven domination,” the letter continues, “a project Larry Ellison and his partners have never been shy about trumpeting – and one they themselves have explicitly linked to their support for the ongoing depredations being visited on the people of Palestine and their silencing of critics of those horrors.”The letter cited theTrump-brokered sale of TikTokby the Chinese company ByteDance to US investors includingOracle; Larry Ellison’s reported $350m in personal funding of the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change amid the former prime minister’sultimately unsuccessful bid, backed by Jared Kushner, tooccupy a key positionon Trump’s transitional board of peace for Gaza; and Oracle executives’ public backing of Israel’s military strikes in Gaza, “which has become an open-air laboratory for AI-driven killing and control technologies” celebrated by Catz and other Oracle officials.“Pointing out the crucial connections between what is happening in Gaza and what is happening in Hollywood is the exact opposite of antisemitism,” the letter said. “It is, for us, the very essence of Jewish ethical duty.”Explore more on these topicsMark RuffaloParamount PicturesTodd HaynesWallace ShawnWarner BrosNaomi KleinOraclenewsShareReuse this content

title: Emily Wilson to retranslate the Odyssey from scratch | Books | The Guardian
description: Wilson, whose 2017 English translation of Homer’s epic poem inspired Christopher Nolan’s box office hit, is revisiting it after criticising the film adaptation
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: Wilson, whose 2017 English translation of Homer’s epic poem inspired Christopher Nolan’s box office hit, is revisiting it after criticising the film adaptation
Content: ‘It’s a complete retranslation. It’s not a revision of the old version’ … Emily Wilson.Photograph: Matt Rourke/APView image in fullscreen‘It’s a complete retranslation. It’s not a revision of the old version’ … Emily Wilson.Photograph: Matt Rourke/APBooksEmily Wilson to retranslate the Odyssey from scratchWilson, whose 2017 English translation of Homer’s epic poem inspired Christopher Nolan’s box office hit, is revisiting it after criticising the film adaptationEmma LoffhagenTue 1 Sep 2026 11.09 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEmily Wilson, the first woman to translate Homer’s Odyssey into English, is to retranslate the ancient Greek epic poem from scratch less than a decade after the publication of her acclaimed version.The announcement comes after Wilson attracted controversy this summer with a scathing assessment of Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster film adaptation of the Odyssey, which sheslammed forits “abysmal” writing and lack of sex scenes.Wilson’s2017 translationbecame a bestseller and was praised for making the 3,000-year-old epic poem modern and accessible.“I’m now retranslating the Odyssey from scratch, with an approach closer to that of my translation of the Iliad, using somewhat more lines than the original, enabling more varied word-length and pacing,” she told the New York Times.“It’s a complete retranslation. It’s not a revision of the old version,” she told the AP. “I’m about halfway through.”Nolan cited Wilson’s 2017 translation, including its opening sentence, “Tell me about a complicated man”, as an influence on his adaptation of the poem, released in Julythis year and starring Tom Holland, Zendaya, Matt Damon and Anne Hathaway.Nolan’s adaptationtook the global box office by storm,making $264m (£196m) during its opening weekend, marking the director’s best ever opening. Book sales saw a huge bump too: UK print sales of the poemincreased by 1,400% in the four weeks to 25 July compared with the same period in 2025, after the film’s release in the middle of the month.Wilson made headlines forher attack on Nolan’s version. Writing in the London Review of Books, she said: “Nolan’s Odyssey lacks many of the elements that make the poem great … The writing is abysmal.”She continued: “None of the characters has convincing motivation for their actions or words. There are no sex scenes, and all the food looks horrible,” adding, “I would be ashamed to have written any part of this script.”Her criticism attracted strong reactions, includingfrom novelist Joyce Carol Oates,whoaccusedWilson of “haughty superiority”.Wilson’s decision to retranslate the poem predates the row over the film. In an interview recorded in the spring for the ancient-history podcast Instant Classics, she discussed her desire to return to Homer and approach the poem differently from her first translation.“I’m proud of my Odyssey translation … I think there are lots of good things about the kinds of compression and choices that I was forced into,” Wilson said then.She has indicated that she will “probably” keep the opening line, “Tell me about a complicated man”. Wilson also added that her original translation relied too heavily on the word “slave”, when more precise terminology could have better reflected the different forms of enslavement depicted in the poem.The new translation will also give readers far more of Wilson’s scholarly commentary. “I’m also going to quadruple the number of endnotes because endnotes are really fun to write,” she said.While Wilson’s decision to retranslate Homer’s poem is unusual, it is not without precedent.“Translators quite often rework or rewrite their own previous translations,” said Matthew Reynolds, professor of English and comparative criticism at Oxford University. “Elizabeth Barrett Browning completely rewrote her translation of Aeschylus’s Prometheus Bound, Ezra Pound repeatedly revised his translations of Guido Cavalcanti, and Yu JongHo (유 종호) translated Jane Eyre into Korean first in 1970 and again in 2004.”He added: “It shows that translation – especially literary translation – is not just a matter of right or wrong, good or bad, but a continual exploratory process of interpretive reimagining and re-making.”Wilson’s new Odyssey does not yet have a publication date.Explore more on these topicsBooksThe OdysseyPoetryChristopher NolanHomerFilm adaptationsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Prolific UK graffiti artist Helch dies | Street art | The Guardian
description: Artist rose to prominence in 2018 by painting his eponymous tag in public spots across southern England
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Artist rose to prominence in 2018 by painting his eponymous tag in public spots across southern England
Content: Helch graffiti in Acton, west London, early 2026.Photograph: Steve Cotton/AlamyView image in fullscreenHelch graffiti in Acton, west London, early 2026.Photograph: Steve Cotton/AlamyStreet artProlific UK graffiti artist Helch diesArtist rose to prominence in 2018 by painting his eponymous tag in public spots across southern EnglandThe graffiti artist who left an indelible mark on high-rise BritainJamie GriersonTue 1 Sep 2026 07.44 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe street artist Helch, known for murals and tags acrossEngland, has died, his gallery has said.Herose to prominencein 2018 by painting his eponymous tag in capital letters across a string of public spots in London as well as bridges on the M4, M1 and M25.View image in fullscreenThe artist’s tag painted in 10-foot letters on a railway viaduct near Windsor Castle, 2019.Photograph: Rex/ShutterstockThe tag was sometimes painted in stylised fonts or different colours, and occasionally appeared just as the simple letter “H”.In 2019, Helch appeared on a bridge over M4 to the north of Bristol. In July that year, the words ‘Boris is …’ were painted on one side of the bridge, visible to westbound traffic. They remained for a few weeks before being painted over by Network Rail. But then the words “Boris is Helch” appeared in the same place.View image in fullscreenHelch graffiti in Bristol in July 2019 before Boris Johnson’s election as prime minister.Photograph: Mr Standfast/AlamyPosting on Sunday on Instagram, BSMT Space, a gallery for street artists in eastLondon, said: “Receiving news today of the untimely passing of Helch has left us broken hearted.“It felt like he stepped into our lives out of the ether.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continue“Prompted by a moment of revelation standing outside of the American Carwash in Shoreditch – a triumph of roller graffiti and an east London landmark – I was so drawn to the enigma and mystery of the word I had to find out more.“It took six months to get him to agree to meet in person, and in 2022 we released his first print which sold out within the hour.View image in fullscreenAmerican Carwash covered in street art, Shoreditch, London, 2022.Photograph: Photozaic/Alamy“A stranger to the gallery world, Helch was a true creature of the night, it’s where he found his vocation and the gallery walls were not always what it was about for him. We often had to recalibrate what this meant as we worked together.“Over the past year, his work progressed exponentially, he was coming into his own as an artist. A true perfectionist – he wouldn’t present anything that wasn’t to his standard and it was an honour to witness.View image in fullscreenTrackside graffiti in Shepherd’s Bush, west London featuring Helch, 2020.Photograph: Mark Charnock/Alamy“An urban landscape without an H in it seems unfathomable. A life unlike any other, he was compelled to leave his mark on this world. There will never be another like him. Rest well H – your rollers have spoken their truth.”The street artist’s identity has never been officially revealed, although one media organisation claimed to name him at the end of last year.View image in fullscreenGraffiti and street art in Shoreditch, east London, featuring Helch.Photograph: Mark Charnock/AlamyExplore more on these topicsStreet artLondonArtEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Beveridge revisited: Simon Callow film celebrates the radical co-founder of Britain’s welfare state | Movies | The Guardian
description: Christine Edzard’s The Man With the Plan tours the country with a timely message about tackling want, disease, squalor, idleness and ignorance
Author: Richard Norton-Taylor
Headline: Christine Edzard’s The Man With the Plan tours the country with a timely message about tackling want, disease, squalor, idleness and ignorance
Content: Grand designs … Simon Callow as William Beveridge in Christine Edzard’s The Man With the Plan.Photograph: Sands Films ProductionView image in fullscreenGrand designs … Simon Callow as William Beveridge in Christine Edzard’s The Man With the Plan.Photograph: Sands Films ProductionMoviesBeveridge revisited: Simon Callow film celebrates the radical co-founder of Britain’s welfare stateChristine Edzard’s The Man With the Plan tours the country with a timely message about tackling want, disease, squalor, idleness and ignoranceRichard Norton-TaylorTue 1 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA new film that addresses issues fundamental to the new prime minister’s declared mission will star Simon Callow as a historical British political figure.The hero of The Man With the Plan isWilliam Beveridge, who helped to lay the foundations of the postwar welfare state. It shows that the Liberal peer was much more radical than is usually assumed – and certainly far more so than Churchill anticipated when he asked Beveridge to draw up a report into the future of Britain’s fragmented social insurance and national health system after the second world war.Despite its misleadingly dull title, Social Insurance and Allied Services, Beveridge’s report caused a sensation: on the day it was published in 1942, a mile-long queue formed outside the government’s stationery office in Kingsway, central London. More than 650,000 copies were sold.Now The Man With the Plan is about to tour the country – with a viewing on the eve of theLabourParty conference in Liverpool – to be shown mainly in small venues including libraries and community centres.It was written and directed by Christine Edzard, who, with Olivier Stockman, the film’s producer, runs Sands Films Studio in Rotherhithe in London, where the film was shot. It is the home of the film studio; the Sands Films Cinema Club, which organises public screenings; a music room which hosts live events and concerts; and an acclaimed collection of period costumes. Edzard and Stockman’s previous films include Little Dorrit, As You Like It and, in 2018, an adaptation of Czech classic The Good Soldier Schwejk.In The Man With the Plan, a young student called Flea, played by newcomer Sophie Jenkin, embarks on a journey and comes across Beveridge’s “five giants”: want, disease, squalor (voiced by Miriam Margolyes), idleness and ignorance. Puzzled by sceptics and opponents of the plan, she confronts a landlord, a skiver, some journalists (portrayed as sheep), politicians and city traders as well as the devil (played by a seductive Alan Cox).Participants in the film include campaigning standup comedian Mark Thomas and Sir Michael Marmot, professor of epidemiology and public health at University College London. Beveridge’s words are spoken verbatim by actor Simon Callow. Prevention of ill health may begin with health centres, says Beveridge, but it also “spreads into problems of sanitation, housing, nutrition. One of the main efforts should be directed to improving housing – there lies the scope for raising standards of living and improving health and defeating the giant squalor.”Beveridge continues: “A satisfactory scheme of social insurance also assumes the maintenance of employment and the prevention of mass unemployment: the giant idleness.”During her travels, Flea faces fierce opposition to a “living wage”, defence spending, the role of the private sector in the NHS, and the privatisation of public utilities. Beveridge’s opponents mock his ambition to abolish want, and the need for an economic policy to maintain productive employment.A sneering choir sings: “Minimum wages cause unemployment … minimum wages cause inflation … minimum wages cause spiralling prices … What of the nation’s debt? Think of the national debt! What of our defence spending? Defence from what?” A narrator intervenes to remind viewers that “the state is the people. The state is not some dictator or Google or Amazon – or ‘they’. The state is you.You!”Flea asks Marmot whether he thinks Beveridge’s plan could be possible today. He replies: “Not just possible today, but necessary, vital, today. We have to address the causes of the causes – and they reside in those five giants of Beveridge. So we need social action, we need to rediscover the public good.”For many people, probably most, this is utopian. But, as this film shows, the charge of utopianism should not be used as an excuse for political leaders simply to reject all his ambitious aims, as successive governments have done. Andy Burnham take note.The Man With the Plan is at Otley Courthouse, Leeds, on 20 September,then touring.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsLabourBenefitsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Wendell Berry, US author, farmer and environmentalist, dies aged 92 | Books | The Guardian
description: Author and Kentucky native, who celebrated the farming world of his home state and warned of the excesses of industrial society, died at home
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Author and Kentucky native, who celebrated the farming world of his home state and warned of the excesses of industrial society, died at home
Content: Wendell Berry, pictured at his home in Port Royal, Kentucky in 2011. He has died aged 92.Photograph: Ed Reinke/APView image in fullscreenWendell Berry, pictured at his home in Port Royal, Kentucky in 2011. He has died aged 92.Photograph: Ed Reinke/APBooksWendell Berry, US author, farmer and environmentalist, dies aged 92Author and Kentucky native, who celebrated the farming world of his home state and warned of the excesses of industrial society, died at homeAssociated PressTue 1 Sep 2026 02.34 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWendell Berry, the Kentucky-born author and agrarian whose poems, stories, novels and essays celebrated the farming communities of his native state and warned of the excesses and misjudgments of an industrial, commercialized society, has died aged 92.His daughter, Mary Berry, confirmed on Monday that he died in his home in Port Royal, Kentucky.“There’s not enough I could say about him to do him justice,” she told the Associated Press.Stand By Me by Wendell Berry review – the soul of KentuckyRead moreBerry was a prolific writer who published more than 40 books, including the novels Nathan Coulter and A Place on Earth, the short story collectionStand By Meand the anthology A Timbered Choir: The Sabbath Poems 1979-1997.His legacy extended well beyond Kentucky: Michael Pollan, author of such bestsellers as The Omnivore’s Dilemma, would say his life was changed by Berry’s declaration that “Eating is an agricultural act.” The chef and food activist Alice Waters cited him as a favorite author and wrote an introduction to Berry’s 1989 essay The Pleasures of Eating.Few authors were more tied to their home than Berry, an intellectual and spiritual heir to Henry David Thoreau and such southern agrarians as Robert Penn Warren and John Crowe Ransom. In prose and poetry that mirrored the uncluttered and deeply felt life he advocated, Berry challenged modern assumptions about prosperity and happiness and renewed the mysteries of birth, love, work and death. He had learned from his own history: Berry was born and raised in a farming town during the Great Depression and watched its seemingly immortal ties unravel by his teens.“Increasingly over the last maybe 40 years, the thought has come to me that the old world in which our people lived by the work of their hands, close to weather and earth, plants and animals, was the true world,” he wrote in his 2006 novel Andy Catlett: Early Travels, “and that the new world of cheap energy and ever cheaper money, honored greed, and dreams of liberation from every restraint, is mostly theater.”“The world I knew as a boy was flawed, surely, but it was substantial and authentic. The households of my grandparents seemed to breathe forth a sense of the real cost and worth of things. Whatever came, came by somebody’s work.”Wendell Berry: ‘for Americans to talk about sustainability is a bit of a joke’Read moreBerry was born in Henry County in 1934, and he moved with his family soon after to New Castle, where his father practised law and all worked on his grandfather’s farm. As a teenager he graduated from the Millersburg Military Institute and entered the University of Kentucky.By his early 20s, he was publishing poems and stories. He received a Wallace Stegner Fellowship from Stanford University in 1958 and stayed on another year as a visiting lecturer. He also lived in New York in the early 1960s, but soon bought Lanes Landing in Kentucky and settled there.Berry and his wife lived without computers, television or phones, but did install solar units in 2005, an act of defiance and of commitment to clean energy in a state powered by coal. He cut ties with the University of Kentucky, his alma mater, after the school accepted $7m for a new basketball dormitory from a group of donors organized by a coal company president. In 2011, he joined a sit-in at the governor’s office in protest of strip-mining.He was among the most prominent authors never to receive a Pulitzer prize or National Book Award, although his honors included a National Humanities Medal and membership in the American Academy of Arts and Letters. In 2016, he was presented a lifetime achievement award from the National Book Critics Circle.“And so I go into the woods. As I go in under the trees, dependably, almost at once, and by nothing I do, things fall into place,” he once wrote. “I enter an order that does not exist outside, in the human spaces. I feel my life take its place among the lives – the trees, the annual plants, the animals and birds, the living of all these and the dead – that go and have gone to make the life of the earth.”Explore more on these topicsBooksKentuckyFictionPoetrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Duane Keith Davis found guilty of 1996 murder of Tupac Shakur | Tupac Shakur | The Guardian
description: Las Vegas jury returns verdict against ex-South Side Compton Crips gang leader in killing of US rap legend
Author: Gabrielle Canon
Headline: Las Vegas jury returns verdict against ex-South Side Compton Crips gang leader in killing of US rap legend
Content: Duane Davis during his murder trial for the 1996 killing of Tupac Shakur, in Las Vegas, Nevada, on 24 August.Photograph: Caroline Brehman/Pool Reuters/APView image in fullscreenDuane Davis during his murder trial for the 1996 killing of Tupac Shakur, in Las Vegas, Nevada, on 24 August.Photograph: Caroline Brehman/Pool Reuters/APTupac ShakurDuane Keith Davis found guilty of 1996 murder of Tupac ShakurLas Vegas jury returns verdict against ex-South Side Compton Crips gang leader in killing of US rap legendThirty years of waiting, a memoir and a trial: conviction in Tupac Shakur killing brings closureGabrielle CanonMon 31 Aug 2026 21.25 EDTFirst published on Mon 31 Aug 2026 20.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Las Vegas jury has found former South Side Compton Crips gang leader Duane Keith Davis guilty of the murder ofTupac Shakur, bringing the case to a close nearly 30 years after the famous rapper was gunned down.The jury took about three hours to reach a guilty verdict in a case that relied heavily on multiple confessions from Davis himself, including his description of the killing in the 2019 memoir Compton Street Legend.Shakur was born in 1971 in East Harlem, New York, and rose to fame in the early 90s, with poetic flow that doubled as sharp commentary on social injustice, including systemic racism, police brutality and the struggles felt by marginalized communities.View image in fullscreenTupac Shakur at the Premiere of I Like It Like That.Photograph: Ron Galella/WireImageRegarded among the greatest rappers to ever live, Shakur affected generations and continued to be celebrated around the world even years after his life was cut short. He was only 25 years old when he died in the hospital days after being shot four times in a car near theLas VegasStrip.Reverence for the rapper has long inspired conspiracy theories about his death as questions swirled around who was involved, why the case remained open for years and even whether Shakur was actually dead.The trial has offered some resolution, even as family members and fans continue to mourn both the man and the years it took to bring details of his death to light.Over the weeks-long trial, Marc DiGiacomo, the Clark county district attorney, and Binu Palal, the chief deputy district attorney, brought 25 witnesses to the stand – including some who had to be ordered by the court because they were reluctant to testify – in their case against Davis.The 63-year-old man who was accused of instigating the deadly shooting, although not pulling the trigger himself, had spent years telling investigators and interviewers alike of his direct involvement before he was arrested in 2023.Davis’s attorney Michael Sanft tried to frame the stories and statements as the exaggerated and embellished claims of a man hoping to benefit from the public interest and unanswered questions around Shakur’s murder.Prosecutors played eight hours of recordings, taken from four separate events in different years, during which Davis shared in his own words what happened the night of 7 September 1996. Davis wrote that he had hatched the plan to retaliate against Shakur after the rapper’s entourage beat his nephew, Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson, in the lobby of the MGM Grand earlier that night. Anderson, who died two years later in an unrelated shootout, was a member of a rival gang in Compton, California.Shakur and the founder of his label, Marion “Suge” Knight, had attended a Mike Tyson boxing match at the casino when the altercation with Anderson took place, and were on their way to an after-party. A white Cadillac pulled up next to them while they were stopped at a red light, and someone in that car began shooting, according to investigators.In his book, Davis claimed to have been in that car, and that he had brought a .40-caliber Glock with him. “Them jumping on my nephew gave us the green light to want to do something to their ass,” he wrote. “Pac chose the wrong game to play.”Tupac’s sister, Sekyiwa “Set” Shakur, cried as the verdict was read, while Davis’s son covered his face with his hand, according to the Associated Press.“It was kinda hard for me to feel so happy at the same time knowing someone is going to jail for so long,” a teary-eyed Shakur fan named Jessica Martin told AP outside the courtroom. “But then I looked over at Tupac’s family and it reminded me of everything they’ve gone through. It’s really emotional.”View image in fullscreenTupac Shakur and Marion Suge Knight, Death Row Records chair, at a voter registration event in Los Angeles in 1996.Photograph: Frank Wiese/APThe Clark county district court judge Carli Kierny scheduled Davis’s sentencing hearing for 13 October. Prosecutors had not sought the death penalty against Davis and, after the verdict, voluntarily dropped their efforts to tack a gang enhancement on to Davis’s conviction.First-degree murderin Nevadacarries penalties ranging from 20 years to life imprisonment. Davis said he plans to appeal the verdict.While the trial has finally come to an end, family members had been left to wonder for years why it took so long for investigators to reach a conclusion in the case.“We’ve been waiting 30 years to grieve properly,” Zayd Akinyela, Shakur’s cousin told reporters outside the courtroom when the trial was under way. “A lot of people don’t get to grieve until they understand what happened to their loved one and how it happened.”A Los Angeles Times review of police missteps on the case, published in 2015, detailed how authorities failed to investigate Anderson even after details about the conflict between him and Shakur’s entourage became known. Police also declined to follow a lead from a member of Shakur’s entourage, who claimed he could identify the shooters. That witness died weeks later in a separate shooting, the Times reported.1:46Jury finds Duane Davis guilty of 1996 murder of Tupac Shakur – videoThe investigation highlighted why many of his followers, members of his family and Black leaders and entertainers have pointed to the case – and the years it took to reach a conclusion – as yet another indication of racism in a broken justice system.Investigators, meanwhile, said it was challenging to prove because they struggled to produce physical evidence and faced strong resistance from potential witnesses, including other members of the rapper’s entourage. Even now, some resisted participating in the case and had to be compelled to come to court.Davis ultimately became the prosecution’s lead witness, despite being the defendant. “Had he decided to never write the book,” DiGiacomosaidduring the trial, “he would not, probably, have ever been prosecuted for the crime.”Explore more on these topicsTupac ShakurGun crimeUS justice systemUS crimeLas VegasNevadaLaw (US)newsShareReuse this content

title: Raygun: Breaking Badly review – the ridiculed Olympic B-girl gets the last laugh … and it’s a total joy | Television | The Guardian
description: She spent the biggest moment of her career at the Paris Olympics thrashing around like a toddler having a tantrum – then went viral globally. Now, a new Netflix film reveals how the much-mocked breakdancer got over it
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: She spent the biggest moment of her career at the Paris Olympics thrashing around like a toddler having a tantrum – then went viral globally. Now, a new Netflix film reveals how the much-mocked breakdancer got over it
Content: Out of step … Rachael Gunn in Untold Raygun: Breaking Badly on Netflix.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixView image in fullscreenOut of step … Rachael Gunn in Untold Raygun: Breaking Badly on Netflix.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixTV reviewTelevisionReviewRaygun: Breaking Badly review – the ridiculed Olympic B-girl gets the last laugh … and it’s a total joyShe spent the biggest moment of her career at the Paris Olympics thrashing around like a toddler having a tantrum – then went viral globally. Now, a new Netflix film reveals how the much-mocked breakdancer got over itStuart HeritageTue 1 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNetflix’s Untold is ostensibly a series of sports documentaries. However, since its inception five years ago, it has been most successful when sport collides with the wider celebrity machine. There have been films about Caitlyn Jenner, Jake Paul and Vinnie Jones. The gold tends to come when the subjects spill over into public notoriety. With that in mind, it was only a matter of time before they made a film about Raygun.You may remember Raygun as the Australian breakdancer who spent the biggest moment of her career at the Paris Olympics thrashing around like a toddler having a tantrum in a supermarket. If you didn’t see her routine, you will almost certainly be aware of the memes she inspired. Adele discussed her during a concert. Rachel Dratch did an impersonation of her on Jimmy Fallon. For months, Raygun was everywhere. As this film demonstrates, she really didn’t want to be.This, of course, is part of the great Olympic tradition. In every competition, a country will put up an athlete who – while perhaps the best in their country – finds themselves wildly out of their league on the international stage. Raygun entered the same Olympic pantheon asEddie the Eagle,Eric Moussambaniand theJamaican bobsleigh team; competitors whose limitations made them more famous than most champions.However, there are a couple of key differences here. The first is that Raygun was competing in a sport that had never previously been held at the Olympics, and whose inclusion was already primed for ridicule. The second is that she was competing in the age of social media, allowing every idiot with a phone to mock her performance in real time. Crashing out of the Olympics with zero points was one thing. Knowing that the world considered you a joke turned out to be far worse.Raygun – real name Dr Rachael Gunn, author of the PhD thesis Deterritorializing Gender in Sydney’s Breakdancing Scene: A B-girl’s Experience of B-boying – is understandably front and centre here, which is good because she turns out to be an intensely charismatic person, in turn open and joyful and infectious. The same can be said for her husband, Sam, a breaker whose professional name (at least before he started training children) was Sammy Sex.View image in fullscreenJoyful … Raygun (left) and B-Girl Flix in Untold Raygun: Breaking Badly.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixIt is through their eyes that this textbook Olympic underdog story is told. A country holds trials for the Olympics. The best person on the day gets through, only to realise fairly quickly that the rest of the world is leagues ahead of them. Gunn watches in dismay as she realises that her unique brand of creative breaking doesn’t mesh with the hardcore power moves of the world elite. In effect, Australia entered an interpretive dancer into a gymnastics competition. Of course she was going to do badly. By her own admission, judged by these criteria, she was “pretty shit”.It’s an opinion that, for a time, the world happened to share. A couple of Australian breakers named Tinylocks and Flix form a Greek chorus here, taking uncomfortably gleeful pleasure in Raygun’s public downfall. But their opinions are amplified by reams of social media posts that gradually balloon out of all proportion, with some falsely claiming that Gunn qualified only because her husband was head of the Olympic committee, and others projecting no end of vitriol about her perceived privilege.It was a truly ugly spectacle. Gunn began to take antidepressants and made a video begging the media to leave her alone. Needless to say, the video made the news, in one case above rolling text reporting the latest tally of dead Palestinians.But once the outrage burned off, people started to notice what Gunn had done. Rather than try to keep up with her more conventionally talented competitors, she entered the Olympics on her own terms. Obviously that didn’t work, because she left the group stage without a single point, but what we saw was a woman being her complete, undiluted self.And isn’t that more relatable than almost anything else at the Olympics? Most Olympians have pushed everything else aside for years, pinning the outcome of their lives on a single moment. Raygun, meanwhile, was a bundle of nerves – underprepared and brimming with impostor syndrome – who was simply trying to get through the day unscathed. In that respect, she may have been the most human athlete there.Untold Raygun: Breaking Badly is on Netflix nowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewreviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: join the jury as a teenager goes on trial for murder | Television | The Guardian
description: The gripping series about controversial real-life verdicts returns. Plus: The Great British Sewing Bee gets bookish. Here’s what to watch today
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: The gripping series about controversial real-life verdicts returns. Plus: The Great British Sewing Bee gets bookish. Here’s what to watch today
Content: Nature v nurture ... The Jury: 14 and on Trial for Murder.Photograph: Lottie O’Neill/Channel 4View image in fullscreenNature v nurture ... The Jury: 14 and on Trial for Murder.Photograph: Lottie O’Neill/Channel 4TV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: join the jury as a teenager goes on trial for murderThe gripping series about controversial real-life verdicts returns. Plus: The Great British Sewing Bee gets bookish. Here’s what to watch todayPhil Harrison,Graeme Virtue,Hollie RichardsonandPriya ElanTue 1 Sep 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Jury: 14 and on Trial for Murder9pm, Channel 4Withtrial by jury under scrutiny, this is a timely moment for the return of this gripping series, which reruns an actual criminal trial and follows the 12 jury members as they reach their verdict. This time, the case of brothers – one of whom is only 14 years old – accused of killing their stepfather causes instant polarisation. Debates around nature and nurture and punishment for its own sake emerge straight away.PhilHarrisonRace Against the Tide7.30pm, BBC TwoThis good vibes sand-sculpting contest should really be called the Great British Scrape Off. With no eliminations last time, the six teams gather in St Andrews to tackle their latest challenge: smoothing a beach into something that evokes the beauty and motion of the ocean.Graeme VirtueThe Great British Sewing Bee8pm, BBC OneView image in fullscreenWho will make it to the next chapter? Judges Esme Young and Patrick Grant in The Great British Sewing Bee.Photograph: BBC/Love Productions LtdA deerstalker fit for Sherlock Holmes; an outfit for a grownup Matilda made out of old school uniforms; a made-to-measure Regency dress inspired by the world of Jane Austen – it can only be literary icons week in the sewing competition. Who will make it to the next chapter?Hollie RichardsonCelebrity MasterChef9pm, BBC OneThis week, the competitors include plum-voiced prankster Max Fosh, who does lots of unintentional Partridge (“Bosh!”); Una from the Saturdays, who likes to talk about potatoes; and Paralympian Lauren Steadman, who says she forces everyone she cooks for to give her marks out of 10 for the food. Sounds relaxing.Priya ElanThe Game9pm, Channel 5The excellent Jason Watkins returns as embattled former detective Huw Miller in the second series of this somewhat hysterical thriller. Huw and his wife, Alice, have retired to a remote coastal home, but the past hasn’t left them behind as letters start to arrive from Robson Green’s imprisoned serial killer, Patrick Harbottle.PHLittle Bird9pm, Sky AtlanticView image in fullscreenDeeply moving drama … Darla Contois in Little Bird.Photograph: Holly Dunphy/©Original Pictures Inc.It’s the concluding double bill of this deeply moving drama about the Sixties Scoop in Canada, when Indigenous children were taken from their families. title: The man who shaped Trump: book sheds fresh light on ruthless Roy Cohn | Books | The Guardian
description: American Scoundrel tells story of McCarthy attack dog, mob lawyer and Trump mentor – will the president be thumbing its pages?
Author: Martin Pengelly
Headline: American Scoundrel tells story of McCarthy attack dog, mob lawyer and Trump mentor – will the president be thumbing its pages?
Content: Donald Trump with Roy Cohn at Trump Tower in Manhattan in 1983.Photograph: Sonia Moskowitz/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump with Roy Cohn at Trump Tower in Manhattan in 1983.Photograph: Sonia Moskowitz/Getty ImagesBooksThe man who shaped Trump: book sheds fresh light on ruthless Roy CohnAmerican Scoundrel tells story of McCarthy attack dog, mob lawyer and Trump mentor – will the president be thumbing its pages?Martin Pengellyin WashingtonTue 1 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 09.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKai Bird and Susan Goldmark have written a book Trumpworld doesn’t want you to read. Published on Tuesday,American Scoundrelis a propulsive, horrifying biography of Roy Cohn, the New York mob lawyer whose extraordinary life charted, as the book’s subtitle has it, a “Dark Journey from Joe McCarthy to Donald Trump”.“I told my publicist to reach out to any of the Fox News hosts and reporters, to Joe Rogan, Steve Bannon,” Bird said. “We haven’t gotten a peep, other than Joe Rogan. He said he looked at the galleys, and he got back to my publicist and said, ‘I’m not interested.’ I’m kind of surprised. This is a serious biography of the president’s mentor, whom he publicly admires and says he still misses.”From the mid-70s to the mid-80s, Cohn guided Trump through the cutthroat world of New York real estate. Everything brutal about Trump, in business and politics, he probably learned from Cohn. How to profit fromties to organized crime? Check. How to stay a step ahead of the law? Check. How to remorselessly lie and never admit wrong or defeat? Check.Small wonder thatin 2017, amid scandal over links to Russia that aides couldn’t master, Trump memorably demanded:“Where’s my Roy Cohn?”Trump does know about American Scoundrel, because Bird called him four times on his personal number.“The interviews were eight, nine, 10 minutes,” Bird said. “He told some stories. They were of use to me. I asked, ‘Well, how did you first meet Roy Cohn?’ And I was expecting what he had said before inThe Art of the Dealand in interviews, and instead he flipped the story all the way upside down. Instead of him going up to the older man, recognizing the powerful lawyer sitting at a nearby table at Le Club in Manhattan [in 1973], he said, ‘Oh, Roy Cohn recognized me. I was making a name for myself as a young developer in Manhattan.’”View image in fullscreenKai Bird and Susan Goldmark.Photograph: ScribnerAnother lesson from Cohn: tell the story however the hell you want.Describing his final Trump call, Bird said: “It’s so weird. You cold-call him, and he picks up. This time, instead of politely listening to my questions, he says, ‘Oh, I can’t do this. I don’t have time for this. You shouldn’t be using this number. I’m the president. I have Russia calling. I have China calling.’ And I say, ‘OK, I understand, Mr President, but I just have two questions.’“And I ask, ‘Did you know that Roy Cohn in 1976 voted for Jimmy Carter?’ And he says, ‘Ah, that’s unbelievable. Why would he do that?’ And I said, ‘Well, Roy was kind of fed up and impatient with the old guard Republican party symbolized by Gerald Ford, and he thought Jimmy Carter was a fresh face.’ And Trump said, ‘Oh, I can understand that. That makes sense.’ You know his frustrations with the Republican party establishment. So that must have resonated with him.“Then I said, ‘Well, Cohn quickly got disillusioned with Carter, particularly over the Panama canal treaty, and of course Trump jumped in and said, ‘Yeah, that was a terrible deal. What a terrible deal!’ He’s trying to get off the phone, and I say, ‘Well, I just want you to know this book is coming out in the autumn, and he says, ‘Oh, terrific, maybe I can promote it. Anything I promote goes to number one.’ And then there’s a pause, and he says, ‘Of course, it would have to be fair.’”American Scoundrel is certainly fair. Birdwon a Pulitzer prizefor American Prometheus, a life of the nuclear scientist J Robert Oppenheimer co-written with Martin J Sherwin and the basis for Christopher Nolan’sOscar-winning biopic. Bird’s last subject wasCarter. Cohn kept cropping up, so Bird and Goldmark (his wife, “director of research” and “muse”) got down to work. Then Trump was re-elected. Cohn was current again.“At 27, Cohn was onthe cover of Time magazine,” Bird said, pointing to a rise that saw Cohn graduate from Columbia Law School at 20, prosecute Julius and Ethel Rosenberg,executed for spying for Russia, then become the GOP senator Joe McCarthy’s aide inthe Red Scare, the brutal 1950s witch-hunt of liberals and homosexuals.“Joe McCarthy is a much less complicated and driven kind of figure than Roy Cohn,” Bird said. “Joe McCarthy was a populist senator from Wisconsin who was simply looking to generate some headlines, and he kind of stumbled on the idea of communists and the government.”Cohn was “the ideologue. He’s the svengali, the real brain, who tells Joe McCarthy how he can take advantage of this issue. He runs the hearings, actually conducts the interrogations of these witnesses and is driven out of ideological certainty that there is a danger to the nation from internal communism, and a desire as a Jewish American – this is, I think, important to his identity – to prove his own loyalty, to prove not all Jews are leftwing.”Cohn’s rightwing credentials were impeccable: he was close to Rupert Murdoch, Ronald Reagan and other major reactionary figures.View image in fullscreenThe cover of American Scoundrel.Photograph: ScribnerAs thehorrorsof McCarthyism now echo in Trump’sextralegal war on “woke”, so do inquisitors’ unenforced errors. The Army-McCarthy hearings, whichbrought McCarthy downin 1954, were spawned by Cohn’s attempts to get another young inquisitor, G David Schine, out of overseas service. Senators insinuated Cohn and Shine were lovers. Cohn was certainly gay but never came out of the closet. He was also, Bird said, “quite definitely attracted to Donald Trump. When he met him, Trump was 27 years old. He was tall, blonde, blue-eyed. Wealthy, somewhat. So he was Roy’s type. I don’t think anything sexual went on between them but there was a dynamic, and a pattern to Roy’s friendships.”Cohn could be generous. Bird considers the case of Gary Belis, who dated Cohn, 25 years his senior, but didn’t sleep with him and remained fond. But that story is told in a chapter titled “Predator”, which also containsthe horrific story of Richard Kerr, a Northern Irish boy abused in care then trafficked around the world, including to Roy Cohn.“He could be very charming with someone like Gary Belis and sort of decent,” Bird said. “He courted him, gave him favors as Roy would, but he backed off when Gary indicated he couldn’t go down that path. And yet Cohn was a sexual addict, and he had these ‘boy toys’” – teen hustlers paid for sex.Cohn is an American villain. He features inAngels in America, Tony Kushner’s stage epic of the Aids crisis. In 2024,Jeremy Strongplayed him in The Apprentice, Ali Abbasi’s Trump biopic. A portion of his archive is owned by Michael Stipe of REM, author of the songExhuming McCarthy.He died in 1986, aged 59, from Aids. As he always denied his sexuality, so he denied his final illness, claiming liver cancer even as he received experimental Aids treatment thanks to Washington connections. Not long before he died, he wasdisbarredfor unethical conduct, three indictments having failed to bring him down. (He still had 36 character witnesses, among them Trump, William F Buckley Jr and the TV host Barbara Walters, once Cohn’s “beard”, or fake romantic interest.) In extremis, Trump is commonly said to have abandoned Cohn, causing him to say: “Donald pisses ice water.” Bird said: “That’s not entirely true.“I quote the switchboard operator Chris Seymour at Cohn’sNew Yorktownhouse law firm. He said that when Trump recognized that Roy was dying of Aids, he began to keep his distance. He didn’t rely on him as much, as his lawyer. The calls were fewer. But that didn’t mean he cut him off. He did invite him down to his new estate in Mar-a-Lago for this fabulous dinner, March 86, so just five months before he dies. And it was a touching farewell dinner, with many toasts.”Cohn’s memorial service was held in midtown Manhattan. A witness saw Trump weeping.American Scoundrel isout nowExplore more on these topicsBooksDonald TrumpNew YorkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Anita Brookner by Hermione Lee review – an enigmatic literary great given her due | Anita Brookner | The Guardian
description: This exhaustive biography of the Booker winner brings her properly out of the shadows for the first time
Author: Lucy Atkins
Headline: This exhaustive biography of the Booker winner brings her properly out of the shadows for the first time
Content: Anita Brookner in 1987.Photograph: Mike Abrahams/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenAnita Brookner in 1987.Photograph: Mike Abrahams/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.Book of the dayAnita BrooknerReviewAnita Brookner by Hermione Lee review – an enigmatic literary great given her dueThis exhaustive biography of the Booker winner brings her properly out of the shadows for the first timeLucy AtkinsTue 1 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 05.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Dr Weiss, at forty, knew that her life had been ruined by literature.” The first fictional sentenceAnita Brooknerever published, aged 53, in A Start in Life, certainly set a tone. If people have heard of Brookner today, Hermione Lee says, they imagine a lonely, cardiganed woman yearning for an absent lover. “This,” says Lee (an emeritus English professor at the University of Oxford), “won’t do.”The cardiganed image confuses the author with her protagonists. Of 24 novels written across 30 years, only the first four – A Start in Life, Providence, Look at Me and Hotel du Lac – are about a single woman pining for love. There is certainly a “Brooknerian” style, characterised by elegance, restraint and melancholia, but her fiction engaged with our emotional lives broadly, examining family, exile, home, trauma, ageing and much more.Born in 1928 and raised in south London by a fearsome Polish-Jewish grandmother and absurdly ineffectual parents (a tobacco salesman and a failed singer), Brookner was a highly academic only child. After a degree at King’s College London, she briefly tasted freedom as a student in Paris, but was soon dragged back to care for her extraordinarily needy mother. Yoked to home for the next decade, she managed, nevertheless, to become a brilliant art critic and a charismatic lecturer at the Courtauld Institute, where she stayed until retirement.In the introduction, Lee describes hearing the author’s voice saying, repeatedly, “Go away”, and Brookner’s 20s and 30s were the “most hidden, the least witnessed” of all. Brookner did her utmost to erase her life, and Lee is forced, therefore, to mine any detail she can find. As well as Brookner’s academic work and extensive reading habits, we get her poor handwriting, fear of trains, love of perfumes and at one particularly desperate point, salary increases over two decades. A couple of love affairs in her 30s fizzled out, but if there was ever a record of her feelings, Brookner expunged it. The first 200 pages, then, can be hard going. She was, says Lee, through gritted teeth, “an object of mystery and puzzlement”.double quotation markPrivate Eye snarked about 'Hotel du Lac of Interest' and a grim pattern of critical disdain was setBut Lee persists – always rake thin, Brookner kept slimming biscuits in her handbag; she loved babies; she doled out tranquillisers to nervous PhD candidates – and just as this enterprise starts to feel doomed, something miraculous happens. The tireless details begin to cohere and Brookner steps out of the shadows, intriguing, contradictory – the super brain who shaved 10 years off her age in her own Who’s Who entry; the self-proclaimed “loneliest woman in London” who had loads of friends.The older she gets, the more interesting this book becomes. In 1979, her beloved Courtauld mentor, friend and boss, Anthony Blunt, was exposed as a Soviet spy. Shaken, Brookner remained loyal until she discovered he’d used her to extract information from a hospitalised colleague.Reeling and depressed, facing another lonely summer, she found herself writing fiction. Her process was extraordinary. Each novel took only three months from start to finish. She’d roam London forming sentences in her head, then simply write them down, at speed. Hilary Mantel, a fervent admirer, said Brookner arrived as a novelist perfectly formed, “as if she had hatched from a marbled egg”. She would repeat this process, annually, for more than two decades.In 1984, her fourth novel, Hotel du Lac,about a woman who jilts her fiancee and retreats to a Swiss hotel,won the Booker prize. Pretty much everyone expected JG Ballard’s Empire of the Sun or Julian Barnes’s Flaubert’s Parrot to win. The misogyny was mind-bending. At the ceremony, Ballard hissed, “You stole my Booker.” Private Eye snarked about “Hotel du Lac of Interest” and a grim pattern of critical disdain was set. For the rest of Brookner’s writing life, critics would carp about “doily” novels and compare her to Mills & Boon. Profiles were invariably illustrated with sad spinsters holding cups of tea. It tormented her. But she kept on writing.She was, personally, far from isolated. She had devoted friends, including the Virago publisher Carmen Callil and fellow writers such as Rosamond Lehmann or Julian Barnes, who offers loving memories here. He was so intimidated by her eloquence when they lunched that he’d feel himself inserting semicolons into his own speech.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWas she a literary genius? She once, brilliantly, described novel-writing as “trying very hard to remember something which has not yet taken place”. Lee offers genuinely transporting literary criticism, unearthing the elegance and complexity of the work, but admits the compulsive production of a book a year diluted the impact and sometimes the quality. Still, she singles out three – Family and Friends, Latecomers and The Next Big Thing–as truly “outstanding” novels. Thankfully, it is no longer cool to Brookner-bash. This astute and tireless biography succeeds, against the odds, in unearthing the author – who would be appalled by our scrutiny. Above all, it shows that the work deserves our full attention.Anita Brookner: Art and Life by Hermione Lee is published by Chatto & Windus (£28). title: Under Story by Chloe Benjamin review – this time-reversal melodrama is quantum hokum | Science fiction books | The Guardian
description: A grieving couple who have lost their son find a way to a mirror universe where time runs backwards – but the narrative machinery is shonky and distracting
Author: Beejay Silcox
Headline: A grieving couple who have lost their son find a way to a mirror universe where time runs backwards – but the narrative machinery is shonky and distracting
Content: ‘Will the suffragettes fight to relinquish the vote?’ … Chloe Benjamin.Photograph: David EnloeView image in fullscreen‘Will the suffragettes fight to relinquish the vote?’ … Chloe Benjamin.Photograph: David EnloeScience fiction booksReviewUnder Story by Chloe Benjamin review – this time-reversal melodrama is quantum hokumA grieving couple who have lost their son find a way to a mirror universe where time runs backwards – but the narrative machinery is shonky and distractingBeejay SilcoxTue 1 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is something farcical – grotesque, even – about life played in reverse. A child falling into a tree. A sandwich emerging from a mouth, bite by reconstituted bite. A doctor unstitching a wound. The world is strange in any order, but rewind helps us notice – makes the ordinary absurd.Novels that pick a fight with forward momentum tend to harness this absurdity, revel in it. InThe Cockroach(2019), Ian McEwan gives us a sneering Brexit fable about political nostalgia. If voters want to turn back the clock, let them. He unleashes “Economic Reversalism”, which sees employees pay for the privilege of work, and every pound sent back to where it came from. In Time’s Arrow (1991), Martin Amis inverts the Holocaust. Just imagine it, he dares us: a network of sanatoriums instead of death camps. A vast machinery of reparation run by benevolent Nazis. How monstrously laughable.Joining this backwards bunch is Chloe Benjamin with her third novel, Under Story. It conjures a universe that mirrors our own (a “duoverse”), populated by doppelgangers; a place where the past might be undone, because it hasn’t happened yet.Here are the fictional facts. In the duoverse, ordinary human life begins underground. Mycelium grow a corpse from rot, like a 3D printer for gizzards. A heart starts beating, for reasons, and a fully grown human crawls up from the soil riddled with elderly ailments, but with a box-fresh brain. Once they’re cleaned up and DNA profiled – the work of “overtakers” – these new/old people are delivered to their children, but in the postal, rather than the obstetric, sense. The doorbell rings.Brains grow older; bodies grow younger. Cancers unbloom. Cataracts fade. Children raise their parents until they’re spry enough to cope on their own. Nursing homes are convalescent kindergartens. And down at the other end of life, kindergartens are dementia clinics full of geriatric toddlers. Death is birth: neonates are shoved up their mothers in maternity morgues, swallowed by the amniotic dark.It’s ghoulish stuff, body horror territory: wards of women surgically forced to eat their babies with their hungry vaginas. You might expect – even hope for – some literary depravity: Benjamin Button reimagined by William Burroughs orAgustina Bazterrica. But Under Story is a love story. We follow a forward-born couple, Laurel and Eli, who are grieving their son, Silas. Could a round trip to the duoverse summon him back? Might it also help them to forgive one another? What follows is a 500-page melodrama of parental devotion and quantum hokum. Imagine Orpheus and Eurydice meets Interstellar, but starring Tom Hanks from Big.Using a combination of speculative physics and prophetic dreams, Laurel and Eli find their way to a portal under the ice of Antarctica and into the duoverse. They adjust quickly to its topsy-turvy logic: September follows October, Obama follows Trump, and the analogue revolution is under way (the record player has just been invented). Handily, the climate is also unravaging – extinct species popping up from the ground like the mushrooms that remade them.double quotation markIt’s meant to make us weep, to rouse mighty questions about love, free will and our connection to the planetThe key to it all is entropy: “this universe moves toward the Big Bang, and entropy is reversed,” Eli explains. He’s a physicist; Laurel is a mycologist. They’ll both do a great deal of explaining.There can be no life without entropy, but that’s not the problem here. Plenty of imagined worlds are nonsense, and gloriously so. The problem is that Benjamin keeps drawing our attention to her shonky narrative machinery. She answers questions we’d never thought to ask. We learn that “Christmas exists here, even though Jesus won’t be born for two thousand years” and that reverse folks can’t choose to procreate, because the decision is already waiting for them when they grovel out of the placental dirt.Benjamin’s last novel, 2018’sThe Immortalists, was also about foretold lives: four siblings who learn the dates of their deaths from a fortune teller. But the point – and lure – of that novel was doubt. Was the prophecy real or self-fulfilling? Is there a difference? Benjamin left those questions with us. In Under Story, she seems unsure her cosmic premise can carry its own mysteries.But the more we learn, the more distracted we are. And that’s before Benjamin busts out some last-act theatrics – mystical anagrams and fortuitous gadgetry – or subjects us to a death-birth. It’s hard to trust a novel that doesn’t trust itself.Part of the problem is length. Rewound life is a gimmick, a thought experiment. The books that do it best are wry, incisive and short (the anticlockwise archetype, F Scott Fitzgerald’s The Curious Case of Benjamin Button, is a fleet 40-page story). The longer Laurel and Eli stay in the duoverse, the more contrived it all feels, because the more contrived it has to be. It’s hard to live backwards with dignity, and Benjamin knows it. And so she picks and chooses which bodily functions work in which direction. People walk and talk normally. Have conceptionless sex. Breathe and eat and excrete. It’s entropy galore, except for the life cycle. The author has her backwards cake, and eats it too.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTop 10 novels that interrupt time | Ross RaisinRead moreBut there are much easier ways to meddle with the past and its sorrows (see Scott Alexander Howard’sThe Other Valleyor Aja Gabel’sLightbreakers), which makes all of Benjamin’s picking and choosing feel particularly gruesome. Her duoverse has been elaborately rigged to produce a scene of filial reunion. She has violated the laws of physics, reanimated the dead and turned women’s bodies into tombs all in order to weaponise parental grief.It’s meant to make us weep, to rouse mighty questions about ageless love, free will and our intimate connection to the planet. But here are some of the questions I scribbled in the margins of Under Story: if every fossil is a future creature, are palaeontologists dino-killers? Will the suffragettes fight to relinquish the vote? If vaginas work backwards, are penises the same: meaty little vacuum cleaners, hoovering up sperm? Once you’ve written a line like that you know your suspension of disbelief has well and truly snapped. And maybe something else has too.Under Story by Chloe Benjamin is published by Tinder (£20). title: ‘Led us down such a dark path’: documentary explores how 9/11 changed America | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: In Netflix film Turning Point: Generation 9/11, the lives of people forever impacted by the terrorist attack in 2001 are explored
Author: David Smith
Headline: In Netflix film Turning Point: Generation 9/11, the lives of people forever impacted by the terrorist attack in 2001 are explored
Content: A still from Turning Point: Generation 9/11.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixView image in fullscreenA still from Turning Point: Generation 9/11.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixDocumentary films‘Led us down such a dark path’: documentary explores how 9/11 changed AmericaIn Netflix film Turning Point: Generation 9/11, the lives of people forever impacted by the terrorist attack in 2001 are exploredDavid Smithin WashingtonTue 1 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 12.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwenty-five years on, memory is giving way to history.
