Soon the US will cross the point where half its population were born after11 September 2001or were too young to remember the day that terrorists crashed planes into the World Trade Center in New York, the Pentagon in northern Virginia and a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania.‘Environmental violence’: inside the fight to save indigenous land from becoming a nuclear dumping groundRead more“When I do that math, I get to the bomb at Hiroshima – that’s how distant it is,” says Brian Knappenberger, 56, director of a new Netflix documentary,Turning Point: Generation 9/11. “When we talk about the second world war, for our generation it seemed like a long time ago but, for the current generation of 20-year-olds, that’s how long ago it was.”Having previously made series about the “war on terror”, cold war and Vietnam war, Knappenberger felt compelled to address a generation for whom 9/11 is an abstraction they might find in a school history textbook, a solemn annual ceremony or, most disorientingly, a meme circulating on TikTok and Instagram.Speaking via Google Meet from Los Angeles, he adds: “This film is coming from a place of respecting that experience, not assuming that people understand what it felt like to live through 9/11, which is so ingrained to those of us that did. It’s to illustrate not just what terrorism meant and how frightening that was but also how the decisions made in the days and weeks and years that followed – maybe more than the events themselves – changed us as a country.”Indeed, Knappenberger’s film captures a paradox: even as 9/11 fades from living memory, we are still living in a vividly 9/11 world. “We are at a place where it is moving into distant history. But I would like people to understand what we went through and record in a documentary what those decisions did to us – and ask what kind of country we want to be.”Turning Point: Generation 9/11 follows in a long line of documentaries recounting the horror ofa day that killed nearly 3,000 people: the morning TV shows jarringly interrupted, the trapped office workers, the final phone calls, the heroic firefighters, the falling towers, the dust-coated commuters, the sombre presidential address.For older generations, it is a day when everyone remembers where they were and what they were doing. “9/11 changed my life,” Knappenberger reflects. “It changed how I saw the world. It changed how I saw the political system in the United States. It changed the course of my career. It’s hard to even describe with hindsight how profound of a change this was.”But for anyone born in the late 1990s or later, 9/11 feels like an inheritance. The documentary focuses on young people whose entire lives were directly shaped by the catastrophe. Among them is Laurel Homer, whose father,LeRoy Homer, was the co-pilot of United Flight 93. Laurel was just 10 months old when her father and passengers fought back against hijackers over Shanksville. In the film, she describes feeling like “collateral” in a narrative that consumed her family.She confides: “I know he was a hero but I wish he didn’t have to be …My entire life was kind of built around this. I’m just still struggling so much and it has taken over, like, my whole life.” Grieving a father she never knew, Laurel finds herself confronting strangers online who send callous direct messages or peddle conspiracy theories claiming the tragedy was an elaborate inside job.There is also An Nguyen, whose father,Khang Nguyen– an immigrant who grew up amid the Vietnam war before emigrating to the US – was killed while working as an electrical engineer at the Pentagon. An was four years old when his father ran out to kiss him goodbye at the preschool bus on that Tuesday morning, never to return.Knappenberger observes: “It’s incredibly profound to understand what the children of people who lost their parents, lost their loved ones on 9/11, went through on those days. But it’s more profound when you think about how it changed their lives and those events have stayed with them through the evolution that our country also went through.”To view the modern US information ecosystem through the eyes of these families exposes the depth of contemporary political cynicism, he continues. There has been “memeification” of the event, where conspiracy theories and jokes aboutOsama bin LadenorGeorge W Bushcirculate on platforms such as TikTok and Instagram.More perniciously,the “truther” movementrejects the official account of 9/11 in favour of conspiracy theories, including that it was orchestrated by the US government itself.The director says: “9/11 gave birth to the truther movement – this incredibly dark movement that rises in a disinformation environment, claiming 9/11 wasn’t real or that jet fuel can’t burn steel, that it was an inside job. When you look at these disinformation campaigns through the eyes of children who actually lost loved ones, that makes it even more profound and telling.”View image in fullscreenAn Nguyen in Turning Point: Generation 9/11.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixKnappenberger traces a thread from early conspiracy theories to today’s fractured political reality. “There is a direct line from the early 9/11 truther movement through all of the rise of conspiracy theories online, and a direct connection from that to figures likeAlex Jones, who became a leading figure in the movement, all the way through the disinformation and misinformation that we see now that divides and tears our country apart.”The timing proved fateful. Facebook launched in 2004, Reddit in 2005 and Twitter in 2006. “These platforms were coming of age right in the shadow of 9/11 and so you had this massive rise of conspiracy theories and this new technology and ways we’re communicating on social media happening at the same time. I don’t think you can separate these things. The truther movement is an early predecessor to some of the chaotic world of misinformation that we see now.”The domestic fallout of September 11 was not confined to the internet. The film tracks how the institutional apparatus constructed in the immediate aftermath of the attacks permanently altered civil liberties at home. It visits Brooklyn’s “Little Pakistan” to capture the experience of shopkeepers and families who lived the American dream before 2001, only to find their neighbourhoods subjected to FBI monitoring, harassment and suspicion almost overnight.Knappenberger highlights the creation of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and the subsequent formation of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) which, under Donald Trump, has been widely condemned for its aggressive enforcement tactics and arrests of people without criminal recordsin cities such as Minneapolis.“The violence we see ICE perpetrating on the streets of America has a direct line to 9/11,” he says. “We became fearful and suspicious of Muslim communities in America, and that infrastructure we built needed another place to go, and it continued. That fear dominates us and politicians have capitalised on that fear in order to get elected and to get power.”He adds: “There’s no question that when you see violence on the streets of America perpetrated by ICE, that is a shock of 9/11. That is the wave of violence that started on 9/11 and a direct result of decisions that were made then.This is a choice about who are we as Americans, what’s important to us and what do we do moving forward. There’s a new generation who will start to have to answer those questions for themselves.”The US has also projected violence abroad over the past quarter of a century at a cost of millions of lives. The foundational pillar of the “forever wars” was erected just three days after the twin towers fell when Congress passed the2001 Authorization for Use of Military Force (AUMF)with only a single dissenting vote. Intended to target al-Qaida and those who harboured them, the statute became an elastic legal justification for military interventions, drone campaigns and indefinite detentions across sovereign nations spanning four presidential administrations.“We created this thing called the AUMF, which is about as simple as it gets,” Knappenberger says. “That’s simply not how it works or the way our country was set up. It’s pretty clear in the constitution that Congress determines if we get a war or not. After 230 years at that point of being a country, of having a constitution, we decided after 9/11 that we weren’t going to do that any more. We decided we’re going to defer that in these cases to the president – not at all how the founders of this country saw our government working.”The long-term consequence, Knappenberger argues, has been a dangerous expansion of executive power. “That was meant to go after al-Qaida, the people that attacked us on 9/11, and it has morphed into the rationale behind lots of other wars that we’ve engaged in. In that sense we’re still feeling the effects of the ‘war on terror’ in the way that it shifted power in the United States to the executive.“It said now the president gets to decide if we’re engaging in these wars or not. That’s a huge difference in how America is supposed to operate. In that sense we’re definitely very much feeling the effects of the ‘war on terror’ still – this nebulous war on terror that can be applied and used as a justification for all these other wars.”View image in fullscreenThe World Trade Center on 9/11.Photograph: Hubert Michael Boesl/EPAIf 9/11 was the opening salvo of a new geopolitical era, the chaotic August 2021 evacuation from Hamid Karzai international airport in Kabul after a 20-year war in Afghanistan was the closing of a chapter. The mission suffered a disaster when an Isis-K suicide bomberdetonated an explosive vest at Abbey Gate, killing 13 US service members and at least 170 Afghan civilians.Knappenberger weaves the harrowing experiences of young US marines stationed at Abbey Gate into the narrative. They describe the strange experience of having to coordinate security with the Taliban – the very enemy the US had invaded to depose two decades earlier.Knappenberger says: “It didn’t seem possible that we would still have troops in Afghanistan 20 years after 9/11, especially with how fast the Taliban was driven out. Here we are 20 years after that with a new generation of people: some weren’t born, some were too young to remember 9/11. They are the ones closing it out in those final harrowing days and of course 13 people were killed in that bombing. It’s profound and on the Taliban side you have people who were also not born yet or were too young to remember the events of that day.”Alongside the US military trauma, the film foregrounds the plight of Afghan allies who placed their faith in the United States. One former Afghan military pilot, Obaidullah Durani, recounts securing evacuation for his two children to Arizona while hissick wife, Shafaro, was separated from themand left behind under Taliban rule, fracturing the family.For Knappenberger, the visual parallels between Kabul in 2021 and Saigon in 1975 represent an indictment. “One season of Turning Point wasabout the Vietnam warand you saw people who believed in the American cause fleeing in fear for their lives at the end of that war. Many people thought this was a tragedy that we should never repeat as a country but it’s something that very much was repeated when the United States left Afghanistan.“Over the course of 20 years, the United States did some good things in Afghanistan, but when we left so many people who bought into the idea of a new society ended up running for their lives. When you look at history, you think: how do we do this twice? There is no more stark example of the ineffectiveness of these efforts than the fact that these images look almost identical.”Looking back across a quarter-century defined by overseas conflict, the erosion of institutional trust, rising domestic division under Trump and military operations launched without congressional authorisation, Knappenberger goes back to the strategy articulated by Bin Laden and hisal-Qaida terrorist network.“Osama bin Laden knew that that they couldn’t take on or destroy America; they couldn’t go to war and hurt that many Americans ultimately. He was aware that they could cause America to devour itself, that there was a way of getting America so involved in these other wars and to divide America within.“That would be a way of destroying America that would be far beyond any kind of terrorist attack. He saw the way to destroy America was to turn it against itself and in that sense it’s hard to overstate the profound effect those actions had on us.”Knappenberger is left with questions and the hope that those born after 9/11 will make a different choice. “Who is an American, what is an American, how do we welcome people into our society? Those decisions were made out of fear and they were made out of suspicion, and they changed who we were. We are a different country after 9/11 than we were before. I would like the next generation to not fall into the fear and suspicion that led us down such a dark path.”Turning Point: Generation 9/11 is out onNetflixon 2 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsSeptember 11 2001NetflixfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Summer box office 2026: what can we learn from the hits and misses? | Film industry | The Guardian
description: It was a bumper season for Hollywood, almost back to pre-pandemic levels, with Tom Holland blockbusters winning out, but there was still a string of disappointments
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: It was a bumper season for Hollywood, almost back to pre-pandemic levels, with Tom Holland blockbusters winning out, but there was still a string of disappointments
Content: This movie season passed the $4bn mark, up 20% from last year.Composite: AlamyView image in fullscreenThis movie season passed the $4bn mark, up 20% from last year.Composite: AlamyFilm industrySummer box office 2026: what can we learn from the hits and misses?It was a bumper season for Hollywood, almost back to pre-pandemic levels, with Tom Holland blockbusters winning out, but there was still a string of disappointmentsBenjamin LeeTue 1 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 09.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs the world continued to burn and temperatures reached worrying highs, most of us decided to take refuge in the cinema this summer. It provided some relief for audiences, but even more so for the industry at large, with the season pushing past the magic $4bn mark to become the biggest since 2019, up 20% from last year. There were the expected hits (Spider-Man never misses), but there were also unprecedented breakouts (we were obsessed with Obsession) and surprise underperformers (are kids Minions-ed out?)Obsessed with Obsession: how a low-budget horror changed the game in HollywoodRead moreSo at the end of a season with epic highs and cavernous lows, what lessons can Hollywood learn?Spider-Man is the king of HollywoodView image in fullscreenSpider-Man: Brand New Day.Photograph: Ent-movie/AlamyAs soon as pundits are ready to admit that the superhero genre is actuallyreallydead this time, a film comes out that almost immediately proves them wrong. Last summer, the underperformance of both Thunderbolts ($382m worldwide) and The Fantastic Four: First Steps ($521m worldwide) was somewhat offset by the decent start for James Gunn’s rebooted Superman ($624m worldwide), alarms temporarily quietened. But it was still a minor win for a type of film that used to enjoy major success, with the last superhero caper to cross the magic $1bn number notably being 2024’s snarky and self-deprecating Deadpool & Wolverine. Sirens were heard across Hollywood once again this summer as DC’sSupergirlcrashed and burned back in June (a pitiful $126m worldwide from an estimated budget of $180m), but like clockwork, a miss was then followed by a hit and this time it was one of genuinely heroic proportions.Web of billions: how Spider-Man became the most heroic franchise in HollywoodRead moreAs July drew to a close,Spider-Man: Brand New Daypremiered to sky-high numbers, a global opening weekend of almost $1bn leading to a current total of well over $2bn, by far the biggest film of the year to date as well as the second biggest superhero film of all time and the fourth biggest film ever, overtaking Titanic. It’s an obvious cause for celebration but one that comes with considerable asterisks. Spider-Man has long been a pioneering superhero character impervious to wider market trends. Sam Raimi’s 2002 original was the first film ever to make over $100m in its opening domestic weekend; even the lowest-performing sequel (2014’s The Amazing Spider-Man 2) made over $700m. Spider-Man: No Way Home became the highest-grossing film during the pandemic and now as Captain America, Supergirl and Thunderbolts flail, Spider-Man remains a considerable draw.Marvel will surely be seeing this as a positive sign of things to come when Avengers: Doomsday hits in December (a film that has more riding on it than arguably anything else this year), but Spider-Man’s success continues to be his and his alone.Gen Z horror profit margins are scary goodView image in fullscreenInde Navarrette and Michael Johnston in Obsession.Photograph: Courtesy of Focus FeaturesHorror has long been Hollywood’s favourite genre for the simple business fact of its profit margin. Typically cheap to produce and not reliant on expensive actors, even an underperformer rarely results in a great, superhero-sized loss. But this summer’s scariest hits were even cheaper and even more successful than the genre typically sees and both were used as proof of a changing of the guard, a new generation of film-makers now taking over.Are you sitting uncomfortably? How Backrooms upended the horror movieRead moreWhile some of the hyperbole surrounding the success ofObsessionandBackrooms, both directed by YouTube-trained twentysomethings, got a little bit overexcited (it’s not quite the new New Hollywood movement just yet), therewassomething undeniably invigorating about seeing two small films outgross far bigger summer options. Obsession came first with a budget of just $750k and after a modest opening weekend, word of mouth propelled it to one of the unlikeliest box office runs in recent memory, the first film since ET to increase its takings for three weekends in a row. It ended its run with a global total of $505m, making it the sixth biggest horror film of all time and the most successful original film of the 2020s. Soon after, A24’s less obviously audience-friendly horror Backrooms, based on the hit web series, became the company’s biggest-ever film with $394m worldwide from a $10m budget, while also making director Kane Parsons the youngest-ever film-maker to open at No 1.As many soon pointed out, the success of two horror films in a landscape already oversaturated with them wasn’t a sign of some great sea change (imagine if two low-budget comedies achieved this, for example) but it did feel like a moment, one that energised a gen Z audience who were able to claim ownership of films made for them by people their age while still proving accessible to other age groups. The successes also came at a mostly underwhelming season for the horror genre elsewhere with more traditional options like Paramount’sPassenger($31m worldwide),Hokum($25m worldwide), Eli Roth’sIce Cream Man($6m worldwide) and evenEvil Dead Burn($72m worldwide down from Evil Dead Rise’s $147m) paling in comparison with these two megahits. The wrong lessons will be learned with studios already buying up the rights to any old creepypasta that they can find, but ideally it encourages more chances to be taken and more rules to be somewhat broken. Hopefully next time in a different genre …For franchises, too much is a bad thingView image in fullscreenDwayne Johnson at the Moana world premiere.Photograph: Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagicThe declining interest in all things Marvel, Star Wars and DC should have taught Hollywood execs a thing or two about a lot of things but the biggest lesson should be one about the importance of scarcity. The more audiences were given of once carefully managed and commercially unbeatable brands, on both big and small screens, the less they felt compelled to keep coming back, an obvious case of more being too much.It’s a thread that partly explains why a number of this summer’s biggest films underperformed: sequels, remakes or spin-offs rushed out before audiences had the chance to crave their return. The Despicable Me/Minions franchise had become the most reliable long-running animated series in Hollywood with over $6bn in the bank globally and the last two films in both intertwining sagas almost reaching $1bn each. But after six titles, the last of which was out in 2024, exhaustion set in and this past July’sMinions & Monstershas so far only made $513m and domestically is at almost half of what the last Minions film made. Last summer might have seen a promising start for the umpteenth Superman reboot but in a bizarrely bullish move, given the precarious state of the superhero genre, DC hurried out itsSupergirlspin-off to be released less than a year later and the film was a bomb, making $126m, a disastrous amount that means Warner Bros is set to lose close to $120m and immediately killing the possibility of sequels. WhileThe Mandalorian and Grogumight have been the first Star Wars film since 2019, in that seven-year period Disney flooded fans with almost 25 seasons of live-action and animated shows, and returning to the big screen with what seemed like an extended episode of a pre-existing series led to an underwhelming $345m worldwide, even less than what ridiculed spin-off Solo: A Star Wars Story made in 2018.And, perhaps the most surprising flop of them all, was Disney’s live-actionMoana, which has only just crossed $308m globally on a budget of $250m. The original animation made $687m in 2016 and became a major hit on Disney+, big enough to transform the follow-up from a streaming miniseries to a theatrical release, one that brought in over $1bn at the end of 2024. While it made a third film inevitable, it also made the live-action remake seem like an unnecessary and dated, piece of fan service.At the same time, the franchises that paid dividends this summer gave fans something they had been missing. Long-awaited nostalgia-bait sequels were big withThe Devil Wears Prada 2making an astonishing $692m globally (over twice what the 2006 original made) andScary Movierising to $231m worldwide (almost three times the amount of the last sequel in 2013), while kids flocked toToy Story 5which made $1.1bn, the highest of any movie in the series to date (the last film was back in 2019). Audiences proved this summer that they were willing to repeatedly come out en masse to the movies but there still needed to be a real reason to do so.Christopher Nolan is bigger than Steven SpielbergView image in fullscreenThe Odyssey is Christopher Nolan’s biggest hit to date.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyAs brands started to steal sway from the power of A-list actors and directors, we found ourselves losing a generation of stars who could be easily relied upon as a box office draw, both in front of and behind the screen. Admittedly the latter bracket has always been considerably smaller but still, until recently it was hard to name many contemporary equivalents to a Quentin Tarantino or a James Cameron. But with the success of Christopher Nolan’s Oppenheimer in 2023 and then Ryan Coogler’s Sinners last year, it seemed like we had two newer film-makers who had finally proven themselves without the help of superhero IP. This summer, Nolan proved this again and then some with his biggest hit to date, an epic adaptation ofThe Odyssey.‘A towering piece of monoculture’: how The Odyssey discourse has dominated this summerRead moreIt has now crossed $1.5bn worldwide making it the highest-grossing R-rated movie ever as well as Nolan’s biggest hit to date. While, yes, it was based on known IP, Homer was unlikely to be the driving force and even though it was cleverly stuffed with stars who had different generational appeal, none could be solely responsible for a hit of such scale. Nolan had already shown that he could turn a talky drama about the atom bomb into a $972m smash and now, at a time when even Gladiator II couldn’t reignite the swords-and-sandals genre, he’s found another unlikely summer success.At the same time, arguably the most well-known commercial director alive Steven Spielberg stumbled withDisclosure Day, his original sci-fi thriller making an underwhelming $241m worldwide from a budget of $115m (reports suggested it needed closer to $300m just to break even). It was a more obviously commercial sell in many ways – Spielberg + aliens – but it just didn’t connect with audiences and after similarly glum returns for both The Fabelmans and West Side Story, it seems like the director’s golden touch might have faded or maybe it’s just time for the baton to pass. Similarly, at the tail end of the season, another older, one-time hitmaker Ridley Scott faced another flop with post-apocalyptic dramaThe Dog Stars, a film with a $110m budget that couldn’t even pass $20m in its global opening weekend. Maybe it’ll inspire both directors to try something a little different next.Original comedies have no one laughingView image in fullscreenMonica Barbaro and Callum Turner in One Night Only.Photograph: Nicole Rivelli/Universal Pictures/APIt was supposed to be another Anyone But You but Will Gluck’s follow-up romcomOne Night Onlyended up as anything but, a calculated sleeper hit that failed to wake up its target younger audience. His Glen Powell-Sydney Sweeney match-up was a surprise hit at the end of 2023, adding a long tail to an underwhelming opening ($7m turned into $88m domestic which ballooned into $220m worldwide) and became the biggest R-rated comedy for almost a decade. But with a move from winter to summer, known leads to relative nobodies and a bizarre dystopian premise (what if sex was only legal for one night?), lightning failed to strike twice and after almost three weeks on release, the film has only crossed a damp $20m worldwide.The failure of Sex Purge was not a great surprise to anyone paying attention (how a 30-second TV spot was supposed to convey that set-up is beyond me) but it came during another summer season that left original comedies out in the cold and spoke to a greater concern over a genre now mostly seen as safe for streaming only. Wider releases likeThe Breadwinner($20m),Spa Weekend($7.6m) andI Love Boosters($9.7m) fizzled alongside medium-sized attempts likePower Ballad($3.4m),Stop! That! Train!($4.3m) andGail Daughtry and the Celebrity Sex Pass($1.4m). And while nostalgia worked for Scary Movie and Prada,Super Troopers 3opened to less than a third of what the second film did.There was one bright spot although just how bright it actually was remains under discussion. At this year’s Sundance, Olivia Wilde’s crowd-pleasing couples comedyThe Invitewas the subject of an intense bidding war, one of the only real sure things at a festival struggling through another off year. Despite a higher offer for a streaming release (something Wilde later referred to as a “bribe”), a theatrical rollout was seen as Paramount and A24 picked it up for an estimated $12m. By summer’s end it had made about $25m in the US and a total of $51m worldwide, a heartening result but given the buzz, reviews, stars attached and wide release, it wasn’t quite the slam-dunk some had hoped for (strong awards chances should help to make it an even more worthwhile purchase come end of year).Studios have still been aggressively buying up buzzy comedy scripts so they’re not going away anytime soon (although next time Sex Purge’s writer comes a knocking, maybe keep that door closed) but still, without IP attached, it remains a risky genre theatrically. Like horror, it probably needs a gen Z transfusion to survive.This article was amended on 1 September 2026. The caption for the picture accompanying the entry forThe Odysseymisidentified the stuntwoman Devyn Dalton as the actor Matt Damon.Explore more on these topicsFilm industrySpider-Man: Brand New ⁠DaySpider-ManThe OdysseyChristopher NolanTom HollandDisclosure DayfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Waking Life: Richard Linklater’s genre-defying indie is a kaleidoscopic masterpiece  | Movies | The Guardian
description: Wiley Wiggins plays a man wandering around Austin, Texas, whose reality-bending encounters make him uncertain whether he’s awake or asleep
Author: Paul F Verhoeven
Headline: Wiley Wiggins plays a man wandering around Austin, Texas, whose reality-bending encounters make him uncertain whether he’s awake or asleep
Content: Julie Delpy and Ethan Hawke in Waking Life, which was originally shot in live action and then animated using the technique known as rotoscoping.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenJulie Delpy and Ethan Hawke in Waking Life, which was originally shot in live action and then animated using the technique known as rotoscoping.Photograph: APStream teamMoviesWaking Life: Richard Linklater’s genre-defying indie is a kaleidoscopic masterpieceWiley Wiggins plays a man wandering around Austin, Texas, whose reality-bending encounters make him uncertain whether he’s awake or asleepPaul F VerhoevenTue 1 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 20.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“I’m gonna tell you about a dream I once had,”Richard Linklater– playing himself in his own film Waking Life – tells Wiley Wiggins, playing the film’s unnamed protagonist. “I know when someone says that usually you’re in for a very boring next few minutes, and you might be,” Linklater adds as he hammers away at a pinball machine. “But it sounds like … what else you gonna do, right?”On paper, that’s the premise – and, if you’re cynical, the central dilemma – of Linklater’s 2001 genre-defying indie masterpiece. Wiggins plays a man wandering around Austin, Texas, who is uncertain whether he’s awake or asleep. He may be stuck in a dream, unable to wake up – or reality might just be this weird.Films often try too hard to capture what dreamsfeellike, with violent, surrealist imagery, or wacky, quasi-Lychian abstractions. In Waking Life, however, Linklater propels our hero through what feels unnervingly like a dream with none of that ham-handed crudeness. We, along with Wiggins’ dreamer, are attempting to stay on track, only to suddenly find ourselves walking down a street talking to a stranger, with no word on why, or how, we got there.That’s what Waking Life is, essentially – a collection of strange, dreamlike moments. We’re riding along with our hero as he meets a kaleidoscopic array of artists, philosophers and eccentrics, who wax lyrical about everything – from dreams, to politics, to the nature of reality itself.“We had a very, very loose script initially which changed a lot as we started shooting,” Wiggins tells me. “There was a sort of open-casting looking for odd characters around town who could speak passionately about special interests, and then that was incorporated. The whole thing was very loose during filming, which was done with little consumer DV handy cams”.Linklater has always told stories about people tussling with big, abstract ideas, whether it’s the walk-and-talk ruminations of Jesse and Céline in the Before trilogy, or the stoner philosophy of Dazed and Confused. His protagonists have the kinds of contemplative conversations wethinkwe’re having when we’re talking the ear off a stranger at a party.View image in fullscreenRichard Linklater in September 2001.Photograph: Wally Skalij/Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesBut Waking Life is not mere dorm room sophistry: it will likely introduce you to some genuinely mind-blowing ideas as you’re carried downstream through its visually sumptuous waters. The entire film is rotoscoped, a technique invented by Max Fleischer back in 1915, where artists hand-draw over each frame of the film, leading to a hyper-real animated style. Each sequence is drawn by a different animator, changing as the film’s tone does.“There were all sorts of people involved in the animation stage, painters, people who might not have any existing animation experience before,” Wiggins says. “It was a very different technique than even other rotoscoped animations … it was jarring to some viewers, but I appreciated that quality.”The Quiet Earth: New Zealand post-apocalyptic classic preys on the fear of being totally aloneRead moreFor some viewers, Waking Life prompted an exploration of lucid dreaming – the act of becoming aware, and maintaining control, during a dream. For others, it made them gently paranoid about whether they were, in fact, awake at all. “It’s funny, but I actually have done the thing where I try to turn lights on and off in a dream and can’t,” Wiggins says (as the film explains, you typically can’t do this in dreams). “I don’t know if that’s an artefact of having been in the movies, or something real.”But does Wiley think he’s awake or asleep right now? He considers this for a moment. “The last 10 years have been a series of rude awakenings, one after another,” he finally says.A great deal has happened since 2001, when Waking Life came out. In the wake of 9/11, Roger Ebert said that the film “could not come at a better time”, praising it for “[celebrating] a series of articulate, intelligent characters who seek out the meaning of their existence and do not have the answers”.“At a time when madmen think they have the right to kill us because of what they think they know about an afterlife, which is by definition unknowable, those who don’t know the answers are the only ones asking sane questions,” Ebert wrote. “True believers owe it to the rest of us to seek solutions that are reasonable in the visible world.”And with that in mind, maybe now is the perfect moment to dive back into this strange film.Waking Life is available to stream on Disney+ in Australia and Prime Video in the US. It’s available to rent or buy on in the UK.Explore more on these topicsFilmStream teamRichard LinklaterAnimation in filmfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Super Nature review – crowd-sourced Super 8 film is a triumphant collage of hope for the natural world | Movies | The Guardian
description: Film-maker Ed Sayers’ project gathered footage from collaborators all over the world, cleverly edited to combine human and animal contributions
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: Film-maker Ed Sayers’ project gathered footage from collaborators all over the world, cleverly edited to combine human and animal contributions
Content: All manner of flora and fauna … Super Nature.Photograph: BFIView image in fullscreenAll manner of flora and fauna … Super Nature.Photograph: BFIMoviesReviewSuper Nature review – crowd-sourced Super 8 film is a triumphant collage of hope for the natural worldFilm-maker Ed Sayers’ project gathered footage from collaborators all over the world, cleverly edited to combine human and animal contributionsLeslie FelperinTue 1 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis delightful, fleet-footed film represents a labour of love both for its writer-director-producer-editor, Briton Ed Sayers, and his many, many collaborators who shot the film’s footage on Super 8 all over the world. Between them they’ve used decades-old rigs in newfangled setups with stock that, like several of the species seen here, would have gone extinct had it not been for the intervention of enthusiasts.The brief from Sayers was simply to film nature, so we get shots of all manner of flora and fauna, ranging from coral reefs to high deserts, places populated by minute bugs all the way up to whales. Given Super 8 reels can only capture a few minutes’ worth of stock, this must have been a fiendishly complex puzzle in the editing room, so all credit to Sayers not just for his own lovely footage and clever vision but for his nimble collaging of the whole thing together.It is a work embellished by a sweet, swoony original score by Alexandra Hamilton-Ayres and some dainty Foley work (sound design is by David McAuley) to lay in, for example, the sound of two ibex butting horns. Super 8 cameras don’t record sound, and in fact one of the contributions comes from a British woman who has lost her hearing, and now finds communing with nature in silence all the sweeter.Indeed, the secret strength of the film is how it includes the film-makers themselves, underscoring the continuum between nature, animals and people, all one big mostly happy, sometimes murderous family across the globe. The mini self-portraits capture characters like the woman filming the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, another who loves snakes in the Mojave, a man who is so close to the white rhinos that he looks after he cuddles up to them in the sun, and a chap with Parkinson’s who reckons his devotion to filming wildlife is one of the reasons his health hasn’t deteriorated too badly yet.Throughout, we get glimpses of Sayers himself filming seals along the Norfolk coast or lying down in the rain to shoot a snail in his garden, talking a bit about how his mother’s death shaped his feelings towards the project. Altogether, this forms the best kind of crowd-sourced art: a work that is intimate, quirky and intensely accessible.Super Nature is in UK and Irish cinemas from 4 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsBiodiversityConservationWildlifereviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Extractor review – Indonesian hostage-rescue thriller has surprising thread of gentleness at its core | Movies | The Guardian
description: Iko Uwais directs and acts in the story of a band of elite soldiers who must rescue a group of researchers taken captive in the jungle
Author: Catherine Bray
Headline: Iko Uwais directs and acts in the story of a band of elite soldiers who must rescue a group of researchers taken captive in the jungle
Content: Well-staged action sequences … The Extractor.Photograph: Signature EntertainmentView image in fullscreenWell-staged action sequences … The Extractor.Photograph: Signature EntertainmentMoviesReviewThe Extractor review – Indonesian hostage-rescue thriller has surprising thread of gentleness at its coreIko Uwais directs and acts in the story of a band of elite soldiers who must rescue a group of researchers taken captive in the jungleCatherine BrayTue 1 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 04.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCan an elite team of soldiers rescue a band of innocent hostages from a bunch of mean old terrorists? Yes, probably, since there are few (if any) action movies in which the hostages are wiped out and the terrorists win. Not to be confused with the Extraction action franchise starring Chris Hemsworth as a mercenary named Tyler, nor with action thriller Escape Plan: The Extractors, starring Dave Bautista as a prison security expert named Trent, this is an Indonesian action thriller in which actor/director Iko Uwais plays a soldier named Timur. The film was actually called Timur originally, but there’s no denying that The Extractor is a more commercial title (unless you are particularly interested inthe medieval Mongol khanates) and will attract more viewers to this tale of hostages, heroes and long-ago childhood friends.In some ways, though, the rebrand is a shame, because the new title suggests the film is more generic than it is. While the basic plot, in which a bunch of researchers are taken hostage in the jungle by an armed group of wrong ’uns, is hardly unique, there are sequences in the film that stand out from the direct-to-video action content mill. InIndonesia, timur means “east”, where the sun rises, and it carries the connotation of hopefulness. That softer feeling in the original title is a key part of the film’s identity, which includes sentimental flashbacks to the childhoods of various characters whose lives have taken tragically different paths. (Can you imagine a world in which a terrorist and a soldier knew each other as children? The Extractor can.)These gentler scenes make for a fun contrast with the rather well-staged action sequences, which are at their best during hand-to-hand combat, but also include arresting interactions between the natural world and military hardware: soldiers advancing underwater watch fish swim past gun barrels; a butterfly alights on the sights of a gun. It doesn’t hit the heights of action maestro John Woo’s use of symbolic white doves, but it’s quirkier than you might expect.The Extractor is on digital platforms from 7 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmThrillersAction and adventure filmsIndonesiaAsia PacificreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Pin de Fartie review – spoonerist remix of Samuel Beckett’s Endgame finds fresh absurdity in Argentina | Movies | The Guardian
description: Beckett’s masterpiece is given a postmodern cinema slant, with characters in different locations, music and humour in a free and fanciful interpretation
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: Beckett’s masterpiece is given a postmodern cinema slant, with characters in different locations, music and humour in a free and fanciful interpretation
Content: Father-daughter dynamics … Cleo Moguillansky as Cleo and Santiago Gobernori as Otto in Pin de Fartie.View image in fullscreenFather-daughter dynamics … Cleo Moguillansky as Cleo and Santiago Gobernori as Otto in Pin de Fartie.MoviesReviewPin de Fartie review – spoonerist remix of Samuel Beckett’s Endgame finds fresh absurdity in ArgentinaBeckett’s masterpiece is given a postmodern cinema slant, with characters in different locations, music and humour in a free and fanciful interpretationLeslie FelperinTue 1 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRemember remixes? Where you take a song and swap out parts of it with new or pre-existing material, changing it just enough to be still recognisable? Argentinean director Alejo Moguillansky applies this quintessentially postmodern aesthetic to film with a funky cinematic remix, or even series of remixes, of Samuel Beckett’s one-act play Fin de Partie, AKA Endgame. The result feels a little retro and possibly a bit too pleased with its own cleverness, and the spoonerist title is juvenile. But in the end this really achieves something with both the source material and the remix that’s fresh, pleasingly provocative, and at times moving.Beckett’s 1957 absurdist masterwork has just four characters on stage throughout, two of whom do most of the talking: cantankerous blind, disabled Hamm banters with his servant/slave Clov, while Hamm’s parents, Nagg and Nell, live in dustbins upstage and talk rather less. There’s an air of apocalyptic doom, much talk of drugs, food and, above all, time running out.Moguillansky offers a series of select cuts from the play with different cast members (no Nagg or Nell for the most part), changing the balance each time simply through casting, performance choice and context. In the first interpretation, Hamm becomes blind but mobile Otto (Santiago Gobernori) and Clov becomes Cleo (Cleo Moguillansky, the director’s daughter), who have a tetchy father-daughter dynamic that unfolds in a lakeside house. Meanwhile, in Buenos Aires a pair of actors (Laura Paredes and Marcos Ferrante) meet furtively in a flat; they are not having an affair but rehearsing Fin de Partie together, falling in love with each other in the process.Elsewhere, an older woman (Margarita Fernández) insists that her son (the director himself) reads her passages from the Spanish translation of Beckett’s play (the same text used throughout), and so on. In addition, Luciana Acuña (the director’s wife, also a performer) and musician Maxi Prietto offer their own omniscient glosses on the play, with Prietto performing folk-inflected ditties about the action that are amusing and quite ridiculous.Would Beckett have approved? Probably not, as he tended to insist on fidelity to his vision, right down to the set-dressing. But while his work is not yet in the public domain, his estate these days seems to feel considerably easier about adaptations, and this interpretation is so free and fanciful, more of an essay or an exercise, it probably falls under the terms of fair use. To be honest an academic slant about the whole exercise that, while compelling, may feel a little too dry for some – although no one could be anything but charmed by a scene where Gobernori and young Moguillansky skip in sync along a lakeside promenade with a raging sunset behind them.Pin de Fartie is at the ICA, London, from 4 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsSamuel BeckettArgentinaAmericasTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: The best theatre to stream this month: Bryan Cranston cranks up the tension in All My Sons | Stage | The Guardian
description: Cranston and Marianne Jean-Baptiste lead a brilliant staging of Arthur Miller’s tragedy, a Shelagh Delaney deep-cut is released and Black Watch turns 20
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Cranston and Marianne Jean-Baptiste lead a brilliant staging of Arthur Miller’s tragedy, a Shelagh Delaney deep-cut is released and Black Watch turns 20
Content: Staggering … Paapa Essiedu (Chris Keller) and Bryan Cranston (Joe Keller) in Miller’s All My Sons. Photo Jan VersweyveldPhotograph: Jan VersweyveldView image in fullscreenStaggering … Paapa Essiedu (Chris Keller) and Bryan Cranston (Joe Keller) in Miller’s All My Sons. Photo Jan VersweyveldPhotograph: Jan VersweyveldThe best theatre to stream this monthStageThe best theatre to stream this month: Bryan Cranston cranks up the tension in All My SonsCranston and Marianne Jean-Baptiste lead a brilliant staging of Arthur Miller’s tragedy, a Shelagh Delaney deep-cut is released and Black Watch turns 20Chris WiegandTue 1 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 01.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAll My SonsIvo van Hove’sstaggering West End productionof Arthur Miller’s tragedy for “the common man” proved every bit as emotionally honed as hisA View from the Bridgein 2014. Named best revivalat this year’s Olivier awards, it brings together Bryan Cranston as compromised factory owner Joe Keller, Marianne Jean-Baptiste as his wife and Paapa Essiedu as his son. Jan Versweyveld’s stark design should look stunning on screen.From NT at Home.Cymbeline“Some pleasing scenes,” was Dr Johnson’s impression of Shakespeare’s late romance. If that sounds like damning with faint praise, he decided not to waste any more words on its “unresisting imbecility”. Director Jennifer Tang makes her case for the play in her 2025Shakespeare’s Globedebut, turning the eponymous ancient king into a queen.View image in fullscreenTake a bow … Shelagh Delaney in the early 1960s.Photograph: Evening Standard/Getty ImagesCatch Me Who CanShelagh Delaneytakes another bowas her previously unperformed play about a schoolgirl runaway is releasedon Spotifyas an audio drama. The cast includes Rita Tushingham, who starred in the 1961 adaptation of Delaney’s A Taste of Honey, and Toby Jones. Available from 23 September.The Jonathan Larson ProjectThis summer’s UK premiere of Jonathan Larson’s lesser-known songs wasa revelation. Alternately satirical and sunny, poignant and political, the collection – including numbers cut from Rent and Tick, Tick … BOOM! – was recorded fora 2019 albumwith a fine cast, including a bluesy Lauren Marcus on Break Out the Booze.Play TimeBBC Radio 4 and the Royal Courtteam up for an audio season including a new 10th-anniversary recording of Lucy Kirkwood’s The Children. It’s accompanied by archive productions, from Look Back in Anger with Ben Whishaw to Cuttin’ It with Susan Wokoma, all selected by Mark Ravenhill. Available onBBC Soundsfrom 26 September.View image in fullscreenUpending … Ali Craig in Black Watch.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianBlack WatchIt’s been 20 years since the nascent National Theatre of Scotland turned a pool table into a tank and had a blistering hit with Gregory Burke’s Black Watch, about a Scottish regiment in Iraq and inspired by interviews with soldiers. “Every one of my suppositions of what drove them to join the army was demolished,”said director John Tiffany. It’s part of a British theatre seasonon BBC iPlayer.CactusAustralian writer-performer Madelaine Nunn was at last year’s Edinburgh fringe with her acclaimed solo show about a nurse, Flick. This earlier two-hander is a funny and frank account of teenagers navigating that prickly final year of high school, with a medical diagnosis that puts the future in a new light. OnMarqueeTV.Caroline – A New MusicalRadio Caroline, the 60s pirate station, inspired this touring musical with “rebellious energy” by Vikki Stone, produced this year by Ipswich’s New Wolsey theatre. A tale of life on the ocean and airwaves, it’s delivered by a cast of actor-musicians whose playlist includes the Kinks, the Who and the Rolling Stones.Available until 19 September.Explore more on these topicsStageThe best theatre to stream this monthTheatreNational TheatreMusicalsAudio dramaLucy KirkwoodBryan CranstonShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s more freaky, more balls to the wall’: how alt-country won over a new generation | Americana | The Guardian
description: From Waxahatchee and Florry in the US to Brown Horse and Little Grandad in the UK, a wave of young songwriters are reinvigorating the subgenre’s earnest emotion and twang
Author: Michael Hann
Headline: From Waxahatchee and Florry in the US to Brown Horse and Little Grandad in the UK, a wave of young songwriters are reinvigorating the subgenre’s earnest emotion and twang
Content: Waxahatchee performing at London’s Kentish Town Forum in 2024.Photograph: Sonja Horsman/Sonja Horsman / The GuardianView image in fullscreenWaxahatchee performing at London’s Kentish Town Forum in 2024.Photograph: Sonja Horsman/Sonja Horsman / The GuardianAmericana‘It’s more freaky, more balls to the wall’: how alt-country won over a new generationFrom Waxahatchee and Florry in the US to Brown Horse and Little Grandad in the UK, a wave of young songwriters are reinvigorating the subgenre’s earnest emotion and twangMichael HannTue 1 Sep 2026 06.14 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 06.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘It’s so important to talk about this before it’s gone,” says Francie Medosch, singer, guitarist and songwriter of the band Florry, “because it’s really a flash in the pan.” The flash she means is a brief moment where it feels as though on both sides of the Atlantic, scores of exciting indie bands are playing something that, without slavish copying, has plainly drawn inspiration from alt-country, the music that emerged in the US in the late 1980s and early 90s, when former punks such as Uncle Tupelo – featuring futureWilcoco-founder Jeff Tweedy – and the Bottle Rockets picked up picked up fiddles, banjos and acoustic guitars.In the UK, Brown Horse and Vegas Water Taxi have the weeping pedal steel, in the former case tied to something very heartland and in the latter paired with a very English indie sensibility.Westside Cowboyand Little Grandad both borrow from the spiky rootsiness of early Wilco, while Wyatt play slacker country rock. Over in the US, where there’s always going to be more of this sort of thing, you can point to the current indie-rock holy trinity ofWaxahatchee, Wednesday andMJ Lenderman, plus Florry, Ratboys, Thomas Dollbaum, Fust, SG Goodman, Lily Seabird, Ryan Davis and the Roadhouse Band and more.View image in fullscreen‘There’s a genuine desire among young people to embrace earnest storytelling’ … Ratboys.Photograph: Miles Kalchik“It seems to be a real language right now in the music world,” says Julia Steiner, singer-guitarist of Ratboys, from the rockier end of this moment, “and I’m stoked about it. It’s been a long time coming – it’s so exciting to me when bands take really simple ingredients and find ways to make really progressive recipes with them. What’s exciting to me about alt-country is that the same cowboy chords are in play here, but the filter they come through is more freaky, more balls to the wall. It’s fun to see how many places people can take these essential ideas.”London quartet Little Grandad, who earlier this summer signed a three-album deal with Communion, didn’t even know about alt-country when they started playing last year. “Tim from [buzzy London venue] Brixton Windmill told me, ‘You’ve got to check out this whole scene of bands,’” says their singer-guitarist Harry Lower. “I knew about Wilco, but I didn’t know about Uncle Tupelo and all of that world. I’ve listened to a lot of music in the last year.”One of those discoveries was Jason Molina, of Songs: Ohia and the Magnolia Electric Co, who died in 2013 of organ failure following long-term alcohol abuse. “I love how fragile he is,” Lower says of the midwestern singer-songwriter. “I just believe him. I believe his songwriting. I watched an interview of him, and he’s saying how he’s so confused that he makes this music because he listens to Metallica and metal bands, and he’s like, ‘How has it turned out like this?’ That makes me feel better about what we make, because you stumble into it.”By chance, in the week all these interviews were conducted, London became alt-country central. On the Tuesday night, the Norfolk band Brown Horse were the house band at a night honouring the songs of Molina, with a rotating cast of singers including Alexis Taylor of Hot Chip and Lottie Pendlebury of Goat Girl. On Wednesday, Wilco were in town, with alt-country band Hovvdy opening and a set that didn’t eschew the country end of their catalogue, and on Thursday and Friday Greg Freeman, from Vermont, played two sold-out club shows.Everyone seems to have taken different routes to get to similar places, though all these musicians in their 20s or early 30s came to it via their own discovery, rather than hearing it in the cars of gen X parents. Steiner grew up with country in the air in Kentucky, and added the alternative rock later. Medosch hailsLucinda Williamsas the source of all things alt-country (a complete music head, she offers an eloquent disquisition on why powerpop, and Big Star in particular, must be considered part of this lineage).View image in fullscreen‘You can say so much with a country song’ … Francie Medosch of Florry.Photograph: John McSweeney“All this stuff comes under Neil Young,” says Lower. Thomas Dollbaum, who lives in New Orleans, remembers hearing the music you can’t avoid, such as Bob Dylan, then having uncles send him John Prine CDs, “because they knew I was interested in that kind of music. And then I found stuff on my own. I listened to a lot of Jason Molina, a lot of Damian Jurado, a lot of Bill Callahan and Richard Buckner growing up. In early college I had a friend and we’d send tapes back and forth.”Brown Horse came to alt-country via a eureka moment. They were already a band, playing an approximation of American folk music, when they were booked to play the Black Deer festival in 2022. “We’d been so fucking bored for a year and a half,” says their pedal steel player, Emma Tovell. “We had a euphoric moment watching Drive-By Truckers. We could really see where they’d come from that kind of gothic old southern country music, but they were really rocking, and we absolutely loved that. And we saw Wilco at that festival, and SG Goodman, who played at 1pm to 30 people. We got home and decided it was time to start amplifying stuff. That felt like a concentration point.”Tovell remembers an early Brown Horse tour of Scandinavia, where “95% of the gigs were seated and the average age of the audience was 65”. In the last few years, the audience for live guitar music seems to have become much younger. It’s hardly rockism’s revenge on poptimism, but in a culture in which people sit in front of screens all day, for work or for leisure, there’s something resonant about seeing people making music in which raggedness is celebrated, in which edges are the result of friction rather than having been generated by computer.“I think there’s a genuine desire among young people – millennials like myself included – to embrace earnest storytelling and our humanity, in the face of this monolith of corporate suits drooling over AI and the internet and trying to tell us what’s cool,” says Steiner. “There’s something to the idea of stripping that away and getting to the bare essentials of storytelling, and putting your perspective out there in ways that feel accessible and honest. I’m just happy that people are trying to make music that feels really human.”View image in fullscreen‘We’d been so fucking bored’ … Emma Tovell of Brown Horse performing at  the Moth Club, London, in 2024.Photograph: Brown Horse/Facebook“You can say so much with a country song,” Medosch says. “You can be so earnest, or you can be detached, you can mess with the form so much.” She was amazed when she realised British bands felt the same. “What’s happening in England is really shocking to American musicians.”Pixar, Catholic shame, and urine-drinking podcast bros: the mixed-up rock of MJ LendermanRead moreWhile the British bands are still forming their futures, many of the American bands have several years and several albums in the books, and they’re already changing. Florry’s next album will have a Broadway show tune and a Caribbean rock song, says Medosch, hence her pleasure in this moment being captured for posterity.Before our call ends, Steiner asks if I am familiar with the term “post-country”. “I’m just curious because I first used that term 10 years ago as a joke, but I’ve seen people using it nowadays. When I first met Dave, our guitar player – he’s my partner – in university and he started showing me all these bands I had never heard of, he was using terms like post-hardcore and post-rock, and I was like, ‘What the fuck? Post-rock? Like, what are you talking about?’ I just thought it was hilarious, and we started calling our music post-country.”This is still a genre in search of a name – one online wag suggested “the Lendermen” – and maybe it’s not a genre at all, so much as a shared sense of purpose. But it’s real, and it sounds wonderful.Among the acts mentioned in this piece, Ratboys, Lily Seabird, Ryan Davis and the Roadhouse Band, SG Goodman and Little Grandad playthe End of the Road festival from 3-6 September. Most have other UK dates around the festival; check artist websites for detailsExplore more on these topicsAmericanaCountryWilcoWaxahatcheeIndiePop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I feel like I’m grieving’: staff on the devastating fallout of widespread layoffs at Xbox | Games | The Guardian
description: Last month, Microsoft’s gaming division told its workforce it was cutting 3,200 jobs, which some say will have big ramifications for game development – as well as taking a huge personal toll
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: Last month, Microsoft’s gaming division told its workforce it was cutting 3,200 jobs, which some say will have big ramifications for game development – as well as taking a huge personal toll
Content: ‘It never made any sense’ … a rally against the layoffs at Xbox outside the Activision building in Austin, Texas, this month.Photograph: Emilio González/Communications Workers of AmericaView image in fullscreen‘It never made any sense’ … a rally against the layoffs at Xbox outside the Activision building in Austin, Texas, this month.Photograph: Emilio González/Communications Workers of AmericaGames‘I feel like I’m grieving’: staff on the devastating fallout of widespread layoffs at XboxLast month, Microsoft’s gaming division told its workforce it was cutting 3,200 jobs, which some say will have big ramifications for game development – as well as taking a huge personal tollKeith StuartTue 1 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 08.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the morning of 6 July, an email went out from Asha Sharma, the chief executive of Xbox, to all of the division’s employees around the world. Under the headline “Resetting Xbox”, it announced the most significant restructuring in the history of Microsoft’s console business: 3,200 staff would be laid off throughout the financial year to 2027, and 1,600 of those roles would be eliminated immediately.An hour later, at studios throughout company, the Teams meeting invites started arriving. “It was a virtual call with our studio manager,” says Anne Barrett, who was laid off from Bethesda Game Studios Austin. “All of our cameras and microphones were turned off so we weren’t able to say anything or react to anything. We were just brought in, told the news and it was like: ‘You guys are going to lose access to your Slack channel.’ So you saw a flurry of goodbye messages before everything was just shut off.”View image in fullscreenMotion graphics artist Alyssa Gobelle at a rally against the layoffs at the ZeniMax Online Studios office in Maryland.Photograph: Communications Workers of AmericaThis, it seems, was the routine, at least at studios in North America: a Teams call with a studio head, a prepared statement read, then a warning about Slack (the group messaging app widely used at game development studios). Emails, the staff were told, would be turned off a few days later. “We’re primarily a remote studio, so Slack is the main mode of conversation with our teammates,” says Morgan Goin, who worked at ZeniMax Online Studios. “All through the morning, everyone was sending their goodbyes … ‘Hey, it’s been great working with you. Here’s my contact information. I’ve loved working here. I will miss all of you.’” Then silence.Bethesda Games Studios and Zenimax Online Studios were unionised in 2024 and both Goin and Barrett are on the bargaining committees for their respective studios, currently in talks withMicrosoft. In the US, the Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) act is a federal law that requires companies with 100 or more employees to give its workers 60 days’ notice before major closures or mass staff layoffs. Consequently, affected staff at US studios will be paid until 4 September. Union reps at Bethesda are undertaking a bargaining process with Microsoft to negotiate severance packages and any benefits owed, and is attempting to get at least some affected members re-employed. Rallies are taking place outside studio buildings across North America, with the Bethesda union seeking support from gamers via social media.double quotation markBethesda is Skyrim, it’s Fallout ... We thought that the work we were doing was going to keep us safeStaff say rumours had been circulating about a new wave of lay-offs for several weeks, and that they sawthe Bloomberg articleon 10 June warning of coming job cuts. “There was an impending sense of doom, and it was like, man, is it going to be us?” says Barrett. “We thought we were safe. I mean, Bethesda Games Studios is Skyrim, it’s Fallout. We have really highly anticipated stuff coming out. We thought that the work we were doing was going to keep us safe. And instead, we got brought into a meeting that was two minutes long, to end, in some cases, decades of career at the company. It was just devastating.”“I remember, I laughed the whole day because I was in complete disbelief,” Barrett adds. “I was like, there’s no way they’re doing this. That’s how I processed it. Some of my co-workers were just devastated. I mean, breaking down. They did not understand what was going on. We had people who were just in really dark places. I think it hit me probably the next day. I felt like, wow – I just spent seven years doing all this. In college, people called me Bethesda because it was my dream to work here. And that was just … gone.”View image in fullscreen‘Our titles have a very well-known visual identity’ … Fallout 76.Illustration: Bethesda Game StudiosThis is what doesn’t get reported with the statistics of mass redundancies: the sheer human cost of it. “I’m very tired, my sleep schedule is all kinds of messed up, my eating has not been great,” says Goin. “I have to ask myself daily: have you had enough food and water? Have you had enough sunlight? When was the last time you took a shower? We’re doing the depression symptoms, that’s what’s happening. I feel like I’m grieving.”Simon Préfontaine has a similar story. Previously a designer at Bethesda Game Studios Montreal, he is a single father concerned about the future without work, and without the health insurance his job came with. “It’s very stressful,” he says. “I’ve heard of other people who have been laid off for over a year and haven’t been able to find work. I know I’m not the only single parent in the Montreal studio, I know there are people that have health issues.” But as with Goin, it is about more than financial stability. “It might seem like an overstatement or a dramatisation, but I do feel like I went through the stages of grief. You work with these people for years and years and years, and then suddenly you don’t get to see them any more.”What has been most bewildering to staff is that there seemed to be no structure to the layoffs, no clear reasoning behind who was affected. “I’m on the character art team, and we lost two people who had been there for decades,” says Alex Nguyen, a union bargainer still employed at BethesdaGamesStudios Dallas. “They did everything that was asked, they were very passionate, they were great at their jobs. They worked on all this stuff that made our creatures, characters and armour feel real. Outstanding employees. It never made any sense.”double quotation markI don’t know how you create games at the quality level we were without the knowledge that’s been lostIt is likely, after all that, there will be ramifications for games being produced at these studios – including content delays and project cancellations. Id Software, creator of Doom and Quake, lost 136 staff in the cuts – a majority of its workforce. One staff member affected, VFX artist Derek Best, claimed ina LinkedIn postthat the developer had been relegated to “support studio size”.Barrett makes a similar assertion about Bethesda, where the redundancies have been less severe but where key staff have been affected. “I don’t know how you create games at the quality level we were without the institutional knowledge that’s been lost. We have proprietary tech. Our titles have a very well-known visual identity. And when you lose the people who built the tech, when you lose the people who were improving it, you can’t just throw new people at that problem, right? You can’t replace an artist with someone brand new and say: ‘Now replicate what they were doing 15, 20 years ago.’ The company has said that they can do it. I disagree.”View image in fullscreen‘My view of the industry has definitely been damaged’ … protesters in Montreal.Photograph: Communications Workers of AmericaNobody knows what happens next. Barrett could only provide a brief statement on how the union’s talks with Microsoft are faring: “Effects bargaining continues with each side exchanging counterproposals. In their counter, the employer has not made enough substantial movement to care for the very real consequences impacted members are facing (loss of employment; loss of income; and disruption of benefits for their families). We (the union) have indicated that we are prepared to work toward an agreement but we cannot accept a proposal where the burden of compromise falls almost entirely on the employees.”A Microsoft spokesperson provided the following statement on the bargaining process: “Effects bargaining for our union-represented ZeniMax colleagues is under way and on track, and we have offered severance terms comparable to the generous package provided to our non-union represented colleagues, including up to 39 weeks of severance, six months of company-paid Cobra [Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act], and 16 weeks of outplacement support. We are committed to reaching an agreement that supports impacted colleagues as they move forward.”At least 1,600 more redundancies are coming atXboxstudios as the “reset” of the division continues. During that time, there will likely be mass lay-off events at other large companies in the industry. All of the staff I spoke to echoed a familiar feeling about mainstream games development – that something has gone drastically wrong and that mass redundancies point to a wider malaise. “Publishers have to be prepared for multi-year development cycles,” says Nguyen. “If that cost is too high, or those timelines are too long, then the game needs to scale back in some way. That might mean more indie and AA games and fewer blockbuster titles. What doesn’t work is investing in a long-term game product, and expecting profits on a yearly basis.”Barrett concurs. “My view of the industry has definitely been damaged,” she says. “There’s been a loss of sight over why AAA games were so valuable to players. It wasn’t just that they were big and shiny. It was that [the studios] had the resources to invest in creativity. What I see now is the same formula over and over and over again. In any entertainment industry, if you do that enough times, people get tired of it. I would love for us as an industry to get back to actually being creative and investing in that creativity.”Explore more on these topicsGamesXboxMicrosoftfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A walking tour of Andalucía’s historic white villages: ‘Nightingales serenade us as we wind along lush river valleys’ | Andalucia holidays | The Guardian
description: The famous pueblos blancos in southern Spain’s Sierra de Grazalema natural park teem with wildlife amid a limestone wonderland of peaks
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The famous pueblos blancos in southern Spain’s Sierra de Grazalema natural park teem with wildlife amid a limestone wonderland of peaks
Content: ‘The conditions couldn’t be more perfect’ … Zahara de la Sierra in Andalucía.Photograph: Antonio Ciero Reina/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘The conditions couldn’t be more perfect’ … Zahara de la Sierra in Andalucía.Photograph: Antonio Ciero Reina/AlamyAndalucia holidaysA walking tour of Andalucía’s historic white villages: ‘Nightingales serenade us as we wind along lush river valleys’The famous pueblos blancos in southern Spain’s Sierra de Grazalema natural park teem with wildlife amid a limestone wonderland of peaksMike UnwinTue 1 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 04.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘The wind is in from Africa / Last night I couldn’t sleep.” Joni Mitchell has ear-wormed her way into my head as my wife and I step out from Zahara de la Sierra into the mountains of Sierra de Grazalema natural park. The Africa bit probably comes from yesterday’s visit to Zahara’s castle museum. Here, high above the tiled terracotta mosaic of village rooftops, we learned how the recapture of this picturesque hill town was a turning point in theReconquista– the military campaign of the 1400s that saw the Catholics retake southern Spain after seven centuries of Moorish control. As for sleep deprivation, I may just have overdone it on last night’s tapas.Either way, Africa feels present as we tramp through the countryside of Andalucía, if only in the wildlife. The painted lady butterflies drifting over the flower-spangled verges, the turtle doves purring from the olive groves and the booted eagle drifting overhead: all are summer visitors recently blown in from the great continent to our south.View image in fullscreenBee-eaters in Sierra de Grazalema natural park.Photograph: Nature Picture Library/AlamyIt’s day two of our White Villages of the Ronda Mountains walking tour, a self-guided seven-day route from On Foot Holidays that explores this alluring corner of southern Spain. We arrived yesterday by bus from Málaga, winding up through the mountains until the whitewashed dwellings of Zahara appeared like teeth in the hillside ahead. This was the first of the week’s fourpueblos blancos, all tucked picturesquely into the natural park’s rugged 51,695 hectares (127,740 acres) of limestone peaks and serpentine river valleys.I’ve walked with On Foot before, so the routine is familiar: water bottles and packed lunches stashed in daypacks, laminated map around neck on lanyard and route app open on phone (belt-and-braces navigation). Best of all, our luggage is already wending its way by taxi to the next destination.double quotation markLunch is in a high meadow, where we unwrap our bocadillos while bees buzz and butterflies busy themselves among the bloomsThe conditions couldn’t be more perfect. The hillsides burst with blossom and birdsong, the May temperature is a pleasant mid-20s (midsummer out here would be punishing), and the peaks stand proud against the clear blue sky. It’s hard to believe February brought such heavy rains that much of our route was then impassable – and some areas of the park were affected by wildfires later in the summer.View image in fullscreenWalking to GrazalemaBut each month here has its own character. September/October – also prime walking season – sees the chestnuts and cork oak forests turn russet and gold, and the spring irises and orchids replaced by the post-summer bloom of wild asparagus and autumn crocus. Overhead, those booted eagles will be massing for their return journey – along with bee-eaters, honey buzzards and other winged voyagers – back to Africa.Eight of the best secluded and affordable places to stay in Andalucía, SpainRead moreToday’s hike takes us south towards Grazalema:pueblo blanconumber two. We skirt a reservoir then wind along a lush river valley, nightingales serenading us from the oleander thickets, and by late morning are rising into the mountains, the vista gaining grandeur as we gain height.Lunch is in a high meadow, where we unwrap ourbocadilloswhile bees buzz and butterflies busy themselves among the blooms. Afternoon brings a long uphill slog, then finally a cool descent through shady pines to sleepy Grazalema. Another 11 miles (18km) under our belts.We stay two nights in Grazalema at theHotel la Mejorana, meeting wild ibex on a mountain circuit high above town, and eating at the cosyCádiz el Chicorestaurant, where a menu featuring partridge and wild boar (though, thankfully, not ibex) reflects the region’s hunting traditions. At night, the cobbled streets are quiet beneath a canopy of stars.Benaoján, the third of ourpueblos blancos, lies about 16 miles to the south-east. We exit Grazalema early in the morning, beneath the Los Peñascosmirador. Roosting griffon vultures line the cliffs like pterodactyls, warming up in the morning sun before, one at a time, flapping off on table-top wings for another day combing the plains.View image in fullscreenBenaoján.Photograph: Japhotos/AlamyOur route leads down through the oak woods before rising again into the hills. Here we enter a limestone wonderland, the karst formations sculpted by wind and rain into Henry Moore-like statues. Bee-eaters dart overhead, their liquid chirrups audible long before we lay eyes on them. A passing walker greets us with a cheery “Buen camino!” He’s returning with his father to see the farmhouse where they grew up. We find Dad sitting on a nearby rock, devouring an empanada. They’re the only other walkers we meet all day.Our hideaway at Benaoján is theMolino del Santohotel, where we dine beside a chuckling stream on a terrace crowded with potted geraniums. From here, it takes us two hours to hike to theCueva de la Pileta, an immense cave system discovered in 1905 when a local farmer spotted bats streaming from a fissure in the hillside.Local guide Ainhoa Bullón leads us down cool, narrow passages into measureless caverns, her thin torch beam illuminating flowstone formations as enormous and elaborate as a Gaudí cathedral – formed, she explains, by the drip-drip of lime at the rate of 1cm every 400 years. The farthest recesses hold exquisite shamanic rock art, some more than 25,000 years old. Ainhoa overflows with information, talking us through the cave’s successive ages of antiquity, from Neanderthal to Neolithic. Most important, she delivers us safely back to the blazing sunshine outside.View image in fullscreenRonda, perched atop El Tajo gorge.Photograph: M Viliam /AlamyOur week ends at Ronda, perched atop the precipitous El Tajo gorge. The celebrated clifftop town seems to beckon us onward like some mythical sky citadel as we tramp our final kilometres towards it. Below the cliffs, we find ourselves back in tourist land, sharing the steep climb to the top with a gaggle of selfie-snapping day trippers.We make it, slumping at the first available cafe table to lever off boots, fold away the map and order a celebratory coldcerveza. Tomorrow, we catch our bus back to Málaga. For now, a final night lies ahead, with a stirring panorama from our room at theParador de Rondaand the promise of a slap-up meal down in the old town. Our beers arrive, and any lingering strains of Joni are soon lost to a busker’s volley of flamenco guitar.The trip was provided byOn Foot Holidays.It costs from £985pp for aseven-night self-guided route in Grazalemanaturalpark, ending in Ronda;five-,six- andeight-night routes also available.The walking season is February-May and September-December (April, May, Septemberand October being optimum)Explore more on these topicsAndalucia holidaysSpain holidaysEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Smart ideas for preserving summer fruit and veg | Chefs | The Guardian
description: From fermenting plums in honey and pickling courgettes in vinegar brine to a British take on kimchi, there are many ways to make the most of the warm-weather harvest
Author: Anna Berrill
Headline: From fermenting plums in honey and pickling courgettes in vinegar brine to a British take on kimchi, there are many ways to make the most of the warm-weather harvest
Content: Kenji Morimoto’s mirepoix kimchi is a great way to preserve late-summer vegetables.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull.View image in fullscreenKenji Morimoto’s mirepoix kimchi is a great way to preserve late-summer vegetables.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull.Kitchen aideChefsSmart ideas for preserving summer fruit and vegFrom fermenting plums in honey and pickling courgettes in vinegar brine to a British take on kimchi, there are many ways to make the most of the warm-weather harvestAnna BerrillTue 1 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 08.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat’s the best way to preserve late-summer fruit and veg?Jess,by emailFruit, fruit everywhere, so try fermenting it in honey, says Rachel de Thample, author ofThe Fermentation Year(published in September). “I’m currently looking at a jar of blackberries, but whole plums would be gorgeous, too,” she says, especially when eaten with blue cheese – “or any cheese, really” – meat or fish; you can also use the syrup like maple syrup or cordial. De Thample packs the fruit into sterilised jars and pours in just enough honey to cover it: “If the fruit has a low acidity, add a spoonful of lemon juice or a splash of cider vinegar as well.” Pop on the lid and leave for a few weeks. “It gets fizzy, but it doesn’t get to that explosive stage, because it has quite a concentrated sugar content.
