It’ll keep for up to a year at room temperature, but I normally pop it in the fridge after a few weeks.”Kimchi is another option to keep Jess enjoying summer fruits all year round. “In Korea, apples and pears are traditional, but there’s a kimchi for every season and region,” says De Thample, who takes a British approach with a courgette, blackcurrant and strawberry number: “You can use up tomatoes in the paste, too.” Otherwise, if you have plums and damsons, take inspiration from Japanese umeboshi: “That has a high percentage of salt – I use 15% per 100g fruit. Layer the salt and plums in jars and, if it’s really dry, pour over water; otherwise, just crush a couple of the plums so their juices create a brine with the salt.” The brine can then be used like a plummy soy sauce, De Thample says: “Having a few jars stored away always makes me feel like I’m winning.” Damsons are also a dream in flavoured liquors, says Kenji Morimoto, regular Guardian contributor and author ofFerment: “That’s a really nice way to capture their flavour, and all you need is vodka, the fruit and rock [or granulated] sugar.Cheong, a Korean form of maceration, will also prolong the goodbyes, Morimoto says. “It’s an easy concept: you want equal parts sugar and fruit, then let that sit, stirring occasionally, and you’ll end up with this candied fruit and a delicious syrup, or just a delicious syrup.” That’s good for glazing tarts, spooning over ice-cream or drizzling over cakes, and in cocktails, as well as for adding a balancing sweetness to savoury dishes such as stews.Otherwise, Morimoto would bring “a bite of effervescence and briny tang” to the winter dearth by making lacto-fermented cherry tomatoes, which he stores and uses chopped in grain bowls and salsas, and in pasta and other savoury sauces. And there aren’t many summer vegetables that won’t taste great pickled, though courgettes in a classic sweet vinegar brine should be high on Jess’s list. “In many ways, courgettes are better to pickle than cucumbers, because they retain that crunch,” Morimoto says, so slice them, salt them, drain them, then add the brine. “You can then take them in any flavour direction you fancy: mustard seeds, fennel seeds and celery seeds; soy sauce, ginger and garlic; dill and allspice.”Whichever route you go down is sure to get you out of a pickle come autumn.Got a culinary dilemma? title: Sami Tamimi’s recipes for musabaha (warm chickpea dip) and turmeric and nigella seed flatbreads | Food | The Guardian
description: This rubbly cousin of hummus is flavourful and satisfying at any time of day, served warm, topped with a colourful salad and just made to eat with homemade flatbreads
Author: Sami Tamimi
Headline: This rubbly cousin of hummus is flavourful and satisfying at any time of day, served warm, topped with a colourful salad and just made to eat with homemade flatbreads
Content: Sami Tamimi’smusabaha, or warm chickpeas with spicy cherry tomato and coriander salad, served with turmeric and nigella seed flatbread.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Georgia Rudd.View image in fullscreenSami Tamimi’smusabaha, or warm chickpeas with spicy cherry tomato and coriander salad, served with turmeric and nigella seed flatbread.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Georgia Rudd.FoodSami Tamimi’s recipes for musabaha (warm chickpea dip) and turmeric and nigella seed flatbreadsThis rubbly cousin of hummus is flavourful and satisfying at any time of day, served warm, topped with a colourful salad and just made to eat with homemade flatbreadsSami TamimiTue 1 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFew things make me happier than a bowl of warmmusabahaserved with freshly baked bread straight from the pan. It’s a combination that shouts comfort, generosity and the simple pleasure of sharing food. Across the Levant, musabaha is a much-loved breakfast or brunch dish, though I’d happily eat it at any time of day. Served with the buttery, soft turmeric and nigella-seed flatbreads, it becomes a meal that is nourishing, intensely satisfying and perfect for gathering family and friends around the table.Musabaha(warm chickpeas with spicy cherry tomato and coriander salad)View image in fullscreenSami Tamimi’smusabaha, or warm chickpeas with spicy cherry tomato and coriander salad.When I’m short of time but craving something nourishing, full of flavour and genuinely satisfying, I turn to murabaha time and again. Unlike hummus, the chickpeas are left whole, then gently warmed and topped with a vibrant salad of spicy cherry tomatoes, fresh coriander and good olive oil. Serve with plenty of the warm flatbreads below for scooping.Prep15 minCook15 minServes42400g tins chickpeas,drained3 tbsp olive oil, plus extra to drizzle5 large garlic cloves, peeled and crushed1 large green chilli, finely chopped seeds and all1 tbsp ground cumin100g tahini, plus extra to serve120ggreek-style yoghurt3 tbsp lemon juiceSaltFor the cherry tomato salad150g cherry tomatoes,halved1 mini cucumber(100g), finely diced½ red pepper(75g), finely diced20g fresh coriander, finely chopped2 spring onions, trimmed and very thinly sliced1 green chilli, thinly sliced seeds and all1 large garlic clove,peeled and crushed2 tbsp lemon juice1 tbsp white-wine vinegar2 tbsp olive oil1 tbsp sumac1 tsp dried mint½ tsp aleppo chilli, plus extra for sprinklingPut the chickpeas in a medium saucepan with enough water just to cover them., put on a medium heat and bring to a simmer. Leave to cook for about five minutes, just to soften them a bit more, then drain, reserving about 300ml of the cooking liquid.Meanwhile, put all ingredients for the cherry tomato salad in a medium bowl with half a teaspoon of salt, and mix well.Put the oil in a medium saucepan on a medium heat. Add the garlic and cook, stirring often, for two minutes, until the garlic starts to colour, then add the chilli and cook for another minute. Add the drained chickpeas, the reserved cooking liquid, cumin, tahini, yoghurt, lemon juice and a teaspoon of salt, bring to a boil, then turn down the heat to low and simmer, stirring from time to time, for two minutes.To serve, transfer the warm chickpeas to a large serving plate with a lip or a wide, shallow bowl. Drizzle over some tahini, then spoon the cherry tomato salad on top. Finish with a good drizzle of olive oil and a sprinkling of aleppo chilli, and serve with the flatbreads below.Turmeric and nigella seed flatbreadView image in fullscreenSami Tamimi’s turmeric and nigella seed flatbread.I come from a culture where offering freshly baked, warm bread is one of the greatest traditions of hospitality. Whether welcoming unexpected guests or gathering loved ones around the table, bread is always the first thing shared. These golden flatbreads, scented with earthy turmeric and nutty ghee, are perfect for scooping up the warm chickpeas and spicy tomato salad oppositebelow, but they’re equally delicious served with dips or simply drizzled with good olive oil.Prep5 minRest10 minCook25 minMakes8150gfull-fatgreek yoghurt1 tsp bicarbonate of soda350g 00 flour, or plain flour,plus extra for dusting100g wholewheat flour¾ tsp ground turmeric1 tbsp nigella seeds1½ tsp salt35g ghee, or butter, meltedPut the yoghurt and bicarb in the bowl of a free-standing mixer with the dough hook attached, and stir well with a spoon. The mix should start bubbling. Add 150ml water, stir again, then add all the remaining ingredients apart from the ghee and mix on low speed for five minutes, until the dough is soft but not sticky.Divide the dough in 10 equal pieces of about 110g each. Roll each piece into a ball, cover with a damp towel and leave to rest for 10 minutes – this will stop the dough drying out.On a lightly floured surface, roll out each piece of dough into a 16cm disc about ½cm thick.Heat a grill pan until it’s very hot. Lay in one or two dough discs and cook for a minute or two on each side, until the bread is cooked through and has char marks. Remove from the pan, keep warm and repeat with the remaining dough. Brush each flatbread with melted ghee or butter, and serve.Explore more on these topicsFoodBeans, pulses and legumesMain courseSaladBreadBakingHerbs and spicesrecipesShareReuse this content
